title: Preface
content: Preface This volume is for a reader who knows school algebra and has never been asked to write a proof. It teaches one skill: to read a mathematical statement exactly, and to prove it in sentences that a reader can check line by line. It teaches logic as the grammar of proof. A proof is first written as a derivation, a chain in which every line is a premise, an assumption, or one application of a rule, so that checking it needs no idea: for each line we ask which rule produced it and from which lines. Each rule is introduced beside the sentence a mathematician writes when using it, and it is practiced at once, in short derivations and in proofs about numbers. The last chapter turns derivations back into ordinary mathematical prose, and shows that the rules are still there underneath. What it covers. Eight chapters, in three parts. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Part Chapter What it does ------------------------ ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- I. Propositional logic 1 The format of a derivation, with its boxes and scope rule, and the rules for “and”, “implies” and “or” 2 The rules for “not” and “if and only if”, derived rules, and proof by contradiction with the other classical rules 3 How to find a derivation: a search method, four kinds of task, and turning a written argument into a derivation 4 Formulas as objects, induction, truth tables, and the theorems that the rules are sound and complete; then normal forms, and compactness (optional) II. First-order logic 5 “For every” and “there exists”: terms, formulas and substitution, the four quantifier rules and their side conditions, equality, unique existence and counting 6 Translating mathematics into formulas, the laws for negating and moving quantifiers, searching for first-order derivations, and one theorem of analysis derived rule by rule 7 Structures and counter-models, theories and their models, definability and isomorphism; first-order soundness and the limits of first-order logic (both optional) III. Proof in prose 8 From derivations to mathematical prose: the rules in sentences, four levels of one proof, habits for reading, writing and checking proofs, a catalogue of the errors that recur, and the dispute over excluded middle ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ How to read it. Read the chapters in order: each uses the ones before it. A first reading takes Chapters 1–3, Sections 4.1–4.8, Chapters 5 and 6, Sections 7.1, 7.2 and 7.4 with Section 7.5 up to its isomorphisms, and Sections 8.1–8.7. Section 4.9 and the rest of Section 7.5 wait for a second pass. Sections 4.10, 7.3, 7.6 and 8.8 are optional. Before Sets and Functions, a reader needs the core of Chapters 1–6 and 8, and Sections 7.1–7.2 before its Section 4.1; Sections 7.4–7.5 are recommended. Every section has Quick checks with folded answers; answer each one before you unfold it. The exercises of a section come in three groups, A to check understanding, B for practice and C to go deeper, and the last core sections of each chapter add R items that reach back to earlier chapters. Do the derivations on paper, line by line, before reading the solution. A chapter’s opening page lists what it needs, with links, and the time it takes. Second-reading folds hold edge cases and longer justifications; they can be left closed on a first reading, but they are not optional, since later proofs may use what they contain. Sections and results marked optional can be skipped, and nothing outside them depends on them. How long it takes. The core track, as each chapter’s opening page counts it (the first-reading sections with all of A, one B and one C per section, and the exit checks), takes about 250 hours in all. Everything, folds and optional sections included, takes about 440 hours. Why rules before truth tables. Many logic books begin with truth tables, where the row “a false hypothesis makes P \to Q true” has to be accepted as a convention. This book starts from the rules. Section 1.1 reads that row informally, as a promise that is not broken; Section 2.1 derives it from the rules, as vacuous truth; and Chapter 4 brings in the tables and proves that rules and tables agree: what the rules derive is true in every row (Section 4.7), and what is true in every row the rules derive (Section 4.8). The quantifiers take the same road. Chapters 5 and 6 give their rules and use them; Chapter 7 gives them their meaning in structures, where a counter-model shows that a derivation cannot exist. What comes next. Sets and Functions puts the logic to work on sets, functions, relations, induction and the sizes of infinite sets. Its first three chapters are what Analysis on the Real Line assumes. Number Systems: From \nN to \nR builds the numbers themselves out of sets.

title: Connectives and Derivations
content: Connectives and Derivations Section 1.1 opens with two arguments that every integer with an even square is even. Every claim in both is true, and yet only one is a proof. The other, Argument B, starts from “n is even”, reaches “n^2 is even”, and then announces the reverse. Spotting the flaw once it is pointed out is easy. Naming it, so that the same flaw can be caught in an argument we have never seen, needs an answer to a harder question: when is a list of true claims a proof? The motivating problem of this chapter is to name exactly what is wrong with Argument B, and the answer arrives in Section 1.4. This chapter builds the calculus that answers it: a proof is a chain in which every line is a premise, an assumption, or one application of a rule. It gives the rules for “and”, “implies” and “or”, one at a time; Chapter 2 adds “not”, “iff” and proof by contradiction. Before you start: five tempting misreadings. Each is a misreading that this chapter corrects; decide each now, and check again when you reach the section named. 1. Let x be a real number. “If x > 3, then x^2 > 9” is false at x = 1, since x > 3 fails there. 2. Let n be an integer. “n is divisible by 4 only if n is even” says that every even number is divisible by 4. 3. In a proof that begins “Suppose x > 2” and derives x^2 > 4, the line x^2 > 4 may be used anywhere later. 4. “5 \ge 0” is false, because 5 \ne 0. 5. Let x be a real number. From “x \ge 1 or x \le 2” and “x \ge 1” it follows that x \le 2 fails. 1. No. An implication breaks only when its hypothesis holds and its conclusion fails; at x = 1 it promises nothing (Section 1.1, “When is an implication broken?”). 2. No. “P only if Q” is P \to Q: divisible by 4 implies even, which is true. The claim reads the converse, false at n = 2 (Section 1.1). 3. No. It holds only inside the supposition’s box. Outside it, only “if x > 2, then x^2 > 4” may be used, and x^2 > 4 fails at x = 0 (Section 1.4). 4. No. 5 \ge 0 is (5 > 0) \vee (5 = 0), and an inclusive “or” needs one true side: 5 > 0 is true (Section 1.5). 5. No. At x = \tfrac32 both sides hold. The form “from P \vee Q and P, conclude not Q” is affirming a disjunct, a bad form (Sections 1.1 and 1.6). What you need. School algebra only: the rules of signs, adding and multiplying inequalities, and the facts that every integer is even or odd and every real number is non-negative or negative. They are used as facts in examples; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves the order facts from the axioms for the real numbers. No earlier chapter is needed. Time. About 40 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 65 hours for everything. Minimum before Sets and Functions. Chapters 1–6 and 8, core; Sections 7.1–7.2 before its Section 4.1. Roadmap - Statements, Arguments and How to Break One. Statements and the connectives, a phrase book for the English that hides them, the promise reading of “if … then”, and how to break a bad argument form by making its counterexample set true. - Derivations, Starting with And. The format of a derivation, with numbered lines, premises and a justification on every line, and the first two rules of logic, \rulename{\wedge I} and \rulename{\wedge E}. - Using an Implication: Modus Ponens. The rule \rulename{{\to}E}, and chains of implications found forwards and backwards. - Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box. The rule \rulename{{\to}I}, the box and the scope rule for citing lines, and a diagnosis of exactly what Argument B did wrong. - Or, Introduced. The rule \rulename{\vee I}, and the habit of postponing a disjunctive goal until one side is in hand. - Using Or: Proof by Cases. The rule \rulename{\vee E}, the laws of “or” and the constructive dilemma, case proofs about absolute values, and the whole chapter’s rule card. Named moves - Try to break it. To test a form, put statements in for the letters that make every premise true and the conclusion false; one such choice shows the form is bad. (Section 1.1) - Two ways to attack an argument. Show a premise false, or show a step’s form bad; the two attacks are independent. (Section 1.1) - Read the skeleton off the goal. The goal’s main connective chooses the introduction rule: \wedge gives two subgoals, \to a box, \vee a choice to postpone. (Section 1.2) - Use a premise by its main connective. Its elimination rule says what you may do with it: take a conjunction apart, feed an implication its hypothesis, split a disjunction into cases. (Section 1.2) - Open a box, close a box. An assumption lives exactly as long as its box. (Section 1.4) - Work from both ends. Premises at the top, the goal at the bottom; fill the gap from both sides. (Section 1.2) - Postpone a disjunction. Choose a side of a goal P \vee Q only when that side is in hand. (Section 1.5) - Cases end in the current goal. Both boxes of \rulename{\vee E} close on the statement you are trying to reach. (Section 1.6) The chapter’s eight moves are collected again at the end of Section 1.6, beside the rules that make them. Summary A proof is a chain in which every line is a premise, an assumption, or one step of a rule, and checking one needs no idea. The chapter gave the six rules for “and”, “implies” and “or”, with repetition, and with them derived that “and” commutes and regroups (@prp-and-commutes, @prp-and-associative), that implications chain (@prp-implication-transitive), that two hypotheses may be taken at once or one at a time (@prp-curry), that “or” commutes and regroups (@exm-disjunction-first-derivations, @exm-disjunction-regroup), that “and” distributes over “or” (@prp-distributivity) and the constructive dilemma (@exm-constructive-dilemma). It named Argument B’s error: a box opened at the wrong end proves the converse. A form is bad when some choice of statements makes its counterexample set true, and breaking a form is how a bad step is shown bad. Still open: the chapter has no rules for “not” or for contradiction, and the fact Argument B set out to prove waits for them. That is Chapter 2’s question. Terms - argument form, good and bad: bad if some choice of statements breaks it (@def-counterexample-set). - assumption, discharged: an assumption whose box has closed (@def-rules-implication). - available: citable at a line, by the scope rule (@def-derivation). - box: a block of lines opened by an assumption (@def-derivation). - box-free derivation: premises, then one rule step per line (@def-box-free-derivation). - conjunction rules \rulename{\wedge I}, \rulename{\wedge E}: build from both sides; take apart (@def-rules-conjunction). - counterexample set: the premises together with the negated conclusion (@def-counterexample-set). - derivable, \Gamma \vdash \psi: some derivation from premises in \Gamma ends with \psi (@def-derivable). - derivation: each line a premise, assumption, repetition or rule step (@def-derivation). - disjunction rules \rulename{\vee I}, \rulename{\vee E}, proof by cases: weaken to a disjunction; split one into cases (@def-rules-disjunction). - implication rules \rulename{{\to}I}, \rulename{{\to}E}: prove by a box; use by modus ponens (@def-rules-implication). - main connective: the connective applied last in building a statement (@def-main-connective). - modus ponens: from \varphi \to \psi and \varphi, conclude \psi (@def-rule-implication-elimination). - or-introduction: from one side, conclude the disjunction (@def-rule-disjunction-introduction). - repetition \rulename{R}: copy the statement of an available line (@def-derivation). - rule schema: given lines above, one new line below (@def-rule-schema). - sequent, turnstile: P_1, \dots, P_n \vdash Q, the claim that Q is derivable (@def-sequent). - statement: a declarative sentence, either true or false (@def-statement).

title: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content:
Statements, Arguments and How to Break One When is an argument a proof? This section says what the sentences of a proof are, how they are built from smaller ones, and how to test the form of an argument by trying to break it. Two arguments about squares Recall that an integer n is even when n = 2k for some integer k, and odd when n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. Here is a fact about integers. For every integer n, if n^2 is even, then n is even. Read the following two arguments for it. Each is written in the style of a textbook proof, and each claim in each of them is true. Argument A. Suppose n is odd, say n = 2k + 1 for an integer k. Then n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, so n^2 is odd, and therefore n^2 is not even. So an odd n never has an even square. Since every integer is even or odd, an integer with an even square must be even. Argument B. Suppose n is even, say n = 2k for an integer k. Then n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2), and 2k^2 is an integer, so n^2 is even. Hence if n^2 is even, then n is even. Argument A is a correct proof. Argument B is not, although none of its claims is false. It starts from “n is even” and arrives at “n^2 is even”. That is a perfectly good proof of a different statement: “if n is even, then n^2 is even”. The claim asks for the journey in the opposite direction, from the square back to the number, and the last sentence of B announces a conclusion that the argument never reached. Seeing this is easy once it is pointed out. Saying in general what went wrong is harder, and that is what this chapter and the next are for. To name the error we need to know what the rules of proof are, and before that, what they act on. So we start with the smallest pieces: the sentences a proof is made of. Statements A proof is written in sentences, but not every sentence can appear in one. “Is 91 prime?” asserts nothing, so it cannot serve as a premise or a conclusion; neither can “Let us now turn to the case n = 0.” The sentences a proof asserts are the ones that make a claim. A proof also has steps of another kind, such as “Suppose n is odd”, which assert nothing but set up a temporary hypothesis; their rules come in Section 1.4. A statement is a sentence that is either true or false. [Statement] A statement is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, and not both. In words: a statement makes a claim, and the claim is either correct or incorrect. The definition asks that one of the two is the case. It does not ask that we know which one. A statement whose truth nobody has settled is still a statement. [Statements and nonstatements] Decide which of the following are statements. 1. 7 is a prime number. 2. 0.999 > 1. 3. There are infinitely many primes p for which p + 2 is also prime. 4. Is 2^{11} - 1 prime? 5. x > 2. 6. 3 > 2. (a) This is a statement, and it is true. (b) This is a statement, and it is false. A false sentence is as much a statement as a true one. (c) This is a statement. It is the twin prime conjecture, and at the time of writing nobody knows whether it is true. It is certainly true or false, which is all the definition asks. (d) This is a question, so it is not a statement. The sentence “2^{11} - 1 is prime” is a statement, and a false one, since 2^{11} - 1 = 2047 = 23 \cdot 89. (e) This is not a statement. Whether it is true depends on what x is: it is true when x = 3 and false when x = 0, and as written nothing says which. Such a sentence is called an open sentence. (f) This is the sentence of (e) with x replaced by 3, and it is a true statement. Items (e) and (f) differ by one symbol, and the difference is the whole point. The open sentence x > 2 becomes a statement in two ways. We can put a number in for x, as in (f). Or we can say which x we mean in some other way, as in “for every real number x, x > 2” (a false statement) or “for some real number x, x > 2” (a true one). The words “for every” and “for some” are the quantifiers. Convention: a fixed but arbitrary number. When an example says “let x be a real number” and then talks about x, the letter names one number, fixed for the whole example, that we are not told. Every sentence about x is then a statement, true or false according to which number x is: with x = 3, “x > 2” is true; with x = 0, it is false; and the example does not know which x it has. So an argument about x may use only what holds whatever x is, and an argument that never peeks at x works for x = 3, for x = 0, and for every other number at once. Let x be a real number. Is “x > 2 or x \le 2” a statement? Is it true? Yes: by the convention it is a claim about one fixed number x. And it is true whatever x is, since every real number is either greater than 2 or at most 2. The book reserves the words “proposition” and “theorem” for proved results, so it calls the sentences of logic statements. Other books call them propositions, which is where the name propositional logic, for what this chapter and the next study, comes from. The connectives Most statements in mathematics are built from smaller ones. “0 < x and x < 1” is built from “0 < x” and “x < 1” with the word “and”. “If n^2 is even, then n is even” is built from two statements with “if … then”. The words that do the building are the connectives. A statement built from smaller statements by a connective is compound; one that is not is atomic. For this chapter, “x > 0” is atomic: it has an inner structure, a number and an order, but no connective joins parts of it. We write P, Q, R, S for statements whose inner structure we are ignoring. They stand for arbitrary statements, atomic or compound. There are five connectives. In the last column, x is a real number, and every example is true whatever x is. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Symbol Name Read Example --------------------- --------------- -------------------- --------------------------------- P \wedge Q conjunction P and Q x^2 \ge 0 and x^2 + 1 > 0 P \vee Q disjunction P or Q x \ge 0 or x < 0 P 	o Q implication if P, then Q if x > 1, then x^2 > 1 P \leftrightarrow Q biconditional P if and only if Q x^2 = 0 if and only if x = 0 
eg P negation not P not x^2 < 0, that is, x^2 \ge 0 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- To the five connectives we add one statement with no parts at all, written  ot and read “contradiction”. It stands for a statement that is false however things stand: 0 = 1 will do. A proof that reaches  ot has shown that the situation it was working in cannot occur. That is the heart of proof by contradiction, and the rules for  ot come with those for “not”. In P 	o Q, the statement P is the hypothesis (or antecedent) and Q the conclusion (or consequent). “If and only if” is often shortened to iff. Several English words become \wedge: “but”, “although”, and “while” all assert both parts, and add a tone of contrast that logic ignores. “2 is prime but not odd” is a conjunction. So is “neither … nor”, in disguise: “9 is neither even nor prime” asserts that 9 is not even and that 9 is not prime, which is 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q with P: “9 is even” and Q: “9 is prime”. Chained inequalities are conjunctions in disguise too. 0 < x < 1 abbreviates (0 < x) \wedge (x < 1), and a \le b \le c abbreviates (a \le b) \wedge (b \le c). The symbol \le itself hides a disjunction: a \le b means (a < b) \vee (a = b). And a 
e b is the negation 
eg(a = b). All three facts are used often in the sections that follow. In theorem statements the book writes \Rightarrow and \iff, as mathematicians usually do, and in running prose it says “implies” and “if and only if”. The arrows 	o and \leftrightarrow are kept for statements written in logical symbols, as in this section, whether built from letters like P 	o Q or from formulas like (x > 1) 	o (x^2 > 1), and for the formal derivations that start in the next. Nothing but typography separates the two pairs. In everyday English, “or” is often exclusive: “soup or salad” on a menu means one but not both. In mathematics, P \vee Q is inclusive: it is true when P is true, when Q is true, and when both are. For a real number x, “x \ge 0 or x \le 0” is true whatever x is; at x = 0 both parts are true, and that does not spoil it. An exclusive “or” must be said in full: “P or Q, but not both”, which is (P \vee Q) \wedge 
eg (P \wedge Q). The word “if” means different things in a theorem and in a definition. In a theorem, “if P, then Q” is one direction only: “if n is divisible by 4, then n is even” is true, and its converse is false at n = 2. In a definition, “a number is even if it is twice an integer” is meant as “if and only if”: a number that is not twice an integer is not called even. When is an implication broken? Read P 	o Q as a promise: whenever P holds, Q holds too. A promise is broken only when its condition is met and the promised thing fails. An implication is broken only when its hypothesis holds and its conclusion fails. Take the table’s example, “if x > 1, then x^2 > 1”. Its two parts can be true or false in four combinations: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- P: x > 1 Q: x^2 > 1 the promise a value of x ----------------- ----------------- ----------------------------- ------------------------------------------------- true true kept x = 3 true false broken none: this is why the promise holds for every x false true not broken: it says nothing x = -3 false false not broken: it says nothing x = 0 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- : Informal: a reading of “if”, not yet a rule of proof. (No value lands in the second row: if x > 1, then x^2 > x > 1.) This answers the question “what if P is false?”: then P 	o Q is not broken, so it counts as true. To show P 	o Q false, exhibit one case with P true and Q false. Which of x = 3, x = -3, x = 1 breaks “if x^2 > 4, then x > 2”? Only x = -3: 9 > 4 holds and -3 > 2 fails. At x = 3 both parts hold; at x = 1 the hypothesis fails, so nothing is promised. “Only if”, “necessary” and “sufficient” English has many ways of saying P 	o Q: “P implies Q”, “Q if P”, “Q whenever P”, “P only if Q”, “P is sufficient for Q”, and “Q is necessary for P”. To sort out the last three, ask of each sentence: when is it broken? Let x be a real number, with P: “x > 2” and Q: “x^2 > 4”. - “x > 2 only if x^2 > 4” says that x > 2 never happens without x^2 > 4. It is broken exactly when x > 2 and x^2 \le 4, which is exactly when P 	o Q is broken. So “P only if Q” is P 	o Q. It is true here: if x > 2, then x^2 > 2x > 4. - The reverse, “x^2 > 4 only if x > 2”, is Q 	o P, broken by x = -3 (the Quick check above). - “x^2 > 4 is necessary for x > 2” says that there is no x > 2 without x^2 > 4: again P 	o Q. “x > 2 is sufficient for x^2 > 4” says that x > 2 is enough to guarantee x^2 > 4: P 	o Q once more. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- English broken when symbols ----------------------- ----------------------- ----------------------- P only if Q P true, Q false P 	o Q Q if P P true, Q false P 	o Q Q is necessary for P P true, Q false P 	o Q P is sufficient for Q P true, Q false P 	o Q ----------------------------------------------------------------------- “If” and “only if” put the same two statements in opposite directions: “Q if P” is P 	o Q, while “Q only if P” is Q 	o P. Confusing them is Argument B’s mistake. Translating a sentence Translating into symbols is a skill of its own, best learned slowly, in three steps. Find the atomic statements, the smallest pieces that make a claim, and give each a letter. Find the connectives, whatever English words carry them. Then decide how the pieces group. Take “if 12 is divisible by 3 and by 4, then 12 is divisible by 6”. The atomic statements are P: “12 is divisible by 3”, Q: “12 is divisible by 4” and R: “12 is divisible by 6”. English lets “12 is divisible by” be said once and shared; logic writes each piece in full. The words “if … then” carry 	o, and “and” carries \wedge. The hypothesis is everything between “if” and “then”, so the statement is (P \wedge Q) 	o R, not P \wedge (Q 	o R). The second reading would claim P outright, and the English sentence claims nothing outright: it only says what follows from what. A second example shows a connective hidden inside a word. Let x be a real number, and read “x is non-zero, and if x is positive, then so is x^3”. With Z: “x = 0”, P: “x > 0” and C: “x^3 > 0”, “non-zero” is 
eg Z, and the whole sentence is 
eg Z \wedge (P 	o C). Letters that recall their statements, as here, often help; a letter is only a name. In both examples the English word order is a poor guide to the grouping. When in doubt, ask of each connective: which two statements does it join? A phrase book Many English phrases carry a connective in disguise. The table collects the common ones; in each row, ask the question of “Only if”: when is the sentence broken? In the examples, n is an integer and x is a real number. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- English paraphrase symbols example ------------------------- ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------- P provided Q if Q, then P Q 	o P x^2 > 4 provided x > 2 P whenever Q if Q, then P Q 	o P n^2 is even whenever n is even P but Q P and Q P \wedge Q 2 is prime but even neither P nor Q not P, and not Q 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q 9 is neither even nor prime not both P and Q not (P and Q) 
eg(P \wedge Q) 9 is not both odd and prime exactly one of P, Q P or Q, and not both (P \vee Q) \wedge 
eg(P \wedge Q) exactly one of x > 0, x < 1 at least two of P, Q, R some two of them hold ((P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R)) \vee (Q \wedge R) at least two of: n even, n > 0, n a multiple of 3 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- “Unless” is Exercise C1. “Neither … nor” and “not both” differ by one word and say different things. At n = 3, “n is neither even nor prime” is false, since 3 is prime, while “n is not both even and prime” is true. In the “exactly one” row, at x = 2 exactly one part holds (2 > 0, and 2 < 1 fails); at x = 	frac12 both hold, so “exactly one” fails. In the last row, n = 6 satisfies all three parts, and n = -3 only one: it is a multiple of 3, but odd and negative. Let n be an integer, with E: “n is even” and P: “n is prime”. Translate “exactly one of: n is even, n is prime”, and decide it at n = 2, n = 9 and n = 7. (E \vee P) \wedge 
eg(E \wedge P). It is false at 2, where both parts hold; false at 9, where neither does; and true at 7, which is prime and not even. Not every “and” joins two statements. Some sentences with “and” in them make one claim about several things together. - “4 and 9 are coprime.” Not: “4 is coprime \wedge 9 is coprime”. Coprime is a relation between two numbers (their only common positive divisor is 1), so the sentence is one atomic statement about a pair. Contrast “4 and 9 are squares”, which is a conjunction. - “The points A, B, C are collinear.” Not: a conjunction of three statements about single points. Collinearity is one statement about all three points at once. - “1.414 is an approximate root of x^2 - 2 = 0.” Not: “1.414 is approximate \wedge 1.414 is a root”. It is not a root, since 1.414^2 = 1.999396. “Approximate” changes the meaning of “root”, and nothing here is a conjunction. By contrast, “12 is a positive even number” is the conjunction of “12 > 0” and “12 is even”. Everyday readings. Four kinds of word mean something different in mathematics from what they mean in conversation, and the everyday reading translates wrongly. - “Or” is inclusive: the first warning of “The connectives” above. - In a definition, “if” is read more strongly, as “if and only if”: the second warning there. - “Some” never says “not all”. “Some solutions of x^2 = x are non-negative” is true, although every solution (0 and 1) is non-negative. - A word without a sharp boundary makes no statement. “x is large” is not a statement until a bound is fixed, as in “x > 10^6”. Reading a statement: precedence and the main connective Connectives can be combined without limit, and a string of symbols is only useful if it can be read in one way. Consider 
eg P \wedge Q. Does it deny P and then assert Q, or does it deny the whole of P \wedge Q? These are different claims. With P: “n is even” and Q: “n > 0”, the first says that n is odd and positive, while the second says only that n is not a positive even number, which n = -4 satisfies. Parentheses settle every such question, and a few conventions let us drop the ones that would only add clutter. 1. 
eg binds most tightly: it applies to the smallest complete statement that follows it. So 
eg P \wedge Q means (
eg P) \wedge Q, and to deny P \wedge Q we write 
eg(P \wedge Q). 2. \wedge and \vee bind more tightly than 	o and \leftrightarrow. So P \wedge Q 	o R means (P \wedge Q) 	o R. In a mixture of \wedge and \vee, or of 	o and \leftrightarrow, the parentheses are always written. When parentheses in a chain of arrows are dropped, they group to the right: P 	o Q 	o R means P 	o (Q 	o R). This chapter always writes them. In this chapter we parse by eye. The conventions only decide where parentheses may be dropped. The next definition names the one piece of information that reading a statement is for. [Main Connective] The main connective of a compound statement is the connective applied last when the statement is built up from its parts. An atomic statement has no main connective. The main connective is found by undoing the construction from the outside. Take 
eg(P \wedge Q) 	o R . By convention (1), the 
eg applies only to the parenthesized P \wedge Q. That leaves a single connective outside the parentheses, the 	o, joining 
eg(P \wedge Q) on its left and R on its right. So the last step joined

The form of an argument Here are two short arguments, one about integers and one about real numbers. If n is odd, then n^2 is odd. And n is odd. So n^2 is odd. If x > 2, then x^2 > 4. And x > 2. So x^2 > 4. They are about different things, and yet they are the same argument. Write P for “n is odd” and Q for “n^2 is odd” in the first, and P for “x > 2” and Q for “x^2 > 4” in the second. Both then read: from P 	o Q and P, conclude Q. What makes the step correct has nothing to do with odd numbers or squares. It depends only on the shape of the premises, on the fact that one of them is an implication and the other is its hypothesis. That shape is the argument’s form, and the part of the argument that lives in the letters is its content. Logic studies the forms of arguments, not their content. Separating the two has a payoff. Once a form has been shown to be correct, every argument of that form is correct, whatever its content; we check the form once and use it forever. An argument form is written with its premises above a line and its conclusion below it:  egin{array}{l} P 	o Q \ P \ \hline Q \end{array} In running text the same form is written “from P 	o Q and P, conclude Q”. Try to break it Breaking a form means making several statements true at once, and the list of them deserves a name. [Counterexample Set] The counterexample set of an argument form is the list of its premises together with the negation of its conclusion. A counterexample to the form is an argument of that form whose premises are all true and whose conclusion is false, that is, a choice of statements for the letters that makes every member of the counterexample set true. A form is bad if it has a counterexample, and good if no choice of statements can break it. For “from P 	o Q and Q, conclude P” the counterexample set is P 	o Q, Q, 
eg P. To test a form, try to break it: put statements in for the letters that make every premise true and the conclusion false. One counterexample settles that the form is bad. Failing to find one settles nothing yet: showing that a form is good takes a reason that covers every choice of statements at once. Write the form of each argument, and try to break it. 1. If n is divisible by 4, then n is even. And n is even. So n is divisible by 4. 2. If x > 0 and y > 0, then xy > 0. And x > 0 and y > 0. So xy > 0. (i) With P: “n is divisible by 4” and Q: “n is even”, the form is “from P 	o Q and Q, conclude P”: the second premise is the conclusion of the implication, not its hypothesis. And n = 2 breaks it. The first premise is true for every integer, since a multiple of 4 is 4k = 2(2k); the second is true, since 2 is even; yet 2 is not divisible by 4. The form is bad. (ii) With P the compound statement “x > 0 and y > 0” (a letter may stand for one) and Q: “xy > 0”, the form is “from P 	o Q and P, conclude Q”. It cannot be broken. By the promise table, P 	o Q is false only when P is true and Q false; so when P 	o Q and P are both true, Q is true. The form is good. Where to look first. Make the conclusion false first: that fixes some letters, and the premises must then be made true around it. eg Q. Take P: “x > 1” and Q: “x > 0”. The first member holds for every real x, since a number greater than 1 is greater than 0. At x = -1 the second holds too, since -1 > 0 is false. So both are true at once, and the form is bad. Argument B, tried. B’s reasoning shows “if n is even, then n^2 is even”, and its last sentence concludes the converse, “if n^2 is even, then n is even”. That step has the form “from P 	o Q, conclude Q 	o P”, and it breaks: take P: “n is divisible by 4” and Q: “n is even”. The premise is true for every integer, and the conclusion fails at n = 2. With B’s own content no integer breaks the repair, since every integer with an even square is even (the fact B set out to prove); but the form breaks. A true conclusion reached by a bad form is still not proved. Breaking the last step of Argument B shows that the step proves nothing. It does not show that “if n^2 is even, then n is even” is false, and Argument A proves that it is true. A bad form may even have instances whose premises always give the conclusion. The form “from P, conclude Q” is bad: any true P with a false Q breaks it. Yet in its instance “x > 2; so x > 1” no number breaks the step, since every real number greater than 2 is greater than 1. The guarantee there comes from a fact about numbers, not from the form. Logic certifies only forms; the content of a step may still be checked by other means. Many true cases are evidence, not a proof. The number n^2 + n + 41 is prime for n = 0, 1, 2, and so on all the way to n = 39: forty cases without a failure. At n = 40 it is 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41^2. An argument from many checked cases can be strong, but it is not of a good form: its premises can all be true while its conclusion is false. Logic books call a good form valid, and logic studies only form. That is why this book asks of every step not “is it convincing?” but “could this form be broken?” A list of checked cases says something about the cases checked, and perhaps about most cases; a proof says something about every case. A scientist who reasons “if the hypothesis is right, we shall observe this; we observe it; so the hypothesis is right” uses the bad form of Quick check (i), “from P 	o Q and Q, conclude P” (Section 1.3 names it affirming the consequent). The reasoning is a sensible guide to what to test next, and it is not a proof. Some books call an argument of a good form with true premises sound; this book keeps that word for a property of rules. Two ways to attack an argument An argument can be attacked in two ways, and the two are independent. Attack a premise: show that it is false, as with the argument about 6 above. Attack a step: show that its form is bad by breaking it, as with Argument B. A false premise says nothing about the steps, and a broken step says nothing about the premises. A defended argument needs both: good forms, and premises the reader accepts. To doubt an argument, doubt a premise or break a step. The two attacks, in the order a checker makes them: Failing to break a step is not the “no” answer: the arrow down from the first question needs every step shown good, by a reason that covers every choice of statements. Each connective, two rules We now come to the idea that organizes this chapter and the next. Think about what a mathematician does with the word “and”. There are exactly two things to do with it. - To prove a statement of the form P \wedge Q, prove P and prove Q. - To use a statement of the form P \wedge Q that is already known, take either half. Nobody needs to be taught these two moves. They are also, and this is the point, all there is to know about “and” for the purpose of writing proofs. Every other fact about \wedge, such as that P \wedge Q and Q \wedge P say the same thing, follows from the two moves, as Section 1.2 shows. The first move is called the introduction rule for \wedge, written ulename{\wedge I}, because it is how a \wedge gets into a proof. The second is the elimination rule, ulename{\wedge E}, because it is how a \wedge is taken apart. The table below is an informal preview. Hence 0 < x < 1.” ulename{\wedge E} from P \wedge Q, conclude P; also Q “Since 0 < x < 1, in particular x > 0.” --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every connective works the same way. (T) has the form “from P 	o Q and P 	o R, conclude Q 	o R”, with P: “12 is divisible by 6”, Q: “12 is even”, R: “12 is divisible by 3”. The two premises share their hypothesis, and the conclusion joins their two conclusions. (a) and (b) have this form. In (a), P is “x > 2”, Q is “x^2 > 4” and R is “x > 1”; in (b), P is “\Delta is equilateral”, Q is “\Delta is isosceles” and R is “each angle of \Delta is 60^\circ”. (b) has the form “from P 	o Q and Q 	o R, conclude P 	o R”: the second premise starts where the first ends. That is the form of B4(b), which cannot be broken. (c) has the form “from P 	o Q and P 	o R, conclude P 	o (Q \wedge R)”. It is the look-alike: the same premises as (T), and a different conclusion. It cannot be broken either. To make its conclusion false, P must be true and Q \wedge R false, so Q or R is false; then P 	o Q or P 	o R has a true hypothesis and a false conclusion, and a premise is false. Section 1.4 derives the forms of (c) and (d). Breaking the form of (T). Let n be an integer, with P: “n is divisible by 6”, Q: “n is even” and R: “n is divisible by 3”. Both premises hold for every integer, since 6k = 2 \cdot 3k = 3 \cdot 2k. At n = 2 the conclusion Q 	o R is broken: 2 is even and not divisible by 3. So the counterexample set P 	o Q, P 	o R, 
eg(Q 	o R) is true at n = 2, and the form is bad. Argument (a) breaks with its own content, at x = -3: both premises hold for every x, and (-3)^2 = 9 > 4 while -3 > 1 fails. (T) itself. Its conclusion is true, since 12 = 3 \cdot 4, so an even 12 is divisible by 3. But (T) does not prove it: its form is bad, and the truth of the conclusion comes from a fact about 12, not from the premises. C. Going deeper [C1: “Only if” and “unless”, used later] Let P and Q be statements. 1. Explain why “P only if Q” means P 	o Q, and not Q 	o P. (Ask: which situation would make “P only if Q” false?) 2. Explain why “P unless Q” means 
eg Q 	o P. 3. Let x be a real number. Decide whether each sentence is true for every real x. Justify your answer, giving a value of x that makes it false where there is one. - “x^2 = 4 if x = 2.” - “x^2 = 4 only if x = 2.” - “x^2 > 0 unless x = 0.” (a) “P only if Q” says that P does not happen without Q. It is broken exactly when P holds and Q fails. That is also exactly when P 	o Q is broken: an implication promises Q whenever P, and the promise fails only when P holds without Q. So the two say the same thing. By contrast, Q 	o P is broken when Q holds and P fails, a different situation. For example, “a number is divisible by 4 only if it is even” is true, while “a number is even only if it is divisible by 4” is false (take 2). (b) “P unless Q” says that P holds in every situation except possibly those where Q holds. So once we know that Q fails, we may conclude P, which is 
eg Q 	o P. For instance, “the equation ax = 1 has a solution unless a = 0” says: if a 
e 0, then ax = 1 has a solution. (c) The first sentence is (x = 2) 	o (x^2 = 4). It is true for every x: when x = 2, x^2 = 4, and when x 
e 2 it promises nothing. The second is (x^2 = 4) 	o (x = 2), the same two parts in the opposite direction. It is false for x = -2, where x^2 = 4 but x 
e 2. The third is 
eg(x = 0) 	o (x^2 > 0), by (b). It is true for every x: a non-zero real number is positive or negative, and in both cases its square is positive. The first two sentences differ by one word, and they are implications in opposite directions. Confusing them is exactly the mistake of Argument B at the start of this section.

title: 1.2 Derivations, Starting with And
content: Derivations, Starting with And The previous section stated a slogan: a proof is a chain in which every line is a premise, an assumption, or one application of a rule. This section makes the premises and the rule steps exact (assumptions wait until Section 1.4): what a derivation is, how each line carries its reason, and how anyone can check one. Then it gives the first two rules of logic, the rules for “and”. Why check by matching A proof in a research paper can run to hundreds of steps, too many to hold in mind at once, so it is checked one step at a time. Two careful readers can disagree about whether a step is “obvious”; a rule that says exactly which steps are allowed settles it, since a step matches the rule or does not. And programs that check proofs work in the same spirit: each step must match a pattern. Here is a small case: the chain 0 < \tfrac{1}{3} < \tfrac{1}{2} < 1 makes three claims, 0 < \tfrac13, \tfrac13 < \tfrac12, and \tfrac12 < 1, and a reader who accepts them concludes 0 < 1. The justification is one fact, used twice: if a < b and b < c, then a < c. From 0 < \tfrac13 and \tfrac13 < \tfrac12 it gives 0 < \tfrac12. From 0 < \tfrac12 and \tfrac12 < 1 it gives 0 < 1. To check those two steps, a reader needs nothing about fractions and nothing about what < means. It is enough to see that the two inequalities used in each step have the same expression in the middle, and that the new inequality joins the outer two. A clerk who had never seen a number could do it. So a proof can be checked without being understood: a proof is correct when every step matches its pattern, and matching is mechanical. A rule is a pattern We borrow one fact about real numbers and use it as a rule. - Tr (for “transitivity”, or chaining): from a < b and b < c, write a < c. It is a fact about numbers used as a rule, for practice; it is not a rule of logic. A rule is applied by matching against a small picture of the lines it needs and the line it writes. A rule is a pattern: given these lines, you may write that line. [Rule Schema] A rule schema is a pattern of lines: given lines at the top, possibly none, and exactly one new line at the bottom, whose justification names the rule and cites the given lines. Line numbers in a schema are written i, j, k. The letters in the pattern stand for arbitrary expressions of the right kind, and a use of the rule replaces them consistently: the same letter by the same expression, symbol for symbol, everywhere it occurs. A line is justified by the rule when it and the lines it cites, with their numbers, are an instance of a schema of the rule: the pattern with every letter replaced in this way. The schema of \mathrm{Tr} is Here a, b, c stand for expressions for numbers. In three points: - The given lines may stand anywhere above the new line, in any order on the page, and need not be next to each other or to it. - The citation’s order says which line plays which part: “\mathrm{Tr} \ i, j” makes line i play a < b and line j play b < c, unless the rule says otherwise (\rulename{\wedge I}, below, accepts either order). - Letters are replaced consistently, symbol for symbol. The middle letter b occurs in both given lines, so it must be replaced by the same string of symbols in both, not merely by the same number. An instance first. Take i = 3, j = 5, k = 6, and replace a by 0, b by \tfrac12, and c by 1. The pattern becomes: line 3 is 0 < \tfrac12, line 5 is \tfrac12 < 1, and line 6 is 0 < 1, justified “\mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 5”. Now a noninstance, by a minimal change. Keep line 3 as 0 < \tfrac12, and let line 5 be \tfrac13 < 1. Is “6. 0 < 1, \mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 5” justified? Line 3 forces b to be \tfrac12, and line 5 forces it to be \tfrac13, so these lines are not an instance of the schema. Line 6 is true, but \mathrm{Tr} was not applied, so the line has no justification. Why define rules this way? Because a rule applied by matching can be checked by someone who knows nothing about the subject. The schema turns “this step is obviously fine” into “this step matches that pattern”, a claim anyone can test. From the rules of logic on, the letters in a schema are Greek: \varphi, \psi, \chi (phi, psi, chi). A Greek letter is a hole in a rule’s pattern; a capital P is a statement we are reasoning about. A pattern works like the formula (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, whose a and b are holes to be filled with any expression, the same one wherever the hole appears. Filling the holes of a schema works the same way, with parentheses put around a compound statement where they are needed. For example, if a schema has the given lines \varphi and \psi and the new line \varphi \wedge \psi, then the three lines P \to Q, R, and (P \to Q) \wedge R are an instance of it, with \varphi replaced by P \to Q and \psi by R. The middle expression must match exactly, symbol for symbol. The step “0 < \tfrac24 and \tfrac12 < 1, so 0 < 1” is tempting, because \tfrac24 = \tfrac12 and every line in it is true, but it is not an application of \mathrm{Tr}: the two middle expressions are different strings. A checker who had to notice that they are equal would need arithmetic, and the point of a schema is that a checker needs nothing. Compare symbols, not values. Derivations without boxes A proof strings steps together, each using what earlier steps produced. The next definition says exactly how. [Box-Free Derivation] Fix a list of rules, each given by schemas. A box-free derivation is a finite list of numbered lines 1, 2, \dots, n, where n \ge 1, each carrying one statement and a justification, such that: 1. the first lines, possibly none and possibly all, are premises, justified by nothing; a short horizontal rule is drawn under the last premise; 2. every later line is justified by one rule of the list, citing earlier lines, and it and the cited lines form an instance of a schema of that rule. The premises of the derivation are its premise lines, and its conclusion is its last line. In words. Clause (i) says where a derivation starts: with the statements it is given, which are not proved and need no reason. Clause (ii) says how it goes on: each further line is one step of one rule, and the only lines it may use are ones already written. The word “earlier” is the only condition on which lines may be cited for now. Section 1.4 adds assumptions made inside boxes, and then “earlier” is refined to “available”: an earlier line may become unusable once the box it sits in has closed. The layout is always the same. Line numbers run down the left, statements sit in the middle, and each justification is on the right: the rule’s name, then the cited line numbers. A vertical bar runs down the left, and a short horizontal rule under the last premise separates what is given from what is derived. From Section 1.4 on, a box draws a second, shorter bar, and the bars beside a line show which assumptions it depends on. First derivations Here are two derivations with \mathrm{Tr}, each with the reasoning that found it. The reasoning is the part to watch: a derivation on the page runs from the top down, but it is rarely found that way. [Chaining] Let x, y, u, v, w, z be real numbers. Using the rule \mathrm{Tr} only, write a box-free derivation of each conclusion from the given premises. 1. Premises 0 < x, x < y, y < 1; conclusion 0 < 1. 2. Premises u < v, w < z, v < w; conclusion u < z. (a) Idea. The premises form a chain 0 < x < y < 1, each link sharing its right end with the next link’s left end. So we work forwards, from what we have: chain the first two links at their shared middle x, then the result with the third link at y. Read it back. Lines 1–3 are the premises. Line 4: lines 1 and 2 are an instance of \mathrm{Tr}, with a, b, c replaced by 0, x, y. Line 5: lines 4 and 3 are one, with a, b, c replaced by 0, y, 1. The letters are replaced afresh at each use: the b of line 4 has nothing to do with the b of line 5. (b) Idea. This time the chain is scrambled, so we work backwards, from what we want. The goal u < z can come from \mathrm{Tr} only if we have some u < m and m < z for a single expression m. The only premise starting with u is u < v, so try m = v; the remaining need is v < z, a new, smaller goal. It can come from \mathrm{Tr} with some v < m' and m' < z; the only premise starting with v is v < w, and with m' = w the second need, w < z, is a premise. The search has reached the premises, and the derivation is its record, written forwards. The search could have started instead from w < z, the premise ending in z: with m = w it needs u < w, which is \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 3, and then u < z is \mathrm{Tr} \ 4, 2. That is a different correct derivation. The same premises and conclusion usually have many derivations, and any one of them shows that the conclusion follows from the premises. Part (b) was found backwards, from the goal; part (a) forwards. The rest of this section names the two directions. Line 1 of a derivation is 0 < x and line 3 is x < 1. Which is correct: “4. 0 < 1, \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 3” or “4. 0 < 1, \mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 1”? The first. With the citation “1, 3”, line 1 plays a < b and line 3 plays b < c: a is 0, b is x in both lines, and c is 1, so the new line a < c is 0 < 1. With “3, 1”, line 3 would play a < b and line 1 would play b < c, so b would have to be 1 (from line 3) and 0 (from line 1) at once. Reading a derivation Finding a derivation may need an idea, as part (b) of @exm-chaining-derivation did. Checking one never does. For each line after the premises, ask three questions. 1. Which rule? Name the rule the justification cites, and check that it is on the list of rules. 2. Do the cited lines and this line form an instance of that rule’s schema? Find the replacement of the letters: read it off the cited lines in the order the citation gives them (or, for a rule whose lines may be cited in either order, try both: the new line decides), and check that every letter gets the same expression each time it occurs, and that the new line is what the pattern then says. 3. Are the cited lines earlier? Each cited number must be smaller than the number of the line doing the citing. A line that passes all three is correct, whatever it says and whether or not it is true. Here is the check run on part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Rule Cites Instance (the letters’ values) Earlier? -------------- -------------- -------------- -------------------------------- --------------- 1–3 premises — — — 4 \mathrm{Tr} 1, 2 a: 0; b: x; c: y 1, 2 < 4: yes 5 \mathrm{Tr} 4, 3 a: 0; b: y; c: 1 4, 3 < 5: yes --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every line passes, so the list is a derivation. Section 1.4 extends this table, when “earlier” becomes “available”. Finding a derivation may need an idea; checking one never does. A line can fail one question and pass the others. The next example breaks a correct derivation in two ways, each time with the smallest change that does it. [Not a derivation] Each list below is the derivation of part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation with one change. Say which of the three questions of “Reading a derivation” fails, and at which line. 1. The statements of lines 4 and 5 are swapped, each taking its justification with it, so that line 4 is now “0 < 1, \mathrm{Tr} \ 5, 3” and line 5 is “0 < y, \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 2”. 2. Line 5 is justified “\mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 4” instead of “\mathrm{Tr} \ 4, 3”. (a) The list is the following. Line 5 passes all three questions, exactly as line 4 did before. Line 4 passes the first two: lines 5, 3, and 4 are an instance of \mathrm{Tr} with a, b, c replaced by 0, y, 1. It fails the third, because it cites line 5, which is not earlier. So the list is not a derivation. (It would also be useless if it were one: its last line is now 0 < y, not 0 < 1.) (b) Line 5 is now “0 < 1, \mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 4”. Lines 3 and 4 are earlier, so the third question passes, and the rule is named, so the first passes. The second fails. The citation makes line 3, y < 1, play a < b, so a is y and b is 1; and it makes line 4, 0 < y, play b < c, so b is 0. The letter b cannot be both 1 and 0, so there is no instance. The lines are the right ones in the wrong roles. Change (b) shows why the citation order is part of the justification, and change (a) why the order of the lines is. Exercise C2 below asks what would go wrong if a line were allowed to cite a later one. What a derivation proves A derivation shows that its conclusion follows from its premises. The symbol \vdash says that such a derivation exists. [Derivable] Let \Gamma be a list of statements \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n, where n \ge 0, and let \psi be a statement. We say \psi is derivable from \Gamma, and write \Gamma \vdash \psi , if there is a derivation, using the rules of logic, whose premises all belong to \Gamma and whose last line is \psi. We write \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \vdash \psi for \Gamma \vdash \psi, and \vdash \psi when \Gamma is empty. Here \Gamma (capital gamma) is just a name for a list of statements. [Sequent] Let P_1, \dots, P_n and Q be statements, where n \ge 0. The expression P_1, \dots, P_n \vdash Q, read “P_1 to P_n prove Q”, is a sequent. It is the claim that Q is derivable from P_1, \dots, P_n in the sense of @def-derivable. The statements P_1, \dots, P_n are its premises and Q is its conclusion; when n = 0 we write \vdash Q. The symbol \vdash is called the turnstile. A sequent is not true merely because its conclusion is true: it claims that a derivation exists, and it is proved by exhibiting one. In words, three remarks. 1. Which derivations? Until Section 1.4, “derivation” means a box-free derivation (@def-box-free-derivation). Section 1.4 widens the word to allow boxes; nothing proved before changes, since a box-free derivation is still a derivation. 2. Not every premise must be used. A derivation may ignore some statements of \Gamma, and it may even have no premise lines at all. It may not use a premise that is not in \Gamma. 3. Relative to a list of rules. The symbol \vdash always refers to a list of rules. From “The rules for and” below on, it is the rules of logic introduced so far; adding a rule never destroys a derivation, so a sequent once derived stays derived. Before that, we name the rule: “\Gamma \vdash \psi with \mathrm{Tr}”. For instance, part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation shows 0 < x, \ x < y, \ y < 1 \vdash 0 < 1 with \mathrm{Tr}. In the derivations from here on, the capital letters P, Q, R, S stand for arbitrary statements, as in Section 1.1. A derivation written with them proves not one sequent but infinitely many at once, one for each way of putting statements in for the letters. So a line written with letters is justified only if it is an instance of the rule whatever statements the letters stand for, different statements for different letters included. When we ask whether such a line is an instance, we therefore compare the lines as written, with different letters counted as different symbols: Q is not a conjunct of (P \wedge Q) \wedge R, even though it would be one if R happened to be Q. What sequent “with \mathrm{Tr}” does part (b) of @exm-chaining-derivation show? u < v, \ w < z, \ v < w \vdash u < z with \mathrm{Tr}. The premises of the derivation are lines 1–3, and its last line is u < z. [Derivations, simplest first] Decide whether each of the following is a derivation, and if so, what it shows. 1. The single line 1 \quad P \quad \text{premise}. 2. The empty list, with no lines at all. 3. The derivation of part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation, for the list of rules consisting of \mathrm{Tr} alone. (a) Yes. Its only line is a premise, so clause (i) of @def-box-free-derivation holds, and clause (ii) has no lines to speak about. Its last line is P. It shows P \vdash P: every statement is derivable from itself. No rule was used, so this holds whatever the list of rules is. Parts (b) and (c) are answered in the fold below. A derivation of one line. The degenerate case is worth a look. A single premise line, with nothing after it, satisfies both clauses of @def-box-free-derivation: clause (i) holds, and clause (ii) has no lines to speak about. So it is a derivation, and its premise is its conclusion. Part (b) of @exm-derivations. No. The definition asks for n \ge 1 lines, and a derivation must have a last line to be its conclusion. So the empty list derives nothing. In the same way, a list with no premises can never get started with \mathrm{Tr}, or any rule that cites a line: its first line would have to cite an earlier line, and there is none. Every rule met before Section 1.4 cites at least one line, so until then \vdash \psi holds for no \psi. Section 1.4 changes that. Part (c) of @exm-derivations. Yes. Lines 1–3 are premises, with the rule drawn under line 3: clause (i). Line 4 cites lines 1 and 2, which are earlier, and lines 1, 2, 4 are an instance of \mathrm{Tr} with a, b, c replaced by 0, x, y. Line 5 cites lines 4 and 3, which are earlier, and lines 4, 3, 5 are an instance with a, b, c replaced by 0, y, 1. So clause (ii) holds for both later lines. The premises are the three premise lines and the conclusion is 0 < 1. A premise is given, not proved: from the false premises 1 < 0 and 0 < -1, the rule \mathrm{Tr} gives the false line 1 < -1, in a correct derivation. What a correct derivation guarantees is only that if the premises are true, so is the conclusion, and even that only for rules that never lead from true lines to a false one. The rules for and Analysis is full of chains such as 0 < x < 1, which says 0 < x and x < 1. A proof that uses it often needs one half: “in particular x > 0, so we may divide by x.” A proof that proves it must prove both halves; one half is not the whole claim. Section 1.1 previewed these two moves informally. Here they become rules, checked by matching, as \mathrm{Tr} was. To prove “\varphi and \psi”, prove each; to use it, take either. [Rules for Conjunction] The first schema is the rule \rulename{\wedge I} (and-introduction). Its two given lines may be cited in either order: the new line shows which statement is its left conjunct, so question 2 of “Reading a derivation” tries both orders. The second and third are the two forms of the rule \rulename{\wedge E} (and-elimination), one writing the left conjunct and one the right. \rulename{\wedge I}. - Schema: the first one in the block above. - Reading: two lines in hand, anywhere above and cited in either order; write their conjunction. - Example: from line 2, P, and line 5, Q, “\rulename{\wedge I} 5, 2” (or “2, 5”) writes Q \wedge P. \rulename{\wedge E}. - Schema: the other two in the block. - Reading: one line whose main connective (@def-main-connective) is \wedge; write either side, one layer at a time. - Example: from (P \wedge Q) \wedge R it writes P \wedge Q or R, never P. If \varphi and \psi are true, so is \varphi \wedge \psi; if \varphi \wedge \psi is true, so is each side. \rulename{\wedge E} reaches one layer at a time. From line 1, (P \wedge Q) \wedge R, the line “Q — \rulename{\wedge E} 1” is not an instance of either \rulename{\wedge E} schema, because line 1’s conjuncts are P \wedge Q and R. The line is wrong even though Q does follow; the repair costs one line: P \wedge Q by \rulename{\wedge E} 1 first, then Q from it. Which statements can \rulename{\wedge E} write, in one application each, from the line (P \wedge Q) \wedge (R \wedge S)? Only P \wedge Q and R \wedge S. The main connective is the middle \wedge, so \varphi is P \wedge Q and \psi is R \wedge S. Each of P, Q, R, S needs a second application, to one of those two lines. Line 1 is (P \wedge Q) \to R. May “P \wedge Q — \rulename{\wedge E} 1” be written? No. Line 1’s main connective is \to, so \rulename{\wedge E} cannot take it apart, although \wedge occurs in it. Two directions of reasoning A derivation has premises at the top and its goal, the conclusion we want, at the bottom. Between them is a gap, and finding a derivation means filling the gap. There are two places to start. From the goal. Ask: what is the goal’s main connective? If it is \wedge, the last line can be written by \rulename{\wedge I}, and then the goal \varphi \wedge \psi splits into two subgoals, \varphi and \psi, each to be reached on some line above. This is goal-directed reasoning. It works backwards, up from the bottom of the gap, and asks which introduction rule builds the goal’s main connective. From the premises. Ask: what are the main connectives of the lines we already have? A line whose main connective is \wedge can be taken apart by \rulename{\wedge E}, and each conjunct becomes a new line to work with. This is premise-directed reasoning. It works forwards, down from the top of the gap, and asks which elimination rule uses the line’s main connective. Work from both ends: take the premises apart, and build the goal from its parts. The derivation is finished when the two ends meet. Part (b) of @exm-chaining-derivation already worked backwards, with \mathrm{Tr} in the part that introduction rules play from now on. Scratch work for a search fits in a two-column table: the Givens, what is in hand (premises and lines derived so far), and the Goal, what is still needed. A goal-directed step replaces a goal by its subgoals; a premise-directed step adds to the Givens. The search is finished when every goal is among the Givens. The search for P \wedge Q \vdash Q \wedge P, one row per step: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ---------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------- P \wedge Q Q \wedge P P \wedge Q Q, P (\rulename{\wedge I} splits the goal) P \wedge Q, P, Q (\rulename{\wedge E}) Q \checkmark, P \checkmark ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The derivation this search finds is @prp-and-commutes below. A goal line may carry its rule before its citation is known. When the goal Q \wedge P is written at the bottom and the plan is \rulename{\wedge I}, write “\rulename{\wedge I}” beside it and leave the line numbers blank, to be filled when the subgoals stand on lines; the left picture in the Idea of @prp-and-commutes does this. First derivations with and [Two warm-ups] Give a derivation of each sequent. 1. P, \ Q \vdash Q \wedge P. 2. P \wedge Q \vdash Q. (a) Idea. The goal Q \wedge P has main connective \wedge, so, goal-directed, its last line is \rulename{\wedge I} with subgoals Q and P. Both subgoals are premises, so the two ends meet at once. The citation “2, 1” lists Q’s line first; “1, 2” would do as well, since the line shows the order. (b) Idea. The goal Q is a letter, with no main connective, so the goal suggests no rule. The premise has main connective \wedge, so, premise-directed, take it apart; its right conjunct is the goal. Line 2 is the second form of \rulename{\wedge E}, with \varphi \coloneqq P and \psi \coloneqq Q. The two derivations are box-free derivations in the sense of @def-box-free-derivation, with \rulename{\wedge I} and \rulename{\wedge E} as the list of rules: premises first, and every later line an instance of a schema whose given lines are earlier. By @def-derivable they show the two sequents. When the goal is a letter, as in (b), only the premises can suggest a step; when every subgoal is a premise, as in (a), the premises need no taking apart. The first proposition below needs both ends. One line cited twice. Nothing in the schema of \rulename{\wedge I} says that i and j are different lines. With i = j, the letters \varphi and \psi are replaced by the same statement, and the rule writes \varphi \wedge \varphi. It is a silly line, and a legal one. For instance, P \vdash P \wedge P: the goal is a conjunction, so \rulename{\wedge I}, with the subgoals P and P, and the one premise meets both. The first result is that the order of a conjunction does not matter. [Conjunction Commutes] P \wedge Q \vdash Q \wedge P. Write the premise at the top, the goal at the bottom, and leave a gap, and write \rulename{\wedge I} beside the goal, with its citation still blank (left picture; the lines carry the numbers they will have at the end). Start from the goal. Its main connective is \wedge, so the last line will be \rulename{\wedge I}, and we need P and Q on earlier lines (right picture: two subgoals, not yet justified). Now start from the premise. Its main connective is \wedge, so \rulename{\wedge E} gives P and gives Q. That closes the gap: the pieces the goal asks for are the pieces the premise supplies. (This is the search of the Givens/Goal table above.) The following is a box-free derivation with the single premise P \wedge Q and last line Q \wedge P. Lines 2 and 3 are the two forms of \rulename{\wedge E} applied to line 1, and line 4 is \rulename{\wedge I} applied to lines 3 and 2, and the line shows Q on the left. By @def-derivable, P \wedge Q \vdash Q \wedge P. Read back in words, the derivation is a short paragraph: We are given that P and Q. In particular P holds. In particular Q holds. So Q and P both hold. Each sentence is one line, and each “in particular” is one application of \rulename{\wedge E}. Nothing in the derivation looks at what P and Q say: with P: “0 < x” and Q: “x < 1” it turns “0 < x and x < 1” into “x < 1 and 0 < x”, and it does the same for any two statements. Because the letters stand for arbitrary statements, one derivation written with letters proves every such instance at once. The second result is that the grouping of a conjunction does not matter either. It needs the premise taken apart in two layers. [Conjunction Is Associative] (P \wedge Q) \wedge R \vdash P \wedge (Q \wedge R). From the goal: its main connective is the outer \wedge, so the last line is \rulename{\wedge I} with the subgoals P and Q \wedge R, and the second splits again into Q and R. From the premise: \rulename{\wedge E} gives P \wedge Q and R, and again, on P \wedge Q, gives P and Q. Both searches stop at the three letters, and the ends meet there. Since \rulename{\wedge E} reaches one layer at a time, the premise must be peeled in two rounds. In pictures: the goal below a gap; then the first round of \rulename{\wedge E} as lines 2–3, a gap for lines 4–5, and the subgoal Q \wedge R as line 6, lines 6 and 7 not yet justified (line 7 will be \rulename{\wedge I} 4, 6). The following is a box-free derivation with the single premise (P \wedge Q) \wedge R and last line P \wedge (Q \wedge R). Lines 2 and 3 apply \rulename{\wedge E} to line 1, with \varphi \coloneqq P \wedge Q and \psi \coloneqq R. Lines 4 and 5 apply \rulename{\wedge E} to line 2, with \varphi \coloneqq P and \psi \coloneqq Q. Line 6 applies \rulename{\wedge I} to lines 5 and 3, and line 7 applies \rulename{\wedge I} to lines 4 and 6, with \varphi \coloneqq P and \psi \coloneqq Q \wedge R. By @def-derivable, (P \wedge Q) \wedge R \vdash P \wedge (Q \wedge R). The lines could come in other orders. Line 3 could come after lines 4 and 5, for instance, since it is used only at line 6. What cannot move is the dependence: every line must come after each line it cites. The converse, P \wedge (Q \wedge R) \vdash (P \wedge Q) \wedge R, is derived the same way, peeling the premise’s inner conjunction on the right instead of the left; Exercise B1 asks you to write it out. With both directions, the brackets in a chain of conjunctions carry no information, which is why the chain 0 < x < 1 < y is written without any. A line is not used up A line of a derivation is a statement that has been established. Citing it does not consume it: it can be cited again, by as many later lines as need it. The derivation of P \wedge Q, \ R \vdash (P \wedge R) \wedge (Q \wedge R) shows this. From the goal: \rulename{\wedge I} at the bottom, with subgoals P \wedge R and Q \wedge R, each split again by \rulename{\wedge I}. From the premises: \rulename{\wedge E} on line 1 gives P and Q, and R is already a premise. Both subgoals that need R cite the same line 2. In pictures: the goal below a gap; then the subgoals as lines 5–6, not yet justified. Line 2 is cited by lines 5 and 6, and line 1 by lines 3 and 4. In a written proof this is the everyday “we use the hypothesis x > 0 again”. Take everything apart, rebuild in the new order. One more derivation rearranges four letters: (P \wedge Q) \wedge (R \wedge S) \vdash (S \wedge Q) \wedge (P \wedge R). From the premise: two layers of \wedge, so \rulename{\wedge E} twice on line 1 and then twice on each of the two new lines, which leaves the four letters on lines 4 to 7. From the goal: two layers of \wedge, so \rulename{\wedge I} builds S \wedge Q and P \wedge R from the letters and then joins them. There is nothing to choose; the only care needed is the order of each citation. The recipe visibly does not depend on these particular letters or brackets. Take the premise apart with \rulename{\wedge E} until only letters remain, then build the goal from the letters with \rulename{\wedge I}, inside out. It works whenever the premise and the goal are both built from letters by \wedge alone and every letter of the goal occurs in the premise, whatever the bracketing and the order on either side. So “\wedge is commutative and associative” is, in the end, the observation that \rulename{\wedge E} can always take a conjunction down to its letters and \rulename{\wedge I} can always build one back up. How this looks in a mathematical proof Real proofs mix the logical rules with facts about their subject. [A product of numbers in the unit interval] Let x and y be real numbers with 0 < x < 1 and 0 < y < 1. Show that 0 < xy < 1, and name the rule behind each logical step. The hypothesis 0 < x < 1 is the conjunction (0 < x) \wedge (x < 1). By \rulename{\wedge E} we have 0 < x and x < 1 separately, and likewise 0 < y and y < 1. Since x > 0 and y > 0, the product xy is positive. Since y < 1 and x > 0, multiplying by x gives xy < x; together with x < 1 this gives xy < 1. These steps are school algebra, not logic. Finally, from 0 < xy and xy < 1, \rulename{\wedge I} gives (0 < xy) \wedge (xy < 1), which is 0 < xy < 1. As a derivation, the same proof reads as follows. Lines 7 and 8 are justified “algebra”: each is a step by a fact about numbers used as a rule, exactly as Tr was used above, and not a rule of logic. Line 7 uses “a product of two positive numbers is positive”; line 8 uses “if 0 < a, a < 1 and b < 1, then ab < 1”, one fact about numbers (it holds because multiplying b < 1 by the positive a gives ab < a, and a < 1). The facts about numbers supply the content of the solution; the rules supply the joints, taking statements apart and putting the pieces back together. The goal-directed reading is visible in the prose too: “show 0 < xy < 1” is a conjunction, so the solution sets itself two subgoals, and it says “finally” when the two meet. A proof about sequences might contain the line 0 < \frac{1}{n+1} < \frac{1}{n} \le 1 \qquad \text{for } n \in \nZ_{>0} . It asserts three links: 0 < \frac{1}{n+1}, \frac{1}{n+1} < \frac1n, and \frac1n \le 1. A reader who takes from it a claim about its two ends, 0 < 1, performs two steps in silence. The first is one application of chaining: 0 < \frac{1}{n+1} and \frac{1}{n+1} < \frac1n give 0 < \frac1n. The second joins 0 < \frac1n with \frac1n \le 1, and it is not \mathrm{Tr}: the line \frac1n \le 1 has \le, not <, so the lines do not match the schema. It is a different pattern, “from a < b and b \le c, write a < c”, another true fact about numbers. That is exactly why a justification must name the pattern it uses. “By the chain” does not say which one. Written chains like this one are everywhere in analysis, and they are derivations with the justifications left off. Nobody writes the justifications out in a real proof about numbers. But a reader checking a hard chain does what the table of “Reading a derivation” does: for each step, which fact, applied to which earlier lines. Common errors Besides \rulename{\wedge E} applied through a layer, one more error is common. \rulename{\wedge E} applies only to a line whose main connective is \wedge. The line (P \wedge Q) \to R contains a \wedge, but its main connective is \to, so “P — \rulename{\wedge E} 1” is illegal. With x a real number, P: “x > 0”, Q: “x > 1” and R: “x^2 > 1”, the premise “if x > 0 and x > 1, then x^2 > 1” is true for every x, yet at x = -1 the line x > 0 is false. The illegal step leads from a true premise to a false line, so no rule that allowed it could be safe.
