[C4: Challenge: What conjunction cannot do] In this exercise read P, Q, R as three different letters, each a symbol with no inner structure. Show that no box-free derivation whose only premise is P \wedge Q, and whose only rules are \rulename{\wedge I} and \rulename{\wedge E}, has a line whose statement contains the letter R. Deduce that, with these two rules, P \wedge Q \vdash P \wedge R cannot be shown. [Hint 1] Suppose some line does contain R, and look at the first such line. [Hint 2] That first line is not a premise. Which rule wrote it, and which letters can that rule write? Suppose, for a contradiction, that some line of such a derivation contains R. The derivation has finitely many lines, so there is a first such line; call it line k. Every line before line k is free of R. Line k is not a premise, because every premise is P \wedge Q, which does not contain R (P and Q being letters other than R). So line k is justified by one of the two rules, citing earlier lines (@def-box-free-derivation). If it is \rulename{\wedge I}, citing lines i and j, then its statement is \varphi \wedge \psi, where \varphi and \psi are the statements of lines i and j. Both are earlier than k, so neither contains R, and neither does \varphi \wedge \psi. If it is \rulename{\wedge E}, citing line i, then its statement is one conjunct of the statement of line i: a part of it. Line i is earlier than k and free of R, so the part is free of R too. Either way line k does not contain R, which contradicts the choice of k. So no line contains R. In particular no such derivation has the last line P \wedge R, and P \wedge Q \vdash P \wedge R cannot be shown with these rules. The hypothesis on the letters matters. If R were the same statement as P, the sequent would be P \wedge Q \vdash P \wedge P, which \rulename{\wedge E} followed by \rulename{\wedge I} 2, 2 derives (as in “One line cited twice”). What the argument shows is that no single derivation works for every choice of R. The argument, “look at the first bad line; it cannot be a premise, and no rule can create it from good lines”, is an induction on the lines of a derivation; Chapter 4 makes such arguments exact. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: considers a first line containing R, and says why a first one exists (finitely many lines); or, equally, goes down the derivation line by line, showing each line free of R because every line it cites is. - 2: rules out a premise (P \wedge Q does not contain R, since P, Q, R are different letters). - 2: \rulename{\wedge I} case: the new line is built from the statements of two earlier, R-free lines. - 2: \rulename{\wedge E} case: the new line is part of an earlier, R-free line. - 2: concludes that no line contains R, and so that P \wedge R is never a last line. Fatal errors (0 for the step): arguing about one particular derivation instead of every derivation; arguing that R is “not true” instead of about which symbols the rules can write.

title: 1.3 Using an Implication: Modus Ponens
content: Using an Implication: Modus Ponens Section 1.2 gave the two rules for “and”. This section gives one rule for “implies”: the rule that uses an implication already in hand. Proving one needs a new device, the subject of Section 1.4; using one is what a proof does every time it applies a theorem. The work is to see exactly what the rule allows, and to find chains of implications forwards and backwards. Four cards Before the rule, a puzzle about what “if … then” says. Four cards Each of four cards has a whole number on one side and a color on the other. They lie on a table showing 6, \qquad 7, \qquad \text{red}, \qquad \text{green} . Someone claims: if a card shows an even number on one side, then its other side is red. Which cards must be turned over to find out whether the claim is true of these four cards? Decide before reading the solution. For each card, try to break the claim: can its hidden side make a card that is even and not red? (By the promise reading of Section 1.1, that is the only way to break it.) The card showing 6. Its number is even, so the hypothesis of the implication holds, and the claim says its other side is red. If that side is green, the claim is false. This card must be turned. The card showing 7. Its number is odd, so the hypothesis fails, and the claim says nothing about this card. Whatever its color, the card cannot contradict the claim. Leave it. The red card. Its color is the conclusion of the implication. If its number is even, the card fits the claim; if its number is odd, the card still fits, since the claim says only what even cards look like and nothing about which cards are red. No hidden number can contradict the claim. Leave it. The green card. If its number is even, it is an even card that is not red, and the claim is false. This card must be turned. So the answer is the 6 and the green card. Many people choose the 6 and the red card. The red card is the tell: choosing it means reading the claim as if it also said “if a card is red, then its number is even”, which is the converse. An implication and its converse are different claims, and the claim here is only the first. Two of the cards show the two ways an implication meets a case: the 6 and the red card (not the pair that must be turned). The 6 shows the hypothesis, and an implication together with its hypothesis gives its conclusion: that is the rule of this section. The red card shows the conclusion, and an implication together with its conclusion gives nothing: that is the most important thing the rule does not allow. The green card shows that the conclusion fails; saying exactly what follows from that needs the rules for “not”. The rule An implication fires on its hypothesis, and gives its conclusion. [Implication Elimination] This rule is called \rulename{{\to}E} (implication-elimination, or modus ponens). We read it in four bullets. - Two given lines. One line is an implication \varphi \to \psi, the other is \varphi. Both stand earlier in the derivation, anywhere above line k and in either order on the page. - Read \varphi and \psi off the main connective. To see a line as \varphi \to \psi, its main connective (@def-main-connective) must be \to. Then \varphi, the hypothesis, is everything that this \to joins on its left, and \psi, the conclusion, is everything on its right. In (P \wedge Q) \to R, the hypothesis is P \wedge Q and the conclusion is R. In P \to (Q \to R), the hypothesis is P and the conclusion is Q \to R, itself an implication. - The hypothesis must match exactly. Line j must be the statement \varphi, symbol for symbol: the letter \varphi occurs in both given lines, and a use of the rule replaces it by the same statement in both (@def-rule-schema). A part of \varphi will not do, and neither will a statement that “says the same thing”. From (P \wedge Q) \to R and Q \wedge P, the rule gives nothing, although Q \wedge P and P \wedge Q are each derivable from the other (@prp-and-commutes); the hypothesis must first be rebuilt as P \wedge Q, by \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{\wedge I}. - The new line is the whole conclusion. The rule writes \psi, the whole of what stands right of the main \to, and nothing else. If \psi is Q \wedge R, the rule writes Q \wedge R, and getting Q takes one more line, by \rulename{\wedge E}. The citation lists the implication first and its hypothesis second, always: “\rulename{{\to}E} i, j”, as in the schema. Only \psi can come out, so the order changes nothing; it makes every \rulename{{\to}E} line read the same way. The statements \varphi and \psi may be the same. From P \to P and P, the rule writes P, which was already there. The line is legal and useless. Why this rule. It is what “by Theorem so-and-so” means. For integers d and n, write d \mid n, read “d divides n”, when n = dk for some integer k. A theorem of school arithmetic says: if an integer is divisible by 2 and by 3, then it is divisible by 6. For n = 42 it says \bigl( (2 \mid 42) \wedge (3 \mid 42) \bigr) \to (6 \mid 42) . We know 2 \mid 42 (42 = 2 \cdot 21) and 3 \mid 42 (42 = 3 \cdot 14). \rulename{\wedge I} builds the hypothesis, and \rulename{{\to}E} fires: 6 \mid 42, which is right, as 42 = 6 \cdot 7. As a derivation, with the theorem’s instance and the two facts as premises: Every application of a theorem has this shape: check the theorem’s hypotheses, assemble them into exactly the theorem’s hypothesis, and fire. To get “36 divides 72” from the theorem “if 4 and 9 divide n, then 36 divides n” at n = 72, which line, besides the theorem’s instance itself, must stand on the page before \rulename{{\to}E} fires? The conjunction (4 \mid 72) \wedge (9 \mid 72), exactly: the theorem’s hypothesis at n = 72. It is built by \rulename{\wedge I} from the lines 4 \mid 72 and 9 \mid 72, which hold because 72 = 4 \cdot 18 and 72 = 9 \cdot 8. Then \rulename{{\to}E} gives 36 \mid 72, and indeed 72 = 36 \cdot 2. Why it is safe. If \varphi \to \psi and \varphi are true, then \psi is true: that is what the promise says. Why nothing more. From \varphi \to \psi alone, \rulename{{\to}E} cannot fire: an implication by itself asserts neither its hypothesis nor its conclusion. And \rulename{{\to}E} does not run backwards: from \varphi \to \psi together with its conclusion \psi, it gives nothing about \varphi. That pattern, \varphi \to \psi, \ \psi \ \text{ therefore } \ \varphi , is called affirming the consequent, and it is the red card of the puzzle. It is not an instance of \rulename{{\to}E}, because the second given line of \rulename{{\to}E} must be the hypothesis \varphi, and here it is the conclusion \psi. It is a bad form: Section 1.1 broke it at n = 2. It is also the step that would repair Argument B. Affirming the consequent looks like modus ponens and is not. Let x be a real number. “If x > 2, then x^2 > 4” is true for every x, and at x = -3 we have x^2 = 9 > 4; but x > 2 is false there. From an implication and its conclusion, nothing follows about the hypothesis. Line 1 is P \to (Q \to R). What does \rulename{{\to}E} give from line 1 and a line Q? And from line 1 and a line P? From line 1 and Q: nothing. The main connective of line 1 is the first \to, so its hypothesis is P, and Q does not match it. From line 1 and P: the conclusion Q \to R. A second application, to Q \to R and the line Q, would then give R. The hypothesis can itself be an implication, and then the brackets put it on the left. Line 1 is (P \to Q) \to (R \wedge P) and line 2 is P \to Q. What does \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2 give? And what does \rulename{{\to}E} give from line 1 and a line P? R \wedge P. The main connective of line 1 is the \to outside the brackets, so its hypothesis is P \to Q, and line 2 is that whole hypothesis. From line 1 and P: nothing. P is only a part of the hypothesis P \to Q. At this point an implication can be used but not proved. A derivation can write an implication only by taking it out of a line that already contains it: \rulename{\wedge E} applied to (P \to Q) \wedge R, or \rulename{{\to}E} applied to P \to (Q \to R) and P. No rule so far builds a new \to. Section 1.4 gives the rule that does. Picture a reader who grants both “if x > 2, then x^2 > 4” and “x > 2”, yet will not write “x^2 > 4”. We might try to persuade this reader by adding the step itself as a third premise. With P: “x > 2” and Q: “x^2 > 4”, the new premise is \bigl( (P \to Q) \wedge P \bigr) \to Q , “if (if x > 2, then x^2 > 4) and x > 2, then x^2 > 4”. Nothing is gained. Getting from the three premises to Q still takes two steps of the rules: \rulename{\wedge I} to join the first two premises into one line, and \rulename{{\to}E} to fire the new premise on that line. A reader who would not take one step may refuse these two in the same way. A fourth premise that states this passage would call for a fifth, and so on without end: a step that is written down as a premise never gets taken. So \rulename{{\to}E} is not a statement standing among the premises. It is a permission to write a line, and that is why a derivation names its rules apart from its premises (@def-box-free-derivation). The puzzle is an old one: it was first told, as a dialogue, in 1895. Chains of implications With \rulename{{\to}E}, a derivation can pass along a chain: from P and P \to Q to Q, from Q and Q \to R to R, and so on. Such a chain can be found from either end. Forwards, from the premises. An available implication (for now, one on an earlier line) whose hypothesis is also available can fire: \rulename{{\to}E} writes its conclusion, which becomes available in turn and may be the hypothesis of another implication. Keep firing until the goal appears. This is premise-directed reasoning, as in Section 1.2. Backwards, from the goal. Suppose the goal is \psi. Look among the available lines for an implication whose conclusion is \psi, say \varphi \to \psi. If there is one, it is enough to reach \varphi: then \rulename{{\to}E} writes \psi. So \varphi becomes the new goal, and we repeat. This is goal-directed reasoning of a new kind: in Section 1.2 the goal’s main connective chose an introduction rule, but here the goal may be a letter, and it still tells us which implication to look for. The two directions meet in the middle, when a line reached forwards is a goal reached backwards. In written mathematics the backward step has a standard phrase, “to show \psi, it suffices to show \varphi”. In the Givens/Goal table, \rulename{{\to}E} fired forwards adds \psi to the Givens; worked backwards, when \varphi \to \psi is among the Givens, it replaces the goal \psi by \varphi. The premises are P, P \to R, Q \to S, and R \to S, and the goal is S. Search backwards: which implications could give the goal, and which of them leads to a derivation? Two premises have conclusion S: Q \to S and R \to S. The first makes Q the new goal, and no line is Q or has conclusion Q, so that branch is a dead end. The second makes R the new goal; P \to R has conclusion R, and its hypothesis P is a premise. So the derivation is R by \rulename{{\to}E} from P \to R and P, then S by \rulename{{\to}E} from R \to S and R. A backward search may branch, and a branch that stalls is abandoned for the next one. A picture shows the search at a glance. Draw each statement as a dot and each implication as an arrow from its hypothesis to its conclusion. Forwards, follow the arrows out of what you have; backwards, follow the arrows into the goal. Backwards from S, two arrows arrive. One comes from Q, which no arrow reaches and no premise gives: a dead end. The other comes from R, which P reaches. Chains of implications Give a derivation of each sequent. 1. P \to Q, \ P \vdash Q. 2. P, \ P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash R. 3. P \wedge Q, \ P \to (Q \to R) \vdash R. 4. (P \wedge Q) \to R, \ P, \ Q \vdash R. 5. (P \to Q) \wedge (R \to S), \ P \wedge R \vdash Q \wedge S. (a) Idea. There is nothing to choose: the premises are an implication and its hypothesis, and the rule fires once. This is the form of the two short arguments at the start of “The form of an argument” in Section 1.1 (n odd, so n^2 odd; x > 2, so x^2 > 4), now shown as a sequent: a derivation with these premises and this last line exists. (b) Idea, forwards. The premise P \to Q has its hypothesis P available, so it fires and gives Q. Now Q \to R has its hypothesis available, so it fires and gives R, the goal. Idea, backwards. The goal R is a letter. Which available implication has conclusion R? Only Q \to R, so it suffices to reach Q (left picture: the goal at the bottom, its new subgoal Q above it). Which implication has conclusion Q? Only P \to Q, so it suffices to reach P; and P is a premise, so the gap closes (right picture). Both searches write the same five lines, the forward one from the top and the backward one from the last line up. Exercise B3 has a case where the backward search is much shorter. (c) Idea. The goal R is a letter. From the goal: the only line that mentions R is P \to (Q \to R), but its conclusion is Q \to R, not R; the R sits one implication deeper. From the premises: P \wedge Q is a conjunction, so take it apart by \rulename{\wedge E}, giving P and Q. Now P is exactly the hypothesis of P \to (Q \to R), which fires and gives Q \to R. This new line is an implication whose hypothesis Q is available, so it fires too. In the pictures, the goal stands alone at first; then \rulename{\wedge E} writes lines 3 and 4, and only line 5 is missing; line 6 stays unjustified until line 5 is there for \rulename{{\to}E} to cite. Line 6 is the first line in this chapter where \rulename{{\to}E} fires on an implication that was itself written by \rulename{{\to}E}, not given as a premise. (d) Idea. This time the goal leads. The goal R is the conclusion of (P \wedge Q) \to R, so it suffices to reach its hypothesis P \wedge Q. That subgoal is a conjunction, so, goal-directed as in Section 1.2, it comes from \rulename{\wedge I} with subgoals P and Q, and both are premises. In the pictures, the goal stands alone at first; then the subgoal P \wedge Q, read off line 1, sits above it as line 4, still unjustified. Compare (c). There the implication took its two hypotheses one at a time, P \to (Q \to R), and the conjunction was a premise to be taken apart. Here the implication takes both hypotheses at once, (P \wedge Q) \to R, and the conjunction is a subgoal to be built. The content is the same; the brackets decide which rules the derivation uses. (Section 1.4 shows that each of the two implications is derivable from the other.) (e) Idea. Both ends at once. From the goal: Q \wedge S is a conjunction, so its last line is \rulename{\wedge I}, with subgoals Q and S. From the premises: both are conjunctions, so \rulename{\wedge E} takes each apart, giving P \to Q, R \to S, P, and R. The two ends meet through \rulename{{\to}E}: P \to Q fires on P and gives the subgoal Q, and R \to S fires on R and gives the subgoal S. In the second picture lines 3–6 came from the premises and line 9 from the goal; lines 7–8, still unjustified, are where the two searches meet. Each derivation in the example is a box-free derivation (@def-box-free-derivation) with \rulename{\wedge I}, \rulename{\wedge E}, and \rulename{{\to}E} as its rules, so by @def-derivable each shows its sequent. Checking a line of modus ponens Finding a chain can take some searching; checking one never does. For a line justified “\rulename{{\to}E} i, j”, the questions of Section 1.2 (which rule? is it an instance? are the cited lines earlier?) become four small ones: 1. Are lines i and j earlier than this line? 2. Is the main connective of line i a \to? If so, read off \varphi (its left side) and \psi (its right side). 3. Is line j exactly \varphi, symbol for symbol? 4. Is this line exactly \psi? Here is the check run on lines 5 and 6 of (c), and on a tempting wrong line that might replace them, “R — \rulename{{\to}E} 2, 4”. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Cites \varphi, \psi read off line i Line j is \varphi? Line is \psi? -------------- -------------- ------------------------------- -------------------- ----------------------- 5: Q \to R 2, 3 P, Q \to R yes (P) yes 6: R 5, 4 Q, R yes (Q) yes wrong: R 2, 4 P, Q \to R no (Q is not P) no (R is not Q \to R) ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The wrong line fails twice: it feeds line 2 the wrong hypothesis and takes out a part of the conclusion. The main connective settles it: the first \to is the one applied last, so everything after it, Q \to R, is the conclusion. Two chains about numbers The chains so far were made of letters. Here are two made of facts about numbers, one found forwards and one backwards. In both, the premises are true school facts, and the work is to see which implication fires on what. Two chains about numbers 1. Let n be an integer. From the five premises \begin{aligned} &6 \mid n, \qquad (6 \mid n) \to \bigl( (2 \mid n) \wedge (3 \mid n) \bigr), \qquad (2 \mid n) \to (4 \mid n^2), \\ &(3 \mid n) \to (9 \mid n^2), \qquad \bigl( (4 \mid n^2) \wedge (9 \mid n^2) \bigr) \to (36 \mid n^2), \end{aligned} derive 36 \mid n^2. 2. Let x and y be real numbers. From the six premises \begin{aligned} &x > 1, \qquad y > 1, \qquad (x > 1) \to (x^2 > 1), \qquad (y > 1) \to (y^2 > 1), \\ &\bigl( (x^2 > 1) \wedge (y^2 > 1) \bigr) \to (x^2 + y^2 > 2), \qquad (x > 2) \to (x^2 + y^2 > 2), \end{aligned} derive x^2 + y^2 > 2. (a) The premises. Each implication is a fact about every integer. If n = 6k, then n = 2(3k) and n = 3(2k). If n = 2k, then n^2 = 4k^2; if n = 3k, then n^2 = 9k^2. And a number divisible by 4 and by 9 is divisible by 36, the theorem of the Quick check on 72. Idea, forwards. Fire every implication whose hypothesis is in hand. Only the second premise can fire at first, on 6 \mid n. Its conclusion is a conjunction, which \rulename{\wedge E} splits into 2 \mid n and 3 \mid n. Now the third and fourth premises fire. The last premise wants its whole hypothesis on one line, so \rulename{\wedge I} assembles it exactly, and the last premise fires. In the pictures, the goal stands alone at first; then lines 6–8 are written forwards, and line 11, still unjustified, is the hypothesis the last premise asks for. Then lines 6–8, written forwards: The finished derivation: Read back, the twelve lines say: if 6 divides n, then 36 divides n^2. (b) The premises. Each is true for all real x and y. If x > 1, then x^2 = x \cdot x > x > 1, and the same for y. If x^2 > 1 and y^2 > 1, adding gives x^2 + y^2 > 2. If x > 2, then x^2 > 4, and y^2 \ge 0, so x^2 + y^2 > 4 > 2. Idea, backwards. Two premises end in the goal. The last one makes x > 2 the subgoal, but no line is x > 2 and no implication ends in it: a dead end, abandoned. The fifth premise makes its hypothesis, a conjunction, the subgoal. \rulename{\wedge I} splits it into x^2 > 1 and y^2 > 1, and each of these is the conclusion of an implication whose hypothesis is a premise. In the pictures, the goal stands alone at first; then the subgoal read off premise 5 sits above it as line 9, still unjustified. Then the subgoal read off premise 5: The finished derivation: Premise 6 is true and never cited. A true premise can still be a dead end: what decides a backward search is whether the subgoal can be reached, not whether the implication is true. In (b), why is premise 6 never fired? Its hypothesis x > 2 stands on no line, and no line has it as its conclusion, so \rulename{{\to}E} has nothing to fire it on. How this looks in a mathematical proof Let x be a real number with x > 2. Suppose we know two facts of school algebra: - if x > 2, then x^2 > 4 (since x > 2 > 0, multiplying x > 2 by x gives x^2 > 2x, and 2x > 4); - if x^2 > 4, then x^2 + 1 > 5 (add 1 to both sides). A written proof that x^2 + 1 > 5 takes one sentence: Since x > 2, we have x^2 > 4, and so x^2 + 1 > 5. As a derivation, with the two facts and the hypothesis as premises, it reads as follows. Each piece of the sentence is one line. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Sentence ----------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------- 3 “Since x > 2, …” (the hypothesis) 4 “… we have x^2 > 4, …” (\rulename{{\to}E}, firing the first fact) 5 “… and so x^2 + 1 > 5.” (\rulename{{\to}E}, firing the second fact) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The sentence never mentions lines 1 and 2: writers leave a known implication unstated. Each “since \varphi, \psi” in a proof is one application of \rulename{{\to}E} to an implication the reader is trusted to supply. When a proof is hard to follow, writing those implications down is often how one finds the gap: an implication is false, or its hypothesis was never established. Common errors The first warning of this section was about the wrong given line: the conclusion in place of the hypothesis. Another common error is a hypothesis that is only partly there. \rulename{{\to}E} needs the whole hypothesis. From (P \wedge Q) \to R and P alone, it gives nothing. Take the true theorem “if x > 0 and y > 0, then xy > 0” and the line x > 0: at x = 1, y = -1 the theorem and x > 0 are true, and xy > 0 is false. This is the commonest slip in analysis: “f is continuous, so by the theorem f attains a maximum”. The theorem meant has a second hypothesis, that f is defined on a closed bounded interval, and without it the conclusion fails: f(x) = x on the open interval (0, 1) is continuous and has no largest value, since \frac{a + 1}{2} is a larger value than a for every a in (0, 1). A near relative is a hypothesis in the wrong order, as in the third bullet of the rule’s reading: Q \wedge P is not the hypothesis of (P \wedge Q) \to R. The repair is two \rulename{\wedge E} lines and one \rulename{\wedge I} line, and Exercise B1 asks for it. A third error: firing an arrow that is not the whole line. \rulename{{\to}E} fires only on a whole line whose main connective is \to. From P \wedge (Q \to R) and Q, first take out Q \to R by \rulename{\wedge E}; the step straight to R is not an instance of the rule, although it never leads from truth to falsehood. From (P \to Q) \vee R and P, \rulename{{\to}E} cannot fire at all, and the line Q does not follow. Let x be a real number, with P: “x > 2”, Q: “x > 4”, R: “x \le 4”. The first line holds for every x: if x \le 4, then R is true, and if x > 4, then Q is true, so P \to Q is. At x = 3 the line P is true and Q is false. The rule card Before the card, the rule at work on large statements. Each row is one use of \rulename{{\to}E}: the two given lines, and the line it writes. [Instances of \rulename{{\to}E}] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \varphi \psi The implication The hypothesis line New line -------------------------- --------------------- ------------------------------------------------------ -------------------------- --------------------- P \wedge (Q \vee R) S \to P (P \wedge (Q \vee R)) \to (S \to P) P \wedge (Q \vee R) S \to P P \to Q R \wedge (S \vee P) (P \to Q) \to (R \wedge (S \vee P)) P \to Q R \wedge (S \vee P) (P \vee Q) \wedge \neg R (P \wedge S) \vee Q ((P \vee Q) \wedge \neg R) \to ((P \wedge S) \vee Q) (P \vee Q) \wedge \neg R (P \wedge S) \vee Q -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Not an instance. From (P \to Q) \to R and P, \rulename{{\to}E} writes neither Q nor R: the hypothesis is P \to Q, and P is only a part of it. The card of Section 1.2 grows by one row. Shape shows the given lines, then the new line; You write is the phrase a written proof uses for the rule. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule Shape You write Lean --------------------- ------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------- ----------------- \rulename{\wedge I} \varphi, \psi \Longrightarrow \varphi \wedge \psi “We show P, and we show Q.” constructor \rulename{\wedge E} \varphi \wedge \psi \Longrightarrow \varphi (or \psi) “In particular, P.” h.1 (and h.2) \rulename{{\to}E} \varphi \to \psi, \varphi \Longrightarrow \psi “Since P implies Q, and P holds, Q.” exact h hp -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In the Lean column, h is the implication and hp the proof of its hypothesis; h hp applies the one to the other, which is modus ponens. [Not allowed: \rulename{{\to}E}] Each step below is wrong, for the reason after the colon; the reason names the bullet of the rule’s reading that it breaks. - “R from P \to (Q \to R) and Q”: Q is not the hypothesis, which is P (the hypothesis must match exactly). - “P from P \to Q and Q”: the second given line must be the hypothesis, not the conclusion; this is affirming the consequent (two given lines). - “R from (P \wedge Q) \to R and P”: the whole hypothesis must stand on a line (the hypothesis must match exactly). - “Q from P \to (Q \wedge R) and P”: the new line is the whole conclusion, Q \wedge R (the new line is the whole conclusion). - “R from P \wedge (Q \to R) and Q”: the cited line’s main connective is \wedge; take out Q \to R first (read \varphi and \psi off the main connective). [Looking ahead] Chapter 4 proves more than “affirming the consequent is a bad form”: no derivation, however long, works for every choice of P and Q and leads from P \to Q and Q to P. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the schema of \rulename{{\to}E} from memory. 2. Lines 1 and 2 of a derivation are P \to (Q \wedge R) and P. Which of the following can line 3 be, by one application of \rulename{{\to}E}? Q \wedge R; Q; R \wedge Q; P \to Q. 3. In @exm-wason-selection, why is the red card not worth turning? 4. True or false, with a reason: from lines P \to Q and Q \to R, \rulename{{\to}E} gives P \to R. (a) Given lines i: \varphi \to \psi and j: \varphi; new line k: \psi, justified “\rulename{{\to}E} i, j” (@def-rule-implication-elimination). (b) Only Q \wedge R, the conclusion of line 1. The line Q needs a further \rulename{\wedge E}, and R \wedge Q two further \rulename{\wedge E} lines and a \rulename{\wedge I} line. The line P \to Q is not the conclusion of line 1, so \rulename{{\to}E} cannot write it. (c) The claim is “even \to red”, and the red card shows the conclusion. An odd number behind it would not contradict the claim, which says nothing about which cards are red; an even number would fit it. Inferring anything about its number from its color would be affirming the consequent. (d) False. \rulename{{\to}E} needs an implication and a line that is its hypothesis. The hypothesis of Q \to R is Q, and P \to Q is not Q; the hypothesis of P \to Q is P, which is not a line. So \rulename{{\to}E} does not apply at all. (The sequent P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash P \to R does hold, but its derivation needs the rule of Section 1.4.) [A2: Drill] Each part takes a line or two. Lines are numbered as in a derivation. The parts run from one step, through a missing line, a justification column and steps to judge, to short derivations. 1. Lines 1 (P \vee Q) \to R, 2 P \vee Q. What does “\rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2” give? 2. Lines 1 P \to Q \wedge R, 2 P. What does “\rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2” give? 3. Lines 1 ((P \vee Q) \wedge R) \to (S \to P), 2 (P \vee Q) \wedge R. What does “\rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2” give? 4. Line 7 is R \wedge S, justified “\rulename{{\to}E} 4, 6”, and line 6 is P \to Q. What is line 4? 5. Line 5 is Q, justified “\rulename{{\to}E} 2, 3”, and line 2 is (R \wedge S) \to Q. What is line 3? 6. Justify each line, the first two being premises: 1 (P \to Q) \wedge R, 2 R \to P, 3 P \to Q, 4 R, 5 P, 6 Q. 7. Lines 1 P \to (Q \to R), 2 Q. Is “\rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2” legal? 8. Lines 1 (P \wedge Q) \to R, 2 Q \wedge P. Is “R — \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2” legal? 9. Lines 1 P \to Q, 2 R, 3 R \wedge P. Is “4. Q — \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 3” legal? 10. Lines 1 (P \to Q) \wedge R, 2 P. Is “3. Q — \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2” legal? If not, repair it. 11. Break the form of “if n is divisible by 6, then by 3; n is divisible by 3; so n is divisible by 6”. 12. Premises P \to Q, R \to Q, R; goal Q. Searching backwards, which implication leads to a derivation? 13. Derive P \wedge (P \to Q) \vdash Q. 14. Derive P \to (Q \to R), \ P, \ Q \vdash R. 15. Derive P \to (Q \wedge R), \ (Q \wedge R) \to S, \ P \vdash S \wedge Q. (a) R, the conclusion of line 1, whose hypothesis P \vee Q is line 2 exactly. (b) Q \wedge R: since \wedge binds more tightly, line 1 is P \to (Q \wedge R). Getting Q needs one more \rulename{\wedge E} line. (c) S \to P: the hypothesis of line 1 is (P \vee Q) \wedge R, which is line 2 exactly, and its conclusion is the implication S \to P. (d) (P \to Q) \to (R \wedge S). \rulename{{\to}E} cites the implication first, so line 4 is an implication whose hypothesis is line 6 and whose conclusion is line 7. (e) R \wedge S, the hypothesis of line 2, exactly. (f) Lines 1 and 2 are premises; 3 is \rulename{\wedge E} 1; 4 is \rulename{\wedge E} 1; 5 is \rulename{{\to}E} 2, 4; 6 is \rulename{{\to}E} 3, 5. An implication cut out of a conjunction fires on a line that \rulename{{\to}E} wrote. (g) No: the hypothesis of line 1 is P, and line 2 is Q. (h) No: the hypothesis must be P \wedge Q exactly, and Q \wedge P is a different statement. (i) No: line 3 is R \wedge P, not the hypothesis P. First write P by \rulename{\wedge E} 3 as line 4, then Q by \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 4. (j) No: the main connective of line 1 is \wedge, so line 1 is not an implication, and \rulename{{\to}E} cannot fire on it. Repair: 3 P \to Q, \rulename{\wedge E} 1; 4 Q, \rulename{{\to}E} 3, 2. (k) Take n = 3. The first premise is true for every integer, since 6k = 3 \cdot 2k; the second is true, since 3 = 3 \cdot 1; and 3 is not divisible by 6. Both premises true, conclusion false: the form is affirming the consequent. (l) R \to Q: its hypothesis R is a premise, so \rulename{{\to}E} fires at once. The other, P \to Q, makes P the new goal, and nothing gives P: a dead end. (m) 2 P, \rulename{\wedge E} 1; 3 P \to Q, \rulename{\wedge E} 1; 4 Q, \rulename{{\to}E} 3, 2. (n) 4 Q \to R, \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2; 5 R, \rulename{{\to}E} 4, 3. (o) 4 Q \wedge R, \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 3; 5 S, \rulename{{\to}E} 2, 4; 6 Q, \rulename{\wedge E} 4; 7 S \wedge Q, \rulename{\wedge I} 5, 6. B. Practice [B1: Two chains] Give a derivation of each sequent. For each, say which step you found first, and whether it came from the goal or from a premise. 1. P, \ P \to Q, \ Q \to (R \wedge S) \vdash S \wedge Q. 2. (P \wedge Q) \to R, \ Q \wedge P \vdash R. (a) The first step found was from the goal: S \wedge Q is a conjunction, so the last line is \rulename{\wedge I} with subgoals S and Q. Then from the premises: P \to Q fires on P and gives Q, and Q \to (R \wedge S) fires on Q and gives R \wedge S, which \rulename{\wedge E} takes apart. Line 4 is cited twice, by line 5 and by line 7. (b) The first step found was from the goal: R is the conclusion of line 1, so it suffices to reach P \wedge Q exactly. The premise Q \wedge P is not it. So take the premise apart and rebuild in the right order. [B2: Two facts and a number] Let x be a real number. Take as premises the two facts “if 0 < x < 1, then x^2 < x” and “if x^2 < x, then x^3 < x^2”, and the hypothesis 0 < x < 1. Derive x^3 < x^2, naming the rule on each line. Then write the argument as one or two sentences of prose. The hypothesis 0 < x < 1 is the conjunction (0 < x) \wedge (x < 1), which is exactly the hypothesis of the first fact, so the first fact fires on it at once. In prose: Since 0 < x < 1, we have x^2 < x, and therefore x^3 < x^2. Both facts are true for every real x: if 0 < x < 1, multiplying x < 1 by x > 0 gives x^2 < x; and if x^2 < x, then x(x - 1) < 0, so x > 0, and multiplying x^2 < x by x gives x^3 < x^2. [B3: Which premises are needed?] Find a derivation of P, \ P \to Q, \ P \to R, \ R \to S, \ S \to U, \ Q \to T \ \vdash \ T , and list the premises it uses. Explain why a backward search finds the needed premises faster than a forward one here. Search backwards. The goal T is the conclusion of Q \to T only, so it suffices to reach Q. The goal Q is the conclusion of P \to Q only, so it suffices to reach P, a premise. It uses premises 1, 2, and 6. The others are never cited, which is allowed: a derivation need not use every premise (@def-derivable). Deleting lines 3–5 and renumbering gives a derivation of P, \ P \to Q, \ Q \to T \vdash T. A forward search fires every implication whose hypothesis is available, relevant or not: from P it writes Q and R, then S from R, then U from S, and T from Q — five new lines, three of them useless. The backward search looks only at implications whose conclusion is the current goal, and at each stage exactly one qualifies, so it writes only the two lines the derivation needs. [B4: Assemble the hypothesis] A search for P \to (Q \wedge R), \ (R \wedge P) \to S, \ P \vdash S has reached the stage below. Name the move, then complete it. The move is to work backwards from the goal. The goal S is the conclusion of line 2, so it suffices to reach line 2’s hypothesis R \wedge P, exactly, and then fire. That subgoal is a conjunction: P is line 3, and R comes from line 1, which fires on P and gives Q \wedge R, whose right half is R. Line 6 writes R \wedge P, with R on the left, because that is how the hypothesis of line 2 is written; P \wedge R would not match it. Line 3 is cited twice, by lines 4 and 6. [B5: Supply the missing premise] In (a)–(c), add one premise, not the conclusion itself, so that the sequent can be derived with \rulename{\wedge I}, \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{{\to}E}, and give the derivation. In (d), each sentence about an integer n leaves an implication unsaid: write it, and decide whether it is true for every integer n. 1. P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash R. 2. P, \ (P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash R. 3. P, \ Q \vdash R \wedge P. 4. (i) “Since 4 divides n, n is even.” (ii) “Since n is even, n^2 is divisible by 4.” (iii) “Since n^2 is even, n is even.” (iv) “Since n^2 is divisible by 4, n is divisible by 4.” (a) Several premises work. Add P: Or add Q: then 4 R, \rulename{{\to}E} 2, 3. Any premise from which these rules reach P or Q (for instance P \wedge Q) is right too. (b) Several premises work. Add Q: Or add P \wedge Q itself (then one \rulename{{\to}E} line), or Q \wedge P (then two \rulename{\wedge E} lines and one \rulename{\wedge I} line first). Any premise from which these rules reach Q or P \wedge Q is right. (c) Several premises work: any premise from which, together with P and Q, these rules reach R. For instance P \to R: Q \to R works the same way, and so does (P \wedge Q) \to R, with an \rulename{\wedge I} line first. The premise R alone also works, and it says the most: it hands over the new part of the conclusion outright. (d) (i) “If 4 \mid n, then n is even”: true, since 4k = 2(2k). (ii) “If n is even, then 4 \mid n^2”: true, since n = 2k gives n^2 = 4k^2. (iii) “If n^2 is even, then n is even”: true, by Argument A of Section 1.1. (iv) “If 4 \mid n^2, then 4 \mid n”: false at n = 2, where 4 \mid 4 and 4 does not divide 2. The sentence in (iv) looks just like the other three. A missing premise is where a hidden error hides. C. Going deeper [C1: Find the error] Here is an argument, followed by the derivation its author offers for it. If 10 is divisible by 6, then 10 is even. And 10 is even. So 10 is divisible by 6. With D: “10 is divisible by 6” and E: “10 is even”: 1. Name the line that fails, and say why it is not an instance of the schema of \rulename{{\to}E}. 2. Show that the step can lead from true premises to a false conclusion. 3. What new statement about divisibility can be correctly derived from the two premises with the rules so far? (a) Line 3. The schema needs, besides the implication \varphi \to \psi, a line that is its hypothesis \varphi. Matching line 1 gives \varphi \coloneqq D and \psi \coloneqq E, so the second cited line would have to be D; line 2 is E, which is \psi. The line affirms the consequent. (b) Try to break the step: this instance already does. The first premise is true, because every multiple of 6 is even (6k = 2(3k)); the second is true, since 10 = 2 \cdot 5; and the conclusion is false: 6k is at most 6 when k \le 1 and at least 12 when k \ge 2, so 10 = 6k for no integer k. So the step at line 3 leads from two true premises to a false line, and no safe rule can allow it. (c) None. Go down any derivation from these premises line by line, as in @exr-derivations-c4: every line is D \to E, E, or a conjunction built from them by \wedge alone. A premise is of this kind. \rulename{\wedge I} joins two such lines into another one. \rulename{\wedge E} gives back a conjunct of such a line, which is again of this kind. \rulename{{\to}E} would need, besides the implication D \to E, a line D, and D is not of this kind; so \rulename{{\to}E} never fires, and no line is D. What we can reach are the premises and conjunctions of them, such as (D \to E) \wedge E, which say nothing the premises did not. The premises tell us nothing about whether 10 is divisible by 6, which is why the conclusion had to be smuggled in. [C2: Both ends] Consider the sequent P \to (Q \to R), \ S \to P, \ S \wedge Q \ \vdash \ R \wedge S . 1. Describe a search for a derivation in words, in three parts: what the goal asks for; what the premises give; where the two meet. 2. Write the derivation, naming the rule on every line. [Hint 1] Two premises have main connective \to and one has \wedge; the goal has \wedge. Write down what each main connective lets you do. [Hint 2] The goal splits into R and S. Which available implication could end in R, and after how many firings? (a) From the goal: R \wedge S is a conjunction, so the last line is \rulename{\wedge I} with subgoals R and S. The only line mentioning R is P \to (Q \to R), whose conclusion is Q \to R; so R needs Q \to R and Q, and Q \to R needs P. From the premises: S \wedge Q splits by \rulename{\wedge E} into S and Q; then S \to P fires on S and gives P. Where they meet: S is at once a subgoal and a piece of the premise; P, reached forwards, is the hypothesis the backward search asked for; and Q, from \rulename{\wedge E}, is the last hypothesis R needs. (b) The derivation, with the rule on every line: Line 4 is cited twice, by line 6 and by line 9. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: from the goal, splits R \wedge S into the subgoals R and S for a final \rulename{\wedge I}. - 2: takes S \wedge Q apart by \rulename{\wedge E}. - 3: fires S \to P, then P \to (Q \to R), then Q \to R, each \rulename{{\to}E} citing an implication and exactly its hypothesis. - 2: the final \rulename{\wedge I}, whose line is R \wedge S. - 1: the three-part description names where the searches meet. Any other correct derivation earns the same points step for step (its lines may come in another order, as long as each cites only earlier lines). Fatal errors (0 for the step): \rulename{{\to}E} on P \to (Q \to R) with Q (the wrong hypothesis); affirming the consequent anywhere.

title: 1.4 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box Sections 1.2 and 1.3 gave three rules. \rulename{\wedge I} builds a conjunction; \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{{\to}E} take a line apart or use it. With them we can use an implication, but we cannot prove one. This section fills that gap with the rule \rulename{{\to}I}. The rule asks us to do something new: to assume a statement we do not know, inside a boundary that says where the assumption holds. The boundary is a box. With the box we can name the error of Argument B, and say exactly which earlier lines a line may cite. Supposing something we do not know Here is a small theorem about a real number x. If x > 2, then x^2 > 4. The proof everyone would write goes like this. Suppose x > 2. Then x > 0, so multiplying x > 2 by x gives x^2 > 2x. Also 2x > 4. Hence x^2 > 4. Then, often without saying it: this proves that if x > 2, then x^2 > 4. Look at the first sentence. We do not know that x > 2. The number x is arbitrary, and it may well be 0. So “suppose x > 2” asserts nothing. It opens a temporary world, one in which x > 2 holds, and asks what else holds there. Inside that world, the sentences “x^2 > 2x”, “2x > 4”, and “x^2 > 4” are true. Outside it they are not: at x = 0 all three are false. Only the last sentence of the proof leaves the temporary world. What it carries out is not “x^2 > 4” but the implication “if x > 2, then x^2 > 4”, and that is true for every real x. None of the rules so far can do this: \rulename{\wedge I} writes a conjunction, and \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{{\to}E} write a piece of a line that is already there. To prove “if x > 2, then x^2 > 4” from nothing, we must be allowed to suppose. A supposition is only safe if it has a boundary. Without one, the proof above could go on: “… Hence x^2 > 4. So x^2 > 4 for every real x.” That is false at x = 0. The error is not in any computation; it is that a sentence from inside the temporary world was used outside it. A derivation draws the boundary as a box. The assumption opens the box: it is written with a vertical bar to its left and a short horizontal rule under it. Every line derived under the assumption carries the same bar. When the box closes, the bar stops, and exactly one thing leaves: the implication from the assumption to the box’s last line. To prove “if \varphi, then \psi”, assume \varphi in a box, reach \psi inside it, and close the box. The introduction rule for implication From now on the given part of a schema may also be a box, cited as a range of lines from its first line to its last; nothing else in @def-rule-schema changes. Here is the rule, as a pattern. Beside it, for reference, is the rule \rulename{{\to}E} of @def-rule-implication-elimination, so that the two rules for “implies” stand in one place. [Rules for Implication] The left schema is the rule \rulename{{\to}I} (implication-introduction); the right one is \rulename{{\to}E} (@def-rule-implication-elimination). In \rulename{{\to}I}, the line \varphi is an assumption, which opens the box, and the assumption is discharged when the box closes. The line \psi is a line of that box itself, not of a box inside it. As in every schema (@def-rule-schema), \varphi and \psi stand for any statements, replaced consistently, and i, j, k for line numbers. This rule has conditions that matter; read each one. 1. Open a box whose first line is the assumption \varphi. The assumption may be any statement: true or false, related to the premises or not. Its justification is “assumption”, printed “asm, for \rulename{{\to}I}”: the annotation names the rule that will close the box. The price of assuming anything we like is the box. 2. Inside the box, work as usual. Every rule may be used. A line inside may cite the assumption and every earlier line that is not inside a box that has already closed: the premises, the lines above the box that are still in force, and the lines derived inside the box so far. 3. The last line of the box is \psi. It must be a line of this box itself, not a line of some further box opened inside it. (The drawing cannot show this, which is why the definition says it in words.) 4. Close the box, and write \varphi \to \psi on a later line outside it, in practice the very next line. The justification cites the whole box as the range \lines{i}{j}, from its assumption to its last line, not its lines one by one. 5. After the box closes, nothing inside it may be cited again. The assumption is discharged, and everything derived under it goes with it. Only the implication leaves. Clause 5 is the boundary of the temporary world. The subsection “Which lines a line may cite” below turns clause 5 into an exact rule. What each box is for. From now on every assumption says, in its justification column, what its box is for. “asm, for \rulename{{\to}I}” says that the box was opened to prove an implication, and that a \rulename{{\to}I} line will close it. In a written proof the same line is the word “suppose”. While a derivation is still growing and its closing line is not yet written, the annotation records the plan. The degenerate case is i = j: a box of one line, whose assumption is also its last line. Then \psi is \varphi, and the rule writes \varphi \to \varphi. Nothing in the rule asks the box to contain more than its assumption. Why the rule is right. The implication \varphi \to \psi claims only that \psi holds whenever \varphi does. The box shows exactly that: starting from \varphi, and from facts that hold anyway, the rules lead to \psi. Why the box closes. The lines inside hold only under the assumption. If the assumption is false, as x > 2 is at x = 0, they may be false too. Closing the box is what stops them being used where the assumption is not in force. A first box: implication is transitive The first result proved with a box is the chaining of implications. Section 1.3 used chains of implications forwards, firing each on a hypothesis already in hand. Here the hypothesis is not in hand, and we still want the chain. [Implication Is Transitive] P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash P \to R. Start from the goal. Its main connective is \to, so the last line will be \rulename{{\to}I}, and that needs a box that opens with P and ends with R. Inside the box, the new goal is R. Reason backwards: R is the conclusion of the premise Q \to R, so \rulename{{\to}E} gives it once Q is on a line. And Q is the conclusion of P \to Q, so \rulename{{\to}E} gives it from P, which the box has just assumed. In the Givens/Goal table, \rulename{{\to}I} moves the hypothesis into the Givens and makes the conclusion the goal. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ----------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------- P \to Q, Q \to R P \to R P \to Q, Q \to R, P (box opened) R P \to Q, Q \to R, P, Q (\rulename{{\to}E}) R P \to Q, Q \to R, P, Q, R (\rulename{{\to}E}) R ✓ ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The same search as a growing derivation: the box opened, its goal R at the bottom (left); then line 4 written forwards (right). The following derivation has premises P \to Q and Q \to R, and last line P \to R. Line 3 opens a box with the assumption P. Lines 4 and 5 apply \rulename{{\to}E} inside it, each citing a premise and a line of the box. Line 5, R, is the last line of the box. Line 6 closes it and writes P \to R, citing the box \lines{3}{5}. By @def-derivable, this proves the proposition. Read the drawing once more. The bar that starts at line 3 stops after line 5. The statements P, Q, and R on lines 3–5 were never established outright; they hold inside the temporary world where P is assumed. Only P \to R stands outside, next to the premises. Now give the letters some content. Let x be a real number, and let P : x > 3, \qquad Q : x^2 > 9, \qquad R : x^2 > 4 . The premise P \to Q holds: when x > 3, we have x > 0, so x^2 = x \cdot x > 3x > 9. The premise Q \to R holds because 4 < 9: if x^2 > 9, then x^2 > 4. With the premises in hand, lines 3–6 become a paragraph, one sentence per line. Line Sentence ------ ------------------------------------------------ 3 Suppose x > 3. 4 Since x > 3 implies x^2 > 9, we get x^2 > 9. 5 Since x^2 > 9 implies x^2 > 4, we get x^2 > 4. 6 Hence, if x > 3, then x^2 > 4. A practiced writer would compress this to “if x > 3, then x^2 > 9 > 4”: the same derivation with its joints hidden. When a proof is hard to follow, expanding it back into this form is how one finds the gap. The same result holds with the two premises joined into one, (P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to R) \vdash P \to R. Two \rulename{\wedge E} lines take the premise apart first (premise-directed), and the rest is the derivation above, renumbered. Argument B, diagnosed Section 1.1 broke the form of Argument B’s last step. Here is the rule B misused. With E: “n is even” and S: “n^2 is even”, B’s prose is this derivation. Line 1 is B’s “Suppose n is even, say n = 2k”. Line 2 is its computation n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2), a step of algebra, as in @exm-product-in-unit-interval. Line 3 is what the box earns; set it beside what B claimed. B’s box opens with E and closes on S, so \rulename{{\to}I} lets it write E \to S: the converse of the claim. B’s last sentence wrote S \to E. The rule asks the box to open with the hypothesis of the implication being proved, here S, and B never opened that box. The repair fails. Keep E \to S, open a box with S, and inside it use S to reach E: that step goes from E \to S and S to E. It is affirming the consequent, the bad form of Section 1.3. Try to break it. Take “if x > 2, then x^2 > 4” and “x^2 > 4”. At x = -3 both are true, since 9 > 4, and “x > 2” is false. So B cannot be saved by moving its lines around: a \rulename{{\to}I} proof of S \to E opens its box with S. The box of \rulename{{\to}I} opens with the hypothesis of the implication to be proved, never with its conclusion: Argument B used \rulename{{\to}I} with the box opened at the wrong end. A proof of “if x^3 > 8, then x > 2” begins “Suppose x > 2.” and ends “Hence x^3 > 8.” What does its box earn? Is the claim it was meant to prove true? Its box opens with x > 2 and closes on x^3 > 8, so it earns (x > 2) \to (x^3 > 8), the converse of the claim. The claim itself is true: if x \le 2, then x^3 \le 2^3 = 8, since a larger real number has a larger cube, so x^3 > 8 forces x > 2. But this box does not prove it. [Two errors that cancel] Let x be a real number. Here is a “proof” that if x > 3, then x^2 > 9: Suppose x^2 > 9. Then x > 3. Hence, if x > 3, then x^2 > 9. Is the conclusion true? Is it proved? As a derivation, the “proof” reads as follows. Two lines fail. Line 2 is no fact about numbers: at x = -4 we have x^2 = 16 > 9, and x > 3 fails. Line 3 writes the converse of what the box earns. The box opens with x^2 > 9 and ends with x > 3, so \rulename{{\to}I} would write (x^2 > 9) \to (x > 3). The two errors cancel. The implication the box would earn is false, and reversed it is the true claim: if x > 3, then x > 0, so x^2 = x \cdot x > 3x > 9. A reader who compares only the last line with the claim sees nothing wrong; a checker who reads every line finds both errors. A correct conclusion is no evidence that the lines above it are correct. A box must end on a line of its own Try to derive \vdash P \to (Q \to P). The goal is an implication, so open a box with P; the new goal Q \to P is again an implication, so open a box with Q inside the first. The statement P is already on line 1, so it is tempting to close the inner box at once. A checker reads the box \lines{2}{2}: its assumption is Q, and its last line is Q. So \rulename{{\to}I} may write only Q \to Q from it, and line 3 is rejected. The statement P stands on line 1, outside the inner box, and clause 3 asks for \psi as a line of the box itself. The fix is bookkeeping: copy P into the inner box. Copying an available line is the rule \rulename{R} (repetition), made official as clause (D3) of the definition below. The copy “P, R 1” then ends the inner box. Some books let a box end on any line available inside it. This book copies the line in, so that every \rulename{{\to}I} line can be checked by looking only at the box it cites. The corrected derivation is @exm-first-boxes (b) below. Which lines a line may cite In a derivation without boxes (@def-box-free-derivation), a line may cite any earlier line. With boxes that is no longer enough: after the derivation of @prp-implication-transitive, a line 7 citing line 5 would write R outside the box, the “x^2 > 4 for every x” error of the first subsection. What matters is which earlier lines are still available, and the bars show it. A line inside a box may be cited only from inside that box. Once a box has closed above you, nothing inside it can be cited; the boxes you are in may be left across their tops, and passing beside a closed box is fine. Open a box, close a box: an assumption lives exactly as long as its box. A whole box, cited by \rulename{{\to}I}, has its own condition: the citing line must stand in exactly the boxes that the cited box stands in, other than the cited box itself. For single lines: - a line in no box is available at every later line; - a line inside a box is available further down that box, and inside every box opened within it; - once its box closes, the line is available nowhere. The figure shows eleven lines without statements: box A is lines 2–4, box B lines 6–10, and box C, lines 7–8, sits inside B. An arrow runs from a citing line up to the line it cites, solid and marked \checkmark if legal, dashed and marked \times if not. A bracket on the left marks a whole box cited. A line can be cited from below only while every box containing it is still open. Line 8 leaves box C across its top to cite line 6, and line 11 passes beside the closed box B to cite line 5. Lines 5 and 11 stand in no box, and neither do the boxes A and B they cite whole. In the figure, which of lines 1–9 may line 10 cite? Lines 1, 5, 6 and 9. Lines 1 and 5 are in no box; lines 6 and 9 are in box B, which contains line 10. Lines 2–4 are not available (box A has closed), and neither are lines 7–8 (box C has closed). It may also cite the whole box 7–8, which, like line 10, stands in box B alone. Here is the official version, the one a checker uses. [Derivation] Fix a list of rules. A derivation is a finite list of numbered lines 1, 2, \dots, n, each carrying one statement and a justification, together with a set of boxes. A box is a block of consecutive lines whose first line is an assumption. Any two boxes are either disjoint or one inside the other. A box ends at one of its lines and is closed after it. The last line of the derivation lies outside every box. The scope rule. Line i is available at line k if i < k and every box containing line i also contains line k. A box is available at line k if it ends before line k and the boxes other than itself that contain it are exactly the boxes containing line k. A line may cite only lines and boxes available at it. Every line is exactly one of the following: 1. a premise; the premises are the first lines, above every box, with a short rule under the last of them; 2. an assumption, which may be any statement, and opens a new box; 3. a repetition of the statement on a line available at this one, justified “R” and the line repeated; 4. the conclusion of one rule of the list, applied to lines and boxes available at this one, such that this line and the cited lines and boxes form an instance of the rule’s schema. Clause (D3) is the rule \rulename{R} (repetition), whose schema is where line i must be available at line k. (D1)–(D4) say: given, assumed, copied, or one step of one rule, always from what is still available. The scope rule is the definition’s real content: line i is available at line k when every assumption that line i was derived under is still in force at line k: the picture rule above, in words a checker can apply. Well defined. Whether a line is available is decided by looking at the boxes; nothing about the meaning of the statements enters. Checking a derivation stays mechanical. Nothing earlier changes. A derivation with no boxes is a box-free derivation of @def-box-free-derivation for the same rules with \rulename{R} added: with no boxes, “available” means just “earlier”. So every derivation of Sections 1.2 and 1.3 is a derivation in the new sense, and @def-derivable is read from now on with this definition. The sequent \Gamma \vdash \psi still means: there is a derivation whose premises all belong to \Gamma and whose last line is \psi. Its last line lies in no box, so it depends on the premises and on nothing that was merely assumed. The typical use of \rulename{R} copies a line into a box opened below it. Line i is available at line k exactly when every box containing line i contains line k; in this drawing, line i is in no box that has closed, so the copy is legal. The worked example @exm-first-boxes below uses it. A box that is never closed cannot end a derivation. If the last line of a list is still inside a box, it depends on an assumption that was never discharged, and @def-derivation does not count the list as a derivation at all. “Suppose x > 2. Then x^2 > 4”, with nothing after it, proves nothing about x: the implication is the only thing the supposition was allowed to produce, and it was never written. How to check a derivation Section 1.2 checked a line by asking which rule it uses, which lines it cites, and whether they are earlier. With boxes the third question becomes: are they available here? For each line after the premises, ask: 1. Which rule? Name it. An assumption opens a box; \rulename{R} repeats; every other line applies one rule. 2. Which lines or boxes does it cite, and do they form an instance of the rule’s schema? \rulename{{\to}E} cites an implication and exactly its hypothesis; \rulename{{\to}I} cites one box, whose assumption and last line must be the two sides of the implication written. 3. Are they available here? Apply the scope rule to each cited line and box. Finding a derivation may need an idea; checking one never does. Two hypotheses, or one at a time A theorem with two hypotheses, “if x > 0 and y > 0, then xy > 0”, is often written with one hypothesis at a time: “let x > 0; then, if y > 0, xy > 0”. The two forms are (P \wedge Q) \to R and P \to (Q \to R). Each can be derived from the other, so a writer may use whichever reads better.
