Line (i) needs a box from P to R, which must lie inside the box of Q, since (i) is a line of that box; so (ix) opens the inner box, whose last line is (iii). Inside it, (viii) needs the premise and (ix), and (iii) needs (viii) and (ii). Opening the box of P first and the box of Q inside it would not do: the inner \rulename{{\to}I} would then give Q \to R, and the outer one P \to (Q \to R), the premise again. (iv) cannot be used where it is placed. Directly below (i), the inner box has closed, and line (iii) lies inside it; so (iii) is not available there, and (D3) repeats only an available line (the scope rule of @def-derivation). It is the error of @exm-illegal-citation. (v) cannot be used. \rulename{{\to}I} proves P \to R from a box opened by P, the hypothesis. A box opened by R would prove an implication with hypothesis R: the converse error of Argument B. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: a line from a closed box] A student wants to show (P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash (P \to (Q \to R)) \wedge (Q \to (P \to R)), and offers the following derivation. Lines 1–7 are the first derivation in the proof of @prp-curry. 1. Find the first illegal line, and name the clause of @def-derivation that it breaks. 2. Is the student’s conclusion derivable from the premise? Justify your answer. 3. The student defends line 10: “at line 10, both P and Q are assumed, exactly as they were at line 5, so R holds there too.” Explain why @def-derivation does not accept this defense, and show by an instance with real numbers that the move “repeat a line of a closed box” cannot be allowed. [Hint 1] For (a), check each line’s citations against the scope rule; for (b), keep the student’s idea and change one step. [Hint 2] For (b), inside the box of P at line 9, the assumptions Q (line 8) and P (line 9) are both available. What did lines 4 and 5 do with such a pair? (a) Line 10 is the first illegal line. It claims to repeat line 5 by (D3), but line 5 lies in the boxes \lines{2}{6} and \lines{3}{5}, and neither contains line 10. So line 5 is not available at line 10, and (D3) allows repeating only an available line. Lines 1–9 are correct, and lines 11–13 would be correct if line 10 were. (b) Yes: the sequent is derivable. Replace line 10 by two lines that do inside the new boxes what lines 4 and 5 did inside the old ones. Every box containing line 8 or line 9 contains line 10, and line 1 lies in no box; the other lines check as before. The student’s derivation was wrong and its conclusion right: a flawed argument can have a true conclusion. (c) Availability is about boxes, not about which statements happen to be assumed. The boxes \lines{8}{11} and \lines{9}{10} of the student’s derivation are new boxes; that their assumptions repeat those of the old boxes gives line 10 no access to what was derived inside the old ones. And the move, once allowed, can be used anywhere. Used outside every box, as a line 8 “R, R 5” after lines 1–7, it would derive (P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash R. Let x be a real number, and take P: “x > 2”, Q: “x > 3” and R: “x > 1”. The premise “if x > 2 and x > 3, then x > 1” is true whatever x is, and at x = 0 the conclusion x > 1 is false. A move that leads from a true premise to a false conclusion cannot be a step of proof. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: names line 10, because line 5 lies in boxes that do not contain it. - 3: gives any correct derivation of the sequent, every citation available. - 1: says the conclusion is derivable although the argument is wrong. - 3: explains that availability depends on boxes, not on repeated assumptions, with an instance where the move leads from a true premise to a false conclusion. Fatal errors (0 for the step): naming line 5 or line 9; claiming the sequent is not derivable; refuting the conclusion instead of the move. [C2: A hypothesis inside a hypothesis] Show that (P \to Q) \to (P \to R) \vdash P \to (Q \to R). Then say, in one sentence, why the premise cannot be used until a third box is opened. [Hint 1] Read the boxes off the goal. The premise’s hypothesis is P \to Q: what would you need to derive it? [Hint 2] Start: line 2 assumes P and line 3 assumes Q, read off the goal. The last line of the box of Q must be R, and line 1 gives P \to R only once P \to Q is on an available line. The goal P \to (Q \to R) asks for a box with P and, inside it, a box with Q whose last line is R. The premise gives P \to R as soon as we have P \to Q, and P \to R with the available P gives R. So the task is to derive P \to Q inside the box of Q, and that takes a third box. Line 5 is a legal repetition: both boxes containing line 3 contain line 5. Line 8 may cite line 2 because the box \lines{2}{9}, the only box containing line 2, contains line 8. The sentence: the premise fires only on an available line P \to Q, and no available line is P \to Q or has it as a conjunct or as the conclusion of an implication, so it can come only from \rulename{{\to}I}, which needs a box of its own. Line 1 does not help, since \rulename{{\to}E} on it would need P \to Q already. The third box assumes P again although line 2 already did: \rulename{{\to}I} needs the box, not new information. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: opens a box with P and inside it a box with Q, read off the goal. - 3: derives P \to Q inside the box of Q by a box whose last line is Q. - 2: obtains P \to R, then R, by \rulename{{\to}E} on available lines. - 2: closes the boxes inner first, each \rulename{{\to}I} citing an available box. - 1: the sentence says P \to Q must be a line that no elimination rule can supply, hence needs a box. Fatal errors (0 for the step): citing a line outside the box that contains it; writing P \to Q with no box. [C3: Exit check: a derivation and its prose] 1. Write a derivation of P \to Q, \ (Q \to R) \wedge (R \to S) \vdash P \to S, with every line justified. 2. Let x be a real number, and take P: “x > 5”, Q: “x > 4”, R: “x^2 > 16”, S: “x^2 > 9”. Say why each premise is true for every real x. Then write your derivation as fluent prose about x, one sentence per step. (a) Premise-directed first: the second premise is a conjunction, so \rulename{\wedge E} takes it apart. Goal-directed next: the goal is an implication, so open a box with its hypothesis P, and reach S by firing the three implications in turn. Lines 1–4 lie in no box, so they are available inside the box \lines{5}{8}; line 9 cites that box, which has ended, and neither it nor line 9 lies in another box. (b) The premise P \to Q holds because 5 > 4: if x > 5, then x > 4. For Q \to R: if x > 4, then x > 0, so x^2 = x \cdot x > 4x > 16. For R \to S: if x^2 > 16, then x^2 > 9, since 16 > 9. So both premises (the second a conjunction of two true implications) hold for every real x. In prose: We know that x > 5 implies x > 4, and that x > 4 implies x^2 > 16 and x^2 > 16 implies x^2 > 9. In particular, x > 4 implies x^2 > 16. In particular, x^2 > 16 implies x^2 > 9. Suppose x > 5. Then x > 4. Hence x^2 > 16. So x^2 > 9. This proves that if x > 5, then x^2 > 9. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: takes the conjunctive premise apart by two \rulename{\wedge E} lines (inside or outside the box). - 2: opens a box with P (not S) and closes it on S, a line of that box. - 2: reaches S inside the box of P by \rulename{{\to}E} steps, each citing an implication and exactly its hypothesis, every cited line available. - 1: each closing \rulename{{\to}I} cites its box as a range. - 3: prose with one sentence per step, “suppose” for the assumption, and a closing sentence stating the implication. A route that first derives Q \to S in a box of Q (as in @prp-implication-transitive) and then uses it in the box of P earns the same points: its \rulename{{\to}E} steps in both boxes count for the third line, and its two \rulename{{\to}I} steps for the fourth. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a box opened with the conclusion S (the converse error); citing a line of the box after it has closed. [C4: The assumptions a line depends on, used later] Each line of a derivation depends on the premises and on the assumptions of the boxes it sits in. Take the first derivation in the proof of @prp-curry (lines 1–7). 1. Beside each line, write the set of line numbers of the premises and assumptions it depends on. 2. For line 5 and for line 6, write the sequent whose premises are the statements on the lines of that set and whose conclusion is the statement of the line. Show that each is derivable, by turning the open assumptions into premises. 3. (Challenge.) Show that, in any derivation, the set of a line cited by an \rulename{\wedge I}, \rulename{\wedge E} or \rulename{{\to}E} line is contained in the set of the citing line. Then say how the set of a \rulename{{\to}I} line compares with the set of the last line of the box it cites. (a) Line 1: \{1\}. Line 2: \{1, 2\}. Lines 3, 4 and 5: \{1, 2, 3\}. Line 6: \{1, 2\}. Line 7: \{1\}. The premise is in every set; the assumption of line 3 only in the sets of lines 3–5, the lines of its box; the assumption of line 2 in the sets of lines 2–6. (b) Line 5 gives (P \wedge Q) \to R, \ P, \ Q \vdash R: Line 6 gives (P \wedge Q) \to R, \ P \vdash Q \to R; here the box of Q is kept, since line 6 lies outside it: In each, the lines down to the chosen one, with the assumptions of the boxes still open there made premises, form a derivation. (c) A line’s set consists of the premises and the assumptions of the boxes containing it. Let line k cite line i by \rulename{\wedge I}, \rulename{\wedge E} or \rulename{{\to}E}. Then line i is available at line k, so by the scope rule of @def-derivation every box containing line i also contains line k. Hence the assumption of every such box is in the set of line k, and the premises are in both sets: the set of i is contained in the set of k. For \rulename{{\to}I}: the box’s last line is a line of the box itself, so it lies in the cited box and in the boxes around it. The \rulename{{\to}I} line lies in exactly the boxes around the cited box (the condition for a box to be available). So the set of the \rulename{{\to}I} line is the set of the box’s last line with one member removed: the line number of the box’s assumption. That is the discharge, seen as a set. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: all seven sets correct (the premise in every set; line 3’s assumption only in the sets of lines 3–5). - 2: line 5’s sequent, with a correct derivation. - 2: line 6’s sequent, with the box of Q kept. - 3: (c) uses the scope rule for the containment, and names the one assumption that a \rulename{{\to}I} line drops. Fatal errors (0 for the step): putting line 3 in the set of line 6 or line 7; treating an assumption as a premise of the whole derivation.

title: 1.5 Or, Introduced
content: Or, Introduced Sections 1.2 to 1.4 gave the rules for “and” and “implies”. With them we can take a conjunction apart, fire an implication on its hypothesis, and prove an implication by opening a box. This section starts on the third connective of the chapter, “or”. It gives the rule that proves a disjunction, \rulename{\vee I}, and a habit that goes with it: when the goal is a disjunction, commit to one of its sides only when that side is in hand. Near its end it meets a goal that the rules still cannot reach, and that goal is the question the next section answers. Throwing information away on purpose Suppose a proof has just shown that a real number x satisfies x > 0, and the definition it is checking asks for x \ge 0. Every writer takes the step “so x \ge 0” without a pause. Look at what the step does. Section 1.1 noted that the symbol \le hides a disjunction, so x \ge 0 is the statement (x > 0) \vee (x = 0) . The step turns a statement into a disjunction of which it is one side. The step loses something. “x > 0” tells us that x is not 0; “x \ge 0” no longer does. A proof that takes the step throws information away, and it does so on purpose: the definition asks for the weaker statement, and the stronger one is not in the form it asks for. Convention: inequalities written out. When a rule has to see the disjunction inside a \le b, a derivation writes it out as (a < b) \vee (a = b), and a \ge b as (a > b) \vee (a = b): a checker compares symbols, so \rulename{\vee I} can write “x \ge 0” from “x > 0”, and \rulename{\vee E} can split on it, only in the written-out form. Otherwise a \le b may stand in a derivation as one statement, and prose keeps the short forms. The same move appears whenever a known fact has a disjunction as its hypothesis. School algebra says that if a = 0 or b = 0, then a \cdot b = 0. To use this on a product whose first factor we know to be 0, we must hand the fact its hypothesis, “a = 0 or b = 0”. What we have is only “a = 0”. So again the step goes from one side to the whole disjunction, and only then does the fact fire. Both steps are instances of one rule. This section states it as a pattern, reads it in three bullets, and then uses it in two ways: when the goal is a disjunction, and when a premise needs one. The rule of or-introduction To prove a disjunction, it is enough to prove one of its two sides. The rule is defined, like every rule since Section 1.2, by its schema (@def-rule-schema). The Greek letters stand for arbitrary statements, and i, k for line numbers. The rule has two forms, one for each side, so it is printed as two schemas. [Or-Introduction] The rule given by these two schemas is called \rulename{\vee I} (or-introduction). - Schema: the two in the block above, one for each side. - Reading: one available line (an earlier line, not inside a box that has closed), cited alone; write a disjunction with that line’s statement as one whole side, left or right, and any statement as the other side: true or false, related or not. - Example: if line 4 is x > 0, then “\rulename{\vee I} 4” may write (x > 0) \vee (x = 0), or (x = 0) \vee (x > 0), or the silly but correct (x > 0) \vee (x < -7). In mathematics “or” is inclusive (Section 1.1): \varphi \vee \psi is true when \varphi is true, when \psi is true, and when both are. So \varphi \vee \psi is true whenever \varphi is, whatever \psi says. The rule is this first clause read as a permission. \rulename{\vee I} loses information, never truth. The degenerate case is \psi equal to \varphi. From P the rule writes P \vee P, and then the two schemas give the same line. It is a legal step, and the next section uses the statement P \vee P once. The near misses, steps that look like \rulename{\vee I} and are not, are listed after the rule card at the end of this section. Do not read “or” as “one but not both” when checking a step. From x = 2, \rulename{\vee I} gives “x = 2 or x \le 5”, although at x = 2 both sides are true. The step is correct: the disjunction is inclusive, and the rule never claims that the added side is false. \rulename{\vee I} runs one way only. From \varphi it gives \varphi \vee \psi; from \varphi \vee \psi it gives nothing, and in general \varphi does not follow from \varphi \vee \psi at all. The phrase “in particular” belongs to \rulename{\wedge E}, not to “or”. For a concrete failure, let x be a real number: “x \ge 0 or x < 0” is true whatever x is, and “in particular x \ge 0” is false at x = -1. Let x be a real number, and suppose line 1 of a derivation is x = 2. Which of the following may line 2 be, justified by one application of \rulename{\vee I} to line 1? 1. (x = 2) \vee (x = 3). 2. (x = 3) \vee (x = 2). 3. (x = 2) \vee (1 = 0). 4. x \ge 2. (i) Yes, by the first schema, with \psi replaced by x = 3. (ii) Yes, by the second schema. (iii) Yes, by the first schema, with \psi replaced by the false statement 1 = 0. The line is true, since its left side is, and it is useless; the rule allows it. (iv) Only once x \ge 2 is written out as (x > 2) \vee (x = 2), as the convention on inequalities above asks when a rule must see the disjunction. In that form it is an instance of the second schema, with \varphi replaced by x = 2. A checker who matches symbols sees the difference. A disjunction as a goal Section 1.2 asked two questions before writing any line: what is the goal’s main connective? (goal-directed reasoning, from the bottom up) and what are the available lines’ main connectives? (premise-directed reasoning, from the top down). Each rule so far added an answer. A conjunction as a goal splits into two subgoals, both needed (\rulename{\wedge I}); an implication as a goal opens a box (\rulename{{\to}I}, @def-rules-implication). Now \vee joins the list of goals. If the goal is \varphi \vee \psi, its last line can be \rulename{\vee I}, and then the subgoal is \varphi or \psi: one of the two, of our choosing. That choice is new, and a wrong choice can leave us working towards a statement that does not follow from what we have. Suppose the premise is x > 1 and the goal is (x > 3) \vee (x > 0). Choose the left side, and the new goal x > 3 does not follow from the premise: try to break the step, and x = 2 does, since there x > 1 holds and x > 3 fails. Choose the right side, and x > 0 follows from x > 1. In the Givens/Goal table, \rulename{\vee I} replaces the goal \varphi \vee \psi by the side you choose. So the goal-directed step for \vee comes with a caution: Postpone a disjunction: choose a side of a goal \varphi \vee \psi only when that side is in hand. “In hand” means that the side stands on an available line. Until then, work from the premises: take conjunctions apart, fire implications, open the boxes the goal asks for, and look at what appears. When one side of the goal turns up, the choice has been made for us. Let x be a real number. The premise is 0 < x < 1 and the goal is (x < 0) \vee (x < 2). Which side should \rulename{\vee I} take, and why not the other? The right side, x < 2: it follows from x < 1, the right half of the premise. The left side x < 0 does not follow: at x = \tfrac12 the premise holds and x < 0 fails. A side chosen too early is worth watching once, all the way to the point where the search stalls, and then once more done right. [A side chosen too early] Show that P \to R \vdash (P \wedge Q) \to (S \vee R). The box. The goal is an implication, so we open a box with its hypothesis P \wedge Q, and the goal inside is S \vee R. The first picture shows the box with its goal at the bottom, and the line that will close it, not yet justified; line 2 records the plan, “asm, for \rulename{{\to}I}”. The early choice. S is the left side of the goal, so suppose we aim at it at once: line 5 becomes “S \vee R, \rulename{\vee I} 4”, and line 4, S, is the new subgoal (the second picture). Now the search stalls. Nothing mentions S except the goal: no premise, no assumption, no part of either. Try to break the subgoal. Let x be a real number, and take P: “x > 1”, Q: “x > 0”, R: “x^2 > x”, S: “x > 5”. The premise P \to R holds for every x: if x > 1, then x^2 = x \cdot x > x. At x = 2 the assumption P \wedge Q is true and S is false. So S does not follow from the lines in hand. The goal was not at fault, since at x = 2 its right side R is true (4 > 2); the choice was. Redone. Go back to the choice and postpone it. Work from the lines in hand: \rulename{\wedge E} takes P out of the assumption, the premise fires on it, and R, the right side of the goal, is in hand. Only now does \rulename{\vee I} choose a side. Line 5 uses the second schema, with R on the right. A stalled branch is abandoned, not defended: go back to the last choice and make it later. In @exm-early-choice, which side would \rulename{\vee I} take if the premise were P \to S instead? The left side, S: with the premise P \to S, the lines \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{{\to}E} would put S in hand at line 4. The postponing is the same; the choice is made when a side appears. The habit of this section as a picture: Here are four derivations, in order of difficulty. Each Idea says, for each rule, whether it was chosen by the goal or by a premise. [Derivations with or-introduction] Show that: 1. P \vdash P \vee Q, and P \vdash Q \vee P; 2. P \wedge Q \vdash P \vee Q; 3. P \to Q \vdash P \to (Q \vee R); 4. (P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash P \to (Q \to (R \vee S)). (a) Idea. The goal is a disjunction, and one of its sides, P, is the premise: in hand from the start. The only choice is which schema, and the goal decides it: P sits on the left of P \vee Q and on the right of Q \vee P. In the first, line 2 is the first schema with \varphi replaced by P and \psi by Q; in the second, it is the second schema with the same replacement. The letter Q appears in no premise. That is the Reading’s “any statement” at work. (b) Idea. The goal P \vee Q is a disjunction, and neither side stands on a line yet, so we postpone it. Premise-directed: the premise’s main connective is \wedge, so \rulename{\wedge E} takes it apart. After that, both sides of the goal are in hand, and either choice finishes. The left derivation chose the left side (first schema); the right one chose the right side (second schema). Both are correct, and the choice was free precisely because both sides were in hand. That will not usually be so. (c) Idea. The goal’s main connective is the outer \to; the \vee sits inside its conclusion. Goal-directed: open a box with the hypothesis P, and the new goal inside it is Q \vee R, a disjunction, so we postpone it. Premise-directed: the premise P \to Q is an implication whose hypothesis P is now on a line, so \rulename{{\to}E} fires and gives Q. The left side of the goal is in hand; \rulename{\vee I} takes it, and \rulename{{\to}I} closes the box. The pictures show the box opened with its goal at the bottom, and then the box with the side Q written; only the justification of line 4, marked “?”, is left. Line 3 cites line 1, which lies in no box, and line 2, the assumption of the box that contains line 3. Line 4 is a line of the box itself, so \rulename{{\to}I} may cite the box \lines{2}{4}. (d) Idea. The goal has two arrows at the top of its structure, P \to (Q \to \cdots), so, as in @prp-curry, we open two nested boxes, first P, then Q; the inner one will close first. The innermost goal is R \vee S: postpone. Premise-directed: the only line that mentions R is the premise (P \wedge Q) \to R. Its hypothesis is P \wedge Q, which is not on any line, but both of its halves are: the two assumptions. So \rulename{\wedge I} builds it, \rulename{{\to}E} fires, and R is in hand. Then \rulename{\vee I}, and the two boxes close. In the pictures, the two boxes are open with the innermost goal at the bottom; then lines 4 and 5 are written, and only the justification of line 6 is left. This derivation uses every rule of the chapter so far except \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{R}. Line 4 cites line 2, from the outer box, which is still open at line 4. Line 5 cites line 1 from inside two boxes: a line in no box is available everywhere below it. Line 7 is a line of the outer box itself, which is why \rulename{{\to}I} at line 8 may cite \lines{2}{7}. Choosing the wrong side of a disjunctive goal too early can leave a goal that does not follow. Derivation (c) is where postponing pays. Had we committed at once, inside the box, to the goal’s right side, planning to reach Q \vee R from R, the box would need R itself, from the premise P \to Q and the assumption P alone. With x a real number, P: “x > 2”, Q: “x > 1” and R: “x > 3”, the premise and the assumption hold at x = 2.5, and R fails there, so R does not follow. Keep the goal as the whole disjunction until one side appears on a line. Manufacturing a hypothesis In every derivation so far, \rulename{\vee I} produced the goal, or the goal of a box. It has a second use. A premise whose hypothesis is a disjunction can fire only when that disjunction stands on a line, exactly as written (the matching clause of @def-rule-implication-elimination). If one side of it is in hand, \rulename{\vee I} builds the whole hypothesis. [A disjunctive hypothesis splits into two implications] Show that (P \vee Q) \to R \vdash (P \to R) \wedge (Q \to R). Idea. Goal-directed: the goal is a conjunction, so \rulename{\wedge I} splits it into two subgoals, P \to R and Q \to R, and each is an implication, so each gets its own box. Inside the box of P, the goal is R. Premise-directed: the only line that mentions R is the premise, and \rulename{{\to}E} on it needs its hypothesis P \vee Q on a line. We have P, one side of that hypothesis. So \rulename{\vee I} manufactures P \vee Q, and the premise fires. Here \rulename{\vee I} is chosen not because the goal is a disjunction (the goal is R) but because a premise’s hypothesis is one. The box of Q is the same, with the other schema. In the pictures, both boxes are open with their goals at the bottom; then the \rulename{\vee I} lines that manufacture the hypothesis are written, and only the \rulename{{\to}E} lines are left. Line 3 uses the first schema of @def-rule-disjunction-introduction (P on the left), line 7 the second (Q on the right). Both produce the same statement P \vee Q, the one the premise asks for. The two boxes are separate: the second opens after the first has closed, and nothing in it cites a line of the first. Line 10 cites lines 5 and 9, which lie in no box. The product example below, and several exercises, use \rulename{\vee I} the same way. Weakening is how a strong fact is fed to a rule, or a theorem, that asks for a weaker one. In mathematical terms, the derivation says that a theorem with a hypothesis “P or Q” splits into two theorems. Let x be a real number, and suppose we know “if x \ge 0, then x^3 \ge 0”, that is, “if x > 0 or x = 0, then x^3 \ge 0”. Then we know “if x > 0, then x^3 \ge 0” and “if x = 0, then x^3 \ge 0”. The way back, from the two implications to the single one with the disjunctive hypothesis, needs the rule of the next section; it is derived there. In the derivation of @exm-or-hypothesis-split, line 3 could not have been skipped by letting line 4 cite line 2 directly, as “R — \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2”. Why not? \rulename{{\to}E} (@def-rule-implication-elimination) needs the implication on one cited line and its hypothesis, exactly, on the other. The hypothesis of line 1 is P \vee Q, and line 2 is P, which does not match it symbol for symbol. Line 3 writes the hypothesis out, and only then does line 1 fire. A goal we cannot reach yet The most obvious fact about “or” is that the order of its sides does not matter: P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P. Try to derive it with the rules so far. The goal Q \vee P is a disjunction, so we postpone it and look at the premise. Its main connective is \vee, and no rule so far takes a disjunction apart. \rulename{\wedge E} needs a conjunction and \rulename{{\to}E} an implication; \rulename{\wedge I}, \rulename{\vee I}, and \rulename{R} may cite P \vee Q, but only to copy it or to build something larger around it. So the premise gives us nothing, and working from it alone, neither side of the goal ever comes into hand. We can get this far, though. Each side of the premise, assumed in a box, leads to the goal: This derivation is correct, but it shows P \vee Q \vdash Q \to (Q \vee P), and line 1 is never cited. (A derivation need not use every premise, @def-derivable.) What we would like is to put the three lines 1, 4, and 7 together: one of P, Q holds, and either one leads to Q \vee P; so Q \vee P. That is a proof by cases, and none of the rules so far performs it. With them we cannot find a derivation of P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P. The missing move is to use a disjunction, as \rulename{\wedge E} uses a conjunction and \rulename{{\to}E} uses an implication. The next section gives the rule that does this, and with it the six-line derivation that this attempt lacks. Derive it or break it From here on, some exercises list claims \Gamma \vdash \varphi without saying which hold. For each, either give a derivation, or break the claim: find statements that make its counterexample set \Gamma, \neg\varphi (@def-counterexample-set) true all at once. For instance, P \wedge (Q \vee R) \vdash Q breaks. Let x be a real number, and take P: “x > 0”, Q: “x > 2”, R: “x < 3”. At x = 1 the set P \wedge (Q \vee R), \neg Q is true: 1 > 0, 1 < 3, and 1 > 2 fails. A claim can also be of neither kind yet. P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P cannot be broken: if P \vee Q is true, one of its sides is, and that side makes Q \vee P true. And with the rules so far no derivation of it has been found: the attempt in “A goal we cannot reach yet” stalls, and the claim waits for the next section’s rule. The lists in this section’s exercises contain only claims that the rules so far settle. How this looks in a mathematical proof In written mathematics \rulename{\vee I} is almost always silent. Here are the two steps of the opening, written out as derivations. [A product with a zero factor] Let a and b be real numbers, and take as known the school fact “if a = 0 or b = 0, then a \cdot b = 0”. Prove that if a = 0, then a \cdot b = 0, naming the rule behind each step. Then write the step from x > 0 to x \ge 0 as a derivation. The goal is an implication, so the proof supposes a = 0 (a box). Inside, the fact needs its hypothesis “a = 0 or b = 0”, which \rulename{\vee I} manufactures, as in @exm-or-hypothesis-split. In prose, with each step’s rule in brackets: Suppose a = 0. Then a = 0 or b = 0 [\rulename{\vee I}]. So, by the school fact, a \cdot b = 0 [\rulename{{\to}E}]. Hence, if a = 0, then a \cdot b = 0 [\rulename{{\to}I}]. As a derivation, with the school fact as the premise: A written proof would say “if a = 0, then a \cdot b = 0 by the fact”, and leave out the words “a = 0 or b = 0”. The derivation shows what that sentence leaves out: a box, a weakening, and one use of the fact. For the second step, let x be a real number with x > 0. Written out, x \ge 0 is (x > 0) \vee (x = 0), and the step is one application of the first schema: Line 2 is x \ge 0, written out. Every “so x \ge 0” after x > 0, every “so \abs{t} \le 1” after \abs{t} < 1, and every “so n is even or n > 5” after “n is even” is this rule. A reader who checks a proof line by line should see it, even where the writer did not name it. It is a step that never leads from a truth to a falsehood, and it is also the step that explains why a conclusion can say less than the proof knew. The rule card Before the card, the new rule at work on statements larger than single letters. The schema sees only the whole cited line; how much is inside it does not matter. [Instances of \rulename{\vee I}] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Schema \varphi \psi Cited line New line -------------- -------------------- ----------------- -------------------- ----------------------------------- first P \to Q R \wedge \neg S P \to Q (P \to Q) \vee (R \wedge \neg S) second P \vee Q P \wedge \neg R P \vee Q (P \wedge \neg R) \vee (P \vee Q) second (P \wedge Q) \to R \neg R (P \wedge Q) \to R \neg R \vee ((P \wedge Q) \to R) -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Not an instance. From P \vee Q, the line P \vee (Q \vee R) is not written by \rulename{\vee I}: the rule adds a side to the whole cited line, giving (P \vee Q) \vee R or R \vee (P \vee Q); it never reaches inside. The card grows by one row. Shape shows the given lines (or box), then the new line. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Rule Shape You write Lean --------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------ -------------------------------------- ---------------------------- \rulename{\wedge I} \varphi, \psi \Longrightarrow \varphi \wedge \psi “We show P, and we show Q.” constructor \rulename{\wedge E} \varphi \wedge \psi \Longrightarrow \varphi (or \psi) “In particular, P.” h.1 (and h.2) \rulename{{\to}E} \varphi \to \psi, \varphi \Longrightarrow \psi “Since P implies Q, and P holds, Q.” exact h hp \rulename{{\to}I} box \varphi … \psi \Longrightarrow \varphi \to \psi “Assume P. … Hence Q.” intro hp \rulename{R} \varphi (available) \Longrightarrow \varphi, copied “As shown above, P.” exact hp \rulename{\vee I} \varphi \Longrightarrow \varphi \vee \psi (or \psi \vee \varphi) “So P or Q holds.” left (or Or.inl hp); right ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ The phrase is different from the “in particular” of \rulename{\wedge E} on purpose. “In particular” announces that a part is being taken out of something bigger; “so P or Q” announces that something bigger, and weaker, is being built. [Not allowed: \rulename{\vee I}] Each step is offered as one application of \rulename{\vee I}; each breaks the Reading of the rule where shown. - “P from P \vee Q”: it runs the rule backwards. The cited line is a side of the new line, never the other way round. - “P \wedge Q from P”: the new line must be a disjunction. - “Q \vee P from P \vee Q”: the cited line must be one whole side of the new line. - “P \vee (Q \vee R) from P \vee Q”: the rule never reaches inside the cited line. - “x \ge 0 from x > 0, as written”: a checker compares symbols. Write x \ge 0 out first, as the convention on inequalities at the start of this section asks. Line 3 is Q. Which of Q \vee (P \wedge R), (P \wedge R) \vee Q, Q \vee Q, Q \wedge Q may “\rulename{\vee I} 3” write? The first three. The first is the first schema and the second the second schema, with \psi replaced by P \wedge R; the third is either schema, with \psi replaced by Q itself. Q \wedge Q is a conjunction, written by \rulename{\wedge I} 3, 3. [Looking ahead] Chapter 4 proves that a claim that breaks has no derivation, with any of the rules of Chapters 1 and 2, and that a claim that cannot be broken has a derivation with them. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the two schemas of @def-rule-disjunction-introduction from memory, and say which letter in them may stand for a statement that appears in no earlier line. 2. Which of the following sentences, taken from proofs about a real number x or real numbers a, b, use \rulename{\vee I}? For each of the others, name the rule it uses. - “We have x < 3, so x \le 3.” - “We found that a = 0. So a = 0 or b = 0, and therefore a \cdot b = 0.” - “Since 0 < x < 1, in particular x < 1.” - “Since \abs{x - 2} < 1 implies 1 < x < 3, and \abs{x - 2} < 1, we get 1 < x < 3.” 3. True or false, with a reason: \rulename{\vee I} may introduce a side that is false. 4. To show Q, \ (P \vee Q) \to (Q \to R) \vdash R, which rule writes the first line after the premises, and what is that line? Why is that rule used, although the goal is not a disjunction? (a) From a line i holding \varphi, a line k holding \varphi \vee \psi, justified “\rulename{\vee I} i”; and, from the same line, a line k holding \psi \vee \varphi, with the same justification (@def-rule-disjunction-introduction). The letter \psi appears in no given line: it may be any statement. (b) The first uses \rulename{\vee I}: x \le 3 is (x < 3) \vee (x = 3), and its left side is in hand. The second uses \rulename{\vee I} to build “a = 0 or b = 0” from its left side, and then \rulename{{\to}E} on the fact about products, as in @exm-product-zero. The third uses \rulename{\wedge E}: 0 < x < 1 is (0 < x) \wedge (x < 1), and the sentence takes out its right half. The fourth uses \rulename{{\to}E}, with the implication first and its hypothesis second. (c) True. The added side \psi may be any statement, false ones included, as in the line (x = 2) \vee (1 = 0) of the Quick check after the definition. The new line is still true whenever the cited line is, because “or” is inclusive: one true side is enough. (d) The rule is \rulename{\vee I}, by its second schema, and line 3 is P \vee Q, from line 1. It is used because a premise’s hypothesis is a disjunction. The goal R occurs only in the premise (P \vee Q) \to (Q \to R), and \rulename{{\to}E} fires on that premise only when P \vee Q itself stands on a line. Only its right side Q is on a line, and \rulename{\vee I} turns it into P \vee Q. Then Q \to R follows by \rulename{{\to}E} 2, 3, and R by \rulename{{\to}E} 4, 1. The move is the one of @exm-or-hypothesis-split, where \rulename{\vee I} builds a premise’s hypothesis. [A2: Drill] Each part takes a line or two. The parts run from single steps, through a missing line and a justification column, to whole derivations. Let x be a real number and n an integer. 1. Line 2 is (P \to Q) \wedge R. Write two lines that “\rulename{\vee I} 2” can give, one by each schema. 2. Line 6 is (R \wedge S) \vee (P \to Q), justified “\rulename{\vee I} 4”. What can line 4 be? 3. Justify each line: 1 P \wedge Q, premise; 2 R, premise; 3 Q; 4 Q \vee R; 5 (Q \vee R) \wedge R; 6 S \vee ((Q \vee R) \wedge R). 4. Line 1 is x = 5. Which of these may be written as “\rulename{\vee I} 1”? (i) (x = 5) \vee (x = 6); (ii) (x > 4) \vee (x = 5); (iii) x \ge 5, as written; (iv) (x = 5) \wedge (x \ge 0). 5. Line 1 is P \wedge Q. Is “P \vee Q — \rulename{\vee I} 1” legal? 6. Line 1 is Q \vee P. Is “P \vee Q — \rulename{\vee I} 1” legal? 7. Is “x > 0, so x \ge 0” one step of \rulename{\vee I}? 8. Line 4 is P \wedge Q. Is “(P \vee R) \wedge Q — \rulename{\vee I} 4” correct? If not, how many lines does it take? 9. “We have n = 4. So n is even or n > 10.” Which steps does this sentence take? 10. The premise is x < -1 and the goal is (x < -5) \vee (x < 0). Which side should \rulename{\vee I} take? 11. Derive P \vdash (P \vee Q) \wedge (R \vee P). 12. Derive P \wedge Q \vdash Q \vee R. 13. Derive P \to Q \vdash P \to (R \vee Q). 14. Derive (P \vee Q) \to R, \ Q \vdash R. 15. Derive P \to (Q \wedge R) \vdash P \to (S \vee R). (a) ((P \to Q) \wedge R) \vee S by the first schema and S \vee ((P \to Q) \wedge R) by the second, with any statement for S. (b) R \wedge S (first schema) or P \to Q (second schema): line 4 is one whole side of line 6. (c) 3 \rulename{\wedge E} 1; 4 \rulename{\vee I} 3 (first schema); 5 \rulename{\wedge I} 4, 2; 6 \rulename{\vee I} 5 (second schema). (d) (i) Yes, by the first schema. (ii) Yes, by the second schema: x = 5 is the right side. (iii) No: as written, x \ge 5 is one statement. Written out as (x > 5) \vee (x = 5), it is the second schema. (iv) No: the new line is not a disjunction. (e) No: P \wedge Q is not a side of P \vee Q. From line 1, \rulename{\vee I} could write (P \wedge Q) \vee R. (f) No: Q \vee P is not a whole side of P \vee Q. (g) Yes, once x \ge 0 is written out as (x > 0) \vee (x = 0): it is the first schema. (h) No. The new line of \rulename{\vee I} is a disjunction with line 4 as one whole side; this line is a conjunction, and it reaches inside line 4. It takes four lines: 5 P, \rulename{\wedge E} 4; 6 Q, \rulename{\wedge E} 4; 7 P \vee R, \rulename{\vee I} 5; 8 (P \vee R) \wedge Q, \rulename{\wedge I} 7, 6. (i) Two steps: algebra (4 = 2 \cdot 2, so n is even), then \rulename{\vee I}. From “n = 4” itself, \rulename{\vee I} gives only “n = 4 or …”. (j) The right side, x < 0, which follows from x < -1. The left side fails at x = -2, where the premise holds and x < -5 does not. (k) 2 P \vee Q, \rulename{\vee I} 1; 3 R \vee P, \rulename{\vee I} 1; 4 (P \vee Q) \wedge (R \vee P), \rulename{\wedge I} 2, 3. (l) 2 Q, \rulename{\wedge E} 1; 3 Q \vee R, \rulename{\vee I} 2. (m) A box opened with P: 2 P, assumption, for \rulename{{\to}I}; 3 Q, \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2; 4 R \vee Q, \rulename{\vee I} 3; then 5 P \to (R \vee Q), \rulename{{\to}I} 2–4. (n) 3 P \vee Q, \rulename{\vee I} 2; 4 R, \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 3. (o) A box opened with P: 2 P, assumption, for \rulename{{\to}I}; 3 Q \wedge R, \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2; 4 R, \rulename{\wedge E} 3; 5 S \vee R, \rulename{\vee I} 4; then 6 P \to (S \vee R), \rulename{{\to}I} 2–5. B. Practice [B1: Committing to a side] Show that P \wedge (Q \to R) \vdash Q \to (R \vee S), and that P \vdash (Q \vee P) \vee R. For each derivation, say at which line you committed to a side of a disjunctive goal, and why that was safe. For the first, the goal is an implication, so open a box with Q; the goal inside is R \vee S, which we postpone. Premise-directed, \rulename{\wedge E} takes out Q \to R, and \rulename{{\to}E} fires on the assumption Q. We committed at line 5, to the left side R, and only after line 4 had put R on a line. The other conjunct of the premise, P, is never used. For the second, the goal (Q \vee P) \vee R is a disjunction whose left side, Q \vee P, is itself a disjunction, and P is one side of that. Line 2 uses the second schema (P on the right) and line 3 the first, with \varphi replaced by Q \vee P. We committed twice, at lines 2 and 3, and both times the side was in hand: at line 2 the side P was the premise, and at line 3 the side Q \vee P was line 2. Choosing the side R at the outer level would have left the subgoal R, which does not follow from P: take P true and R false. [B2: The last line] A search for P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash P \to (S \vee R) has reached the stage below; only the last line is missing. Name the move, then complete it. The move is the one read off the goal: an implication goal opens a box with its hypothesis, and the box is closed by \rulename{{\to}I} once its last line is the implication’s conclusion. The box opened with P at line 3, and its last line, line 6, is S \vee R, the conclusion of the goal. So line 7 closes the box: Line 7 cites the box as the range \lines{3}{6}, not its lines one by one. Inside the box, the disjunction S \vee R was postponed until R came into hand at line 5; the side in hand was the right one, so line 6 uses the second schema. [B3: A theorem with a weaker hypothesis] Let x be a real number, and take as known the school fact “if x \ge 1, then x^2 \ge x”. Prove that if x > 1, then x^2 \ge x. Write the proof as a derivation whose premise is the school fact, with x \ge 1 written out as a disjunction, and then as two or three sentences of prose. Written out, x \ge 1 is (x > 1) \vee (x = 1), so the premise is an implication whose hypothesis is a disjunction. The goal is an implication: open a box with x > 1. Inside, \rulename{\vee I} manufactures the premise’s hypothesis, and \rulename{{\to}E} fires. In prose: Suppose x > 1. Then x \ge 1, so x^2 \ge x by the fact. Hence if x > 1, then x^2 \ge x. The words “then x \ge 1” are line 3. For instance, at x = 3 the conclusion reads 9 \ge 3. [B4: Derive or break] For each claim, either derive it with the rules of Sections 1.2–1.5, or break it by statements about a real number x that make its counterexample set true. 1. P \vdash P \vee (Q \wedge R). 2. P \vdash P \wedge (Q \vee R). 3. P \to R \vdash (P \vee Q) \to R. 4. (P \vee Q) \to R \vdash P \to R. 5. (P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash (Q \wedge P) \to (R \vee S). 6. (P \to Q) \wedge (P \to R) \vdash P \to (Q \vee R). 7. P \to (Q \vee R) \vdash P \to Q. (a) Derive. The side P of the goal is the premise. (b) Break. Take P: “x > 0”, Q: “x > 5”, R: “x < -5”. At x = 1, P is true and Q \vee R is false (1 > 5 and 1 < -5 both fail), so P \wedge (Q \vee R) is false. The counterexample set P, \neg(P \wedge (Q \vee R)) is true. (c) Break. Take P: “x > 3”, Q: “x < 0”, R: “x > 1”. The premise P \to R holds for every x. At x = -1, P \vee Q is true (-1 < 0) and R is false, so (P \vee Q) \to R is false, and the counterexample set P \to R, \neg((P \vee Q) \to R) is true. (d) Derive. Inside the box of P, \rulename{\vee I} manufactures the premise’s hypothesis, as in @exm-or-hypothesis-split. (e) Derive. The premise’s hypothesis is P \wedge Q, and the box gives Q \wedge P: take it apart and join it the other way round, then postpone the goal R \vee S until R is in hand. (f) Derive. One half of the premise is enough. (g) Break. Take P: “x > 0”, Q: “x > 5”, R: “x < 6”. The premise P \to (Q \vee R) holds for every x, since every real number is > 5 or < 6. At x = 1, P is true and Q is false, so the counterexample set P \to (Q \vee R), \neg(P \to Q) is true. Apart from (e), which simply derives, the claims come in pairs. (a) and (b) are look-alikes, with \vee and \wedge traded; (c) and (d) are converses; (g) is a look-alike of (f), with premise and conclusion traded and weakened. In each pair one claim derives and the other breaks. C. Going deeper [C1: Which new rules are safe?] Suppose someone proposes new rules for the derivations of this chapter. Let x be a real number. 1. Take the rule “from \varphi \vee \psi, write \varphi”. Starting from the premise “x \ge 0 or x < 0”, which is true for every real x, derive with it a line that is false at x = -1. 2. \rulename{\vee I} adds a side \psi that may be any statement at all. Explain why it can never lead from a true line to a false one. 3. Is the rule “from \varphi, write \varphi \wedge \psi, for any statement \psi” safe in the same sense? Justify your answer with an instance. (a) With \varphi replaced by x \ge 0 and \psi by x < 0, the proposed rule turns the premise into the line x \ge 0. At x = -1 the premise is true, since -1 < 0, and the line -1 \ge 0 is false. So the rule can lead from a true line to a false one. (b) Suppose the cited line \varphi is true. The new line \varphi \vee \psi (or \psi \vee \varphi) is true when at least one of its sides is true, because “or” is inclusive (Section 1.1), and its side \varphi is true. So the new line is true, whatever \psi is. The truth or falsity of \psi never enters. (c) No. The new line \varphi \wedge \psi is true only when both sides are, and \psi is arbitrary. With \varphi replaced by x = -1 and \psi by x \ge 0, at x = -1 the cited line is true and the new line, “x = -1 and x \ge 0”, is false. The contrast with (b) is the whole difference between \vee and \wedge: a disjunction needs one true side, so an arbitrary second side is harmless; a conjunction needs both, so it is not. That is why \rulename{\wedge I} asks for both sides on lines. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) applies the proposed rule to the premise to get x \ge 0, and checks at x = -1 that the premise is true and the new line false. - 3: (b) argues from the inclusive meaning of “or”: one true side makes the disjunction true, whatever the other side is. - 3: (c) answers no, with an instance in which \varphi is true and \varphi \wedge \psi is false. - 1: (c) names the difference: a conjunction needs both sides true. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (a), a premise that is false at x = -1; in (b), an argument that assumes \psi is true; in (c), “safe” on the grounds that \varphi is true. [C2: Predicting the manufacture] 1. Show that (P \vee Q) \to (R \wedge S) \vdash P \to S. 2. Show that (P \vee Q) \to R \vdash (P \wedge Q) \to R. 3. In each derivation, which rule built the hypothesis of the premise? Could you have predicted, from the premise’s main connective and the shape of its hypothesis alone, that this rule would be needed? (a) The goal is an implication: open a box with P; the goal inside is S. The only line mentioning S is the premise, whose conclusion R \wedge S contains it; to use the premise, \rulename{{\to}E} needs P \vee Q, built from P by \rulename{\vee I}. Then \rulename{\wedge E} takes out S. (b) The goal is an implication: open a box with P \wedge Q; the goal inside is R. The premise fires on P \vee Q. The assumption gives P by \rulename{\wedge E}, and \rulename{\vee I} builds P \vee Q. Taking Q at line 3 instead, and building P \vee Q by the second schema, works equally well. (c) In both, \rulename{\vee I} built the hypothesis (line 3 in (a), line 4 in (b)), and in both it could be predicted. The premise’s main connective is \to, so the premise is used by \rulename{{\to}E}, which needs its hypothesis P \vee Q on a line of its own, exactly. That disjunction occurs only inside the premise, as its hypothesis, and no rule takes the hypothesis out of an implication (\rulename{{\to}E} gives the conclusion). So it had to be built, and the only rule of the chapter so far that builds a disjunction is \rulename{\vee I}. The one question left was which side would be in hand; in (b) the conjunction P \wedge Q offered both.

title: 1.6 Using Or: Proof by Cases
content: Using Or: Proof by Cases The previous section met a goal the rules could not reach: from P \vee Q, derive Q \vee P. The rules could build a disjunction (\rulename{\vee I}, @def-rule-disjunction-introduction), but none of them could use one. This section gives the rule that uses a disjunction, \rulename{\vee E}. It is the most familiar move in mathematics after “suppose”: the split into cases, “if x \ge 0, then …; if x < 0, then …”. It is also the last rule of this chapter. We use it to reach the stalled goal, to prove the laws that let “and” and “or” be rearranged, and to prove three facts about absolute values; the section ends with all the rules of the chapter on one page. A proof that needs two cases The absolute value of a real number is defined in two cases: \abs{x} \coloneqq \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0 . \end{cases} Suppose we want to prove that \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y} for all real numbers x and y. There is no single computation to do. Which formula gives \abs{xy} depends on the sign of xy, and that depends on the signs of x and y. Yet once the signs are fixed, each case is one line: if x > 0 and y < 0, for instance, then \abs{xy} = -xy = x \cdot (-y) = \abs{x}\abs{y}. So the proof we want has the shape “every real number is \ge 0 or < 0; in the first case …; in the second case …; so in every case …”. The rules so far cannot say this. The attempt at P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P in Section 1.5 met the same wall from the other side. It derived that each side of the premise, assumed in a box, leads to the goal: lines 4 and 7 there were P \to (Q \vee P) and Q \to (Q \vee P). What it lacked was a rule to say “one of P, Q holds, and either one leads to Q \vee P; so Q \vee P”: a rule that takes “\varphi or \psi”, which does not say which side holds, and still reaches a definite conclusion. That is the job of the elimination rule for “or”. The rule of or-elimination To use “\varphi or \psi”, reach your goal from \varphi, and reach it again from \psi. The definition block states both rules for disjunction, so that the pair stands in one place: the new rule first, then the two schemas of \rulename{\vee I} recalled from Section 1.5. As in every schema (@def-rule-schema), the Greek letters stand for arbitrary statements and i, j, k, l, m, n for line numbers. [Rules for Disjunction] The first schema is the rule \rulename{\vee E} (or-elimination, or proof by cases); the other two are \rulename{\vee I}, as in @def-rule-disjunction-introduction. In \rulename{\vee E}, each line \chi (line k and line m) is a line of its box itself, not of a box inside it. This rule has conditions that matter; read each one. - The disjunction. Line i holds a disjunction \varphi \vee \psi, available at line n. The cases are not ours to invent: they are the two sides of a disjunction we already have, as a premise, an assumption, or a line derived earlier. Writing “Case 1 … Case 2 …” does not create it. - Two boxes. The first box opens with the left side \varphi as its assumption, the second with the right side \psi. They are separate: the second opens after the first has closed, and the drawing shows a break in the vertical bar between them. So, by the scope rule of @def-derivation, no line of the second box may cite a line of the first. The disjunction does not tell us which side holds, so we must be ready for both, and each case’s assumption is in force only inside its own box. Each case box’s assumption is printed “asm, for \rulename{\vee E}”; read it as “Case 1: …” and “Case 2: …”. - The same last line. Both boxes end in the same statement \chi, and in each box \chi is a line of that box itself, not of a box opened inside it. The rule then writes \chi a third time, outside both boxes, where neither \varphi nor \psi is assumed. That is honest only because \chi was reached whichever case holds. - Three citations. The justification “\rulename{\vee E} i, \lines{j}{k}, \lines{l}{m}” cites the disjunction first, then the box of the left side, then the box of the right side, each box as a range. Both boxes must be available at line n: closed, and sitting directly in the part of the derivation where line n is (@def-derivation). - Any conclusion. The statement \chi need not mention \varphi or \psi. It is whatever we are trying to reach. The next subsection says how to choose it. The degenerate case is a box of one line, whose assumption is already \chi. Nothing in the rule asks a box to contain more than its assumption, just as nothing in \rulename{{\to}I} did (@exm-first-boxes). The second derivation below has two such boxes. A case may use only its own assumption. Here is the error in its usual form. Let x be a real number, and split on “x \ge 0 or x < 0”. Case x \ge 0: then \abs{x} = x. Case x < 0: since x \ge 0, again \abs{x} = x. So \abs{x} = x. The second case cites the assumption of the first, whose box has closed, which the scope rule forbids. The conclusion is false at x = -1. Cases end in the current goal Section 1.2 set up two questions: what is the goal’s main connective? and what are the available lines’ main connectives? Section 1.5 answered the first for \vee: postpone a disjunctive goal until one side is in hand. Now we can answer the second. A disjunction on an available line invites \rulename{\vee E}: split on it. What should the two boxes end in? The rule leaves \chi to us, and the choice is always the same. It is the current goal: whatever we are trying to reach at the point where the split is made. That may be the goal of the whole derivation, or a subgoal inside other boxes. The boxes of the split end in it, and the \rulename{\vee E} line that closes the split then writes it outside both boxes, exactly where it was wanted. Cases end in the current goal. From a skeleton to a proof about numbers Almost every proof by cases in analysis has the same skeleton. A known fact supplies the cases, and each case is handled by a separate argument, a small lemma that turns the case’s assumption into the goal. As a derivation, with the fact and the two lemmas as premises: The idea behind it is the whole method of this section at its simplest. The goal R is atomic, so the goal suggests nothing. Premise-directed, the disjunction on line 1 is split, both boxes ending in the current goal R. In each box the matching lemma fires on the case’s assumption. (@exm-cases-on-hypothesis did the same with the two lemmas packed into one conjunction, and inside a box.) In a proof about real numbers, the disjunction is usually a fact about the order. The facts about \le and the absolute value used below are school algebra: every real number a satisfies a \ge 0 or a < 0; the rules of signs for products; adding two inequalities of the same direction. Here we take them as known. In the language of this chapter, “every real number a satisfies a \ge 0 or a < 0” is a supply of disjunctions: for each number we meet, it gives a line (a \ge 0) \vee (a < 0) that \rulename{\vee E} may cite. The first example is the smallest, and it is written twice: as a proof in which every step carries its rule in brackets, and as a derivation. [A number is at most its absolute value] Let x be a real number. Prove that \abs{x} \ge x, by cases, labeling each step with its rule. The goal \abs{x} \ge x is the disjunction (\abs{x} > x) \vee (\abs{x} = x), and neither side is known for every x (the first fails at x = 1, the second at x = -1), so we postpone it. The fact “x \ge 0 or x < 0” is a disjunction to split on. In prose: We have x \ge 0 or x < 0, and we argue by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]. Case x \ge 0. By the definition of the absolute value, \abs{x} = x [\rulename{{\to}E}]. So \abs{x} \ge x [\rulename{\vee I}]. Case x < 0. By the definition, \abs{x} = -x, and -x > 0 > x; so \abs{x} > x [\rulename{{\to}E}], which is the school-algebra fact “if x < 0, then \abs{x} > x” used on the case’s assumption. So \abs{x} \ge x [\rulename{\vee I}]. In either case \abs{x} \ge x, so \abs{x} \ge x. As a derivation, with the order fact, the definition’s first clause, and the school-algebra fact about negative numbers as premises, and with \abs{x} \ge x written out: It is the skeleton above, with a weakening at the end of each box: line 6 takes the right side of the goal (second schema of \rulename{\vee I}) and line 9 the left side (first schema). Each case took the side it had in hand. At x = 3, the first case applies and line 6 reads 3 > 3 or 3 = 3; at x = -2, the second applies and line 8 reads 2 > -2. In the derivation of @exm-abs-at-least-x, which statement do lines 6 and 9 both write, and why must they agree? Both write (\abs{x} > x) \vee (\abs{x} = x), the current goal written out. They must agree because \rulename{\vee E} closes a split only when both case boxes end in the same statement. The next two examples are longer, and in each the case split is doing real work. [The absolute value of a product] Let x and y be real numbers. Prove that \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y}. We use that \abs{a} = -a whenever a \le 0: for a < 0 this is the definition, and for a = 0 both sides are 0. The number x satisfies x \ge 0 or x < 0, and we argue by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]. Inside each case, y \ge 0 or y < 0, and we argue by cases again. Case x \ge 0, y \ge 0. Then xy \ge 0, so \abs{xy} = xy = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Case x \ge 0, y < 0. Then xy \le 0, so \abs{xy} = -xy = x \cdot (-y) = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Case x < 0, y \ge 0. Then xy \le 0, so \abs{xy} = -xy = (-x) \cdot y = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Case x < 0, y < 0. Then xy > 0, so \abs{xy} = xy = (-x)(-y) = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Each inner case split reaches \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y}, so each outer case does, and hence the equation holds. The structure is two uses of \rulename{\vee E}, one inside each box of the other: two outer boxes (the sign of x), each containing two inner boxes (the sign of y), and every one of the four inner boxes ending in the same equation, the current goal. The second and third cases needed the remark about a \le 0. When x = 0 and y < 0, the product is 0, not negative, and without the remark the case would have a hole at exactly that point. A case split need not be the obvious one. The triangle inequality has an equally short proof with two cases, if we split on the sign of the right quantity. [The triangle inequality by cases] Let x and y be real numbers. Prove that \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. First, every real number a satisfies a \le \abs{a} and -a \le \abs{a}. This is itself a proof by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]: if a \ge 0, then \abs{a} = a, so a \le \abs{a}, and -a \le 0 \le a = \abs{a}; if a < 0, then \abs{a} = -a, so -a \le \abs{a}, and a < 0 < -a = \abs{a}. Now x + y \ge 0 or x + y < 0, and we argue by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]. Case x + y \ge 0. Then \abs{x + y} = x + y \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, adding x \le \abs{x} and y \le \abs{y}. Case x + y < 0. Then \abs{x + y} = -x - y = (-x) + (-y) \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, adding -x \le \abs{x} and -y \le \abs{y}. Both cases reach \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, so it holds. Two case splits appear here, one after the other rather than one inside the other. The first proves a small lemma for an arbitrary number a, both halves at once, and its first half, a \le \abs{a}, is @exm-abs-at-least-x again. The second uses both halves of the lemma, for a = x and for a = y. Splitting on the sign of x + y instead of the signs of x and y is what saves two cases: the absolute value in the goal is \abs{x + y}, and its sign is the only one the goal’s left side cares about. A case split must cover every possibility. A common faulty proof of the triangle inequality treats “x \ge 0 and y \ge 0” and “x < 0 and y < 0”, checks both, and stops. The disjunction of these two cases is not a fact: x = 1, y = -1 satisfies neither. So there is no line \varphi \vee \psi for \rulename{\vee E} to cite, and the rule was never legally applied. The missing mixed-sign cases are the interesting ones: at x = 1, y = -1 the inequality reads 0 \le 2, and it is strict. Cases must exhaust, and a split that silently drops a value is a missing case in disguise. “Every real x satisfies x > 0 or x < 0” is false: x = 0 satisfies neither. A proof that splits into x > 0 and x < 0 cites a disjunction that is not available, and proves nothing about x = 0. The true disjunctions are “x \ge 0 or x < 0”, and “x > 0, or x = 0, or x < 0”. Cases may overlap, however. “x \ge 0 or x \le 0” is true for every real x, and x = 0 lies in both cases. Nothing in \rulename{\vee E} forbids this: the rule asks that the goal be reached in each case, not that the cases be disjoint. (This is the inclusive “or” of Section 1.1.) Because “or” is inclusive, knowing one side of a disjunction says nothing about the other. The form “from P \vee Q and P, conclude \neg Q” is called affirming a disjunct, and it is bad. Let n be an integer, with P: “n is even”, Q: “n is a multiple of 3”; at n = 6 both premises are true and \neg Q is false. No step of \rulename{\vee E} does this: its cases end in one common statement, never in the falsity of a side. Each of the following begins a proof that x^2 \ge 0 for every real number x. Which case splits are exhaustive, so that \rulename{\vee E} may be applied? 1. Case x \ge 0; case x < 0. 2. Case x > 0; case x < 0. 3. Case x \ge 0; case x \le 0. (i) Exhaustive: every real number is \ge 0 or < 0. (ii) Not exhaustive: x = 0 is in neither case, so the disjunction cited is false. The claim is still true at 0, but this split never proves it there. (iii) Exhaustive. The cases overlap at x = 0, which does no harm: x^2 = 0 \ge 0 is reached in both. Letters in the number column stand for line numbers; every cited line must be available (@def-derivation), and each box rule needs the box’s last line as a line of that box itself. To test a form, put statements in for the letters that make every premise true and the conclusion false; one such choice shows the form is bad. (Section 1.1) - Two ways to attack an argument. Show a premise false, or show a step’s form bad; the two attacks are independent. (Section 1.1) - Read the skeleton off the goal. The goal’s main connective chooses the introduction rule: \wedge gives two subgoals, \to a box, \vee a choice to postpone. (Section 1.2) - Use a premise by its main connective. Its elimination rule says what you may do with it: take a conjunction apart, feed an implication its hypothesis, split a disjunction into cases. (Section 1.2) - Open a box, close a box. An assumption lives exactly as long as its box. (Section 1.4) - Work from both ends. Premises at the top, the goal at the bottom; fill the gap from both sides. (Section 1.2) - Postpone a disjunction. Write x as a sum of two numbers whose absolute values appear in the goal. [Hint 2] In the case \abs{x} \ge \abs{y}, the left side is \abs{x} - \abs{y}. Start from x = (x - y) + y. We use two school facts: for real numbers a, b, either a \ge b or a < b; and \abs{-a} = \abs{a} for every real a (if a \ge 0 then -a \le 0, so \abs{-a} = -(-a) = a = \abs{a}, using, as in @exm-abs-product-cases, that \abs{b} = -b whenever b \le 0; if a < 0 then -a > 0, so \abs{-a} = -a = \abs{a}). By the first fact, \abs{x} \ge \abs{y} or \abs{x} < \abs{y}, and we argue by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]. Case \abs{x} \ge \abs{y}. Then \abs{x} - \abs{y} \ge 0, so \bigl\lvert \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr\rvert = \abs{x} - \abs{y}. By @exm-triangle-inequality-cases applied to the numbers x - y and y, \abs{x} = \abs{(x - y) + y} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y} , so \abs{x} - \abs{y} \le \abs{x - y}, which is the goal in this case. Case \abs{x} < \abs{y}. Then \abs{x} - \abs{y} < 0, so \bigl\lvert \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr\rvert = \abs{y} - \abs{x}. By @exm-triangle-inequality-cases applied to y - x and x, \abs{y} = \abs{(y - x) + x} \le \abs{y - x} + \abs{x} , so \abs{y} - \abs{x} \le \abs{y - x} = \abs{-(x - y)} = \abs{x - y}.
