Then \abs{y} = -y, and x - y > 0, so \abs{x - y} = x - y = \abs{x} + \abs{y}. Case 2: x < 0. Then \abs{x} = -x. Case 2a: y \ge 0. Then \abs{y} = y, and x - y < 0, so \abs{x - y} = y - x = \abs{y} + \abs{x}. Case 2b: y < 0. Then \abs{y} = -y. Since x \ge 0 and y < 0, we have x - y > 0, so \abs{x - y} = x - y \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, because x \le \abs{x} and -y = \abs{y}. All four cases give \abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. 1. Is the statement true? 2. Find the line that is not justified, and name the rule whose conditions it breaks. 3. Show with specific numbers that the step fails. 4. Repair Case 2b. (a) Yes. For instance, it follows from @exm-triangle-inequality-cases applied to x and -y, since \abs{-y} = \abs{y} (shown in the solution of @exr-disjunction-and-cases-c1). So the question is not whether the conclusion holds but whether this argument proves it. (b) The sentence “Since x \ge 0 and y < 0, we have x - y > 0” in Case 2b. The assumption x \ge 0 is the assumption of Case 1. In derivation terms, it opens the first box of the outer \rulename{\vee E}, and Case 2b lies inside the second box, which is opened by x < 0. Once the first box has closed, its lines are not available (the scope rule of @def-derivation), so Case 2b may not cite x \ge 0: the rule broken is \rulename{\vee E}, each of whose boxes may cite only lines available at it by the scope rule: its own assumption, what has been derived inside it, and what was available before the box opened; so nothing from the first box, which has closed. The sentence is the reasoning of Case 1b copied into Case 2b, where its assumption is no longer in force. So the box of Case 2 does not reach the goal from the lines available to it, and the final \rulename{\vee E} has no right to cite it. (c) Take x = -3 and y = -1, which is Case 2b. Then x - y = -2, which is not > 0, and \abs{x - y} = 2 \ne -2 = x - y. The conclusion of Case 2b still holds here (2 \le 3 + 1), but the step used to reach it is false. (d) In Case 2b, x < 0 and y < 0, so \abs{x} = -x and \abs{y} = -y. The number \abs{x - y} is x - y or y - x. Since x < 0, we have x - y < -y = \abs{y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. Since y < 0, we have y - x < -x = \abs{x} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. So in either case \abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, using only the assumptions of Case 2b. [C3: Exit check: a distributive law, rule by rule] Derive (P \wedge Q) \vee (R \wedge Q) \vdash (P \vee R) \wedge Q, naming the rule and the cited lines on every line. Then say which steps would change if the premise were (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) and the goal P \wedge (Q \vee R), and which would stay the same. The chart would build the conjunction by \rulename{\wedge I}, with subgoals P \vee R and Q, and reach each one by splitting the premise; that route works (it is the second route below). Here one split is enough: the premise is a disjunction, so we split on it first and build the whole goal in each case; both cases end in the current goal (P \vee R) \wedge Q. In each case, \rulename{\wedge E} takes the assumption apart, \rulename{\vee I} builds P \vee R from the side in hand, and \rulename{\wedge I} builds the goal. Line by line: 1 is the premise; 2 is the assumption of the first case; 3 and 4 are \rulename{\wedge E} on line 2; 5 is \rulename{\vee I} on line 3, first schema; 6 is \rulename{\wedge I} on lines 5 and 4, written with P \vee R as the left conjunct; 7 is the assumption of the second case; 8 and 9 are \rulename{\wedge E} on line 7; 10 is \rulename{\vee I} on line 8, second schema; 11 is \rulename{\wedge I} on lines 10 and 9; 12 is \rulename{\vee E}, citing the disjunction on line 1 and the boxes \lines{2}{6} and \lines{7}{11}, both of which end in the goal as lines of their own. No line of the second box cites the first. With premise (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) and goal P \wedge (Q \vee R), the shape stays the same: a split on the premise, \rulename{\wedge E} twice in each box, one \rulename{\vee I} and one \rulename{\wedge I} in each box, and \rulename{\vee E} at the end. What changes is which part is weakened and where it goes. The common conjunct is now P, and the parts that differ between the cases are Q and R; so the \rulename{\vee I} lines build Q \vee R (from Q in the first box, first schema; from R in the second, second schema), and the \rulename{\wedge I} lines write P as the left conjunct, as in the goal. That derivation is the second one of @prp-distributivity. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: splits on the premise by \rulename{\vee E}, with two boxes opened by its two sides. - 2: in each box, takes the assumption apart by \rulename{\wedge E} into both conjuncts. - 2: in each box, uses \rulename{\vee I} to build P \vee R from the side in hand, with the correct schema. - 2: in each box, builds the goal by \rulename{\wedge I}, so that both boxes end in the same line, the goal. - 2: the \rulename{\vee E} line cites the disjunction and both boxes as ranges, and the final sentences name the changed steps (the \rulename{\vee I} lines, now building Q \vee R, and the \rulename{\wedge I} lines, now with P on the left). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a line in one box citing a line of the other box; a conclusion drawn inside one box only and then used outside it. A second route is also correct: split the premise twice, once ending both boxes in P \vee R and once ending both in Q, and then join the two results by \rulename{\wedge I} outside every box (14 lines). Its points map as follows: 2 for either split with two boxes opened by the premise’s sides; 2 for the \rulename{\wedge E} lines in the boxes; 2 for the \rulename{\vee I} sides; 2 for the final \rulename{\wedge I}, with the boxes of each split ending in the same line; 2 for the citations and the final sentences. [C4: The second half] A search for Q \vee R, \ Q \to (P \to S), \ R \to S \vdash P \to S has written the premises and opened one box; the rest is blank. The finished derivation has 11 lines. Name the move, then complete it. [Hint 1] Inside the box, what is the current goal, and which available line is a disjunction? [Hint 2] Line 5 is Q, the assumption of a first case box opened inside the box of P; like the second case box, it must end in the current goal S. The moves are two. First, the box of line 4 was read off the goal: P \to S is an implication, so the box opened with P, and its current goal is S; it will be closed by \rulename{{\to}I}. Second, inside it, the available disjunction Q \vee R (line 1, in no box, so available inside the box) is split, and both case boxes end in the current goal S. In the case Q, line 2 fires to give P \to S, which fires on line 4; in the case R, line 3 fires. Line 7 cites line 4, the assumption of the outer box, which contains line 7. Line 10 is a line of the box \lines{4}{10} itself (the case boxes have closed), so \rulename{{\to}I} may cite that box at line 11. Splitting outside the box instead, with both case boxes ending in P \to S, is also a correct derivation of the sequent; it does not complete the lines given, because it would split before line 4, not after. R. Review [R1] Let f be a function and [a, b] an interval. Take the atomic statements C: “f is continuous on [a, b]”, B: “f is bounded on [a, b]” and I: “f is integrable on [a, b]”; you need not know what the words mean. Translate the argument “If f is continuous on [a, b] and bounded there, then f is integrable on [a, b]. f is bounded on [a, b]. f is continuous on [a, b]. So f is integrable on [a, b] and bounded there.” into a sequent, and derive it. The sequent is (C \wedge B) \to I, \ B, \ C \vdash I \wedge B: three premises and a conclusion, as in @def-sequent. The goal is a conjunction, so it splits into the subgoals I and B. B is a premise. The only line that mentions I is the first premise, whose hypothesis C \wedge B is built by \rulename{\wedge I} (@def-rules-conjunction) from two premises; then \rulename{{\to}E} (@def-rule-implication-elimination) gives I. Line 4 writes C \wedge B, with C on the left as in the hypothesis of line 1 (\rulename{\wedge I} may cite 3, 2 or 2, 3); the hypothesis must match exactly. Line 2 is cited twice, at lines 4 and 6: a line is not used up by being cited. [R2] Show that (P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to R), \ P \wedge S \vdash R \wedge S, and say in one sentence which step you found by working backwards from the goal. Premise-directed, both premises are conjunctions and are taken apart by \rulename{\wedge E} (@def-rules-conjunction); goal-directed, the goal R \wedge S splits into R and S, and S is already in hand. For R, work backwards as in @exm-implication-chains: Q \to R is available, so Q becomes the subgoal; P \to Q is available, so P does; and P is in hand. The chain of lines 7 and 8 was found backwards, from the subgoal R to Q to P, and written forwards. [R3] Is \vdash (P \wedge (P \to Q)) \to (Q \vee R)? Justify your answer. Yes. The goal’s main connective is the outer \to, so the move is to open a box with its hypothesis P \wedge (P \to Q) (@def-rules-implication). Inside, the current goal is Q \vee R, which we postpone. The assumption is a conjunction, so \rulename{\wedge E} gives P and P \to Q; \rulename{{\to}E} gives Q; now the left side of the goal is in hand, and \rulename{\vee I} (@def-rule-disjunction-introduction) takes it. The derivation has no premises, so it shows \vdash (P \wedge (P \to Q)) \to (Q \vee R). The look-alike start fails: the statement contains \vee, and one might begin with \rulename{\vee I} on the whole goal. But the goal’s main connective is \to, not \vee, so \rulename{\vee I} cannot produce it; and even inside the box, choosing the side R of Q \vee R would have left the subgoal R, which nothing supplies; the side Q is the one lines 2–4 supply.

title: Negation and Classical Logic
content:
Negation and Classical Logic Is there a rational number whose square is 2? Is x^2 + 1 ever 0 for a real number x? Is “if x^2 < 0, then x = 7” true? Chapter 1 could prove that things are so, but not that something is not so, and it read the third sentence only informally, as a promise not broken: no rule yet derives it. By the end of this chapter you will be able to prove that something is not so; you will know when “suppose not” is a different kind of step from the others, and why that one step is all that classical logic adds. Two questions stay open at the end. How do you find a derivation when none comes to mind? Chapter 3 answers it. And how could you ever show that something is not derivable? Chapter 4 answers that. Steps about “every” and “some”. Proofs in this chapter apply facts about every integer to one integer, pass from an arbitrary rational number to all of them, and name the k in “n = 2k + 1”. These are steps about “every” and “some”. Here they are used as ordinary reasoning, as in school algebra; Chapter 5 gives them rules. What you need. All of Chapter 1: the rules for “and”, “implies”, and “or”, and above all the definition of a derivation, with its boxes and its scope rule (@def-derivation). School algebra about integers and real numbers is used in examples, as facts. Time. About 30 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 50 hours for everything. Minimum before Sets and Functions. Chapters 1–6 and 8, core; Sections 7.1–7.2 before its Section 4.1. Roadmap - Contradiction: Using a Negation. The rules ulename{
eg E} and ulename{ ot E}: what a clash is, what it buys, why an impossible case closes itself and an implication with an impossible hypothesis is true, and the two sequents called the paradoxes of material implication. - Proving a Negation. The rule ulename{
eg I}, and with it the irrationality of \sqrt 2, then of \sqrt p for a prime p. - Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules. A proved sequent used as one line; modus tollens, the contrapositive and disjunctive syllogism; and why pasting a proved sequent into a derivation is safe (weakening and cut). - Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says. The rules for \leftrightarrow, provable equivalence, why a definition’s “if” means “if and only if”, chains of equivalences, and why no statement is equivalent to its own negation. - Proof by Contradiction and the Classical Rules. The rule ulename{RAA}, the classical laws it gives (double-negation elimination, excluded middle, De Morgan, Peirce), where the classical step is needed, and why three of its forms stand or fall together. Named moves - Goal  ot: find a clash. Look for \varphi and 
eg\varphi among the available lines, or make \varphi a subgoal for some 
eg\varphi you have. (Section 2.1) - An impossible case closes itself. In a proof by cases, a case that reaches  ot ends by ulename{ ot E} on the current goal. (Section 2.1) - To prove “not \varphi”, assume \varphi. The box opens with the unnegated statement and ends on  ot. (Section 2.2) - Use a derived rule as one line. A proved sequent is a new rule. (Section 2.3) - Two boxes for an iff. One box for each direction, each ending on the other side. (Section 2.4) - When stuck, assume the negation of the goal. Proof by contradiction, and then hunt for a clash. (Section 2.5) - A disjunction with neither side within reach: expect the classical step. When each side of a disjunctive goal breaks on its own, aim at the disjunction by ulename{RAA}. (Section 2.5) Section 3.1 gathers these moves and Chapter 1’s into one table, and all thirteen rules onto one card. Summary The chapter added the rules for 
eg,  ot and \leftrightarrow and the rule ulename{RAA}, which with Chapter 1’s seven make the thirteen primitive rules. It proved that a clash gives anything (@prp-ex-falso) and that an impossible hypothesis makes an implication true (@prp-vacuous-implication); it proved the theorem Argument B set out to prove (@thm-square-even-implies-even) and that \sqrt 2 is irrational (@thm-sqrt2-irrational). It turned proved sequents into rules, with weakening and cut as the reason pasting is safe (@lem-weakening-cut). It showed that an iff is two implications, that a definition’s “if” is an iff, and that no statement is equivalent to its own negation (@lem-not-iff-own-negation). With ulename{RAA} it derived double negation, excluded middle, De Morgan’s laws and Peirce’s law, and showed ulename{RAA}, ulename{
eg
eg E} and ulename{LEM} to be one principle (@thm-classical-rules-interderivable). Still open: a method for finding derivations (Chapter 3), and a way to show that a sequent has no derivation (Chapter 4), which also settles whether the classical rule could be done without. Terms - biconditional rules ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}: prove by two boxes; use either direction (@def-rules-biconditional). - classical rules ulename{RAA}, ulename{
eg
eg E}, ulename{LEM}: interderivable; one principle (@thm-classical-rules-interderivable). - contradiction  ot: the line a clash produces (@def-rules-contradiction). - contradiction rules ulename{
eg E}, ulename{ ot E}: a clash gives  ot;  ot gives anything (@def-rules-contradiction). - contrapositive: 
eg\psi 	o 
eg\varphi, derivable from \varphi 	o \psi (@prp-contrapositive). - cut: a proved lemma may be pasted in (@lem-weakening-cut). - De Morgan’s laws: how negation passes through “and” and “or” (@prp-de-morgan). - derived rule: a proved sequent used as one line (@def-derived-rule). - disjunctive syllogism ulename{DS}: from \varphi \vee \psi and 
eg\varphi, conclude \psi (@prp-disjunctive-syllogism). - double negation: 
eg
eg\varphi and \varphi, each from the other (@prp-double-negation). - ex falso: from a clash, anything follows (@prp-ex-falso). - excluded middle ulename{LEM}: \varphi \vee 
eg\varphi, with no premises (@prp-excluded-middle). - modus tollens ulename{MT}: from \varphi 	o \psi and 
eg\psi, conclude 
eg\varphi (@prp-modus-tollens). - negation rule ulename{
eg I}: assume \varphi, reach  ot, conclude 
eg\varphi (@def-rules-negation). - Peirce’s law: ((\varphi 	o \psi) 	o \varphi) 	o \varphi (@prp-peirce). - provably equivalent, \dashv\vdash: each derivable from the other (@def-provable-equivalence). - reductio ad absurdum ulename{RAA}: assume 
eg\varphi, reach  ot, conclude \varphi (@def-rule-raa). - vacuously true: an implication whose hypothesis cannot hold (@prp-vacuous-implication). - weakening: extra premises never spoil a derivation (@lem-weakening-cut).

title: 2.1 Contradiction: Using a Negation
content:
Contradiction: Using a Negation Chapter 1 gave rules for “and”, “implies”, and “or”, and not one of them mentions “not”. Yet written proofs are full of sentences such as “this is impossible”, “this case cannot occur”, and “which contradicts what we assumed”. This section gives the two rules that use a negation: the first says exactly what a clash between two lines is, and the second says what a clash buys. The rule that proves a negation is the subject of the next section. A case that cannot occur Here is Argument A of Section 1.1, told as a proof by cases. Let n be an integer whose square is even. Every integer is even or odd, so there are two cases. If n is even, we are done. If n is odd, then n^2 is odd; but n^2 is even, and no integer is both, so this case cannot occur. Hence n is even. Chapter 1 has a rule for a proof by cases: ulename{\vee E} of @def-rules-disjunction. It asks for a disjunction and two boxes, one opened by each disjunct, and both boxes must end on the same line, the goal. In the argument above the goal is “n is even”. The first box reaches it at once. The second box does not reach it at all. It reaches “impossible”, and then simply declares itself finished. Two things are missing, and no rule of Chapter 1 supplies them. - A way to record the impossibility: the lines “n^2 is even” and “n^2 is odd”, together with “no integer is both”, should produce a line that says “contradiction”. - A way to close the impossible box with the goal: from the line “contradiction”, the box should be allowed to write “n is even”, so that both boxes end on the same line and ulename{\vee E} applies. Section 1.1 introduced the symbols for both. The connective 
eg forms the negation 
eg\varphi, read “not \varphi”. The constant  ot, read “contradiction”, is a statement that is false however things stand. There they were symbols only. The two rules below give them their first uses. The rules for a clash The rule for recording a clash has a simple content. The statement 
eg\varphi says that \varphi fails, so a derivation that has both \varphi and 
eg\varphi available is working in a situation that cannot occur. The rule writes this down as the line  ot. A second rule then says what such a line is good for. A statement and its negation clash; from a clash, anything follows. [Rules for Contradiction] The left schema is ulename{
eg E} (not-elimination): if \varphi and 
eg\varphi stand on lines i and j available at line k, write  ot, citing both, the unnegated line first. The right schema is ulename{ ot E} (contradiction-elimination, or ex falso): if  ot stands on a line i available at line k, write any statement \varphi, citing line i. Why may ulename{ ot E} write anything? A line  ot can stand only where the premises and open assumptions cannot all hold together: a derivation that reaches  ot describes a situation that never happens. Nothing said there can ever be caught false, just as a promise whose condition is never met is never broken; the subsection “Vacuous truth” below returns to this. As in every schema (@def-rule-schema), \varphi is one statement, the same wherever it occurs, and i, j, k are line numbers. We read ulename{
eg E} in four bullets. - Two given lines, both available (the scope rule of @def-derivation), in either order on the page. - Exactly \varphi and 
eg\varphi: the second is the first with one 
eg in front of the whole of it, symbol for symbol. “Contradicts it in spirit” is not enough: x < 1 and x > 1 cannot both hold, but neither is the other’s negation as written (the box below). - The citation lists the unnegated line first: “ulename{
eg E} i, j” says that line i is \varphi. - The new line is  ot and nothing else; what to do with the clash is the business of ulename{ ot E}. And ulename{ ot E} in three. - Schema. The right one in the block above. - Reading. One available line  ot, cited alone; write any statement, related to nothing above, a negation or  ot itself included. - Example. From line 4  ot, “ulename{ ot E} 4” writes R, or 
eg R, or x = 7. Two more observations complete the reading. First, ulename{ ot E} is the elimination rule of  ot: it says how a line  ot is used. There is no introduction rule of its own for  ot. Other rules can pass a  ot along (ulename{ ot E} may write it again, and ulename{{	o}E} writes it from \varphi 	o  ot and \varphi), but each of them (ulename{R}, ulename{\wedge E}, ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{\vee E}, whenever their new line is  ot) needs  ot already written, perhaps inside a longer statement, in a line it uses (ulename{\vee I} can bring  ot in, but only inside a disjunction). Unless  ot already occurs in a premise or an assumption, the first line of a derivation that is  ot itself is written by ulename{
eg E}: it is the one rule whose new line is always  ot, from lines in which  ot need not occur. So ulename{
eg E} plays two parts at once: it is the way a negation is used, and it is the way  ot is produced. Second, why is ulename{ ot E} honest? A rule should never lead from lines that hold to a line that fails. A line  ot can stand only in a part of a derivation where the premises and the open assumptions cannot all hold together, at least when the  ot was written by ulename{
eg E}, from some \varphi and 
eg\varphi that were both available there; that the rules which only pass a  ot along keep this property is part of what Section 1.2’s Looking-ahead box promised for every rule. In such a place there is no situation in which the conclusion of ulename{ ot E} would have to be checked, so it cannot be caught failing. In the Givens/Goal table, ulename{
eg E} adds  ot to the Givens once \varphi and 
eg\varphi are both there; and with  ot among the Givens, ulename{ ot E} ticks off any goal. Which of these pairs of lines are, as written, an instance of the given lines of ulename{
eg E}, and in which order must each be cited? The pairs are (i) Q \wedge R and 
eg(Q \wedge R); (ii) 
eg P and 
eg
eg P; (iii) P 	o Q and 
eg P 	o Q. (i) Yes, with \varphi = Q \wedge R; cite the line Q \wedge R first. (ii) Yes, with \varphi = 
eg P: the second line is 
eg(
eg P). Cite 
eg P first, then 
eg
eg P. (iii) No. The main connective of 
eg P 	o Q is 	o (@def-main-connective), so it is not a negation at all; the 
eg applies to P alone. The negation of P 	o Q would be 
eg(P 	o Q). Convention: negations of order and equality. For real numbers a and b, exactly one of a < b and a \ge b holds. So a \ge b says the same as 
eg(a < b), and likewise a > b the same as 
eg(a \le b), a \le b as 
eg(a > b), and a < b as 
eg(a \ge b); and a 
e b means 
eg(a = b), by definition. A derivation writes the negation out whenever a rule for “not” must see it (ulename{
eg E} here, and the rule of the next section); otherwise, and in prose, the short forms stay. Together with the box of Section 1.5, which writes a \le b out as (a < b) \vee (a = b) when ulename{\vee I} or ulename{\vee E} must see the disjunction, this fixes how an inequality looks on a line. The fact “no integer is both even and odd” is a negation of a conjunction, 
eg(E \wedge O) with E for “n is even” and O for “n is odd”. It clashes only with a line E \wedge O, which ulename{\wedge I} builds from separate lines E and O. For a real number x, which pairs are a clash as written, once the convention is used? (i) x^2 < 0 and x^2 \ge 0; (ii) x = 2 and x 
e 2; (iii) x < 1 and x > 1. (i) Yes: x^2 \ge 0 is 
eg(x^2 < 0); cite x^2 < 0 first. (ii) Yes: x 
e 2 is 
eg(x = 2); cite x = 2 first. (iii) No: x > 1 is 
eg(x \le 1), and x < 1 is not x \le 1. The line x \le 1, written out, must first be built by ulename{\vee I} (drill A2(l)). A clash must have the exact shape \varphi, 
eg\varphi. And some pairs that look opposed do not clash at all: x \ge 1 and x \le 1 both hold at x = 1. ulename{ ot E} does not run backwards. From  ot we may write \varphi, or 
eg\varphi, or anything; but from a line \varphi alone no rule writes  ot, unless  ot already occurs in it. If it could, the true line x = 1 would give  ot, and then ulename{ ot E} would give the false line x = 2. First derivations with a clash The five examples below grow in difficulty. Each Idea says why each rule was chosen, in the two directions Chapter 1 used: from the goal (what does the goal’s main connective ask for?) and from the premises (what does an available line’s main connective let us do?). This section adds one question to each list. From the goal: when nothing produces the goal, can a clash produce it? From the premises: an available negation 
eg\varphi is used in exactly one way, by ulename{
eg E}, so it asks for \varphi. [The first clashes] Show that (a)  ot \vdash P, and (b) P \wedge Q, \ 
eg Q \vdash R. (a) is the rule ulename{ ot E} itself, the degenerate case with no clash to find. In (b), the first premise is a conjunction, so the premise-directed move takes it apart by ulename{\wedge E}. Its half Q and the premise 
eg Q are exactly a pair \varphi, 
eg\varphi. The goal R has nothing to do with the premises: no rule builds it from them. Only ulename{ ot E} can write it, and ulename{ ot E} needs a line  ot, which the clash supplies. Snapshots for (b): the goal alone; then the goal handed to ulename{ ot E}, with  ot as the new goal. (a) Two lines: the premise, and one application of ulename{ ot E}. (b) Five lines. Line 4 cites line 3 first because line 3 plays \varphi and line 2 plays 
eg\varphi, with \varphi = Q. The half P of the first premise is never used; a derivation need not use every premise (@def-derivable). The next result is the pattern of (b) with nothing extra around it. We state it as a proposition, because later sections cite it. [Contradictory Premises Prove Anything] P, \ 
eg P \vdash Q. The premises are a clash as they stand, so ulename{
eg E} writes  ot at once, and ulename{ ot E} writes the goal, which nothing else could produce. The derivation has premises P and 
eg P and last line Q. This proves the proposition. In the next derivation the clash happens inside a box, and the rule ulename{ ot E} writes the box’s goal. [Vacuous Implication] 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q. The goal is an implication, so the goal-directed move of Chapter 1 (ulename{{	o}I}, @def-rules-implication) opens a box with its hypothesis P; the new goal is Q. Nothing available mentions Q, so no rule can build it. But inside the box, the assumption P and the premise 
eg P clash, and ulename{ ot E} writes the box’s goal Q. This is the section’s goal-directed move: when nothing produces the goal, look for a clash. Snapshots: the box with its goal Q; then the clash named as the subgoal. The derivation has premise 
eg P and last line P 	o Q. Line 3 may cite line 1, which lies in no box. This proves the proposition. How the rules look in a mathematical proof We can now prove the fact of Argument A in Section 1.1, with every rule named. Three school facts about integers enter as premises. An integer n is even if n = 2k for some integer k, and odd if n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. And: 1. every integer is even or odd; 2. no integer is both even and odd; 3. the square of an odd integer is odd. The third is a computation. If n = 2k + 1 for an integer k, then n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1 , and 2k^2 + 2k is an integer, so n^2 is odd. [Even Square, Even Number] Let n be an integer. If n^2 is even, then n is even. The hypothesis “n^2 is even” hands us nothing to compute with: it says n^2 = 2j for some integer j, and no algebra turns that into a statement about n. The word “odd” does hand us something, since n = 2k + 1 can be squared. So we split on (E1) and show that the odd case is impossible: there (E3) makes n^2 odd, which clashes with the hypothesis through (E2). The impossible case then closes itself. Suppose n^2 is even [	ext{assumption for } ulename{{	o}I}]. By (E1), n is even or n is odd, and we argue by cases [ulename{\vee E}]. Case n even. This is the goal. Case n odd. By (E3), n^2 is odd [ulename{{	o}E}]. So n^2 is both even and odd [ulename{\wedge I}]; this contradicts (E2) [ulename{
eg E}]. So this case cannot occur, and in it n is even [ulename{ ot E}]. In both cases n is even [ulename{\vee E}]. This proves that if n^2 is even, then n is even [ulename{{	o}I}]. The logic of the proof fits in a derivation. Write E for “n is even”, O for “n is odd”, S for “n^2 is even”, and T for “n^2 is odd”. Then (E1) for n is E \vee O, (E2) for n^2 is 
eg(S \wedge T), and (E3) for n is O 	o T; these are the premises. Each line is one sentence of the proof. Vacuous truth We can now settle the question that makes many readers distrust logic. Is the sentence if x^2 < 0, then x = 7 true, for a real number x? The hypothesis never holds, and the conclusion has nothing to do with it. Everyday intuition is unsure what to say. The rules are not unsure. [An implication with an impossible hypothesis] Let x be a real number. Show that if x^2 < 0, then x = 7. The goal is an implication, so open a box with x^2 < 0, aiming at x = 7. Nothing produces x = 7, so look for a clash: the school fact x^2 \ge 0 is 
eg(x^2 < 0), which clashes with the assumption. This is exactly the derivation of @prp-vacuous-implication, with P read as “x^2 < 0” and Q as “x = 7”. With the school fact as the premise: In prose: suppose x^2 < 0; this contradicts x^2 \ge 0; so this case cannot occur, and in it x = 7; hence if x^2 < 0, then x = 7. We wrote out all five lines rather than citing @prp-vacuous-implication as a single step. Using an already proved sequent as one line of a new derivation is a genuine new permission, and Section 2.3 grants it; until then, a derivation repeats the steps. An implication whose hypothesis cannot hold is called vacuously true. Nothing about it was decided by convention. It is forced by two rules that each look harmless: ulename{{	o}I}, which proves an implication by assuming its hypothesis, and ulename{ ot E}, which closes an impossible case. Everyday language agrees. A friend says: “if you finish the exercises by Friday, I will buy you lunch”. You do not finish them. Whatever your friend does on Friday, the promise has not been broken. A promise never tested is never broken. Vacuous truth is not a curiosity; it is what makes case splits work. In @exm-impossible-case, line 7 closed the impossible case by ulename{ ot E}, and line 10 of the derivation of @thm-square-even-implies-even did the same. “True” is not “useful”. The statements “if x^2 < 0, then x = 7” and “if x^2 < 0, then x 
e 7” are both true, and neither says anything about x or about 7. Likewise “if n is an even prime greater than 2, then n = 17” is true and empty. When a hypothesis turns out to be impossible, suspect the hypothesis; do not believe the conclusion. Two sequents that sound wrong Two sequents in hand sound wrong when read aloud with unrelated statements. The first is Q \vdash P 	o Q: a box opened with P, whose only other line repeats Q (line 1 lies in no box), closed by ulename{{	o}I}, as in Exercise B2 of Section 1.4. The second is 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q, @prp-vacuous-implication. Read aloud: “7 is odd; so, if every square is negative, then 7 is odd”, and “7 is not even; so, if 7 is even, then every square is negative”. They are called the paradoxes of material implication. Each comes from a rule, so whoever rejects one must say which rule goes: the first rests on ulename{{	o}I} closing a box whose assumption no line uses (with ulename{R} copying a line in from outside), the second on ulename{ ot E}. Some logics, built for purposes other than mathematics, do drop ulename{ ot E}; this book keeps it, and Exercise B3 of Section 2.5 shows that the classical rule would bring it back anyway. The same rule gives @prp-ex-falso: from a clash, anything. Mathematics does not suffer: its “if” almost always sits under “every”, joining two statements about one variable, as in “for every integer n, if n is a multiple of 4, then n is even”. Instances with a false hypothesis (“if 3 is a multiple of 4, then 3 is even”) are true and empty, as the paradoxes say; the content lies where the hypothesis holds, and there the promise is exact. Nobody wants to prove a sentence whose two parts share nothing. Let x be a real number. Which of the two sequents makes “if x^2 < 0, then x > 5” true, and which makes “if x < -3, then x^2 + 1 > 0” true? The first by 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q, since x^2 < 0 fails (x^2 \ge 0 is 
eg(x^2 < 0), the convention box); the second by Q \vdash P 	o Q, since x^2 + 1 > 0 holds whatever x is. “If 7 were even, 7 would be divisible by 2” sounds true, and “if 7 were even, 7 would be divisible by 3” sounds false, though the two share the false hypothesis “7 is even”. By 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q, both material implications are true. So the subjunctive “if” of everyday talk is not the connective 	o: whether it holds depends on more than the truth of its two parts. Mathematics rarely uses it. When a proof says “if n were odd, then n^2 would be odd”, it is working inside a box whose assumption is “n is odd”, and its “if” is the material one. Suppose instead ulename{{	o}I} were allowed only when the box’s assumption is cited by some line of the box or is itself the box’s last line. Which of the two derivations of (a) is lost? Is the one-line box of \vdash P 	o P lost? Is the sequent Q \vdash P 	o Q lost? 4. Let n be an integer. For n = 3, n = 6 and n = 8, write the instance of “if n is a multiple of 4, then n is even”, and say for each whether the first sequent of (a), the second, or neither, decides its truth. (a) 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q: ulename{{	o}I}, ulename{
eg E}, ulename{ ot E} (@prp-vacuous-implication). Q \vdash P 	o Q: ulename{{	o}I} and repetition. (b) Four lines: It stops at  ot inside the box, where the derivation of @prp-vacuous-implication wrote Q: the step from  ot to Q was ulename{ ot E}’s. What survives says only that P leads to a contradiction. (c) The derivation of Q \vdash P 	o Q is lost: no line of its box cites the assumption P (line 3 repeats line 1). The box of \vdash P 	o P is kept: its last line is its assumption, which the restriction allows. The derivation of @prp-vacuous-implication is kept: line 3 cites the assumption. But the sequent Q \vdash P 	o Q is not lost. This derivation meets the restriction, since line 3 cites the assumption: The restriction kills one derivation, not the sequent; a logic that really rejects the paradox has to restrict more than one rule. (d) n = 3: “if 3 is a multiple of 4, then 3 is even”; hypothesis and conclusion are both false, so only 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q decides it. n = 6: “if 6 is a multiple of 4, then 6 is even”; the hypothesis is false and the conclusion true, so either sequent decides it. n = 8: “if 8 is a multiple of 4, then 8 is even”; both parts are true (8 = 4 \cdot 2), so the first sequent does not apply and the second does, since the conclusion is true. This is the one instance of the three whose hypothesis holds, the kind in which the theorem says something: here it can be fired by ulename{{	o}E}. Marking scheme. (10 points) 2: (a), both rule lists. 2: (b), a correct four-line derivation (1) and the remark that the step to Q is ulename{ ot E}’s (1). 3: (c), the right derivation lost and the reason, that the assumption is never cited (1); \vdash P 	o P kept (1); and a derivation of Q \vdash P 	o Q that meets the restriction (1). 3: (d), one point per value: the truth values of hypothesis and conclusion, and the right sequent (n = 3: the first only; n = 6: either; n = 8: the second). Fatal error (0 for (b)): a derivation of P 	o Q itself without ulename{ ot E} that cites a line inside a closed box. C. Going deeper [C1: A disjunct that cannot hold] 1. Show that P \vee (Q \wedge 
eg Q) \vdash P. 2. What does (a) say about the statement “x > 0, or x = 1 and x 
e 1”, for a real number x? (a) The premise is a disjunction, so split it by ulename{\vee E}, with both boxes ending in the goal P. The box of P is a one-line box. The box of Q \wedge 
eg Q is impossible: ulename{\wedge E} gives a clash, and ulename{ ot E} closes the case. (b) With P: “x > 0” and Q: “x = 1”, the statement is P \vee (Q \wedge 
eg Q), since x 
e 1 is 
eg(x = 1). By (a), it gives x > 0. So the second disjunct adds nothing: a disjunct that can never hold is an impossible case, and it closes itself. (Conversely, x > 0 gives the whole statement by ulename{\vee I}, so the two say the same thing.) [C2: A clash that escaped its box] A student wants to show 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q and writes: 1. Is the sequent 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q derivable? 2. Find the first line that is not justified, and name the clause of @def-derivation it breaks. 3. Show that the move made at that line can lead from a true premise to a false conclusion. 4. Write a correct derivation. (a) Yes: it is @prp-vacuous-implication. The conclusion is true; the question is whether this argument proves it. (b) Line 4. It cites line 3, which lies inside the box \lines{2}{3}, and that box has closed before line 4. By the scope rule of @def-derivation, a line inside a closed box is not available. (Lines 1–3 are fine: a box may close without a rule discharging it, although nothing then leaves it. Lines 5–7 would be fine if line 4 were.) (c) Lines 1–4 alone would “derive” 
eg P \vdash Q by the same move. Read P as “x > 0” and Q as “x = 7”, and take x = -1. The premise 
eg(x > 0) is true, and the conclusion x = 7 is false. So the move “write, outside a box, what a closed box’s  ot would allow” can lead from a true premise to a false line. The line  ot on line 3 holds only under the assumption P; once the box closes, that assumption is gone, and so is the clash. (d) Move the ulename{ ot E} inside the box, where the clash is: Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: answers (a) yes, citing @prp-vacuous-implication or giving a derivation. - 3: names line 4 as the first failure and the scope rule (a line inside a closed box is not available) as the clause broken. - 3: gives a counterexample to the step, not only to some conclusion: a reading of P, Q under which lines 1–4 go from a true premise to a false line. - 2: a correct derivation, with every citation available. Fatal errors (0 for the step): blaming line 7 or line 6 (they are correct once line 4 is); saying that ulename{ ot E} itself is the error.

title: 2.2 Proving a Negation
2.3 Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules
content:
Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules Section 2.1 closed an impossible case by hand, and Section 2.2 proved negations by hand, one box at a time. By now the same few patterns keep coming back: the impossible case of @exm-impossible-case, and a box that turns a known implication round. Mathematicians give such patterns names (“by contraposition”, “since P fails, Q”) and use them in one breath. This section proves three of them once, from the rules we have, and then allows each to be used as a single line. The one new thing is that permission: a derived rule. A box that keeps coming back Here are two short arguments from different corners of mathematics. Let n be an integer whose square is not even. Suppose n is even. Then n^2 is even, which contradicts the hypothesis. Hence n is not even. Let x be a real number with x^2 < 1. Suppose x \ge 1. Then x^2 \ge x \ge 1, which contradicts x^2 < 1. Hence x < 1. The subjects differ; the steps are the same. Each has a known implication (“if n is even, then n^2 is even”; “if x \ge 1, then x^2 \ge 1”), and a fact saying that the implication’s conclusion fails. Each then opens a box on the implication’s hypothesis, fires the implication inside it by ulename{{	o}E}, meets the clash with ulename{
eg E}, and closes the box by ulename{
eg I} (@def-rules-negation). (For reals, x^2 < 1 and x < 1 are the exact negations of x^2 \ge 1 and x \ge 1.) The same four lines appear whenever an implication is used backwards, from the failure of its conclusion to the failure of its hypothesis. A mathematician does not write these four lines. She writes “since n^2 is not even, n is not even”, or “by contraposition”, and moves on: the lines are the same every time. But a derivation is checked line by line against the rules, and “by contraposition” is not one of the rules. What licenses the short form? First we derive the pattern once, as a sequent, with the rules we have. Then we say exactly when a sequent already derived may be used as a single line. Modus tollens, from the rules we have The pattern of the two arguments is: from an implication and the negation of its conclusion, infer the negation of its hypothesis. [Modus Tollens] P 	o Q, \; 
eg Q \vdash 
eg P. Read the skeleton off the goal. The goal 
eg P is a negation, and Section 2.2’s move for a negated goal is a box opened on what is negated, here P, with goal  ot. Inside the box, look for a clash (Section 2.1’s move for the goal  ot). The premise 
eg Q will clash with Q, so Q is the subgoal, and the premise P 	o Q gives it from the box’s own assumption. In the pictures, the box on P stands with its goal  ot; then ulename{
eg E} writes  ot from the subgoal Q, still unjustified. The following is a derivation with premises P 	o Q and 
eg Q, and last line 
eg P. Line 5 cites the premise on line 2, which lies in no box and so is available everywhere below it. The box \lines{3}{5} ends in  ot as a line of its own, so ulename{
eg I} closes it on line 6. This proves the proposition. The name is Latin for “the mode that takes away”: denying the conclusion takes away the hypothesis. Its partner, from P 	o Q and P to Q, is ulename{{	o}E}, traditionally modus ponens, “the mode that puts” (@def-rule-implication-elimination). The derivation uses ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{
eg E}, and ulename{
eg I}, and nothing else. A second form of the same fact packs the two premises into one implication. It is the form in which mathematicians state it: an implication implies its contrapositive. [Contrapositive] P 	o Q \vdash 
eg Q 	o 
eg P. The goal is an implication, so Chapter 1’s first goal-directed move applies: open a box with its hypothesis 
eg Q, and the new goal is 
eg P. That goal is a negation, so open a second box, on P, inside the first. Inside both boxes we are exactly where the proof of @prp-modus-tollens was: P and P 	o Q give Q, which clashes with 
eg Q. The following is a derivation with premise P 	o Q and last line 
eg Q 	o 
eg P. Line 5 may cite line 2, because the only box containing line 2, the box \lines{2}{6}, also contains line 5 (the scope rule of @def-derivation). The inner box closes on line 6, a line of the outer box itself, and line 7 closes the outer box. This proves the proposition. The statement 
eg Q 	o 
eg P is called the contrapositive of P 	o Q. Like modus tollens, its derivation uses only the rules so far: ulename{{	o}I}, ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{
eg I}, and ulename{
eg E}. The passage back, from 
eg Q 	o 
eg P to P 	o Q, is a different matter (Common errors, below). Now compare the two derivations. Lines 3–6 of the derivation of @prp-modus-tollens are, line for line and citation for citation, lines 3–6 of the derivation of @prp-contrapositive: P, then Q by ulename{{	o}E}\ 1, 3, then  ot by ulename{
eg E}\ 4, 2, then 
eg P by ulename{
eg I}\ \lines{3}{5}. And they are the four lines of the two arguments that opened this section. Writing them out every time buries the argument in bookkeeping. What a derived rule is A sequent that has been derived may be used as a rule. This is what a mathematician does when she writes “by Lemma 3”: the lemma was proved once, and each use of it is a single step. For derivations we must say exactly what that step may do. [Derived Rule] Let \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n \vdash  eta be a sequent, written with statement letters, that has already been derived earlier in the book. In a later derivation, replace each letter in \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n,  eta by a statement, the same statement for every occurrence of the same letter. If lines i_1, \dots, i_n, all available at line k, hold the resulting instances of \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n, we may write the resulting instance of  eta on line k. The justification names the result and cites i_1, \dots, i_n. A sequent used in this way is a derived rule. For example, @prp-modus-tollens becomes the rule ulename{MT}: In words: a proved sequent is a new rule. Its premises become the cited lines, its conclusion the line written, and its letters the metavariables of a schema (@def-rule-schema). Read the definition clause by clause. 1. “Already derived.” The sequent must have been derived before the line that uses it: earlier in the book, and never inside its own derivation. A derivation that used a sequent to derive that same sequent would prove nothing. 2. “Replace each letter … the same statement for every occurrence.” The letters of a derived sequent stood for arbitrary statements all along (@def-derivable), so they may be replaced by any statements, provided the replacement is uniform. From (A \wedge B) 	o C and 
eg C, the rule ulename{MT} gives 
eg(A \wedge B), with the letters P and Q of @prp-modus-tollens (written \varphi and \psi in the schema) replaced by A \wedge B and C. 3. “Available at line k.” The scope rule of @def-derivation still governs every citation. A derived rule may not reach into a closed box, just as a primitive rule may not. 4. “The resulting instance of  eta.” The rule writes the conclusion, with the same replacement, and nothing else. The derived rule does not open or close any box of the derivation that uses it. We give the derived rules of this section short tags: ulename{MT} for @prp-modus-tollens, ulename{CP} for @prp-contrapositive, and, once it is proved below, ulename{DS} for @prp-disjunctive-syllogism. Every other derived sequent is a derived rule too, cited by its name: the four lines 2–5 of @exm-vacuous-square, for instance, are now one line citing @prp-vacuous-implication. Left: with the derived rule. Right: written out. Line 3 on the left stands for lines 3–6 on the right: the same premises, the same last line. A derived rule is shorthand for lines we could always write out, so it lets us prove nothing that the primitive rules could not. In the figure, which lines does line 3 on the left cite, and which lines on the right use those same two premises? Lines 1 and 2. On the right, line 4 cites line 1 and line 5 cites line 2. Convenience, not power. A derived-rule line abbreviates a stretch of derivation that we could write out in full. To expand it, repeat each cited line by (D3) of @def-derivation, then copy the derivation of the sequent below the repetitions, with its letters replaced, its premises replaced by the repetitions, and its line numbers shifted. Every citation inside the copy points inside the copy or to a repetition, all in the current box, so every citation is available. The copy’s boxes close before its last line, which is the instance of  eta. If the copy itself uses derived rules, expand those lines in the same way; this stops, because each derivation cites only results proved before it. So whatever can be derived with derived rules can be derived with the primitive rules alone. The degenerate case is a sequent with nothing done to its premise, P \vdash P, whose derivation is the single premise line (part (a) of @exm-derivations): as a derived rule it copies an available line, which repetition already does. The first use with content is modus tollens proved a second time, with ulename{CP} as a rule. The premise P 	o Q invites ulename{CP}, and its conclusion 
eg Q 	o 
eg P is an implication whose hypothesis is the other premise. Line 3 is the instance of @prp-contrapositive with P and Q replaced by themselves; line 4 is modus ponens on it. Written out in full, line 3 would become a repetition of line 1 followed by lines 2–7 of the derivation of @prp-contrapositive. This is honest because @prp-contrapositive was derived from the primitive rules, not from @prp-modus-tollens: the chain of derived rules ends in primitive rules, without a loop. A derived rule must match its sequent exactly, under one uniform replacement of letters. From P 	o Q and 
eg R, ulename{MT} gives nothing: no single statement in place of \psi turns the pair into \varphi 	o \psi and 
eg\psi. Equally, from P 	o 
eg Q and Q, ulename{MT} gives nothing yet: it needs the negation of the conclusion, 
eg
eg Q, and Q is not that line. (Here ulename{
eg I} would give 
eg
eg Q first, as in @exm-double-negation-introduction, and then ulename{MT} applies.) Likewise ulename{DS}, as stated below, refutes the left disjunct; applied blindly to P \vee Q and 
eg Q, it does not match. In the Givens/Goal table, a derived rule adds its conclusion to the Givens in one row, as an elimination rule does. Pasting whole derivations: weakening and cut The figure expands one derived-rule line inside a derivation. Outside every box there is a cleaner statement, about whole derivations: two derivations can be joined end to end, and premises that are never used do no harm. [Weakening and Cut] Let \Gamma and \Delta be lists of statements, and let \varphi, \psi, \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m (m \ge 1), and  eta be statements. 1. Weakening. If \Gamma \vdash \psi and every member of \Gamma is a member of \Delta, then \Delta \vdash \psi. In particular, \Gamma \vdash \psi implies \Gamma, \varphi \vdash \psi. 2. Cut. If \Gamma \vdash \varphi and \Gamma, \varphi \vdash \psi, then \Gamma \vdash \psi. 3. Chaining. If \Gamma \vdash \alpha_i for every i = 1, \dots, m, and \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m \vdash  eta, then \Gamma \vdash  eta. In words: (a) extra premises never hurt; (b) a statement that has been derived may be used as a premise; (c) a sequent already proved can be applied to statements already derived. Part (c) is @def-derived-rule for whole derivations, outside every box; inside a box, the expansion of the fold “Why a derived rule adds no power” does the same job. Chaining and cut are the reason a derived-rule line outside every box is legitimate: the lines it cites lie in no box, so the derivation up to each of them derives it from \Gamma, and (c) then derives the instance of the sequent’s conclusion from \Gamma; by (b), the rest of the derivation may use that instance. Part (a) is read off @def-derivable, which asks only that the premises of the derivation belong to the list. For (b) and (c), write the derivations one after another and let the last one cite, instead of its premise \alpha_i, the last line of the derivation of \alpha_i. The only thing to check is the scope rule of @def-derivation: the last line of a derivation lies in no box, so it stays available to everything written after it. (a) A derivation witnessing \Gamma \vdash \psi has premises that belong to \Gamma, hence to \Delta, and its last line is \psi. By @def-derivable it witnesses \Delta \vdash \psi. The second sentence is the case where \Delta is \Gamma, \varphi. For (b) and (c) we prove one statement that contains both: (\ast) If \Gamma \vdash \alpha_i for every i = 1, \dots, m, and \Gamma, \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m \vdash  eta, then \Gamma \vdash  eta. Part (b) is (\ast) with m = 1, \alpha_1 = \varphi and  eta = \psi. Part (c) follows from (\ast), since \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m \vdash  eta gives \Gamma, \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m \vdash  eta by (a). To prove (\ast), let D_i be a derivation of \alpha_i with premises in \Gamma, for each i, and let E be a derivation of  eta with premises in \Gamma, \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m. If the last line of E is one of its premises, then  eta is a member of \Gamma, and the one-line derivation whose only line is the premise  eta shows \Gamma \vdash  eta; or  eta is some \alpha_i, and D_i shows \Gamma \vdash  eta. Otherwise, build a list of lines F as follows. 1. First, as premises, every premise of D_1, \dots, D_m, and every premise of E that is a member of \Gamma. 2. Then the lines of D_1 that are not premises, then those of D_2, and so on up to D_m, each with its boxes. 3. Then the lines of E that are not premises, with its boxes. Renumber the lines, and change each citation as follows. A citation of a premise that is in \Gamma now cites the premise line of step 1 carrying that statement. A citation in E of a premise \alpha_i that is not in \Gamma now cites the last line of D_i; that line is not a premise of D_i, because the premises of D_i are in \Gamma and \alpha_i is not, so it was copied in step 2. Every other citation follows its line to its new number. We check that F is a derivation (@def-derivation). The premises come first and lie in no box. The boxes are those of the D_i and of E, moved as blocks, so two boxes are still disjoint or nested, each still begins with its assumption, and each line lies in exactly the boxes it lay in before. Hence a line and a box that were available at a citing line are still available there, since the boxes containing each are unchanged. A premise line of step 1 lies in no box and comes first, so it is available at every later line. The last line of D_i lies in no box (it was the last line of a derivation) and comes before every line of E, so it is available at every line of E. Each line carries the same statement and the same justification as before, citing lines with the same statements, so it is an instance of the same rule. Finally, the last line of F is the last line of E, namely  eta, and it lies in no box. The premises of F are all in \Gamma. Therefore \Gamma \vdash  eta, which proves (\ast). Given @prp-modus-tollens, which part of @lem-weakening-cut gives P 	o Q, \ 
eg Q, \ R \vdash 
eg P at once? Given also @prp-vacuous-implication, which part gives P 	o Q, \ 
eg Q \vdash P 	o R? Part (a), weakening, with R as the extra premise. Part (c), chaining, with m = 1, \alpha_1 = 
eg P and  eta = P 	o R: @prp-modus-tollens gives P 	o Q, \ 
eg Q \vdash 
eg P, and @prp-vacuous-implication with R in place of Q gives 
eg P \vdash P 	o R. (Part (a) and then part (b) do the same.) Disjunctive syllogism: the impossible case, filed The second pattern is the impossible case of Section 2.1. Every integer is even or odd; this one is not even; so it is odd. A disjunction, one side refuted, the other side left. [Disjunctive Syllogism] P \vee Q, \; 
eg P \vdash Q. This is @exm-impossible-case with a simpler clash. There, the case P produced R by ulename{{	o}E}, which clashed with 
eg R. Here the case P clashes with the premise 
eg P at once. So: split the premise P \vee Q by ulename{\vee E}, both boxes ending in the current goal Q. The Q box is its own assumption. The P box cannot reach Q honestly, so it reaches a clash and closes by ulename{ ot E}: an impossible case closes itself. The following is a derivation with premises P \vee Q and 
eg P, and last line Q. The two boxes \lines{3}{5} and \lines{6}{6} are separate. The second consists of its assumption alone, which is already the statement Q that ulename{\vee E} needs. This proves the proposition. Set the derivation beside that of @exm-impossible-case. Both split P \vee Q into the same two boxes, and in both the Q box is one line long. Inside the P box, two lines reached  ot there (lines 5–6) and one line does here (line 4); then ulename{ ot E} closes the box in the same way. From now on this whole stretch is one line, tagged ulename{DS}. The rule as stated refutes the left disjunct. To refute the right one, first put the disjunction in the other order; that, too, is now one line, since @exm-disjunction-first-derivations derived P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P. (Exercise B1 derives the mirror image directly.) [Derived rules in use] 1. Show that P 	o Q, \; Q 	o R, \; 
eg R \vdash 
eg P, and then write the derivation out with primitive rules only. 2. Show that P \vee Q, \; 
eg P, \; Q 	o R \vdash R. Idea. A derived rule is a premise-directed shortcut: a line \varphi 	o \psi with a line 
eg\psi invites ulename{MT}; a disjunction with one side refuted invites ulename{DS}. This is the move this section adds to the search for derivations: before opening a box by hand, ask whether a derived rule takes the step at once. (a) Work backwards from the goal 
eg P. The premise P 	o Q would give it by ulename{MT} if 
eg Q were available. And 
eg Q comes by ulename{MT} from Q 	o R and 
eg R. So ulename{MT} is used twice, the second time on the conclusion of the first. Line 4 is the instance with \varphi replaced by Q and \psi by R; line 5 the instance with P and Q. In primitive rules, each ulename{MT} line becomes its four lines, as in lines 3–6 of the derivation of @prp-modus-tollens: a box on the hypothesis, ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{
eg E}, ulename{
eg I}. This natural expansion has eleven lines. The literal expansion of the fold “Why a derived rule adds no power” adds a repetition of each cited line and is longer; the natural one cites the available lines directly. (b) The disjunction P \vee Q has its left side refuted by 
eg P, so ulename{DS} gives Q, and then Q 	o R fires. Expanded, line 4 becomes lines 3–7 of the derivation of @prp-disjunctive-syllogism (five lines), with a case split on line 1 and the case P closed by ulename{ ot E}. Which derived rule of this section, if any, gives a new line in one step from each pair of available lines? (i) P 	o Q and 
eg Q. (ii) P \vee Q and 
eg P. (iii) P \vee Q and Q 	o R. (iv) P 	o 
eg Q and Q. (i) ulename{MT} gives 
eg P. (ii) ulename{DS} gives Q. (iii) None: nothing is known about the case P. (iv) None in one step: ulename{MT} needs the negation of the conclusion 
eg Q, which is 
eg
eg Q, not Q. A ulename{
eg I} box gives 
eg
eg Q from Q first, as in @exm-double-negation-introduction, and then ulename{MT} gives 
eg P. Modus tollens on numbers, and the green card In a mathematical proof, ulename{MT} is the step “since the conclusion fails, the hypothesis fails”. Here it is with numbers. [Modus tollens on numbers] Let x be a real number with x^2 \le 4. Use the implication “if x > 2, then x^2 > 4” to show that x \le 2, naming the derived rule. Take P: “x > 2” and Q: “x^2 > 4”. The implication is P 	o Q. (It holds because x > 2 > 0 gives x^2 = x \cdot x > 2x > 4.) The hypothesis x^2 \le 4 is 
eg Q, since for real numbers x^2 \le 4 and x^2 > 4 are exact negations of each other. By ulename{MT} (@prp-modus-tollens), 
eg P, that is, 
eg(x > 2), which is x \le 2. The claim of @exm-wason-selection (Section 1.3), for one card, is E 	o R, with E: “this card’s number is even” and R: “its color side is red”. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The card shows So we have What a rule gives Turn it? ----------------- ----------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------- 6 E ulename{{	o}E}: R; the back must be red yes: a green back would break the claim 7 
eg E nothing about R: no rule takes E 	o R and 
eg E to R or to 
eg R no red R nothing about E: concluding E would be affirming the consequent no green 
eg R ulename{MT}: 
eg E; the number must be odd yes: an even number would break the claim ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Turning the green card tests exactly the line ulename{MT} wrote: an even number there gives E, and with 
eg R and E 	o R, ulename{{	o}E} and ulename{
eg E} reach  ot. Modus tollens is the step people skip. ulename{CP} turns the claim into its contrapositive 
eg R 	o 
eg E, “a card whose color is not red has an odd number”, which carries the claim’s content to the green card; Section 2.5 derives the passage back, so the two say the same. The converse R 	o E, “a red card has an even number”, is a different claim, and the card rule never made it. Which card would ulename{MT} settle if the claim were “if a card’s color side is red, then its number is even”? The 7. The claim is R 	o E, the 7 shows 
eg E, and ulename{MT} gives 
eg R, so its back must not be red: turn it. A claim about every integer of a kind makes one prediction per instance. “For every prime p, the number 2^p - 1 is prime” predicts that 3, 7, 31 and 127 are prime, for p = 2, 3, 5, 7, and all four are.
