As a derivation: The computation is right: (2k)^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2), and 2k^2 is an integer. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: identifies the frame as ulename{{	o}I}, with the box opened on the hypothesis “n^2 is odd”. - 2: identifies “n^2 is not even” as ulename{
eg I}, naming the clash (with “no integer is both”, by ulename{
eg E}). - 3: identifies ulename{CP} (then ulename{{	o}E}), or ulename{MT}, applied to “if n is even, then n^2 is even”, with that antecedent and consequent. Reading the “if n were even” sentence as a premise or as a ulename{{	o}I} box that proves the implication earns these points equally. - 2: identifies ulename{DS} on “every integer is even or odd”, naming “even” as the refuted side. - 1: names the closing ulename{{	o}I}. Fatal errors (0 for the step): naming anything but ulename{
eg I} for the “not even” step (it concludes a negation from a box on the unnegated statement); applying ulename{CP} to the converse, “if n^2 is even, then n is even”.

title: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content:
Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says One connective is still without rules: “if and only if”. Theorems say “n is odd if and only if n^2 is odd”, and every definition, though written with a plain “if”, is used as an “if and only if”. Section 1.1 warned that “if” means different things in a theorem and in a definition; this section explains why. The one new thing here is the pair of rules for \leftrightarrow; the rest of the section (provable equivalence, the layout of an “iff” proof, the convention about definitions, chains of equivalences) is what the rules are used for. The rules for “if and only if” “P if and only if Q” combines “P if Q”, which is Q 	o P, with “P only if Q”, which is P 	o Q, as Section 1.1 explained. A proof of it travels both ways; a use of it, either way. An implication is proved by a box, opened on the hypothesis and closed on the conclusion (@def-rules-implication); an “if and only if” needs two such boxes. An “if and only if” is two implications, and proving it takes two proofs. [Rules for the Biconditional] The first schema is the rule ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} (iff-introduction); its two assumptions are discharged when their boxes close, and each box’s last line (\psi in the first, \varphi in the second) is a line of that box itself, not of a box inside it. The two schemas below it are the two forms of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} (iff-elimination). As in every schema (@def-rule-schema), \varphi and \psi stand for any statements, replaced consistently, and i, j, k, l, m for line numbers. Read the rules clause by clause. 1. Two boxes. ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} needs two available boxes: one opened by \varphi and ending in \psi, the other opened by \psi and ending in \varphi, each last line a line of its own box. Each is exactly the box ulename{{	o}I} would need for one direction. Their order does not matter, but both must be there: a single box from \varphi to \psi proves \varphi 	o \psi and nothing more. Each box’s assumption is printed “asm, for ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}”; in a written proof the two boxes are the paragraphs (\Rightarrow) and (\Leftarrow). 2. Separate boxes. The boxes are siblings, not nested, so nothing in the second may cite a line of the first (the scope rule of @def-derivation). Each direction is a proof on its own. 3. Citation. The justification cites both boxes as ranges, as in ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}\ \lines{2}{4}, \lines{5}{7}. 4. Elimination, either way. From \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi and \varphi on available lines, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} writes \psi; from \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi and \psi, it writes \varphi. It is modus ponens in whichever direction we need, citing the biconditional first. In the Givens/Goal table, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} splits a row in two: \varphi added to the Givens with the goal \psi, and \psi added with the goal \varphi. First derivations with iff The section’s goal-directed move: a goal \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi opens two boxes, one on each side, and each box’s goal is the other side. [An iff read both ways] 1. Show that P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash Q \leftrightarrow P. 2. Show that P \leftrightarrow Q, \; 
eg Q \vdash 
eg P. (a) Idea. The goal is an iff, so the last line is ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}, and we need a box from Q to P and a box from P to Q. Each box’s goal is one ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} away: the premise crosses from its assumption to the other side. The goal at the foot (left), then its two boxes (right). The finished derivation: Line 3 uses the second form of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} (right to left), line 5 the first. (b) Idea. The goal 
eg P is a negation, so open a box on P and aim at  ot (Section 2.2). Inside, the premise P \leftrightarrow Q turns P into Q, and Q clashes with 
eg Q. This is the derivation of @prp-modus-tollens with ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} on line 4: if two statements are equivalent and one fails, so does the other. The rules say nothing that the two implications do not say. The next result makes this exact. [An Iff Is Two Implications] P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P), and (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P) \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q. Each goal chooses its rule. For the first, the goal is a conjunction of two implications: ulename{\wedge I} needs both, and each is built in its own ulename{{	o}I} box, crossing the premise with ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} inside. For the second, the goal is an iff: open its two boxes. The premise is a conjunction, so take it apart first (premise-directed), and cross each box with one of its halves by ulename{{	o}E}. First claim: the two implications as goals (left), then their boxes (right). Second claim: the premise taken apart (left), then the two boxes (right). For the first claim, the following is a derivation with premise P \leftrightarrow Q and last line (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P). For the second claim, the following is a derivation with premise (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P) and last line P \leftrightarrow Q. Lines 2 and 3 lie in no box, so both boxes may cite them. This proves both claims. So \leftrightarrow could have been an abbreviation for (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P). We keep it as a connective with its own rules, so that every connective is proved by an introduction rule and used by an elimination rule. [Negating both sides of an iff] Show that P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash 
eg P \leftrightarrow 
eg Q. Idea. The goal is an iff, so there are two boxes, one opened by 
eg P and reaching 
eg Q, the other the reverse. Each box’s goal is a negation, so each contains a ulename{
eg I} box: the goal-directed move applied twice, one inside the other. Inside the inner box, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} crosses from one side of the premise to the other, and the result clashes with the outer assumption. The second half is part (b) of @exm-iff-symmetric, run inside a box; the first is its mirror image, with the other form of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. The outer boxes (left), then a ulename{
eg I} box inside each (right). The finished derivation: The two halves are mirror images. In the derivation of @exm-iff-negations, which line does line 5 cite as 
eg\varphi, and why may it? Line 2, 
eg P, the assumption of the outer box \lines{2}{6}, which is still open at line 5. The derivation uses only the rules of this section and of Sections 2.1–2.2. Its converse, 
eg P \leftrightarrow 
eg Q \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q, is also derivable, with the rule of Section 2.5: in the box of P it must produce the positive statement Q, and the natural box, on 
eg Q, closes to 
eg
eg Q, not Q. @exm-iff-negations negated both sides of an iff. Can one side be the negation of the other, a statement equivalent to its own negation? [No Statement Is Equivalent to Its Negation] \vdash 
eg(P \leftrightarrow 
eg P). The goal is a negation: open a ulename{
eg I} box on P \leftrightarrow 
eg P, with goal  ot. ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} needs one side of the iff on a line, and neither is. So make 
eg P a subgoal, by a ulename{
eg I} box on P: inside it ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} gives 
eg P, which clashes with P. With 
eg P in hand, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} the other way gives P, and the two clash again. The outer box (left), then the subgoal 
eg P with its box (right). The following is a derivation with no premises and last line 
eg(P \leftrightarrow 
eg P). Line 5 may be cited at lines 6 and 7: it lies in the box \lines{1}{7}, as they do. No rule of Section 2.5 is used. In words: no statement is equivalent to its own negation; a definition that made a term mean the failure of that very term would define nothing. For an instance, let x be a real number. The sentence “x > 0 if and only if x \le 0” is false whatever x is: by the convention of Section 2.1, x \le 0 is 
eg(x > 0), so the sentence is an instance of P \leftrightarrow 
eg P, and the lemma, used as a derived rule, refutes every instance. In the proof of @lem-not-iff-own-negation, which two lines use the biconditional, and in which direction? Line 3, from the left side P (line 2) to the right side 
eg P; and line 6, from the right side 
eg P (line 5) back to the left side P. Provable equivalence @prp-iff-two-implications is a pair of sequents, one in each direction. It is not the first such pair: @prp-curry and @prp-distributivity are pairs too. When two statements can each be derived from the other, either may stand in for the other in any derivation, and the situation deserves a name. Two statements are provably equivalent when each can be derived from the other. Provable Equivalence Statements P and Q are provably equivalent, written P \dashv\vdash Q, if P \vdash Q and Q \vdash P. In words: there is a derivation with premise P and last line Q, and another with premise Q and last line P. The symbol is the turnstile of @def-derivable written twice, back to back; two derivations prove the claim. A first example is P \wedge Q \dashv\vdash Q \wedge P: @prp-and-commutes derives Q \wedge P from P \wedge Q, and the same derivation with P and Q exchanged derives P \wedge Q from Q \wedge P. By the same exchange, @exm-disjunction-first-derivations gives P \vee Q \dashv\vdash Q \vee P, and part (a) of @exm-iff-symmetric gives P \leftrightarrow Q \dashv\vdash Q \leftrightarrow P. The degenerate example is P \dashv\vdash P: the one-line derivation of part (a) of @exm-derivations serves in both directions. A minimal change gives a one-way street. @exm-double-negation-introduction derived P \vdash 
eg
eg P, but the converse, 
eg
eg P \vdash P, would have to remove two negations, and no rule met so far removes one. So we cannot claim P \dashv\vdash 
eg
eg P: the clause “Q \vdash P” is the one missing. (It holds once Section 2.5 adds its rule.) Likewise @prp-contrapositive derives 
eg Q 	o 
eg P from P 	o Q, but not yet the reverse. The connective \leftrightarrow and the relation \dashv\vdash are two sides of one idea; the next result makes the link exact, and shows that \dashv\vdash behaves as an equivalence should. [Provable Equivalence and the Biconditional] For all statements P, Q, R: 1. P \dashv\vdash Q if and only if \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q; 2. P \dashv\vdash P; if P \dashv\vdash Q, then Q \dashv\vdash P; and if P \dashv\vdash Q and Q \dashv\vdash R, then P \dashv\vdash R. In words: one derivation of P \leftrightarrow Q from no premises is worth two derivations, one each way; and \dashv\vdash can be used like = in a calculation. Everything here moves whole derivations around. To prove \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q, the two boxes of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} are the two given derivations, with their premises turned into the boxes’ assumptions. To use \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q, write out its derivation and apply ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. For transitivity, run one derivation into the next: the last line of the first is the premise of the second. We use one observation twice. Let D be a derivation, and copy its lines, in order and with their numbers shifted, to some place in another derivation, with every line of the copy inside the same boxes as that place. Then every citation inside the copy is still available: if line i of D is available at line k of D, every box of D containing line i contains line k, and the boxes added around the copy contain both lines. Closed boxes cited in D are handled the same way. So each copied line is justified by the same rule as before. (\Rightarrow) in (a). Suppose P \vdash Q and Q \vdash P, by derivations D_1 and D_2. Build a derivation with no premises as follows. Open a box with the assumption P and, below it, copy D_1, turning each of its premise lines P into a repetition of the assumption by (D3) of @def-derivation. By the observation, the copy is justified, and its last line Q is a line of the box itself, since the last line of D_1 lies in none of D_1’s boxes. Close the box. Open a second box with Q, copy D_2 in the same way, and close it on P. Then ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} on the two boxes gives P \leftrightarrow Q. So \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q. (\Leftarrow) in (a). Suppose \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q, by a derivation D with no premises. For P \vdash Q, start with the premise P, copy D below it, and write Q by ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} from the last line of the copy, P \leftrightarrow Q, and line 1. Both cited lines lie in no box, so both are available. For Q \vdash P, do the same with premise Q, using the other form of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. So P \dashv\vdash Q. (b) The one-line derivation consisting of the premise P shows P \vdash P, in both directions, so P \dashv\vdash P. Symmetry holds because @def-provable-equivalence says the same thing about P, Q as about Q, P. For transitivity it is enough to show that P \vdash Q and Q \vdash R give P \vdash R, since the reverse direction is the same statement with P and R exchanged. Take a derivation D_1 of Q from P, and below its last line copy a derivation D_2 of R from Q, turning each premise line Q of D_2 into a repetition of the last line of D_1. That line lies in no box, so it is available everywhere below it, and by the observation the rest of the copy is justified. The result has premise P and last line R. This proves the proposition. Here are equivalences derived so far. Each row gives two derived rules (@def-derived-rule), one in each direction. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Provable equivalence Derived in ----------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- P \wedge Q \dashv\vdash Q \wedge P @prp-and-commutes, with the letters exchanged for the converse P \vee Q \dashv\vdash Q \vee P @exm-disjunction-first-derivations, likewise (P \wedge Q) 	o R \dashv\vdash P 	o (Q 	o R) @prp-curry P \wedge (Q \vee R) \dashv\vdash (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) @prp-distributivity (P 	o R) \wedge (Q 	o R) \dashv\vdash (P \vee Q) 	o R @exm-cases-on-hypothesis and @exm-or-hypothesis-split P \leftrightarrow Q \dashv\vdash (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P) @prp-iff-two-implications P \leftrightarrow Q \dashv\vdash Q \leftrightarrow P @exm-iff-symmetric (a), with the letters exchanged 
eg
eg
eg P \dashv\vdash 
eg P @exm-triple-negation, and @exm-double-negation-introduction (a) with 
eg P for P ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The fourth row is distributivity of \wedge over \vee as a provable equivalence. Some familiar laws are not in the table, because the text has derived them in one direction only; associativity of \vee is one (@exm-disjunction-regroup). A sequent in one direction is not an equivalence. P \wedge Q \vdash P holds by ulename{\wedge E}, but the form “from P conclude P \wedge Q” breaks: take P: “2 > 1” and Q: “1 > 2”, and the premise is true while the conclusion is false. Before writing \dashv\vdash, check that both derivations exist. Proving an iff: two directions In a written proof, the two boxes of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} become two paragraphs: (\Rightarrow) assumes the left side and reaches the right, (\Leftarrow) the reverse. Neither may borrow the other’s assumption: they are two separate boxes. The first example completes the story of parity. We use the facts (E1)–(E3) of Section 2.1: every integer is even or odd; no integer is both even and odd; the square of an odd integer is odd. [Odd Square, Odd Number] Let n be an integer. Then n is odd if and only if n^2 is odd. Two boxes. Forwards is (E3). Backwards, “n^2 is odd” gives nothing to compute with, so split on (E1) and show the even case impossible, as in @exm-impossible-case. (\Rightarrow) This is (E3). (\Leftarrow) Suppose n^2 is odd [	ext{assumption for the second box}]. By (E1), n is even or odd, and we argue by cases [ulename{\vee E}]. If n is odd, we are done. If n is even, say n = 2k with k an integer, then n^2 = 2(2k^2) is even; so n^2 is both even and odd [ulename{\wedge I}], which contradicts (E2) [ulename{
eg E}]. So this case cannot occur, and n is odd in it too [ulename{ ot E}]. In both cases n is odd. This proves the theorem [ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}]. With the derived rules of Section 2.3, (\Leftarrow) fits in one breath, “n cannot be even, since then n^2 would be even; so n is odd”: ulename{
eg I} with (E2), then ulename{MT}, then ulename{DS} on (E1). The next example is about real numbers, and its two directions do different work. Each hypothesis is needed: dropping either one breaks one of the two directions, as the remark after the proof shows. [Squaring Preserves Order] Let x and y be real numbers with x \ge 0 and y \ge 0. Then x \le y \iff x^2 \le y^2 . Forwards, multiply x \le y by x \ge 0 and by y \ge 0, and chain. Backwards, nothing undoes squaring without square roots, so we split instead: either x \le y, which is the goal, or y < x. In the second case the forward argument, run with a strict inequality, gives y^2 < x^2, which clashes with the hypothesis: an impossible case, closed by ulename{ ot E}. (\Rightarrow) Suppose x \le y. Multiplying by x \ge 0 gives x^2 \le xy, and multiplying by y \ge 0 gives xy \le y^2. Hence x^2 \le y^2. (\Leftarrow) Suppose x^2 \le y^2. For real numbers, x \le y or y < x, and we argue by cases [ulename{\vee E}]. If x \le y, we are done. If y < x, then x > y \ge 0, so x > 0. Multiplying y < x by x > 0 gives xy < x^2, and multiplying y < x by y \ge 0 gives y^2 \le xy. Hence y^2 < x^2, which contradicts x^2 \le y^2 [ulename{
eg E}]; so this case cannot occur, and x \le y holds in it [ulename{ ot E}]. In both cases x \le y. This proves the theorem [ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}]. Each hypothesis has a job. The direction (\Rightarrow) needs x \ge 0, and fails without it: x = -2, y = 1 gives x \le y but x^2 = 4 > 1 = y^2. (Its proof also multiplied by y \ge 0, but there y \ge 0 already follows from y \ge x \ge 0.) The direction (\Leftarrow) used only y \ge 0, and fails without it: x = 1, y = -2 gives x^2 = 1 \le 4 = y^2 but x > y. A payoff comes at once. For a, b \ge 0, apply @thm-squares-order to x = \sqrt{a} and y = \sqrt{b}: \sqrt{a} \le \sqrt{b} if and only if a \le b. Taking square roots preserves order, a fact used constantly in estimates. (That square roots of non-negative numbers exist is a school fact here.) Here is a proof of the statement “for a real number x, x^2 = 1 if and only if x = 1 or x = -1”. If x = 1, then x^2 = 1 \cdot 1 = 1. If x = -1, then x^2 = (-1)(-1) = 1. This proves the claim. Which direction has been proved, and which is missing? Supply the missing one. The proof assumes the right side, “x = 1 or x = -1”, splits it into its two cases, and reaches x^2 = 1 in both. So it proves (\Leftarrow), by ulename{\vee E}. The direction (\Rightarrow) is missing. (\Rightarrow) Suppose x^2 = 1. Then (x - 1)(x + 1) = x^2 - 1 = 0. A product of real numbers is zero only if one of the factors is zero, so x - 1 = 0 or x + 1 = 0, that is, x = 1 or x = -1. A proof of an iff can prove one direction twice and look complete. For “n is odd if and only if n^2 is odd”, a proof that shows “if n is odd, then n^2 is odd” and then “if n^2 is not odd, then n is not odd” has proved (\Rightarrow) and its contrapositive (@prp-contrapositive), which is (\Rightarrow) again. The direction (\Leftarrow), “if n^2 is odd, then n is odd”, is still missing; its contrapositive would be “if n is not odd, then n^2 is not odd”. Before writing “this proves the theorem”, check that one paragraph assumes each side. What a definition says Here is a definition written the way this book and most others write definitions. A function f \colon 
R 	o 
R is strictly increasing if, for all real numbers x and y, x < y implies f(x) < f(y). Grammatically the sentence is an implication, “f is strictly increasing if [condition]”, and read as a theorem it would allow only one move, from the condition to the term. But a definition is not a theorem. It introduces a new term, and the new term means exactly the condition: no more, since nothing else was said about the term, and no less, since the condition is all the term was made to express. So the definition is used in both directions, as an \leftrightarrow between the term and the condition, and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} is how it is used. In a definition, “if” means “if and only if”. This is a convention of mathematical language, not a rule of logic. Some books write “iff” or :\Leftrightarrow in definitions; this book, like most, writes “if” and puts the term defined in bold, which signals that the “if” is an “iff”. Here it is used three ways. [A definition used in both directions] 1. Show that f(x) = 3x - 5 defines a strictly increasing function f \colon 
R 	o 
R. 2. Suppose g \colon 
R 	o 
R is strictly increasing. Show that g(1) < g(2). 3. Show that h(x) = x^2 does not define a strictly increasing function h \colon 
R 	o 
R. (a) Let x and y be real numbers with x < y. Multiplying by 3 > 0 gives 3x < 3y, and subtracting 5 gives 3x - 5 < 3y - 5, that is, f(x) < f(y). So f satisfies the condition, and by the definition, read from right to left, f is strictly increasing [ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}]. (b) Since g is strictly increasing, the definition, read from left to right, says that x < y implies g(x) < g(y) for all real x and y [ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}]. Taking x = 1 and y = 2, and using 1 < 2, we get g(1) < g(2) [ulename{{	o}E}]. (c) Suppose h were strictly increasing [	ext{assumption for } ulename{
eg I}]. By the definition read from left to right, as in (b), -1 < 0 would give h(-1) < h(0), that is, 1 < 0, which is false [ulename{
eg E}]. So h is not strictly increasing [ulename{
eg I}]. Part (a) uses the definition from the condition to the term; parts (b) and (c) use it from the term to the condition. A definition read only as an “if” would permit (a) and nothing else. Because the term means exactly the condition, a candidate condition is judged against the intended meaning. Had the definition said “x < y implies f(x) \le f(y)”, it would be too broad: the constant function f(x) = 0 would count as strictly increasing. Had it said “x < y implies f(y) - f(x) \ge 1”, it would be too narrow: f(x) = x would not count, since 0 <  rac{1}{2} and  rac{1}{2} - 0 < 1. The convention is for definitions only. In a theorem, “if” means “if”, one direction. The theorem “if 6 \mid n, then n is even” is true for every integer n: n = 6k = 2(3k). Its converse, “if n is even, then 6 \mid n”, breaks at n = 4. Reading a theorem’s “if” as “iff” means proving its converse without a proof, which is the error of Argument B in Section 1.1. A familiar theorem of calculus says: if f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a. Its converse is false. The function f(x) = \abs{x} is continuous at 0, but it is not differentiable there, since its graph has a corner: the quotient \abs{h}/h is 1 for h > 0 and -1 for h < 0. Write the converse of “if a real number x satisfies x > 2, then x^2 > 4”, and break it. The converse is “if x^2 > 4, then x > 2”. The value x = -3 breaks it: (-3)^2 = 9 > 4, and -3 > 2 fails. Chains of equivalences “The following are equivalent: (a), (b), (c)” means that any two of the three are equivalent: three iff statements, or six implications. Three implications suffice, if they go round in a cycle: 	ext{(a)} \Rightarrow 	ext{(b)} \Rightarrow 	ext{(c)} \Rightarrow 	ext{(a)} . Once the cycle is proved, any condition leads to any other by following the arrows round. Here is the derivation behind that sentence. [Proving Equivalence by a Cycle] P 	o Q, \; Q 	o R, \; R 	o P \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q. Likewise, from the same three premises, Q \leftrightarrow R and R \leftrightarrow P are derivable. The goal is an iff, so there are two boxes. From P, one step along the cycle reaches Q. From Q, the cycle reaches P the long way round, through R: a backward chain of ulename{{	o}E}, as in Section 1.3. The other two equivalences need no new work, because the three premises do not change when the letters are rotated. The goal at the foot (left), then its two boxes (right). The following is a derivation with the three premises and last line P \leftrightarrow Q. Now replace P, Q, R throughout by Q, R, P respectively. The premises P 	o Q, Q 	o R, R 	o P become Q 	o R, R 	o P, P 	o Q, the same three statements in a different order, and every line remains justified by the same rule, since the letters stood for any statements (as in clause 2 after @def-derived-rule). So the renamed derivation derives Q \leftrightarrow R from the same premises. Rotating once more gives R \leftrightarrow P. This proves the proposition. In a cycle every condition reaches every other along the arrows; longer cycles work the same way, with longer chains of ulename{{	o}E} in the boxes. Two arrows back and forth are not a cycle through three conditions. Proving (a) \Rightarrow (b) and (b) \Rightarrow (a) shows that (a) and (b) are equivalent and says nothing about (c): no arrow enters or leaves it. For a real number x, take (a) “x > 0”, (b) “2x > 0”, and (c) “x > 1”. Both arrows between (a) and (b) are true, and (c) is not equivalent to them: x =  rac{1}{2} satisfies (a) and (b) but not (c). Every condition in the list must lie on the cycle. [Three descriptions of the unit interval] Let x be a real number. Prove that the following are equivalent. 1. 0 < x < 1. 2. x^2 < x. 3. x > 0 and 1/x > 1. By @prp-equivalence-cycle it suffices to prove (a) \Rightarrow (b) \Rightarrow (c) \Rightarrow (a). (a) \Rightarrow (b). Suppose 0 < x < 1. Multiplying x < 1 by x > 0 gives x^2 < x. (b) \Rightarrow (c). Suppose x^2 < x. First, x > 0: otherwise x \le 0, and then x \le 0 \le x^2, so x \le x^2, which contradicts x^2 < x. (In rules: we have x \le 0 or x > 0; the first is refuted by a ulename{
eg I} box, and ulename{DS} (@prp-disjunctive-syllogism) leaves the second.) Since x > 0, we may divide x^2 < x by x, which gives x < 1, and then divide x < 1 by x, which gives 1 < 1/x. In each, the premises are used as bridges, one after the other, by ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. Lines 4 and 8 use P \leftrightarrow Q in opposite directions, as do lines 5 and 7 with Q \leftrightarrow R. [B2: A parity equivalence] Let n be an integer. Prove that n is even if and only if n + 3 is odd. (\Rightarrow) Suppose n is even, say n = 2k with k an integer. Then n + 3 = 2k + 2 + 1 = 2(k + 1) + 1, and k + 1 is an integer, so n + 3 is odd. (\Leftarrow) Suppose n + 3 is odd, say n + 3 = 2j + 1 with j an integer. Then n = 2j - 2 = 2(j - 1), and j - 1 is an integer, so n is even. This proves the equivalence. [B3: Strict inequalities] Let x and y be real numbers with x \ge 0 and y \ge 0. Deduce from @thm-squares-order and @exm-iff-negations that x < y if and only if x^2 < y^2. You may use that, for real numbers a and b, a < b holds exactly when b \le a fails. 1. Apply @thm-squares-order with the roles of x and y exchanged. What does it say? 2. Use @exm-iff-negations as a derived rule on (a): with which statements in place of P and Q, and what does it give? 3. Translate both sides of (b) with the fact quoted. 4. What have you proved? (a) The exchange is allowed, since both numbers are non-negative: y \le x if and only if y^2 \le x^2. (b) With P: “y \le x” and Q: “y^2 \le x^2”, @exm-iff-negations, used as a derived rule (@def-derived-rule), gives: y \le x fails if and only if y^2 \le x^2 fails. (c) By the fact quoted, the left side says x < y and the right side says x^2 < y^2. (d) That x < y if and only if x^2 < y^2. [B4: Both directions] A search for P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash (P \wedge R) \leftrightarrow (Q \wedge R) has reached the stage below. Name the move, then complete it. The move is two boxes for an iff: the goal’s main connective is \leftrightarrow, so line 12 will be ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}, with a box from P \wedge R to Q \wedge R and a box back. Inside each, take the conjunction apart, cross with ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}, and rebuild. The second box never cites a line of the first: line 10 gets P afresh from line 8. [B5: Criticize the definition] For real numbers a, b, x, we want to define “x lies strictly between a and b”, meaning that one of a, b is less than x and x is less than the other. Here are five candidate conditions. 1. a < x and x < b. 2. a < x or x < b. 3. (a < x and x < b) or (b < x and x < a). 4. (x - a)(x - b) < 0. 5. x \le a fails and b \le x fails. 1. For each, say whether it is too broad (it admits a triple a, b, x that should be excluded), too narrow (it excludes one that should be admitted), or right, giving a triple for each fault. 2. A definition is read as an iff. Prove that (iii) and (iv) are equivalent. 3. Which candidates would make “if x lies strictly between a and b, then x lies strictly between b and a” false? Give one triple that shows it for all of them. (a) (i) Too narrow: a = 5, b = 2, x = 3 lies between and fails (i). It is not too broad: (i) gives one of the wanted orders. (ii) Too broad: a = 2, b = 5, x = 100 satisfies 2 < 100 but does not lie between. And too narrow: a = 5, b = 2, x = 3 lies between, but 5 < 3 and 3 < 2 both fail (the triple of (c)). (iii) Right: it lists the two possible orders. (iv) Right, by (b). (v) This is (i) in negative dress: by the convention of Section 2.1, “x \le a fails” is a < x and “b \le x fails” is x < b. So it is too narrow, by the same triple as (i), and needlessly negative. (b) (\Rightarrow) In the case a < x < b, x - a > 0 and x - b < 0, so the product is negative. In the case b < x < a, x - a < 0 and x - b > 0, so again the product is negative. The two cases are ulename{\vee E} on (iii). (\Leftarrow) Suppose the product is negative. Then neither factor is 0, and the two factors cannot have the same sign, since a product of two positive or of two negative numbers is positive. So x - a > 0 > x - b, that is a < x < b, or x - a < 0 < x - b, that is b < x < a. (c) (i), (ii) and (v). With a = 2, b = 5, x = 3, each holds for the ends 2, 5 and fails for the ends 5, 2 (for (ii): 2 < 3, while neither 5 < 3 nor 3 < 2). A definition of “between” should not depend on the order of the two ends; (iii) and (iv) do not, since exchanging a and b exchanges the two disjuncts of (iii) and the two factors of (iv). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 4: (a), one point each for (i) and (v) with a correct triple, one for (ii) with both triples (too broad and too narrow), and one for calling (iii) and (iv) right. - 4: (b), each direction 2; the second must say why the factors have opposite signs. - 2: (c), (i), (ii) and (v) with one triple. Fatal error (0 for (b)): proving only one direction and calling the conditions equivalent. [B6: Four conditions, one cycle] Let n be an integer. Prove by one cycle of four implications that the following are equivalent. 1. n is odd. 2. n + 1 is even. 3. 8 \mid n^2 - 1. 4. n^2 is odd. You may use @thm-odd-iff-square-odd and the fact that k(k - 1) is even for every integer k. Then: a proof that proved only (i) \Leftrightarrow (ii) and (iii) \Leftrightarrow (iv) would be incomplete; which two implications would complete it most cheaply? We prove the cycle (i) \Rightarrow (ii) \Rightarrow (iii) \Rightarrow (iv) \Rightarrow (i). It suffices by the argument of @prp-equivalence-cycle: for any two conditions, each reaches the other by a chain of ulename{{	o}E} along the arrows, inside the two boxes of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}. (i) \Rightarrow (ii). If n = 2k + 1, then n + 1 = 2(k + 1). (ii) \Rightarrow (iii). If n + 1 = 2j, then n - 1 = 2(j - 1), so n^2 - 1 = (n - 1)(n + 1) = 4j(j - 1). By the fact quoted, j(j - 1) = 2m for an integer m, so n^2 - 1 = 8m. (iii) \Rightarrow (iv). If n^2 - 1 = 8m, then n^2 = 2(4m) + 1, which is odd. (iv) \Rightarrow (i). This is @thm-odd-iff-square-odd, read from right to left. (Exercise B3 of Section 1.6 met the fact (i) \Rightarrow (iii) by another route.) For the second question: (i) \Rightarrow (iv) and (iv) \Rightarrow (i). Both are @thm-odd-iff-square-odd, so they cost nothing. Any two implications joining the two pairs, one in each direction, would do, for instance (ii) \Rightarrow (iii) and (iv) \Rightarrow (i); with them every condition reaches every other. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: a cycle through all four conditions, citing the argument of @prp-equivalence-cycle or arguing that it suffices. - 8: 2 for each of the four arrows. - 1: the completion question. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a “cycle” that omits a condition; (iii) \Rightarrow (iv) or (iv) \Rightarrow (i) argued by examples. [B7: Derive or break] For each claim, derive it with the rules of Chapter 1 and Sections 2.1–2.4, or break it by statements about a real number x that make its counterexample set true. 1. P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash (P \vee R) \leftrightarrow (Q \vee R). 2. (P \vee R) \leftrightarrow (Q \vee R) \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q. 3. P \leftrightarrow (Q \wedge R) \vdash P 	o Q. 4. P \leftrightarrow (Q \wedge R) \vdash Q 	o P. 5. P \leftrightarrow Q, \ Q \leftrightarrow 
eg R \vdash 
eg(P \wedge R). 6. P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash 
eg(P \wedge 
eg Q). 7. 
eg(P \wedge 
eg Q) \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q. 8. P \leftrightarrow Q, \ P \vee Q \vdash P \wedge Q. (a) Derive. Two boxes for the iff, and a case split inside each. (b) Break. Take P: “x > 0”, Q: “x > 5”, R: “x > -1”. At x = 1, P \vee R and Q \vee R are both true, so the premise is true; P is true and Q false, so P \leftrightarrow Q is false. The counterexample set (@def-counterexample-set) (P \vee R) \leftrightarrow (Q \vee R), 
eg(P \leftrightarrow Q) is true at x = 1. (c) Derive. (d) Break. Take P: “x > 5”, Q: “x > 0”, R: “x > 3”. At x = 1, Q \wedge R and P are both false, so the premise is true, while Q 	o P is false, since Q is true and P false. The counterexample set is true at x = 1. (e) Derive. (f) Derive. (g) Break. Take P: “x > 5”, Q: “x > 0”. At x = 1, P \wedge 
eg Q is false, since P is, so the premise is true; P is false and Q true, so P \leftrightarrow Q is false. The counterexample set is true at x = 1. (h) Derive. Split on the second premise; in each case ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} supplies the other letter. (b) and (g) are the converses of (a) and (f), and (d) replaces the conclusion of (c) by its converse; each of the three breaks. (a) is the \vee-twin of @exr-biconditional-and-definitions-b4, with a case split inside each box. Marking scheme. (16 points) For each claim: 1 for the verdict; 1 for a derivation every line of which checks, or for a choice of statements and one value of x at which every member of the counterexample set is true. Fatal errors (0 for the claim): a “break” at which a premise fails; RAA in a derivation; a box of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} citing its sibling. C. Going deeper [C1: Divisibility by six] For integers d and n, write d \mid n if n = dk for some integer k. Let n be an integer. Prove that the following three conditions are equivalent, by a single cycle of three implications. 1. 6 \mid n; 2. 2 \mid n and 3 \mid n; 3. 6 \mid n^2. You may use @thm-square-even-implies-even and part (a) of @exr-negation-and-contradiction-b3. [Hint 1] Choose the order of the cycle so that each arrow is short. The two results you may use both pass from a square to the number itself. [Hint 2] Try (i) \Rightarrow (iii) \Rightarrow (ii) \Rightarrow (i). The last arrow is the one that needs an idea: the two halves of (ii) must be used together, not one at a time. We prove (i) \Rightarrow (iii) \Rightarrow (ii) \Rightarrow (i), which suffices by @prp-equivalence-cycle. (i) \Rightarrow (iii). Suppose n = 6k. Then n^2 = 36k^2 = 6(6k^2), so 6 \mid n^2. (iii) \Rightarrow (ii). Suppose n^2 = 6j. Then n^2 = 2(3j) is even, so n is even by @thm-square-even-implies-even, that is, 2 \mid n. Also n^2 = 3(2j), so 3 \mid n^2, and by part (a) of @exr-negation-and-contradiction-b3, 3 \mid n. Hence 2 \mid n and 3 \mid n [ulename{\wedge I}]. (ii) \Rightarrow (i). Suppose 2 \mid n and 3 \mid n, and write n = 3b with b an integer. The integer b is odd or even. If b were odd, then n = 3b would be odd: writing b = 2c + 1 gives 3b = 6c + 3 = 2(3c + 1) + 1. But n is even, and no integer is both, so this case cannot occur [ulename{
eg E}, ulename{ ot E}]. Hence b is even, say b = 2c, and n = 6c, so 6 \mid n. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: names a cycle through all three conditions and cites @prp-equivalence-cycle (or proves the needed implications explicitly). - 2: (i) \Rightarrow (iii) by computation. - 3: (iii) \Rightarrow (ii), citing @thm-square-even-implies-even for the factor 2 and part (a) of @exr-negation-and-contradiction-b3 for the factor 3. - 4: (ii) \Rightarrow (i), combining the two factors correctly (ruling out b odd, or n = 3n - 2n, or otherwise). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a “cycle” that omits a condition; using “2 \mid n and 3 \mid n gives 6 \mid n” without proof; using “6 \mid n^2 implies 6 \mid n” as known. Any other cycle through the three conditions earns full marks if each of its arrows is proved: 1 point for the cycle and its citation, and 3 points for each of its three arrows. [C2: Dropping a hypothesis, and repairing the statement] 1. Suppose only y \ge 0 is assumed in @thm-squares-order, and x is an arbitrary real number. The remark after it says that (\Leftarrow) survives. Which steps of its proof use y \ge 0, and why is x \ge 0 never needed? Refute (\Rightarrow) with a new pair. 2. Prove that for all real numbers x and y, \abs{x} \le \abs{y} if and only if x^2 \le y^2. Hint: for (b), apply @thm-squares-order to the right pair of numbers. (a) The proof of (\Leftarrow) uses y \ge 0 twice: for x > 0 from x > y, and for y^2 \le xy. Its other multiplication is by the derived x > 0, so x \ge 0 is never used. For (\Rightarrow), take x = -3, y = 1: x \le y and y \ge 0, but x^2 = 9 > 1 = y^2. (b) Let x and y be real numbers. Then \abs{x} \ge 0 and \abs{y} \ge 0, so @thm-squares-order applies to the pair \abs{x}, \abs{y} and gives \abs{x} \le \abs{y} if and only if \abs{x}^2 \le \abs{y}^2. Finally \abs{x}^2 = x^2, since \abs{x} is x or -x and (-x)^2 = x^2, and likewise \abs{y}^2 = y^2. This proves that \abs{x} \le \abs{y} if and only if x^2 \le y^2.

Proof by Contradiction and the Classical Rules Every rule so far either builds a statement or takes one apart. The rules for negation are no exception: ulename{
eg I} (@def-rules-negation) builds 
eg\varphi from a box that opens with \varphi and ends in  ot, and ulename{
eg E} (@def-rules-contradiction) uses 
eg\varphi against \varphi. Yet in three places this chapter has stopped one step short of a goal. This section adds the one rule that takes a negation away, reductio ad absurdum. It then derives from it the classical laws that mathematics uses without noticing, and shows that three of them are one principle in three forms. Two boxes that look alike Here are two arguments that a mathematician would both call “proof by contradiction”. The first is the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational. It fixes a rational number r, supposes r^2 = 2, reaches a contradiction, and concludes that r^2 
e 2. In the language of @def-rules-negation, it opens a box with the assumption P (“r^2 = 2”), reaches  ot inside it, and closes the box to get 
eg P. That is ulename{
eg I}. The second is about a real number. [A number whose square is at most itself] Let x be a real number with x^2 \le x. Prove that x \le 1. Suppose, for a contradiction, that x \le 1 fails, that is, x > 1. Then x > 0, and multiplying x > 1 by x gives x^2 > x. This contradicts x^2 \le x. Hence x \le 1. Look at its shape. The box opens with the assumption 
eg P, where P is “x \le 1”, reaches  ot, and closes to give P. If we tried to justify the last line by ulename{
eg I}, we would get the negation of the box’s assumption, 
eg
eg P: “it is not the case that x \le 1 fails”. That is not P. The two arguments put their negations in different places. ulename{
eg I} puts a 
eg into the conclusion; the second argument takes one out. Where the rules so far stop short The second argument is not a curiosity. Three times already in this chapter a derivation has stopped short in the same way: it reached a negation where the goal was not one. 1. Section 2.2 noted that a box opened with 
eg(x > 0) and closed by ulename{
eg I} gives 
eg
eg(x > 0), and no rule so far gets from there to x > 0. 2. If you did Exercise C1 of Section 2.3, you met a second: @exr-derived-rules-c1 led from P 	o Q and 
eg P 	o R to 
eg(
eg Q \wedge 
eg R), and not to Q \vee R. 3. Section 2.4 noted, after @exm-iff-negations, that its converse, 
eg P \leftrightarrow 
eg Q \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q, resists the rules so far. The natural box on 
eg Q, inside the box of P, closes to 
eg
eg Q, not Q. Try the smallest case, P from 
eg
eg P. The goal P is a letter, so no introduction rule applies: the goal-directed moves have nothing to say. The premise 
eg
eg P is a negation, and a negation can be used only by ulename{
eg E}, against the statement it negates, 
eg P. So we assume 
eg P in a box. The box reaches  ot at once, and ulename{
eg I} closes it with 
eg

The book keeps both for the reason the remark after @thm-classical-rules-interderivable gives for ulename{ ot E}: the primitive rules other than ulename{RAA} are to form a system of their own. By (E1), n is even or n is odd, and we argue by cases [ulename{\vee E}]. Case n even. Write n = 2k with k an integer. Then n^2 + 3n = 4k^2 + 6k = 2(2k^2 + 3k), which is even. Case n odd. Write n = 2k + 1 with k an integer. Then n^2 + 3n = (4k^2 + 4k + 1) + (6k + 3) = 2(2k^2 + 5k + 2), which is even. Both cases reach the goal, so n^2 + 3n is even [ulename{\vee E}]. title: Finding Derivations
content: Finding Derivations Chapters 1 and 2 gave every connective a rule for using it and a rule for proving it, and a derivation, once written, can be checked line by line with no idea at all. Finding one is another matter. An assumption may be any statement whatever, and nothing in the rules says which one to make; yet every Idea so far found its derivation with a handful of moves. “You know every propositional rule. Given a sequent, how do you find a derivation, or decide to stop looking?” The chapter answers in three steps. Section 3.1 puts the moves in order as one method, says why the order loses nothing, and watches the method succeed and fail. Section 3.2 shows that the task shapes the search, and names the syntactic idea behind every task: an inconsistent list, one from which \bot is derivable. Section 3.3 starts from a paragraph of mathematics instead of a sequent. The chapter ends on a question its methods cannot answer: a search that fails proves nothing, so how could anyone show that something is not derivable? What you need. Chapters 1 and 2: the rules for every connective; derivations with boxes and the scope rule (@def-derivation); derived rules (@def-derived-rule) and @lem-weakening-cut; the classical rules of Section 2.5; and from Section 1.1 the counterexample set (@def-counterexample-set) and the move try to break it. Steps about “every” and “some”, such as “say m = 2k”, are used as ordinary reasoning, as in Chapter 2, until Chapter 5 gives them their rules. Time. About 15 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 25 hours for everything. Minimum before Sets and Functions. Chapters 1–6 and 8, core; Sections 7.1–7.2 before its Section 4.1. Roadmap - How to Find a Derivation. The moves of Chapters 1 and 2 put in order as one method, the reason the order loses nothing, four refinements including the detour rule, searches that succeed and one that fails, and every rule on one card. - Four Kinds of Task. Theorems, equivalences, inconsistent lists and claims whose verdict is withheld: how each task starts its search, and why all four are one question, whether a list derives \bot. - From Argument to Derivation. Extracting the argument from a paragraph, naming the facts it leaves unsaid, writing a proof and its derivation side by side, and a library of standard sequents grouped by what they are for. Named moves - Work from both ends. The method: read the skeleton off the goal, use the resources by their main connectives, keep the classical step for last. (Section 3.1) - Find the goal among the resources. If the current goal is already available, cite it or copy it by \rulename{R}. (Section 3.1) - Derive what needs nothing new before opening a box. Lines written outside the boxes are available in all of them. (Section 3.1) - Look first for a clash partner already on a line. For the goal \bot, aim at the statement whose negation you already have. (Section 3.1) - No detours. Never build a line by an introduction rule and take it apart at once by the matching elimination. (Section 3.1) - Let the task choose the search. A theorem starts at the goal, an equivalence needs two derivations, an inconsistency aims at a clash. (Section 3.2) - Try to break it first. Before searching, try to make the counterexample set true. An attempt that is forced into a clash at every turn is usually a derivation read backwards: its forced statements suggest the boxes, and its clash the \bot. (Section 3.2) - Name the unstated fact. An argument in prose leaves premises unsaid; write each one down and check it. (Section 3.3) - Two columns. Write the proof beside the derivation it mirrors, and see which lines the prose leaves silent. (Section 3.3) Summary The search method reads boxes off the goal and eliminations off the resources, and its goal steps and its classical step never turn a gap that can be filled into one that cannot (the fold of Section 3.1). Postponing a disjunction and the four refinements make it efficient. Every task in Section 3.2 is a question about derivability, and every question about derivability is a question about whether a list is inconsistent (@prp-derivable-iff-negation-inconsistent): deriving \varphi from \Gamma is showing the counterexample set \Gamma, \neg\varphi inconsistent. An inconsistent list derives every statement (@prp-inconsistent-derives-everything). Arguments in prose become sequents once their unstated facts are named, and the library of Section 3.3 sorts the standard sequents by what they are for. Every method of the chapter can show that something is derivable, and none can show that something is not: a claim that breaks, or a search that stalls, has not been shown underivable. That is Chapter 4’s question. Terms - consistent list: a list from which \bot is not derivable (@def-inconsistent-set). - counterexample set (recalled): the premises together with the negated conclusion (@def-counterexample-set). - current goal: the written line below a gap (@def-partial-derivation). - gap: a stretch of a partial derivation still missing (@def-partial-derivation). - inconsistent list: a list from which \bot is derivable (@def-inconsistent-set). - partial derivation: a derivation with gaps still to fill (@def-partial-derivation). - provably equivalent (recalled): each derivable from the other (@def-provable-equivalence). - resources: the lines available at a gap’s current goal (@def-partial-derivation). - theorem (of logic): a statement derivable from no premises, \vdash \varphi (@def-derivable).

title: 3.1 How to Find a Derivation
content:
How to Find a Derivation We now have every rule for the connectives. Checking a derivation is mechanical, as @def-derivation makes it: for each line, which rule, which lines, and are they available. Finding one is not, since an assumption may be any statement at all. Yet every Idea in Chapters 1 and 2 found its derivation with the same handful of moves. This section introduces no new rule. It collects those moves into one method, puts them in order, says why the order is right, and then watches the method work: on five searches that succeed, one that fails, and one mathematical goal. It ends with every rule in one place. The moves so far Each section since Section 1.2 has added a move, either to the list read off the goal (goal-directed: which introduction rule builds the goal’s main connective?) or to the list read off the premises (premise-directed: which elimination rule uses an available line’s main connective?). Here they are together, with the section where each first appeared. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The situation The move First met --------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------- goal \varphi \wedge \psi two subgoals, \varphi and \psi, joined by ulename{\wedge I} Section 1.2 resource \varphi \wedge \psi take it apart by ulename{\wedge E} Section 1.2 resource \varphi 	o \psi fire it on \varphi by ulename{{	o}E}; if \varphi is missing, make it a subgoal Section 1.3 goal \varphi 	o \psi a box opened with \varphi, with the new goal \psi Section 1.4 goal \varphi \vee \psi postpone; choose a side only when it is in hand Section 1.5 resource \varphi \vee \psi two cases, each ending in the current goal Section 1.6 goal  ot find a clash, or manufacture one; an impossible case closes itself by ulename{ ot E} Section 2.1 resource 
eg\varphi clash it by ulename{
eg E}: make \varphi a subgoal Section 2.1 goal 
eg\varphi a box opened with \varphi, with the new goal  ot Section 2.2 a pattern with a name use the derived rule as one line (ulename{MT}, ulename{DS}, …) Section 2.3 goal \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi two boxes, one for each direction Section 2.4 resource \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi cross it by ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} once one side is on a line Section 2.4 stuck assume the negation of the goal (ulename{RAA}), or split on \chi \vee 
eg\chi (ulename{LEM}) Section 2.5 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Thirteen moves is a lot to hold in mind at a blank page. The method below turns them into an order of attack. Every assumption a search opens says, in its justification column, which move opened it: “asm, for ulename{{	o}I}” is the goal step for 	o, “asm, for ulename{\vee E}” the resource step for \vee, “asm, for ulename{RAA}” step 5. To state it we need a name for a derivation that is only half written. Partial derivations Here is the first snapshot of the first search below, for P 	o 
eg Q \vdash 
eg(P \wedge Q) \wedge (Q 	o 
eg P), drawn as in every section since Section 1.2: Each row \vdots is a gap. The written line just below a gap, here line 7 or line 13, is the gap’s current goal; it has no justification yet. The lines available at that goal, here the premise for the first gap and the premise and line 7 for the second, are the gap’s resources. The definition says the same thing exactly. [Partial Derivation] A partial derivation is a list of lines laid out as a derivation (@def-derivation), except that some stretches of lines are still missing. Each missing stretch is a gap, drawn as a row \vdots. The line just below a gap is its current goal; it is already written, but it has no justification yet, since the lines of the gap are to supply one. The lines available at the current goal, in the sense of @def-derivation, are the gap’s resources. In words: every line that has been written is a premise, an assumption, a current goal, or a line justified by a rule from lines and boxes available to it; the boxes are nested and closed as in any derivation; only the gaps are missing. A search starts with a single gap, below the premises and above the conclusion, and each step replaces a gap by lines, boxes, and smaller gaps. It ends when no gap is left, and then the partial derivation is a derivation. The snapshots in the worked searches below are all partial derivations; a line carries the number it will have in the finished derivation, and a line whose place is not yet fixed carries no number. On paper you would number the lines at the end. Nonexample. Take a snapshot and leave one of its boxes open at the bottom, so that the conclusion sits inside the box. That is not a partial derivation, even though every line is correct so far: @def-derivation asks that every box close and that the last line lie outside every box, and a gap cannot repair that, since filling a gap adds lines only above its current goal. The method Work from both ends: let the goal choose the boxes, let the premises choose the eliminations, and meet in the middle. Searching for a derivation of \Gamma \vdash \varphi. 1. Set up. Write the premises \Gamma at the top and \varphi at the bottom, with one gap between. 2. Goal-directed step. Take the main connective of the current goal (@def-main-connective) and set up its introduction rule: - \psi \wedge \chi: two gaps, with goals \psi and \chi (Section 1.2); - \psi 	o \chi: a box opened with \psi; inside it, the new goal is \chi (Section 1.4); - 
eg\psi: a box opened with \psi; inside it, the new goal is  ot (Section 2.2); - \psi \leftrightarrow \chi: two boxes, one from \psi to \chi and one from \chi to \psi (Section 2.4); - \psi \vee \chi: postpone; do not choose a side yet (Section 1.5). Repeat while the current goal is a \wedge, 	o, 
eg, or \leftrightarrow. 3. Premise-directed step. Take the main connective of a resource and apply its elimination rule: ulename{\wedge E} freely (Section 1.2); ulename{{	o}E} and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} when the other statement they need is a resource, or can be made a new goal (Sections 1.3 and 2.4); ulename{\vee E} by opening two boxes, one per disjunct, each ending in the current goal (Section 1.6). A derived rule may do the work of several lines (Section 2.3): a resource \psi 	o \chi with 
eg\chi available gives 
eg\psi by ulename{MT}; a resource \psi \vee \chi with 
eg\psi available gives \chi by ulename{DS}. 4. Clash. If the current goal is  ot, look for a pair \chi, 
eg\chi among the resources, or make \chi the new goal for some resource 
eg\chi and manufacture it, starting again at step 2 for that goal. Whatever the current goal, if the resources clash, or a clash with a resource 
eg\chi can be manufactured, write  ot and then the goal by ulename{ ot E}: an impossible case closes itself (Section 2.1). When the clash needs a disjunction whose negation is a resource, either side may be chosen to build it: once the disjunction is written,  ot follows. 5. Stuck. Use ulename{RAA}: open a box with the negation of the current goal, whose new goal is  ot; if that gives nothing, try the same with a goal further out whose box contains the stalled gap. Or use ulename{LEM} on a well-chosen statement \chi, and split on \chi \vee 
eg\chi by ulename{\vee E}. Then return to step 3 (Section 2.5). When no gap is left, number the lines and check the derivation as @def-derivation says. The steps are listed in the order in which to try them, and the order has reasons. - Step 2 loses nothing. If a gap with the goal \psi 	o \chi can be filled at all, so can the gap inside a box on \psi with the goal \chi. - Choosing a side of \vee can leave a goal that does not follow. From P \vee Q, with P true and Q false, the step to Q breaks. - Step 5 loses nothing either, and still comes last. The goal  ot gives step 2 nothing to work with, and a good statement to split on must be chosen. The goal-directed steps lose nothing. Suppose the goal \psi 	o \chi is derivable from the resources \Gamma at all, by some derivation D. Then \chi is derivable from \Gamma together with \psi: add \psi to the premises of D (@def-derivable asks only that the premises belong to the list), and append the line \chi by ulename{{	o}E}, citing the last line of D and the premise \psi. A derivation from \Gamma and \psi can be written inside the box, its premises from \Gamma cited as available lines and \psi as the box’s assumption (the pasting of @lem-weakening-cut). So opening a box on \psi never turns a derivable gap into an underivable one. With ulename{\wedge E}, ulename{
eg E}, or ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} as the appended line, the same argument covers \wedge, 
eg, and \leftrightarrow. That is why step 2 may be applied without thinking. Choosing a side of \vee can leave a goal that does not follow. A disjunction can be derivable when neither side follows from the resources. From P \vee Q the goal Q \vee P is derivable (@exm-disjunction-first-derivations), but P \vee Q does not say which side holds, so a last line ulename{\vee I} from Q, or from P, leaves a gap whose goal does not follow from its resources: P true and Q false makes P \vee Q true and Q false. Choosing a side is safe only once the resources decide it, typically inside a case of ulename{\vee E}, or when the disjunction is being manufactured for a clash (step 4) with a resource that is its negation: then the resources derive  ot as soon as they derive the disjunction, and from  ot every statement, either side included, by ulename{ ot E}. Step 5 also loses nothing, and still comes last. If \varphi is derivable from the resources, then  ot is derivable from them together with 
eg\varphi, by one appended ulename{
eg E}; so an ulename{RAA} box is always safe. A split on \chi \vee 
eg\chi is safe too, since each case only adds a resource. A mathematical goal The method reads the frame of a proof off the goal whether the statements are letters or facts about numbers. In ordinary mathematics its payoff is that the first and last sentences of a proof, and its division into parts, are fixed before any mathematics is done. [Building a skeleton] Let m and n be integers. Prove that if mn is odd, then m is odd and n is odd. The skeleton. The main connective is “if … then”, so step 2 opens a ulename{{	o}I} box: “Assume mn is odd. … Hence m is odd and n is odd.” The new goal is a conjunction, so step 2 again: two separate proofs, one that m is odd and one that n is odd. Each is a letter as far as logic can see, and the one resource, “mn is odd”, cannot be taken apart. So step 3 brings in facts we can compute with: “if m is even then mn is even” is one, and ulename{CP} (@prp-contrapositive) turns it into “if mn is not even then m is not even”, which the resource can feed. Then “every integer is even or odd” and ulename{DS} finish. The givens and the goal are tabulated in the fold below. The proof. Assume mn is odd. We show that m is odd and that n is odd. First, if m is even, say m = 2k with k an integer, then mn = 2(kn) is even. By the contrapositive (@prp-contrapositive), if mn is not even, then m is not even. Now mn is odd, so it is not even, since no integer is both; hence m is not even. Since every integer is even or odd, m is odd, by @prp-disjunctive-syllogism. Exchanging the roles of m and n in the previous paragraph shows that n is odd. Hence m and n are both odd. What the method did. It fixed the first sentence, the two paragraphs, and the last sentence; the only computation is mn = 2(kn). To derive a goal \varphi, it is tempting to open a box with \varphi. The box reaches \varphi at once, but after it closes it gives \varphi 	o \varphi, not \varphi, and its assumption is gone. An assumption is useful when the goal asks for it: the hypothesis of an implication (step 2), the negated goal of ulename{RAA} (step 5), a disjunct of a resource (step 3). Opening the box on the conclusion of an implication is the converse error of Argument B, diagnosed in Section 1.4. A derivation of \Gamma \vdash \varphi says that whoever accepts every member of \Gamma is committed to \varphi. It does not say that \varphi should now be believed. If \varphi is plainly false, say 0 = 1, the derivation is a reason to give up a member of \Gamma, and it does not say which. A mathematician who derives 0 = 1 from the hypotheses of a lemma has learned that those hypotheses cannot hold together; Section 3.2 calls such a list inconsistent, and a proof by contradiction is built to reach exactly that. title: 3.2 Four Kinds of Task
content:
Four Kinds of Task The method of Section 3.1 answers one kind of question: here are premises, here is a conclusion, find a derivation. Mathematics asks others as well: - prove a statement from nothing; - show that two statements say the same thing; - show that some conditions cannot all be met at once; - decide whether a conclusion follows at all, when nobody says whether it does. Each of these changes where a search starts and what counts as its end. This section takes the four tasks in turn. Underneath, it finds, they are one question. Four tasks, one method Let the task choose the search. The four tasks use the same rules and the same method. What differs is the first move and the finish line. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Task The claim Where the search starts What ends it ----------------- ------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------- theorem \vdash \varphi step 2 on the goal; every resource is an assumption the goal asks for the goal, reached outside every box equivalence \varphi \dashv\vdash \psi (@def-provable-equivalence) two searches, one from each side two derivations inconsistency \Gamma \vdash  ot step 4: the goal is  ot; look for a clash partner already on a line  ot, outside every box derive or break \Gamma \vdash \varphi? (verdict withheld) try to break it first a derivation, or statements that make the counterexample set true --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Only the last task leaves open which way it ends. The other three state their claim: a failed search leaves the question open, as Section 3.1’s failed search did, and a break ends the task against the claim. Which task is each? (i) \vdash P \vee 
eg P. (ii) P \wedge Q \dashv\vdash Q \wedge P. (iii) Show that P, 
eg P \vee Q and 
eg Q cannot all be accepted together. (iv) Does P 	o Q, \ Q \vdash P hold? (i) A theorem. (ii) An equivalence. (iii) An inconsistency: the claim P, \ 
eg P \vee Q, \ 
eg Q \vdash  ot. (iv) Derive or break; it breaks, since it is affirming the consequent (Section 1.3). Theorems A theorem of logic is a statement derivable from no premises, \vdash \varphi (@def-derivable with the list empty). [A statement that implies a contradiction] Find a derivation of \vdash (P 	o (Q \wedge 
eg Q)) 	o 
eg P. In words: a statement that implies a contradiction is false. Every proof that begins “suppose P” and ends “which is impossible” has this shape. There are no premises, so step 1 writes only the goal. Step 2 opens a box on P 	o (Q \wedge 
eg Q) with the goal 
eg P, and then, inside it, a box on P with the goal  ot: Now there are two resources, both assumptions the goal asked for. Step 3 fires the first on the second, giving Q \wedge 
eg Q, and splits it by ulename{\wedge E}. Step 4 finds the clash. A theorem has no premises, so the goal does all the early work. Once proved, it is a derived rule with nothing above the line (@def-derived-rule): any derivation, from any premises, may write an instance of it as a line, as derivations already write ulename{LEM}. Equivalences [Proving a disjunction by refuting one side] Show that P 	o (Q \vee R) \dashv\vdash (P \wedge 
eg Q) 	o R. This is how mathematics proves a disjunction: to show that ab = 0 implies a = 0 or b = 0, assume ab = 0 and a 
e 0, and show b = 0 (divide by a). The equivalence says that this changes nothing. (\Rightarrow) The goal is an implication, so a box on P \wedge 
eg Q. ulename{\wedge E} splits it, the premise fires on P, and ulename{DS} removes the refuted side. (\Leftarrow) The goal is an implication: a box on P, with the goal Q \vee R. That goal is a disjunction, so it is postponed (step 2). The premise waits for P \wedge 
eg Q: P is in hand, 
eg Q is not, and nothing clashes. That is step 5, and the well-chosen statement is Q, whose negation the premise waits for: ulename{LEM} on Q. In the case Q, ulename{\vee I} gives the left side. In the case 
eg Q, ulename{\wedge I} builds P \wedge 
eg Q, the premise gives R, and ulename{\vee I} gives the right side. An equivalence is two searches, and they need not be alike. The direction (\Rightarrow) used a derived rule and no classical step. The direction (\Leftarrow) reached step 5, because its goal was a disjunction with no side in hand. When one direction is easy, do it first: it checks that the statements are worth comparing, and its lines often suggest the other direction’s split. Inconsistent lists Sometimes the task is not to reach a conclusion but to show that some statements cannot be accepted together: a puzzle’s conditions that no number meets, the hypotheses of a lemma that contradict each other, or the assumption of a proof by contradiction together with what is given. Section 2.5 (@exr-reductio-and-classical-rules-b5) already read an ulename{RAA} derivation as a derivation of  ot from the counterexample set. A derivation of  ot does this job, and the list it starts from gets a name. [Inconsistent and Consistent Lists] Let \Gamma be a list of statements \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n, where n \ge 0. The list \Gamma is inconsistent if \Gamma \vdash  ot: some derivation whose premises all belong to \Gamma has  ot as its last line. It is consistent if it is not inconsistent, that is, if no derivation with premises in \Gamma ends with  ot. In words: a list is inconsistent when a derivation from it reaches  ot outside every box. The definition speaks only of derivations, and says nothing about whether the statements are true. The list P, 
eg P is inconsistent, by one ulename{
eg E} line, and so is any list with  ot as a member. To show a list inconsistent, exhibit a derivation. To show one consistent, one would have to rule out every derivation, and nothing in this chapter can do that. [An Inconsistent List Proves Everything] For a list of statements \Gamma, the following are equivalent: 1. \Gamma is inconsistent; 2. \Gamma \vdash \psi for every statement \psi; 3. \Gamma \vdash \chi and \Gamma \vdash 
eg\chi for some statement \chi. In words: an inconsistent list proves every statement, and a list that proves some statement and its negation is inconsistent. This is @prp-ex-falso grown from two premises to any inconsistent list. Its proof is in the fold of the next subsection. Without writing a derivation, explain why P, \ 
eg P \vdash Q \wedge 
eg Q. The list P, 
eg P is inconsistent (one ulename{
eg E} line), so by @prp-inconsistent-derives-everything, (i) \Rightarrow (ii), it derives every statement, Q \wedge 
eg Q included. [Four conditions that no integer meets] Let n be an integer. A puzzle asks for an n such that: 1. if n is even, then n is a multiple of 4; 2. n is even or a multiple of 3; 3. if n is a multiple of 3, then n is even; 4. n is not a multiple of 4. With E: “n is even”, F: “n is a multiple of 4” and T: “n is a multiple of 3”, show that the list E 	o F, \ E \vee T, \ T 	o E, \ 
eg F is inconsistent. The goal is  ot. Look first for a clash partner already on a line (Section 3.1): line 4 is 
eg F, so aim at F. F is the conclusion of line 1, so the new goal is E, a letter. Line 3 gives E from T, but T is not in hand, and E \vee T does not say which side holds. So use line 2 by ulename{\vee E}, with both cases ending in E. The case E is a one-line box; the case T fires line 3. Read as a proof about n, the derivation shows that no integer meets all four conditions: by (2) and (3), n is even in either case; by (1) it is a multiple of 4; and (4) says it is not. Yet any three of the conditions can be met together: n = 6 meets all but (1), n = 1 all but (2), n = 3 all but (3), and n = 12 all but (4). The inconsistency belongs to the four together. The derivation does not say which condition to drop (the fold “Logic permits; it does not choose” in Section 3.1). Which integers between 1 and 10 meet conditions (1), (2) and (4) of @exm-inconsistency-search, and which condition does each break? 3 and 9: they are odd, so (1) promises nothing; they are multiples of 3, so (2) holds; and they are not multiples of 4. Each breaks (3). Here are three more inconsistent lists, each with compound members, and one list that only looks inconsistent. title: 3.3 From Argument to Derivation
content:
From Argument to Derivation Most searches in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 started from a sequent: its letters, its premises and its conclusion were given. Mathematics starts from a paragraph. Its premises are scattered among words such as “since” and “so”; some of them are not written at all; and its letters must be chosen. This section turns paragraphs into sequents and derives them. Then it goes the other way, and writes a proof beside the derivation it mirrors. A last page collects the sequents that searches keep needing. One key for the section Section 1.1, Exercise B5, fixed one key for an integer n, and this section keeps it: E: “n is even”, P: “n is prime”, T: “n is a multiple of 3”, G: “n > 10” (@exr-statements-and-connectives-b5). A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. Three facts about integers will serve as premises: - F1 (P \wedge E) 	o 
eg G: an even prime is at most 10. The only even prime is 2, since an even n > 2 has the divisor 2. - F2 (P \wedge T) 	o 
eg G: a prime multiple of 3 is at most 10. The only one is 3, since a multiple of 3 greater than 3 has the divisor 3. - F3 (E \wedge T) 	o 
eg P: no even multiple of 3 is prime. Such an integer is a multiple of 6. A positive multiple of 6 has the divisor 2 and is greater than 2, and 0 and the negative integers are not prime. Each fact is true for every integer n. An argument may use any of them as a premise, and a derivation lists the ones it uses. A translation is checked by reading it back, letter by letter, as in Section 1.1: F3 reads back as “if n is even and a multiple of 3, then n is not prime”. On the key, translate “n is an odd prime greater than 10”. Then read back G 	o 
eg(P \wedge E). (
eg E \wedge P) \wedge G. And G 	o 
eg(P \wedge E) reads back as “if n > 10, then n is not an even prime”. Extracting an argument To turn a paragraph into a sequent, work through five steps. 1. Find the conclusion. Words such as so, hence, therefore, thus and it follows that introduce it. 2. Find the stated premises. Words such as since, because, for and given that introduce them. A supposition (“suppose …”, “let n be …”) is a premise, or the assumption of a box. 3. Name the unstated facts. The 7-line ending ulename{{	o}E} 5, 6 earns full marks; the detour remark is not required. - 3: (b), the conclusion that no statement meets the condition, with the inconsistency. - 3: (c), the rules of the reader’s own derivation named correctly, and the point that a derivation using only ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}, ulename{{	o}I} and ulename{{	o}E} exists (the model), so no negation rule is needed. Fatal error (0 for (a)): Q obtained inside the box and carried out of it. R. Review [R1] For real numbers a and b, let \max(a, b) \coloneqq a and \min(a, b) \coloneqq b if a \ge b, and \max(a, b) \coloneqq b and \min(a, b) \coloneqq a if a < b. Prove that \max(a, b) + \min(a, b) = a + b. Since a \ge b or a < b, and these two cases cover every pair of real numbers, we argue by cases (ulename{\vee E}, @def-rules-disjunction), as in @exm-abs-product-cases. Case a \ge b. Then \max(a, b) = a and \min(a, b) = b, so \max(a, b) + \min(a, b) = a + b. Case a < b. Then \max(a, b) = b and \min(a, b) = a, so \max(a, b) + \min(a, b) = b + a = a + b. In either case the equation holds, which proves it. Both cases end in the same statement, the goal, as ulename{\vee E} requires. [R2] Let x be a real number. Write N for “x < 0”, M for “x > 1”, and S for “x = 7”. Translate the argument below into a sequent in these letters, and derive it. x is neither negative nor greater than 1. Therefore x is not negative, and if x is greater than 1, then x = 7. The phrase book (Section 1.1) gives “neither … nor” as

eg I} box on N), and the second an implication (a box on M). In both boxes ulename{\vee I} builds N \vee M, which clashes with the premise; in the second box ulename{ ot E} then gives S. Lines 2–5 are half of @prp-de-morgan (a), which turns 
eg(N \vee M) into the phrase book’s

The implication M 	o S is vacuously true, as in @prp-vacuous-implication: the premise rules out M, and a promise never tested is never broken, whatever S says. [R3] Is (P 	o Q) 	o R \vdash P 	o (Q 	o R) derivable? Derive or break its converse, P 	o (Q 	o R) \vdash (P 	o Q) 	o R. The first is derivable, by the search method of Section 3.1. The goal gives a box on P, then a box on Q, with the goal R. The premise gives R by ulename{{	o}E} once we produce P 	o Q, a new goal: a box on P whose last line repeats Q. The repetition at line 5 puts Q inside the box of line 4, as ulename{{	o}I} requires (clause (D3) of @def-derivation). Two look-alike tools do not apply. @prp-curry moves a conjunction in and out of a hypothesis, (P \wedge Q) 	o R \dashv\vdash P 	o (Q 	o R), and the premise here has P 	o Q, not P \wedge Q, in that place. And @prp-implication-transitive chains two implications, which we do not have. The converse breaks: with P and R false (and Q either way), the premise P 	o (Q 	o R) is true because P is false, while P 	o Q is true and R is false, so the conclusion is false. Chapter 4 proves that such a choice rules out every derivation, so that a search for it can only stall: the chapter’s open question, in a new place. [R4] Ana and Ben talk about a real number. Ana. Let x be a real number with x^2 < x. Then x is positive. Ben. Why can’t it be negative? Ana. A negative number is less than its square. Ben. And zero? Ana. At zero, x^2 equals x. And x is less than 1, because for x \ge 1 we would have x^2 \ge x. Ben. So 0 < x < 1. But you never said why x^2 \ge x when x \ge 1. Ana. Multiply x \ge 1 by x, which is positive. 1. What is the conclusion, and who states it? 2. Turn the dialogue into a derivation. 3. Is Ana’s last answer enough? (a) “0 < x < 1”, stated by Ben. Ana’s first line, “x is positive”, is an intermediate step. (b) With, for instance, N: “x < 0”, Z: “x = 0”, B: “x \ge 1”, L: “x^2 < x”, the premise is L. The facts: - N 	o
