title: Truth, Soundness and Completeness
content:
Truth, Soundness and Completeness Chapter 3 ended on a question: we show that something is derivable by exhibiting a derivation, but how could we ever show that something is not derivable? Section 3.1 searched for a derivation of P 	o Q \vdash Q 	o P, and every route stalled. A search that fails proves nothing: a cleverer derivation might exist. Here is something that does prove it. p q p 	o q q 	o p --- --- --------- --------- ---------- T T T T T F F T F T T F this row F F T T In the third row the premise p 	o q (Section 4.1 says why the letters are now lower-case) is true, because its hypothesis is false (the promise reading of Section 1.1), and the conclusion q 	o p is false. By the end of this chapter this one row is a proof that no derivation of q 	o p from p 	o q exists, however long. The answer is to give formulas a meaning. Soundness says that whatever can be derived is true in every row where the premises are true; so one such row with a false conclusion proves that no derivation exists. Completeness says that whatever is true in every such row can be derived. To prove them, formulas become objects and induction arrives. Between the two theorems sits a search (Section 4.6) that, for any finite list of premises and any conclusion, finds a refuting row or shows that there is none. The core ends with completeness; normal forms, the constructive content of completeness (second pass), and compactness (optional) follow. What you need. Chapters 1–3: the rules for every connective, the definition of a derivation with its boxes and its scope rule (@def-derivation), derived rules and @lem-weakening-cut (Section 2.3), the classical rules of Section 2.5, above all @prp-excluded-middle, the search method of Section 3.1, and the four kinds of task of Section 3.2 with its word consistent (@def-inconsistent-set). The arithmetic and order of the natural numbers are school facts. Time. About 45 hours on the core track (Sections 4.1–4.8: all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 90 hours for everything. Minimum before Sets and Functions. Chapters 1–6 and 8, core; Sections 7.1–7.2 before its Section 4.1. How to read this chapter. A first reading takes Sections 4.1–4.8 with every second-reading fold closed. Each section’s main line teaches the section, and every A and B exercise can be done from it. The folds hold the proofs of structural induction, the parenthesis count and structural recursion, the bookkeeping lemmas, the proof that the search of Section 4.6 decides, and the descent in the completeness proof. They are not optional: later proofs use those results, and the proofs are complete. Section 4.9, on normal forms, is a second-pass section; nothing in Chapters 5–8 uses it. Section 4.10, on compactness, is optional; nothing outside it depends on it. Roadmap - Formulas as Objects. The exact definition of a formula, parse trees, the object language and the metalanguage, and substitution into a derivation. - Induction on the Natural Numbers. The principle, strong induction, a checklist for every induction, and proving more in order to prove less. - Induction and Recursion on Formulas. Structural induction, a count of parentheses, the proof that every formula is read in only one way, and definitions by recursion, which fail without it. - Valuations and Truth Tables. The value of every formula computed from its atoms, 2^n rows for n atoms, truth-functional connectives, and a game for the clauses. - Tautologies, Entailment and Equivalence. \Gamma \models \psi, satisfiable and contingent formulas, contradictory and contrary pairs, replacement and substitution, and every question reduced to one: is this list unsatisfiable? - Hunting for a Refuting Row. Forced moves, splits, the search drawn as a tree, and why a closed tree proves an entailment. - Soundness. Every rule checked against the tables, by induction on the lines of a derivation, so that one refuting row rules out every derivation; and the move test the subgoal. - Completeness. The rules prove their own truth tables row by row, and excluded middle glues the rows; consistent and satisfiable coincide; a truth-table step, TAUT. - Normal Forms and Adequate Connectives (second pass). Normal forms, adequate connectives, calculating with equivalences, and why a stronger hypothesis gives a weaker theorem. - Compactness and Maximal Consistent Sets (optional). Infinitely many premises, Lindenbaum’s construction, and why every finite part satisfiable means the whole is. Named moves - Induction on the shape of a formula. Prove it for atoms and  ot, then for each connective from the parts. (Section 4.3) - Check the induction. Objects, property, base cases, steps, principle. (Section 4.2) - Prove more to prove less. Strengthen the claim until the step goes through. (Sections 4.2, 4.3) - Define by recursion on formulas. One clause per way of building a formula. (Section 4.3) - Work backwards from F. Assume the formula false and follow what is forced. (Section 4.4) - Reduce to unsatisfiability. Every semantic question asks whether some list is unsatisfiable. (Section 4.5) - Search for a refuting row. Forced moves first, split when nothing is forced, close branches early. (Section 4.6) - Refute with one row. One refuting row proves \Gamma 
vdash \psi, by soundness. (Section 4.7) - Test the subgoal. Before chasing a subgoal, look for a row that refutes it. (Section 4.7) - Induction on the lines of a derivation. Show that every rule preserves the property. (Section 4.7) - Split on an atom. With p \vee 
eg p and ulename{\vee E}, prove the goal under p and under 
eg p. (Section 4.8) Where this goes. Chapter 5 looks inside the atoms: it gives “every” and “some” their rules and their meaning. Chapter 8 says what reductio asserts that the other rules do not, and who objected to it. Chapter 7 gives the formulas of predicate logic structures in place of rows; it shows a theory consistent, and an axiom independent, by exhibiting a model (Section 7.4), asks which sets a formula can define (Section 7.5), and states completeness and compactness for predicate logic (Section 7.6, optional). Three later volumes take up threads of this chapter. Sets and Functions makes “the smallest collection of strings closed under the building steps” and “function” exact (Chapter 1). It proves induction equivalent to the well-ordering principle and shows a famous false induction that breaks at its first step (Chapter 2). Number Systems: From 
N to 
R derives induction from the axioms of set theory (Chapter 1). Analysis on the Real Line takes the least upper bound axiom as given, as this chapter takes induction (Chapter 1). Summary Formulas are strings built by the clauses of @def-formula, and each is read in only one way (@thm-unique-readability), so a function on formulas can be defined by one clause per connective. Induction, on the numbers and on formulas, is the tool for statements about all of them; its checklist and its strengthening are the two habits it needs. A valuation gives every formula a truth value, and entailment, satisfiable, contingent and the pair relations are defined from rows. Every semantic question reduces to whether some list is unsatisfiable, and a search tree decides it (@prp-search-decides). Soundness (@thm-soundness) says that a refuting row rules out every derivation, and completeness (@thm-completeness) that every valid sequent has a derivation; so \vdash and \models coincide, and so do consistent and satisfiable, and derivability is decided by a finite table. TAUT records a truth-table step as one line. All of this is proved for propositional formulas and finitely many premises (infinitely many in the optional Section 4.10). What is open is the inside of an atom: “for every \varepsilon > 0 there is an N” is one letter to a truth table, and how to reason inside it is Chapter 5’s question. Also still open: which tautologies need reductio (the optional @thm-raa-independent settles two), and how short a derivation can be. Terms - adequate set of connectives: expresses every truth function (@def-adequate). - atom: one letter such as p, q, p_1, a formula alone (@def-formula). - conjunctive, disjunctive normal form: an “and” of “or”s; an “or” of “and”s (@def-cnf, @def-dnf). - contingent formula: true in some row and false in another (@def-tautology). - contradiction: a formula false in every row (@def-tautology). - contradictory, contrary, subcontrary: exactly one true; never both true; never both false (@def-pair-relations). - entailment, \Gamma \models \psi: no refuting row (@def-valid-argument). - formula: a string built from atoms and  ot by the connectives (@def-formula). - height: the nodes on a longest branch of the parse tree (@def-height). - induction: from P(0) and each step, P(n) for every n (@ax-induction). - literal: an atom or the negation of an atom (@def-literal). - parse tree: the tree showing how a formula is built (@def-parse-tree). - positive, negative occurrence: a part’s sign, flipped by 
eg and by hypotheses (@def-occurrence-polarity). - premises, infinitely many: \vdash and \models for a collection (@def-infinite-entailment). - refuting row: premises true and conclusion false (@def-valid-argument). - satisfiable: some row makes every member true (@def-satisfiable). - search tree: the hunt for a refuting row, drawn (@def-search-tree). - semantic equivalence, \equiv: the same value in every row (@def-semantic-equivalence). - subformula: a formula met while building another (@def-subformula). - TAUT: one line for a truth-table step (@def-rule-taut). - tautology: a formula true in every row (@def-tautology). - truth function: a truth value for each list of truth values (@def-truth-function). - truth table: a formula’s value in each of the 2^n rows (@def-truth-table). - truth value: T or F, computed from the atoms (@def-truth-value). - valuation: a choice of T or F for each atom (@def-valuation).

title: 4.1 Formulas as Objects
content:
Formulas as Objects Chapter 3 ended on a question that no derivation can answer. We show that a sequent holds by writing a derivation of it; but how could we show that one does not hold, that no derivation of Q 	o P from P 	o Q exists, however long and however clever? This chapter’s answer is a theorem about every derivation of every formula, and such a theorem needs, first of all, an exact description of what a formula is. This section gives it. Why formulas must become objects Here is the theorem that Section 4.7 proves, stated loosely: If \psi can be derived from premises \Gamma, then \psi is true in every situation in which all the premises are true. Read it as a mathematician reads a statement about all integers. “For every integer n, n^2 - n is even” can be proved only by someone who knows what an integer is: every integer is even or odd, and each kind can be handled. A proof needs a way to take hold of an arbitrary object of the kind the statement is about. The loose theorem above is about arbitrary derivations, and a derivation is a list of formulas, so the proof will need a way to take hold of an arbitrary formula. Chapters 1–3 never needed one. There we read statements by eye: we found the main connective of 
eg(P \wedge Q) 	o R (@def-main-connective) by looking, and we drew its tree by hand. That is fine for one statement at a time. It is useless for a claim about all statements, because “all the strings we would recognize as statements” is not a description anyone can reason from. So we now say exactly which objects we mean, in a form that later proofs can use. The description has three parts. First, the alphabet, the symbols formulas are written with. Second, the formation rules, which say how formulas are built. Third, a closing clause saying that nothing else is a formula. The third is the one that is easy to forget and that makes everything else work. The alphabet Formulas are strings of symbols. A string is a finite list of symbols written one after another, and its length is the number of symbols in it. The symbols are these. - Atoms: p, q, r, p_1, p_2, p_3, \dots, infinitely many of them. Each atom is one symbol: p_1 is a single symbol whose name happens to carry a subscript, not the two symbols p and 1. - The constant  ot, read “contradiction”, as in Chapter 1. - The connectives: 
eg (the only one that takes one part) and \wedge, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow (the binary connectives, which take two). - The parentheses ( and ). An atom plays the part that a letter played in Chapters 1–3: a statement whose inner structure we ignore. In those chapters the letters were capitals, P, Q, R, and they stood for arbitrary statements, atomic or compound. From now on we keep two kinds of letter apart, because the theorems of this chapter need the difference. Who is who: the letters of this chapter. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Letter Stands for Inside a formula? Example --------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------- ---------------------------------------------- p, q, r, p_1, p_2, \dots an atom, one symbol of the language yes (p \wedge 
eg q) \varphi, \psi, \chi (phi, psi, chi) any formula: a metavariable, a name we use when talking about formulas never “if \varphi is a formula, so is 
eg\varphi” \Gamma, \Delta (capital gamma, delta) a finite list of formulas, as in the sequents of Chapter 1 (@def-derivable) never \Gamma \vdash \psi P, Q, R of Chapters 1–3 arbitrary statements; read from now on as atoms, or as any formulas (the last part of this section) they are replaced P 	o Q read as p 	o q ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Chapter 1 already used the three letters \varphi, \psi, \chi in exactly this way, in the schemas of its rules (@def-rule-schema). Which of these is a formula, and which is a name for formulas or for a list: (p 	o q); (\varphi 	o q); \Gamma? (p 	o q) is a formula. (\varphi 	o q) is not a formula, since \varphi is no symbol of the language; it is a pattern, and each formula put in for \varphi gives a formula. \Gamma names a list of formulas. Two languages. Everything in this chapter is said in two languages at once. The object language is the language of formulas: its expressions are strings over the alphabet above, such as (p 	o q). The metalanguage is the language in which we talk about those strings: English with ordinary mathematics, together with names for formulas (\varphi, \psi) and for lists (\Gamma), and claims such as \Gamma \vdash \psi and, from Section 4.5 on, \Gamma \models \psi. Neither \vdash nor \models is a symbol of the alphabet. The sentence “(p 	o q) has length 5” belongs to the metalanguage and speaks about a string of the object language; (p 	o q) on its own is a string, not a claim. The theorems of this chapter, unique readability, soundness and completeness, are theorems about the object language, proved in the metalanguage by ordinary mathematics: induction, cases, counting. To speak about a symbol we name it, as we name a word. “p is an atom” mentions the symbol p, in the way that “‘seven’ has five letters” mentions a word. Sort into strings of the object language, claims of the metalanguage, and neither: 1. ((p \wedge q) 	o p) 2. p \wedge q \vdash p 3. the main connective of ((p \wedge q) 	o p) is 	o 4. (\varphi \wedge q) 5. 
eg ot is a formula (a) A string of the object language: a formula. (b) A claim of the metalanguage, since \vdash is not a symbol of the alphabet. It is true, by ulename{\wedge E}. (c) A claim of the metalanguage, and true. (d) Neither. The letter \varphi is a metavariable, not a symbol, so the expression is a pattern; each formula put in for \varphi gives a formula. (e) A claim of the metalanguage, and true:  ot is a formula, and 
eg in front of a formula gives a formula (clauses (F1) and (F2) of the definition below). Formulas Chapter 1 described a statement as something “built from smaller ones by a connective”. The definition below says exactly how the building goes. It is an inductive definition: it names the starting pieces, names the ways of building new formulas from old, and then closes the door on everything else. Building one formula. Here is the formula ((p \wedge 
eg q) 	o p) built one step at a time. Each entry is an atom, or is built from earlier entries by one connective. The atom p is used twice and listed once. A list like this is called a formation sequence. The definition below has one more clause than the building steps. Its clause (F4) says that the formulas are exactly the last entries of such lists: the list you just saw, in general. In clause (F4) below, \circ stands for any one of the four binary connectives, as \varphi stands for any formula: (\chi_j \circ \chi_l) means any one of (\chi_j \wedge \chi_l), (\chi_j \vee \chi_l), (\chi_j 	o \chi_l), (\chi_j \leftrightarrow \chi_l). A formula is a string built from atoms and  ot by the connectives, one step at a time, with a pair of parentheses around every binary step. [Formula] The formulas are the strings given by the following clauses. 1. Every atom is a formula, and  ot is a formula. 2. If \varphi is a formula, then 
eg\varphi is a formula. 3. If \varphi and \psi are formulas, then (\varphi \wedge \psi), (\varphi \vee \psi), (\varphi 	o \psi) and (\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) are formulas. 4. Nothing else is a formula: a string is a formula only if it is the last entry of a formation sequence. A formation sequence is a finite list of strings \chi_1, \dots, \chi_m, with m \ge 1, in which every entry \chi_i is an atom or  ot, or is 
eg\chi_j for some earlier entry \chi_j (so j < i), or is (\chi_j \circ \chi_l) for some earlier entries \chi_j and \chi_l (so j, l < i; j = l is allowed) and some binary connective \circ. In words, clause by clause. - (F1), the starting pieces. A single atom is a formula, and so is  ot. These are the only formulas of length one. - (F2), negation. Writing 
eg in front of a formula gives a formula. No parentheses are added: 
eg p and 
eg
eg p are formulas, and 
eg
eg p is 
eg in front of the formula 
eg p. - (F3), the binary connectives. Writing a binary connective between two formulas and wrapping the result in one pair of parentheses gives a formula. The two formulas may be the same: (p \wedge p) is a formula. - (F4), nothing else. Clauses (F1)–(F3) say which strings are formulas. They do not say that other strings are not. Clause (F4) does: a formula is exactly something we can reach from atoms and  ot by finitely many uses of (F2) and (F3), and the formation sequence is the written record of such a reaching. Think of building blocks: (F1) lists the blocks, (F2) and (F3) the two ways of joining them, and (F4) says that only what is built in this way counts. Two facts about formation sequences are used constantly, and both are immediate from the definition. First, every entry of a formation sequence is a formula. Walk along the list. The first entry \chi_1 is an atom or  ot, so it is a formula by (F1). Each later entry is an atom or  ot, a formula by (F1), or it is 
eg\chi_j or (\chi_j \circ \chi_l) for earlier entries that are already formulas, and so it is a formula by (F2) or (F3). (Section 4.3 makes this walk exact with strong induction, in the fold “Sets built from a base”.) Second, every formula was made by one of the clauses from formulas. Take a formula \chi and a formation sequence ending in it. Its last entry \chi is an atom or  ot, or it is 
eg\chi_j, or it is (\chi_j \circ \chi_l), where the earlier entries \chi_j, \chi_l are formulas by the first fact. So every formula is an atom, or  ot, or 
eg\varphi for a formula \varphi, or (\varphi \circ \psi) for formulas \varphi, \psi. We will call this looking at the last step of a formula. Looking at the last step already tells us something about the first symbol. A formula of the form 
eg\varphi begins with 
eg, and one of the form (\varphi \circ \psi) begins with ( and ends with ). So: The first-symbol test. A formula of length one is an atom or  ot. A longer formula begins with 
eg or with (, and if it begins with (, it is (\varphi \circ \psi) for formulas \varphi, \psi and ends with ). (A formula of the form 
eg\varphi has length at least 2, and one of the form (\varphi \circ \psi) has length at least 5, since \varphi and \psi each have at least one symbol. So a formula of length one is made by (F1).) Write a formation sequence for 
eg(p \vee  ot), and say which earlier entries each entry uses. p, \  ot, \ (p \vee  ot), \ 
eg(p \vee  ot). Entry 3 uses entries 1 and 2, and entry 4 uses entry 3; entries 1 and 2 use none. [Formation sequences] Write down a formation sequence for each of the strings p,  ot, 
eg
eg q and (
eg p \vee (q 	o  ot)), which shows that each is a formula. For p, the one-entry list p is a formation sequence: its only entry is an atom. Likewise the list  ot. These are the degenerate cases, and they matter: a formula need not have been built at all. Every structural argument in Section 4.3 has to deal with them. For 
eg
eg q: q, \quad 
eg q, \quad 
eg
eg q . The first entry is an atom; the second is 
eg in front of the first; the third is 
eg in front of the second. For (
eg p \vee (q 	o  ot)): p, \quad 
eg p, \quad q, \quad  ot, \quad (q 	o  ot), \quad (
eg p \vee (q 	o  ot)) . Entries 1, 3 and 4 are atoms or  ot. Entry 2 is 
eg in front of entry 1. Entry 5 is (\chi_3 	o \chi_4), and entry 6 is (\chi_2 \vee \chi_5). A formula has many formation sequences. In @exm-formation-sequences we could have listed q before p in the last list, or added entries that are never used, such as r or 
eg r. The definition asks only that some formation sequence ends in the string, and nothing in this chapter depends on which one we take. To show that a string is a formula, we exhibit a formation sequence, just as we show that a sequent holds by exhibiting a derivation. To show that a string is not a formula, exhibiting is not enough; we need a property that every formula has and the string lacks. The first-symbol test supplies such properties. [Strings that are not formulas] Show that none of the strings p \wedge 	o q, (p \wedge q, (
eg p) and p \wedge q is a formula. p \wedge 	o q: it has length 4, so by the first-symbol test a formula would begin with 
eg or (. It begins with p. Not a formula. (p \wedge q: it begins with (, so by the first-symbol test a formula would end with ). It ends with q. Not a formula. (The missing parenthesis is the whole problem: (p \wedge q) is a formula.) (
eg p): it begins with (, so a formula would have to be (\varphi \circ \psi), with the two symbols 
eg p between the parentheses equal to \varphi \circ \psi, and so containing a binary connective. The string 
eg p contains none. Not a formula. The official language puts no parentheses around a negation; (F2) adds none. p \wedge q: it has length 3 and begins with p. Not a formula. This one is a surprise at first, since we have written p \wedge q all along. It is shorthand for the formula (p \wedge q), in the way explained later in this section. The last two strings are ones Chapter 1 wrote freely, and that is no mistake in Chapter 1. Chapter 1 used a convenient shorthand; the official formulas carry every parenthesis that (F3) puts in and none that it does not. We come back to the shorthand below. Which of the following strings are formulas? For each, give a formation sequence or name the test it fails. 1. 
eg(p 	o  ot) 2. (p 	o 
eg) 3.  ot ot (a) A formula: p, \  ot, \ (p 	o  ot), \ 
eg(p 	o  ot) is a formation sequence. (b) Not a formula. It begins with (, so it would be (\varphi 	o \psi) with \varphi the string p and \psi the string 
eg (the only binary connective is the 	o). But 
eg is a string of length one that is neither an atom nor  ot, so by the first-symbol test it is not a formula. (c) Not a formula. It has length 2, so it would begin with 
eg or (; it begins with  ot. Why this definition Each feature of the definition is there because something breaks without it. Without (F4), clauses (F1)–(F3) would be satisfied by far too many collections of strings. The collection of all strings contains every atom and  ot, and is closed under writing 
eg in front and under wrapping two strings with a connective in parentheses; so (F1)–(F3) alone cannot tell us that p \wedge 	o q is excluded. Clause (F4) says the formulas are only those strings that the building steps reach. In other words, the formulas are the smallest collection of strings closed under (F1)–(F3). Without the parentheses in (F3), a string could be read in two ways. Take p \wedge q \vee r. Built one way, it is “p \wedge q” joined to r by \vee; built the other way, it is p joined to “q \vee r” by \wedge. The two constructions have different parse trees (defined below), and they say different things (the everyday reading of Chapter 1 is enough here): if p is false and r is true, then “p and q, or r” is true, because r is, while “p, and q or r” is false, because p is. With the parentheses of (F3) the two constructions give two different strings, ((p \wedge q) \vee r) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad (p \wedge (q \vee r)) , and the ambiguity disappears. Section 4.3 proves that it disappears for every formula: a formula can be built in only one way (the unique readability theorem). Why not parentheses around a negation too? Nothing would break, but nothing would be gained. The symbol 
eg always stands in front of what it negates, so 
eg\varphi can be read in only one way without help. Keeping the official language as lean as possible makes the proofs about it shorter. Why atoms, and not sentences like “x > 0”? Because the theorems of this chapter are about forms, and the form of an argument is what remains when the content of its atomic statements is forgotten (Chapter 1’s slogan: logic studies the forms of arguments). An atom is a statement reduced to a name. A formula is a string of symbols, and questions about formulas are questions about strings. “Is (p \wedge p) the same formula as p?” has the answer no: the first has length 5 and the second length 1, even though they always have the same truth value (Section 4.4 gives the means to check this). Sameness of formulas is letter-for-letter identity; sameness of meaning is a different relation, which Section 4.5 names. Parse trees A formation sequence records how a formula was built, but it is a list, and a list hides the shape of the building. Chapter 1 drew the shape as a tree, with the main connective at the top (the tree after @def-main-connective). We now make that drawing official. A parse tree is a formula’s construction drawn upside down: the last step at the root, the atoms at the leaves. [Parse Tree] A parse tree for a formula is defined along the clauses of @def-formula. 1. For an atom or  ot: a single node, labeled by that atom or by  ot. 2. If T is a parse tree for \varphi, then the tree whose root is labeled 
eg and has T hanging below it as its only subtree is a parse tree for 
eg\varphi. 3. If T and T' are parse trees for \varphi and \psi, then the tree whose root is labeled \circ, with T hanging below it on the left and T' on the right, is a parse tree for (\varphi \circ \psi). 4. Nothing else is a parse tree: a tree is a parse tree for a formula \varphi only if that follows from finitely many uses of (T1)–(T3). In particular, a parse tree for 
eg\varphi is made by (T2), and a parse tree for (\varphi \circ \psi) by (T3). The leaves are the nodes with nothing below them; a branch is a path from the root down to a leaf. In words: (T1) is the tree of a formula that was not built at all, a single node. (T2) puts a new root 
eg on top of an existing tree. (T3) joins two existing trees under a new root carrying the connective, keeping left and right apart, because (p 	o q) and (q 	o p) are different formulas. (T4), as (F4) did for formulas, says that only trees built this way count; Section 4.3 uses it when it asks how a given tree could have been made. Parentheses do not appear in a parse tree: their only job in the string was to show the grouping, and the tree shows the grouping by its shape. Every formula has a parse tree. Take a formation sequence of the formula and build a tree for each entry in turn: an atom or  ot gets (T1), and an entry 
eg\chi_j or (\chi_j \circ \chi_l) gets (T2) or (T3) from the trees already built for the earlier entries. The tree built for the last entry is a parse tree for the formula. Could a formula have two different parse trees? That would happen if one string could be built in two different ways, as p \wedge q \vee r could if parentheses were not written. Section 4.3 proves that it never happens (the unique readability theorem); until then we say “a parse tree”. After that section, every formula has exactly one, and we speak of the parse tree. [Three parse trees] Draw a parse tree for each formula: (a) p; (b) 
eg(p \wedge 
eg q); (c) ((p \leftrightarrow 
eg q) \vee (r \wedge ( ot 	o p))), which uses every connective and  ot. (a) A single node labeled p, by (T1). This is the degenerate tree: its root is also its only leaf, and its only branch has one node. (b) By (T1) the atoms p and q get one-node trees; (T2) puts 
eg above q; (T3) joins p and 
eg q under \wedge; (T2) puts 
eg on top. (c) The main connective is the \vee: it is the last step, joining (p \leftrightarrow 
eg q) on the left to (r \wedge ( ot 	o p)) on the right. Each side is taken apart in the same way. The leaves are p, q, r,  ot and p again: the atom p occurs twice in the formula, and each occurrence is its own leaf. To draw a parse tree from a string, find the last step, draw it as the root, and repeat on the parts. For a formula (\varphi \circ \psi), the last step is the binary connective that sits inside exactly one pair of parentheses; in (c), it is the \vee, and every other binary connective sits inside at least two pairs. Section 4.3 proves that this recipe always finds the main connective, and only it. Subformulas Each node of a parse tree is the root of the part of the tree below it, and that part is itself a parse tree, built by the same clauses, for a formula. The formulas that arise in this way are the pieces a formula is built from. [Subformula] The subformulas of a formula \varphi are the formulas whose parse trees hang from the nodes of a parse tree for \varphi: for each node, the formula of which the part of the tree from that node downwards is a parse tree. The formulas at the children of the root are the immediate subformulas of \varphi. Until Section 4.3 this depends, as far as we know, on the parse tree chosen; Section 4.3 shows there is only one, so the subformulas of \varphi are determined by \varphi. So the subformulas of \varphi include \varphi itself (at the root) and each atom that occurs in \varphi (at the leaves). A formula of the form 
eg\varphi has one immediate subformula, \varphi; a formula (\varphi \circ \psi) has the two immediate subformulas \varphi and \psi (one, if \varphi and \psi are the same formula); an atom or  ot has none. When we list the subformulas, a formula that sits at several nodes is listed once. For the formula (c) of @exm-parse-trees, the subformulas are  egin{gathered} ((p \leftrightarrow 
eg q) \vee (r \wedge ( ot 	o p))), \quad (p \leftrightarrow 
eg q), \quad (r \wedge ( ot 	o p)), \ 
eg q, \quad ( ot 	o p), \quad p, \quad q, \quad r, \quad  ot , \end{gathered} nine in all. The tree has ten nodes, \vee, \leftrightarrow, p, 
eg, q, \wedge, r, 	o,  ot and p again, and only p sits at two of them; so ten nodes give nine distinct subformulas. Counting by eye is easy to get wrong, and the safe method is to walk the tree node by node, as we just did. A string that merely appears inside a formula need not be a subformula. The formula ((p \wedge q) \vee r) contains the string q) \vee r, which is not a formula at all, and it contains the string p \wedge q, which is only the shorthand of a formula. Its subformulas are the formulas at the nodes: ((p \wedge q) \vee r), (p \wedge q), p, q and r. Draw the parse tree of (
eg p \vee q) \leftrightarrow 
eg(r \wedge p) (in official form, ((
eg p \vee q) \leftrightarrow 
eg(r \wedge p))) and list its subformulas. The root is \leftrightarrow. Its left subtree is \vee over 
eg p and q, where 
eg p is 
eg over the leaf p. Its right subtree is 
eg over \wedge, and \wedge has the leaves r and p. The subformulas are the formula itself, (
eg p \vee q), 
eg(r \wedge p), 
eg p, q, (r \wedge p), p and r: eight, with p listed once although it sits at two leaves. A parse tree is not a truth table. The tree records how a formula is built, and it is the same whatever the atoms stand for; nothing in it is true or false. Values come in Section 4.4, where they are computed along the tree, from the leaves up. Mixing the two, for instance writing “T” beside a node while drawing the tree, is a habit worth not forming: the same tree carries different values under different assignments. Shorthand and official formulas Nobody wants to write (((p \wedge q) 	o r) \leftrightarrow (p 	o (q 	o r))). Chapter 1 used conventions that let us drop parentheses (Section 1.1, the conventions before @def-main-connective), and we keep using them. What changes is their status: they are not part of the definition of a formula. A string written with the conventions is shorthand, and it stands for exactly one official formula, the one obtained by putting the dropped parentheses back. The translation, from shorthand to official form, goes as follows. 1. Put back the outer pair of parentheses of a formula whose main connective is binary: p \wedge q stands for (p \wedge q). 2. 
eg binds most tightly: it applies to the smallest formula that follows it. So 
eg p \wedge q stands for (
eg p \wedge q), not for 
eg(p \wedge q). 3. \wedge and \vee bind more tightly than 	o and \leftrightarrow: p \wedge q 	o r stands for ((p \wedge q) 	o r). 4. 	o groups to the right: p 	o q 	o r stands for (p 	o (q 	o r)). 5. Chapter 1 sometimes wrote a negation in parentheses for emphasis, as in (
eg P) 	o Q; such parentheses are simply removed. In a mixture of \wedge with \vee, or of 	o with \leftrightarrow, the shorthand keeps the parentheses (Chapter 1’s rule for such mixtures), so no rule is needed for those. [Two groupings of three implications] Write the official formula for the shorthand p 	o q 	o r, draw its parse tree beside that of ((p 	o q) 	o r), and find a situation in which the two formulas say different things. By rule 4, p 	o q 	o r stands for (p 	o (q 	o r)): the first 	o is the main connective, and its conclusion is (q 	o r). The other grouping, ((p 	o q) 	o r), has the second 	o as main connective, and its hypothesis is (p 	o q). Left, (p 	o (q 	o r)); right, ((p 	o q) 	o r). The two trees are mirror images in shape, and they say different things. Suppose p, q and r are all false. The left formula is an implication whose hypothesis p is false, so it is true (vacuous truth, Section 2.1). The right formula has the true hypothesis p 	o q (again vacuous, since p is false) and the false conclusion r, so it is false. The everyday reading of Chapters 1 and 2 is enough to see this; Section 4.4 makes it a computation. This is why the grouping convention matters. Grouping to the right is the useful choice, because statements of the form “if P, then if Q, then R” are common and (P 	o Q) 	o R is rare. Going the other way, from official to shorthand, we drop every pair of parentheses the rules would put back. (
eg(p \vee q) \leftrightarrow (
eg p \wedge 
eg q)) becomes 
eg(p \vee q) \leftrightarrow 
eg p \wedge 
eg q: the outer pair goes by rule 1, the pair around 
eg p \wedge 
eg q by rule 3, and the pair after the first 
eg must stay, since without it rule 2 would read 
eg p \vee q. From now on we write formulas in shorthand whenever that is clearer, and every statement about “the formula p \wedge q” is about the official formula (p \wedge q). Where the official form matters, as in counting parentheses or symbols, we write it out. Letters, metavariables and substitution We can now say exactly what the letters of Chapters 1–3 were. Every rule was stated as a schema (@def-rule-schema), with metavariables: ulename{\wedge I} writes \varphi \wedge \psi from \varphi and \psi, for any formulas \varphi and \psi. The derivations of those chapters were written with capital letters, as in the derivation of @prp-implication-transitive: In the language of this chapter, read the letters P, Q, R as three atoms. Then this is a derivation of p 	o q, \ q 	o r \vdash p 	o r in the official sense, written in shorthand. But Chapter 1 meant more: the derivation was a pattern, good for any statements put in for the letters. Here is that promise made exact. A derivation written with letters is a template. Substitution. Replace each atom of a derivation by a formula, the same formula at every occurrence of the same atom, and all such replacements at once. The result is again a derivation. The fold below checks that every line stays a formula and stays justified. Here is why. First, each line becomes a formula. Replacing atoms by formulas in a formula \chi gives a formula: take a formation sequence of \chi, write in front of it a formation sequence of each formula put in for an atom, and replace the atoms inside the old entries. Each old entry that was an atom has become the last entry of one of the sequences written in front; each old entry built by (F2) or (F3) is now built by the same clause from the replaced versions of the same earlier entries. So the new list is a formation sequence, and its last entry is the replaced \chi. Second, each line is still justified. Each line of the old derivation was a premise, an assumption, a repetition, or an instance of a rule’s schema (@def-derivation, clauses (D1)–(D4)). Being an instance means: the line and the lines it cites are the schema with its metavariables replaced by certain formulas. The schema’s own symbols are connectives,  ot and parentheses, never atoms, so replacing atoms in the lines is the same as replacing atoms inside those certain formulas. The new lines are therefore the same schema with its metavariables replaced by the new formulas: an instance of the same rule. Third, nothing about citations changes. The line numbers, the boxes, and which line cites which are untouched, and whether a line or a box is available depends on nothing else (@def-derivation, the scope rule). So the result is a derivation, with the replaced premises and the replaced last line. For instance, put (p_1 \wedge p_2) for P, 
eg p_1 for Q, and (p_2 \vee p_1) for R in the derivation above: Line 4 is still ulename{{	o}E}: lines 1 and 3 are \varphi 	o \psi and \varphi with \varphi the formula p_1 \wedge p_2 and \psi the formula 
eg p_1. Line 6 is still ulename{{	o}I} with the same box. The fact is immediate rule by rule, because every rule was stated for arbitrary formulas from the start. It is what the phrase “the letters stand for arbitrary statements” (Chapter 1, Section 1.2) and the clause “replace each letter … the same statement for every occurrence” of @def-derived-rule were relying on. We use it twice later in the chapter, in the soundness proof of Section 4.7 and in the completeness proof of Section 4.8. The replacement must be uniform. Replacing only the first P of the derivation above by p_1 \wedge p_2, and leaving the P on line 3 alone, would break line 4, which needs the hypothesis of line 1 to be literally the formula on line 3. [Looking ahead] Section 4.3 proves that every formula is built in only one way. Then “the parse tree” of a formula makes sense, and with it the height of a formula. Exercises A. Give a formation sequence for each formula, and for each nonformula name the test or clause it fails: (i) (p \vee  ot); (ii)

eg(p \vee q)) in which (p \vee q) is listed once. 4. Why does clause (F3) of @def-formula put parentheses around its result, while (F2) does not? 5. Explain why clauses (F1)–(F3) alone do not show that 	o p is not a formula, and which clause does. (a) (i) A formula: p, \  ot, \ (p \vee  ot). (ii) A formula: p, \ 
eg p, \

eg p. (iii) Not a formula. It begins with (, so by the first-symbol test it would be (\varphi \circ \psi), and the string p 
eg q between the parentheses would contain a binary connective. It contains none. (iv) Not a formula. It begins with (, so it would be (\varphi \circ \psi) with \varphi \circ \psi the string (p 	o q). The only binary connective in that string is the 	o, so \varphi would be the string (p, of length 2. A formula of length 2 begins with 
eg, by the first-symbol test (one beginning with ( has length at least 5). So (p is not a formula, and neither is the string. So here the doubled outer pair is not official. (v) Not a formula. It would be (\varphi \wedge \psi) with the \wedge one of the two. If it is the first, \psi is the string q \wedge r; if the second, \varphi is p \wedge q. Each has length 3 and begins with an atom, so by the first-symbol test neither is a formula. (Chapter 1’s conventions give no reading of the shorthand p \wedge q \wedge r; Section 4.5 introduces it for the right-grouped (p \wedge (q \wedge r)) and explains why either grouping would do.) (b) The formula is (
eg(p 	o q) \vee q). Its subformulas are (
eg(p 	o q) \vee q), 
eg(p 	o q), (p 	o q), p and q: five, with q listed once although it sits at two leaves. (c) p, \ q, \ (p \vee q), \ 
eg(p \vee q), \ ((p \vee q) \wedge

(d) A binary connective joins two formulas, and without parentheses a string such as p \wedge q \vee r could be built in two ways, with different meanings (see “Why this definition”). A negation stands in front of the one formula it negates, so there is nothing to group. (e) Clauses (F1)–(F3) say which strings are formulas and never which are not: the collection of all strings satisfies them. Clause (F4) says a formula is the last entry of a formation sequence, and from it follows the first-symbol test: 	o p has length 2 and does not begin with 
eg or (. [A2: Drill] Answer each part in a line or two. 1. Is

eg \ r \ ). (d) No. It is a claim of the metalanguage about two formulas; \vdash is not a symbol of the alphabet. (e) 	o; officially the formula is (
eg(p \wedge q) 	o r). (f) (p \wedge q) and r. The string q) 	o r is not a formula. (q 	o r) is a formula, but no node of the tree carries it. (g) (p \wedge 
eg q): the string begins with (, so by the first-symbol test it must end with ). (h) Delete all four parentheses, leaving 
eg p. The string has no binary connective, and a pair of parentheses is official only around a binary step; so the only formulas made of its symbols are 
eg p and p. (i) ((p \vee q) \vee r) and (p \vee (q \vee r)). (j) ((
eg p \vee q) 	o r). (k) Root 	o; on the left the leaf p, on the right 	o over q and p. The leaves are p, q, p. (l) Yes. Lines 1–6 become q 	o q, q 	o p, q, q, p, q 	o p, and lines 4, 5, 6 are still instances of ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{{	o}I}. A substitution may put the same formula for two letters. B. Practice [B1: Trees from Chapter 1] Each formula below appears, with capital letters, in a result of Chapter 1 (@prp-curry and @prp-distributivity); here the letters are atoms. For each, write the official formula, draw its parse tree, and list its subformulas. 1. (p \wedge q) 	o r 2. p 	o (q 	o r) 3. (p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge r) (a) Official form ((p \wedge q) 	o r). Root 	o; left subtree \wedge with leaves p, q; right subtree the leaf r. Subformulas: ((p \wedge q) 	o r), (p \wedge q), p, q, r. (b) Official form (p 	o (q 	o r)). The formulas of (a) and (b) have different trees; @prp-curry says that each can be derived from the other.) (c) Official form ((p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge r)). Root \vee; left subtree \wedge with leaves p, q; right subtree \wedge with leaves p, r. Subformulas: ((p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge r)), (p \wedge q), (p \wedge r), p, q, r: six, with p listed once although it sits at two leaves. [B2: Shorthand and back] 1. Write in shorthand, dropping every pair of parentheses the conventions allow: ((p \wedge q) 	o (r 	o p)) and (
eg(p \vee q) 	o (
eg p \wedge 
eg q)). 2. Write the official formula for: p 	o q \vee r 	o 
eg p and 
eg p \wedge q \leftrightarrow r. (a) p \wedge q 	o r 	o p. The outer pair goes by rule 1; (p \wedge q) loses its pair because \wedge binds more tightly than 	o (rule 3); (r 	o p) loses its pair because 	o groups to the right (rule 4). 
eg(p \vee q) 	o 
eg p \wedge 
eg q. The outer pair goes; the pair around 
eg p \wedge 
eg q goes by rule 3. The pair after the first 
eg stays: without it, rule 2 would make the 
eg apply to p alone. (b) (p 	o ((q \vee r) 	o 
eg p)). Rule 3 groups q \vee r first; rule 4 then makes the first 	o the main connective, with conclusion ((q \vee r) 	o 
eg p). ((
eg p \wedge q) \leftrightarrow r). Rule 2 makes 
eg apply to p alone; rule 3 groups 
eg p \wedge q before \leftrightarrow. C. Going deeper [C1: Forgetting the grouping convention] Suppose we forgot rule 4 of the shorthand, so that p 	o q 	o r 	o s could stand for any official formula obtained by inserting parentheses into it. 1. List every official formula it could stand for, and draw the shape of each parse tree. 2. How many are there? Say how the count is found, by splitting at the main connective. 3. Which of them is the one rule 4 chooses? [Hint 1] The main connective is one of the three arrows. Choose it first. [Hint 2] Write c_n for the number of groupings of a chain of n atoms, and find c_1, c_2 and c_3 first. (a) The main connective is one of the three arrows; what lies on each side is then grouped in every possible way. - Main connective the first arrow: p on the left, and q 	o r 	o s on the right, grouped in one of two ways. This gives (p 	o (q 	o (r 	o s))) and (p 	o ((q 	o r) 	o s)). - Main connective the second arrow: (p 	o q) on the left and (r 	o s) on the right, each grouped in one way. This gives ((p 	o q) 	o (r 	o s)). - Main connective the third arrow: p 	o q 	o r on the left, grouped in one of two ways, and s on the right. This gives ((p 	o (q 	o r)) 	o s) and (((p 	o q) 	o r) 	o s). Their parse trees have the root 	o in each case: in the first two, the leaf p on the left and a chain of two arrows on the right (leaning right, or leaning left); in the third, two one-arrow trees side by side; in the last two, a chain of two arrows on the left and the leaf s on the right. (b) There are 5. Write c_n for the number of groupings of a chain of n atoms joined by one binary connective. A chain of one or two atoms has one grouping: c_1 = c_2 = 1. For three atoms the main connective is the first or the second arrow, and the side with two atoms has one grouping: c_3 = c_1 c_2 + c_2 c_1 = 2. For four atoms, choosing the main connective splits the chain into a left part of k atoms and a right part of 4 - k atoms, for k = 1, 2, 3, and the two parts are grouped independently: c_4 = c_1 c_3 + c_2 c_2 + c_3 c_1 = 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 . The three terms are the three bullets of (a). (c) Rule 4 groups to the right, so the main connective is the first arrow and its right side is grouped to the right again: (p 	o (q 	o (r 	o s))), the first formula of the list. The numbers 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, \dots produced by this splitting are the Catalan numbers; they grow quickly: a chain of eleven atoms joined by ten connectives already has 16{,}796 readings. Parentheses, or a fixed convention, are not pedantry.

title: 4.2 Induction on the Natural Numbers
content:
Induction on the Natural Numbers Section 4.1 made formulas into objects: strings built from atoms and  ot by the clauses of @def-formula, and by nothing else. There are infinitely many of them, and the theorems this chapter is heading for are about all of them. This section supplies the tool for proving anything about infinitely many objects at once. It is induction on the natural numbers, where it is familiar. Section 4.3 carries it over to formulas, where the chapter needs it most. One argument for infinitely many cases Here is a claim about every formula: every formula has as many left parentheses as right ones. It is believable. The clause (F3) of @def-formula adds one of each, and the other clauses add none. But the claim is about infinitely many strings, and checking them one by one never ends. The belief already contains the shape of a proof. Every formula is reached by finitely many building steps from atoms and  ot (clause (F4)). The starting pieces have no parentheses, so they have equally many of each kind. Each building step turns formulas that balance into a formula that balances. So, step by step along any formation sequence, balance is never lost, and every formula balances. Exactly the same shape appears with numbers. To show that some property holds for every natural number, show that it holds for 0, and that it passes from each number to the next. Every natural number is reached from 0 by finitely many steps of “add one”, so the property is never lost. This is induction. We state it for numbers first, because it is simpler there, then prove the version for formulas from it. As in Chapters 1 and 2, “for every n \in 
N” and “there is a k” are used in their everyday sense. As in the rest of the book, 
N = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\} starts at 0, and the arithmetic and order of the natural numbers are school facts. The principle of induction A property of natural numbers is an open sentence P(n) about a natural number n, such as “n^2 \ge n” or “2^n > n”: for each particular n it becomes a statement, true or false (compare the open sentence x > 2 of @exm-statements, which became a statement once x was fixed). If a property holds for 0, and passes from each number to the next, then it holds for every number. [Principle of Induction] Let P(n) be a property of natural numbers. Suppose that 1. P(0) holds, and 2. for every n \in 
N, if P(n) holds, then P(n + 1) holds. Then P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. In symbols (here  orall abbreviates the words “for every”): \Bigl( P(0) \ \wedge \  orall n \in 
N \  igl( P(n) 	o P(n + 1)  igr) \Bigr) \ 	o \  orall n \in 
N \ P(n) . In words: hypothesis (i) is the base case. Hypothesis (ii) is the inductive step, and inside it, the assumption “P(n) holds” is the induction hypothesis. The step is one implication, proved once, for a number n about which we assume nothing except that it is a natural number with P(n). The conclusion is about every natural number at once. Its status. We take @ax-induction as a basic property of 
N, given and not proved. It is, in a precise sense, what the three dots in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\} mean: the natural numbers are what we reach from 0 by adding one, again and again, and nothing else. Every later use cites this principle. Dominoes. The usual picture is a row of dominoes, one for each natural number. The base case knocks over the first. The inductive step says that each domino, if it falls, knocks over the next. Then every domino falls. The picture carries the one point that matters: the step must work for every n, the first transition from 0 to 1 included. A single domino standing too far from the next stops the whole row, however well the others are placed. Not an infinite derivation. From P(0) and the instances P(0) 	o P(1), P(1) 	o P(2), of the step we could derive P(1) by ulename{{	o}E}, then P(2), and so on; each single P(n) has a finite derivation, n lines long or so. But no finite derivation contains all of them, and “and so on” is not a rule. The principle of induction is what licenses the passage, in one step, from the two hypotheses to “for every n”. It is a rule about 
N, not a rule of logic. The step as a box. In the language of Chapter 1, the inductive step is proved by a ulename{{	o}I} box. We fix a natural number n, knowing nothing about it except what the step allows, and open a box assuming P(n); inside the box we reach P(n + 1); closing the box gives the implication. For now, “let n \in 
N” means what Chapter 1 made it mean (Section 1.1): one fixed number, not further specified. Starting from another number. Often a property is claimed only from some b \in 
N on, as in “for every n \ge 1”. Then it suffices to prove P(b), and, for every n \in 
N with n \ge b, that P(n) implies P(n + 1). Indeed, apply @ax-induction to the property Q(m): “P(b + m) holds”. Its base case Q(0) is P(b), and its step from Q(m) to Q(m + 1) is the step from P(b + m) to P(b + m + 1), where b + m \ge b. So Q(m) holds for every m \in 
N, and every natural number n \ge b is b + m for the natural number m = n - b. We call this induction started at b; it is @ax-induction applied to Q. Here is the first proof by induction, with every part labeled. [A sum of products of neighbors] Prove that for every natural number n \ge 1, 1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 + \dots + n(n + 1) =  rac{n(n + 1)(n + 2)}{3} . Let P(n) be the displayed equation. Its left side is the sum of the n terms k(k + 1) for k = 1, \dots, n, so the left side for n + 1 is the left side for n plus the one new term (n + 1)(n + 2). Before proving anything, test small cases. For n = 1, 2, 3 the left side is 2, 2 + 6 = 8 and 8 + 12 = 20, and the right side is  rac{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3}{3} = 2,  rac{2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4}{3} = 8 and  rac{3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5}{3} = 20. The claim is plausible. It starts at n = 1, so we use induction started at 1 (see above). Base case. For n = 1 the left side is the single term 1 \cdot 2 = 2, and the right side is  rac{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3}{3} = 2. So P(1) holds. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N with n \ge 1, and suppose P(n) holds (the induction hypothesis). Then  egin{aligned} 1 \cdot 2 + \dots + n(n + 1) + (n + 1)(n + 2) &=  rac{n(n + 1)(n + 2)}{3} + (n + 1)(n + 2) \ &=  rac{(n + 1)(n + 2)(n + 3)}{3} , \end{aligned} where the first equality is the induction hypothesis and the second takes out the common factor (n + 1)(n + 2), leaving  rac{n}{3} + 1 =  rac{n + 3}{3}. The last expression is the right side of P(n + 1). So P(n) implies P(n + 1). Conclusion. By @ax-induction, started at 1, P(n) holds for every natural number n \ge 1. Notice where the induction hypothesis entered: exactly once, to replace the sum of the first n terms by a closed expression. A proof by induction that never uses its induction hypothesis is either not an induction or is hiding a gap. The inductive step of an inequality usually has a second ingredient besides the hypothesis: a crude estimate that finishes the job. [An inequality by induction] Prove that 3^n \ge 2n + 1 for every n \in 
N. Let P(n) be “3^n \ge 2n + 1”. Base case. 3^0 = 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1, so P(0) holds. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N and suppose 3^n \ge 2n + 1. Then 3^{n + 1} = 3 \cdot 3^n \ge 3(2n + 1) = 6n + 3 \ge 2n + 3 = 2(n + 1) + 1 , where the first inequality multiplies the induction hypothesis by the positive number 3, and the second uses 6n \ge 2n, true because n \ge 0. So P(n + 1) holds. Conclusion. By @ax-induction, 3^n \ge 2n + 1 for every n \in 
N. The estimate 6n + 3 \ge 2n + 3 throws away a great deal. That is typical: the step needs only to reach P(n + 1), not to reach it tightly, and a generous estimate that is obviously true is better than a sharp one that needs its own proof. For the claim “5^n - 1 is divisible by 4 for every n \in 
N”, write down the base case and the statement of the inductive step, without proving the step. Base case: 5^0 - 1 = 0 = 4 \cdot 0. Step: for every n \in 
N, if 4 \mid 5^n - 1, then 4 \mid 5^{n + 1} - 1. (It holds, since 5^{n + 1} - 1 = 5(5^n - 1) + 4.) The inductive step must hold for every n, including the first transition. Try to prove “2^n \ge n^2 for every n \in 
N”: the base case 1 \ge 0 holds, and the step 2^{n + 1} = 2 \cdot 2^n \ge 2n^2 \ge (n + 1)^2 looks fine, but its last inequality holds only for n \ge 3, so the steps from 0 to 1, from 1 to 2 and from 2 to 3 are not covered. The claim survives the first two gaps (at n = 1, 2 \ge 1, and at n = 2 both sides are 4), but it is false at n = 3, where 2^3 = 8 < 9 = 3^2; it is true again from n = 4 on. A checklist for a proof by induction. Before writing, and again after, answer five questions. 1. Objects. What does the induction run over: the natural numbers from 0, from some m, the formulas, the lines of a derivation? 2. Property. Write P as an open sentence about one object. Everything the step will need must be inside it, restrictions such as “if n \ge 8” included. 3. Base cases. Which objects does the step not reach from earlier ones: those not built from others, or, in strong induction, those whose step would reach outside the range? Check every one of them. 4. Steps. One for each way of building, proved for an arbitrary object, using the hypothesis only for objects built earlier: the one before, any earlier one, or the immediate parts. 5. Principle. Name it (@ax-induction, @thm-strong-induction) and say what it gives. Every induction in this chapter can be checked against these five questions, and Sections 4.3 and 4.7 do so. Strong induction Sometimes the step from n to n + 1 is the wrong shape. The immediate parts of a formula (\varphi \circ \psi) are shorter than it, but not by exactly one symbol; a natural number may be best understood through a smaller one that is not its predecessor. In such cases we want to assume the property not just for n, but for every smaller number. If a property holds for n whenever it holds for all smaller numbers, then it holds for every number. Strong Induction Let P(n) be a property of natural numbers. Suppose that for every n \in 
N: if P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < n, then P(n) holds. Then P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. This form is also called course-of-values induction: the hypothesis may use the whole course of values P(0), \dots, P(n - 1), not just the last one. Its induction hypothesis is stronger (we assume more), so its step is easier to prove; the theorem says we lose nothing by it. There seems to be no base case. There is one, hidden. For n = 0, the hypothesis says: if P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < 0, then P(0) holds. No natural number is less than 0, so “P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < 0” is vacuously true: for each k \in 
N, the implication “if k < 0, then P(k)” has a false hypothesis, and an implication with a false hypothesis holds (@prp-vacuous-implication: from 
eg (k < 0) we get (k < 0) 	o P(k)). So at n = 0 the hypothesis of the theorem hands us P(0) outright. In practice, the proof of the step usually treats small n separately, and that is where the base cases live. Strong induction is ordinary induction applied to a stronger property. Let Q(n) say “P(k) holds for every k \le n”. Then Q(n) is exactly the hypothesis the theorem needs at n + 1, since the numbers below n + 1 are those up to n; so the theorem’s hypothesis moves us from Q(n) to Q(n + 1). Ordinary induction on Q does the rest, and Q(n) contains P(n). Suppose the hypothesis of the theorem holds. For n \in 
N, let Q(n) be the property “P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k \le n”. We prove Q(n) for every n by @ax-induction. Base case. No natural number is less than 0, so P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < 0, vacuously. By the hypothesis of the theorem at n = 0, P(0) holds. The only k \in 
N with k \le 0 is 0, so Q(0) holds. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N and suppose Q(n). The natural numbers k < n + 1 are exactly those with k \le n, since no natural number lies strictly between n and n + 1. So Q(n) says that P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < n + 1, and the hypothesis of the theorem at n + 1 gives P(n + 1). A natural number k \le n + 1 satisfies k \le n or k = n + 1, and P(k) holds in both cases. Hence Q(n + 1). By @ax-induction, Q(n) holds for every n \in 
N. Given n \in 
N, Q(n) applied to k = n gives P(n). This proves the theorem. In the proof of @thm-strong-induction, to which property is @ax-induction applied, and why is it not applied to P(n) itself? To Q(n): “P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k \le n”. Applied to P(n) itself, ordinary induction would give us only P(n) as induction hypothesis, while the hypothesis of the theorem at n + 1 asks for P(k) at every k \le n. The property Q carries exactly that information from one step to the next. The first use shows the typical shape: the step splits into a few small cases, handled directly, and a general case that reaches back further than one. [Threes and fives] Prove that every natural number n \ge 8 is a sum of threes and fives: n = 3a + 5b for some integers a, b \ge 0. Ordinary induction is awkward here. From n = 3a + 5b we cannot easily reach n + 1: we would have to trade some threes for fives or the other way round, and there may be none of the kind we want to trade. Going back three steps is easy instead: if n - 3 is a sum of threes and fives, add one more three. So we use strong induction. For n \in 
N, let P(n) be “if n \ge 8, then n = 3a + 5b for some integers a, b \ge 0”. Let n \in 
N, and suppose P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < n. We show P(n). Case n < 8. Then the hypothesis “n \ge 8” of P(n) is false, and P(n) holds vacuously. Cases n = 8, 9, 10. Directly: 8 = 3 + 5, 9 = 3 \cdot 3, 10 = 5 \cdot 2. Case n \ge 11. Let k = n - 3. Then k \ge 8, so k \in 
N, and k < n. By the induction hypothesis P(k), there are integers a, b \ge 0 with n - 3 = 3a + 5b. Then n = 3(a + 1) + 5b, with a + 1 \ge 0 and b \ge 0. In every case P(n) holds. By @thm-strong-induction, P(n) holds for every n \in 
N: every n \ge 8 is a sum of threes and fives. The three direct cases are the base cases. They are needed because the general case reaches back three steps: for n = 8, 9, 10, the number n - 3 is 5, 6, 7, which is below 8, and there the induction hypothesis P(n - 3) is vacuous and gives us nothing. The bound 8 cannot be lowered: 7 is not a sum of threes and fives, since neither 7 nor 7 - 5 = 2 is a multiple of 3. Proving more to prove less Sometimes the step will not go through although the claim is true. The cure is surprising: prove more. [Prove more to prove less] For n \ge 1 let S_n =  rac{1}{1 \cdot 2} +  rac{1}{2 \cdot 3} + \dots +  rac{1}{n(n + 1)} . Show that S_n < 1 for every n \ge 1. First try. Let P(n) be “S_n < 1”. The base case holds: S_1 =  rac12. In the step, S_{n+1} = S_n +  rac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}, and the hypothesis S_n < 1 tells us nothing more about S_n: a number x < 1 may exceed 1 -  rac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}, and then x +  rac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)} > 1. From S_n < 1 alone we cannot reach S_{n+1} < 1. The hypothesis is too weak to give P(n + 1). The claim is not to blame; the hypothesis is. Guess more. S_1 =  rac12, S_2 =  rac12 +  rac16 =  rac23, S_3 =  rac23 +  rac{1}{12} =  rac34. Let Q(n) be “S_n =  rac{n}{n+1}”. Base case. S_1 =  rac12 =  rac{1}{1 + 1}. Inductive step. Let n \ge 1 and suppose S_n =  rac{n}{n+1}. Then S_{n+1} =  rac{n}{n+1} +  rac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)} =  rac{n(n+2) + 1}{(n+1)(n+2)} =  rac{(n+1)^2}{(n+1)(n+2)} =  rac{n+1}{n+2} , which is Q(n + 1). Conclusion. By @ax-induction started at 1 (“Starting from another number”), Q(n) holds for every n \ge 1, and  rac{n}{n+1} < 1 gives the claim. A stronger claim gives the step a stronger hypothesis to use, and asks the step to deliver more; here it can. The same need returns with formulas in Section 4.3, where facts about parentheses are proved together, because one of them, alone, does not pass through the step. Run the checklist on @exm-threes-and-fives. Objects: the natural numbers. Property: “if n \ge 8, then n = 3a + 5b for some integers a, b \ge 0”, with the restriction inside. Base cases: 8, 9, 10, the numbers whose step would reach below 8 (for n < 8 the property holds vacuously). Step: for n \ge 11, the hypothesis for n - 3 \ge 8, an earlier number, and one more 3. Principle: @thm-strong-induction. N. Let P(n) be “2^n \ge n + 1”. Base case. 2^0 = 1 = 0 + 1, so P(0) holds. Inductive step. Let n \in

N. [B2: Divisible by six] Prove by induction that n^3 - n is divisible by 6 for every n \in 
N. You may use that n(n + 1) is even for every n \in 
N. Let P(n) be “6 \mid n^3 - n”. Base case. 0^3 - 0 = 0 = 6 \cdot 0, so P(0) holds. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N and suppose 6 \mid n^3 - n. Expanding, (n + 1)^3 - (n + 1) = n^3 + 3n^2 + 2n = (n^3 - n) + 3n(n + 1) . By the induction hypothesis, 6 \mid n^3 - n. N. Marking scheme.
