The step multiplies by 1 -  rac{1}{(n+1)^2} < 1, and the hypothesis R_n >  rac12 tells us nothing more about R_n: for a number x just above  rac12, such as x =  rac12 +  rac{1}{4(n+1)^2}, the number x  igl(1 -  rac{1}{(n+1)^2} igr) is below  rac12, so the hypothesis alone does not give the claim for n + 1. Prove more. R_2 =  rac34, R_3 =  rac34 \cdot  rac89 =  rac23, R_4 =  rac23 \cdot  rac{15}{16} =  rac58 suggest R_n =  rac{n+1}{2n}. Base case n = 2: R_2 =  rac34 =  rac{2 + 1}{2 \cdot 2}. Step: let n \ge 2 and suppose R_n =  rac{n+1}{2n}. Then R_{n+1} =  rac{n+1}{2n} \cdot  rac{(n+1)^2 - 1}{(n+1)^2} =  rac{n+1}{2n} \cdot  rac{n(n+2)}{(n+1)^2} =  rac{n+2}{2(n+1)} . By @ax-induction started at 2, R_n =  rac{n+1}{2n} for every n \ge 2, and so R_n =  rac12 +  rac{1}{2n} >  rac12. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: argues that the plain claim does not pass through the step. - 2: states the stronger claim. - 2: base case. - 3: the algebra of the step. - 1: the conclusion, naming the principle. Fatal error (0 for the step): “proving” the step from R_n >  rac12 alone.

title: 4.3 Induction and Recursion on Formulas
content:
Induction and Recursion on Formulas Section 4.2 proved statements about every natural number. This section proves statements about every formula in the same way, and with them answers the question Section 4.1 left open, whether every formula is read in only one way, and with it a second: does a definition with one clause per connective define exactly one thing? On the way it shows what goes wrong when an object can be built in two ways. Structural induction We return to formulas. The formation sequence of a formula plays the part that “0, 1, 2, \dots” plays for numbers: every formula is reached from atoms and  ot by finitely many uses of the clauses. So a property of formulas can be proved in the same two parts. A property of formulas is a statement P(\varphi) about a formula \varphi, true or false for each particular formula: “\varphi has as many left as right parentheses”, “\varphi contains the atom p”. If every atom and  ot has a property, and each way of building a formula passes the property from the parts to the whole, then every formula has it. Structural Induction Let P(\varphi) be a property of formulas. Suppose that 1. P(p) holds for every atom p, and P( ot) holds; 2. for every formula \varphi, if P(\varphi) holds, then P(
eg\varphi) holds; 3. for all formulas \varphi, \psi and each binary connective \circ, if P(\varphi) and P(\psi) hold, then P((\varphi \circ \psi)) holds. Then P(\varphi) holds for every formula \varphi. In words: (i) is the base case, one for each kind of formula of length one. (ii) and (iii) are the inductive steps, one for each building clause of @def-formula, and inside them “P(\varphi) and P(\psi)” is the induction hypothesis, assumed for the immediate parts of the formula being built. There are seven cases in all (atoms,  ot, 
eg, and the four binary connectives); often the four binary ones are handled at once, with \circ left unspecified. Section 4.2’s checklist reads: objects, the formulas; property, P(\varphi), with any restriction inside it; base cases, every atom and  ot; steps, one for 
eg and one for each binary connective; principle, @thm-structural-induction. For example, take the property “\varphi has as many left as right parentheses”. Base cases: an atom and  ot have no parentheses, none of either. Step for 
eg: if \varphi has k of each, so has 
eg\varphi, since 
eg is not a parenthesis. Step for \circ: if \varphi has k of each and \psi has l of each, then (\varphi \circ \psi) has k + l + 1 of each, the outer pair adding one of each. By @thm-structural-induction, every formula has as many left as right parentheses. This is part (a) of @lem-parenthesis-count below; its other parts need more care. Take any formula and a formation sequence ending in it. Walk along the sequence: each entry is an atom or  ot, which has the property by (i), or is built from earlier entries, which have it already, by (ii) or (iii). “Earlier entries, any of them” is exactly the shape of strong induction, applied to the position in the list. The property spreads from left to right. Each entry gets its check mark from (i), or from entries to its left that already have one. The proof, in the fold below, makes “from left to right” exact with strong induction on the position in the list. Suppose (i)–(iii) hold, and let \chi be a formula. By @def-formula (F4) there is a formation sequence \chi_1, \dots, \chi_m with \chi_m = \chi. For i \in 
N, let Q(i) be the property “if 1 \le i \le m, then P(\chi_i) holds”. We prove Q(i) for every i \in 
N by @thm-strong-induction. Let i \in 
N, and suppose Q(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < i. If i = 0 or i > m, then Q(i) holds vacuously. So let 1 \le i \le m. By the definition of a formation sequence, one of three things is true. - \chi_i is an atom or  ot. Then P(\chi_i) holds by (i). - \chi_i = 
eg\chi_j for some j < i. Then 1 \le j \le m, and Q(j) gives P(\chi_j). The entry \chi_j is a formula (every entry of a formation sequence is one, Section 4.1), so (ii) applies and gives P(\chi_i). - \chi_i = (\chi_j \circ \chi_l) for some j, l < i and a binary connective \circ. Then 1 \le j, l \le m, and Q(j) and Q(l) give P(\chi_j) and P(\chi_l), both entries are formulas, and (iii) gives P(\chi_i). So Q(i) holds. By @thm-strong-induction, Q(i) holds for every i \in 
N; in particular Q(m) gives P(\chi_m), that is, P(\chi). Since \chi was an arbitrary formula, this proves the theorem. The proof uses strong induction, because an entry of a formation sequence may be built from any earlier entries, not only from the one just before it. A tempting alternative is induction on the height of a formula (the number of nodes on a longest branch of its parse tree, defined later in this section). That route is circular here. The height is read off the parse tree, and that a formula has only one parse tree is proved below from unique readability, whose proof uses structural induction. Inducting on the position in a formation sequence needs nothing but @def-formula. A structural induction must cover every clause, the base case  ot and the step for 
eg included. Try to prove “every formula contains an atom”: it holds for atoms, and the steps for 
eg and for (\varphi \circ \psi) keep it, since the atoms of the parts are atoms of the whole. But the case  ot fails, and so does the claim:  ot, 
eg ot and ( ot 	o  ot) contain no atom. A proof that “forgets”  ot proves something false. Which clause of @def-formula makes step (ii) of @thm-structural-induction necessary? Give a property of formulas that holds for every atom and for  ot, passes from \varphi and \psi to (\varphi \circ \psi) for every binary connective, and yet fails for some formula. Clause (F2), which builds 
eg\varphi from \varphi: step (ii) is the step for that clause. Without it, the formulas made by (F2) would be missed. One such property: “\varphi is an atom, or is  ot, or begins with (”. Atoms and  ot have it, and every formula (\varphi \circ \psi) begins with (, whatever its parts are. But 
eg p does not have it. So (i) and (iii) alone do not prove a property of every formula; the property fails exactly at a formula made by the forgotten clause. Section 4.1 called the formulas the smallest collection of strings closed under (F1)–(F3). Here is that sentence made exact. Call a collection C of strings closed if it contains every atom and  ot, contains 
eg s whenever it contains s, and contains (s \circ t) whenever it contains s and t, for each binary connective \circ. The collection of all strings is closed, and closed collections can be much larger than we want. (i) Every closed collection C contains every formula. Given a formula and a formation sequence \chi_1, \dots, \chi_m ending in it, show “if 1 \le i \le m, then \chi_i \in C” for every i \in 
N by @thm-strong-induction, case by case as in the proof of @thm-structural-induction: each entry is an atom or  ot, or is built by one clause from earlier entries, which are in C already. The last entry is the formula. (ii) The formulas form a closed collection, by (F1)–(F3). So the formulas are the smallest closed collection: contained in every closed collection, and one of them. Structural induction is (i) applied to one particular collection. If a property P satisfies (i)–(iii) of @thm-structural-induction, the collection of formulas that have P is closed: it contains every atom and  ot by (i), and the formulas built from members of it are formulas with P, by (ii) and (iii). So it contains every formula. The top-down description (“the smallest closed collection”) and the bottom-up one (“whatever a formation sequence reaches”) pick out the same strings. The word “collection” keeps its everyday sense here. Counting parentheses: the depth profile Section 4.1 met the string p \wedge q \vee r, which can be read as (p \wedge q) \vee r or as p \wedge (q \vee r). With p and q false and r true, the first reading is true and the second false. Section 4.4 defines the truth value of a formula one clause per connective, and the clause to use is decided by the main connective. A string with two main connectives would get two values. Formulas carry parentheses, and the parentheses are meant to settle the reading. This subsection and the next prove that they do, for every formula. The tool is a count. Read a formula from left to right, keeping a running count: add one at each (, subtract one at each ). The count just before a symbol is its depth: how many pairs of parentheses are open around it. The depth profile of ((p \wedge q) \vee r). It starts at 0, stays at 1 or more strictly inside, comes back to 0 only after the last symbol, and the only binary connective at depth 1 is the main connective. For every formula of the form (\varphi \circ \psi) the lemma below says the same: (a) the count returns to 0, (b) it never goes below 0 and stays at 1 or more strictly inside, (c) every binary connective is at depth 1 or more. The remark after the proof adds that only the main connective is at depth exactly 1. We count parentheses in strings, and for this some words about strings. An initial segment of a string s is the string of the first k symbols of s, for some k with 0 \le k \le the length of s. For k = 0 it is the empty string, with no symbols; for k equal to the length it is s itself. An initial segment is proper if it is shorter than s. The excess of a string s is \operatorname{ex}(s) \coloneqq (	ext{number of } ( 	ext{ in } s) - (	ext{number of } ) 	ext{ in } s) . So a left parenthesis has excess 1, a right parenthesis -1, and any other symbol 0; and the excess of a string written as two strings one after the other is the sum of their excesses, since the counts add. For example, \operatorname{ex}(\,(p \wedge (q\,) = 2: after reading (p \wedge (q we are inside two pairs of parentheses that have not yet closed. That is the picture to keep: the excess of an initial segment is the depth we are at when we have read that far. So the depth of a symbol is the excess of the initial segment that ends just before it. [Parenthesis Count] Let \chi be a formula. 1. \operatorname{ex}(\chi) = 0: \chi has as many left as right parentheses. 2. Every initial segment u of \chi has \operatorname{ex}(u) \ge 0. If moreover \chi has the form (\varphi \circ \psi) and u is proper and non-empty, then \operatorname{ex}(u) \ge 1. 3. For every occurrence of a binary connective in \chi, the initial segment of \chi that ends just before that occurrence has excess at least 1. In words: (a) is balance. (b) says that reading a formula from the left, we never close more parentheses than we have opened, and that inside a formula (\varphi \circ \psi) we stay at depth at least 1 until the very last symbol. (c) says that no binary connective lies outside all parentheses. Part (a) is the balance proved above, repeated in the proof because (b) and (c) need it for the parts; (c), with (a), is what the unique readability theorem needs, and (b), with (a), is the key to showing that no proper initial segment of a formula is a formula (Exercise C1). The steps for (b) and (c) use (a) for the parts, so the three are proved together. Part (b)’s second sentence, alone, does not pass through the step; that is why the lemma proves more, as @exm-strengthen-the-claim did (fold below). Induction on the shape of a formula, all three parts at once. For 
eg\varphi, the extra 
eg changes no count. For (\varphi \circ \psi), list its initial segments by where they stop: before anything, inside \varphi, at the connective, inside \psi, at the end. Each is “(” followed by pieces whose excess the induction hypothesis controls. We prove, by @thm-structural-induction, that every formula \chi has the property P(\chi): “(a), (b), and (c) hold for \chi”. Atoms and  ot. The formula is one symbol, not a parenthesis. (a) Its excess is 0. (b) Its initial segments are the empty string and the formula itself, both of excess 0; and it does not have the form (\varphi \circ \psi), which has length at least 5. (c) It contains no binary connective. Negation. Let \varphi be a formula with P(\varphi); we show P(
eg\varphi). (a) \operatorname{ex}(
eg\varphi) = 0 + \operatorname{ex}(\varphi) = 0, by (a) for \varphi. (b) An initial segment of 
eg\varphi is either empty, of excess 0, or 
eg followed by an initial segment u' of \varphi, of excess \operatorname{ex}(u') \ge 0 by (b) for \varphi. The formula 
eg\varphi begins with 
eg, so it does not have the form (\varphi' \circ \psi'), and the second sentence of (b) says nothing about it. (c) A binary connective in 
eg\varphi lies in \varphi, and the initial segment of 
eg\varphi before it is 
eg followed by the initial segment of \varphi before it, whose excess is at least 1 by (c) for \varphi. Binary connectives. Let \varphi, \psi be formulas with P(\varphi) and P(\psi), let \circ be a binary connective, and let \chi = (\varphi \circ \psi). (a) \operatorname{ex}(\chi) = 1 + \operatorname{ex}(\varphi) + 0 + \operatorname{ex}(\psi) - 1 = 0, by (a) for \varphi and for \psi. (b) Every initial segment of \chi is of exactly one of the following five kinds, and its excess is as shown: - the empty string: excess 0; - ( followed by an initial segment u' of \varphi: excess 1 + \operatorname{ex}(u') \ge 1, by (b) for \varphi; - (\varphi\,\circ: excess 1 + \operatorname{ex}(\varphi) + 0 = 1, by (a) for \varphi; - (\varphi\,\circ followed by a non-empty initial segment v' of \psi: excess 1 + 0 + \operatorname{ex}(v') \ge 1, by (a) for \varphi and (b) for \psi; - \chi itself: excess 0, by (a) for \chi. All five have excess at least 0. The proper non-empty ones are those of the middle three kinds, and they have excess at least 1. (c) An occurrence of a binary connective in \chi is the connective \circ between \varphi and \psi, or lies in \varphi, or lies in \psi. Before \circ stands (\varphi, of excess 1. Before an occurrence in \varphi stands ( followed by the initial segment of \varphi before it, of excess at least 1 + 1 = 2 by (c) for \varphi. Before an occurrence in \psi stands (\varphi\,\circ followed by the initial segment of \psi before it, of excess at least 1 + 0 + 1 = 2 by (a) for \varphi and (c) for \psi. In all three cases the excess is at least 1. So P(\chi) holds. By @thm-structural-induction, every formula has the property P, which proves the lemma. The three parts were proved together for a reason. The second sentence of (b), alone, cannot be proved by structural induction. For (
eg(p \wedge q) \wedge r), the initial segment (
eg(p is ( followed by the initial segment 
eg(p of the formula 
eg(p \wedge q), and its excess is 1 + \operatorname{ex}(
eg(p); to know that this is at least 1, we need \operatorname{ex}(
eg(p) \ge 0, a fact about an initial segment of a negation, which the second sentence of (b) does not cover. The first sentence of (b) does. A property that is too weak to pass through the induction must be strengthened until it does, and here the strengthening is (b)’s first sentence, as the strengthening of @exm-strengthen-the-claim was S_n =  rac{n}{n+1}. The proof (in the fold) gives a little more than (c) states, and the next proof uses the extra. In a formula (\varphi \circ \psi), the initial segment before the connective \circ has excess exactly 1, and the initial segment before any other binary connective has excess at least 2. In the language of depth: the main connective is the only binary connective at depth one. That is the recipe of Section 4.1 for finding the root of a parse tree. Write down the depth of each symbol of (p \wedge (q \vee r)). Which binary connective is at depth 1? ( 0, p 1, \wedge 1, ( 1, q 2, \vee 2, r 2, ) 2, ) 1, and 0 after the last symbol. The \wedge is at depth 1, and it is the main connective. Compare the figure, whose main connective was the \vee. Unique readability We can now prove what Section 4.1 promised: a formula can be built in only one way. Unique Readability Let \chi be a formula that is neither an atom nor  ot. Then exactly one of the following holds: 1. \chi = 
eg\varphi for a formula \varphi; 2. \chi = (\varphi \circ \psi) for formulas \varphi, \psi and a binary connective \circ. In case (i), \varphi is uniquely determined by \chi; in case (ii), \circ, \varphi and \psi are uniquely determined by \chi. In words: every compound formula has one main connective, and one way of being split into its immediate parts. This is the precise form of Chapter 1’s claim that a statement built from letters by connectives can be read in only one way. Existence is the easy half; the content is uniqueness. The danger it excludes is a string such as p \wedge q \vee r, which, if it were a formula, could be split at \wedge or at \vee. Some form holds, by looking at the last step (Section 4.1); the first symbol tells the two forms apart. For case (ii), suppose \chi = (\varphi \circ \psi) = (\varphi' \circ' \psi'). By the remark after @lem-parenthesis-count, each main connective is the only binary connective at depth one; so both sit at the same position of the string, and everything else is forced. By Section 4.1 (looking at the last step), \chi is an atom,  ot, 
eg\varphi for a formula \varphi, or (\varphi \circ \psi) for formulas \varphi, \psi; by hypothesis it is one of the last two. It cannot be both, since a string of the form 
eg\varphi begins with 
eg and one of the form (\varphi \circ \psi) begins with (. Case (i). If \chi = 
eg\varphi = 
eg\varphi', removing the first symbol gives \varphi = \varphi'. Case (ii). Let \chi = (\varphi \circ \psi). Before the connective \circ stands the initial segment (\varphi, of excess 1 + \operatorname{ex}(\varphi) = 1 by @lem-parenthesis-count (a). Before a binary connective inside \varphi stands ( followed by an initial segment of \varphi of excess at least 1, by @lem-parenthesis-count (c); so the excess is at least 2. Before a binary connective inside \psi stands (\varphi\,\circ followed by an initial segment of \psi of excess at least 1, by (c) for \psi and (a) for \varphi; so again at least 2. Hence the position of \circ in \chi is the only position of a binary connective in \chi whose initial segment before it has excess 1, and this description mentions only the string \chi. Now suppose also \chi = (\varphi' \circ' \psi') for formulas \varphi', \psi' and a binary connective \circ'. By the same argument, the position of \circ' is the only position with that description. So \circ and \circ' stand at the same position of \chi, and \circ = \circ'. That position is the one just after ( and \varphi, and also the one just after ( and \varphi', so \varphi and \varphi' have the same length; both are the string of symbols of \chi between the first symbol and that position, so \varphi = \varphi'. Likewise \psi and \psi' are both the string of symbols between that position and the last symbol, so \psi = \psi'. This proves the theorem. The theorem settles the question Section 4.1 left open about parse trees. Every formula has exactly one parse tree. We know it has one. That it has only one is proved by structural induction. By (T4) of @def-parse-tree, every parse tree is made by one of (T1)–(T3). An atom or  ot has only the one-node tree, since a tree made by (T2) or (T3) of @def-parse-tree is a tree for a string beginning with 
eg or (. A parse tree for 
eg\varphi must have been made by (T2), from a parse tree for some \varphi' with 
eg\varphi' = 
eg\varphi; so \varphi' = \varphi, and by the induction hypothesis the tree below the root is the one parse tree of \varphi. A parse tree for (\varphi \circ \psi) must have been made by (T3), from parse trees for some \varphi', \psi' and a connective \circ' with (\varphi' \circ' \psi') = (\varphi \circ \psi); by @thm-unique-readability, \circ' = \circ, \varphi' = \varphi and \psi' = \psi, and by the induction hypothesis the two subtrees are the parse trees of \varphi and \psi. From now on we speak of the parse tree of a formula. With one parse tree for each formula, a measurement of that tree is a measurement of the formula. [Height] The height of a formula \varphi, written \hgt(\varphi), is the number of nodes on a longest branch of its parse tree. Atoms and  ot have height 1: their tree is one node, and its only branch has one node. (Some books count edges instead of nodes and give atoms height 0; with nodes, every formula has height at least 1.) In @exm-parse-trees, (b) has height 4, along the branch 
eg, \wedge, 
eg, q, and (c) has height 4 too, along \vee, \leftrightarrow, 
eg, q or along \vee, \wedge, 	o,  ot. The height counts the nodes on the longest branch, not the symbols of the formula. The formula 
eg(p \wedge 
eg q) has seven symbols, 
eg, (, p, \wedge, 
eg, q, ), and height 4; the formula ((p \wedge q) \wedge (r \wedge p)) has thirteen symbols and height only 3. Parentheses never count towards the height, and a wide tree can be shallow. Definition by recursion Height, the set of atoms, the number of connectives: each is naturally defined one clause per way of building a formula. The height of 
eg\varphi is one more than that of \varphi; the atoms of (\varphi \circ \psi) are those of \varphi together with those of \psi. Such a definition is called recursive: it defines the value at a formula through the values at its immediate parts. The question is whether it really defines something. For a string that could be split in two ways, the clauses might assign two different values, and then they would define nothing. Unique readability says this never happens. We say function on formulas for a rule that assigns to each formula exactly one value; the values may be numbers, truth values, formulas, or collections of atoms. Nothing here needs more than this everyday sense of “function”. Give a value for each atom and for  ot, and say how to get the value of a compound formula from its parts; then exactly one function on formulas obeys these clauses. [Structural Recursion] Suppose we are given - a value a_p for each atom p, and a value a_ ot; - a rule g_
eg that produces a value g_
eg(\varphi, x) from any formula \varphi and any value x; - for each binary connective \circ, a rule g_\circ that produces a value g_\circ(\varphi, \psi, x, y) from any formulas \varphi, \psi and any values x, y. Then there is exactly one function f on formulas such that, for every atom p, all formulas \varphi, \psi and every binary connective \circ,  egin{aligned} f(p) &= a_p, \qquad f( ot) = a_ ot, \ f(
eg\varphi) &= g_
eg igl(\varphi, f(\varphi) igr), \ f igl((\varphi \circ \psi) igr) &= g_\circ igl(\varphi, \psi, f(\varphi), f(\psi) igr). \end{aligned} In words: the three lines are the clauses of a recursive definition, one for each clause of @def-formula. The rules g_
eg and g_\circ may look at the immediate parts themselves as well as at their values; most definitions use only the values, and the list of subformulas below uses the parts. The theorem says the clauses define a function (existence) and only one (uniqueness). Build the function on short formulas first. A formula with one symbol is an atom or  ot, and the first clauses fix its value. A longer formula has immediate parts that are shorter, whose values are already fixed, and unique readability says which clause applies and to which parts, with no choice left. So the value at each formula is forced, length by length. Formally: an ordinary induction on n, proving that there is exactly one function on the formulas of length at most n that obeys the clauses. For n \in 
N with n \ge 1, call a function h, defined on the formulas of length at most n, n-good if it obeys the three clauses at every formula of length at most n. This makes sense: the immediate parts of a formula are shorter than it, so the clauses at a formula of length at most n mention values of h only at formulas of length at most n. Let S(n) be “there is exactly one n-good function”; we prove S(n) for every n \ge 1 by @ax-induction, started at 1 (“Starting from another number”, Section 4.2). Base case. By the first-symbol test (Section 4.1), the formulas of length 1 are the atoms and  ot. A 1-good function must give each atom p the value a_p and  ot the value a_ ot, and the function that does so is 1-good, since the other two clauses concern no formula of length 1. So S(1) holds. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N with n \ge 1, suppose S(n), and let h_n be the n-good function. Define h on the formulas of length at most n + 1 as follows. At a formula of length at most n, let h agree with h_n. Let \chi have length n + 1 \ge 2; it is neither an atom nor  ot, so by @thm-unique-readability it is either 
eg\varphi for exactly one formula \varphi, or (\varphi \circ \psi) for exactly one \circ, \varphi, \psi; the parts have length at most n. Let h(\chi) \coloneqq g_
eg(\varphi, h_n(\varphi)) in the first case and h(\chi) \coloneqq g_\circ(\varphi, \psi, h_n(\varphi), h_n(\psi)) in the second. Unique readability leaves no choice of case or of parts, so this is one value. The function h is (n + 1)-good: at formulas of length at most n it agrees with the n-good h_n, including at their parts, and at formulas of length n + 1 it obeys the clauses by construction. For uniqueness, let h' be any (n + 1)-good function. Its restriction to the formulas of length at most n is n-good, so it is h_n, by S(n). At a formula \chi = 
eg\varphi of length n + 1, the clause for 
eg gives h'(\chi) = g_
eg(\varphi, h'(\varphi)) = g_
eg(\varphi, h_n(\varphi)) = h(\chi); at \chi = (\varphi \circ \psi) the same argument with g_\circ gives h'(\chi) = h(\chi). So h' = h, and S(n + 1) holds. By @ax-induction, started at 1, S(n) holds for every n \ge 1; let h_n denote the n-good function. The function f. If m \ge n, the restriction of h_m to the formulas of length at most n is n-good, so it is h_n. For a formula \chi of length n, let f(\chi) \coloneqq h_n(\chi); then f(\chi) = h_m(\chi) for every m \ge n. The function f obeys the clauses: for \chi = 
eg\varphi of length m, f(\chi) = h_m(\chi) = g_
eg(\varphi, h_m(\varphi)) = g_
eg(\varphi, f(\varphi)), and likewise for the other two clauses. And it is the only one: a function f' on formulas obeying the clauses restricts, for each n, to an n-good function, which is h_n; so f'(\chi) = h_n(\chi) = f(\chi) for a formula \chi of length n. This proves the theorem. Unique readability was used at one place: to define h(\chi) by exactly one clause, applied to exactly one choice of parts. Without it, the clauses could demand two different values at one string, and then no function would obey them. What goes wrong without it. The positive integers are built from 1 by two steps, “add one” and “double”; adding one alone reaches every positive integer. Try to define a function one clause per building step: g(1) \coloneqq 0, g(n + 1) \coloneqq g(n) + 1, g(2n) \coloneqq g(n). The number 2 is built in two ways, as 1 + 1 and as twice 1. The first clause gives g(2) = g(1) + 1 = 1, the second g(2) = g(1) = 0, and no function obeys both. The positive integers are not built freely by these two steps: one number can come out of two different steps, which is exactly what @thm-unique-readability rules out for formulas. Do the clauses h(1) \coloneqq 1, h(n + 1) \coloneqq h(n) + 2, h(2n) \coloneqq 2h(n) define a function on the positive integers? No. At 2, the first step clause gives h(2) = h(1) + 2 = 3 and the second h(2) = 2h(1) = 2. [Four recursive definitions] Each of the following is a function on formulas by @thm-structural-recursion. - Height: \hgt(p) = \hgt( ot) = 1, \hgt(

eg(p \vee (q \leftrightarrow r)) as Polish formulas. 2. Prove that every Polish formula has weight 1, and that every proper initial segment of it (the empty one included) has weight at most 0. 3. Deduce that if \mathsf{K}\varphi\psi and \mathsf{K}\varphi'\psi' are the same string, for Polish formulas \varphi, \psi, \varphi', \psi', then \varphi = \varphi' and \psi = \psi'. 4. Read \mathsf{C}\mathsf{A}pq\mathsf{N}r by the count, and write it in ordinary notation. [Hint 1] (b) is an induction over the Polish clauses, set up as in the fold “Sets built from a base”: the Polish formulas with the property form a collection closed under the Polish clauses. Use a strengthened property, as in @lem-parenthesis-count. [Hint 2] (c): if \varphi 
e \varphi', one of them is a proper initial segment of the other. (a) \mathsf{C}\mathsf{K}p\mathsf{N}qp and \mathsf{N}\mathsf{A}p\mathsf{E}qr. Read “nothing else is” as in the fold “Sets built from a base”: the Polish formulas are the smallest collection of strings that contains every atom and  ot and is closed under the Polish clauses. So if a property holds at atoms and  ot and passes from the parts to the whole at each clause, the Polish formulas with it form such a collection and include every Polish formula. In the same way every Polish formula is non-empty, and is an atom,  ot, \mathsf{N}\varphi, or \mathsf{K}\varphi\psi, \mathsf{A}\varphi\psi, \mathsf{C}\varphi\psi, \mathsf{E}\varphi\psi for Polish \varphi, \psi (the strings of these forms make such a collection); (c) and (d) use this. (b) By induction over the clauses, the property being “weight 1, and every proper initial segment has weight \le 0”. Atom or  ot. Weight 1; its only proper initial segment is the empty string, of weight 0. \mathsf{N}\varphi. Weight 0 + 1 = 1. A proper initial segment is empty (weight 0), or \mathsf{N} followed by a proper initial segment u of \varphi (weight 0 + w(u) \le 0). \mathsf{K}\varphi\psi (and likewise \mathsf{A}, \mathsf{C}, \mathsf{E}). Weight -1 + 1 + 1 = 1. A proper initial segment is of one of four kinds: empty (weight 0); \mathsf{K} followed by an initial segment u of \varphi other than \varphi itself (weight -1 + w(u) \le -1); \mathsf{K}\varphi (weight -1 + 1 = 0); or \mathsf{K}\varphi followed by a proper non-empty initial segment u of \psi (weight 0 + w(u) \le 0). (c) Both \varphi and \varphi' begin at the second symbol. If they differ, the shorter is an initial segment of the longer (both are initial segments of the string after \mathsf{K}), a proper one, and non-empty, since every Polish formula has a symbol. By (b) the shorter has weight 1, and as a proper initial segment of the longer it has weight \le 0: impossible. So \varphi = \varphi', and \psi, \psi' are both what follows \mathsf{K}\varphi: equal. (d) Read from the symbol after \mathsf{C}: the running weight is -1 after \mathsf{A}, 0 after p, and first reaches 1 after q. By (b), a Polish formula ends exactly where its running weight first reaches 1, so the first part of \mathsf{C} is \mathsf{A}pq and the second is \mathsf{N}r. (From the first symbol the running weight is -1, -2, -1, 0, 0, 1, reaching 1 only at the end.) In ordinary notation: ((p \vee q) 	o 
eg r). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a). - 4: (b), with the induction set up over the clauses and all three kinds of non-empty proper initial segment of \mathsf{K}\varphi\psi. - 3: (c), with the non-emptiness of the shorter part named. - 1: (d). Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (b), proving only “weight 1” (then (c) has nothing to use: the strengthening is the point); in (c), assuming the two parts have equal length.

title: 4.4 Valuations and Truth Tables
content:
Valuations and Truth Tables Sections 4.1 and 4.3 made formulas into objects: every formula is built from atoms and  ot by the connectives in exactly one way, and so a function on formulas can be defined one clause per connective. So far a formula is only a string of symbols. It says nothing, and it is neither true nor false. This section gives formulas a meaning. We say what it takes to fix the truth or falsity of every atom, and then compute the truth value of every formula from the values of its atoms, one connective at a time. The result is the truth table, the second way of looking at a formula that Chapters 1 and 2 kept promising. Throughout, formulas are those of @def-formula, with atoms p, q, r, p_1, p_2, \dots, and we use Chapter 1’s shorthand for them (outer parentheses dropped, the usual precedence, 	o grouped to the right), as Section 4.1 allows. Reading a table off the rules Before any definition, a question. Suppose we want to call each statement true or false, and we want the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 to be safe: whenever the lines a rule cites are true, the line it writes is true. How must “true” behave for each connective? The rules answer almost completely. This subsection is motivation only; nothing later rests on it, and Section 4.8 makes it exact. Conjunction. Take statements \varphi and \psi. If both are true, ulename{\wedge I} writes \varphi \wedge \psi from them, so \varphi \wedge \psi must be true. If \varphi \wedge \psi is true, ulename{\wedge E} writes \varphi and writes \psi, so both must be true; turned around, if either of them is false, then \varphi \wedge \psi must be false. All four combinations of values are settled:  egin{array}{cc|c} \varphi & \psi & \varphi \wedge \psi \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \end{array} Here \mathrm{T} stands for “true” and \mathrm{F} for “false”. Contradiction. The rule ulename{ ot E} writes any statement from  ot. If  ot were ever true, ulename{ ot E} would lead from a true line to every statement, false ones included. So  ot must be false, always. Negation. The rule ulename{
eg E} writes  ot from \varphi and 
eg\varphi. Since  ot is false, \varphi and 
eg\varphi are never both true: if \varphi is true, 
eg\varphi is false. And @prp-excluded-middle derives \varphi \vee 
eg\varphi from no premises at all, so at least one of the two is true: if \varphi is false, 
eg\varphi is true. Negation flips the value. Implication. The rule ulename{{	o}E} writes \psi from \varphi 	o \psi and \varphi. So in the combination “\varphi true, \psi false”, the implication cannot be true: that is the one row where \varphi 	o \psi is false. The other three rows are forced by derivations. @prp-vacuous-implication derives P 	o Q from 
eg P, so whenever P is false (and 
eg P therefore true), P 	o Q must be true, whatever Q is. And P 	o Q is derivable from Q alone (@exr-proving-an-implication-b2 (a) of Section 1.4): so whenever Q is true, P 	o Q must be true. That settles the rows with P false (by the first derivation) and the row with both true (by the second). The vacuous rows of 	o, “if P is false, then P 	o Q is true”, are often presented as a convention to be swallowed. Here they are forced by ulename{ ot E}, the rule that closes an impossible case, exactly as Section 2.1 said they would be. The rows of \vee and \leftrightarrow can be read off their rules in the same way, and Exercise C3 of Section 4.5 asks for a sharper version of the argument for 	o. We now turn the answers into a definition. The rules of Chapters 1 and 2 determine their tables almost completely. Not every pair of rules does. Invent a connective \diamond with an introduction rule “from \varphi, infer \varphi \diamond \psi” and an elimination rule “from \varphi \diamond \psi, infer \psi”, and read a table off them as above. The first rule needs \varphi \diamond \psi true whenever \varphi is; the second needs \psi true whenever \varphi \diamond \psi is. In a row with \varphi true and \psi false the two demands clash, so no table makes both rules safe. Worse, the two rules together derive anything from anything: from p, the first gives p \diamond q, and the second then gives q. (Logicians call this connective tonk.) A pair of rules does not give a connective a meaning just by being written down. Section 4.8 shows that the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 do, row by row. Valuations A formula such as p \wedge 
eg q cannot be true or false on its own, because p and q are atoms: letters with no content. What decides its value is a choice of which atoms are true. We need a word for one such choice. A valuation is one possible situation, described by saying which atoms are true and which are false. [Valuation] A valuation v assigns to every atom p exactly one of the two truth values \mathrm{T} and \mathrm{F}. We write v(p) for the value it assigns to p, and say that p is true under v if v(p) = \mathrm{T}, false under v if v(p) = \mathrm{F}. In words: a valuation answers, for each atom separately, the question “true or false?”, and it answers every such question. Two valuations are equal when they give every atom the same value. Nothing links the values of different atoms: v(p) and v(q) may be chosen freely, and that freedom is the whole point. We let a valuation decide every atom so that one valuation gives a value to every formula at once. In practice only the few atoms a formula contains matter, and the Coincidence Lemma below says so. Some valuations, simplest first. - The all-T valuation gives every atom the value \mathrm{T}; the all-F valuation gives every atom \mathrm{F}. They are the two extreme cases, and both will return as tests. - The valuation with v(p) = \mathrm{T}, v(q) = \mathrm{F} and v(r) = \mathrm{F} for every other atom r. This is the typical way to describe a valuation: give the values of the few atoms we care about, and fix the rest once and for all. The value of a formula A valuation fixes the atoms. The value of every other formula should then follow, computed from the values of its parts by the tables of the first subsection. Since formulas are built by the clauses of @def-formula, this is a definition by recursion. The value of a formula is computed from the bottom of its parse tree upwards, one connective at a time. [Truth Value of a Formula] Let v be a valuation. The truth value v(\varphi) of a formula \varphi under v is defined by recursion on \varphi: 1. for an atom p, v(p) is the value the valuation assigns to p; and v( ot) \coloneqq \mathrm{F}; 2. v(
eg\varphi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}, and v(
eg\varphi) \coloneqq \mathrm{F} if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}; 3. v(\varphi \wedge \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}; otherwise \mathrm{F}; 4. v(\varphi \vee \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} or v(\psi) = \mathrm{T} (or both); otherwise \mathrm{F}; 5. v(\varphi 	o \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{F} if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v(\psi) = \mathrm{F}; otherwise \mathrm{T}; 6. v(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if v(\varphi) = v(\psi); otherwise \mathrm{F}. We say \varphi is true under v, or v makes \varphi true, if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}; otherwise \varphi is false under v. Clauses (V2)–(V6) say that the value of a compound formula depends only on the values of its immediate parts, and they are summed up in the tables of the five connectives:  egin{array}{c|c} \varphi & 
eg\varphi \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} \qquad  egin{array}{cc|cccc} \varphi & \psi & \varphi \wedge \psi & \varphi \vee \psi & \varphi 	o \psi & \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} Read them clause by clause. (V1): an atom has the value the valuation gives it, and  ot is false under every valuation. (V2): negation flips. (V3): a conjunction needs both parts. (V4): a disjunction needs at least one part; “or” is inclusive, as the rule ulename{\vee I} of Section 1.5 already said, so the row with both parts true gives \mathrm{T}. (V5): an implication is false in exactly one case, a true hypothesis with a false conclusion. (V6): a biconditional says the two sides agree. The columns for 
eg, \wedge and 	o, and the value of  ot, are the ones the first subsection read off the rules. Section 4.8 proves that every row of every table is, in a precise sense, a derivable sequent. Well defined. Clause (V1) gives a value to every atom and to  ot, and each of (V2)–(V6) gives a rule computing the value of a compound formula from the values of its immediate parts. By @thm-structural-recursion, such clauses define exactly one function on all formulas. This is what Section 4.3 was for. Section 4.3 showed the danger with the string p \wedge q \vee r, whose two readings take different values when p and q are false and r is true. A formula of @def-formula carries its parentheses, and has one value. [Computing a value] Let v be a valuation with v(p) = \mathrm{F}, v(q) = \mathrm{T} and v(r) = \mathrm{F}. Compute v(\varphi) for \varphi = (p \vee 
eg q) 	o (q \wedge r) . Work from the leaves of the parse tree up to its root, one node at a time, each time using one clause of @def-truth-value. List the subformulas so that each comes after its immediate parts: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Subformula Clause Value ---------------------------------- ------------------------------------ ------------------------------------ p, q, r (V1) \mathrm{F}, \mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F} 
eg q (V2): v(q) = \mathrm{T} \mathrm{F} p \vee 
eg q (V4): both parts \mathrm{F} \mathrm{F} q \wedge r (V3): v(r) = \mathrm{F} \mathrm{F} (p \vee 
eg q) 	o (q \wedge r) (V5): the hypothesis is \mathrm{F} \mathrm{T} ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ So v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}. The last step did not need the value of q \wedge r: a false hypothesis makes an implication true whatever its conclusion is. Computing by hand, one may stop a branch as soon as its value is decided. Nonexample. “p is true” and “p is false” together do not describe a valuation: the definition asks for exactly one value per atom. And a list that gives p the value \mathrm{T} and says nothing about the other atoms is not a valuation either, since it fails “every atom”. We never need more than such a partial list, but we complete it (by \mathrm{F}, say) so that the definition applies. Nonexample. The rule “every formula gets the value \mathrm{T}” agrees with the all-T valuation on every atom, but it is not the truth value of @def-truth-value under any valuation. It breaks (V1) at  ot, and it breaks (V2) at 
eg p, where p and 
eg p would both be \mathrm{T}. The truth value under the all-T valuation is the function that (V1)–(V6) produce from it, and it makes 
eg p false. Values do not distribute over connectives the way symbols seem to. The value of 
eg(p \wedge q) is not computed by negating p and q and keeping the \wedge: under a valuation with v(p) = \mathrm{T} and v(q) = \mathrm{F}, the formula 
eg(p \wedge q) is \mathrm{T} (since p \wedge q is \mathrm{F}), while 
eg p \wedge 
eg q is \mathrm{F} (since 
eg p is \mathrm{F}). Always follow the parse tree: the main connective is applied last. Let v(p) = \mathrm{F}, v(q) = \mathrm{T}, v(r) = \mathrm{T}. What is v igl( (p \vee q) 	o 
eg r  igr)? \mathrm{F}. Bottom up: p \vee q is \mathrm{T}, by (V4), since q is \mathrm{T}; 
eg r is \mathrm{F}, by (V2); and an implication with a true hypothesis and a false conclusion is \mathrm{F}, by (V5). Let v(p) = \mathrm{T} and v(q) = \mathrm{F}. What is v(
eg p \vee (q \leftrightarrow  ot))? \mathrm{T}. 
eg p is \mathrm{F} by (V2). q \leftrightarrow  ot is \mathrm{T} by (V6), since both sides are \mathrm{F} ( ot by (V1)). So the disjunction is \mathrm{T} by (V4). A game for the clauses. Clauses (V2)–(V4) can be acted out. Two players argue about a formula built from atoms by 
eg, \wedge and \vee, under a valuation v. The verifier claims that the formula is true under v, the falsifier that it is false. Play starts at the whole formula and moves down its parse tree. At \varphi \wedge \psi the falsifier chooses a conjunct to dispute, and play goes on there; at \varphi \vee \psi the verifier chooses a disjunct to defend. At 
eg\varphi the two players swap roles, and play goes on at \varphi. At an atom p the game ends: the verifier wins if v(p) = \mathrm{T}, the falsifier if v(p) = \mathrm{F}. Run it once on 
eg(p \wedge q), with v(p) = \mathrm{T} and v(q) = \mathrm{F}. At the 
eg the players swap, so the verifier of 
eg(p \wedge q) now disputes p \wedge q. At the \wedge the choice is hers: she picks q, and she wins. A formula is true under v exactly when the verifier can always win, whatever the falsifier does; Exercise C3 proves it, and nothing later rests on the game. Only the atoms of a formula matter A valuation fixes infinitely many values, but a formula contains only finitely many atoms. We expect the value of a formula to depend only on the values of its own atoms. That is the fact that makes truth tables finite, and it is our first proof by structural induction about meaning. Recall from Section 4.3 that \atoms(\varphi), the set of atoms occurring in \varphi, is defined by recursion: \atoms(p) = \{ p \} for an atom p, \atoms( ot) is empty, \atoms(
eg\varphi) = \atoms(\varphi), and the atoms of \varphi \circ \psi, for each binary connective \circ, are those of \varphi together with those of \psi. Two valuations v and w agree on a set of atoms if v(p) = w(p) for every atom p in it. [Coincidence Lemma] Let \varphi be a formula, and let v and w be valuations that agree on \atoms(\varphi). Then v(\varphi) = w(\varphi). Structural induction on \varphi, with the property “for all valuations v, w that agree on the atoms of \varphi, v(\varphi) = w(\varphi)”. At an atom, the two valuations agree by hypothesis. At a compound formula, both values are computed by the same clause from the values of the immediate parts, and every atom of a part is an atom of the whole, so the two valuations agree on the atoms of each part and the hypothesis for the parts applies. We apply @thm-structural-induction to the property C(\varphi): for all valuations v and w that agree on \atoms(\varphi), v(\varphi) = w(\varphi). Atoms. Let p be an atom and let v, w agree on \atoms(p) = \{ p \}. Then v(p) = w(p), which is C(p).  ot. By (V1), v( ot) = \mathrm{F} = w( ot) for all valuations v, w. So C( ot) holds. Negation. Assume C(\varphi), and let v, w agree on \atoms(
eg\varphi). Since \atoms(
eg\varphi) = \atoms(\varphi), they agree on \atoms(\varphi), so v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) by C(\varphi). By (V2), v(
eg\varphi) is determined by v(\varphi) and w(
eg\varphi) by w(\varphi) through the same rule, so v(
eg\varphi) = w(
eg\varphi). This proves C(
eg\varphi). Conjunction. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let v, w agree on \atoms(\varphi \wedge \psi). Every atom of \varphi is an atom of \varphi \wedge \psi, so v and w agree on \atoms(\varphi), and v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) by C(\varphi). In the same way v(\psi) = w(\psi) by C(\psi). By (V3), v(\varphi \wedge \psi) = \mathrm{T} exactly when v(\varphi) = v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, that is, exactly when w(\varphi) = w(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, that is, exactly when w(\varphi \wedge \psi) = \mathrm{T}. Hence v(\varphi \wedge \psi) = w(\varphi \wedge \psi), which is C(\varphi \wedge \psi). Disjunction, implication, biconditional. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let v, w agree on the atoms of \varphi \circ \psi. As in the conjunction case, v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) and v(\psi) = w(\psi). One clause of @def-truth-value then turns these equal inputs into equal outputs: ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \circ Clause Why v(\varphi \circ \psi) = w(\varphi \circ \psi) ----------------------- ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \vee (V4) \mathrm{T} exactly when one of the two parts is \mathrm{T}, and the parts have the same values under v and under w 	o (V5) \mathrm{F} exactly when the first part is \mathrm{T} and the second \mathrm{F}, and the parts have the same values under v and under w \leftrightarrow (V6) \mathrm{T} exactly when the two parts have equal values, and the parts have the same values under v and under w ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every clause of @def-formula has been covered, so by @thm-structural-induction, C(\varphi) holds for every formula \varphi. This proves the lemma. The table’s three cases are the conjunction case again, with another clause. The fold writes each one out in words. Disjunction. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let v, w agree on \atoms(\varphi \vee \psi). As in the previous case, v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) and v(\psi) = w(\psi). By (V4), v(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T} exactly when one of v(\varphi), v(\psi) is \mathrm{T}, that is, when one of w(\varphi), w(\psi) is \mathrm{T}, that is, when w(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T}. So C(\varphi \vee \psi). Implication. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let v, w agree on \atoms(\varphi 	o \psi). Again v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) and v(\psi) = w(\psi). By (V5), v(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{F} exactly when v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v(\psi) = \mathrm{F}, that is, when w(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and w(\psi) = \mathrm{F}, that is, when w(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{F}. So C(\varphi 	o \psi). Biconditional. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let v, w agree on \atoms(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi). Again v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) and v(\psi) = w(\psi). By (V6), v(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) = \mathrm{T} exactly when v(\varphi) = v(\psi), that is, when w(\varphi) = w(\psi), that is, when w(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) = \mathrm{T}. So C(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi). Two consequences. First, to know v(\varphi) we need only the values of v on the finitely many atoms of \varphi: if \varphi has n atoms, it has exactly 2^n different “situations”, one for each way of giving its atoms the values \mathrm{T} and \mathrm{F}. (Each atom has two choices, and the choices are independent, so the number of ways doubles with each new atom: 2, 4, 8, \dots, 2^n. This count is itself a small induction on n, by @ax-induction.) Second, the extra atoms a valuation happens to fix are irrelevant: two valuations that differ only on atoms not in \varphi give \varphi the same value. Let \varphi = p 	o (q \vee p). Two valuations v and w agree on p and q but disagree on r and on every p_n. What does @lem-coincidence say about v(\varphi) and w(\varphi)? Does it say anything about v(\varphi \wedge r) and w(\varphi \wedge r)? \atoms(\varphi) = \{ p, q \}, and v, w agree there, so v(\varphi) = w(\varphi). For \varphi \wedge r the atoms are p, q, r, and the valuations disagree on r, so the lemma does not apply. Indeed the values can differ: \varphi is true under every valuation (if p is true, so is q \vee p), so v(\varphi \wedge r) = v(r) and w(\varphi \wedge r) = w(r), which differ. Truth tables @lem-coincidence says that a formula’s value is decided by finitely many choices, and so it can be tabulated once and for all. A truth table lists the value of a formula in every possible situation, one row per way of giving its atoms values. [Truth Table] Let \varphi be a formula and let p_1, \dots, p_n be a list of distinct atoms that includes every atom of \varphi. A row is an assignment of a truth value to each of p_1, \dots, p_n. The truth table of \varphi (on p_1, \dots, p_n) lists, for each of the 2^n rows, the value v(\varphi) for a valuation v that agrees with the row on p_1, \dots, p_n. We say \varphi is true (or false) in the row. Well defined. Two things must be checked. Existence: every row comes from a valuation, for instance the one that gives p_1, \dots, p_n the row’s values and every other atom \mathrm{F}. Independence of the choice: two valuations that agree with the same row agree on p_1, \dots, p_n, hence on \atoms(\varphi), so by @lem-coincidence they give \varphi the same value. Without the lemma, “the value in a row” would not make sense, since a row says nothing about the infinitely many other atoms. The list p_1, \dots, p_n is allowed to contain atoms that do not occur in \varphi; then pairs of rows that differ only there show the same value. This freedom lets us compare several formulas in one table, over the atoms of all of them, and Section 4.5 does that constantly. When \varphi has no atoms at all, as 
eg ot or  ot 	o  ot do, the list may be empty, and the table has 2^0 = 1 row: such a formula has the same value under every valuation. Conventions. The atom columns come first. The rows are listed with \mathrm{T} before \mathrm{F}, the last atom alternating fastest: for two atoms, TT, TF, FT, FF. In practice we add a column for each subformula, building up to \varphi in the order of the parse tree, as in @exm-value-down-the-tree, but now for every row at once. [The truth table of modus ponens] Make the truth table of ((p 	o q) \wedge p) 	o q on p, q, and read off from it what ulename{{	o}E} does. Columns for the two atoms, then for each subformula in turn:  egin{array}{cc|ccc} p & q & p 	o q & (p 	o q) \wedge p & ((p 	o q) \wedge p) 	o q \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} The third column is (V5): \mathrm{F} only in the row TF. The fourth is (V3) applied to the third column and the p column: \mathrm{T} only in the first row. The last is (V5) again, with the fourth column as hypothesis and q as conclusion: the hypothesis is false in rows 2–4, so those rows are \mathrm{T}, and in row 1 the conclusion q is \mathrm{T}. So the formula is true in every row. Read as a statement about ulename{{	o}E}: the only row in which both given lines p 	o q and p are true is row 1, and in that row the line the rule writes, q, is true as well. The rule never leads from true lines to a false one, at least when \varphi and \psi are the atoms p and q. Section 4.7 proves this for every rule and every formula. Now a table built column by column for a biconditional, whose two sides Chapter 2 related by derivations. [An implication and its contrapositive] Make the truth table of (p 	o q) \leftrightarrow (
eg q 	o 
eg p).  egin{array}{cc|ccccc} p & q & p 	o q & 
eg q & 
eg p & 
eg q 	o

Nothing else about the parts enters: not what they say, not how long they are. The general form of such a rule has a name. [Truth Function] Let n \ge 1. A truth function f with n inputs assigns to each list (a_1, \dots, a_n) of truth values (each a_i is \mathrm{T} or \mathrm{F}) a truth value f(a_1, \dots, a_n). A formula \varphi expresses f if v(\varphi) = f igl(v(p_1), \dots, v(p_n) igr) \quad 	ext{for every valuation } v . (3) If v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, then v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V4), since at least one part is true. (4) If v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, then v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V5), because v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{F} and an implication with a false hypothesis is true. This covers every clause, and proves the claim. 1. Is the claim true? 2. Name the line that fails and say exactly what is wrong with it. 3. Give a formula on which the reason given in that line is false. 4. Repair the line. (a) Yes. The claim is true, and the repaired proof in (d) proves it. So no formula is a counterexample to the claim; the error is in the argument only. (b) Line (4). Its hypothesis states v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, and its reason states v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}. The reason contradicts the induction hypothesis it is supposed to use: it quotes the vacuous row of (V5), which does not apply here. The conclusion v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T} is correct, but not for the reason given. (c) p 	o q. Under v_{\mathrm{T}}, v_{\mathrm{T}}(p) = \mathrm{T}, so the stated reason “v_{\mathrm{T}}(p) = \mathrm{F}” is false, although v_{\mathrm{T}}(p 	o q) = \mathrm{T} holds. (d) (4) If v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, then v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V5), because the conclusion \psi is true, so we are not in the one row (true hypothesis, false conclusion) where an implication is false. With this line the induction is correct, and the claim follows. Section 4.9 uses this fact to show that \wedge, \vee and 	o cannot express negation. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the claim is true (with the reason: the repaired proof). - 3: names line (4), and says its reason contradicts the hypothesis v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} of that very case. - 2: a formula, such as p 	o q, on which the stated reason fails. - 3: the repair, citing the row of (V5) that actually applies (conclusion true). Fatal errors (0 for the step): calling the claim false; locating the error in line (3) (at least one part true is correct) or in the handling of  ot, 
eg, \leftrightarrow. [C3: The game and the clauses] Fix a valuation v. For formulas built from atoms by 
eg, \wedge, \vee alone, define by recursion (@thm-structural-recursion, applied to the pair of truth values of the two statements as one function, since each clause for 
eg calls on the other statement; give  ot, 	o and \leftrightarrow any values, they play no part) two statements, \mathrm{Ver}(\varphi) (“the verifier can always win at \varphi”) and \mathrm{Fal}(\varphi) (“the falsifier can always win at \varphi”): ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \varphi \mathrm{Ver}(\varphi) holds iff \mathrm{Fal}(\varphi) holds iff ----------------------- --------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------- an atom p v(p) = \mathrm{T} v(p) = \mathrm{F}

Say in words why each clause matches the rules of the game. 2. Prove by structural induction that for every such formula \varphi, \mathrm{Ver}(\varphi) holds iff v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, and \mathrm{Fal}(\varphi) holds iff v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}. 3. Why must the two statements of (b) be proved together? [Hint 1] Put “if \varphi is built from 
eg, \wedge, \vee” inside the property. [Hint 2] The step for 
eg needs the claim about \mathrm{Fal} for the part. (a) At an atom the game ends, and the value of the atom decides the winner. At \wedge the falsifier chooses, so the verifier wins only if she can win at both parts, whichever he picks, and the falsifier wins if he can win at one of them, by picking it. At \vee the verifier chooses, so the roles are reversed: she needs one part, he needs both. At 
eg the players swap, so winning as verifier at 
eg	heta is winning as falsifier at 	heta, and the other way round. (b) The property is C(\varphi): if \varphi is built from 
eg, \wedge, \vee, then (\mathrm{Ver}(\varphi) iff v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}) and (\mathrm{Fal}(\varphi) iff v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}). For  ot, 	o and \leftrightarrow it is vacuous. For an atom both halves are the definition. Negation. Assume C(	heta). Then \mathrm{Ver}(

eg	heta) = \mathrm{T}, by (V2). Likewise \mathrm{Fal}(
eg	heta) iff \mathrm{Ver}(	heta) iff v(	heta) = \mathrm{T} iff v(
eg	heta) = \mathrm{F}. Conjunction. Assume C(	heta) and C(\chi). \mathrm{Ver}(	heta \wedge \chi) iff both \mathrm{Ver}(	heta) and \mathrm{Ver}(\chi), iff both parts are true, iff v(	heta \wedge \chi) = \mathrm{T}, by (V3). \mathrm{Fal}(	heta \wedge \chi) iff \mathrm{Fal} holds of one part, iff one part is false, iff v(	heta \wedge \chi) = \mathrm{F}. Disjunction. The same with (V4): \mathrm{Ver} iff one part is true, \mathrm{Fal} iff both parts are false. Every clause of @def-formula is covered, so @thm-structural-induction gives C(\varphi) for every formula. (c) The

title: 4.5 Tautologies, Entailment and Equivalence
content:
Tautologies, Entailment and Equivalence Section 4.4 gave every formula a value under every valuation, and collected the values in a truth table. One formula at a time, though, is not what Chapters 1 and 2 were about. They were about sequents: premises on the left, a conclusion on the right, and the claim that the conclusion can be derived. This section defines the counterpart of a sequent in terms of truth, \Gamma \models \psi: every valuation that makes the premises true makes the conclusion true. On the way it names the formulas that are true in every row, and the pairs of formulas that are true in the same rows. It then proves two lemmas about changing a formula, by replacing one part or by putting formulas in for its atoms, that later sections use, and ends by sorting the section’s questions by whether one row or every row settles them, and by setting \models beside \vdash. Tautologies and contradictions Some tables of Section 4.4 had a last column made entirely of \mathrm{T}: the formula ((p 	o q) \wedge p) 	o q of @exm-truth-table-modus-ponens, and the biconditional of @exm-table-contrapositive. Their truth does not depend on the situation. One table in Exercise A1 there, that of p \leftrightarrow 
eg p, was all \mathrm{F}. These extremes deserve names. A tautology is true for reasons of form alone: whatever the atoms mean, it comes out true. [Tautology and Contradiction] A formula \varphi is a tautology if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} for every valuation v. It is a contradiction if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F} for every valuation v. By @lem-coincidence, the value of \varphi under a valuation depends only on the row the valuation gives to the atoms of \varphi. So \varphi is a tautology exactly when its truth table has \mathrm{T} in every row, and a contradiction exactly when it has \mathrm{F} in every row. Infinitely many valuations, finitely many rows to check. Examples, simplest first. - p 	o p and p \vee 
eg p are tautologies: in the row p = \mathrm{T} both are true, and in the row p = \mathrm{F}, p 	o p has a false hypothesis and 
eg p is true. - p \wedge 
eg p and p \leftrightarrow 
eg p are contradictions: in each row one of p, 
eg p is false, and the two sides of the biconditional differ. - Nonexample. p 	o q is neither: it is \mathrm{T} in the row TT and \mathrm{F} in the row TF. Most formulas are like this. Changing one symbol of the tautology p 	o p, to get p 	o q, loses the property: the rows in which the hypothesis and conclusion differ are no longer excluded by their being the same atom. A formula that is true in some rows and false in others, such as p 	o q, is called contingent: every formula is a tautology, a contradiction, or contingent. A formula with no atoms, such as  ot or 
eg ot, has the same value under every valuation (its table has one row). So it is either a contradiction, like  ot, or a tautology, like 
eg ot. This degenerate case is the only one in which “not a tautology” forces “a contradiction”. Lists of formulas need a word too, because a list of premises can fail to be true together even when each premise alone can be true. [Satisfiable] A formula \varphi is satisfiable if there is a valuation v with v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}. A list of formulas \Gamma = \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n, where n \ge 0, is satisfiable if there is a valuation that makes every \varphi_i true. A formula or list that is not satisfiable is unsatisfiable. In words: a formula is satisfiable if some row makes it true, and a list is satisfiable if some single row makes all its members true at once. So a formula is unsatisfiable exactly when it is a contradiction. The empty list (n = 0) is satisfiable: every valuation makes all of its members true, since it has none to check. The list p, 
eg p is unsatisfiable, although each of its members is satisfiable: a row making p true makes 
eg p false. Satisfiability of a list is about a common row, not about each formula separately. And the list p 	o q, \ q 	o r, \ r 	o 
eg p is satisfiable, by the row with p false and q, r true (the first two have true conclusions, and the third has conclusion 
eg p, which is true); in fact p is false in every row that makes all three true. Tautologies and unsatisfiable formulas are two sides of one coin. For every formula \psi, \psi 	ext{ is a tautology} \iff 
eg\psi 	ext{ is unsatisfiable.} Indeed, by (V2) of @def-truth-value, v(
eg\psi) = \mathrm{T} exactly when v(\psi) = \mathrm{F}. So “no valuation makes 
eg\psi true” says “no valuation makes \psi false”, which is “every valuation makes \psi true”. Sections 4.6 and 4.9 use it to pass between the two kinds of question. Satisfiable and consistent. Section 3.2 called a list \Gamma inconsistent if \Gamma \vdash  ot (@def-inconsistent-set), and consistent otherwise: a word about derivations. Satisfiable is its twin about truth: some row makes every member of the list true. Nothing yet connects the two words. Section 4.7 proves that a satisfiable list is consistent, and Section 4.8 the converse; until then we keep them apart. The counterexample set lives in both worlds: \Gamma \vdash \psi exactly when \Gamma, 
eg\psi is inconsistent (@prp-derivable-iff-negation-inconsistent (b)), and \Gamma \models \psi exactly when \Gamma, 
eg\psi is unsatisfiable (below). “Not a tautology” does not mean “a contradiction”. The formula p 	o q is neither: some rows make it true and some false. To show a formula is not a tautology, one row making it false is enough; to show it is a contradiction, every row must make it false. Semantic entailment Now the counterpart of a sequent. A derivation from premises \Gamma to a conclusion \psi is a promise that \psi follows from \Gamma. In terms of truth, “follows” should mean: no situation makes the premises true and the conclusion false. We want to prove, in Sections 4.7 and 4.8, that the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 derive exactly the sequents that pass this test; for that we need a precise name for the test. An argument is valid when its conclusion is true in every row in which all its premises are true. Semantic Entailment Let \Gamma = \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n be a list of formulas, where n \ge 0, and let \psi be a formula. We say \Gamma semantically entails \psi, and write \Gamma \models \psi , if every valuation that makes all of \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n true also makes \psi true. We then also call the argument from \Gamma to \psi valid. We write \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \models \psi for \Gamma \models \psi, and \models \psi when \Gamma is empty. If \Gamma \models \psi fails, we write \Gamma 
ot\models \psi, and a valuation that makes every formula of \Gamma true and \psi false is a refuting valuation, or refuting row. Clause by clause. “Every valuation”: the condition is checked in all situations, not in the actual one; a valid argument cannot be spoiled by what the atoms happen to mean. “That makes all of \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n true”: rows in which some premise is false are ignored, whatever the conclusion does there. “Also makes \psi true”: in the remaining rows, the conclusion must hold. In symbols, for every valuation v,  igl( v(\varphi_1) = \mathrm{T} 	ext{ and } \dots 	ext{ and } v(\varphi_n) = \mathrm{T}  igr) \ \Rightarrow \ v(\psi) = \mathrm{T} . And \Gamma 
ot\models \psi says: there is a valuation making every premise true and the conclusion false. One refuting row is enough. Checking it. By @lem-coincidence, whether a valuation makes the premises and the conclusion true depends only on its row on the atoms occurring in \Gamma and \psi. So \Gamma \models \psi can be decided by one truth table on those atoms (@def-truth-table allows extra atoms in the list): find the rows in which every premise is \mathrm{T}, and look at the conclusion there. First examples. Row 1 of @exm-truth-table-modus-ponens is the only row making p 	o q and p true, and q is true there, so p 	o q, \ p \models q. By @exm-table-contrapositive, p 	o q \models 
eg q 	o 
eg p and 
eg q 	o 
eg p \models p 	o q, since the two columns are equal. The empty list. When \Gamma is empty, every valuation makes “all of \Gamma” true, so \models \psi says that every valuation makes \psi true: \models \psi holds exactly when \psi is a tautology. Unsatisfiable premises. If \Gamma is unsatisfiable, no valuation makes all of \Gamma true, so the condition has no row to check and holds: \Gamma \models \psi for every formula \psi. For example p, 
eg p \models q and  ot \models q. This is the table’s version of @prp-ex-falso, P, 
eg P \vdash Q, and of ulename{ ot E}. More premises. If \Gamma \models \psi, and \Delta is a list containing every formula of \Gamma (and perhaps others), then \Delta \models \psi: a valuation making all of \Delta true makes all of \Gamma true, and so makes \psi true. Adding premises never destroys an entailment. In the same way, the order of the premises and repetitions among them do not matter: only which formulas occur in the list does. Four facts about \models need nothing but the definition. Reflexivity: \Gamma \models \varphi whenever \varphi is a member of \Gamma, since a row making all of \Gamma true makes \varphi true. Weakening: adding premises keeps an entailment, as just shown. Order and repetition: rearranging \Gamma, or repeating a member, changes nothing. Cut: if \Gamma \models \varphi and \Gamma, \varphi \models \psi, then \Gamma \models \psi. Indeed, let a row make every member of \Gamma true. By the first entailment it makes \varphi true, so it makes every member of \Gamma, \varphi true, and by the second it makes \psi true. Section 2.3 proved weakening and cut for \vdash (@lem-weakening-cut) by pasting derivations, and its weakening, which asks only that every member of \Gamma be a member of \Delta, covers order and repetition; reflexivity for \vdash is the derivation whose only line is the premise \varphi. Here each fact is one line about rows. Section 4.8 sets the two lists side by side. A test by satisfiability. Finally, for every list \Gamma and formula \psi, \Gamma \models \psi \iff 	ext{the list } \Gamma, 
eg\psi 	ext{ is unsatisfiable.} Both sides say that no valuation makes every formula of \Gamma true and \psi false, because v(
eg\psi) = \mathrm{T} exactly when v(\psi) = \mathrm{F}. With \Gamma empty this is the equivalence between tautologies and unsatisfiable negations above. The list \Gamma, 
eg\psi is the counterexample set of the claim (@def-counterexample-set): an argument is valid exactly when its counterexample set cannot be made true by any row. Rows as regions. A table on p and q has four rows, and they can be drawn as the four regions of a picture. Each row of the table on p, q is a region. A formula marks the rows where it is true: p \wedge q the lens, p \vee q both circles, 
eg p everything outside p’s circle. \Gamma \models \psi says that the region where all of \Gamma is true lies inside the region of \psi: p \wedge q \models p \vee q. Equivalent formulas mark the same region, a tautology marks the whole rectangle, and an unsatisfiable list marks nothing in common. Does p \wedge q \models p \vee r hold? Does p \vee r \models p \wedge q? The first holds: a row making p \wedge q true makes p true, so p \vee r is true. The second fails, for instance at p = \mathrm{F}, r = \mathrm{T} (any q), which makes p \vee r true and p \wedge q false. [Affirming the consequent is not valid] Show that p 	o q, \ q 
ot\models p. We need one row making both premises true and the conclusion false. The conclusion p must be \mathrm{F}, and the premise q must be \mathrm{T}. In the row p = \mathrm{F}, q = \mathrm{T}, the premise p 	o q is \mathrm{T}, since its hypothesis is false. So this row makes p 	o q and q true and p false: it is a refuting row. The pattern is the one of Section 1.3, “from \varphi 	o \psi and \psi, infer \varphi”, which is not an instance of ulename{{	o}E}. Section 1.1’s Quick check gave the row a face: with P: “n is divisible by 4” and Q: “n is even”, at n = 2 the premises P 	o Q and Q are true and P is false. It is also the step that would repair Argument B of Section 1.1: from “if n is even, then n^2 is even” and “n^2 is even”, conclude “n is even”. The conclusion of that instance happens to be true for every integer n, as Argument A proves; the refuting row shows that the form does not guarantee it, so the step proves nothing. Section 4.7 upgrades this row from “not valid” to “not derivable by any derivation”. A valid argument with several premises is checked in the same way, and working backwards from F often settles it without a table. [Two cases, two conclusions] Show that p \vee q, \ p 	o r, \ q 	o s \models r \vee s. Suppose a valuation v makes all three premises true and the conclusion false; we derive a contradiction. Since r \vee s is \mathrm{F}, both r and s are \mathrm{F} (V4). Since p 	o r is \mathrm{T} and r is \mathrm{F}, the hypothesis p is \mathrm{F} (V5). In the same way q 	o s forces q to be \mathrm{F}. But then p \vee q is \mathrm{F}, contradicting the first premise. So no refuting valuation exists, and the entailment holds. The search replaced a table of 2^4 = 16 rows by four forced steps. The entailment is the table’s picture of a proof by cases with ulename{\vee E}: in the case p, the second premise gives r, and ulename{\vee I} gives r \vee s; in the case q, the third gives s, and ulename{\vee I} again. Changing the grouping of a formula can change what it entails. [One grouping entails the other, not conversely] Decide whether (p 	o q) 	o r \models p 	o (q 	o r), and whether p 	o (q 	o r) \models (p 	o q) 	o r. The first holds. Suppose a valuation makes (p 	o q) 	o r true and p 	o (q 	o r) false. The latter forces p = \mathrm{T} and q 	o r false, so q = \mathrm{T} and r = \mathrm{F}. Then p 	o q is \mathrm{T}, and (p 	o q) 	o r has a true hypothesis and a false conclusion, so it is \mathrm{F}, a contradiction. The second fails. Take p = \mathrm{F} and r = \mathrm{F}, with q either value. Then p 	o (q 	o r) is \mathrm{T}, since its hypothesis is false. But p 	o q is \mathrm{T} for the same reason, so (p 	o q) 	o r is \mathrm{T} 	o \mathrm{F}, which is \mathrm{F}. These two rows are refuting rows. So the two groupings are not interchangeable, which is why Chapter 1 fixed a convention (	o groups to the right) and why the convention matters. \models is not 	o. The formula \varphi 	o \psi is a formula: it has a value in each row and can be a part of larger formulas. The statement \varphi \models \psi is not a formula at all. It is a claim about two formulas, true or false once and for all, like \varphi \vdash \psi. They are related (Exercise B3 below asks you to prove that \varphi \models \psi holds exactly when \varphi 	o \psi is a tautology), but writing p \models q \models r, or 
eg(p \models q) inside a formula, mixes the two levels and means nothing. Is p, 
eg p \models q? Is p 	o q, \ 
eg p \models 
eg q? The first holds: the list p, 
eg p is unsatisfiable, so there is no row to check. The second fails: the row p = \mathrm{F}, q = \mathrm{T} makes p 	o q true (false hypothesis) and 
eg p true, and 
eg q false. It is the pattern “denying the hypothesis”, the mirror image of affirming the consequent. Semantic equivalence Two formulas can be different strings and still say the same thing in every situation, as p 	o q and 
eg q 	o 
eg p did in @exm-table-contrapositive. Chapter 2 had a word for formulas that derive each other, provable equivalence (@def-provable-equivalence). Here is the counterpart in terms of truth. Two formulas are equivalent when they have the same truth table. Semantic Equivalence Formulas \varphi and \psi are semantically equivalent, written \varphi \equiv \psi, if \varphi \models \psi and \psi \models \varphi. In words, each entails the other. Equivalently, v(\varphi) = v(\psi) for every valuation v. Indeed, if \varphi \equiv \psi and v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, then v(\psi) = \mathrm{T} by \varphi \models \psi; if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}, then v(\psi) cannot be \mathrm{T}, since \psi \models \varphi would make v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}. The converse is plain. By (V6) of @def-truth-value, “v(\varphi) = v(\psi) for every v” says that \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi is true under every v, so \varphi \equiv \psi \iff \models \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi . From “same value under every valuation” it follows at once that \equiv is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive: \varphi \equiv \varphi; if \varphi \equiv \psi, then \psi \equiv \varphi; if \varphi \equiv \psi and \psi \equiv \chi, then \varphi \equiv \chi. Examples: p \wedge q \equiv q \wedge p (the clause (V3) does not care about the order); p \equiv 
eg
eg p (two flips); p \vee 
eg p \equiv 
eg ot (both are true under every valuation). The degenerate case: any two tautologies are equivalent, and so are any two contradictions. Nonexample: p \wedge q and p are not equivalent. One direction holds, p \wedge q \models p, but the other fails in the row p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F}. Entailment in one direction is not equivalence. Nor is equivalence identity: p \wedge q and q \wedge p are different formulas, with different parse trees, and ulename{{	o}E} treats them as different (Section 1.3). The equivalences used most often are collected below. They are stated for arbitrary formulas \varphi, \psi, \chi, not just atoms, since Section 4.9 applies them to compound formulas. [Standard Equivalences] For all formulas \varphi, \psi and \chi: 1. (contrapositive) \varphi 	o \psi \equiv
