eg\varphi \equiv \varphi; 5. (biconditional) \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi \equiv (\varphi 	o \psi) \wedge (\psi 	o \varphi); 6. (commutativity) \varphi \wedge \psi \equiv \psi \wedge \varphi and \varphi \vee \psi \equiv \psi \vee \varphi; 7. (distributivity) \varphi \wedge (\psi \vee \chi) \equiv (\varphi \wedge \psi) \vee (\varphi \wedge \chi) and \varphi \vee (\psi \wedge \chi) \equiv (\varphi \vee \psi) \wedge (\varphi \vee \chi); 8. (associativity) (\varphi \wedge \psi) \wedge \chi \equiv \varphi \wedge (\psi \wedge \chi) and (\varphi \vee \psi) \vee \chi \equiv \varphi \vee (\psi \vee \chi). For atoms these are truth-table checks. For arbitrary formulas the same tables work, with \varphi, \psi, \chi in the place of atoms: under a fixed valuation, each of \varphi, \psi, \chi has some value, and both sides are computed from those values by the clauses (V2)–(V6), exactly as in a table whose first columns are \varphi, \psi, \chi. Fix a valuation v, and let a = v(\varphi), b = v(\psi), c = v(\chi). Each side of each equivalence is built from \varphi, \psi, \chi by connectives, so by (V2)–(V6) of @def-truth-value its value under v is computed from a, b, c by the clauses of those connectives. The combination (a, b), or (a, b, c), is one row of the tables below, whose first columns list all 4 (or 8) combinations. In each table the columns of the two sides of each equivalence agree in every row, as the reader can check column by column. Hence both sides have the same value under v, and since v was arbitrary, they are equivalent by the paraphrase of @def-semantic-equivalence. title: 4.6 Hunting for a Refuting Row
content:
Hunting for a Refuting Row Section 4.5 reduced every question about rows to one: is this list unsatisfiable? A truth table answers it by brute force, and with n atoms it has 2^n rows. Working backwards from F (@exm-backwards-from-f) is faster: assume the conclusion false and follow what is forced. But where a value leaves a choice, as a false conjunction or a true disjunction does, it only says “split into cases”, and keeps no record of the cases. This section turns working backwards into a method that keeps that record: take the forced steps first, and when nothing is forced, split into cases and follow every case. On paper the method is a tree. A branch that closes is a case with no row; a branch that stays open hands us a row. The answers are about truth, “valid” or “here is a refuting row”; what they say about derivations is the next section’s business. The rules of the search To decide \Gamma \models \psi, we look for one row that makes every formula of the counterexample set \Gamma, 
eg\psi true; the entailment holds exactly when there is none. To decide whether a list \Delta is satisfiable, we look for one row that makes all of \Delta true. Requirements on the row are kept as formulas: “\varphi must be true” is written \varphi, and “\varphi must be false” is written 
eg\varphi. From the tables of (V3)–(V5), counting each way as a condition on one or both parts: in how many ways can \varphi \wedge \psi be true? In how many ways can it be false? In how many ways can \varphi 	o \psi be false? In how many ways can it be true? \varphi \wedge \psi is true in one way (both parts true) and false in two (\varphi false, or \psi false; the row with both false is covered by either). \varphi 	o \psi is false in one way (\varphi true and \psi false) and true in two (\varphi false, or \psi true). Each requirement on a compound formula is traded for requirements on its parts, read off its clause. These are the search rules; first the requirements met in only one way. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- On the branch Its requirement, read off Adds ------------------------- ----------------------------------------- ----------------------- \varphi \wedge \psi (V3): both parts true \varphi, \psi 
eg(\varphi \vee \psi) (V4): both parts false 
eg\varphi, 
eg\psi 
eg(\varphi 	o \psi) (V5): hypothesis true, conclusion false \varphi, 
eg\psi 
eg
eg\varphi (V2) twice: \varphi true \varphi ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Then the requirements met in two ways; each splits the search into two cases. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- On the branch Its requirement, read off Adds ------------------------------------ -------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------- \varphi \vee \psi (V4): some part true \varphi or \psi 
eg(\varphi \wedge \psi) (V3): some part false 
eg\varphi or 
eg\psi \varphi 	o \psi (V5): hypothesis false, or conclusion true 
eg\varphi or \psi \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi (V6): the parts agree \varphi, \psi or 
eg\varphi, 
eg\psi 
eg(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) (V6): the parts differ \varphi, 
eg\psi or 
eg\varphi, \psi -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- An atom, a negated atom, and 
eg ot (true in every row) need no rule. A list of requirements that holds some formula together with its negation, or holds  ot, describes no row at all: it is closed. The one-way rules are the forced steps of working backwards from F, with 
eg
eg added; the two-way rules are where it split into cases, with \leftrightarrow added. The two ways of a split need not exclude each other (a row may make both \varphi and \psi true); they need only cover every row that makes the formula true. The search, drawn as a tree [Search Tree] Let \Delta be a finite list of formulas. A search tree for \Delta is built in stages. It begins as one node, the root, carrying the formulas of \Delta. At each stage, choose an open branch B and a formula \chi on B that is not an atom, a negated atom,  ot or 
eg ot, and that is not yet used on B; then, below the last node of B, add \chi’s rule: one new node with the formulas of its one way, or two new nodes side by side with the formulas of its two ways. On each new branch, \chi (and every formula equal to it) is now used: a formula is used on a branch exactly when the branch passes through a node added by its rule, so it stays used on every branch extending that one. Being used is a property of a formula on a branch: a formula at the root may be used on one branch and not on another. A branch is a path from the root down to a node with nothing below it, and its formulas are those on its nodes. A branch is closed if it holds some formula together with its negation, or holds  ot; otherwise it is open. An open branch is finished if every formula on it, other than an atom, a negated atom or 
eg ot, is used on it. A search tree is finished if each of its branches is closed or finished. In words: a search tree is a record of a backwards computation with every choice followed. A closed branch is a case with no row; a finished open branch is a case that has survived every requirement. We draw search trees with three marks. A closed branch ends in 	imes, and a finished open branch in \circ. A formula is ticked (\checkmark) once its rule has been applied below it on some branch; the nodes its rule added show on which branches it is used. The formulas that a one-way rule adds are written straight under the stack they extend, with no new edge. [A tree that closes] Decide whether p 	o (q \vee r), \ q 	o s, \ r 	o s \models p 	o s. This is the list of Section 3.2’s exit check (@exr-four-kinds-of-task-c1), which derived the claim; now a search shows it valid. The root carries the counterexample set: the three premises and 
eg(p 	o s). - Stage 1, the one-way rule for 
eg(p 	o s): add p, 
eg s. - Stage 2, p 	o (q \vee r): 
eg p or q \vee r. The branch 
eg p closes against p. - Stage 3, q \vee r: q or r. - Stage 4, on the branch q: q 	o s gives 
eg q, which closes against q, or s, which closes against 
eg s. - Stage 5, on the branch r: r 	o s gives 
eg r or s, both closed. (The branch r closes without q 	o s, so that formula is never used there.) Every branch is closed: no row makes the counterexample set true, and the entailment holds. A tick marks a formula whose rule was applied below it: q 	o s was used on the branch through q, and r 	o s on the branch through r. Each branch closed before the other formula was needed. Five closed branches replace the 2^4 = 16 rows of a table. Read as a proof by cases, the tree says: p is forced, so q \vee r; in the case q, s follows, against 
eg s; in the case r, likewise. [A branch that stays open] Decide whether p 	o (q \vee r), \ q 	o s \models p 	o s. The first three stages are the same as before. On the branch q, the rule of q 	o s closes both sides, as before. On the branch r, at a stage of its own, q 	o s gives 
eg q or s. (A formula used on one branch may be used again on another.) The side s closes against 
eg s; the side 
eg q does not. That branch carries p 	o (q \vee r) (used), q 	o s (used), 
eg(p 	o s) (used), p, 
eg s, q \vee r (used), r and 
eg q: it is open and finished. Its row: the atoms on it, p and r, are true; the atoms that stand negated on it, q and s, are false. Check against the root. p 	o (q \vee r) is \mathrm{T} 	o \mathrm{T}, true. q 	o s has a false hypothesis, so it is true. p 	o s is \mathrm{T} 	o \mathrm{F}, false. So this row refutes the claim. The premise r 	o s of the first example is exactly what closed this branch. Dropping it breaks the claim, as replacing it by r 	o t did in part (d) of @exr-four-kinds-of-task-c1, and now the search finds the row. The search may stop at the first finished open branch: one refuting row settles the question. On the open branch of the second tree, check that its row makes every formula on the branch true, the used ones included. p, r, 
eg q and 
eg s are true; q \vee r is true, by r; p 	o (q \vee r) is true, its conclusion being true; q 	o s is true, its hypothesis being false; and 
eg(p 	o s) is true, since p 	o s is false. What a closed tree proves Each rule passes a row on. If a row makes every formula on a branch true and a rule is applied there, the row makes true all the formulas of at least one new node, since each rule was read off its table. So a row making the root true runs down some branch to its end with every formula true there. A closed branch holds \varphi and 
eg\varphi, or  ot, which no row makes true. An open finished branch hands over a row. Make the atoms that stand on it true and all other atoms false. A negated atom on it is then true, since its atom is not on the open branch; every other formula on it is used, so the branch carries the shorter formulas of one of its ways, and it is true by its clause once they are. From the shortest up, every formula on the branch is true. [The Search Decides] Let \Delta be a finite list of formulas. 1. Every search tree for \Delta can be continued until it is finished, and it has only finitely many stages. 2. If every branch of a search tree for \Delta is closed, then \Delta is unsatisfiable. 3. If a search tree for \Delta has an open finished branch B, then the valuation v_B that makes the atoms on B true and every other atom false makes every formula on B true, in particular every formula of \Delta. So, for a list \Gamma and a formula \psi: a search tree for \Gamma, 
eg\psi, continued as in (a), either closes, and then \Gamma \models \psi, or has an open finished branch, whose row refutes \Gamma \models \psi. In words: the search always ends; a closed tree proves unsatisfiability, and an open finished branch exhibits a satisfying row. Since (b) and (c) cannot both apply to finished trees of one list, every order of moves gives the same verdict. (a) Every new formula is shorter than the one whose rule added it, and is a subformula of a root formula or the negation of one. (b) and (c) are the two observations, made exact by induction (on the stages for (b), on the length of a formula for (c)). The proof is in the fold below. (a) Let N be the number of formulas that are subformulas of formulas of \Delta, or negations of such. Every formula ever added to the tree is one of these. Each rule adds immediate parts of the used formula, or negations of them, or, for 
eg
eg\varphi, the formula \varphi; and if the used formula is a subformula of a root formula or the negation of one, then so are the formulas it adds. Once a formula is used on a branch, it and every formula equal to it stay used on every branch below, so a stage below a given node never uses a formula already used above it. Hence each of the N formulas is used at most once along a branch, and a branch has at most N stages below the root. A stage adds at most two nodes, below one branch, so a branch splits at most N times, and the tree never has more than 2^N branches, each with at most N + 1 nodes. Each stage adds a node, so there are only finitely many stages. When no stage is possible, no open branch carries an unused formula other than an atom, a negated atom,  ot or 
eg ot; since  ot is on no open branch, every branch is closed or finished. (b) Claim: at every stage, if a valuation v makes every formula of \Delta true, then some branch has all its formulas true under v. At the start this is the root. title: 4.7 Soundness
content:
Soundness Chapter 3 ended on a question it could not answer. Section 3.1 searched for a derivation of P 	o Q \vdash Q 	o P, and every route came back to the same gap; but a search that fails proves nothing, since a cleverer derivation might exist. The row that refutes affirming the consequent in Section 4.5, p = \mathrm{F} and q = \mathrm{T}, finds what the search could not: it makes p 	o q true and q 	o p false, and the search of Section 4.6 finds such rows whenever they exist. This section proves the theorem that turns such a row into a proof that no derivation exists. It is called soundness: whatever the rules derive is true in every row where the premises are true. The proof is the book’s first long proof about proofs, and it is an induction on the lines of a derivation. What must be proved, and why it is not obvious Two levels. This section speaks about the calculus from outside it. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Object level: written in the language Meta level: claims about it, proved in ordinary mathematics ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- formulas; derivations, with their lines, boxes, justifications and printed purposes (“asm, for →I”, which the proof reads as the rule whose case applies) “\Gamma \vdash \psi”, “\Gamma \models \psi”, “line k is justified by ulename{\vee E}”, “\Gamma_k \models \varphi_k” ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Section 4.2’s checklist reads: objects, the lines of one derivation; property, \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k (contexts are defined below); base cases, the premises and assumptions, which cite nothing; steps, one for each rule; principle, @thm-strong-induction. The proof below argues by cases (“if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F} … if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}”) and by contradiction, in the metalanguage: the very patterns that ulename{\vee E} and ulename{RAA} record in the object language. That is not circular. The theorem is not meant to persuade someone who rejects reasoning by cases. It is a theorem of ordinary mathematics about a calculus, and what it rules out is a mismatch between the rules and the tables, of the kind the connective in the fold of Section 4.4 has. Chapters 1 and 2 checked each rule as it arrived. ulename{\wedge I} is safe because two true statements make a true conjunction (Section 1.2); ulename{{	o}E} is safe because that is what “if … then” asserts (Section 1.3). Section 1.2 said once that Chapter 4 would prove it for every rule of Chapters 1 and 2 at once. Why is that more than collecting the separate checks? The first attempt at a proof is: go down a derivation, line by line, and show that each line is true in every row in which the premises are true. For a derivation without boxes this works. Each line is a premise, or comes from earlier lines by a rule, and the rule turns true lines into a true line. But it fails at the first box. Here is the derivation of @prp-contrapositive, written with atoms: Line 3 is p, and the row p = \mathrm{F}, q = \mathrm{F} makes the premise p 	o q true and line 3 false. Line 5 is  ot, which is false in every row. So the lines inside a box are not true in the rows where the premises are true, and the first attempt collapses. Yet the derivation is correct, and its last line 
eg q 	o 
eg p is true in every row making p 	o q true (@exm-table-contrapositive). What goes wrong is that a line inside a box is not claimed on the strength of the premises alone. Line 4 says: if p 	o q, 
eg q and p all hold, then q holds. That is a true claim about rows. Every line depends on the premises and on the assumptions of the boxes around it, and a correct statement about each line must mention both. Below we give this list a name: the context of the line. Derivations of formulas From now on the lines of a derivation carry formulas in the sense of @def-formula, with atoms p, q, r, \dots. Nothing in the rules changes. Every rule was stated as a schema, whose letters \varphi, \psi, \chi stand for arbitrary statements (@def-rule-schema), so it applies to formulas as it stands, and @def-derivation and @def-derivable read the same with “formula” for “statement”. As Section 4.1 said, a derivation written with Chapter 2’s letters P, Q is a pattern, and reading its letters as atoms, or as any formulas, gives a derivation of formulas. Two conventions for the rest of the section. The primitive rules are those of Chapters 1 and 2 collected in Section 3.1: ulename{R}, ulename{\wedge I}, ulename{\wedge E}, ulename{{	o}I}, ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{\vee I}, ulename{\vee E}, ulename{
eg I}, ulename{

eg I}, ulename{RAA}, ulename{\vee E} and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}. The other eight, ulename{R} included, cite only lines; we call them the one-step rules. The proof reads both parts off the scope rule; it is in the fold below. (a) The premises belong to every context. Any other formula of \Gamma_i is the assumption of a box containing line i. Since line i is available at line k, every box containing line i also contains line k, by the scope rule of @def-derivation. So that assumption belongs to \Gamma_k. (b) Let B be the box from line a to line b. Since line k cites B, the box B is available at line k. By the scope rule, it ends before line k, and the boxes containing B are exactly the boxes containing line k. We find the boxes containing line b. Every box containing line k contains B, and so contains line b; and B contains line b. Conversely, let C be a box containing line b. By @def-derivation, two boxes are either disjoint or one inside the other; C and B share line b, so C = B, or C contains B, or C lies inside B. The last is impossible: then line b, the last line of B, would be a line of a box inside B, and every box rule requires the last line of its box to be a line of that box itself, not of a box inside it (@def-rules-implication, @def-rules-negation, @def-rule-raa, @def-rules-disjunction, @def-rules-biconditional). So C = B, or C is one of the boxes containing B, which are the boxes containing line k. Hence the boxes containing line b are B and the boxes containing line k. The assumption of B is \varphi_a, so \Gamma_b consists of the premises, the assumptions of the boxes containing line k, and \varphi_a, which is \Gamma_k together with \varphi_a. The soundness theorem We can now state the theorem that Chapters 1 and 2 kept pointing to. Soundness Let \Gamma be a list of formulas and \psi a formula. If \Gamma \vdash \psi, then \Gamma \models \psi. Try it first (ten minutes): suppose line k is \varphi 	o \psi, by ulename{{	o}I} from a box that opens with \varphi and ends with \psi. Suppose you already know that every row making the context of line k and \varphi true makes \psi true. Why is \varphi 	o \psi true in every row making the context of line k true? What happens in the rows where \varphi is false? An attempt at the ulename{{	o}I} case runs into two things. First, knowledge about the box’s last line is knowledge about rows making its own context true, which contains the assumption \varphi; that is why the claim must carry contexts, and why @lem-context-inclusion (b) is needed. Second, the rows in which \varphi is false are not covered by the box at all, and they need nothing: there \varphi 	o \psi is true by (V5). The same two moves handle every box rule. The Step roadmap: ① Prove the stronger claim \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k for every line k of a derivation in primitive rules. ② Use strong induction on k (@thm-strong-induction): a rule may cite any earlier line, not only the line just above, so the hypothesis must be available for all earlier lines at once. ③ Split on how line k is justified. A premise or an assumption belongs to its own context. A one-step rule: apply the hypothesis to the cited lines, move their contexts into \Gamma_k by @lem-context-inclusion (a), and use one clause of @def-truth-value. A box rule: apply the hypothesis to each box’s last line, whose context is \Gamma_k plus the box’s assumption by @lem-context-inclusion (b), and argue about the rows where that assumption is true or false. ④ The last line lies in no box, so its context is the premises, all in \Gamma; adding the other formulas of \Gamma keeps the entailment. A technique, named. The proof is an instance of a general technique: to show that a rule cannot be derived from the others, find a new notion of “true” under which the other rules are sound and that rule is not. Here the notion has three values; Exercise C4 uses two values with  ot read as an ordinary letter, and Exercise C5 two other three-valued tables. Each notion is a different semantics. For the two-valued tables the rules are not only sound but complete, which is Section 4.8’s theorem.

title: 4.8 Completeness
content:
Completeness Soundness (@thm-soundness) says that the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 never lead from true premises to a false conclusion: whatever can be derived is true in every row where the premises are. That answers half of the chapter’s question. The other half is the converse. Could the rules be too weak, so that some sequent is true in every row and yet no derivation of it exists? This section proves that they are not: every truth-table consequence has a derivation. The proof reads a derivation off the truth table, one row at a time, and then glues the rows together with excluded middle. The question soundness leaves open Recall the two relations from Section 4.5. \Gamma \vdash \psi says that there is a derivation of \psi from premises in \Gamma (@def-derivable). \Gamma \models \psi says that every valuation making all of \Gamma true makes \psi true (@def-valid-argument). Soundness is the implication \Gamma \vdash \psi \ \Rightarrow \ \Gamma \models \psi . Its converse is not automatic. The rules are a list that people wrote down, and a list can leave something out. Suppose, as a thought experiment, that we struck ulename{RAA} (@def-rule-raa) from the list. Every derivation that remains is still a derivation, so soundness still holds. But the tautology p \vee 
eg p would then have no derivation (this is the optional @thm-raa-independent of Section 4.7). So a sound list of rules can be too short. The question is whether our list is long enough. Here is a sequent to keep in mind. The formula (p 	o q) \vee (q 	o p) is a tautology: if q is true then p 	o q is true, and if q is false then q 	o p is true. Chapter 3 found a derivation of it (@exr-finding-derivations-c2), but only after reaching for ulename{LEM}, and nothing in Chapter 3 proved that a derivation would be there to find. We want a theorem that promises it in advance, for every tautology and every valid sequent. We are going to prove: If \Gamma is a list of formulas and \Gamma \models \psi, then \Gamma \vdash \psi. The plan has two ideas, one per row and one for all the rows together. 1. One row gives one derivation. Fix a row of the truth table, that is, a valuation v. Write each atom as it stands in that row: p if v makes p true, 
eg p if v makes it false. From these signed atoms we will derive the formula \psi if \psi is true in the row, and 
eg\psi if it is false. The derivation climbs the parse tree of \psi, one connective at a time. 2. The rows are glued by excluded middle. If \Gamma \models \psi, the first idea gives \psi from \Gamma and the signed atoms of each row. Two rows that differ only at the atom p have derivations from “\ldots, p” and from “\ldots, 
eg p”. The rule ulename{\vee E} applied to p \vee 
eg p merges them into one derivation that no longer mentions p. Removing the atoms one at a time leaves a derivation from \Gamma alone. We keep the premises \Gamma throughout, and we isolate the two ingredients as lemmas so that each can be checked on its own. Before either, we need a little bookkeeping about derivations. The first idea is known as Kalmár’s lemma, and gluing rows by excluded middle is the standard way to finish; the route is the classical one. Bookkeeping: adding premises and chaining derivations In Chapter 2 we learned to use a proved sequent as a single line (@def-derived-rule), and Section 2.3 proved what that gives, @lem-weakening-cut: (a) extra premises never hurt; (b) a statement already derived may be used as a premise; (c) a sequent already proved may be applied to statements already derived. The completeness proof uses (a) and (c) dozens of times. They also made Step 1 of the proof of @thm-soundness honest: for whole derivations, part (c) is the precise form of “abbreviates”. Suppose \Gamma \vdash \alpha and \Gamma \vdash 
eg\alpha. Which part of @lem-weakening-cut, applied to which proved sequent, gives \Gamma \vdash \chi for every formula \chi? Part (c) with m = 2, \alpha_1 = \alpha, \alpha_2 = 
eg\alpha and  eta = \chi, applied to @prp-ex-falso, P, 
eg P \vdash Q, with \alpha for P and \chi for Q. The rules prove their own truth tables Each line of the truth table of a connective says something like “with \alpha true and  eta false, \alpha 	o  eta comes out false”. Read with signs, that line is a sequent: from \alpha and 
eg eta, conclude

For a valuation v and a formula \varphi, the signed formula \varphi^{v} is \varphi^{v} \coloneqq  egin{cases} \varphi & 	ext{if } v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, \

In particular, whether \Gamma \vdash \psi holds can be decided by checking the 2^n rows of a truth table, where n is the number of atoms occurring in \Gamma and \psi. (\Rightarrow) is @thm-soundness and (\Leftarrow) is @thm-completeness. For the second sentence, let p_1, \dots, p_n be the atoms occurring in \Gamma and \psi. If \Gamma \vdash \psi, then \psi follows informally: each rule is an inference every mathematician accepts, and a chain of accepted inferences is accepted. If \psi follows informally from \Gamma by form alone, then \Gamma \models \psi: an inference valid by its form cannot have a row, which is one way of reading the atoms, making the premises true and the conclusion false. Therefore m + n is not even.” Translate it into a sequent, using atoms e: “m + n is even”, a: “m is even”, b: “n is even”, and decide whether the premises entail the conclusion. “P only if Q” is P 	o Q (Section 1.1, and @exr-statements-and-connectives-c1). “Both odd” is 
eg a \wedge 
eg b, since an integer is odd exactly when it is not even. So the sequent is e 	o ((a \wedge b) \vee (
eg a \wedge 
eg b)), \ \ a \wedge 
eg b \ \models \ 
eg e . Work backwards from F. A refuting row needs 
eg e false, so e = \mathrm{T}, and the second premise true, so a = \mathrm{T}, b = \mathrm{F}. In that row a \wedge b and 
eg a \wedge 
eg b are both F, so the first premise is \mathrm{T} 	o \mathrm{F}, which is F. So no row makes both premises true and the conclusion false: the entailment holds. By @thm-completeness, the sequent is also derivable. (The eight-row table gives the same answer; working backwards found the only candidate row at once.) [R3] Is (p \wedge (q \vee r)) 	o ((p \wedge q) \vee r) a tautology? Is it derivable without ulename{RAA}? A tautology. Work backwards from F (Section 4.4). The formula is false only if p \wedge (q \vee r) is true and (p \wedge q) \vee r is false. The second needs r false and p \wedge q false; the first needs p true and q \vee r true, so with r false, q true. But then p \wedge q is true. No row makes the formula false, so it is a tautology (@def-tautology). Derivable without ulename{RAA}. Completeness (@thm-completeness) says it is derivable, but not how, and its proof uses ulename{LEM} in @lem-atom-splitting, so it does not answer the second question. A search does: the goal is an implication, so a box on p \wedge (q \vee r); split it by ulename{\wedge E} and use q \vee r by ulename{\vee E}. No ulename{RAA} is used: the boxes close by ulename{\vee E} and ulename{{	o}I}. The tools: truth values (@def-truth-value) for the first question, the search of Chapter 3 for the second. The look-alike tool, completeness, answers only “derivable with all the rules”.

title: 4.9 Normal Forms and Adequate Connectives
content:
Normal Forms and Adequate Connectives The proof of completeness wrote each row of a truth table as a list of signed atoms p_1^{v}, \dots, p_n^{v} (Section 4.8). Join the signed atoms of one row by \wedge, and you get a formula that is true in that row and in no other. Join those formulas, one for each row where a given formula \varphi is true, by \vee, and you get a formula with the same truth table as \varphi. This section turns that observation into two standard shapes for formulas, the disjunctive and the conjunctive normal form. It then reads validity off the conjunctive shape at a glance, and asks how few connectives are really needed. On a first reading this section may wait: it is a second-pass section, and nothing in Chapters 5–8 uses it. Conjunctions and disjunctions of many formulas Normal forms are long conjunctions and disjunctions. Section 4.5 fixed how to write them, in the paragraph on long conjunctions after @prp-standard-equivalences. For formulas \chi_1, \dots, \chi_k with k \ge 1, \chi_1 \wedge \chi_2 \wedge \dots \wedge \chi_k is the conjunction grouped to the right, \chi_1 \wedge (\chi_2 \wedge (\cdots \wedge \chi_k)), and likewise for \vee; for k = 1 it is \chi_1 itself. That paragraph proved, by induction on the number of terms, how such formulas are evaluated: for every valuation v,  egin{aligned} v(\chi_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \chi_k) = \mathrm{T} &\iff v(\chi_i) = \mathrm{T} 	ext{ for every } i = 1, \dots, k, \ v(\chi_1 \vee \dots \vee \chi_k) = \mathrm{T} &\iff v(\chi_i) = \mathrm{T} 	ext{ for some } i = 1, \dots, k. \end{aligned} {#eq-many-term-values} We use these two lines constantly below, and we cite them by this display. So a long conjunction is true when all its parts are, and a long disjunction when at least one is, just as the words say. Literals, clauses and the two normal forms The building blocks are the smallest formulas that still carry a sign. [Literal] A literal is an atom or the negation of an atom. So p, 
eg p, q_7 and 
eg q_7 are literals. The signed atom p^{v} of Section 4.8 is always a literal. The formulas 
eg
eg p, 
eg(p \wedge q) and  ot are not: in the first two, 
eg is applied to something other than an atom, and  ot is neither an atom nor a negation. The opposite of a literal is 
eg p if the literal is p, and p if it is 
eg p. By the clause for 
eg in @def-truth-value, a literal and its opposite take opposite values under every valuation. From literals we build two kinds of blocks and two kinds of formulas. - A clause joins one or more literals by \vee, such as p \vee 
eg q \vee r, or 
eg q alone. - A conjunctive clause joins one or more literals by \wedge, such as p \wedge 
eg q \wedge r, or 
eg q alone. (We do not shorten it to “conjunct”, which keeps its ordinary meaning, one side of a conjunction.) A normal form is a formula whose connectives come in fixed layers: negations only on atoms, then one layer of one connective, then one layer of the other. [Disjunctive Normal Form] A formula has disjunctive normal form (DNF), or is in DNF, when it has the shape C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k, with k \ge 1, where every C_i joins one or more literals by \wedge. Conjunctive Normal Form A formula has conjunctive normal form (CNF), or is in CNF, when it has the shape K_1 \wedge \dots \wedge K_k, with k \ge 1, where every K_i joins one or more literals by \vee. In words: a DNF is an “or of ands” and a CNF an “and of ors”, and in both the only negations sit directly on atoms. Read a DNF as a list of situations, any one of which makes it true; read a CNF as a list of requirements, all of which must be met. Check some formulas against the definitions, clause by clause. 1. (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (
eg p \wedge q) is in DNF: two conjunctive clauses, each a conjunction of literals. It is not in CNF: as a conjunction of clauses it would have to be a single clause (it is not a conjunction), and a clause cannot contain \wedge. 2. (p \vee q) \wedge (
eg p \vee 
eg q) is in CNF, with two clauses, and not in DNF. 3. p \wedge 
eg q is in both: in DNF with one conjunctive clause, and in CNF with two clauses of one literal each. Likewise p \vee 
eg q is in both. 4. A single literal, 
eg r, is in both forms: one conjunctive clause of one literal, and one clause of one literal. This degenerate case matters, because a formula such as 
eg r must count as already normal. A nonexample by a minimal change: (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee r is in DNF, but 
eg(p \wedge q) \vee r is not in either form. Only one symbol moved, and the literal condition fails: 
eg now stands on the conjunction p \wedge q, not on an atom. The formula p 	o q is in neither form either, since 	o is not allowed at all. Why these layers? Because they are the shapes that the truth table hands us, as the next theorem shows, and because in these shapes some questions become easy: the subsection “Reading validity off a CNF” below decides validity of a CNF without a table. A literal is an atom with at most one 
eg, and nothing else. 
eg
eg p is equivalent to the literal p but is not a literal, so 
eg
eg p \vee q is not in CNF as written. Likewise  ot is not a literal, so a “normal form” containing  ot is not one; that is why the constructions below never use it. Which of the following are in CNF, and which are in DNF? (i) (p \vee 
eg q) \wedge r; (ii) 
eg(p \vee q); (iii) p \vee (
eg q \wedge r). (i) CNF, with clauses p \vee 
eg q and r; not DNF, since the conjunctive clause would have to be the whole formula and p \vee 
eg q is not a literal. (ii) Neither: 
eg stands on a disjunction. (iii) DNF, with conjunctive clauses p and 
eg q \wedge r; not CNF, since the one clause would contain \wedge. Reading a DNF off the truth table Take a valuation v and atoms p_1, \dots, p_n with n \ge 1, and form the minterm of the row of v, the conjunctive clause of its signed atoms, C_v \coloneqq p_1^{v} \wedge \dots \wedge p_n^{v} . For every valuation w, each p_i^{v} is true under w exactly when w(p_i) = v(p_i): if v(p_i) = \mathrm{T}, then p_i^{v} = p_i; if v(p_i) = \mathrm{F}, then p_i^{v} = 
eg p_i, which is true under w exactly when w(p_i) = \mathrm{F}. By @eq-many-term-values, w(C_v) = \mathrm{T} \iff w(p_i) = v(p_i) 	ext{ for every } i = 1, \dots, n . {#eq-row-conjunct} So C_v is true in the row of v and in no other row. It is a formula that “names” one row. [Exactly one of two] Find a formula in DNF that is true exactly when exactly one of p, q is true, and check it. The rows with exactly one of p, q true are (p, q) = (\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F}) and (\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{T}). Their minterms are p \wedge 
eg q and 
eg p \wedge q, so the answer is (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (
eg p \wedge q). Check against the table: in the row T, F the first minterm is true; in F, T the second is; in T, T each minterm has a false literal (
eg q, 
eg p); in F, F likewise (p, q). So the formula is true in exactly the two rows wanted. The same recipe works for any formula. [Disjunctive Normal Form] Every formula \varphi is equivalent to a formula in DNF. If \varphi has at least one atom, the DNF can be chosen so that every atom in it is an atom of \varphi. List the rows where \varphi is true and disjoin their minterms C_v. A valuation makes the disjunction true exactly when it agrees with one of those rows, which by @lem-coincidence is exactly when it makes \varphi true. Two degenerate cases need a convention: a formula with no T-row, whose disjunction would be empty, and a formula with no atoms, which has no rows to speak of. By the paraphrase of @def-semantic-equivalence, two formulas \varphi and \psi are equivalent exactly when v(\varphi) = v(\psi) for every valuation v. Case 1: \varphi has at least one atom. Let p_1, \dots, p_n (n \ge 1) be the atoms of \varphi. A row is a choice of a value for each p_i; there are 2^n rows, and for each we fix a valuation that takes those values at p_1, \dots, p_n (and, say, T at every other atom). By @lem-coincidence, v(\varphi) depends only on the row of v. Let v_1, \dots, v_k be the fixed valuations of the rows in which \varphi is T. If k \ge 1, let D \coloneqq C_{v_1} \vee \dots \vee C_{v_k}, which is in DNF by @def-dnf, with atoms among p_1, \dots, p_n. Let w be any valuation. By @eq-many-term-values and @eq-row-conjunct, w(D) = \mathrm{T} exactly when w agrees with some v_j on p_1, \dots, p_n. If it does, then w(\varphi) = v_j(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} by @lem-coincidence. Conversely, if w(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, then the row of w is one where \varphi is T, so w agrees on p_1, \dots, p_n with the valuation v_j fixed for that row. Hence w(D) = w(\varphi) for every w, and \varphi \equiv D. If k = 0, then \varphi is F in every row, hence under every valuation. The formula p_1 \wedge 
eg p_1 is in DNF (one conjunctive clause of two literals) and is F under every valuation by @def-truth-value. So \varphi \equiv p_1 \wedge 
eg p_1. Case 2: \varphi has no atoms. Any two valuations agree on all the atoms of \varphi (there are none), so by @lem-coincidence v(\varphi) is the same for every v. Let p be an atom. If that value is T, then \varphi \equiv p \vee 
eg p, which is true under every valuation and is in DNF (two conjunctive clauses of one literal); if it is F, then \varphi \equiv p \wedge 
eg p. This proves the theorem. The minterms of different rows are never true together, and in each row exactly one of the 2^n minterms is true: they divide the rows like the pieces of a partition, and a full disjunctive normal form collects the pieces in which the formula is true. The minterms C_v are the signed atoms of Section 4.8 joined by \wedge. There the signed atoms of a row were premises from which \varphi^{v} was derived; here they are joined into a formula that is true in that row only. The proof is the proof of completeness with the derivations taken out. For p \wedge 
eg p we could have written  ot, which is also F under every valuation. We did not, because  ot is not a literal, and because the adequacy theorem at the end of this section reuses the construction in a language without  ot. Conjunctive normal form A DNF lists the rows where a formula is true. A CNF does the opposite: it lists the rows where the formula is false, one clause per row, each clause being false in its row and true in every other. Conjunctive Normal Form Every formula \varphi is equivalent to a formula in CNF. If \varphi has at least one atom, the CNF can be chosen so that every atom in it is an atom of \varphi. Apply @thm-dnf to 
eg\varphi and negate the result: \varphi \equiv 
eg
eg\varphi \equiv 
eg(C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k). Now push the 
eg inwards with De Morgan’s laws and double negation (@prp-standard-equivalences): 
eg(C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k) becomes 
eg C_1 \wedge \dots \wedge 
eg C_k, and each 
eg C_i, the negation of a conjunction of literals, becomes the disjunction of the opposite literals. The proof checks the outcome directly with @eq-many-term-values, which avoids De Morgan’s laws for many terms. By @thm-dnf, 
eg\varphi \equiv C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k for some conjunctive clauses C_1, \dots, C_k (with atoms among those of \varphi if it has any, since 
eg\varphi has the same atoms). For each i, let K_i be the disjunction of the opposites of the literals of C_i, in the same order, and let K \coloneqq K_1 \wedge \dots \wedge K_k. Then K is in CNF, with the same atoms as C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k. Let w be a valuation. Each literal of K_i is true under w exactly when the corresponding literal of C_i is false. By @eq-many-term-values, used at each step:  egin{aligned} w(K) = \mathrm{T} &\iff 	ext{for every } i, \ w(K_i) = \mathrm{T} \ &\iff 	ext{for every } i, 	ext{ some literal of } C_i 	ext{ is false under } w \ &\iff 	ext{for every } i, \ w(C_i) = \mathrm{F} \ &\iff w(C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k) = \mathrm{F} . \end{aligned} Since C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k \equiv 
eg\varphi, the last line holds exactly when w(
eg\varphi) = \mathrm{F}, that is, when w(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}. So w(K) = w(\varphi) for every w, and \varphi \equiv K. Unwinding the construction: the conjunctive clauses C_i of the DNF of 
eg\varphi are the rows where \varphi is false, and K_i is the clause that is false exactly in the row of C_i. So the CNF can be read straight off the table: one clause per F-row, built from the opposites of that row’s signed atoms. In the row p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F}, for instance, the clause is 
eg p \vee q. A formula with no F-row gets, by the proof, the clause of a contradiction’s DNF negated, 
eg p \vee p (from C_1 = p \wedge 
eg p), which is true in every row. On the atoms p, q, r, write the CNF clause for the F-row p = \mathrm{F}, q = \mathrm{T}, r = \mathrm{F}. The row’s signed atoms are 
eg p, q, 
eg r; their opposites give p \vee 
eg q \vee r. It is false exactly when p is F, q is T and r is F, that is, in that row only. Alternatively, a CNF can be reached by rewriting. First replace each  ot, which is not a literal, by p \wedge 
eg p for an atom p; both are false in every row. Replace \alpha \leftrightarrow  eta by (\alpha 	o  eta) \wedge ( eta 	o \alpha) and \alpha 	o  eta by 
eg\alpha \vee  eta; push each 
eg inwards by De Morgan’s laws, and remove 
eg
eg; finally distribute \vee over \wedge, replacing \alpha \vee ( eta \wedge \gamma) by (\alpha \vee  eta) \wedge (\alpha \vee \gamma). Each step replaces a part of the formula by an equivalent one: the equivalences are  ot \equiv p \wedge 
eg p and those of @prp-standard-equivalences, which hold for arbitrary formulas, and @lem-replacement says the whole formula stays equivalent; since \equiv is transitive (Section 4.5), the steps chain. Stopping before the distribution step, and distributing \wedge over \vee instead, gives a DNF. The rewriting route is often much shorter than the table, as the next example shows, but it can also explode, as the warning after it shows. [Two routes to a normal form] Put \varphi = (p 	o q) 	o (
eg q 	o r) into DNF and into CNF, first from its truth table and then by rewriting. The table route. Work backwards from F (Section 4.4): \varphi is false exactly when p 	o q is T and 
eg q 	o r is F. The latter needs 
eg q true and r false, so q = r = \mathrm{F}; then p 	o q true needs p = \mathrm{F}. So \varphi has exactly one F-row, p = q = r = \mathrm{F}, as the table confirms:  egin{array}{ccc|c|c|c} p & q & r & p 	o q & 
eg q 	o r & (p 	o q) 	o (
eg q 	o r) \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \end{array} The DNF of @thm-dnf has one minterm for each of the seven T-rows:  egin{aligned} &(p \wedge q \wedge r) \vee (p \wedge q \wedge 
eg r) \vee (p \wedge 
eg q \wedge r) \vee (p \wedge 
eg q \wedge 
eg r) \ &\quad \vee (
eg p \wedge q \wedge r) \vee (
eg p \wedge q \wedge 
eg r) \vee (
eg p \wedge 
eg q \wedge r). \end{aligned} The CNF of @thm-cnf has one clause for the single F-row, built from the opposites of 
eg p, 
eg q, 
eg r: it is the single clause p \vee q \vee r. The rewriting route. Eliminate the three implications, then push the negation in:  egin{aligned} \varphi &\equiv 
eg(
eg p \vee q) \vee (
eg
eg q \vee r) \ &\equiv (
eg
eg p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (q \vee r) \ &\equiv (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee q \vee r , \end{aligned} using (c) of @prp-standard-equivalences three times, then De Morgan’s law (b) for 
eg(\alpha \vee  eta), then double negation (d) twice. This is already a DNF, with three conjunctive clauses. For a CNF, distribute, by (g) together with commutativity (f) and associativity (h): (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (q \vee r) \equiv (p \vee q \vee r) \wedge (
eg q \vee q \vee r). The second clause contains q and 
eg q, so it is true in every row, and a conjunction with a part that is true in every row is equivalent to its other part. So \varphi \equiv p \vee q \vee r: one clause, as the table route found. The formula p \vee q \vee r is also a DNF, with three conjunctive clauses of one literal each. So the table’s seven minterms and the rewriting’s three conjunctive clauses can both be replaced by three one-literal conjunctive clauses. Both routes are correct; they differ in length, and neither is guaranteed to give the shortest normal form. A formula has many equivalent CNFs and DNFs; “normal form” does not mean “unique form”. p \vee q \vee r and (p \vee q \vee r) \wedge (
eg q \vee q \vee r) are both CNFs of the formula above. And the two routes have opposite weaknesses. The table route needs all 2^n rows for n atoms. The rewriting route can explode at the distribution step: distributing (p_1 \wedge q_1) \vee (p_2 \wedge q_2) \vee (p_3 \wedge q_3) gives 8 clauses, one for each way of picking p_i or q_i from every conjunctive clause, and m such conjunctive clauses give 2^m clauses. Reading validity off a CNF A CNF is a list of requirements, all of which must hold. That makes one question easy. [Validity of a CNF] 1. A formula in CNF is a tautology exactly when every clause contains some atom together with its negation. 2. A formula in DNF is satisfiable exactly when some conjunctive clause contains no atom together with its negation. Try it first (ten minutes): take a clause in which no atom occurs both with and without 
eg, such as p \vee 
eg q \vee r. Can you find a row that makes it false? What does that row do to a CNF containing this clause? The direction “every clause has a pair \Rightarrow tautology” is the easy one: p \vee 
eg p is true in every row, so a clause containing both is too, and a conjunction of clauses true in every row is true in every row. The attempt above is the other direction. To make a CNF false, it is enough to make one clause false, and a clause is false only when all its literals are. So set every atom of the clause against its literal: F for a plain atom, T for a negated one. The one thing that could stop us is an atom that appears both plain and negated, since it would have to be both F and T. That is exactly the pair the proposition talks about. (a) Let K = K_1 \wedge \dots \wedge K_k be in CNF. (\Leftarrow) Suppose every clause K_i contains some atom p and its negation 
eg p. Let v be a valuation. One of p, 
eg p is true under v, by @def-truth-value, so v(K_i) = \mathrm{T} by @eq-many-term-values. This holds for every i, so v(K) = \mathrm{T} by @eq-many-term-values. As v was arbitrary, K is a tautology (@def-tautology). (\Rightarrow) We prove the contrapositive. Suppose some clause K_i contains no atom together with its negation. Define a valuation v by: v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{F} if the literal p occurs in K_i; v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if the literal 
eg p occurs in K_i; v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} for every other atom. This is well defined, because no atom occurs in K_i both as p and as 
eg p. Every literal of K_i is false under v, so v(K_i) = \mathrm{F} by @eq-many-term-values, and hence v(K) = \mathrm{F}, again by @eq-many-term-values. So K is not a tautology. (b) Let D = C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k be in DNF. (\Leftarrow) Suppose C_i contains no atom together with its negation. Define v by v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if p occurs in C_i, v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{F} if 
eg p occurs in C_i, and v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} otherwise; this is well defined as in (a). Every literal of C_i is true under v, so v(C_i) = \mathrm{T} and v(D) = \mathrm{T} by @eq-many-term-values. So D is satisfiable (@def-satisfiable). (\Rightarrow) If every conjunctive clause contains some p and 
eg p, then under every valuation one of these two literals is false, so every conjunctive clause is false and so is D, by @eq-many-term-values. So D is not satisfiable. This proves the proposition. The two parts are two faces of one fact. Section 4.5 showed that a formula is a tautology exactly when its negation is unsatisfiable (after @def-satisfiable). Let D be in DNF, and let K be the CNF whose clauses are the conjunctive clauses of D with every literal replaced by its opposite. The proof of @thm-cnf, applied to \varphi = 
eg D with D itself as the DNF of 
eg\varphi \equiv D, shows K \equiv 
eg D. A clause of K has an atom together with its negation exactly when the corresponding conjunctive clause of D has. So D is unsatisfiable exactly when 
eg D, and so K, is a tautology, which by (a) happens exactly when every conjunctive clause of D has such a pair. That is (b) again. The proposition trades one kind of work for another. Checking a CNF for validity is now a glance, but getting the CNF in the first place may take the 2^n rows of the table route or the explosion of the rewriting route. Nothing is free: the work has moved, not vanished. [Validity at a glance] Decide whether each formula is a tautology, without a table. 1. (
eg p \vee q \vee p) \wedge (r \vee 
eg q \vee s \vee q) \wedge (
eg s \vee 
eg r \vee s) \wedge (p \vee 
eg r \vee r \vee q). 2. The same formula with the third clause changed to 
eg s \vee 
eg r \vee q. (a) Each clause has a pair: 
eg p, p in the first; 
eg q, q in the second; 
eg s, s in the third; 
eg r, r in the fourth. By @prp-cnf-validity (a), it is a tautology. A table would have needed 16 rows. (b) The new third clause 
eg s \vee 
eg r \vee q has the atoms s, r, q, each once, so it has no pair, and the formula is not a tautology. The proof of @prp-cnf-validity names a refuting row: s = \mathrm{T}, r = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F}, and p = \mathrm{T}, like every atom not in the clause; in fact either value of p works. In that row the third clause is F, so the conjunction is F. Calculating with equivalences Section 4.5 replaced a part of a formula by an equivalent part (@lem-replacement) and chained such steps, since \equiv is transitive. Normal forms can be reached in this way, as the rewriting route did, and so can shorter formulas. Each step cites a law, as each line of a derivation cites a rule. A few more laws make the calculations run; in them, 
eg ot serves as a formula that is true in every row. [Laws of the Constants, Idempotence and Absorption] For all formulas \varphi and \psi: 1. \varphi \wedge 
eg ot \equiv \varphi and \varphi \vee  ot \equiv \varphi; 2. \varphi \wedge  ot \equiv  ot and \varphi \vee 
eg ot \equiv 
eg ot; 3. \varphi \wedge 
eg\varphi \equiv  ot and \varphi \vee 
eg\varphi \equiv

Adequate sets of connectives Our formulas use five connectives and  ot. Chapter 2 already showed that some of them can be traded for others: an implication for a disjunction (@prp-implication-as-disjunction), a biconditional for two implications (@prp-iff-two-implications). How far can this go? Before we can answer, we need to say what a set of connectives must be able to “say”. Every formula whose atoms are among p_1, \dots, p_n has a truth table: a value for each of the 2^n rows. Turn this around, and ask whether every table is the table of some formula. Section 4.4 called such a table a truth function (@def-truth-function): a value for each list of inputs, with no formula attached; a formula expresses it when it has that table. There are 2^n lists of inputs and two choices of output for each, so there are 2^{2^n} truth functions with n inputs: 4 with one input and 16 with two. Examples: the negation function with one input, \mathrm{T} \mapsto \mathrm{F}, \mathrm{F} \mapsto \mathrm{T}, expressed by 
eg p_1; the two-input function that is T only at (\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{T}), expressed by p_1 \wedge p_2; the three-input majority function, T when at least two inputs are T, expressed by (p_1 \wedge p_2) \vee (p_1 \wedge p_3) \vee (p_2 \wedge p_3). A degenerate case: the one-input function that is always T is expressed by p_1 \vee 
eg p_1, and also by p_2 	o p_2, which does not mention p_1 at all. The definition allows that. We say a formula is in a set S of connectives if every connective occurring in it belongs to S, and  ot occurs in it only if  ot belongs to S (for this purpose  ot counts as a connective with no inputs).
