eg(q 	o r) \equiv 
eg p \wedge 
eg(
eg q \vee r) \equiv 
eg p \wedge q \wedge 
eg r. This single conjunctive clause is a DNF, and it is also a CNF with three one-literal clauses. Check: in the row F, T, F it is true, and so is the original (q 	o r is false and p is false); in the row F, T, T it is false, and so is the original (q 	o r is true). [B2: Two connectives from two] Find formulas in \{
eg, \wedge\}, with atoms p and q, equivalent to p \vee q and to p \leftrightarrow q. Check the second by a truth table. p \vee q \equiv 
eg(
eg p \wedge 
eg q): this is the translation t_1 in the proof of @thm-adequate-connectives, and the right side is F exactly when 
eg p and 
eg q are both true, that is, when p \vee q is F. For the biconditional, p \leftrightarrow q says p 	o q and q 	o p, and p 	o q says “not p without q”, that is, 
eg(p \wedge 
eg q). So p \leftrightarrow q \equiv 
eg(p \wedge 
eg q) \wedge 
eg(
eg p \wedge q). The table:  egin{array}{cc|c|c|c|c} p & q & 
eg(p \wedge 
eg q) & 
eg(
eg p \wedge q) & 
eg(p \wedge 
eg q) \wedge 
eg(
eg p \wedge q) & p \leftrightarrow q \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} The last two columns agree in every row. [B3: Odd parity] Give an example of a formula in DNF, with atoms p, q, r, that is true in exactly the rows where an odd number of p, q, r are true. List the properties your answer must have, and check it against them. The rows with an odd number of T’s are those with three T’s, T T T, and those with one, T F F, F T F, and F F T. One minterm per row, as in @thm-dnf: (p \wedge q \wedge r) \vee (p \wedge 
eg q \wedge 
eg r) \vee (
eg p \wedge q \wedge 
eg r) \vee (
eg p \wedge 
eg q \wedge r). The properties an answer must have: (i) it is in DNF (a disjunction of conjunctions of literals); (ii) its atoms are among p, q, r; (iii) it is T in the four rows T T T, T F F, F T F, F F T; (iv) it is F in the other four, T T F, T F T, F T T, F F F. Check: (i) and (ii) hold by inspection. By @eq-row-conjunct, each minterm is T in its own row only, so the disjunction is T exactly in the four rows listed, which gives (iii) and (iv). A different correct answer, for instance the same minterms in another order, or with the literals of a minterm reordered, passes the same checks. No DNF with fewer conjunctive clauses works. A conjunctive clause containing an atom and its negation is T in no row and contributes nothing. Any other conjunctive clause omitting an atom, say p \wedge q, is T in two rows that differ at that atom, and changing one atom always changes the parity, so one of those rows has even parity. So every conjunctive clause that is T somewhere mentions all three atoms and is T in exactly one row, and four T-rows need at least four conjunctive clauses. C. Going deeper [C1: One connective is enough] Add to the language two binary connectives: \alpha \mathbin{|}  eta (“not both”, NAND), which is F exactly when \alpha and  eta are both T, and \alpha \downarrow  eta (“neither”, NOR), which is T exactly when \alpha and  eta are both F. 1. Prove that \{\mathbin{|}\} is adequate. 2. Prove that \{\downarrow\} is adequate. (a) First, two equivalences, checked from the table of \mathbin{|}: \alpha \mathbin{|} \alpha is F exactly when \alpha is T, so \alpha \mathbin{|} \alpha \equiv 
eg\alpha; and (\alpha \mathbin{|}  eta) \mathbin{|} (\alpha \mathbin{|}  eta) \equiv 
eg(\alpha \mathbin{|}  eta), which is T exactly when \alpha and  eta are both T, so it is equivalent to \alpha \wedge  eta. Now define, by recursion on formulas as in @thm-structural-recursion, s(p) \coloneqq p, s(
eg\alpha) \coloneqq s(\alpha) \mathbin{|} s(\alpha), s(\alpha \wedge  eta) \coloneqq (s(\alpha) \mathbin{|} s( eta)) \mathbin{|} (s(\alpha) \mathbin{|} s( eta)) (the other clauses do not matter). By structural induction, exactly as in the Claim in the proof of @thm-adequate-connectives, every formula \varphi in \{
eg, \wedge\} has s(\varphi) in \{\mathbin{|}\} and v(s(\varphi)) = v(\varphi) for every v: the atom case is immediate, and the two equivalences above give the 
eg and \wedge cases from the induction hypothesis. Given a truth function f, @thm-adequate-connectives (a) gives a formula \varphi in \{
eg, \wedge\} expressing it, and then s(\varphi) expresses f and is in \{\mathbin{|}\}. (b) The same, with \{
eg, \vee\}: \alpha \downarrow \alpha is T exactly when \alpha is F, so \alpha \downarrow \alpha \equiv 
eg\alpha; and (\alpha \downarrow  eta) \downarrow (\alpha \downarrow  eta) \equiv 
eg(\alpha \downarrow  eta) \equiv \alpha \vee  eta. The recursive translation s(
eg\alpha) \coloneqq s(\alpha) \downarrow s(\alpha), s(\alpha \vee  eta) \coloneqq (s(\alpha) \downarrow s( eta)) \downarrow (s(\alpha) \downarrow s( eta)) turns a formula in \{
eg, \vee\} expressing f into one in \{\downarrow\}. (Recursion and structural induction for the language with the new connectives hold by the same proofs as @thm-structural-recursion and @thm-structural-induction, with one more formation clause.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) two equivalences expressing the connectives of an adequate set from @thm-adequate-connectives (a) in terms of \mathbin{|}, read off its table (for instance \alpha \mathbin{|} \alpha \equiv 
eg\alpha and (\alpha \mathbin{|}  eta) \mathbin{|} (\alpha \mathbin{|}  eta) \equiv \alpha \wedge  eta). - 3: (a) the recursive translation and the structural induction showing that it keeps the value under every valuation. - 1: (a) the conclusion, via @thm-adequate-connectives (a). - 3: (b) the same for \downarrow, with \{
eg, \vee\}. Fatal errors (0 for the step): checking the translation on examples only, with no induction. [C2: Two sets that are not adequate] 1. Prove that \{\wedge, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow\} is not adequate. 2. Add to the language a three-place connective \mathsf{M}(\alpha,  eta, \gamma), majority, which is T exactly when at least two of \alpha,  eta, \gamma are T. Prove that \{
eg, \mathsf{M}\} is not adequate. [Hint 1] For (b): compare each row with the row in which every atom’s value is flipped. [Hint 2] For (b): show that every formula in 
eg and \mathsf{M} takes opposite values in a row and in its flipped row. (a) Let v_{\mathrm{T}} make every atom true. Every formula in \{\wedge, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow\} is true under v_{\mathrm{T}}, by the structural induction in the proof of @thm-adequate-connectives (b) with one more case: if v_{\mathrm{T}}(\alpha) = v_{\mathrm{T}}( eta) = \mathrm{T}, then v_{\mathrm{T}}(\alpha \leftrightarrow  eta) = \mathrm{T}, since the two values are equal. As there, no such formula expresses negation, which must give F at the input T. (b) For a valuation v, let  ar v be the flipped valuation:  ar v(p) is the opposite of v(p), for every atom p. We show by structural induction that every formula \varphi in \{
eg, \mathsf{M}\} satisfies: for every valuation v,  ar v(\varphi) is the opposite of v(\varphi). For an atom this is the definition of  ar v. If  ar v(\alpha) is the opposite of v(\alpha), then  ar v(
eg\alpha), the opposite of  ar v(\alpha), is v(\alpha), which is the opposite of v(
eg\alpha). If the property holds for \alpha,  eta, \gamma, then flipping v flips all three values; at least two of them are T after the flip exactly when at least two were F before, that is, exactly when at most one was T, that is, exactly when \mathsf{M}(\alpha,  eta, \gamma) was F. So  ar v(\mathsf{M}(\alpha,  eta, \gamma)) is the opposite of v(\mathsf{M}(\alpha,  eta, \gamma)). The other connectives and  ot do not occur in formulas of \{
eg, \mathsf{M}\}, so those cases are vacuous. (Structural induction for the extended language holds by the proof of @thm-structural-induction, with one more formation clause.) Now the two-input function of p_1 \wedge p_2 is F at (\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F}) and at the flipped input (\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{T}). If a formula \varphi in \{
eg, \mathsf{M}\} expressed it, then for a valuation v with v(p_1) = \mathrm{T}, v(p_2) = \mathrm{F} we would have v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F} and  ar v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}, since  ar v(p_1) = \mathrm{F} and  ar v(p_2) = \mathrm{T}. But these values must be opposite. So no formula in \{
eg, \mathsf{M}\} expresses it, and the set is not adequate. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) states the all-T valuation and runs the induction, with the \leftrightarrow case and the vacuous cases (
eg,  ot) named. - 1: (a) names a truth function that is not expressed (negation), with the reason. - 4: (b) states the flipped-row property for every formula in \{
eg, \mathsf{M}\} and proves it by structural induction, including the \mathsf{M} case. - 2: (b) exhibits a truth function that takes the same value on some row and on its flipped row, and concludes. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (b), checking the flipped-row property on a few formulas instead of proving it for all; in (a), an implication case justified by the hypothesis being true rather than by the conclusion. [C3: Exit check: normal forms] Put (p 	o q) 	o (q \wedge r) into DNF and into CNF, by either route, and check one of your answers against the truth table. By rewriting. Eliminate the outer implication and then the inner one, and push the negation in:  egin{aligned} (p 	o q) 	o (q \wedge r) &\equiv 
eg(p 	o q) \vee (q \wedge r) \ &\equiv 
eg(
eg p \vee q) \vee (q \wedge r) \ &\equiv (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (q \wedge r) . \end{aligned} The last line is a DNF. Here 
eg(p 	o q) \equiv p \wedge 
eg q, since an implication is false exactly when its hypothesis is true and its conclusion false. For a CNF, distribute: (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (q \wedge r) \equiv (p \vee q) \wedge (p \vee r) \wedge (
eg q \vee q) \wedge (
eg q \vee r) , and drop the clause 
eg q \vee q, which is true in every row: the CNF is (p \vee q) \wedge (p \vee r) \wedge (
eg q \vee r). (The clause p \vee r is redundant too: (p \vee q) \wedge (
eg q \vee r) is an equivalent CNF, as splitting on q shows. Either is correct.) The check. The formula is false exactly when p 	o q holds and q \wedge r fails. Its table:  egin{array}{ccc|c|c|c} p & q & r & p 	o q & q \wedge r & (p 	o q) 	o (q \wedge r) \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \end{array} The T-rows are T T T, T F T, T F F, and F T T. The DNF (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (q \wedge r) is true in exactly these: p \wedge 
eg q in T F T and T F F, and q \wedge r in T T T and F T T. In each of the four F-rows the CNF has a false clause: 
eg q \vee r in T T F and F T F, p \vee q in F F T and F F F. By the table route, the DNF has four minterms, one per T-row, and the CNF four clauses, one per F-row, for instance 
eg p \vee 
eg q \vee r for the row T T F. Any correct DNF and CNF earns full marks; a CNF is not unique. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the route carried out correctly: 	o eliminated, with 
eg(p 	o q) \equiv p \wedge 
eg q and its reason, or the T-rows and F-rows read off a correct table. - 3: a correct DNF. - 3: a correct CNF, by distribution carried out in full or by one clause per F-row. - 2: the check against the table, covering at least the four F-rows (or the four T-rows). Fatal errors (0 for the step): 
eg(p 	o q) rewritten as 
eg p 	o 
eg q; a “CNF” with a conjunction inside a clause. [C4: From connectives to sets] Let U be a collection, and A, B, E collections of members of U, in the everyday sense; U \setminus A is the collection of members of U not in A. For a member x of U, write a, b, e for the statements x \in A, x \in B, x \in E. 1. Write “x \in U \setminus (A \cap B)” and “x \in (U \setminus A) \cup (U \setminus B)” as formulas in a, b, and deduce from a standard equivalence that the two collections have the same members. 2. Show in the same way that A \cap (B \cup E) and (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap E) have the same members. 3. Show that (a 	o b) 	o ((a \wedge e) 	o (b \wedge e)) is a tautology, and deduce: if every member of A is in B, then every member of A \cap E is in B \cap E. (a) The formulas are 
eg(a \wedge b) and 
eg a \vee 
eg b. They are equivalent by @prp-standard-equivalences (b). Each member x of U gives a valuation of a and b, by whether it lies in A and in B, and under that valuation the two formulas have the same value. So x is in one collection exactly when it is in the other. (b) The formulas are a \wedge (b \vee e) and (a \wedge b) \vee (a \wedge e), equivalent by @prp-standard-equivalences (g); conclude as in (a). (c) Work backwards from F. Falsity needs a 	o b true and (a \wedge e) 	o (b \wedge e) false, so a and e true and b \wedge e false. Then b is true, by a 	o b, so b \wedge e is true: no row makes the formula false, and it is a tautology. For each x, its memberships give a valuation making the formula true: so if “x \in A implies x \in B” holds, then “x \in A \cap E implies x \in B \cap E” holds. If every member of A is in B, the first holds for every x, hence so does the second. Marking scheme. (8 points) - 3: (a), with the step from an equivalence to equal membership argued (each x gives a valuation). - 2: (b). - 3: (c): the tautology, and the step to collections. Fatal errors (0 for the step): checking the set equality on one example collection only. [C5: Counting rows] For a formula \varphi whose atoms are among p_1, \dots, p_n, let \#\varphi be the number of rows of the table on p_1, \dots, p_n in which \varphi is true. 1. Show that \varphi \models \psi implies \#\varphi \le \#\psi, and that the converse fails. 2. Show that \#(\varphi \vee \psi) = \#\varphi + \#\psi - \#(\varphi \wedge \psi). 3. Show that the minterms of two different rows are never true together, and that the disjunction of all 2^n minterms is a tautology. Deduce that, for satisfiable \varphi, the full DNF of \varphi over p_1, \dots, p_n (one minterm on p_1, \dots, p_n for each row on them in which \varphi is true) has exactly \#\varphi minterms. (a) If \varphi \models \psi, every row in which \varphi is true is one in which \psi is true, so there are at least as many of the second. The converse fails: on the atoms p, q, the formulas p and q are each true in two rows, so \#p \le \#q, but p 
ot\models q (the row p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F}). (b) By (V4), the rows of \varphi \vee \psi are those of \varphi together with those of \psi. By (V3), the rows in both are the rows of \varphi \wedge \psi. The sum \#\varphi + \#\psi counts those twice and every other row of \varphi \vee \psi once. (c) Two different rows differ at some p_i; one minterm contains p_i and the other 
eg p_i, and no valuation makes both literals true. Each row makes its own minterm true (@eq-row-conjunct), so the disjunction of all 2^n is true in every row (@eq-many-term-values). The full DNF over p_1, \dots, p_n has one minterm for each row on them in which \varphi is true, and different rows give different minterms, so it has \#\varphi of them. (It is not always the DNF that the proof of @thm-dnf builds. That proof uses only the atoms of \varphi, so when \varphi is satisfiable and has at least one atom, and j of the p_i do not occur in \varphi, it gives \#\varphi / 2^j minterms on the remaining atoms. When \varphi has no atoms it gives p \vee 
eg p or p \wedge 
eg p. When \#\varphi = 0 it gives a contradiction q \wedge 
eg q for some atom q, which is a conjunctive clause but no minterm. Hence the restriction to satisfiable \varphi.) Marking scheme. (8 points) - 2: (a) the inequality; 1: a counterexample to the converse, checked. - 2: (b), with the rows counted twice named. - 3: (c): different rows give minterms never true together; the disjunction of all is a tautology; the count. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (a), a “converse” argued from one pair of formulas that happen to entail each other. [C6: Challenge: Interpolation] 1. For \varphi = p \wedge q and \psi = q \vee r, find a formula 	heta whose only atom is q, with \varphi \models 	heta and 	heta \models \psi. 2. Prove: if \varphi \models \psi, \varphi is satisfiable and \psi is not a tautology, then there is a formula 	heta, all of whose atoms occur both in \varphi and in \psi, with \varphi \models 	heta and 	heta \models \psi. 3. Show that under the hypotheses of (b), \varphi and \psi have at least one atom in common. [Hint 1] Let 	heta say: the shared atoms take values that some row making \varphi true also gives them. [Hint 2] To show 	heta \models \psi, build one row that agrees with a row of \varphi on the atoms of \varphi and with the given row on the other atoms of \psi. (a) 	heta = q: p \wedge q \models q and q \models q \vee r. (c) (Proved first, since (b) uses it.) Suppose no atom is shared. Take a row u making \varphi true, and any row w. The row that agrees with u on the atoms of \varphi and with w on every other atom makes \varphi true (@lem-coincidence), hence \psi; it agrees with w on the atoms of \psi, none of which is an atom of \varphi, so w makes \psi true (@lem-coincidence again). As w was any row, \psi would be a tautology. (b) Let q_1, \dots, q_k be the shared atoms (k \ge 1 by (c)). Call a row s on q_1, \dots, q_k good if some valuation making \varphi true gives the q_i the values of s; there is at least one, since \varphi is satisfiable. Let 	heta be the disjunction of the minterms, on q_1, \dots, q_k, of the good rows. Its atoms are shared. \varphi \models 	heta: a valuation making \varphi true gives the q_i the values of a good row s, so it makes the minterm of s true (@eq-row-conjunct), hence 	heta. 	heta \models \psi: let w make 	heta true. Then w makes the minterm of some good row s true, so w gives the q_i the values of s; and some u making \varphi true does the same. Let u' agree with u on the atoms of \varphi and with w on every other atom. By @lem-coincidence, u' makes \varphi true, so it makes \psi true, since \varphi \models \psi. Now u' agrees with w on every atom of \psi: on the shared atoms both give the values of s, and the other atoms of \psi are not atoms of \varphi. By @lem-coincidence, w makes \psi true. Marking scheme. (12 points) - 1: (a). - 2: the definition of 	heta from the good rows, with its existence (satisfiable \varphi). - 2: \varphi \models 	heta. - 5: 	heta \models \psi, with the glued row and both uses of @lem-coincidence. - 2: (c). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a 	heta with an atom of \varphi alone; a glued row that is not shown to agree with w on every atom of \psi.

title: 4.10 Compactness and Maximal Consistent Sets
content:
Compactness and Maximal Consistent Sets This section is optional, and nothing outside it depends on it. Every list of premises in this chapter has been finite, and the proof of completeness needed that: its Step 1 lists the atoms of \Gamma and \psi, and there are only finitely many of them because \Gamma is a finite list (@thm-completeness). But a statement about infinitely many objects can come with infinitely many premises. Give each n \ge 1 an atom p_n, read “the n-th lamp is on”, and the rules “the first lamp is on” and “if the n-th lamp is on, so is the next” are one premise for each n. This section defines \vdash and \models for such collections of premises, proves completeness for them by a route different from that of Section 4.8, and deduces from it the compactness theorem: a collection of formulas can be made true all at once as soon as each finite part of it can. The word “collection” keeps its everyday sense throughout; nothing here needs more. Infinitely many premises A derivation is finite, so from infinitely many premises it can use only finitely many; a valuation, on the other hand, gives every formula a value at once. [Derivability and Entailment from Infinitely Many Premises] Let \Gamma be a collection of formulas, finite or infinite, and \psi a formula. \Gamma \vdash \psi if \psi is derivable from some finite list of members of \Gamma; \Gamma is consistent if \Gamma 
vdash  ot. \Gamma \models \psi if every valuation that makes every member of \Gamma true makes \psi true; \Gamma is satisfiable if some valuation makes every member of \Gamma true. In words: a derivation has finitely many lines, so it can cite only finitely many premises. That is why \vdash goes through finite lists of members, while \models looks at all of \Gamma at once. For a finite list the new definitions agree with the old. A derivation from part of a list is a derivation from the list, by @lem-weakening-cut (a), so \vdash means what @def-derivable said, and consistent means what @def-inconsistent-set said. The definitions of \models and satisfiable say for a finite list exactly what @def-valid-argument and @def-satisfiable said. “Finite list of members” allows repetitions and any order; neither matters, by @lem-weakening-cut (a) and by the definitions of \models and satisfiable. An example. Let \Gamma consist of p_1 and every formula p_n 	o p_{n+1} with n \ge 1. Then \Gamma \vdash p_3: from the finite list p_1, \ p_1 	o p_2, \ p_2 	o p_3, two ulename{{	o}E} lines give p_2 and then p_3. And \Gamma \models p_n for every n \ge 1: a valuation making every member of \Gamma true makes p_1 true, and makes p_{n+1} true whenever it makes p_n true, so it makes every p_n true, by @ax-induction on n, started at 1. Is the collection consisting of p_1 \vee p_2 and every 
eg p_n with n \ge 2 satisfiable? Is it consistent? Satisfiable: the valuation making p_1 true and every other atom false makes every member true. Hence consistent. A derivation of  ot would use some finite list of members; that list is made true by the same valuation, so it is satisfiable, hence consistent by Section 4.7, and derives no  ot. Listing all formulas The construction below goes through all formulas one at a time, so it needs them in one list. [The Formulas Can Be Listed] There is a list \varphi_0, \varphi_1, \varphi_2, \dots of formulas in which every formula occurs. In words: the atoms are listed already (p, q, r, p_1, p_2, \dots), and each formula is a finite string of symbols, so the formulas can be listed by size, finitely many at each stage. List by size. At stage n, allow only the first n atoms and strings of at most n symbols. Each stage is finite, and every formula fits into some stage. Write the atoms in one list a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots (say p, q, r, p_1, p_2, \dots in this order). For each n \ge 1, consider the strings of length at most n over the n + 8 symbols a_1, \dots, a_n, \  ot, \ 
eg, \ \wedge, \ \vee, \ 	o, \ \leftrightarrow, \ (, \ ) . There are finitely many such strings (at most (n+8)^n of each length up to n), so finitely many of them are formulas. Stage n lists, in any order, the formulas among them that no earlier stage listed. Write the stages one after another and number the entries \varphi_0, \varphi_1, \dots. Each stage n lists at least the atom a_n, which is available for the first time, so the stages together list infinitely many formulas. Every formula occurs. Let \varphi have length \ell, and let its atoms be among a_1, \dots, a_m (with m = 0 if it has none). At stage n = \max\{\ell, m\} (note \ell \ge 1), \varphi is a string of length at most n over the symbols of that stage, so it is listed then, or earlier. Lindenbaum’s construction The new proof of completeness works the other way round from Section 4.8. It does not build a derivation. It starts from a consistent collection and builds a row that makes all of it true. The row is read off a collection that has made up its mind about every formula. A collection \Delta is maximal consistent if it is consistent and, for every formula \varphi, \varphi is in \Delta or 
eg\varphi is. The construction rests on one step. Exercise C2 of Section 3.2 (@exr-four-kinds-of-task-c2) proved it for finite lists; here it is again, for collections, with its proof. The key step. If \Delta is consistent, then \Delta with \varphi added, or \Delta with 
eg\varphi added, is consistent. Suppose both were inconsistent. Then there are finite lists \Delta_1 and \Delta_2 of members of \Delta with \Delta_1, \varphi \vdash  ot and \Delta_2, 
eg\varphi \vdash  ot (if a derivation of  ot does not use \varphi, or 
eg\varphi, adding it as a premise changes nothing, by weakening). By weakening, both hold with the list \Delta_1, \Delta_2 in place of \Delta_1 and of \Delta_2. A ulename{
eg I} box on \varphi gives \Delta_1, \Delta_2 \vdash 
eg\varphi, and an ulename{RAA} box on 
eg\varphi gives \Delta_1, \Delta_2 \vdash \varphi (this is @prp-derivable-iff-negation-inconsistent). Then ulename{
eg E}, by chaining (@lem-weakening-cut (c)), gives \Delta_1, \Delta_2 \vdash  ot, and \Delta would be inconsistent. [Lindenbaum’s Lemma] Every consistent collection of formulas is contained in a maximal consistent collection. Go through the list of all formulas, and add each one or its negation, whichever keeps the collection consistent. The key step says one of them always does. At the end, every formula has been decided, and no contradiction has been let in, because a contradiction would show up at some finite stage. Let \Gamma be consistent, and let \varphi_0, \varphi_1, \dots be the list of @lem-formula-enumeration. Each \Delta_n contains the one before. Let \Delta consist of the formulas that belong to some \Delta_n. Then \Delta contains \Gamma = \Delta_0. \Delta is consistent. A derivation of  ot from \Delta uses a finite list of members of \Delta. Each of them is in some \Delta_n, so all of them are in the \Delta_N with the largest of those indices N (N = 0 if the list is empty), since the collections grow. eg\psi cannot lead to  ot, since an ulename{RAA} box would turn such a derivation into one of \psi. Extend \Gamma with 
eg\psi to a maximal consistent collection and read off its row: it makes every member of \Gamma true and \psi false. We prove the contrapositive of the first sentence. Suppose \Gamma 
vdash \psi. Then \Gamma with

eg\psi to the list if it is not there (weakening), we have \Gamma_0, 
eg\psi \vdash  ot for a finite list \Gamma_0 of members of \Gamma, and an ulename{RAA} box on 
eg\psi gives \Gamma_0 \vdash \psi, so \Gamma \vdash \psi. By @lem-lindenbaum, \Gamma with 
eg\psi is contained in a maximal consistent \Delta. By @lem-truth-lemma, v_\Delta makes every member of \Delta true, in particular every member of \Gamma, and

vdash  ot. So the first sentence with \psi =  ot is the second. Conversely, given the second, if \Gamma 
vdash \psi, then \Gamma with 
eg\psi is consistent, as just shown, hence satisfiable, by a row that refutes \Gamma \models \psi. Two proofs, two prices. Section 4.8 glued the rows of a truth table into one derivation. That is a construction one can carry out, from 2^n row derivations for n atoms, but only for finitely many premises. This section never writes a derivation. It shows that if none exists, then a row exists, by a construction that passes through infinitely many formulas, one at a time, and cannot be finished by hand. The first proof is effective (it writes the derivation down) and limited to finite lists; the second reaches infinite collections and produces no derivation. The second is the route that extends beyond propositional logic. Besides the rules, and the structural induction and recursion of Section 4.3, the proof used one new fact about the formulas: that they can be listed (@lem-formula-enumeration). The construction then decides the formulas in the order of the list, and a different list may give a different \Delta and a different row; any of them refutes \Gamma \models \psi. The proof cites @prp-excluded-middle nowhere, but its key step uses ulename{RAA}, and so does the step from \Gamma 
vdash \psi to the consistency of \Gamma with 
eg\psi. It is classical in the same way as the splitting of Section 4.8, which used excluded middle. Compactness Compactness A collection \Gamma of formulas is satisfiable if and only if every finite list of members of \Gamma is satisfiable. Consequently, \Gamma \models \psi if and only if some finite list of members of \Gamma entails \psi. “Only if”: a valuation making every member of \Gamma true makes every member of each finite list true. “If”: every finite list of members of \Gamma is satisfiable, hence consistent, by Section 4.7. So \Gamma is consistent, since a derivation of  ot from \Gamma would use a finite list of members. By @thm-completeness-infinite, \Gamma is satisfiable. For the second sentence: \Gamma \models \psi iff \Gamma with 
eg\psi added is unsatisfiable (a valuation making \Gamma true and \psi false is exactly one making both \Gamma and 
eg\psi true); iff, by the first sentence, some finite list of its members is unsatisfiable; iff some finite list \Gamma_0 of members of \Gamma has \Gamma_0, 
eg\psi unsatisfiable (adding 
eg\psi to an unsatisfiable list keeps it unsatisfiable, and \Gamma_0, 
eg\psi is itself such a list); iff \Gamma_0 \models \psi, by Section 4.5’s reduction of entailment to unsatisfiability. [Infinitely many premises, finitely many used] Let \Gamma consist of p_1 and every p_n 	o p_{n+1} with n \ge 1, the lamps of the opening. 1. Show \Gamma \models p_{100}, and find a finite list of members of \Gamma that entails p_{100}. 2. Show that a finite list of members of \Gamma that leaves out p_{50} 	o p_{51} does not entail p_{100}. (a) A valuation making every member of \Gamma true makes p_1 true and passes truth from each p_n to p_{n+1}, so it makes every p_n true (@ax-induction, started at 1), p_{100} among them. The hundred formulas p_1, \ p_1 	o p_2, \ \dots, \ p_{99} 	o p_{100} already entail p_{100}: a row making them all true makes p_1, p_2, \dots, p_{100} true, one after another. (b) Take the valuation making p_1, \dots, p_{50} true and every other atom false. It makes p_1 true; it makes p_n 	o p_{n+1} true for n < 50 (true conclusion) and for n > 50 (false hypothesis); only p_{50} 	o p_{51} is false. So it makes every member of the finite list true, and p_{100} false. Compactness says that this is no accident: an entailment from infinitely many premises always rests on finitely many of them. Here every finite list that entails p_{100} must contain all ninety-nine implications up to p_{99} 	o p_{100}, since (b)’s argument works with any p_k 	o p_{k+1}, k < 100, in place of p_{50} 	o p_{51}, and it must contain p_1, since the valuation making every atom false makes all the implications true. Compactness promises one valuation for the whole collection when each finite part has one. The valuations of the finite parts may all differ, and the theorem does not say how to find the single one: its proof went through a maximal consistent collection, which nobody writes down. Prove that the whole graph can. Use atoms c_{n,i}, read “vertex n gets color i” for i = 1, 2, 3, where the c_{n,i} are distinct atoms (for instance, c_{n,i} is p_{3n+i}). eg(c_{n,i} \wedge c_{n,j}), for every vertex n and all i 
e j; - 
eg(c_{m,i} \wedge c_{n,i}), for every joined pair m, n and every i. Each member of \Gamma_0 mentions only vertices of F, and v makes it true: the first kind because \kappa colors every vertex of F, the second because it gives each one color, the third because \kappa colors joined vertices of F differently.
