It is free for \varepsilon in \varphi, because the only quantifiers above the free occurrences of \varepsilon in \varphi are on N and n. Section 5.3’s rule makes this step, and “\varepsilon/2 > 0” then comes from \varepsilon > 0 by arithmetic. “Take N = n.” Now suppose the proof has chosen N, so it knows \psi \ = \  orall n \in 
N \;  igl( n \ge N 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon  igr), with N free. A tempting step is to “apply this with n in place of N”. No rule allows this: N has been chosen, not quantified, so no term may be put in for it. Writing the step out shows how badly it goes wrong, because n is not even free for N in \psi: the occurrence of N lies in the scope of  orall n. The substitution produces  orall n \in 
N \;  igl( n \ge n 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon  igr), which says that every term of the sequence is within \varepsilon of L, a far stronger claim that does not follow. In words, the error is to let the threshold N be “the n we are looking at”, when n is the placeholder of “for all n \ge N”. A proof that needs a statement about a particular index names it with a new letter, say m \ge N, and substitutes m, which is free for n. Induction, as a formula. The display after @ax-induction in Section 4.2 used a property P(n). With substitution it can be written for any formula \varphi in which the variable n is free, as the formula \Bigl( \varphi[0/n] \ \wedge \  orall n \in 
N \,  igl( \varphi 	o \varphi[(n + 1)/n]  igr) \Bigr) \ 	o \  orall n \in 
N \; \varphi , where \varphi[0/n] plays the part of P(0) and \varphi[(n + 1)/n] the part of P(n + 1). The term n + 1 is free for n in \varphi: its only variable is n, and a free occurrence of n never lies in the scope of a quantifier on n. This is how the principle of induction reads in the language of this chapter; its status (a basic property of 
N) is unchanged. Mathematics writes 1/x and \lim a_n, which name nothing for some values: x = 0, or a sequence with no limit. In the language of this chapter every term names an object, because every function symbol is defined everywhere on the domain. Mathematics keeps partial operations out of trouble with hypotheses: 1/x is written only under x 
e 0, as in  orall x\, (x 
e 0 	o x \cdot (1/x) = 1), where the value at 0 is never used; and “the limit” is written only after it has been proved that there is exactly one (Section 5.8). Some logics allow terms that name nothing; this book does not need them. [Looking ahead] Chapter 7 proves, in an optional section, that renaming a bound letter never changes the meaning of a formula. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. For each formula, mark each occurrence of each variable as free or bound, list the free variables, and say whether it is a sentence: (i)  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(y)); (ii) \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y); (iii)  orall x\, (x < y) \wedge \exists y\, (y < x); (iv)  orall \varepsilon\,  igl( \varepsilon > 0 	o \exists \delta\, (\delta > 0 \wedge \delta < \varepsilon)  igr). 2. Which of the following are terms, and which are formulas, for one-place f, two-place g and two-place predicate R? (i) g(f(x), c); (ii) R(f(x), c); (iii) f(R(x, c)); (iv)  orall c\, R(c, c). 3. True or false, with a reason: if t is a variable, then t is free for x in every formula. 4. True or false, with a reason:  igl(  orall x\, P(x) \wedge Q(x)  igr)[c/x] is  orall x\, P(x) \wedge Q(c). (a) (i) The single occurrence of x, in P(x), is bound by  orall x (the x after  orall belongs to the quantifier node and is not an occurrence); the occurrence of y in Q(y) is free (no quantifier on y). Free variables: y. Not a sentence. (ii) The occurrence of x is bound by \exists x, that of y by  orall y. No free variables: a sentence. (iii) By shorthand rule 2 this is ( orall x\, (x < y) \wedge \exists y\, (y < x)). In the left part, x is bound by  orall x and y is free. In the right part, y is bound by \exists y and x is free (the  orall x governs only the left part). Free variables: x and y, each with one free and one bound occurrence. Not a sentence. (iv) Every occurrence of \varepsilon lies below  orall \varepsilon, and both occurrences of \delta lie below \exists \delta; 0 is a constant. A sentence. (b) (i) A term, by (Tm2) twice. (ii) A formula, atomic by (Fm1): the predicate R applied to the terms f(x) and c. (iii) Neither: R(x, c) is a formula, not a term, and (Tm2) applies f only to a term. (iv) Neither: (Fm4) puts a variable after  orall, and c is a constant symbol. (c) False. The variable y is not free for x in \exists y\, (y 
e x), since the free occurrence of x lies in the scope of \exists y. (A variable t is free for x when t is x itself, or when t does not appear in the formula.) (d) True. The formula is ( orall x\, P(x) \wedge Q(x)) by shorthand rule 2. The \wedge passes the substitution to both parts;  orall x\, P(x) is unchanged because its quantifier is on x, and Q(x) becomes Q(c). [A2: Drill] Answer each part in a line or two. 1. In  orall y\, (x < y) \wedge \exists x\, (x = y), which occurrences are free, and what are the free variables? 2. Is  orall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 0) a sentence? 3. Someone writes  orall x\, P(x) 	o Q(x) for “every P is a Q”. Which occurrence of x is free, and what is the repair? 4. Repair  orall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists \delta > 0\; (\abs{x - a} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon), meant as “f is continuous at a”, with a a variable here (not a constant symbol), so that a is its only free variable. 5. Compute  igl( x \le y \wedge \exists y\, (y < x)  igr)[3/x]. 6. Compute  igl(  orall x\, (x \ge y)  igr)[0/y]. 7. Compute  igl(  orall x\, P(x) 	o P(x)  igr)[c/x]. 8. Compute  igl( (x + y = y + x)[y/x]  igr)[x/y]. Is the result the formula with x and y swapped? 9. Compute  igl( P(x, y)[f(y)/x]  igr)[c/y]. 10. Is x free for y in \exists x\, (x > y)? 11. Is z + 1 free for y in \exists x\, (x > y)? Compute. 12. Put x in for y in \exists x\, (x > y), renaming first. (a) The x of x < y and the y of x = y are free; the y of x < y is bound by  orall y and the x of x = y by \exists x. Free variables: x, y. (b) Yes: every occurrence is bound. (c) By shorthand rule 2 the  orall x governs only P(x), so the formula is ( orall x\, P(x)) 	o Q(x) and the x of Q(x) is free. Repair:  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)). (d) As written, x is free, so the formula speaks of one fixed x. Repair:  orall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists \delta > 0\;  orall x\, (\abs{x - a} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon); f is a function symbol, not a variable. (e) 3 \le y \wedge \exists y\, (y < 3). (f)  orall x\, (x \ge 0). (g)  orall x\, P(x) 	o P(c) (shorthand rule 2: the  orall x governs only the first P(x)). (h) y + y = y + y, then x + x = x + x. No: the swap is y + x = x + y. (i) P(f(y), y), then P(f(c), c): the second substitution also reaches the y inside the term put in by the first. (j) No: the free y lies in the scope of \exists x, and x is the variable of the term. (k) Yes: \exists x\, (x > z + 1). (l) Rename x to z: \exists z\, (z > y); then \exists z\, (z > x). B. Practice [B1: Computing substitutions] Compute each substitution. Where the term is not free for the variable, say which quantifier would capture it, rename first, and then substitute. 1.  igl( P(x) \wedge R(x, y)  igr)[f(y)/x]. 2.  igl(  orall x\, R(x, y) 	o P(x)  igr)[c/x]. 3.  igl(  orall y\, (x < y)  igr)[(y + 1)/x]. 4.  igl( \exists x\, (x = 2 \cdot y)  igr)[x/y]. 5.  igl( \exists y\, (y > x) \wedge Q(y)  igr)[(x + 1)/y]. (a) No quantifiers, so f(y) is free for x. Every occurrence of x is replaced: P(f(y)) \wedge R(f(y), y). The y inside f(y) and the y already in R(x, y) now stand side by side; with no quantifier around, both are the same free y, as intended. (b) By shorthand rule 2 the formula is ( orall x\, R(x, y) 	o P(x)). The constant c has no variables, so it is free for x. The left part is unchanged (quantifier on x); the free x in P(x) becomes c:  orall x\, R(x, y) 	o P(c). (c) Not free for: the free occurrence of x lies in the scope of  orall y, and y is a variable of y + 1. Rename y to z, which appears nowhere:  orall z\, (x < z). Then substitute:  orall z\, (y + 1 < z). (Without renaming, the definition would give  orall y\, (y + 1 < y), which says nothing about y + 1.) (d) Not free for: the free occurrence of y lies in the scope of \exists x, and the term is x. Rename x to z: \exists z\, (z = 2 \cdot y), “y doubled is something”, then substitute: \exists z\, (z = 2 \cdot x). (Without renaming, the result would be \exists x\, (x = 2 \cdot x), “some number is its own double”, a claim about no particular number.) (e) By shorthand rule 2 the formula is (\exists y\, (y > x) \wedge Q(y)). The occurrence of y in y > x is bound, and the one in Q(y) is free and not in the scope of any quantifier; so x + 1 is free for y (the \exists y above the bound y is irrelevant, since that occurrence is not replaced). The result is \exists y\, (y > x) \wedge Q(x + 1). [B2: The set of free variables] For a term t, let \mathrm{Var}(t) be the set of variables of t, and for a formula \varphi, let \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) be the set of its free variables. (Here \cup is the union of two sets, \setminus removes elements, and \emptyset is the empty set, all in the everyday sense.) 1. Write down clauses that define \mathrm{Var}(t) by recursion on terms and \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) by recursion on formulas, one clause for each case of @def-term and of @def-first-order-formula. 2. Use your clauses to compute \mathrm{FV} of  orall x\, (x < y) \wedge \exists y\, (y < x) and of  orall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = z), showing each step. (a) For terms:  egin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(x) &= \{x\} \ 	ext{ for a variable } x, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(c) = \emptyset, \ \mathrm{Var} igl( f(t_1, \dots, t_n)  igr) &= \mathrm{Var}(t_1) \cup \dots \cup \mathrm{Var}(t_n). \end{aligned} For formulas:  egin{aligned} \mathrm{FV} igl( R(t_1, \dots, t_n)  igr) &= \mathrm{Var}(t_1) \cup \dots \cup \mathrm{Var}(t_n), \ \mathrm{FV}(t_1 = t_2) &= \mathrm{Var}(t_1) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t_2), \qquad \mathrm{FV}( ot) = \emptyset, \ \mathrm{FV}(
eg\varphi) &= \mathrm{FV}(\varphi), \qquad \mathrm{FV} igl( (\varphi \circ \psi)  igr) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \cup \mathrm{FV}(\psi), \ \mathrm{FV}( orall x\, \varphi) &= \mathrm{FV}(\exists x\, \varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}. \end{aligned} These are the four lines of the recursive description of “free” (in the fold after the examples of free and bound occurrences), rewritten as sets: x \in \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) exactly when x is free in \varphi. By structural recursion (carried over to terms and to first-order formulas), each set of clauses defines exactly one function. (b) First formula. \mathrm{FV}(x < y) = \{x, y\}, so \mathrm{FV}( orall x\, (x < y)) = \{x, y\} \setminus \{x\} = \{y\}. \mathrm{FV}(y < x) = \{x, y\}, so \mathrm{FV}(\exists y\, (y < x)) = \{x\}. The conjunction gives \{y\} \cup \{x\} = \{x, y\}, which agrees with A1(a)(iii). Second formula. \mathrm{FV}(x + y = z) = \mathrm{Var}(x + y) \cup \mathrm{Var}(z) = \{x, y, z\}. Then \mathrm{FV}(\exists y\, (x + y = z)) = \{x, z\}, and \mathrm{FV}( orall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = z)) = \{z\}. So the formula is an open sentence in z alone (over 
R it is true for every z: given x, take y = z - x). [B3: Swapping two letters] Let \varphi = \exists z\,  igl( R(x, z) \wedge R(z, y)  igr). 1. Compute (\varphi[y/x])[x/y], and say whether it is \varphi with x and y swapped. 2. Swap x and y in \varphi with three substitutions through a letter u that appears nowhere, checking at each step that the term is free for the variable. 3. Why would z not do as the go-between? (a) \varphi[y/x] = \exists z\, (R(y, z) \wedge R(z, y)), and then [x/y] gives \exists z\, (R(x, z) \wedge R(z, x)). The swap is \exists z\, (R(y, z) \wedge R(z, x)), a different formula, and it says something different: over 
N with R read as < and x, y naming 2, 0, the swap is true (z = 1), while the computed formula, “some z is above 2 and below 2”, is false. (b) \varphi[u/x] = \exists z\, (R(u, z) \wedge R(z, y)); then [x/y] gives \exists z\, (R(u, z) \wedge R(z, x)); then [y/u] gives \exists z\, (R(y, z) \wedge R(z, x)), the swap. At each step the only quantifier above the replaced occurrence is \exists z, and the term (u, x, y) is not z, so it is free. (c) z is not free for x in \varphi: the x of R(x, z) lies inside \exists z, so \varphi[z/x] would be captured and say \exists z\, (R(z, z) \wedge R(z, y)). The go-between must appear nowhere in \varphi, bound letters included (“appear”, in “Free and bound: drawing the arrows”). Worked examples of these types: “One substitution at a time”; the practical rule “Before you substitute”. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a), both steps computed and the swap written, with the difference shown (by the strings, or by one reading in which they differ). - 4: (b), the three substitutions in the right order, each result correct, and the free-for check stated once for each step. - 3: (c), capture named, with the captured formula written. Fatal error (0 for the part): treating [y/x] and [x/y] as happening at the same time. C. Going deeper [C1: Challenge: What substitution does to the free variables] Let \varphi be a formula, x a variable and t a term, with t free for x in \varphi, and with x free in \varphi. 1. Prove that the free variables of \varphi[t/x] are the free variables of \varphi other than x, together with the variables of t: \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) =  igl( \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}  igr) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t), with the notation of B2. Prove it in the following form, by structural induction on \varphi: for every \varphi in which t is free for x, if x \in \mathrm{FV}(\varphi), then \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = (\mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t); if x 
otin \mathrm{FV}(\varphi), then \varphi[t/x] = \varphi. The term version, the atomic case and the connective cases are done below; prove the case of  orall y\, \varphi (the case of \exists y\, \varphi is the same). 2. Show, with the capture example \exists y\, (y > x), t = y + 1, that the conclusion can fail when t is not free for x. Show also, with an example of your own, that it can fail when x is not free in \varphi. Given for (a). Terms. Let s be a term in which x occurs. Then \mathrm{Var}(s[t/x]) = (\mathrm{Var}(s) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t). By induction on s: if s is the variable x, then s[t/x] = t and both sides are \mathrm{Var}(t). (A constant, or a variable other than x, does not contain x.) If s = f(s_1, \dots, s_n), then s[t/x] = f(s_1[t/x], \dots, s_n[t/x]); for each s_i containing x, the induction hypothesis gives \mathrm{Var}(s_i[t/x]) = (\mathrm{Var}(s_i) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t), and for each s_i not containing x, s_i[t/x] = s_i (as in the proof of the claim in the text). At least one s_i contains x, so the union over i is (\mathrm{Var}(s) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t). Formulas. We prove, by structural induction on \varphi, the statement S(\varphi): if t is free for x in \varphi, then \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = (\mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t) when x \in \mathrm{FV}(\varphi), and \varphi[t/x] = \varphi when x 
otin \mathrm{FV}(\varphi). The second half is the claim proved in the text, for every \varphi; so in each case below we assume x \in \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) and prove the equation. Write E(\chi) for the set (\mathrm{FV}(\chi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t). Atomic. Let \varphi = R(s_1, \dots, s_n) with x occurring in some s_i. By the clause for atomic formulas, \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) is the union over i of the sets \mathrm{Var}(s_i[t/x]). Exactly as in the term case for f(s_1, \dots, s_n) (the result for terms for each s_i containing x, s_i[t/x] = s_i for the others, and at least one s_i containing x), this union is E(\varphi). The same for s_1 = s_2. ( ot has no free variables.) Negation. \mathrm{FV}((
eg\varphi)[t/x]) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = E(\varphi) = E(
eg\varphi), by the induction hypothesis (t is free for x in \varphi, and x is free in \varphi). Binary connective. Let x be free in (\varphi \circ \psi); then t is free for x in both parts, and x is free in at least one. If it is free in both, the induction hypothesis gives E(\varphi) \cup E(\psi) = E((\varphi \circ \psi)). If it is free in \varphi only, then \psi[t/x] = \psi, and E(\varphi) \cup \mathrm{FV}(\psi) = E((\varphi \circ \psi)), because x 
otin \mathrm{FV}(\psi). Symmetrically if it is free in \psi only. [Hint 1] When x is free in  orall y\, \varphi, what does “free for” tell you about y and t? [Hint 2] Start from \mathrm{FV}(( orall y\, \varphi)[t/x]) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) \setminus \{y\} and apply the induction hypothesis to \varphi. Then see where removing y from the resulting set needs something about y and \mathrm{Var}(t). (a) The term version and the atomic, negation and connective cases are given in the statement. It remains to treat the quantifiers. Quantifier. If x is not free in  orall y\, \varphi, then ( orall y\, \varphi)[t/x] =  orall y\, \varphi by the claim of the text. Now let x be free in  orall y\, \varphi. Then y is not x and x is free in \varphi; and since t is free for x in  orall y\, \varphi while x is free there, y 
otin \mathrm{Var}(t) and t is free for x in \varphi (the recursive description of “free for”). So  egin{aligned} \mathrm{FV} igl( ( orall y\, \varphi)[t/x]  igr) &= \mathrm{FV} igl( \varphi[t/x]  igr) \setminus \{y\} =  igl( (\mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t)  igr) \setminus \{y\} \ &=  igl( \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x, y\}  igr) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t) = E( orall y\, \varphi), \end{aligned} where the third equality uses y 
otin \mathrm{Var}(t), and the last uses \mathrm{FV}( orall y\, \varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{y\}. The case of \exists y is the same. This proves S(\varphi) for every formula, and (a) is its first half. (b) With \varphi = \exists y\, (y > x) and t = y + 1: \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) = \{x\}, so the equation would give \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = \{y\}. But \varphi[t/x] = \exists y\, (y > y + 1), whose set of free variables is \emptyset. The y of the term was captured, so it is not free in the result; the quantifier case of the proof fails because y \in \mathrm{Var}(t). For the second hypothesis, take \varphi = P(z) and t = y. Then x is not free in \varphi, and t is free for x (there are no quantifiers). Now \varphi[t/x] = P(z), with free variables \{z\}, while the equation would give \{z\} \cup \{y\} = \{y, z\}. Without a free x, nothing is put in, so the variables of t do not appear. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: the quantifier case reduced to \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) \setminus \{y\} by the definitions. - 3: the use of “free for” to get y 
otin \mathrm{Var}(t) and t free for x in \varphi, naming where it is used. - 1: the case “x not free in  orall y\, \varphi” handled by the claim of the text. - 3: both counterexamples of (b), each checked by computing both sides. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using the equation \mathrm{FV}(\chi[t/x]) = (\mathrm{FV}(\chi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t) for a part \chi in which x is not free (it fails there; see the second example in (b)); removing y from \mathrm{Var}(t) without justification. [C2: Renaming is not swapping] 1. Show that  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) and  orall y\, \exists x\, (y < x) are the same sentence up to renaming bound variables: give a sequence of renamings, each allowed by the condition of the text, leading from the first to the second. 2. Show that  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) and \exists y\,  orall x\, (x < y) are not the same up to renaming. Hint: what does a renaming leave unchanged? (a) A renaming needs a variable that does not appear in the formula, so the two letters cannot be exchanged in one step; go through a third letter z. 1. In  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y), rename the bound x to z, which does not appear:  orall z\, \exists y\, (z < y). 2. Rename the bound y to x, which no longer appears:  orall z\, \exists x\, (z < x). 3. Rename the bound z to y, which no longer appears:  orall y\, \exists x\, (y < x). Each step renames one quantifier and the occurrences it binds, to a letter absent from the formula at that moment. The result is the second sentence. (Over 
N both say “there is no largest natural number”, in two spellings.) (b) A renaming changes only which letters are used. It does not change the parse tree’s shape, which quantifier symbol ( orall or \exists) sits at which node, or which quantifier node binds which occurrence. In  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) the root is a  orall node; in \exists y\,  orall x\, (x < y) the root is an \exists node. No sequence of renamings turns a  orall node into an \exists node, so no sequence of renamings leads from one sentence to the other. The two sentences also say different things: over 
N, the first is true (take y = x + 1) and the second false (for any y, take x = y). This is @exm-quantifier-order-sum again. Renaming changes the names of the placeholders; swapping changes the order in which they are chosen, and the order is what carries the meaning.

title: 5.3 Using "For Every": Instantiation
content:
Using “For Every”: Instantiation Section 5.2 made the language exact and defined the operation \varphi[t/x], “put the term t in for the variable x”, with its one hazard, capture. We can now give the first quantifier rule. It is the rule for using a universal statement: whatever holds for every object holds for the object named by any term we care to write. The rule is called ulename{ orall E}. It is the rule behind every “by the theorem, applied to x = 2”. With it alone, universal statements can be used but not proved, and the section meets exactly that gap (“A stall” below), which Section 5.4 fills. Applying a statement about everything Every application of a general fact to a particular case is one step of logic, and so far that step has been taken on trust. Three earlier places took it. - Section 1.3 used the theorem “if an integer is divisible by 2 and by 3, then it is divisible by 6” at n = 42, taking the step from “every integer” to the one integer 42 on trust. - In @exm-raa-zero (Section 2.5) the hypothesis was “x \le \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0”, and the proof applied it to the one number \varepsilon = x/2. - Section 5.1 opened with the argument “every positive real has a square root; 2 is positive; so 2 has a square root”, which a truth table calls invalid because it sees only three unrelated atoms. The same step happens in each: a statement about every object is applied to one object, named by a term. In the language of Section 5.2, the first premise of the square-root argument is  orall x\, (P(x) 	o S(x)), and applying it to 2 gives  igl( P(x) 	o S(x)  igr)[2/x] \ = \ P(2) 	o S(2), which is part (a) of @exm-computing-substitutions. From there ulename{{	o}E} finishes. All that is missing is a rule that licenses the first step. The rule A universal statement may be applied to any term: remove the quantifier and put the term in for the variable. [Universal Elimination] Here \varphi is a formula, x a variable, and t any term, subject to one side condition: t is free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for). Line i must be available at line k (the scope rule of @def-derivation). This rule is called ulename{ orall E} (universal elimination, or instantiation), and \varphi[t/x] is an instance of  orall x\, \varphi. In words: if a line says that \varphi holds for every x, then any later line, where that line is still available, may write what \varphi says about t. The rule cites one line and no box. - Schema: the block above: one cited line, no box. - Reading: drop the  orall x, put one term in for every free x, and check that no letter of the term gets caught by a quantifier inside. - Example: from  orall x\, (P(x) 	o S(x)), “ulename{ orall E} 1” at the term 2 writes P(2) 	o S(2). Read the definition clause by clause; exercises cite the clauses by number. 1. The cited line’s main symbol is  orall x, with all of \varphi as its scope:  orall x\, P(x) 	o Q(c) is an implication; a  orall buried inside another connective must first be taken out by that connective’s rule, when it can be (ulename{\wedge E} takes  orall x\, P(x) out of  orall x\, P(x) \wedge Q(c)), and a  orall in the hypothesis of an implication cannot be instantiated at all. 2. Any term: a constant, a variable (x itself included) or a compound term. Nothing about it needs to be established first, since every term names an object of the domain. 3. Every free occurrence, by the same term: the new line is \varphi[t/x]; we do not choose which occurrences change. 4. Free for x (@def-free-for): no letter of t is caught by a quantifier of \varphi. This is the rule’s only restriction. 5. Line i is available (the scope rule of @def-derivation), as for every rule. When the universal statement has a bound,  orall x \in A\; \varphi, using it at t also needs the line t \in A. Line 1 is  orall x\, (x + 0 = x). Which of 3 + 0 = 3, y + 0 = y, 3 + 0 = x may line 2 be, by ulename{ orall E}? The first two, at the terms 3 and y; y is free for x, since the formula has no quantifier. The third is not an instance: \varphi[t/x] puts the same term in for every free x, and 3 + 0 = x replaced one x and left the other. If x is not free in \varphi, then \varphi[t/x] = \varphi for every term t (the claim proved in Section 5.2), and ulename{ orall E} simply removes a quantifier that bound nothing: from  orall x\, P(c) it writes P(c). Legal, and dull. One line, many uses. The cited line stays where it is, available as before. A derivation may instantiate the same universal line as often as it likes, at different terms or the same one. Worked derivation (d) below uses one premise twice. Why this rule. It says no more than the word “every”. If every object in the domain satisfies \varphi, then so does the object that t names, whichever object that is. A term always names something, since the domain is never empty (Section 5.1), so the instance always has something to be about. Why “free for”. The instance must say about t what \varphi says about x. Section 5.2 showed that when a variable of t is captured, \varphi[t/x] can say something quite different. The condition rules capture out, and the subsection on common errors below shows the rule going wrong without it. Line 1 of a derivation is  orall x\, \exists z\, (z > x + y). For which terms t may ulename{ orall E} write (\exists z\, (z > x + y))[t/x] on line 2? Is t = y allowed? Is t = z + 1? The only free occurrence of x in \exists z\, (z > x + y) lies in the scope of \exists z, and that is the only quantifier above it. So t is free for x exactly when z is not a variable of t: any term not containing z is allowed. The term y is allowed, and gives \exists z\, (z > y + y); the variable y already occurs free in the line, and that does no harm. The term z + 1 is not allowed: it would give \exists z\, (z > z + 1 + y), where the z of the term has been captured. Nor is z itself. To instantiate at z, rename the bound z first (Section 5.2), say to w: from  orall x\, \exists w\, (w > x + y), ulename{ orall E} at z gives \exists w\, (w > z + y). A long “and”, taken apart. In world W of Section 5.1,  orall x\, \varphi says \varphi[a/x] \wedge \varphi[b/x] \wedge \varphi[c/x] \wedge \varphi[d/x], and ulename{ orall E} at b does what ulename{\wedge E} does: it takes out one conjunct. Over 
N the conjunction cannot be written; ulename{ orall E} takes out any conjunct, at any term, without writing the rest. Four derivations The worked derivations below use ulename{ orall E} and the rules of Chapter 1. Each has an Idea that says why each rule was chosen, continuing the search method of Section 3.1: a goal-directed step looks at the goal’s main symbol, a premise-directed step at a resource’s. The new question is the one that ulename{ orall E} raises every time: at which term? [Instantiation at work] Give a derivation of each sequent. 1.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \ P(c) \vdash Q(c). 2.  orall x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \vdash R(c, c). 3.  orall x\,  orall y\, (R(x, y) 	o R(y, x)), \ R(a, b) \vdash R(b, a). 4.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o P(f(x))), \ P(c) \vdash P(f(f(c))). (a) Idea. The goal Q(c) has no connective or quantifier, so no introduction rule produces it, and the search turns to the premises. The premise P(c) cannot be taken apart. The premise  orall x\, (\dots) begins with  orall, so it can be used only by ulename{ orall E}. At which term? The goal mentions the term c, so instantiate at c. That gives an implication whose hypothesis is a premise and whose conclusion is the goal. Line 3 is (P(x) 	o Q(x))[c/x]; the constant c has no variables, so it is free for x. Read c as 2, P(x) as “x is positive”, and Q(x) as “x has a square root” (Section 5.1 wrote S for this predicate), and the derivation is the square-root argument of Section 5.1, in the four lines promised there. The argument that truth tables rejected is derivable once the rules can see inside its sentences. (b) Idea. The premise has two quantifiers, and ulename{ orall E} removes one at a time, the outermost first: the main symbol of the premise is  orall x, and only after it is gone is  orall y the main symbol. The goal R(c, c) shows the term for both. Line 2 is ( orall y\, R(x, y))[c/x]: the quantifier  orall y is on a variable other than x, so the substitution passes through it (@def-substitution). Line 3 instantiates y at c as well. Nothing forbids putting the same term in for two different variables; “for all x and y” includes the case x = y. (c) Idea. Work backwards from the goal R(b, a). The only line that can produce it is the first premise, through an instance of its inside, R(x, y) 	o R(y, x), followed by ulename{{	o}E}. Which instance has conclusion R(b, a)? Matching R(y, x) with R(b, a) gives y \coloneqq b and x \coloneqq a. Then the hypothesis of that instance is R(a, b), which is the second premise. So the terms are read off the goal: a for x first (the outer quantifier), then b for y. A reader who matches the goal R(b, a) against the hypothesis R(x, y) instead of the conclusion R(y, x) puts b for x and a for y, and gets R(b, a) 	o R(a, b). That is a legal line, but its hypothesis is the goal itself, so ulename{{	o}E} cannot fire. Match the goal against the conclusion of the implication, since that is the part ulename{{	o}E} delivers. (d) Idea, forwards. The premise P(c) is the hypothesis of the instance of the first premise at c, so instantiating at c and firing gives P(f(c)). Now P(f(c)) is the hypothesis of the instance at f(c), so the same premise, instantiated again, fires again and gives P(f(f(c))), the goal. Idea, backwards. The goal P(f(f(c))) has the shape P(f(x)), the conclusion of the inside of the first premise, with x \coloneqq f(c). So the last ulename{ orall E} must be at the compound term f(c), and its hypothesis P(f(c)) becomes the new goal. That has the shape P(f(x)) with x \coloneqq c, and its hypothesis is the premise P(c). Line 5 cites line 1 again: a universal line can be instantiated as often as needed. Its term f(c) contains no variable, so it is free for x, and (P(x) 	o P(f(x)))[f(c)/x] is P(f(c)) 	o P(f(f(c))): every x is replaced by the whole term f(c), including the one inside f(x). An arithmetic reading: over 
N, let f(n) be n + 2, let P(n) say “n is even”, and let c be 0. The first premise says that adding 2 to an even number gives an even number, the second that 0 is even, and the derivation concludes that f(f(0)) = 4 is even. Each further step up the even numbers would cost two more lines. Reaching “every n of the form f(\cdots f(0) \cdots)” at once is a job for induction, not for this rule. In each derivation, the Idea chose the term of every ulename{ orall E} by matching: the goal, or a hypothesis still needed, has a definite shape, and the instance is chosen to have that shape. Instantiating at a term that nothing asks for is legal, and it fills a derivation with lines that lead nowhere. Checking a line of instantiation Choosing the term can take thought; checking a line never does. For a line justified “ulename{ orall E} i”, ask four questions. 1. Is line i available here (@def-derivation)? 2. Is the main symbol of line i a universal quantifier? If so, read off its variable x and its scope \varphi. 3. Is this line \varphi[t/x] for some term t? Find t by comparing the two lines at a free occurrence of x in \varphi; then check that every free occurrence of x became that same t, and that nothing else changed. 4. Is t free for x in \varphi? Run on line 5 of (d): line 1 is available, since no box contains it; its main symbol is  orall x, with scope P(x) 	o P(f(x)); comparing gives t = f(c), and both occurrences of x became f(c); and f(c) has no variables, so it is free for x. The line passes. How this rule looks in a mathematical proof Let a be a real number. A proof might say: Since y^2 \ge 0 for every real y, applying this to a - 1 gives (a - 1)^2 \ge 0, that is, a^2 - 2a + 1 \ge 0. The first half of the sentence is one ulename{ orall E}, at the compound term a - 1. The second half rewrites (a - 1)^2 by school algebra. In a derivation such a step is written as one line justified “arith”, for arithmetic: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Sentence ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 1 “Since y^2 \ge 0 for every real y, …” (the general fact) 2 “… applying this to a - 1 gives (a - 1)^2 \ge 0, …” (ulename{ orall E} at a - 1) 3 “… that is, a^2 - 2a + 1 \ge 0.” (arith) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- A line justified “arith” records a fact of school arithmetic or algebra, used on the lines it cites; here the fact is that (u - 1)^2 and u^2 - 2u + 1 are the same number for every real u. It is not a new rule, and the facts of school algebra are used as facts. Written out in full, an arith line is a universally quantified arithmetic statement, here  orall u\,  igl( (u - 1)^2 \ge 0 	o u^2 - 2 \cdot u + 1 \ge 0  igr), taken as one more premise, instantiated by ulename{ orall E} at the term on the line (here a) and applied by ulename{{	o}E} to the cited line. That is exactly the pattern of (a) above. The book writes it as one line because spelling it out every time would bury the logic under algebra; its bound variables are letters that appear nowhere else in the derivation, and that keeps every term free for them. Section 5.4 will turn this three-line derivation into a proof of x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0 for every real x. That needs a rule this section does not have. A stall Try the sequent  orall x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \vdash  orall x\, P(x) . It is plainly correct: if every x has both properties, then every x has the first. Search for a derivation. The goal begins with  orall, and no rule so far is made for proving a  orall. Apart from ulename{ ot E} (@def-rules-contradiction) and ulename{RAA} (@def-rule-raa), which reach a line only by way of a contradiction, a line beginning with  orall can only be taken out of a line or box that already contains it. So the goal-directed step has nothing to offer, and we turn to the premise. ulename{ orall E} at c gives P(c) \wedge Q(c), and ulename{\wedge E} gives P(c). The same works at d, at f(c), at any term we name. But each line is an instance. No finite list of instances is the statement  orall x\, P(x), which speaks about every object at once, including all the objects that none of our terms happen to name. So with ulename{ orall E} alone, a universal statement can be used but not proved. Leaving aside a detour through a contradiction, a derivation can write  orall x\, \psi only by taking it out of a line or box that already contains it, as line 2 of (b) took  orall y\, R(c, y) out of the premise. Section 1.3 was in the same position with implications, and Section 1.4 filled the gap with a box. Section 5.4 does the same for  orall: it proves P of one name about which nothing is known, and that box finishes this derivation in four lines. Counter-readings. Each error above was shown wrong by a reading, a domain with a meaning for every symbol and a value for each free variable, in which the premises are true and the line is false. Call such a reading a counter-reading: it makes the whole counterexample set of the claim (Section 1.1), its premises and the negation of its line, true at once. A counter-reading shows that a step is unsafe. It is also how this book shows that a sequent has no derivation at all: a search that stalls proves nothing, since a cleverer derivation might exist. Sections 7.1 and 7.2 make readings exact and state that a counter-reading rules out every derivation. Until then, when this chapter says that something does not follow, it gives a counter-reading, and it never treats a stalled search as a proof. R and a, b, c as real numbers. Give a derivation of  orall x\,  orall y\, (x \le y 	o f(x) \le f(y)), \ a \le b, \ b \le c \ \vdash \ f(a) \le f(b) \wedge f(b) \le f(c) , and then write the argument as one sentence of prose. The goal is a conjunction, so its last line is ulename{\wedge I}, with subgoals f(a) \le f(b) and f(b) \le f(c). Each is the conclusion of an instance of the first premise: matching f(x) \le f(y) with f(a) \le f(b) gives x \coloneqq a, y \coloneqq b, and with f(b) \le f(c) gives x \coloneqq b, y \coloneqq c. The hypotheses of the two instances are the other two premises. The premise is instantiated twice, along two different paths: once at a and b, once at b and c. In prose: Since f is increasing and a \le b, we have f(a) \le f(b), and likewise b \le c gives f(b) \le f(c). The word “increasing” carries the first premise, and the two applications of it are the two pairs of ulename{ orall E} lines. [B3: Squares are not negative] Let a and b be real numbers. Give a derivation of  orall x\, (x^2 \ge 0) \vdash (a + b)^2 \ge 0 \wedge (a - b)^2 \ge 0 . Then extend it by one line justified “arith” to a derivation of a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab from the same premise, and say which earlier line the arith line uses. The goal is a conjunction of two instances of the premise, at the compound terms a + b and a - b. Both terms are free for x in x^2 \ge 0, which has no quantifier. Lines 1–4 are the first derivation. For the second goal only line 3 is needed: (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2, so (a - b)^2 \ge 0 says a^2 - 2ab + b^2 \ge 0, and adding 2ab to both sides gives a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab. That algebra is the arith line 5. (Lines 2 and 4 are then unused, which is allowed, and deleting them leaves a three-line derivation of a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab. Line 2 would give a^2 + b^2 \ge -2ab in the same way.) [B4: Read the terms off the goal] A search for  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \  orall x\, (Q(x) 	o R(x)), \  orall x\, P(x) \vdash R(c) \wedge Q(c) has reached the stage below. Name the move, then complete it. The move is instantiate at the term you need: the goal names c, so every ulename{ orall E} is at c. ulename{\wedge I} splits the goal into R(c) and Q(c), and each is the end of a chain of ulename{{	o}E}. [B5: Derive or break] For each claim, either derive it with the rules of Chapters 1–2 and ulename{ orall E}, or break it with a counter-reading: a domain, a meaning for each symbol, and a value for each constant, that make its counterexample set true. Then pair each of the breaks (e) and (g) with the derivable claim in the list that it imitates, and say what separates them. 1.  orall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)), \ 
eg P(c) \vdash Q(c). 2.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \ Q(c) \vdash P(c). 3.  orall x\, R(x, f(x)) \vdash R(c, f(c)) \wedge R(f(c), f(f(c))). 4.  orall x\, R(x, f(x)) \vdash R(f(c), c). 5.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o 
eg P(f(x))), \ P(c) \vdash 
eg P(f(f(c))). 6.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o 
eg P(f(x))), \ P(f(c)) \vdash 
eg P(c) \wedge 
eg P(f(f(c))). 7.  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) \vdash \exists y\, R(y, y). 8.  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) \vdash \exists y\, R(c, y). (a) Derive. Instantiate at c, then take the disjunction apart by cases. (b) Break. The domain \{0\}, c naming 0, P true of nothing, Q true of 0. The first premise holds (its hypothesis is false at 0), Q(c) holds, and P(c) fails. (The form affirms the consequent of an instance.) (c) Derive. Two instances of the one premise, at c and at f(c). (d) Break. The domain \{0, 1\}, c naming 0, f(0) = 1 and f(1) = 1, R true of the pairs (0, 1) and (1, 1) only. The premise holds: R(0, f(0)) is R(0, 1), and R(1, f(1)) is R(1, 1). The conclusion R(f(c), c) is R(1, 0), which is false. (e) Break. The domain \{0, 1\}, c naming 0, f exchanging 0 and 1, P true of 0 only. The first premise holds: at 0, P(0) holds and P(1) does not; at 1, the hypothesis P(1) is false. P(c) holds, and 
eg P(f(f(c))) is 
eg P(0), which is false. (f) Derive. The instance at f(c) gives the right conjunct at once; the instance at c refutes P(c) inside a ulename{
eg I} box. (g) Break. The domain \{0, 1\}, R true of (0, 1) and (1, 0) only (“differs from”). Every element has a partner, and no element is its own. (h) Derive, in one step: the only quantifier inside is on y, and c contains no y. (e) and (f) are look-alikes: the premise about f is used at the wrong term in (e), at the right one in (f). (g) is the capture look-alike of (h): instantiating at the bound letter y would write \exists y\, R(y, y). (b) is the converse look-alike of the square-root step of @exm-universal-elimination-derivations (a). Each break is a counter-reading of the kind in the figure of “Common errors”. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1 for each of the eight verdicts with its derivation or counter-reading. A counter-reading must give the domain, every symbol’s meaning and the value of c, and check each premise and the conclusion. - 2: the closing pairing, (e) with (f) and (g) with (h), with the reason. Fatal errors (0 for the claim): a “break” by a reading in which a premise is false; a ulename{ orall E} at a term that is not free for its variable. C. Going deeper [C1: A partner makes a loop] A relation R is symmetric if R(x, y) gives R(y, x), and transitive if R(x, y) and R(y, z) give R(x, z). Show that in a symmetric and transitive relation, every element that is related to something is related to itself, by giving a derivation of  egin{aligned} & orall x\,  orall y\, (R(x, y) 	o R(y, x)), \ & orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\, ((R(x, y) \wedge R(y, z)) 	o R(x, z)), \ R(a, b) \ \vdash \ R(a, a) . \end{aligned} Explain how each term of each ulename{ orall E} was chosen. [Hint 1] The goal R(a, a) can only come from the transitivity premise. Match its conclusion R(x, z) with the goal. [Hint 2] The match gives x \coloneqq a and z \coloneqq a, and leaves y open. Which y makes the hypothesis R(a, y) \wedge R(y, a) reachable from the premises? The search. The goal R(a, a) is atomic, so it must be the conclusion of an instance of a premise. Symmetry ends in R(y, x), and its instance at a, a is R(a, a) 	o R(a, a), whose hypothesis is the goal itself: a dead end. Transitivity ends in R(x, z). Matching gives x \coloneqq a and z \coloneqq a. The variable y does not occur in the conclusion, so the goal says nothing about it; the hypothesis R(a, y) \wedge R(y, a) must decide. The premise R(a, b) offers R(a, y) with y \coloneqq b. Then the second conjunct is R(b, a), which symmetry gives from R(a, b): the instance of the symmetry premise at x \coloneqq a, y \coloneqq b (read off its needed conclusion R(b, a), as in @exm-universal-elimination-derivations (c)). The terms. Lines 7 and 9 put a in for x and for z: both read off the goal. Line 8 puts b in for y: read off the premise R(a, b), the only available fact of the form R(a, \cdot). Lines 4 and 5 put in a and b: read off the needed line R(b, a). All terms are constants, so every one is free for its variable. The hypothesis “related to something” is needed. In a symmetric and transitive relation an element related to nothing need not be related to itself: on \{0, 1\}, the relation that holds only between 0 and 0 is symmetric and transitive, and R(1, 1) fails. Without a premise like R(a, b) the search has no term for y that makes the hypothesis of line 9 reachable. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: identifies transitivity as the source of the goal and instantiates it with a for x and z. - 2: chooses b for y, with the reason (the premise R(a, b)). - 2: obtains R(b, a) from symmetry at a, b, with ulename{{	o}E}. - 2: builds the conjunction in the right order and fires the transitivity instance. - 2: every ulename{ orall E} removes the outermost quantifier of a cited line and replaces every occurrence of its variable. Fatal errors (0 for the step): removing an inner quantifier before an outer one; instantiating transitivity at a term for y for which neither conjunct of the hypothesis is available. [C2: Instantiating at the variable itself] 1. Show that  orall x\, P(x) \vdash P(x), by a derivation whose one ulename{ orall E} line you check against every clause of @def-rule-universal-elimination. 2. The reverse step, from a line P(x) to  orall x\, P(x), is an instance of no rule so far. Show that it must not be allowed without restriction: give a reading over 
Z, with x naming one particular integer, in which P(x) is true and  orall x\, P(x) is false. (a) Clause 1: the main symbol of line 1 is  orall x, with scope P(x). Clause 2: the term is the variable x itself, and any term is allowed. Clause 3: P(x)[x/x] = P(x), so every free occurrence was replaced, by x. Clause 4: x is free for x in every formula (Section 5.2: a free occurrence of x never lies in the scope of a quantifier on x). Clause 5: line 1 is a premise and lies in no box, so it is available at line 2. So line 2 is legal. Its x is now free: line 2 says “P holds of whatever x names”, which is true whatever x names, since line 1 says that P holds of everything. (b) Read P(x) as “x is even” and let x name 2. Then P(x) is true, and  orall x\, P(x), “every integer is even”, is false, since 1 is odd. A rule allowing the step from P(x) to  orall x\, P(x) in general would lead from a true line to a false one. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 6: (a) the derivation, with each of the five numbered clauses checked (main symbol  orall x; any term; every free occurrence by the same term; free for x; availability), including that x is free for x. - 4: (b) a reading with P(x) true and  orall x\, P(x) false, with the value of x stated. Fatal error (0 for the step): in (b), a reading in which P(x) is false or x has no value.

title: 5.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content:
Proving “For Every”: Let x Be Arbitrary Section 5.3 gave the rule for using a universal statement, and ended at a stall: from  orall x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) it could derive P(c) for every term c we cared to name, but never  orall x\, P(x) itself. No list of instances is a statement about everything. This section gives the rule that proves a universal statement, ulename{ orall I}. It needs one new device, a box that carries a name instead of an assumption, and one new side condition, which turns the mathematician’s “let x be arbitrary” into something a reader can check line by line. One number we know nothing about Here is a fact of school algebra. For every real number x, x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0. We cannot check it number by number; there are too many numbers. The proof everyone writes takes one real number and argues about it: Let x \in 
R. Then x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^2, and a square is never negative. So x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0. Then, often without saying so: since x was arbitrary, this holds for every real x. Chapter 1 adopted a convention for sentences like “let x be a real number”: the letter names one fixed number, not further specified (Section 1.1). It promised that Chapter 5 would explain why an argument of that kind proves a statement about every x at once. Section 2.2 met the same step at the end of the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational, passing from an arbitrary rational r to every rational; Section 4.2 met it in induction, passing from “let n \in 
N” to “for every n”. Each time the step was taken on trust. Here is why it is correct, and when it is not. The argument about x used nothing about x except that it is a real number. It never said “suppose x > 0” or “take x = 3”. So it could be repeated word for word with 0, with -7, with \pi, with any real number in place of x, and it would prove the claim for that number. One argument about a number we know nothing about is a recipe for an argument about each number, and that is what “for every” asks for. Everything depends on “nothing”. If the argument had used a fact about x that not every number has, the recipe would break for some numbers. “Let x be a real number with x > 0. Then x > 0. Since x was arbitrary, every real number is positive” is the same shape, and its conclusion is false. The step “since x was arbitrary” is legitimate only when x was arbitrary: when no premise and no assumption still in force says anything about it. The rule of this section makes that condition exact. The flagged box To prove “for every x”, take a fresh name that nothing is known about, prove the statement for that name, and generalize. In a derivation the argument about the arbitrary x is drawn as a box, as Chapter 1 drew the argument under an assumption. The box opens with no assumption at all. Instead it carries the arbitrary name, written at its top left, and is called a flagged box; the name is its flag. [Rules for the Universal Quantifier] The rule on the left is ulename{ orall I} (universal introduction, or generalization). It cites a flagged box, with flag x_0, from its first line i to its last line j, and writes  orall x\, \varphi on line k. The flag x_0 is a variable. The box’s last line j is \varphi[x_0/x], and it is a line of the flagged box itself, not of a box inside it. The side condition is on the name: at line k, - x_0 appears in no premise, - x_0 appears in no assumption of a box still open at line k, and - x_0 does not appear in  orall x\, \varphi. The rule on the right is ulename{ orall E}, as in @def-rule-universal-elimination: t is any term free for x in \varphi. In words: to prove that \varphi holds for every x, open a box flagged with a new name x_0, prove \varphi[x_0/x], “\varphi holds of x_0”, as the box’s last line, close the box, and write  orall x\, \varphi. The side condition says that x_0 really was arbitrary. A first flagged box: how the rule looks in a mathematical proof Here is the opening proof as a derivation, with the general fact about squares as a premise and the algebra as one line justified “arith” (Section 5.3). The goal is universal, so the box opens first, with the goal’s instance at x_0 as its last line; then the premise is instantiated at the term that last line needs, x_0 - 1. The finished derivation: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Sentence ----------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- box x_0 “Let x \in 
R.” 2 “Then (x - 1)^2 \ge 0, since a square is never negative.” (ulename{ orall E} at x_0 - 1) 3 “That is, x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0.” (arith) 4 “Since x was arbitrary, x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0 for every real x.” (ulename{ orall I}) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Lines 2 and 3 are the derivation of Section 5.3 with the flag x_0 in place of the constant a. What changed is only the name: a was a constant that the language fixed, so nothing could be generalized over it; x_0 is a variable that no premise mentions, so line 4 may generalize. The written proof uses the same letter x for the flag and for the bound variable, and says “let x \in 
R” where the derivation opens the box. Readers of mathematics are expected to supply the box. Since the domain is 
R, “let x \in 
R” asks nothing of x. A proof that says “let \varepsilon > 0” does ask something: inside the box flagged \varepsilon_0, a ulename{{	o}I} box opens with the assumption \varepsilon_0 > 0. Reading the rule Here are the two boxes side by side: the box of ulename{{	o}I} from @def-rules-implication, and the flagged box. Both draw a boundary and both are cited as a range i–j. The ulename{{	o}I} box opens with what we suppose; the flagged box opens with the name we have fixed. In the schema the flagged box begins with a gap \vdots on line i, only so that the range has a first line; in a real derivation line i is whatever the box’s first line is. This rule has conditions that matter; read each one. Read the rule part by part: the flag, the three clauses of the side condition, and the last line. - The flag. Opening the box is the written “let x_0 be arbitrary”. The flag is always a variable, never a constant: a constant has a fixed meaning, while the whole point of x_0 is that it may stand for anything. The book writes flags with a subscript 0, x_0, y_0, \varepsilon_0, so that they stand out. - No premise, no open assumption (the first and second clauses). This is “we know nothing about x_0”. What is known at line k is the premises and the assumptions of the boxes still open there. If none of them mentions x_0, then nothing that was used about x_0 inside the box is special to x_0. - Not in the conclusion (the third clause). The name must not leak out. Inside the box it stood for an arbitrary object, and  orall x\, \varphi is meant to speak about all objects through the bound x. A conclusion that still mentions x_0 ties what it says to the one object x_0 names, while claiming it of everything. - The last line. \varphi[x_0/x] is what was proved about x_0, and it must be a line of the flagged box itself, just as the last line of a ulename{{	o}I} box must be (Section 1.4). A line inside a further box would still depend on that box’s assumption. “Appear” is the word of Section 5.2: written anywhere in the formula, including just after a quantifier symbol. So a box flagged x can never be closed by ulename{ orall I} with  orall x\, \varphi, since x appears in  orall x\, \varphi. That is one more reason the book never uses the quantified letter itself as the flag. In practice: choose as flag a letter written nowhere in the derivation so far, and as the quantified letter x one that does not appear in the box’s last line (if it does, rename that bound letter first, Section 5.2). When the box closes, put x in place of every occurrence of the flag in its last line. Then the last line is \varphi[x_0/x] for the formula \varphi so obtained, and all three clauses hold at once: no premise or open assumption can contain a letter written nowhere, and the conclusion no longer contains the flag. The clauses are what a checker tests, and they allow a little more than this habit does (the fold below). The condition asks about three places only: the premises, the open assumptions, and the conclusion. Lines outside the box may mention x_0, before it or after it. An earlier line  orall y\, R(x_0, y), obtained by ulename{ orall E} from a premise, is harmless; Exercise C1 builds a derivation with such a line. And once a flagged box has closed, its name may flag a later box. A name that satisfies the side condition at the line that closes its box is called fresh there. It need not be new to the whole derivation. A derivation has used the letters x_0, y_0 and u_0 so far, and u_0 appears in an open assumption. Which flag can a new ulename{ orall I} box take without checking anything? Any letter written nowhere yet, for example z_0. (x_0 or y_0 may also be allowed, but only after checking the three clauses; u_0 is not, while its assumption is open.) Why each clause Each clause stops a derivation of a false conclusion from true premises. Here is one failure for each. A name in a premise. If ulename{ orall I} could generalize over a name in a premise, then P(x_0) \vdash  orall x\, P(x): Over 
Z, read P(x) as “x is even” and let x_0 name 2. The premise is true and line 3, “every integer is even”, is false. Line 3 breaks the first clause: x_0 appears in the premise on line 1. The premise does say something about x_0, so x_0 is not arbitrary. A name in an open assumption. Suppose x_0 > 0, and inside that supposition generalize over x_0 (left): On the left, line 3 breaks the second clause, since x_0 appears in the assumption of line 1, whose box is still open at line 3. Read over 
Z with x_0 naming 1: line 4 says “if 1 > 0, then every integer is positive”, which is false at 0, and it rests on no premise at all. This is the “let x be a real number with x > 0 … since x was arbitrary” of the opening, made into lines. One more legal flagged box around everything turns line 4 into a false sentence; the fold shows it. On the right the boxes are nested the other way: the flagged box opens first, the supposition inside it, and ulename{ orall I} generalizes an implication that carries its hypothesis with it. With one more flagged box, the error of the minimal derivation becomes a false sentence: Line 3 breaks the second clause: x_0 appears in the assumption on line 1, whose box is still open at line 3. Every other line is legal, including line 5, where the box of line 1 has closed. The inner box on line 2 is flagged x_0 while the outer box flagged x_0 is still open; the definition allows this, since its side condition asks only about premises, open assumptions and the conclusion. And line 5 says “every positive number makes every number positive”, which over 
Z is false: at y = 1 the hypothesis 1 > 0 holds and  orall x\, (x > 0) fails at x = 0. This is the “let x be a real number with x > 0 … since x was arbitrary” of the opening, made into lines. A name in the conclusion. From the premise  orall x\, (x \le x), true over 
N, open a box flagged y_0: Line 2 is (x \le y_0)[y_0/x], so line 3 has the shape of ulename{ orall I} with \varphi = (x \le y_0). But y_0 appears in the conclusion, which breaks the third clause. Line 3 says “every natural number is at most y_0”, and that is false whatever y_0 names: y_0 + 1 is a counterexample. (Exercise C1 of Section 5.5 turns this into a sentence, “there is a largest natural number”.) The requirement on the last line is the one Chapter 1 already imposed on every box rule, for the same reason. Derivations with flagged boxes The search method of Section 3.1 gets a new goal-directed step: when the goal is  orall x\, \varphi, open a flagged box with a fresh name x_0, and make \varphi[x_0/x] the box’s last line, the new goal. The examples below use it, each with an Idea. [Flagged boxes at work] Give a derivation of each sequent. 1.  orall x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \vdash  orall x\, R(x, x). 2.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \  orall x\, P(x) \vdash  orall x\, Q(x). 3.  orall x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \vdash  orall y\,  orall x\, R(x, y). (a) Idea. The goal begins with  orall x, so the goal-directed step opens a box flagged x_0, and the new goal is R(x, x)[x_0/x] = R(x_0, x_0). That goal names the term for ulename{ orall E} (Section 5.3’s step): instantiate the premise at x_0, twice. The side condition at line 4: x_0 does not appear in the premise, no box is open at line 4, and x_0 does not appear in  orall x\, R(x, x). Lines 2 and 3 instantiate at the variable x_0, which is free for x and for y, since the formulas contain no quantifier on x_0. Compare Section 5.3, (b), which reached only R(c, c): there the term was a constant, a name fixed by the language, and nothing can be generalized over a constant; here it is a flag, a variable that no premise mentions. (b) Idea. The goal is universal: a box flagged x_0, whose last line must be Q(x_0). Both premises are universal; instantiate each at the term the box’s goal names, x_0, and ulename{{	o}E} finishes. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal --------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)),  orall x\, P(x)  orall x\, Q(x) the same, and the fresh name x_0 (ulename{ orall I} opens a box) Q(x_0) + P(x_0) 	o Q(x_0), P(x_0) (ulename{ orall E} at x_0, twice) Q(x_0) + Q(x_0) (ulename{{	o}E}) Q(x_0) ✓ --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- At line 6, x_0 appears in neither premise nor in  orall x\, Q(x), and no box is open. (c) Idea. Read the goal’s quantifiers from the outside:  orall y first, so open a box flagged y_0; the new goal  orall x\, R(x, y_0) is again universal, so open a box flagged x_0 inside it; the innermost goal is R(x_0, y_0). Two boxes, opened in the goal’s order. Now the premise’s quantifiers are removed in its order: ulename{ orall E} at x_0, then at y_0. The box flagged y_0 immediately contains the box flagged x_0, so it has no line of its own before the inner box; following the convention for a flagged box that immediately contains another box (the fine print below), line 5 cites it as \lines{2}{4}, from the first line of the inner box. Its last line is line 4, a line of the outer box itself. At line 4, x_0 is in no premise, the only open box (flagged y_0) has no assumption, and x_0 does not appear in  orall x\, R(x, y_0). At line 5 the same holds for y_0. Nothing in (c) used that the formula under the quantifiers is R(x, y). For any formula \psi and different variables x and y, with flags x_0 and y_0 that are different from each other and from x and y and that do not appear in \psi, the same five lines derive  orall x\,  orall y\, \psi \vdash  orall y\,  orall x\, \psi: line 3 becomes (\psi[x_0/x])[y_0/y], which equals (\psi[y_0/y])[x_0/x], since the two substitutions put two different fresh names in for two different variables and so do not interfere. Exchanging the letters x and y gives the other direction. So two adjacent universal quantifiers may always be swapped:  orall x\,  orall y\, \psi \dashv\vdash  orall y\,  orall x\, \psi. Section 5.1 read this off the game, where the challenger makes both moves; here it is derived. Suppose premise 2 of (b) were P(x_0) in place of  orall x\, P(x). The box still reaches Q(x_0), by ulename{ orall E} 1 and ulename{{	o}E}. May line 6 be written? No: x_0 appears in a premise, so the first clause fails. A counter-reading shows the step is unsafe: over 
Z, with P and Q both read as “even” and x_0 naming 2, both premises are true and  orall x\, Q(x) is false. Could both boxes of (c) be flagged x_0, the outer one standing for y? No. The inner box would end in R(x_0, x_0), and the ulename{ orall I} line that closes it must be  orall x\, R(x, x_0), the instance at x_0 of the outer goal; that line contains the inner flag x_0, so the third clause fails. Here the nested flagged boxes need two names. Section 5.2 took renaming of a bound variable as a convention and promised to derive it at the front of a formula. For a formula \varphi and variables y, z with z not appearing in \varphi,  orall y\, \varphi \dashv\vdash  orall z\, \varphi[z/y]: Take z_0 to be a variable that does not appear in \varphi and is different from y and z. Since z does not appear in \varphi, the formula \varphi[z/y] is \varphi with each free y changed to z, and changing those z’s on to z_0 gives the same result as changing each free y to z_0 at once: (\varphi[z/y])[z_0/z] = \varphi[z_0/y]. So in the left derivation, line 2 is a legal ulename{ orall E} (z_0 does not appear in \varphi, so it is free for y), and it is the instance (\varphi[z/y])[z_0/z] that the ulename{ orall I} on line 3 needs.
