Inside the box, the partner f(x_0) plays the part that b played in Exercise C1 of Section 5.3. At line 13, x_0 is in no premise, no box is open, and x_0 is not in the conclusion. (f) Break. The domain \{0, 1\}, R true of (0, 0), (1, 1) and (0, 1). R is reflexive; R(0, 1) holds and R(1, 0) does not. (g) and (b) are converses, and only (a) derives. (d) is the trap “symmetric and transitive give reflexive”, which breaks at an element related to nothing, and (e) repairs it by giving every element a partner f(x) (Exercise C1 of Section 5.3 shows the same for one element that has a partner). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2 each for (a), (c), (e): flags opened in the order read off the goal, every ulename{ orall E} at the flag (or at f(x_0)) the box needs, the side condition checked once at the last ulename{ orall I}. - 1 each for (b), (d), (f): a counter-reading with the domain and every pair of R listed, each premise and the conclusion checked. - 1: the closing sentence. Fatal errors (0 for the claim): a ulename{ orall I} over a flag that an open assumption mentions; a counter-reading that is not symmetric (in (d)) or not reflexive (in (f)). C. Going deeper [C1: How fresh is fresh?] 1. Give a derivation of  orall x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \vdash R(x_0, x_0) \wedge  orall x\, R(x, x) in which the line R(x_0, x_0) is written before a flagged box that uses the same name x_0. Check every clause of the side condition at the ulename{ orall I} line. 2. A stronger condition is sometimes proposed: “x_0 occurs nowhere in the derivation outside its box”. Does your derivation meet it? Explain why the conclusion of your derivation is nonetheless correct, so that the stronger condition forbids more than it needs to. 3. Could the last line of the flagged box in (a) be obtained by ulename{R}, repeating the earlier line R(x_0, x_0)? Is the result a derivation? [Hint 1] The goal is a conjunction. Derive the left conjunct first, by two ulename{ orall E} lines outside any box. [Hint 2] For the right conjunct, open a box flagged x_0 and instantiate the premise at x_0 again inside it. At the ulename{ orall I} line, list the premises, the open assumptions and the conclusion, and look for x_0 in each. (a) The side condition at line 6. Premises: the only premise is line 1,  orall x\,  orall y\, R(x, y), and x_0 does not appear in it. Open assumptions: no box is open at line 6, so there are none. Conclusion:  orall x\, R(x, x) does not contain x_0. The last line of the box, line 5, is R(x, x)[x_0/x] and is a line of the box itself. So line 6 is legal, and the derivation has 7 lines. Lines 2, 3 and 7 mention x_0 outside the box, and the side condition does not ask about them. (b) No: lines 2, 3 and 7 mention x_0 outside its box. Yet the conclusion is correct. The reason the side condition looks only at premises and open assumptions is that these are the only lines taken without proof, so they are the only lines that can single out what x_0 names; every other available line is derived from them. Lines 2 and 3 were derived from a premise that does not mention x_0; they hold whatever x_0 names. So the argument in the box really is about an arbitrary object, and  orall x\, R(x, x) follows. The stronger condition would reject this derivation, although renaming the box’s flag to a new letter z_0 (lines 4–5 becoming  orall y\, R(z_0, y) and R(z_0, z_0)) gives a derivation that meets it and has the same last line. A condition that rejects a correct derivation for the spelling of a name forbids more than safety needs. (c) Yes. ulename{R} may copy into the box any line available there, and line 3 lies in no box, so it is available at every later line. With line 5 justified “ulename{R} 3” (and line 4 deleted), the box is a single line R(x_0, x_0), and the side condition at the ulename{ orall I} line is checked exactly as in (a): nothing in it looks at where the box’s last line came from. The derivation is legal, and it is correct for the reason in (b): line 3 was derived from a premise that says nothing about x_0. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the left conjunct by two ulename{ orall E} lines at x_0, outside any box. - 2: a flagged box with ulename{ orall E} at the flag and ulename{ orall I} citing it. - 2: the side condition checked clause by clause: premise, open assumptions, conclusion. - 2: (b) explains that lines outside the box that do not rest on premises or assumptions about x_0 cannot make x_0 special. Alternatively, 2 for showing that renaming the box’s flag to a new letter gives a derivation that meets the stronger condition and has the same last line. - 2: (c) correct answer with the availability check for the repeated line. Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming that line 3 makes line 6 illegal; checking the side condition against lines that are not premises, open assumptions or the conclusion. [C2: Find the error] A student offers this proof. Claim. For every real number x, x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0. Proof. (1) Let x be a real number. (2) At x = 0: 0 - 0 + 1 = 1 \ge 0. (3) At x = 1: 1 - 2 + 1 = 0 \ge 0. (4) At x = 2: 4 - 4 + 1 = 1 \ge 0. (5) So x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0, and since x was arbitrary, the claim holds for every real x. 1. Is the claim true? 2. Does the argument prove it? Name the step that fails and the rule it misuses. 3. Show that the step can lead to a false conclusion: give a polynomial g for which the same checks at x = 0, 1, 2 succeed and g(x) \ge 0 fails for some real x. 4. Point to a correct proof. [Hint 1] Write lines (2)–(4) as formulas. Which terms do they mention? [Hint 2] Write the student’s proof as a derivation: open a box flagged x_0 for line (1), and write lines (2)–(4) as lines inside it. What would line (5) have to cite? (a) Yes. For every real x, x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^2 \ge 0, since a square is never negative. (b) No. Lines (2)–(4) are true, and line (1) opens a flagged box, “let x be arbitrary”. The error is in line (5). With \varphi the formula x^2 - 2 \cdot x + 1 \ge 0, lines (2)–(4) establish \varphi[0/x], \varphi[1/x] and \varphi[2/x]: statements about the constants 0, 1, 2. None of them is \varphi[x_0/x] for the flag. Inside the box, nothing about the arbitrary x was ever proved. The first sentence of (5), “so x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0”, has the right form: it is \varphi[x_0/x], with the student’s x as the flag. But nothing the student wrote yields it: lines (2)–(4) are the only lines it rests on, and no rule takes \varphi[0/x], \varphi[1/x] and \varphi[2/x] to \varphi[x_0/x]. So the closing “since x was arbitrary” applies ulename{ orall I} to a box whose last line was never derived: lines (2)–(4) are all instances at constants, not the instance at the flag. Line (1) was idle: the argument never used the x it introduced. (c) Take g(x) = x(x - 1)(x - 2). The same checks succeed: g(0) = 0 \ge 0, g(1) = 0 \ge 0, g(2) = 0 \ge 0. But g(-1) = (-1)(-2)(-3) = -6 < 0, so “g(x) \ge 0 for every real x” is false. So the pattern of (5), concluding “for every x” from checks at a few constants, can lead from true checks to a false conclusion. It is not an instance of ulename{ orall I}, as (b) showed. (A legal step never leads from true premises to a false conclusion; Section 7.2 states this.) The claim in (a) is true for a different reason, one that the argument never gave. (d) The derivation under “A first flagged box” in this section: inside the box flagged x_0, ulename{ orall E} applies “squares are not negative” at x_0 - 1, an arith line rewrites it as x_0^2 - 2x_0 + 1 \ge 0, and that line is \varphi[x_0/x], so ulename{ orall I} applies. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) the claim is true, with a reason (it is a square). - 3: (b) names step (5) and ulename{ orall I}; says that lines (2)–(4) are instances at constants, not the instance at the flag. - 3: (c) a polynomial that passes the three checks and fails somewhere, with both computations shown. - 2: (d) a correct proof, generalizing over a statement proved about the arbitrary x. Fatal errors (0 for the step): answering (b) with “the claim is false”; a “counterexample” in (c) that fails one of the three checks or is non-negative everywhere.

title: 5.5 Proving "There Exists": Exhibit a Witness
content:
Proving “There Exists”: Exhibit a Witness Sections 5.3 and 5.4 gave the two rules for “for every”: ulename{ orall E} uses a universal statement, and ulename{ orall I} proves one. This section starts on the other quantifier. It gives the rule that proves an existential statement, ulename{\exists I}, and the habit that goes with it: when the goal is “there exists”, do not guess the object, but wait until a line of the derivation shows it. The sequent  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x), which no rule so far can finish, is finished here in three lines. Showing that something exists How does a mathematician prove that there is a natural number N with 1/(N + 1) < 1/100? By naming one. “Take N = 100: then 1/(N + 1) = 1/101, and 1/101 < 1/100.” Nobody asks for more, and nobody objects that N = 1000 would also have done. The proof exhibits a witness, checks that it has the property, and stops. Look at what the proof does with the witness at the end. The statement proved, “there is an N with 1/(N + 1) < 1/100”, does not say which N; the 100 still in it belongs to the bound 1/100, not to N. The number was needed to establish the claim and is then forgotten: a reader of the conclusion learns that some N works, not which one. Chapter 1 used the same pattern from its first page. It recalled that an integer n is even when n = 2k for some integer k, and said that the word “some” has rules of its own, to come in Chapter 5. Here is the first of them. To show that 6 is even, take k = 3: then 6 = 2 \cdot 3. The statement “6 is even” is \exists k\, (6 = 2 \cdot k), and the proof passes from the instance 6 = 2 \cdot 3 to it. The second rule for “some”, how to use “n = 2k for some k”, is the subject of Section 5.6. There is a helpful way to see the step, which Section 5.1’s reading of \exists suggests. Over a domain with three elements named a, b, c, the sentence \exists x\, P(x) says what the disjunction P(a) \vee P(b) \vee P(c) says (grouped to the right, as in Section 4.5): at least one of the three has P. An existential is a long “or”, with one disjunct for each object of the domain. Proving a disjunction from one of its sides is ulename{\vee I} (@def-rule-disjunction-introduction), and proving an existential from one instance is the rule of this section. The analogy is only a guide (a domain such as 
N has infinitely many elements, and a formula cannot be infinitely long), but it predicts the rule’s behavior exactly: it throws information away, and it must never be run backwards. The rule of existential introduction To prove that something has a property, show that one particular thing has it. [Existential Introduction] The rule given by this schema is called ulename{\exists I} (existential introduction). Here \varphi is any formula, x any variable, and t any term, subject to one side condition: t is free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for). Line i must be available at line k (@def-derivation). - Schema: the block above: one cited line, no box, no fresh name. - Reading: from a line that says something about the term t, write “something has that property”: mark some occurrences of t with a variable x to get \varphi, and write \exists x\, \varphi. - Example: from 6 = 2 \cdot 3, marking the 3 gives \exists k\, (6 = 2 \cdot k). Which occurrences? Any you like, as the table below shows; the term t is the witness, and it may be a constant, a compound term or a variable: a variable used elsewhere in the derivation, a flag such as x_0, or even the variable x itself. Check two things. First, \varphi[t/x] must be exactly the cited line: choose a variable x that does not appear in the line and mark some occurrences of t with it, and this marking recipe guarantees it; with an x that does appear, check directly (from R(x, c), marking c gives R(x, x), and R(x, x)[c/x] is R(c, c), not the line). Second, t must be free for x in \varphi, the condition of @def-free-for that ulename{ orall E} also carries. With a bound, \exists x \in A\; \varphi, the witness needs the line t \in A too; “A bounded witness” below shows the two steps. One line, several readings. Let line i be R(c, c), with R a two-place predicate symbol and c a constant. The witness is c, and c occurs twice. Each occurrence may be marked with x or left alone, and each choice is a different \varphi: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ \varphi \varphi[c/x] (the cited line) the new line \exists x\, \varphi ----------------------- ------------------------------- ---------------------------------- R(x, c) R(c, c) \exists x\, R(x, c) R(c, x) R(c, c) \exists x\, R(c, x) R(x, x) R(c, c) \exists x\, R(x, x) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ All three are legal steps. Read over 
N with R(x, y) as “x \le y” and c as 5: the cited line says 5 \le 5, and the three useful conclusions say that something is at most 5, that 5 is at most something, and that something is at most itself. Each is a true and weaker statement. A fourth row is legal too: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ \varphi \varphi[c/x] (the cited line) the new line \exists x\, \varphi ----------------------- ------------------------------- ---------------------------------- R(c, c) R(c, c) \exists x\, R(c, c) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ The last row is the degenerate choice: \varphi has no free x, so \varphi[c/x] is \varphi (Section 5.2) and the new line \exists x\, R(c, c) quantifies over nothing. It is legal, and it says nothing that line i did not. Why this rule. Under the reading of Section 5.1, \exists x\, \varphi is true when at least one element of the domain, put in for x, makes \varphi true. If \varphi[t/x] is true, then the object that t names is such an element, so \exists x\, \varphi is true. The side condition is what makes “\varphi[t/x] says about t what \varphi says about x” correct: that was the content of “free for” in Section 5.2. ulename{\exists I} forgets the witness, and keeps the truth. Line 1 is x_0 + 1 > x_0. Give an ulename{\exists I} line with the witness x_0, and one with the witness x_0 + 1. Marking both occurrences of x_0 with y gives \varphi = (y + 1 > y) and the line \exists y\, (y + 1 > y); marking the term x_0 + 1 gives \varphi = (y > x_0) and the line \exists y\, (y > x_0). In both, y appears nowhere in line 1, and the formula has no quantifier, so the witness is free for y. A nonexample: capture. Let line 1 be  orall y\, R(y, y). With \varphi =  orall y\, R(x, y) and t = y, the definition of substitution gives \varphi[y/x] =  orall y\, R(y, y), which is line 1. So it is tempting to write \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) by ulename{\exists I}. Line 2 breaks the side condition: the free occurrence of x in \varphi lies in the scope of  orall y, and y is the variable of the term t, so y is not free for x in \varphi. The step would be wrong. Read over 
Z with R(x, y) as “x \le y”: line 1 says that every integer is at most itself, which is true, and line 2 says that some integer is at most every integer, that is, that there is a least integer, which is false. The y put in for x was meant to name one object, and it was captured by  orall y and made to range over all of them. The witness must be written on a line. “There is an N with 1/(N + 1) < 1/100: take N large enough” is not an application of ulename{\exists I}, because “large enough” is not a term, and the rule asks for an instance \varphi[t/x] on an available line. In a written proof, “large enough” is a promise to name the witness, and the promise is kept by a term such as N = 100, followed by the check that it works (1/101 < 1/100). Until then nothing has been proved. Let line 1 be 2 + 2 = 4. Which of \exists x\, (x + x = 4), \qquad \exists x\, (x + 2 = 4), \qquad \exists x\, (2 + 2 = x) may line 2 be, justified by one application of ulename{\exists I} to line 1? For each that may, name \varphi and the witness t. All three. For \exists x\, (x + x = 4), take \varphi = (x + x = 4) and t = 2: both 2’s of line 1 are marked. For \exists x\, (x + 2 = 4), take \varphi = (x + 2 = 4) and t = 2: only the first 2 is marked, and the second is written out in \varphi. For \exists x\, (2 + 2 = x), take \varphi = (2 + 2 = x) and t = 4: the witness is a different term. In each case \varphi[t/x] is exactly line 1, and \varphi has no quantifier, so t is free for x. From “for every” to “there exists” The sequent  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x) looks like the easiest in the chapter, and it has a small puzzle in it. To use ulename{\exists I}, the goal needs an instance P(t) on a line. The premise gives an instance for every term, by ulename{ orall E}. But the sequent mentions no constant, so which term? [Every Implies Some]  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x). The following is a derivation. Line 2 is ulename{ orall E} at the term x: with \varphi = P(x), the instance \varphi[x/x] is P(x), and the variable x is free for x in every formula (Section 5.2). Line 3 is ulename{\exists I} with the same \varphi and the witness x. This proves the proposition. The puzzle is answered by the paragraph “Which occurrences?” after @def-rule-existential-introduction: the witness may be a variable, the variable x itself included, so no constant is needed. The line P(x) has x free; it says that P holds of whatever x names. Nothing in the derivation says what that is, and nothing needs to. The same three lines prove  orall x\, \varphi \vdash \exists x\, \varphi for every formula \varphi, since \varphi[x/x] = \varphi (Section 5.2). The rules accept this derivation in any case; it leads from a true premise to a true conclusion only because every domain has at least one element, the convention of Section 5.1. Over an empty domain,  orall x\, P(x) would be true with nothing to check and \exists x\, P(x) false with no witness; the convention enters at line 2, where P(x) treats x as naming an object, and there must be one to name. This does not clash with the empty set of Section 5.1, where  orall x \in \emptyset\; \varphi is true and \exists x \in \emptyset\; \varphi is false. A bounded quantifier is an abbreviation (@def-bounded-quantifier):  orall x \in \emptyset\; \varphi is  orall x\, (x \in \emptyset 	o \varphi), and \exists x \in \emptyset\; \varphi is \exists x\, (x \in \emptyset \wedge \varphi). The domain is still non-empty; it is the set \emptyset that has no elements. Running the three lines on the bounded premise gives ulename{ orall E} at x, the line x \in \emptyset 	o \varphi, and then ulename{\exists I} gives only \exists x\, (x \in \emptyset 	o \varphi), an existential with 	o inside. No line x \in \emptyset is available to fire the implication, so the bounded “every implies some” is not derived, and it should not be. An existential goal: postpone the witness The search method of Section 3.1 asks two questions at each gap: what is the goal, and what are the resources? Sections 5.3 and 5.4 added a step for each side of  orall. Now \exists can be a goal. If the goal is \exists x\, \varphi, its last line can be ulename{\exists I}, and then the new goal is \varphi[t/x] for a term t of our choosing. That is the same situation as a goal \varphi \vee \psi, where ulename{\vee I} left us to choose a side, and the danger is the same. A wrong t can leave a goal that does not follow from the resources, although the existential does. Section 3.1 met the danger for \vee and answered it by postponing; the answer here is the same. Postpone the witness: choose the term t of a goal \exists x\, \varphi only when an available line shows an instance \varphi[t/x]. Premises:  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x + 1)) and P(2). The goal is \exists y\, Q(y). Which witness will the search find, and after which steps? The term 2 + 1: ulename{ orall E} at 2 gives P(2) 	o Q(2 + 1), ulename{{	o}E} gives Q(2 + 1), and only then does ulename{\exists I} have an instance to cite. (Writing the witness as 3 instead needs the line 2 + 1 = 3 and the equality rule of Section 5.7.) Until then, work on the premises and on the other goals, and watch what terms appear. Often the witness is a term that only appears late, built by ulename{ orall E} or ulename{{	o}E} from the premises. Here are four derivations, in order of difficulty, each with an Idea that says why each rule was chosen. [Derivations with existential introduction] Show that: 1. P(c) \wedge Q(c) \vdash \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge Q(x)  igr); 2. R(c, c) \vdash \exists x\, R(x, c) \wedge \exists x\, R(x, x); and decide whether one ulename{\exists I} step leads from \exists x\, R(x, x) to \exists x\, R(x, c); 3.  orall x\, R(x, x) \vdash  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y); 4.  orall x\,  igl( P(x) 	o Q(f(x))  igr), \ P(c) \vdash \exists y\, Q(y). (a) Idea. The goal is an existential, and the premise already is an instance of a suitable \varphi: mark both occurrences of c. One goal-directed step finishes. Here \varphi = P(x) \wedge Q(x) and t = c. Marking only the first c, with \varphi = P(x) \wedge Q(c), would give the legal but weaker line \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(c)), which is not the goal. (b) Idea. The goal is a conjunction, so it splits into two goals (Section 1.2), and each is an existential with the line R(c, c) as an instance, read in two different ways (the first and third rows of the table above). The goal at the bottom (left); then the two subgoals that ulename{\wedge I} asks for (right). Line 2 uses \varphi = R(x, c) and line 3 uses \varphi = R(x, x), both with the witness c. Now the second question. From the line \exists x\, R(x, x), the step to \exists x\, R(x, c) is not an ulename{\exists I} step. The new line is \exists x\, \varphi with \varphi = R(x, c), so the cited line would have to be R(t, c) for some term t. The line \exists x\, R(x, x) is not of that form: its main symbol is \exists x, not R. The rule passes from an instance to an existential, never from one existential to another. Nor is the step safe by any other route: read over 
Z with R(x, y) as “x \cdot y = 1” and c as 0, the line \exists x\, R(x, x) is true (take x = 1), and \exists x\, R(x, c), “some integer times 0 is 1”, is false. (c) Idea. The goal is a  orall, so the step of Section 5.4 opens a flagged box with a fresh name x_0, and the new goal is \exists y\, R(x_0, y). That is an existential: postpone it and look at the premise. The premise is a  orall; instantiate it at the term the goal mentions, x_0. The result, R(x_0, x_0), shows the witness: it is x_0 itself, a variable used as a term, as x was in @prp-forall-implies-exists. The box with its postponed goal (left); then the instance that shows the witness (right). Line 3 uses \varphi = R(x_0, y), the variable y, and the witness x_0; it marks the second occurrence of x_0 and keeps the first. Line 4 is ulename{ orall I} with the flag x_0 (@def-rules-universal): x_0 appears in no premise, there is no open assumption, and x_0 does not appear in line 4. The ulename{\exists I} inside the box needed no box of its own, although its witness is a fresh name. Read over 
N with R(x, y) as “x \le y”: every number is at most itself, so every number is at most something. (d) Idea. The goal \exists y\, Q(y) is an existential, and no line yet has the form Q(t). Postpone, and work forwards. The premise  orall x\, (\dots) is a  orall; the only term in sight is c, so instantiate at c (Section 5.3), and ulename{{	o}E} with the premise P(c) fires. The result Q(f(c)) shows the witness: the compound term f(c). In the Givens/Goal table: ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ------------------------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------------  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(f(x))), P(c) \exists y\, Q(y): postponed, no instance yet + P(c) 	o Q(f(c)) (ulename{ orall E} at c) \exists y\, Q(y) + Q(f(c)) (ulename{{	o}E}) \exists y\, Q(y) ✓ by ulename{\exists I}, witness f(c) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The postponed goal (left); then the two forward steps, after which the witness is visible (right). Line 5 uses \varphi = Q(y) and t = f(c). Now see what choosing the witness first would have done. The term in sight at the start is c, and “take y = c” leaves the goal Q(c). Nothing gives it: the premise speaks of Q only at terms of the form f(\dots), and Q(c) need not hold at all. Read over 
Z with P as “odd”, Q as “even”, f(x) as x + 1, and c as 3: the premises say that the successor of every odd integer is even and that 3 is odd, the conclusion says that some integer is even, and the witness the derivation finds is f(3) = 4, while Q(c) says that 3 is even. The search stalls exactly because it chose the witness before the derivation had produced it. The four Ideas share a pattern. In (a) and (b) the witness stood on a premise line from the start; in (c) and (d) it appeared only after other rules had run, and in (d) it was a term that no line mentioned at the start. Postponing costs nothing in (a) to (c), where the right witness was already a term in sight when the existential goal appeared (in (c) the goal names x_0), and it is necessary in (d), where the only term in sight at the start, c, is the wrong witness. How this rule looks in a mathematical proof In a written proof, ulename{\exists I} is the word “take”, followed by a check. “6 is even: take k = 3; then 6 = 2 \cdot 3.” Over 
Z, with one line of school arithmetic justified “arith” as in Section 5.3: Line 2 marks the 3 with k, and keeps the 6 and the 2: \varphi = (6 = 2 \cdot k). In the same way “7 is odd: take k = 3, since 7 = 2 \cdot 3 + 1” is an ulename{\exists I} with \varphi = (7 = 2 \cdot k + 1). A bounded witness. Analysis states its existentials with bounds. “There is an N \in 
N with 1/(N + 1) < 1/100” abbreviates \exists N\,  igl( N \in 
N \wedge 1/(N + 1) < 1/100  igr) (@def-bounded-quantifier), so the witness must satisfy both conjuncts. Taking N = 100 is two steps: ulename{\wedge I} puts the bound and the inequality together, and ulename{\exists I} forgets the witness. Line 4 marks two of the three occurrences of 100 in line 3 and keeps the one on the right. The witness 100 is the least that works, since N = 99 gives 1/100, which is not less than 1/100; but the proof does not need the least witness, only one. A witness built from what is available. Often the witness is a term made from other names. To show that for every integer n there is an odd integer greater than 2n, a proof says “let n be an integer; 2n + 1 will do, since it is odd and greater than 2n”. The words “let n be an integer” open the flagged box of Section 5.4, and “2n + 1 will do” is ulename{\exists I} with the compound witness 2n + 1, as in (d) above. In general, the witness may be any term the reader can check. ulename{\exists I} runs one way only. From P(c) it gives \exists x\, P(x); from \exists x\, P(x) it gives nothing, and in particular not P(c). “Some integer is even” is true and “3 is even” is false: the existential does not say which object has the property, so it cannot be read back as a statement about a named one. Using an existential takes a rule of its own, with a box, and that is Section 5.6. The rule card Before the card, the rule at work on lines larger than R(c, c). The schema sees the cited line as \varphi[t/x] however much is inside t and \varphi. [Instances of ulename{\exists I}] ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Cited line \varphi Witness t New line --------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------- ----------------- ----------------------------------------------------- P(f(f(c))) \wedge Q(f(c)) P(f(x)) \wedge Q(x) f(c) \exists x\, (P(f(x)) \wedge Q(x)) \abs{a - b} < \varepsilon/2 \abs{a - b} < \delta \varepsilon/2 \exists \delta\, (\abs{a - b} < \delta) (n + 1) \cdot (n + 1) = n \cdot n + 2 \cdot n + 1 m \cdot m = n \cdot n + 2 \cdot n + 1 n + 1 \exists m\, (m \cdot m = n \cdot n + 2 \cdot n + 1) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In each row \varphi[t/x] is exactly the cited line, and the marked places are whole occurrences of t (in the third, both factors on the left; the n’s on the right are not occurrences of n + 1, and they stay). Not an instance. From P(c) \wedge Q(d), the line \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) is not written by ulename{\exists I}: \varphi[t/x] puts one term in every marked place, and no single t turns P(x) \wedge Q(x) into P(c) \wedge Q(d). Line 1 is Q(g(c), c). Write the ulename{\exists I} line with the witness c that marks only the c inside g(c), and name its \varphi. \exists x\, Q(g(x), c), with \varphi = Q(g(x), c); \varphi[c/x] is line 1. Chapters 1 and 2’s thirteen rules are on the card at the end of Section 3.1; here are this chapter’s so far. Nothing later depends on the last column, and Section 5.7 collects the whole table. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule Shape Side condition You write Lean ---------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------ ----------------------------- ulename{ orall E}  orall x\, \varphi \Longrightarrow \varphi[t/x] t free for x in \varphi “In particular, for x = t, …”; “applying the hypothesis to t, …” h t (or specialize h t) ulename{ orall I} box [x_0] … \varphi[x_0/x] \Longrightarrow  orall x\, \varphi x_0 in no premise, in no open assumption, not in  orall x\, \varphi “Let x be arbitrary. … Since x was arbitrary, …” intro x ulename{\exists I} \varphi[t/x] \Longrightarrow \exists x\, \varphi t free for x in \varphi “Take x = t. Then …”; “2k + 1 will do.” use t (or Exists.intro t h) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The phrase names the witness and then checks it. A proof that names the witness without the check (“take N = 100.”) has written the line \exists x\, \varphi without the instance \varphi[t/x] it cites; the reader must supply the instance, and should be able to. In the Givens/Goal table, ulename{\exists I} ticks off the goal \exists x\, \varphi once a Given is an instance \varphi[t/x]; until then the goal row waits. [Not allowed: ulename{\exists I}] Each step is offered as one application of ulename{\exists I}; each breaks the rule where shown. - “From P(c) \wedge Q(d), write \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x))”: the cited line must be exactly \varphi[t/x], with one term t in every marked place. - “From  orall y\, (y < y + 1), write \exists x\,  orall y\, (y < x)”: the side condition; the witness y + 1 is not free for x in  orall y\, (y < x). - “From P(t), write \exists x \in A\; P(x)”: the cited line must be the instance; the bounded form is \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge P(x)), whose instance is t \in A \wedge P(t) (“A bounded witness”). The search method: one more step. Each rule section adds a step to the method of Section 3.1. - Goal \exists x\, \varphi. Postpone. Work on the premises and on other goals until an available line is an instance \varphi[t/x], with t free for x in \varphi; then ulename{\exists I}. The witness may be a compound term that appears only after other rules have run, as f(c) did in (d). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State ulename{\exists I} as a schema, with its side condition. 2. Line 1 of a derivation is R(c, f(c)). Which of the following may line 2 be, by one application of ulename{\exists I} to line 1? For each that may, give \varphi and the witness t; for each that may not, say why. (i) \exists x\, R(x, f(c)); (ii) \exists x\, R(c, x); (iii) \exists x\, R(x, f(x)); (iv) \exists x\, R(x, x); (v) \exists x\, R(f(c), x). 3. Line 1 of a derivation is  orall y\, (y \le y \cdot y). Is \exists x\,  orall y\, (y \le x \cdot x) a legal ulename{\exists I} step from line 1? Read both lines over 
Z: which is true? 4. True or false, with a reason: from the line \exists x\, P(x), one application of ulename{\exists I} gives P(c). 5. The current goal of a search is \exists x\, \varphi and no available line is an instance of \varphi. What does the search method say to do, and why not choose a witness now? (a) From \varphi[t/x] on an available line i, write \exists x\, \varphi on line k, justified “ulename{\exists I} i”. Side condition: t is free for x in \varphi. (b) (i) Yes: \varphi = R(x, f(c)), t = c; only the first c is marked. (ii) Yes: \varphi = R(c, x), t = f(c); the witness is the compound term. (iii) Yes: \varphi = R(x, f(x)), t = c; both occurrences of c are marked, and \varphi[c/x] is R(c, f(c)). (iv) No: the conclusion fixes \varphi = R(x, x), whose instances R(t, t) have equal arguments, while the arguments c and f(c) of line 1 differ. (v) No: the conclusion fixes \varphi = R(f(c), x), whose instances R(f(c), t) have f(c) as first argument, while line 1 has c there. (Read over 
N with R(x, y) as “x < y”, f(x) as x + 1, and c as 0: line 1 says 0 < 1, and (v) says that something exceeds 1, true but not by this step; (iv) says that some number is less than itself, which is false.) (c) No. With \varphi =  orall y\, (y \le x \cdot x), the formula \varphi[y/x] is line 1, so the witness would be the variable y; but the free occurrences of x in \varphi lie in the scope of  orall y, so y is not free for x in \varphi. Over 
Z, line 1 is true: for y \le 0, y \le 0 \le y \cdot y, and for y \ge 1, y \le y \cdot y after multiplying 1 \le y by y > 0. The other line is false: whatever integer x is proposed, y = x \cdot x + 1 gives y > x \cdot x. So the step would lead from a true line to a false one, which is what the side condition prevents. (d) False. ulename{\exists I} concludes an existential from an instance; it never concludes an instance. The line P(c) does not follow from \exists x\, P(x) at all: over 
Z with P as “even” and c as 3, the first is true and the second false. (e) Postpone the goal: work on the premises (ulename{ orall E} at the terms the goal mentions, ulename{{	o}E}, and so on) until a line \varphi[t/x] appears, then use ulename{\exists I}. A witness chosen now leaves the goal \varphi[t/x], which may not follow from the resources even when \exists x\, \varphi does, as “take y = c” did in @exm-existential-introduction-derivations (d). [A2: Drill] Each part takes a line or two. The parts run from single steps, through a missing line, a justification column and steps to judge, to short derivations. 1. Line 1 is 3 + 4 = 7. Name \varphi and t so that ulename{\exists I} gives \exists x\, (x + 4 = 7). 2. Line 2 is c + c = 2 \cdot c. Write the ulename{\exists I} lines with the witness c that mark (i) all three occurrences of c, (ii) the two on the left only. 3. Line 1 is P(f(c)). Give two different ulename{\exists I} conclusions. 4. Line 5 is \exists y\, (y > x_0 + 1), justified “ulename{\exists I} 4”. Give two possible lines 4, with their witnesses. 5. Justify each line: 1  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(f(x))), premise; 2 P(c), premise; 3 P(c) 	o Q(f(c)); 4 Q(f(c)); 5 P(c) \wedge Q(f(c)); 6 \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(f(x))). 6. Line 1 is R(c, c). Which of \exists x\, R(x, c), \exists x\, R(c, x), \exists x\, R(x, y) can one ulename{\exists I} not give? 7. Line 1 is  orall y\, (y = y). Is \exists x\,  orall y\, (x = y) a legal ulename{\exists I} line? 8. True or false: ulename{\exists I} may cite \exists x\, P(x) and write P(c). 9. Premises P(a), Q(b); goal \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)). Should a witness be chosen now? 10. Derive P(c) \vdash \exists x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)). 11. Derive  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(f(x)). 12. Derive  orall x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \vdash \exists x\, \exists y\, R(y, x). (a) \varphi = (x + 4 = 7), t = 3. (b) (i) \exists x\, (x + x = 2 \cdot x); (ii) \exists x\, (x + x = 2 \cdot c). (c) \exists x\, P(x) (witness f(c)) and \exists x\, P(f(x)) (witness c). (d) Any line t > x_0 + 1 with t free for y (every term is, since the formula has no quantifier): for example x_0 + 2 > x_0 + 1 (witness x_0 + 2) or 7 > x_0 + 1 (witness 7). (e) 3 ulename{ orall E} 1 (at c); 4 ulename{{	o}E} 3, 2; 5 ulename{\wedge I} 2, 4; 6 ulename{\exists I} 5 (witness c, marking the c of P(c) and the one inside f(c)). (f) \exists x\, R(x, y): its instances R(t, y) have y in the second place, and line 1 has c. (g) No: the witness would be y, which  orall y captures. Over 
Z line 1 is true and the other line, “some integer equals every integer”, false. (h) False: ulename{\exists I} goes from an instance to an existential, never back. (i) No: neither a nor b has both properties on a line. In fact a counter-reading exists: the domain \{a, b\}, with P true of a only and Q of b only. (j) 2 P(c) \vee Q(c), ulename{\vee I} 1; 3 \exists x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)), ulename{\exists I} 2. (k) 2 P(f(x)), ulename{ orall E} 1 (at the term f(x)); 3 \exists x\, P(f(x)), ulename{\exists I} 2 (with \varphi = P(f(x)) and the witness x). (l) 2  orall y\, R(x, y), ulename{ orall E} 1 (at x); 3 R(x, x), ulename{ orall E} 2; 4 \exists y\, R(y, x), ulename{\exists I} 3 (witness x, marking the first place); 5 \exists x\, \exists y\, R(y, x), ulename{\exists I} 4 (witness x). B. Practice [B1: Postpone, then choose] A search for  orall x\,  igl( P(x) 	o Q(x)  igr), \ P(a) \vdash \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge Q(x)  igr) has reached the stage below. Name the move, then complete it, saying for each line whether the goal or a premise chose it. The move is postpone the witness. Idea. The goal is an existential: postpone it. The premise  orall x\, (\dots) is instantiated at the only term in sight, a, and ulename{{	o}E} with P(a) gives Q(a); both steps are premise-directed. Now the witness a is visible, and the instance the goal needs is P(a) \wedge Q(a), which ulename{\wedge I} builds. The last step is the postponed ulename{\exists I}. Line 6 uses \varphi = P(x) \wedge Q(x) and the witness a. [B2] Over 
R, with the premise  orall x\,  igl( x + (-x) = 0  igr), derive  orall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 0), the true sentence (i) of @exm-quantifier-order-sum. Say what the witness is, and what it depends on. Idea. The goal is a  orall: open a flagged box with a fresh name x_0 (Section 5.4); the new goal is \exists y\, (x_0 + y = 0). Postpone it, and instantiate the premise at the term the goal mentions, x_0. The line x_0 + (-x_0) = 0 shows the witness: -x_0. Line 3 uses \varphi = (x_0 + y = 0) and the witness -x_0, which contains no variable bound in \varphi. At line 4, x_0 appears in no premise, there is no open assumption, and x_0 does not appear in the conclusion, so ulename{ orall I} applies (@def-rules-universal). The witness -x_0 is built from x_0, so it depends on x_0: a different number for each x. That is legal, because ulename{\exists I} is applied inside the box, where x_0 is available as a term. It is the box picture of the game of Section 5.1: the \exists y is played after the  orall x, and may use it. [B3] Over 
Z, prove “there is an integer n with n^2 = n + 2” as a derivation whose only line not justified by a rule is one line of arithmetic justified “arith”; write n^2 as n \cdot n. Then write the proof as one sentence. The witness 2 works, since 2 \cdot 2 = 4 = 2 + 2. Line 2 uses \varphi = (n \cdot n = n + 2) with the witness 2. Line 1 contains four 2’s, and \varphi marks three of them: both factors on the left and the first term of the sum on the right. The last 2 is the constant of the statement and stays. Marking all four would give \exists n\, (n \cdot n = n + n), a different statement. In one sentence: Take n = 2; then n^2 = 4 = n + 2. The witness -1 works too, since (-1) \cdot (-1) = 1 = -1 + 2; a proof needs only one. [B4: Derive or break] For each claim, derive it with the rules of Chapters 1–2, ulename{ orall E}, ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists I}, or break it with a counter-reading (Section 5.3). 1.  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \vee Q(x)  igr). 2. \exists x\, P(x) \vdash  orall x\, P(x). 3. R(c, d) \wedge R(d, c) \vdash \exists x\, R(x, x). 4. R(c, d) \wedge R(d, c) \vdash \exists x\, \exists y\,  igl( R(x, y) \wedge R(y, x)  igr). 5.  orall x\, R(x, f(x)) \vdash  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y). 6.  orall x\, R(x, f(x)) \vdash \exists y\,  orall x\, R(x, y). 7. \vdash \exists x\,  igl( P(x) 	o P(x)  igr). (a) Derive. Instantiate at the variable x, weaken, and forget the witness. Line 4 uses \varphi = P(x) \vee Q(x) and the witness x. (b) Break. The domain \{0, 1\}, with P true of 0 only. The premise holds (at 0), and the conclusion fails at 1. (c) Break. The domain \{0, 1\}, with c naming 0, d naming 1, and R true of the pairs (0, 1) and (1, 0) only. The premise holds, and no element is related to itself. (d) Derive. Two witnesses, one for each place, forgotten one at a time. Line 2 uses \varphi = R(c, y) \wedge R(y, c) and the witness d; line 3 uses \varphi = \exists y\, (R(x, y) \wedge R(y, x)) and the witness c, which is free for x since it is a constant. (e) Derive. Fix x_0 first; the witness f(x_0) is found after the flag. At line 4, x_0 appears in no premise, no box is open, and x_0 is not in line 4. (f) Break. The domain \{0, 1\}, with f the identity (f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1) and R true of (0, 0) and (1, 1) only. The premise holds, since each element is related to itself; and no y has both R(0, y) and R(1, y). (g) Derive. A box with its assumption as its only line, then ulename{\exists I} at the variable x. Line 3 has the witness x; the variable names an object, since domains are not empty (Section 5.1). The pairs: (c) and (d) are look-alikes (one witness for both places, against two witnesses); (e) and (f) differ only in the order of  orall and \exists, the swap of Section 5.1, and the witness f(x_0) in (e) depends on the flag; (b) is the converse of @prp-forall-implies-exists. Worked examples of these types: @exm-existential-introduction-derivations; @prp-forall-implies-exists. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1 each: (a), (b), (c), (d), (f), (g), with the derivation or the counter-reading in full. - 2: (e), with the flag opened first and the witness f(x_0) found after it. - 2: the closing pairing. Fatal errors (0 for the claim): an ulename{\exists I} whose witness is not free for the variable; a “break” in which the premise is false. C. Going deeper [C1: The conclusion clause of for-all-introduction, used later] The side condition of ulename{ orall I} (@def-rules-universal) has three clauses about the flag x_0: it appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at the ulename{ orall I} line, and not in the conclusion  orall x\, \varphi. Show that the third clause is needed: give a “derivation” that breaks only that clause, from a premise that is true over 
N to a sentence (@def-sentence) that is false over 
N. Check that every other step is legal. [Hint 1] The conclusion of the illegal ulename{ orall I} still mentions the flag, so it is not yet a sentence. Which rule of this section can replace a name on a line by a bound variable? [Hint 2] Start from the premise  orall x\, (x \le x), and open a flagged box with the name y_0. The illegal line. Line 3 is ulename{ orall I} with the flag y_0 and \varphi = (x \le y_0): the instance \varphi[y_0/x] is y_0 \le y_0, the last line of the box. The flag y_0 appears in no premise (line 1 has no y_0), and there is no open assumption at all. But y_0 appears in the conclusion  orall x\, (x \le y_0), so the third clause fails, and only it. The other lines are legal. Line 2 is ulename{ orall E} at the term y_0, which is free for x in x \le x since that formula has no quantifier. Line 4 is ulename{\exists I} with \varphi =  orall x\, (x \le y) and the witness y_0: \varphi[y_0/y] is line 3, and y_0 is free for y in \varphi, since the only quantifier of \varphi is on x. Over 
N. Line 1 says that every natural number is at most itself: true. Line 4 says that some natural number is at least every natural number, that is, that there is a largest natural number: false, since for any y, x = y + 1 is larger. What the clause prevents. The box proved y_0 \le y_0, a fact about y_0 in which the two sides are the same name. Line 3 generalized only one side and kept the other, so it claimed that one fixed y_0 is at least every x: a claim about y_0 that the box never proved. The flag is “let y_0 be arbitrary”; it must not survive into the statement that “since y_0 was arbitrary” produces. Line 4 then shows the damage, by turning the leaked name into a witness. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: a derivation whose only illegal line is a ulename{ orall I} whose flag appears in its conclusion. - 2: checks the other two clauses at that line (no premise, no open assumption contains the flag). - 2: checks the remaining lines (here ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists I}, with free-for). - 3: shows the premise true and the conclusion false over 
N, with the witness of the falsity (y + 1). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a second illegal line (for instance a capture in ulename{\exists I}); a premise that is false over 
N. [C2: A witness is not a name, used later] Explain why the rules so far (Chapters 1–2 and ulename{ orall E}, ulename{ orall I}, ulename{\exists I}) cannot derive \exists x\, P(x) \vdash P(c). Go through the rules that could produce the last line P(c), and say what each would need. Then say, in one sentence, why no rule for using \exists should give P(c). The argument below is informal: it explains why every search stalls, and it does not by itself prove that no derivation exists. Section 7.2 gives a model in which the premise is true and P(c) is false. With the soundness theorem stated there (and proved in the optional Section 7.3), that model shows no derivation exists. Which rules could write P(c). The line P(c) is atomic, so no introduction rule writes it: ulename{\wedge I}, ulename{{	o}I}, ulename{\vee I}, ulename{
eg I}, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}, ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists I} all write a line whose main symbol is their own connective or quantifier. The remaining rules take P(c) out of something larger: ulename{\wedge E} needs a conjunction with P(c) as a side; ulename{{	o}E} needs an implication \psi 	o P(c) and \psi; ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} a biconditional with P(c) as a side; ulename{\vee E} a disjunction and two boxes each ending in P(c); ulename{ orall E} a universal  orall x\, \psi with \psi[c/x] = P(c); ulename{
eg E} writes only  ot, never P(c); ulename{ ot E} the line  ot; ulename{RAA} a box from 
eg P(c) to  ot; and ulename{R} the line P(c) itself. The derived rules of Chapter 2 abbreviate derivations in these rules (@def-derived-rule), so they add no new way to write P(c). What the premise can supply. The only premise is \exists x\, P(x), whose main symbol is \exists. No rule so far looks inside an existential: each elimination rule needs a cited line that is  ot (for ulename{ ot E}) or whose main symbol is \wedge, 	o, \vee, \leftrightarrow, 
eg or  orall, and ulename{\exists I} produces existentials rather than using them. So the premise can enter a derivation only as a whole: copied, built into a larger formula, set against a line 
eg\exists x\, P(x) by ulename{
eg E}, or cited as the side \psi beside a line \psi 	o \chi or \psi \leftrightarrow \chi by ulename{{	o}E} or ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. None of these reaches the information inside it, and the lines the rules above need (a conjunction containing P(c), an implication ending in it, a biconditional with it as a side, a disjunction for ulename{\vee E}, a universal with it as an instance, a contradiction) have nowhere to come from. A search therefore stalls at once. Why it should stall. The premise says that something has P and does not say what; the conclusion says that the object named c has P. Over 
Z with P as “even” and c as 3, the premise is true and the conclusion false. So no rule for using an existential may give P(c), and the rule of Section 5.6 does not: it names the witness with a fresh variable, about which nothing else is known, instead of with c. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: identifies that P(c) is atomic, so only elimination rules, ulename{ ot E}, ulename{RAA} or ulename{R} can write it, and names what each needs. - 3: observes that no rule so far uses a line whose main symbol is \exists, so the premise cannot supply what those rules need. - 2: says that this explains the stall but is not a proof of non-derivability (that needs a counter-model together with soundness, Sections 7.2–7.3). - 2: gives a reading with the premise true and P(c) false, and the one-sentence reason (the premise does not say which object has P). Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming that ulename{\exists I} read backwards gives P(c); claiming that a failed search proves the sequent underivable.

title: 5.6 Using "There Exists": Name a Witness
content:
Using “There Exists”: Name a Witness Section 5.5 gave the rule that proves an existential statement: exhibit a witness, and forget it. This section gives the rule that uses one, ulename{\exists E}. It is the last of the four quantifier rules, and the subtlest, because an existential says that a witness exists without saying which one it is. The rule handles this with a box and a fresh name, as ulename{ orall I} did, but the name now stands for an object that is not arbitrary, and the side condition keeps it from being treated as if it were. With the rule in hand, the section moves an \exists past a  orall, and shows exactly where the reverse move breaks down. Using a witness whose identity is unknown Chapter 2 proved that if n^2 is even then n is even (@thm-square-even-implies-even). One of the facts it rested on, (E3), says that the square of an odd integer is odd, and it was shown by taking “an integer k with n = 2k + 1” and computing with it. Chapter 2 noted that naming the k of (E3) lay outside its derivation: it is a quantifier step, whose rule had to wait. Here is the simplest proof with the same step. If n is even, then n + 2 is even. Since n is even, choose an integer k with n = 2k. Then n + 2 = 2k + 2 = 2(k + 1), so n + 2 is even. The hypothesis is \exists k\, (n = 2 \cdot k). The proof does not know which integer k is; it does not need to. It gives the unknown witness a name, uses the one fact it has about it, n = 2k, and reaches a conclusion, “n + 2 is even”, in which the name no longer appears. The witness k + 1 of the last step is forgotten by ulename{\exists I}, as in Section 5.5. Why is this correct? Two tempting shortcuts show what the proof is careful not to do. - It does not name the witness by a term that already means something. From “some integer is even” we may not conclude “3 is even”: the existential does not say that the witness is 3, and, as the warning “ulename{\exists I} runs one way only” of Section 5.5 noted, it cannot be read back as a statement about a named object. - It does not let the conclusion mention the name. If it did, the conclusion would be a statement about k, and outside the argument k refers to nothing; the existential promised only that some k works. So the name must be new, the argument may use only what the existential says about it, and the conclusion must not mention it. Then the argument works for the witness, whichever integer it is, because it never used anything else about it. The rule of existential elimination To use “there exists”, give the witness a new name, assume only what the existential says about it, and conclude something that does not mention it. [Rules for the Existential Quantifier] The rule on the left is ulename{\exists E} (existential elimination). It cites a line h holding \exists x\, \varphi and a flagged box with the name x_0, a variable, whose first line is the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] and whose last line j, a line of that box itself, is \chi; line h and the box must be available at line k (@def-derivation, with the flagged boxes of Section 5.4). The new line k repeats \chi. Side condition, at line k: the name x_0 does not appear - in \chi, - in \exists x\, \varphi, - in any premise, or - in any assumption of a box still open at line k. The rule on the right is ulename{\exists I}, recalled from @def-rule-existential-introduction: t is any term free for x in \varphi. The box of ulename{\exists E} is the flagged box of Section 5.4 with one difference: it opens with an assumption, \varphi[x_0/x], “x_0 is a witness”. Clauses 3–5 below, the side condition, are the official test, the one a checker runs. This rule has conditions that matter; read each one. 1. The assumption. The box assumes \varphi[x_0/x]: the formula of the existential, with the new name in place of x. This is “choose x_0 with \varphi”. It is the only thing the box knows about x_0. 2. The last line. The box ends with \chi, a line of the box itself, not of a box inside it, as for ulename{\vee E} and ulename{ orall I}. It is “whatever the witness is, \chi follows”. The new line k then asserts \chi outside the box, where x_0 is no longer assumed to be anything. 3. x_0 does not appear in \chi. The box shows that \chi follows from “x_0 is a witness”; if \chi mentioned x_0, line k would make a claim about a name that, outside the box, is tied to nothing. The subsection “Three ways to break the rule” below shows the damage. 4. x_0 does not appear in a premise or in an assumption of an open box. The name must be new to everything we know at line k. If a premise or an open assumption already said something about x_0, the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] would add to it a claim that x_0 is the witness, which the existential never made. 5. x_0 does not appear in \exists x\, \varphi. The existential must not itself mention the name chosen for its witness. This clause also makes x_0 free for x in \varphi (Section 5.2: a variable that does not appear in \varphi is free for every variable there), so the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] says of x_0 exactly what \varphi says of x. 6. “Still open at line k”. The box’s own assumption \varphi[x_0/x] is closed at line k, so it is not among the assumptions checked. This matters: read inside the box, “an open assumption” would include \varphi[x_0/x], which contains x_0 whenever x is free in \varphi, and the rule could then never be applied in the cases that matter. Using an existential: open the box early When a resource is \exists x\, \varphi, the premise-directed step of the search method is to open its ulename{\exists E} box at once, with a fresh name x_0, and to make the box’s last line the current goal. Name the witness early: open the ulename{\exists E} box as soon as the existential is available, and aim it at the current goal. Why early? Opening early keeps every resource, since every line available before the box is available inside it; and a box aimed at the current goal can always be closed once the goal is reached, since its name was chosen fresh. What the early box gives is the witness’s name, often exactly the term a postponed \exists goal is waiting for. And a box aimed at the current goal \chi can always be closed once \chi is reached: x_0 is chosen, when the box opens, to appear in no premise, in no open assumption, not in \exists x\, \varphi and not in the current goal \chi. The assumptions still open at the line that closes the box are the ones that were open when it opened, so every clause of the side condition holds there. (One caution: a ulename{ orall I} inside the box needs a flag that does not appear in the new assumption; a flag that is fresh at that point has this property.) How this rule looks in a mathematical proof In a written proof, the ulename{\exists E} box is announced by “choose”, “let x_0 be such a point”, “say n = 2k”, “fix such a k”. The assumption of the box is the property in the sentence, and the rest of the paragraph is the inside of the box. The claim the paragraph ends on, usually the clause after the final “so”, must not mention the chosen name, though the computation leading up to it may. If that claim still mentions the name, the paragraph has not finished: a later step must reach a claim without the name before the box can close, often an ulename{\exists I} that forgets it (as in the example below), or a contradiction  ot (as in @exm-existential-elimination-derivations (b)). N. A proof says: Since (a_n) is bounded, choose M with \abs{a_n} \le M for all n \in 
N. Then \abs{2a_n} = 2\abs{a_n} \le 2M for all n \in 
N, so (2a_n) is bounded. With the domain 
R, the sequence as a function symbol a, and the bound on n written out by @def-bounded-quantifier, the proof is this derivation. The sentences match the boxes. “Choose M” opens the ulename{\exists E} box (line 2). “For all n \in

The conclusion mentions neither M_0 nor 2 \cdot M_0, as the side condition requires. Two witnesses, one name. “Let n and m be even, say n = 2k and m = 2k” is a common error in parity proofs. (10 points) - 2: (a) says the conclusion is derivable and gives a correct derivation or cites @prp-exists-and with ulename{\wedge E}. - 3: (b) names line 4, the rule ulename{\exists E}, and the clause “x_0 not in \chi”. - 1: (b) says that the other lines are correct, so the error is in that one line. - 4: (c) gives a derivation that uses the same illegal step and is otherwise legal, with a reading in which the premise is true and the conclusion false. Fatal errors (0 for the step): answering (a) “no” because the derivation is wrong; giving a counterexample to the conclusion of the original sequent (there is none); blaming line 5. [C3: The diagonal of a list] Let A_0, A_1, A_2, \dots be sets of natural numbers, one for each n \in 
N, and let D = \{ n \in 
N : n 
otin A_n \}. 1. Over the domain 
N, read R(x, y) as “x \in A_y”. Follow the proof of @thm-barber in this reading to show that D is none of the sets A_m. 2. Compute D for the list A_n = \{ k \in 
N : k > n \}, and for the list A_n = \{ k \in 
N : k 	ext{ is a multiple of } n + 1 \}. In each case, find a number at which D differs from A_0, from A_1 and from A_2. [Hint] In (a), the existential of line 1 is “some m has D = A_m”. What does the definition of D say about every n, when D = A_m? (a) Suppose D = A_m for some m: this is the existential of line 1, with its witness named m (line 2). By the definition of D, for every n: n \in A_m exactly when n 
otin A_n; that is  orall x\, (R(x, m) \leftrightarrow 
eg R(x, x)). At n = m (line 3): m \in A_m exactly when m 
otin A_m, which is impossible (lines 4–9). So no m has D = A_m. (b) First list: n > n is false, so n 
otin A_n for every n, and D = 
N. D differs from A_m at m: m \in D and m
