(10 points) - 2: the assumption D = A_m set up as the witness of an existential. - 2: the universal  orall x\, (R(x, m) \leftrightarrow 
eg R(x, x)) read off the definition of D. - 2: the instance at m and the contradiction. - 2: the first list’s D, with the three differences. - 2: the second list’s D (the case n = 0 justified), with the three differences. Fatal error (0 for (a)): instantiating at some number other than m.

title: 5.7 Equality
content:
Equality Sections 5.3 to 5.6 gave the four quantifier rules, and with them every logical symbol of the language of Section 5.2 (the connectives,  ot, the quantifiers, and equality) has rules, except one. So far the equals sign has been treated like a predicate symbol: a = b was an atomic formula like P(a), and no rule looked inside it. Yet almost every calculation in mathematics is a chain of equations, and every use of “the” (the limit, the supremum, the inverse) quietly asserts that something is unique. This section adds the two rules for equality, ulename{{=}I} and ulename{{=}E}, which say together that equals may be replaced by equals. Section 5.8 applies them to the phrase “there is exactly one”, which is an existential statement together with an equation. This section ends by completing the table of rules, phrases, and Lean tactics that Chapter 1 began. What the rules so far cannot do with an equation Here is the first line of a calculation any reader has written: Since a = b and a + a = 2a, we have b + b = 2b. Nothing could be simpler, and nothing in Sections 5.3–5.6 derives it: so far the rules treat = as they treat any two-place predicate symbol, and from R(a, b) and P(a) no rule gives P(b). Reading R(a, b) as a < b and P(x) as x < 1 over 
Z, with a = 0 and b = 5, both premises are true and P(b) is false. What makes the step correct is what = means: a and b are names of the same object. Any statement true of the object is true of it whichever name is used. Two things follow, and they are the two rules of this section. 1. Every term names the same object as itself. Nothing needs to be assumed to write t = t. 2. If t_1 and t_2 name the same object, then a statement about t_1 may be rewritten as the same statement about t_2. The first rule is unusual: it cites no earlier line at all. Chapter 1 anticipated this when it defined rules (Section 1.2): the definition of a rule schema (@def-rule-schema) was worded so that a rule of Chapter 5 could have no given lines at all. This is that rule. The rules for equality Everything is equal to itself, and equals may be replaced by equals. [Rules for Equality] The rule ulename{{=}I} (equality introduction, or reflexivity) writes t = t for any term t, at any line, citing nothing. The rule ulename{{=}E} (equality elimination, or substitution of equals) cites an equation t_1 = t_2 on line i and a line j of the form \varphi[t_1/x], both available at line k, and writes \varphi[t_2/x] on line k. Here \varphi is any formula and x any variable, subject to one side condition: both t_1 and t_2 are free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for). In words: ulename{{=}I} says that every term equals itself. ulename{{=}E} says that when t_1 = t_2 is known, a line that says something about t_1 may be rewritten as the same thing said about t_2. The formula \varphi is the “something”: a statement with a hole x, which line j fills with t_1 and line k fills with t_2. Mark the holes first. To use ulename{{=}E} with t_1 = t_2, write down the line you have and draw a box round each occurrence of t_1 you want to replace. The boxes are the holes: \varphi is the line with a variable in each box, and the new line puts t_2 in every box. With a = b:  oxed{a} +  oxed{a} = 2 \cdot  oxed{a} \ 	ext{ gives } \ b + b = 2 \cdot b, \qquad  oxed{a} + a = 2 \cdot a \ 	ext{ gives } \ b + a = 2 \cdot a . Occurrences without a box stay as they are. Read the definition clause by clause. 1. ulename{{=}I} cites nothing. - Schema: the left block above, t = t, citing nothing. - Reading: every term equals itself, so the line may stand anywhere, even first in a derivation with no premises. - Example: “a + b = a + b — ulename{{=}I}”, the first line of every chain below. 2. The equation is read from left to right. The cited equation t_1 = t_2 licenses replacing t_1 by t_2, and not the other way round. From a = b and P(b), the rule does not give P(a), because P(b) is \varphi[b/x] for \varphi = P(x), and the equation would have to be b = a. The reverse direction needs one more step, symmetry, which we derive below. 3. Some or all occurrences. The choice of \varphi decides which occurrences of t_1 are replaced: exactly those that \varphi marks with x (the boxes above). Occurrences of t_1 that \varphi writes out are left alone. Choosing \varphi is the whole art of using the rule. 4. Free for x. Neither term may have a variable captured by a quantifier of \varphi, the condition of @def-free-for that the rules of Sections 5.3 and 5.5 also carry. The nonexample below shows what goes wrong without it. One line, many readings. Take the equation a = b and the line a + a = 2 \cdot a. The term a occurs three times in the line, and \varphi may mark any of them. Some of the choices: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \varphi \varphi[a/x] (the cited line) \varphi[b/x] (the new line) ----------------------- ------------------------------- ----------------------------- x + a = 2 \cdot a a + a = 2 \cdot a b + a = 2 \cdot a a + x = 2 \cdot a a + a = 2 \cdot a a + b = 2 \cdot a a + a = 2 \cdot x a + a = 2 \cdot a a + a = 2 \cdot b x + x = 2 \cdot x a + a = 2 \cdot a b + b = 2 \cdot b ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Each of the three occurrences is marked or not, so there are 2^3 = 8 choices in all, and each is a legal step. The fourth row is the step of the opening calculation. One more row belongs to the table: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \varphi \varphi[a/x] (the cited line) \varphi[b/x] (the new line) ----------------------- ------------------------------- ----------------------------- a + a = 2 \cdot a a + a = 2 \cdot a a + a = 2 \cdot a ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- This row is the degenerate choice: \varphi contains no x, so \varphi[a/x] and \varphi[b/x] are both \varphi, and the rule copies the line unchanged. It is legal and useless, and it shows that “some occurrences” includes “none”. Another degenerate case: the equation may be t = t itself, and then ulename{{=}E} again returns the cited line. From the equation x_0 = 3 and the line x_0 \cdot x_0 > x_0, which formula \varphi makes ulename{{=}E} give 3 \cdot 3 > x_0? Which gives x_0 \cdot 3 > 3? For 3 \cdot 3 > x_0, take \varphi = (z \cdot z > x_0), with a variable z that appears nowhere else: \varphi[x_0/z] is the cited line and \varphi[3/z] is 3 \cdot 3 > x_0. For x_0 \cdot 3 > 3, take \varphi = (x_0 \cdot z > z). The hole has to be a variable other than x_0, since the occurrences of x_0 that stay must be written out in \varphi. From a = b and the line a \cdot a = a + 1, which occurrences do you box to get a \cdot b = b + 1? The second and the third a: \varphi = (a \cdot z = z + 1), and \varphi[a/z] is the given line, \varphi[b/z] the new one. A nonexample: capture. Take the equation a = y, with y a variable, and the line \exists y\, (y < a). It is tempting to “substitute y for a” and write \exists y\, (y < y). With \varphi = \exists y\, (y < x), the cited line is \varphi[a/x], and the new line would be \varphi[y/x]. But y is not free for x in \varphi: the x sits inside \exists y, and the y put there would be captured. The side condition fails, and rightly. Read over 
Z, with a and y both naming 0, the premises say “a = y” (true) and “some integer is less than 0” (true), while \exists y\, (y < y) says that some integer is less than itself (false). Line 3 breaks the side condition of @def-rules-equality. What the argument meant to say needs a different name for the bound variable: \exists z\, (z < a), which is the same sentence up to renaming (Section 5.2), becomes \exists z\, (z < y), which is true when y names 0. Why these two rules. They are exactly the two facts about “same object” listed above, and nothing else about equality needs to be assumed. Symmetry (s = t gives t = s), transitivity (s = t and t = u give s = u), and “applying the same function to both sides” are all derived below. So the two rules play for = the part that the introduction and elimination rules played for each connective: one builds an equation, one uses it. A bound variable is not a place to substitute. From x = 0 and  orall x\, (x = x), the line  orall x\, (0 = x) does not follow: the x’s of  orall x\, (x = x) are bound, and ulename{{=}E} replaces only free occurrences. Over 
Z, with x naming 0, the premises are true and  orall x\, (0 = x) is false. To write  orall x\, (x = x) as \varphi[x/z], either z does not occur free in \varphi, and then \varphi[0/z] is the unchanged line, or z occurs free in \varphi (for instance, \varphi is  orall x\, (z = x)), and then every free z lies inside  orall x, so x is not free for z in \varphi and the side condition fails. Symmetry, transitivity and congruence Everything we expect of equality now follows from the two rules. Each derivation below is short, and the only thought in each is the choice of \varphi. It turns out that the equation in ulename{{=}E} may be read in either direction after all, at the cost of two extra lines (an ulename{{=}I} and an ulename{{=}E}; after the abbreviation (sym) below, just one), and that equations chain: [Equality Is Symmetric and Transitive] For all terms s, t, u: 1. s = t \vdash t = s; 2. s = t, \; t = u \vdash s = u. For (a), the goal t = s must be the last line of an ulename{{=}E} that uses the premise s = t (it is the only equation available), so it has the form \varphi[t/x], and the cited line \varphi[s/x] must already be on a line. Try \varphi = (x = s): then \varphi[t/x] is t = s, the goal, and \varphi[s/x] is s = s, which ulename{{=}I} supplies for free. For (b), rewrite the t of the first premise using the second: \varphi = (s = x). (a) With \varphi \coloneqq (x = s), for a variable x that occurs in neither s nor t, the line s = s is \varphi[s/x] and the goal t = s is \varphi[t/x]. Both terms are free for x in \varphi, since \varphi has no quantifier. So the following is a derivation: (b) With \varphi \coloneqq (s = x), for a variable x that does not occur in s, the first premise s = t is \varphi[t/x] and the goal s = u is \varphi[u/x]; again \varphi has no quantifier. So the following is a derivation: Line 3 of (b) cites the equation t = u on line 2 as the rule’s line i, and s = t on line 1 as its line j. This proves (a) and (b). Notice where the “reflexivity” line went in (a): the equation s = t was not rewritten at all. It was the tool, and the line it rewrote, s = s, was manufactured for the purpose. This is the typical use of ulename{{=}I}: it supplies a line for ulename{{=}E} to work on. From now on, symmetry and transitivity may be used as one line, with the justifications “(sym)” and “(trans)”: each abbreviates the three-line derivation above with the given terms in place of s, t, u. This is the license of @def-derived-rule, extended from statement letters to terms. The extension is harmless for the same reason: the derivations above used nothing about s, t, u except that they are terms, so they can be pasted in with any terms. The next derivation is the rule behind “apply f to both sides”. Let f be a one-place function symbol, and a, b constants. Here \varphi = (f(a) = f(x)): it keeps the first a and marks the second. With \varphi = (f(x) = f(x)) instead, the same two lines would give f(b) = f(b), which is true and useless. Nothing is special about f: the same three lines give a^2 = b^2 from a = b, or a + c = b + c, or \abs{a} = \abs{b}. Every “do the same thing to both sides of an equation” is this derivation. The last result of this group has no premises. It says that equals share every property, and it is called Leibniz’s Law. [Leibniz’s Law] For every one-place predicate symbol P, \vdash  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( x = y 	o (P(x) 	o P(y))  igr). In words: whatever is true of x is true of anything equal to it. The rule ulename{{=}E} is this law for every formula at once; the seven-line derivation is in the fold below. Finding it. The goal is  orall x, so the search method of Section 3.1, with the step of Section 5.4, opens a flagged box for x_0; the new goal  orall y\, (\dots) opens a second flagged box, for y_0. The goal x_0 = y_0 	o (P(x_0) 	o P(y_0)) is an implication, so a box opens with x_0 = y_0, and the new goal P(x_0) 	o P(y_0) opens another, with P(x_0). Now the goal is P(y_0), the resources are x_0 = y_0 and P(x_0), and one ulename{{=}E} with \varphi = P(x) finishes. Every line but one was written by a goal-directed step. The two ulename{ orall I} lines cite the flagged boxes as \lines{1}{5} and \lines{1}{6}: each flagged box immediately contains another box, so its range starts at that box’s first line (the convention of Section 5.4). At line 6 the name y_0 appears in no premise (there are none), in no open assumption (the boxes on lines 1 and 2 have closed), and not in the conclusion; at line 7 the same holds for x_0. The derivation has 7 lines. The claim is one of the classical “axioms of equality”, often taken as a starting point in place of ulename{{=}E}. Here it is a consequence. Conversely, with the claim as a premise, ulename{ orall E} twice and ulename{{	o}E} twice would do the work of ulename{{=}E} for the formula P(x); the rule does it for every formula at once. Words about knowledge are not formulas. ulename{{=}E} rewrites formulas of the language, and “it is obvious that …”, “the pupil checked that …”, “it is known that …” are not among its connectives. A pupil checked that 7 \cdot 13 = 91, and indeed 7 \cdot 13 = 91. Replacing 7 \cdot 13 by 91 inside the report gives “the pupil checked that 91 = 91”, a different claim about what the pupil did. Inside a formula every free occurrence of a term may be rewritten, subject to the side condition of @def-rules-equality; inside words about what someone knows or checked, none may. Equal sets have the same elements Equal Sets Have the Same Elements Read the domain as consisting of sets, with \in a two-place predicate symbol written between its terms (shorthand rule 1 of Section 5.2). Show that \vdash  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( x = y 	o  orall z\, (z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y)  igr). The two boxes of line 4 are one-line boxes, as P 	o P is shown, and each flagged box immediately contains another box and is cited from its first line. Line 5 is ulename{{=}E} with \varphi = (z_0 \in x_0 \leftrightarrow z_0 \in w): line 4 is \varphi[x_0/w], and the equation of line 1 refills the hole with y_0; as in the proof of symmetry, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} manufactured a line for ulename{{=}E} to rewrite. The converse,  orall z\, (z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y) 	o x = y, breaks. Here is a counter-reading to it: two dots a and b, with nothing an element of anything. With x naming a and y naming b, both sides of z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y are false for every z, so the hypothesis is true; and a = b is false. For sets, the converse is taken as an axiom, the axiom of extensionality: a set is determined by its elements. Calculations are chains of substitutions A calculation in a proof looks like this: a + b = 2 \cdot b + b = 2 \cdot 3 + 3 = 9, written under the premises a = 2 \cdot b and b = 3. The chain is a single statement to the eye, but logically it is several equations, each obtained from the last. Here is the derivation it abbreviates, with one line of arithmetic, justified “arith” as in Section 5.3. A chain as a derivation. From b = 3 and a = 2 \cdot b, derive a + b = 9. The choices of \varphi, with z a variable not occurring in the terms: - line 4: \varphi = (a + b = z + b), rewriting the a on the right of line 3 and keeping the one on the left; - line 5: \varphi = (a + b = 2 \cdot z + z), rewriting both remaining b’s on the right at once; - line 7: \varphi = (a + b = z), rewriting the whole right-hand side by the equation of line 6. The pattern is general. A chain t_1 = t_2 = \dots = t_n starts with t_1 = t_1 by ulename{{=}I}, keeps t_1 fixed on the left, and rewrites the right-hand side once per link, each time by ulename{{=}E} with the equation that justifies the link. Each link is either a premise, as on lines 4 and 5, or an arithmetic fact, as on line 7. The last line is t_1 = t_n. Transitivity (@prp-equality-symmetric-transitive (b)) is the same move made once; a chain makes it n - 1 times. A mixed chain, such as a^2 + 1 = 10 \le 10 + b^2 with a = 3, is not made of ulename{{=}E} alone. Its = links are ulename{{=}E} steps as above, and a \le link needs a fact about \le: here that b^2 \ge 0, so that adding b^2 does not decrease a number. The = link before it then carries over by one more ulename{{=}E}, with \varphi = (z \le 10 + b^2) and the equation a^2 + 1 = 10 turned round by symmetry (@prp-equality-symmetric-transitive (a)); transitivity of \le is needed only where two \le links meet, as in x \le y \le z. Those are facts about order, not about equality. They enter derivations as “arith” lines, one per link. Line 5 of the chain rewrites both b’s on the right of line 4 at once. Which \varphi would rewrite only the b inside 2 \cdot b, and what line would it give? How would the chain then reach line 5? Take \varphi = (a + b = 2 \cdot z + b). Then line 4 is \varphi[b/z], and ulename{{=}E} 1, 4 gives \varphi[3/z], the line a + b = 2 \cdot 3 + b. One more ulename{{=}E} with the same equation b = 3 and \varphi = (a + b = 2 \cdot 3 + z) then gives a + b = 2 \cdot 3 + 3, which is line 5. Marking both occurrences at once saves that line. Under the premise a = 2, the chain a + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3 \le 4 has three links. Which is an ulename{{=}E} step, and which are “arith” lines? The first link is ulename{{=}E}: from a + 1 = a + 1 (ulename{{=}I}) and a = 2, with \varphi = (a + 1 = z + 1), it writes a + 1 = 2 + 1. The links 2 + 1 = 3 and 3 \le 4 are facts of school arithmetic, written as “arith” lines, and each is then carried into the chain by one more ulename{{=}E} (with \varphi = (a + 1 = z), then with \varphi = (z \le 4) and the equation turned round); the last link is about order, not equality. What equality sounds like in a proof In a written proof, ulename{{=}E} is the word “substituting”, or no word at all: the chain a + b = 2b + b = 9 is read as a sequence of substitutions, and the reader supplies the \varphi of each link. “By symmetry” or “rewriting the equation as t = s” is @prp-equality-symmetric-transitive (a). “Applying f to both sides”, “squaring both sides”, “adding c to both sides” are the congruence derivation above. And ulename{{=}I} is almost never written, because t = t goes without saying; it is visible only in the first line of a formal chain, and in a proof assistant, where rfl proves t = t. Here is a proof from school algebra, read link by link. Claim. If a + b = 0 and a + c = 0, then b = c. Proof. b = b + 0 = b + (a + c) = (b + a) + c = (a + b) + c = 0 + c = c. The first link is the fact y + 0 = y for every y, applied at y = b (an instance by ulename{ orall E}) and read from right to left: the chain needs b = b + 0, which is the instance b + 0 = b turned round by symmetry. The second link rewrites the 0 by the premise a + c = 0, again turned round, since the chain needs 0 to become a + c. The third and fourth are instances of associativity and commutativity. The fifth rewrites a + b by the premise a + b = 0 in the direction written. The last is the instance 0 + c = c. So the claim says that a number has at most one additive inverse; the facts it uses are the field axioms, here school algebra. The search method: one more step Each of Sections 5.3 to 5.6 added a step to the search method of Section 3.1. Equality adds one. - An equation. When an equation t_1 = t_2 is available and the goal differs from an available line only in some occurrences of t_1 and t_2, look for the \varphi that makes one ulename{{=}E} turn the line into the goal: mark with x exactly the places where they differ. If the equation points the wrong way, turn it round first (sym). If no available line will do, make one with ulename{{=}I}, as the proof of @prp-equality-symmetric-transitive did. In the Givens/Goal table, ulename{{=}E} turns a Given into a new Given with some holes refilled, and ulename{{=}I} adds t = t to the Givens at no cost. [Instances of ulename{{=}E}] In each row the hole is z; the cited line fills it with the left side of the equation, the new line with the right side. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Equation t_1 = t_2 \varphi Cited line \varphi[t_1/z] New line \varphi[t_2/z] ------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------- f(c) = g(c) + 1 P(z) \wedge R(f(c), c) P(f(c)) \wedge R(f(c), c) P(g(c) + 1) \wedge R(f(c), c) \varepsilon/2 = \delta \abs{x - a} < z 	o \abs{h(x) - h(a)} < \varepsilon \abs{x - a} < \varepsilon/2 	o \abs{h(x) - h(a)} < \varepsilon \abs{x - a} < \delta 	o \abs{h(x) - h(a)} < \varepsilon a + b = b + a  orall y\, (z \cdot y = y \cdot (a + b))  orall y\, ((a + b) \cdot y = y \cdot (a + b))  orall y\, ((b + a) \cdot y = y \cdot (a + b)) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In the first row the f(c) inside R(f(c), c) is written out in \varphi and stays; in the third the hole sits under  orall y, and both terms are free for z because neither contains y. Not an instance. From 2 = 1 + 1 and the line 2^5 = 32, the line (1 + 1)^5 = 3(1 + 1), which treats the digit 2 of 32 as an occurrence of the term 2, is not written by ulename{{=}E}: the numeral 32 is one constant, with no occurrence of the term 2 inside it; \varphi = (z^5 = 32) gives only (1 + 1)^5 = 32. The rule, phrase and Lean table, completed Chapter 1 began a table that pairs each rule with the sentence that performs it in a written proof and, for readers who use a proof assistant, with the Lean code that does the same (Sections 1.2–1.6), and Chapter 2 added the rows for negation, the biconditional, and the classical rules (Sections 2.1–2.5). Sections 5.3–5.6 added a row for each quantifier rule, and this section adds the two rows for equality. Here is the whole table for the calculus of this volume. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule Shape You write ------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ulename{\wedge I} \varphi, \psi \Longrightarrow \varphi \wedge \psi “We show P, and we show Q.” ulename{\wedge E} \varphi \wedge \psi \Longrightarrow \varphi (or \psi) “In particular, P.” ulename{{	o}E} \varphi 	o \psi, \varphi \Longrightarrow \psi “Since P implies Q, and P holds, Q.” ulename{{	o}I} box \varphi … \psi \Longrightarrow \varphi 	o \psi “Assume P. … Hence Q.” ulename{R} \varphi (available) \Longrightarrow \varphi, copied “As shown above, P.” ulename{\vee I} \varphi \Longrightarrow \varphi \vee \psi (or \psi \vee \varphi) “So P or Q holds.” ulename{\vee E} \varphi \vee \psi, box \varphi … \chi, box \psi … \chi \Longrightarrow \chi “Case 1: P. … so R. Case 2: Q. … so R. In either case, R.” ulename{
eg E} \varphi, 
eg\varphi \Longrightarrow  ot “…, which contradicts …” ulename{ ot E}  ot \Longrightarrow any \varphi “This case cannot occur.” “So there is nothing to prove.” ulename{
eg I} box \varphi …  ot \Longrightarrow 
eg\varphi “Suppose \varphi. … This is a contradiction. Hence not \varphi.” ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} box \varphi … \psi, box \psi … \varphi \Longrightarrow \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi “(\Rightarrow) Suppose P. … so Q. (\Leftarrow) Suppose Q. … so P.” ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi, \varphi \Longrightarrow \psi (or with \psi, \varphi) “Since P holds if and only if Q does, and P holds, so does Q.” ulename{RAA} box

(A reflexive relation contains equality.) B. Practice [B1: The identity is unique] A set with an operation \cdot has an identity e if e \cdot x = x and x \cdot e = x for every x. Derive  orall x\, (e \cdot x = x \wedge x \cdot e = x), \;\;  orall x\, (e' \cdot x = x \wedge x \cdot e' = x) \;\vdash\; e = e', where e and e' are constants. Which half of “there is exactly one identity” does this prove? Hint: look at the one element that both premises can say something about. The goal is an equation between e and e', and the only term that both premises can connect to both is the product e \cdot e'. Instantiate the first premise at e' and the second at e (ulename{ orall E}, reading the terms off the goal): Line 7 uses the equation e \cdot e' = e of line 6 to rewrite the left side of line 4, with \varphi = (z = e'): \varphi[e \cdot e'/z] is line 4, and \varphi[e/z] is e = e'. In prose: e = e \cdot e' = e', the first equation because e' is an identity and the second because e is. This is the “at most one” half: any two identities are equal. It says nothing about whether an identity exists. Section 5.8 shows how such an argument combines with existence. [B2: Rewrite, and turn round] A search for a = b, \ b = c, \ P(a) \vdash P(c) \wedge c = a has reached the stage below. Name the move, then complete it, giving for each ulename{{=}E} line its holes. The move is the search step “An equation” of this section: mark the holes, and turn the equation round with an ulename{{=}I} line if it points the wrong way. Lines 4 and 5: \varphi = P(z). Line 6: \varphi = (a = z), so line 1 is \varphi[b/z] and the equation b = c refills the hole with c. Line 8: \varphi = (z = a); line 7 is \varphi[a/z], and the equation a = c refills the box with c. title: 5.8 Unique Existence, Counting and Descriptions
content:
Unique Existence, Counting and Descriptions Mathematics says “the limit”, “the maximum”, “the inverse”, and it defines new words all the time: “we define \abs{x} to be …”, “call n even if …”. This section is about the logic behind both habits. It starts with “there is exactly one”, which licenses “the”. Then it counts with equality, turns “the x such that \varphi” into a name that may be used only after uniqueness is proved, and sets a function symbol beside its graph. Last, it shows why introducing a new symbol by a definition never proves anything new about the old ones. No new rule is needed: equality and the quantifiers do all the work. Unique existence Mathematics says “the limit of the sequence”, “the supremum of A”, “the additive inverse of a”. Each “the” makes two claims. There is such an object, and there is only one, so that the name picks it out. The second claim is the one that is easy to forget, and the one the claim at the start of Section 5.7 was about. “There is exactly one x with \varphi”: there is one, and any other is it. Unique Existence Let \varphi be a formula, x a variable, and y a variable other than x that does not appear in \varphi (Section 5.2). Then \exists! x\, \varphi \quad 	ext{abbreviates} \quad \exists x\,  igl( \varphi \wedge  orall y\, (\varphi[y/x] 	o y = x)  igr). We read \exists! x\, \varphi as “there is exactly one x such that \varphi”, or “there is a unique x with \varphi”. In words: there is an x that satisfies \varphi, and every y that satisfies \varphi (that is, satisfies \varphi with y in place of x) is equal to that x. The first conjunct is existence. The second is uniqueness, and it is a statement about the x already found: any other candidate coincides with it. Like the bounded quantifiers of @def-bounded-quantifier, \exists! is not a new symbol of the language but shorthand, and every rule applies to the formula it abbreviates. Well-definedness. The abbreviation does not depend on the choice of y, up to renaming a bound variable. The argument, in the fold below, rests on one fact about substitution that the proof of @prp-unique-existence-use uses again: if y does not appear in \varphi, then (\varphi[y/x])[t/y] is \varphi[t/x]. This is a structural induction on \varphi of the kind in Section 5.2. In a term, the y’s of s[y/x] are exactly the former x’s, so (s[y/x])[t/y] = s[t/x]; atomic formulas,  ot and the connectives follow clause by clause. For  orall x\, \psi, both sides are  orall x\, \psi, since substitution for x stops at  orall x and y does not appear in \psi (the second fact of Section 5.2). For  orall z\, \psi with z not x, also z is not y, because y does not appear in \varphi; so both substitutions pass under the quantifier and the induction hypothesis applies, and \exists is the same. Now let y and y' be two admissible choices. If they are the same variable there is nothing to show. Otherwise y' does not appear in \varphi[y/x] 	o y = x, since it is neither x nor y and does not appear in \varphi; so the bound y of  orall y\, (\varphi[y/x] 	o y = x) may be renamed y', which gives  orall y'\,  igl( (\varphi[y/x])[y'/y] 	o y' = x  igr). By the fact with t = y', this is  orall y'\, (\varphi[y'/x] 	o y' = x), the formula written with y'. Examples. Simplest first; each is read over the domain named, with the informal truth of Section 5.1. 1. Over 
R, \exists! x\, (x + 2 = 5) is true. Existence: 3 + 2 = 5. Uniqueness: if y + 2 = 5, then subtracting 2 gives y = 3, so y is the x already found. 2. Over 
N, \exists! x\, (x \cdot x = 4) is true. Existence: 2 \cdot 2 = 4. Uniqueness: for a natural number y, if y \le 1 then y \cdot y \le 1, and if y \ge 3 then y \cdot y \ge 9; so y \cdot y = 4 forces y = 2. 3. Over 
R, \exists! x\,  orall y\, (x + y = y) is true: 0 is the unique additive identity. Existence: 0 + y = y for every y. Uniqueness: suppose z + y = y for every y. Apply this to the one instance y = 0 (by ulename{ orall E}): z + 0 = 0. Since also z + 0 = z, symmetry and transitivity give z = 0. The whole uniqueness proof is the choice of the instance y = 0. Nonexample by minimal change. Keep example 2 and change the domain to 
Z. Existence still holds, with the same witness 2. Uniqueness fails: y = -2 also satisfies y \cdot y = 4, and -2 
e 2. So over 
Z, \exists! x\, (x \cdot x = 4) is false, and the failing clause is exactly the second conjunct. Is \exists! x\, (x < 1) true over 
N? Over 
Z? Over 
N, yes: 0 < 1, and every natural number below 1 is 0. Over 
Z, no: existence holds, and uniqueness fails, since 0 and -1 are both below 1. Why y must not appear in \varphi. The condition keeps the new quantifier  orall y from capturing anything of \varphi’s own. Take \varphi = (x \le y), in which y is free, and read over 
N with y naming 0. “There is exactly one natural number x with x \le 0” is true: x = 0. The formula written with the forbidden bound variable y is \exists x\,  igl( x \le y \wedge  orall y\, (y \le y 	o y = x)  igr), because (x \le y)[y/x] is y \le y. Its second conjunct says that every natural number equals x, which is false. The free y of \varphi, which was to name 0, has been captured by  orall y. With an admissible variable, say z, the formula is \exists x\,  igl( x \le y \wedge  orall z\, (z \le y 	o z = x)  igr), which is true. Degenerate. For any constant c, \exists! x\, (x = c) holds in every domain, and it is derivable from no premises (the derivation follows). By contrast, \exists! x\, (x = x) says that the domain has exactly one element, which is false in 
N, 
Z and 
R: existence holds and uniqueness fails. The derivation of \exists! x\, (x = c), with the abbreviation written out, shows that \exists! needs no rules of its own: Line 3 closes a box whose only line is its assumption: the box shows y_0 = c 	o y_0 = c, as P 	o P is shown in Chapter 1. Line 6 is ulename{\exists I} with the witness c, and it reads line 5 as \psi[c/x] for \psi =  igl( x = c \wedge  orall y\, (y = c 	o y = x)  igr), which marks with x the first c and the last one, and keeps the other two. The choice of which occurrences to mark is the one discussed with @def-rule-existential-introduction. Uniqueness is not existence. A uniqueness argument (“suppose y also satisfies \varphi; then y = x”) proves nothing about whether anything satisfies \varphi. Over 
R, every two solutions of x^2 = -1 are equal, vacuously, because there are none; yet no real number is “the” square root of -1. Conversely, an existence proof does not give uniqueness: x^2 = 1 has the solution 1, and “the solution” would be wrong, since -1 is another. Before writing “the”, check both halves. How uniqueness is used and proved A proof of “exactly one” rarely follows the shape of @def-unique-existence, which ties the uniqueness clause to the witness just found. It proves two separate statements: there is at least one, and there is at most one. The second is “any two objects with the property are equal”, and it makes no mention of a witness. The next result says that the two shapes say the same thing. [Two Halves of Unique Existence] Let \varphi be a formula, x a variable, and y a variable other than x that does not appear in \varphi. Then \exists! x\, \varphi \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists x\, \varphi \wedge  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( \varphi \wedge \varphi[y/x] 	o x = y  igr). The right-hand side is “existence and at most one”. Its second conjunct is what a mathematician proves under the heading “uniqueness”: take two objects x and y with the property, and show x = y. Both directions are searches in the style of Section 3.1 with the quantifier steps. For \vdash, the premise is an \exists, so open its ulename{\exists E} box first, with a witness x_0: inside it, \varphi[x_0/x] gives existence at once by ulename{\exists I}, and “at most one” is a  orall orall goal, which opens two flagged boxes u_0, v_0. Two objects u_0, v_0 with the property are each equal to the witness x_0, by the uniqueness clause, and so equal to each other: the witness is the “third point” that links them. For \dashv, open the ulename{\exists E} box on \exists x\, \varphi with a witness x_0; the goal inside is \exists! x\, \varphi, whose witness will be x_0 again, and the uniqueness clause for x_0 comes from “at most one” applied to the pair x_0, y_0. The two derivations that carry this out are in the fold below. Choose four distinct variables x_0, u_0, v_0, y_0 that do not appear in \varphi, and none of which is x or y. Three facts about substitution are used throughout. First, since y does not appear in \varphi, (\varphi[y/x])[t/y] is \varphi[t/x] for every term t, the fact proved for the well-definedness of @def-unique-existence. Second, \varphi[y/x] has no free x (every free x became y), so it is unchanged by a substitution for x. Third, for a term t that does not contain y, \varphi[t/x] contains no y, so it is unchanged by a substitution for y. (\vdash) The following is a derivation with premise \exists! x\, \varphi, written out. Lines 9 and 11 are ulename{ orall E} on line 4 at u_0 and at v_0, by the first substitution fact; each term is a variable not bound in \varphi[y/x] 	o y = x_0, so it is free for y there. Lines 13 and 14 are the symmetry of @prp-equality-symmetric-transitive (a), written out; line 15 is ulename{{=}E} with the equation x_0 = v_0 and \psi = (u_0 = z), which turns line 10 into u_0 = v_0. Line 17 is ulename{ orall I} with the flag v_0: line 16 is its instance at v_0 (by the third and first substitution facts), and v_0 appears in no premise, in no assumption still open at line 17 (only line 2 is, and v_0 is not in it), and not in line 17. Line 18 is ulename{ orall I} with the flag u_0 in the same way; its instance at u_0 is line 17, by the second substitution fact. Finally, line 20 closes the ulename{\exists E} box: its last line 19 does not contain x_0, and x_0 is in neither line 1 nor any open assumption. (\dashv) The following is a derivation with the right-hand side as premise. Line 6 is ulename{ orall E} at x_0 on line 3, by the second substitution fact, and line 7 is ulename{ orall E} at y_0 on line 6, by the third and first. Lines 10 and 11 are symmetry, written out. Line 13 is ulename{ orall I} with the flag y_0: line 12 is its instance at y_0, by the first substitution fact; at line 13 the open assumptions are line 4, which does not contain y_0, the premise does not contain it either, and neither does line 13. Lines 4 and 5 instantiate the premise for f at the compound terms g(x_0) and g(y_0): the move instantiate at the term you need. In prose: “Let x and y satisfy f(g(x)) = f(g(y)). Since f is one-to-one, g(x) = g(y), and since g is one-to-one, x = y.” Marking scheme. (10 points) 2: the two flags and the ulename{{	o}I} box. 4: the ulename{ orall E} steps at g(x_0), g(y_0), then at x_0, y_0, each with ulename{{	o}E}. 2: the closing ulename{ orall I} lines with the flag checks. 2: the prose, one sentence per use of one-to-one. Fatal error (0 for the derivation): the premise for f instantiated at x_0, y_0. C. Going deeper [C1: Two unique quantifiers do not commute] Show that \exists! x\, \exists! y\, R(x, y) and \exists! y\, \exists! x\, R(x, y) can have different truth values, by giving a finite domain D and a two-place relation R on it for which the first is true and the second false. Check both, reading \exists! informally. Hint: first say in words what each sentence claims about the rows and columns of a table of R. What any answer must satisfy. Call x single if exactly one y has R(x, y), and call y co-single if exactly one x has R(x, y). The first sentence says that exactly one element is single. The second says that exactly one element is co-single. So an answer needs exactly one single element and a number of co-single elements other than one: none, or two or more. An example. Take D = \{0, 1, 2\} and R = \{(1, 2), (2, 0), (2, 1)\}. - Single elements: 0 has no partner, 1 has exactly one (2), and 2 has two (0 and 1). So 1 is the only single element, and \exists! x\, \exists! y\, R(x, y) is true, with the witness 1. - Co-single elements: y = 0 is reached only from x = 2; y = 1 only from x = 2; y = 2 only from x = 1. All three are co-single, so there is not exactly one, and \exists! y\, \exists! x\, R(x, y) is false. No example exists on one or two elements (there are only 2 + 16 = 18 relations on such domains). On one element, 0 is single and co-single exactly when R(0, 0) holds, so the two sentences agree. On two elements, suppose exactly one element is single; after relabeling, call it 0, and let c be its only partner. Then 1 is not single, so it has no partners or two. If it has none, column c has one entry and the other column has none. If it has two, column c has two entries and the other column has one. Either way exactly one element is co-single. Exchanging the roles of rows and columns gives the converse, so the two sentences have the same truth value. Three elements is therefore the smallest possible domain. The moral: \exists! is not a quantifier that commutes with its own kind, as two \exists’s do. “Exactly one” hides a  orall (the uniqueness clause), and the order of a  orall and an \exists matters. [C2: “At most one”, two ways] Let P be a one-place predicate symbol. Derive both directions of  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( P(x) \wedge P(y) 	o x = y  igr) \;\dashv\vdash\; 
eg\exists x\, \exists y\,  igl( (P(x) \wedge P(y)) \wedge x 
e y  igr), and say which of your two derivations uses ulename{RAA}, and at which line. [Hint 1] The right-hand side is a negation: for \vdash, open a ulename{

By @prp-unique-existence-use, the first premise gives \exists x\, P(x) and “at most one P”, and the second gives \exists x\, Q(x) and “at most one Q” (ulename{\wedge E}). 2. Without it the conclusion breaks: the domain \{0\} with P and Q both true of 0 makes the first two premises true, and only one object satisfies P(x) \vee Q(x). Marking scheme. (10 points) 2: the two halves of each premise by @prp-unique-existence-use. 1: two ulename{\exists E} boxes with different names. 2: a_0

Review [R1] Consider the terms built from variables, the constant 0 and the two-place function symbol +. Show that in every such term the number of occurrences of + is one less than the number of occurrences of variables and constants, counted together. Check it on (x + 0) + (y + x). For a term t, let a(t) count the occurrences of variables and constants in t, and p(t) those of +. We show p(t) = a(t) - 1 for every t, by induction on the clauses of @def-term, the method of @thm-structural-induction (Section 4.3). Base: t is a variable or 0. Then p(t) = 0 and a(t) = 1. Step: t is t_1 + t_2, and the claim holds for t_1 and t_2. Then p(t) = p(t_1) + p(t_2) + 1 = (a(t_1) - 1) + (a(t_2) - 1) + 1 = a(t_1) + a(t_2) - 1 = a(t) - 1. title: Working with Quantifiers: Translation, Laws and Search
content:
Working with Quantifiers: Translation, Laws and Search A first course in analysis defines “a_n 	o L” with three quantifiers and two bounds, then asks for a proof that a sequence does not converge, which starts from its negation. Chapter 5 gave the rules one per section; this chapter puts them to work: turning a definition into a formula, negating and rearranging it by laws, and finding the derivation a claim needs. You know every quantifier rule. Can you turn a definition from analysis into a formula, negate it without error, and find the derivation it needs? It ends where Chapter 5 began: why “uniformly continuous implies continuous” has a short derivation and a false converse. [Looking back] Chapter 3 did for the connectives what this chapter does for the quantifiers. Section 3.3 turned arguments in words into derivations; Section 6.1 does the same for definitions with quantifiers. Section 3.2 sorted the tasks, and Section 3.1 gave the search method; Section 6.3 does both again, with flags and witnesses. Section 6.2 collects the equivalences the tasks keep using. Section 6.4 has no twin: it is the chapter’s capstone. What you need. Chapters 1–5. From Chapter 3: the search method (Section 3.1) and the four kinds of task (Section 3.2). From Chapter 4: truth tables and semantic entailment (@def-valid-argument), completeness (@thm-completeness), the move test the subgoal (Section 4.7) and the TAUT step for propositional formulas (@def-rule-taut). From Chapter 5: the four quantifier rules with their side conditions (@def-rules-universal, @def-rules-existential), bounded quantifiers and the convention for mixing kinds of number (@def-bounded-quantifier), substitution, free-for and renaming (Section 5.2), equality (Section 5.7), and counter-readings (Section 5.3). School arithmetic and the order of 
N, 
Z, 
R are used in examples as facts. Time. About 20 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 35 hours for everything. Minimum before Sets and Functions. Chapters 1–6 and 8, core; Sections 7.1–7.2 before its Section 4.1. How to read this chapter. Every section is on the first reading, with its folds closed. The folds hold the proofs of the bounded rules, of the replacement rule and of TAUT on the skeleton, the derivations of the distribution and passage laws, and short remarks on edge cases. They are not optional: later proofs may use them. Roadmap - Translating mathematics. Definitions from analysis as formulas, worked from the outside in; the bounded rules; five traps, each shown wrong by a reading; “infinitely many” against “eventually”. - Negating and moving quantifiers. “Not every” is “some not”; negation pushed inward by the replacement rule; the four forms A, E, I, O and their square; the laws that move a quantifier across a connective, and prenex form. - Finding first-order derivations. The search method with flags and witnesses; TAUT on the skeleton; the propositional core; the four kinds of task; a library of sequents and a battery. - Uniformly continuous implies continuous, rule by rule. The capstone derivation, the lines where the converse breaks, x^2 as the counter-reading, and witness functions \delta(\varepsilon) against \delta(x, \varepsilon). Named moves - Read it back. Read a translation back into words before using it. (Section 6.1) - Negate quantifier by quantifier. Push 
eg inward, swapping  orall and \exists, keeping the bounds. (Section 6.2) - Name the witness early, then instantiate at the term you need. Chapter 5’s two moves, in that order. (Section 6.3) - The propositional core. Instantiate at the names in play, reason propositionally, with TAUT, then close the boxes. (Section 6.3) - Test the subgoal by a counter-reading. Section 4.7’s move, with quantifiers. (Section 6.3) - Read the dependency off the boxes. A witness may depend only on the flags whose boxes enclose it. (Section 6.4) Where this goes. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves from the real-number axioms the facts about 
N in 
R and absolute value that Sections 6.1 and 6.2 use as school facts, and it uses “not every” gives “some not” (Section 6.2) in its proof of the Archimedean property. Its Chapters 5 and 6 define continuity and uniform continuity, which Section 6.4 uses only as quantifier patterns. Picking a witness for every \varepsilon at once, as one function (Section 6.4), in general appeals to the axiom of choice, which Sets and Functions, Chapter 6 states. Summary The bounded rules add no power (@prp-bounded-quantifier-rules). “Not every” is “some not”, with one direction classical (@prp-quantifier-negation); a negated implication is a conjunction (@prp-negated-implication); a bound stays with its quantifier (@prp-bounded-quantifier-negation). A part may be replaced anywhere by a provably equivalent part, by a syntactic induction (@prp-replacement); a step right for propositional reasons alone is derivable (@prp-taut-skeleton). The chapter translated and negated the definitions of analysis, and took the search method and the four tasks to quantifiers. The capstone derived “uniformly continuous implies continuous” (@exm-uniform-implies-continuous) and located the side conditions that stop the converse. What is open: every “break” here was a counter-reading. Does one rule out every derivation? Chapter 7 asks. Terms - A, E, I, O forms: every, no, some, some not (Section 6.2). - alternation: a  orall/\exists change in a prefix (Section 6.2). - bounded rules: abbreviations, no new power (@prp-bounded-quantifier-rules). - contradictory, contrary: exactly one true; never both true (Section 6.2). - negated implication: 
eg(\varphi 	o \psi) is \varphi \wedge 
eg\psi (@prp-negated-implication). - passage laws: move a quantifier across a connective (@prp-quantifier-passage). - prenex form: every quantifier at the front (Section 6.2). - propositional core: instantiate, reason propositionally, close (Section 6.3). - propositional skeleton: prime parts read as letters (@def-propositional-skeleton). - quantifier distribution:  orall over \wedge, \exists over \vee (@prp-quantifier-distribution). - quantifier negation: “not every” is “some not” (@prp-quantifier-negation). - replacement of provable equivalents: swap a part for an equivalent (@prp-replacement). - TAUT step, on the skeleton: propositionally right (@prp-taut-skeleton). - uniformly continuous: one \delta for all points (Section 6.4). - witness function: a witness depending on flags (Section 6.4).

title: 6.1 Translating Mathematics: Nested and Bounded Quantifiers
content:
Translating Mathematics: Nested and Bounded Quantifiers The calculus is now complete: Sections 5.3–5.7 gave a rule for using and a rule for proving each quantifier, and the two rules for equality. Before any of those rules can act on a definition from analysis, the definition has to be written as a formula, and written correctly. The definitions of analysis have three or four quantifiers stacked in a fixed order, most of them carrying a bound such as \varepsilon > 0 or n \ge N, and every bound costs extra lines in a derivation. This section does three things. It translates the standard definitions into formulas, by a procedure that works from the outside in. It turns each quantifier rule into a bounded rule that handles the bound in the same step. And it collects the traps that make a translation wrong, each with a reading that shows the wrong formula wrong. [Looking back] Section 3.3 turned an argument in words into a derivation, with one key for a whole paragraph. This section does the same for definitions with quantifiers. What is new is the order of the quantifiers and the bounds they carry, which the propositional key never had. Four pieces in one sentence “The sequence (a_n) converges to L” is written a_n 	o L, and a first course defines it in one breath: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is N \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for all n \ge N. The sentence has three quantifiers, each with a bound (\varepsilon > 0, N \in 
N, n \in 
N), and a fourth condition, n \ge N, hidden in “for all n \ge N”, which will turn out to sit under an implication. Each piece has a job, and a slip in any piece changes the meaning: - drop the bound \varepsilon > 0, and the challenger may choose \varepsilon = -1; then \abs{a_n - L} < -1 is impossible, and no sequence converges; - swap “for every \varepsilon” and “there is N”, and one N must serve every \varepsilon; then only sequences that are eventually equal to L converge; - read “for all n \ge N” as “for all n”, and the first terms must already be close to L; then 1,  rac12,  rac13, \dots converges to nothing. So translation deserves a procedure, and the rules deserve a form that handles bounds without fuss. We take them in that order. Translation from the outside in Find the outermost claim, name its quantifier and its bound, then translate what it claims about each object, in the same way. The procedure, in three steps: 1. Fix the domain. State what the variables range over. The logic of this book has a single domain for all the variables of a formula. Mathematics often mixes kinds of objects in one sentence: in “for every \varepsilon > 0 there is an N \in 
N such that for every n \ge N, …”, the letter \varepsilon is a real number, while N and n are natural numbers. The convention is: the domain is the larger kind (here 
R), and the smaller kind enters as a bound (\exists N \in 
N,  orall n \in 
N). So the sentence begins  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists N \in 
N \;  orall n \in 
N \;  igl( n \ge N 	o \dots  igr), and n ranges over real numbers that happen to be required, by the bound, to be natural numbers. A sequence (a_n) becomes a function symbol a, with a(n), written a_n, the n-th term. Its values at real numbers that are not natural numbers are never used, because a is only ever applied to variables bounded by n \in 
N. Section 5.1 stated this convention in one sentence (“Mixing kinds of number”); here it is in full, and every translation in this chapter follows it. 2. Find the outermost claim. Ask what the sentence says first, before any detail: “every \varepsilon > 0 has a property”, “there is an M with a property”, “no prime is largest”. That gives the outermost quantifier (or connective) and its bound. 3. Recurse. Translate the property, which is a sentence about the object just quantified, by the same two steps. Stop at atomic formulas: equations, inequalities, membership, and predicate symbols such as \mathrm{Prime}(m). A bound is attached to its own quantifier with the connective of @def-bounded-quantifier: 	o under  orall, \wedge under \exists. The bounded notation  orall \varepsilon > 0, \exists N \in 
N does this automatically, which is why we use it. A mixed stage. Halfway through, a translation is part words and part symbols, and writing that stage down catches most slips. Take “for every positive \varepsilon, some element of A lies within \varepsilon of s”. Each line below translates one more quantifier and leaves the rest in words, in square brackets, until no words are left:  egin{aligned} & orall \varepsilon > 0 \; [	ext{some element of } A 	ext{ lies within } \varepsilon 	ext{ of } s] \ & orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists x \in A \; [x 	ext{ lies within } \varepsilon 	ext{ of } s] \ & orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists x \in A \; (\abs{x - s} < \varepsilon) \end{aligned} Read the last line back, symbol by symbol, into words: if the words are the sentence you began with, the translation is done. [Five definitions, translated] Translate each sentence into a formula, stating the domain. 1. a_n 	o L: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is N \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N. 2. The set A of real numbers is bounded above. 3. The function f \colon 
R 	o 
R is continuous at a: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon for every real x with \abs{x - a} < \delta. 4. There is no largest prime. 5. Every integer greater than 1 has a prime divisor. (a) Domain 
R. The outermost claim is about every \varepsilon > 0:  orall \varepsilon > 0. What it says about \varepsilon is that some natural number N works: \exists N \in 
N. What it says about N is that every natural number n from N on is good:  orall n \in 
N, with the further condition n \ge N under an implication. So  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists N \in 
N \;  orall n \in 
N \;  igl( n \ge N 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon  igr). The phrase “for every n \ge N” carries two bounds on n, membership in 
N and n \ge N; the first is a bounded quantifier, the second the hypothesis of the implication. The free variable is L (and the statement is also about the function symbol a, which is not a variable). (b) Domain 
R; A names a set of reals, and x \in A is a one-place predicate of x (Section 5.1). “Bounded above” means that some real number is at least every element of A. Outermost claim: there is an M. Rules for Bounded Quantifiers Let A be a fixed set, so that \in A is a one-place predicate symbol (Section 5.2), x a variable and \varphi a formula. The following four rules, the bounded rules, may be used in derivations, with the rule names of the unbounded rules and the same side conditions: in  orall x \in A \; ulename{E} and \exists x \in A \; ulename{I}, the term t is free for x in \varphi; in  orall x \in A \; ulename{I}, the name x_0 appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at line k, and not in  orall x \in A\; \varphi; in \exists x \in A \; ulename{E}, it appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at line k, and not in \chi or in \exists x \in A\; \varphi. The last line of each box is a line of that box itself. Every use of a bounded rule can be replaced by a block of steps of the unbounded rules (Sections 5.3–5.6) and of Chapter 1, with the same premises, the same assumptions open, and the same last line. Hence any derivation that uses the bounded rules converts into one that does not. The same holds with x \in A and t \in A replaced by x > a and t > a, or by the bounds \ge a, < a, \le a, for a term a in which x does not occur. In words: to use “every x in A has \varphi”, produce an element t of A and conclude \varphi for t. To prove “some x in A has \varphi”, exhibit an element t of A with \varphi. To prove “every x in A has \varphi”, let x_0 be an arbitrary element of A (the box opens with the assumption x_0 \in A) and prove \varphi for it. To use “some x in A has \varphi”, take such an element x_0, with both facts about it as assumptions, and derive something that does not mention it. These are exactly the sentences a mathematician writes: “let \varepsilon > 0”, “since \delta > 0, the hypothesis applies to \delta”, “take N = 7 \in 
N”, “choose \delta > 0 such that …”. The bounded ulename{ orall I} box is the only flagged box with an assumption that closes by ulename{ orall I}. Its assumption x_0 \in A mentions the flag, and that is allowed: the side condition asks about assumptions of boxes still open at line k, and the box’s own assumption has closed there.
