N and 2 3 + 3 = 6. What does the bounded ulename{\exists I} 1, 2 give, with \varphi the formula n + n = 6? 12. How many lines does a bounded ulename{\exists E} save over the unbounded rule? (a) \exists M\;  orall x \in A\; (f(x) \le M). (b)  orall x \in A\; \exists y \in B\; (x < y). (c) \exists x \in A\;  orall y \in B\; (x < y). (d) \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge  orall y\, (y \in B 	o x < y)). (e)  orall x \in A\; [	ext{some element of } A 	ext{ is larger than } x], then  orall x \in A\; \exists y \in A\; (x < y). (f) \exists N \in 
N\;  orall n \in 
N\; (n \ge N 	o a_n > 0). (g)  orall N \in 
N\; \exists n \in 
N\; (n \ge N \wedge a_n \le 0). (h) 
eg orall x \in A\; (x > 0), true for \{-1, 1\} (because of -1); 
eg\exists x \in A\; (x > 0), or  orall x \in A\; 
eg(x > 0), false (because of 1). One word apart, opposite truth values. (i) \exists x\, (x \cdot x < 0) 	o 0 = 1: “any” after “if” is “some”. It is true, since no real square is negative. (j) \varphi[1/\varepsilon]. (k) \exists n \in 
N\; (n + n = 6). (l) One: two assumptions in place of one assumption and two ulename{\wedge E} lines. B. Practice [B1: Three definitions] Formalize each statement, stating the domain and the kind of each symbol (variable, constant, function symbol, predicate symbol; membership \in A in a fixed set A is a one-place predicate symbol, as in Section 5.2). 1. The set A of real numbers is bounded (above and below). 2. The function f \colon 
R 	o 
R is increasing on A: for all x, y \in A, x < y implies f(x) \le f(y). 3. The sequence (a_n) is bounded: there is a real M with \abs{a_n} \le M for all n. Then, for (c), write the formula with the two quantifiers in the other order, and say why it holds for every sequence. No constants occur in any of the three parts. (a) Domain 
R; m, M, x variables (all bound); \in A a one-place and \le a two-place predicate symbol. \exists m\, \exists M\,  orall x \in A\, (m \le x \wedge x \le M). The two witnesses are chosen before x, so they must work for every element of A. (b) Domain 
R; x, y variables (bound); f a one-place function symbol; \in A a one-place and <, \le two-place predicate symbols.  orall x \in A\;  orall y \in A\;  igl( x < y 	o f(x) \le f(y)  igr). (c) Domain 
R; M, n variables (bound); a a one-place function symbol (the one-domain convention, step 1 of the procedure), and \abs{\cdot} a one-place function symbol; \in 
N a one-place and \le a two-place predicate symbol. \exists M\;  orall n \in 
N\; (\abs{a_n} \le M). Swapped:  orall n \in 
N\; \exists M\; (\abs{a_n} \le M). It holds for every sequence, because the witness may depend on n: take M = \abs{a_n}. The sequence a_n = n, which is not bounded, satisfies it. As in @exm-quantifier-order-sum, the swap turns a statement about one M for all n into a statement about each term separately. [B2: A bounded rehearsal] Using the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules, derive  orall x \in A \; (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \;\; \exists x \in A \; P(x) \;\vdash\; \exists x \in A \; Q(x). Then say how many lines the derivation would have with the unbounded rules only. The goal is an \exists: postpone it. The second premise is an \exists: open its bounded ulename{\exists E} box at once, with a witness x_0 and the two assumptions x_0 \in A and P(x_0), and aim for the goal as the box’s last line. Inside, the first premise is a  orall x \in A, and the term the box offers is x_0, with its bound on a line. The witness for the goal is x_0 again. At line 8, x_0 is not in line 8, not in line 2, and not in either premise; no other box is open. The derivation uses three bounded steps (lines 5, 7 and 8), each of which costs one more line unbounded, so the unbounded derivation has 8 + 3 = 11 lines: the ulename{\exists E} box assumes x_0 \in A \wedge P(x_0) and splits it with two ulename{\wedge E} lines; line 5 becomes ulename{ orall E} then ulename{{	o}E}; line 7 becomes ulename{\wedge I} then ulename{\exists I}. The bound is the whole point of the exercise: the witness x_0 must carry its membership in A from the premise to the conclusion, and the bounded rules make that one assumption and one citation. [B3: One key, twenty sentences] The domain is 
N = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}. Use only \mathrm{Prime}(x) (“x is prime”), \mathrm{Even}(x), x < y, x \mid y (“x divides y”, that is, y = x \cdot k for some k), = and the constants 1, 2, 9, with variables x, y, z. Translate sentences 1–18 into formulas. Then translate 19 and 20 into English and decide whether each is true. 1. 2 is an even prime. 2. Some prime divides 9. 3. Every prime greater than 2 is odd. 4. No prime is less than 2. 5. Every even number is divisible by 2. 6. Only odd numbers divide 9. 7. 1 divides every number. 8. Some number divides every number. 9. Every number is divisible by some number. 10. There is no largest prime. 11. There are infinitely many primes. 12. Every number greater than 1 has a prime divisor. 13. The only divisors of a prime are 1 and the prime itself. 14. If a number divides 2, it is 1 or 2. 15. Not every odd number is prime. 16. Between any two numbers, one less than the other, there is a third. 17. Some prime divides every even number. 18. Every divisor of 1 is 1. 19.  orall x\,  orall y\, ((x \mid y \wedge y \mid x) 	o x = y). 20.  orall x\, (\mathrm{Even}(x) 	o \exists y\, (\mathrm{Prime}(y) \wedge y \mid x \wedge 
eg(y = 2))). 1. \mathrm{Even}(2) \wedge \mathrm{Prime}(2). 2. \exists x\, (\mathrm{Prime}(x) \wedge x \mid 9). 3.  orall x\, ((\mathrm{Prime}(x) \wedge 2 < x) 	o 
eg\mathrm{Even}(x)). 4. 
eg\exists x\, (\mathrm{Prime}(x) \wedge x < 2), or  orall x\, (\mathrm{Prime}(x) 	o 
eg(x < 2)). 5.  orall x\, (\mathrm{Even}(x) 	o 2 \mid x). 6.  orall x\, (x \mid 9 	o 
eg\mathrm{Even}(x)). 7.  orall x\, (1 \mid x). 8. \exists x\,  orall y\, (x \mid y). 9.  orall y\, \exists x\, (x \mid y). 10.  orall x\, (\mathrm{Prime}(x) 	o \exists y\, (\mathrm{Prime}(y) \wedge x < y)). 11.  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y \wedge \mathrm{Prime}(y)). 12.  orall x\, (1 < x 	o \exists y\, (\mathrm{Prime}(y) \wedge y \mid x)). 13.  orall x\, (\mathrm{Prime}(x) 	o  orall y\, (y \mid x 	o (y = 1 \vee y = x))). 14.  orall x\, (x \mid 2 	o (x = 1 \vee x = 2)). 15. 
eg orall x\, (
eg\mathrm{Even}(x) 	o \mathrm{Prime}(x)). 16.  orall x\,  orall y\, (x < y 	o \exists z\, (x < z \wedge z < y)). 17. \exists x\, (\mathrm{Prime}(x) \wedge  orall y\, (\mathrm{Even}(y) 	o x \mid y)). 18.  orall x\, (x \mid 1 	o x = 1). 19. “Two numbers that divide each other are equal.” True in 
N: if y = xk and x = yl, then x = xkl, so either x = 0, and then y = 0 too, or kl = 1, which in 
N means k = l = 1. 20. “Every even number has a prime divisor other than 2.” False: at x = 2, and at every power of 2 (4, 8, 16, 32, \dots), the only prime divisor is 2. Sentence 10 restricts x to primes and 11 does not; both are true, and in 
N each follows from the other. Sentence 16 is false (take x = 0, y = 1), and its translation is still correct: a correct translation of a false sentence is a false formula. [B4: Unfold, then fold back] Over 
R, for fixed sets A, B, C of reals, write A \subseteq B for “every element of A is an element of B”, A \cup B for the set of reals in A or in B, and A \cap B for the set of those in both. Use only the predicates \in A, \in B, \in C. 1. Unfold A \subseteq B \cap C. 2. Unfold A \cup B \subseteq C. 3. Unfold “A \cap B has no element”. 4. Fold back  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in B) \wedge  orall x\, (x \in B 	o x \in C). 5. Fold back  orall x\, ((x \in A \wedge x \in B) 	o x \in C). 6. A reader unfolds A \cup B \subseteq C as the formula in (e). Give sets that separate the two, and say why the reader’s formula is wrong. (a)  orall x\, (x \in A 	o (x \in B \wedge x \in C)). (b)  orall x\, ((x \in A \vee x \in B) 	o x \in C). (c) 
eg\exists x\, (x \in A \wedge x \in B). (d) A \subseteq B and B \subseteq C. (e) A \cap B \subseteq C. (f) A = \{1\}, B = \{2\}, C = \emptyset. Then A \cup B \subseteq C is false, since 1 \in A \cup B and 1 
otin C. The formula of (e) is true, because A \cap B has no element, so its hypothesis x \in A \wedge x \in B is false for every x. The reader’s mistake is trap (b) of the section: “in A or in B” is the restriction of (b), and it must be written with \vee; the “and” of “every element of A and of B” is an “or” in the restriction. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a)–(c) together, with every bound attached by 	o under  orall (and by \wedge under the \exists of (c)). - 2: (d) and (e). - 3: (f): the two sets, with one sentence on each truth value. - 3: the reason in words that the restriction of (b) is an “or”. Fatal error (0 for (f)): a pair of sets on which the two formulas agree. C. Going deeper [C1: Where the  orall x stands] Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R and A \subseteq 
R. Translate, over 
R: 1. f is uniformly continuous on A: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that for all x, y \in A, \abs{x - y} < \delta implies \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon; 2. f is continuous at every point of A: for every x \in A and every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that for every y \in A, \abs{x - y} < \delta implies \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon. Then describe, in one sentence, the only difference between the two formulas, and say what it means for the choice of \delta. (a)  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon  igr). (b)  orall x \in A \;  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall y \in A \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon  igr). The only difference is the position of  orall x \in A: in (a) it stands after \exists \delta > 0, in (b) before it. In (b) the defender chooses \delta knowing x, so \delta may depend on x and on \varepsilon; in (a) \delta is chosen before any x is given, so one \delta must serve every x \in A at once, and it depends on \varepsilon only. Section 6.4 derives (b) from (a) and shows that x^2 on 
R satisfies (b) but not (a); Section 7.2 turns this example into a counter-model, so (b) does not derive (a). [C2: Six orders, four statements] Fix a formula \mu (the “matrix”) in the variables x, y, z, and consider the six sentences obtained by putting the prefixes  orall x, \exists y,  orall z in front of \mu in the six possible orders:  orall x\, \exists y\,  orall z\, \mu,  orall z\, \exists y\,  orall x\, \mu, and so on. Call two of these orders essentially the same if the two sentences are provably equivalent (\dashv\vdash) for every matrix \mu, and essentially different if some matrix over 
Z gives them different truth values (read informally, as in Section 5.1). 1. Show that the six orders fall into four groups, with any two orders in one group essentially the same. 2. Using the matrices y > x and y > z over 
Z, show that any two orders from different groups are essentially different. So the six orders say four different things. [Hint 1] Two  orall’s side by side can be exchanged: that was one of the derivations of @exm-universal-introduction-derivations. What is left to decide is where \exists y stands. [Hint 2] List the six orders by the position of \exists y: first, middle or last. When it is first or last, the two  orall’s are side by side. (a) Sort the orders by the position of \exists y. - \exists y first: \exists y\,  orall x\,  orall z\, \mu and \exists y\,  orall z\,  orall x\, \mu. - \exists y last:  orall x\,  orall z\, \exists y\, \mu and  orall z\,  orall x\, \exists y\, \mu. - \exists y in the middle:  orall x\, \exists y\,  orall z\, \mu, and  orall z\, \exists y\,  orall x\, \mu. Two adjacent  orall’s may be exchanged:  orall x\,  orall z\, \psi \dashv\vdash  orall z\,  orall x\, \psi for every formula \psi, by the derivation of @exm-universal-introduction-derivations that exchanges two universal quantifiers (it uses nothing about its matrix but that it is a formula). This gives the “last” pair at once. For the “first” pair the  orall’s sit under \exists y: open the ulename{\exists E} box on \exists y\,  orall x\,  orall z\, \mu with a witness y_0, exchange the two  orall’s inside it, and close with ulename{\exists I} at y_0; the other direction is the same. So there are at most four groups: \{\exists y\,  orall x\,  orall z, \ \exists y\,  orall z\,  orall x\}, \{ orall x\,  orall z\, \exists y, \  orall z\,  orall x\, \exists y\}, \{ orall x\, \exists y\,  orall z\} and \{ orall z\, \exists y\,  orall x\}. (b) Call the groups F (\exists y first), L (last), M_x ( orall x\, \exists y\,  orall z) and M_z ( orall z\, \exists y\,  orall x). Over 
Z, evaluate each group with the two matrices, reading informally (Section 5.1): ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Group \mu = (y > x) \mu = (y > z) ----------------------- ---------------------------------- ------------------------------- F false: no y exceeds every x false: no y exceeds every z L true: given x, z, take y = x + 1 true: take y = z + 1 M_x true: given x, take y = x + 1 false: no y exceeds every z M_z false: no y exceeds every x true: given z, take y = z + 1 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Every two rows differ in at least one column, so every two groups are separated by one of the two matrices: F from L, from M_x and from M_z by the column in which the other group has “true”; L from M_x by y > z and from M_z by y > x; M_x from M_z by either. So the six orders say four different things: within a group the sentences are provably equivalent by (a), and across groups some matrix over 
Z tells them apart. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: lists the six orders and sorts them by the position of \exists y. - 3: justifies the two collapses, citing the exchange of adjacent  orall’s, and handles the pair under \exists y (by an ulename{\exists E} box, or equivalently). - 3: gives, for each of the six pairs of groups, a matrix and the two truth values, with witnesses for the true sentences. - 2: concludes that the six orders say four different things, combining (a) and (b). Fatal errors (0 for the step): exchanging  orall with \exists; a “separation” in which the two sentences have the same truth value. [C3: Eventually, therefore infinitely often] 1. With the bounded rules, derive \exists N \in 
N\;  orall n \in 
N\; (n \ge N 	o P(n)) \;\vdash\;  orall M \in 
N\; \exists n \in 
N\; (n \ge M \wedge P(n)). Lines of arithmetic may be justified “arith”. 2. For the converse, give a reading of P over 
N under which the premise is true and the conclusion false. (a) The goal is a bounded  orall: open its box first, with M_0 \in 
N. The premise is a bounded \exists: open its box early, with N_0 \in 
N and its property. The postponed goal \exists n \in 
N needs a term that is at least M_0 and at which the premise applies, so at least N_0: the sum N_0 + M_0 is both. Lines 7 and 9 use M_0 \ge 0 and N_0 \ge 0, which hold for natural numbers. The side conditions: - At line 12, N_0 is not in line 12, not in line 1, not in the premise, and not in the open assumption on line 2. - At line 13, M_0 is not in the premise and not in line 13, and no assumption is open. - At lines 6 and 11, the term N_0 + M_0 is free for n. The witness N_0 + M_0 is built from the two names in play: fix M_0, obtain N_0, choose a term made from both. (b) Let P(n) be “n is even”. The premise of the converse,  orall M \in 
N\; \exists n \in 
N\; (n \ge M \wedge P(n)), is true: beyond any M there is an even number, such as 2M. Its conclusion, \exists N \in 
N\;  orall n \in 
N\; (n \ge N 	o P(n)), is false: beyond any N there is an odd number, 2N + 1. This is a counter-reading (Section 7.2). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: opens the flagged box of M_0 and the ulename{\exists E} box on the premise (in either nesting) before choosing the witness. - 3: a witness that depends on both names, with both bounds checked by arith lines. - 2: checks the side conditions at lines 12 and 13. - 3: (b): a reading, with both truth values justified. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a witness chosen before M_0 is given; the witness N_0 itself, which need not be at least M_0.

title: 6.2 Negating and Moving Quantifiers
content:
Negating and Moving Quantifiers To prove that a sequence does not converge, or that a function is not uniformly continuous, we must use the negation of a definition, and a negation is only usable once the 
eg has been pushed all the way in. “It is not the case that for every \varepsilon > 0 there is an N …” gives a proof nothing to hold. “There is an \varepsilon > 0 such that for every N there is an n \ge N with …” tells it what to find. Section 5.1 read the step from the first form to the second informally, as the challenger and the defender changing sides. This section derives the laws that make it exact, with the rules of Sections 5.3–5.6. Once they are proved, negating a definition is mechanical: one law per symbol, from the outside in. It then shows the laws at work, in an analysis proof in which a negation and a well-chosen \varepsilon do the work, and ends with the laws that move a quantifier across a connective, and with prenex form, where every quantifier stands at the front. [Looking back] Section 3.2 proved two statements equivalent by two derivations, one each way. Every law of this section is such a pair. What is new is that a law may now be used on a part of a formula buried under quantifiers, and the subsection on negating a definition says why that is safe. Not every, and some not Section 5.1 called the two quantifiers mirror images: a single counterexample refutes a “for every”, and a single witness confirms a “there exists”. The mirror suggests four sequents. “Not every x satisfies \varphi” should say the same as “some x fails \varphi”, and “no x satisfies \varphi” the same as “every x fails \varphi”. Three of the four directions come straight out of the search method. The fourth does not, and the reason it does not is worth a close look. To negate a quantifier, flip it and move the 
eg inside. In the derivations of this section, 
eg\varphi[x_0/x] means (
eg\varphi)[x_0/x], which is 
eg(\varphi[x_0/x]) by @def-substitution; the two readings give the same formula. The fresh name x_0 is always a variable different from x that does not appear in \varphi (or in \psi, when there is one); so it does not appear in  orall x\, \varphi or \exists x\, \varphi either. The side conditions of ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} need this, and it also makes x_0 free for x in \varphi (Section 5.2). [Quantifier Negation] Let \varphi be a formula and x a variable. 1. 
eg orall x\, \varphi \vdash \exists x\, 
eg\varphi, by a derivation that uses ulename{RAA}; 2. \exists x\, 
eg\varphi \vdash 
eg orall x\, \varphi, by a derivation that does not; 3. 
eg\exists x\, \varphi \dashv\vdash  orall x\, 
eg\varphi, both directions by derivations that do not use ulename{RAA}. Try it first (ten minutes): run the search method of Section 3.1, with the quantifier steps of Sections 5.3–5.6, on (a). Which rule should give the last line, and what would that rule need from the premise? Start with (a), and with the obstacle. The goal \exists x\, 
eg\varphi is an \exists, so the search postpones it until an available line shows an instance 
eg\varphi[t/x]. None ever does. The premise 
eg orall x\, \varphi is a negation, and a negation is used only by clashing it with what it negates,  orall x\, \varphi. It says that a counterexample exists and names none, so ulename{\exists I} has nothing to act on. We are stuck, and the last step of the method applies: assume 
eg\exists x\, 
eg\varphi, “no x fails \varphi”, and hunt for a clash. The clash will be with the premise, so the new goal is  orall x\, \varphi. Open a flagged box for it, with the goal \varphi[x_0/x]. That goal is again stuck (we know nothing about \varphi), so a second ulename{RAA} assumes 
eg\varphi[x_0/x]; and now an instance of 
eg\varphi is on a line, so ulename{\exists I} produces \exists x\, 
eg\varphi, which clashes with the outer assumption. For (b) and (c) the method runs without getting stuck. A negated goal opens a ulename{
eg I} box (Section 2.2); an \exists premise opens an ulename{\exists E} box early (Section 5.6); a  orall goal opens a flagged box (Section 5.4). The clash comes in one of two ways. In (b), and in (c) right to left, the instance assumed in the ulename{\exists E} box clashes with the matching instance that ulename{ orall E} takes from the  orall line. In (c) left to right, ulename{\exists I} turns the instance into \exists x\, \varphi, which meets the premise 
eg\exists x\, \varphi. For (a), the derivation: Line 4 is ulename{\exists I} at the term x_0, which is free for x in 
eg\varphi. At line 7 the side condition of ulename{ orall I} holds: x_0 does not appear in the premise, in the assumption 
eg\exists x\, 
eg\varphi still open at line 7, or in  orall x\, \varphi, since it is not x and does not appear in \varphi; and line 6 is the last line of the flagged box. For (b): At line 6, x_0 does not appear in  ot, in \exists x\, 
eg\varphi, in the premise, or in the assumption  orall x\, \varphi still open there. For (c), left to right and right to left: In the first, line 5 is the instance of 
eg\varphi at x_0, as ulename{ orall I} requires, and x_0 appears neither in the premise nor in  orall x\, 
eg\varphi; no assumption is open at line 6. In the second, the side condition of ulename{\exists E} at line 6 is checked as in (b). No line of the derivations of (b) and (c) is justified by ulename{RAA}, and the derivation of (a) uses it twice, at lines 6 and 9. This proves the proposition. So “not every” and “some not” are interderivable, and so are “none” and “every not”. The direction that cost two ulename{RAA} boxes is the one that produces an existential statement from a negative one. That is not an accident of our derivation: no derivation of (a) avoids ulename{RAA}. This is a claim about all derivations, which no search can establish, and we state it without proof (Chapter 4’s optional @thm-raa-independent proves the propositional analogue for 
eg
eg P \vdash P). From the line 
eg orall x\, P(x), may a derivation write 
eg P(c) for a constant c? If not, what may it write, and what does a derivation do next to use it? No. 
eg orall x\, P(x) says that some element fails P, not that the element named c does: over 
Z, with P read as “is even” and c as 0, 
eg orall x\, P(x) is true and 
eg P(0) is false. By (a) the derivation may write \exists x\, 
eg P(x). To use that line it opens an ulename{\exists E} box with a fresh witness x_0 and the assumption 
eg P(x_0) (Section 5.6), and nothing about c follows. The laws as one line. From now on a derivation may use any law of this section as one line, citing it, in the way @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules allows a bounded rule: the line abbreviates the derivation printed here, with \varphi (and \psi) replaced by the formulas at hand and the fresh name chosen so that it appears nowhere in the larger derivation. Then every side condition inside the pasted block still holds, since the block’s premises become lines of the larger derivation and the name is new to all of them. In a derivation the justification is a short tag: QN (a) for @prp-quantifier-negation (a), NIm for @prp-negated-implication below, and VI for @prp-vacuous-implication. The negation of an implication Every definition with a bounded  orall contains an implication,  orall x\, (x \in A 	o \varphi), so negating it means negating an implication. The answer is the one Section 5.1 found for the wrong translation of a bounded \exists: an implication fails exactly when its hypothesis holds and its conclusion does not. Chapter 3 met this law only as an exercise (@exr-finding-derivations-b1 (b)), and a proof in the text may not rest on an exercise, so we prove it here. [Negated Implication] For all formulas \varphi and \psi, 
eg(\varphi 	o \psi) \dashv\vdash \varphi \wedge 
eg\psi . The direction \vdash is derived with ulename{RAA}, and the direction \dashv without it. For \vdash the goal is a conjunction, so ulename{\wedge I} asks for \varphi and 
eg\psi separately. The premise is a negation, usable only to clash with \varphi 	o \psi, so in each part we manufacture \varphi 	o \psi. For 
eg\psi: open a ulename{
eg I} box on \psi; then \varphi 	o \psi follows by ulename{{	o}I}, whose box repeats \psi. For \varphi we are stuck, since \varphi has no known main connective; so ulename{RAA} assumes 
eg\varphi, and 
eg\varphi gives \varphi 	o \psi by @prp-vacuous-implication. For \dashv, the goal is a negation: assume \varphi 	o \psi and clash \psi with 
eg\psi. The two derivations: Line 3 of the first derivation uses @prp-vacuous-implication as a derived rule (@def-derived-rule), and line 8 repeats line 6 into the box, since ulename{{	o}I} needs \psi as a line of its own box. The only ulename{RAA} is at line 5. The derivations use only the rules of Chapters 1 and 2, so the law holds for statements as well as formulas, and it may be used as a derived rule in the sense of @def-derived-rule. Going deeper [C1: Two prenex forms] A formula is in prenex form when all its quantifiers stand at the front, before a part with no quantifier. Using the laws of @prp-quantifier-passage, bring  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y) into prenex form in two ways, ending with \exists x\, \exists y\, (P(x) 	o Q(y)) and with \exists y\, \exists x\, (P(x) 	o Q(y)). Justify each step, and say which directions of the laws are classical. [Hint 1] The formula is an implication with a quantifier on each side. Law (d) moves the quantifier out of the hypothesis, and law (e) moves it out of the conclusion. [Hint 2] For the first route, start with law (d), taking \psi to be the whole conclusion \exists y\, Q(y). First route: x out first. Law (d) of @prp-quantifier-passage, with \varphi the formula P(x) and \psi the formula \exists y\, Q(y), in which x is not free:  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y) \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists x\,  igl( P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y)  igr). Then law (e) under \exists x, with \psi the formula P(x), \varphi the formula Q(y), and y as the moving variable (y is not free in P(x)): P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y) \dashv\vdash \exists y\, (P(x) 	o Q(y)). A provable equivalence may be used under a quantifier (@prp-replacement), so \exists x\,  igl( P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y)  igr) \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists x\, \exists y\,  igl( P(x) 	o Q(y)  igr). Second route: y out first. Law (e), with \psi the formula  orall x\, P(x), \varphi the formula Q(y), and y as the moving variable (y is not free in  orall x\, P(x)):  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y) \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists y\,  igl(  orall x\, P(x) 	o Q(y)  igr). Then law (d) under \exists y, with \varphi the formula P(x) and \psi the formula Q(y) (x is not free in Q(y)): \exists y\,  igl(  orall x\, P(x) 	o Q(y)  igr) \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists y\, \exists x\,  igl( P(x) 	o Q(y)  igr). Classical steps. Going from the given formula towards the prenex form, every step of both routes uses the direction \dashv of (d) or of (e): the direction from the implication to the \exists. These are exactly the two directions that @prp-quantifier-passage derives with ulename{LEM}. The way back uses only the intuitionistic directions. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: first route, with law (d) then law (e), each with \varphi, \psi and the moving variable named, and the “not free” condition checked. - 3: second route, likewise with (e) then (d). - 2: says why a law may be applied under \exists x or \exists y (an equivalence used under a quantifier, by an ulename{\exists E} box closed with ulename{\exists I}). - 2: identifies the \dashv directions of (d) and (e) as the classical ones, used in every step towards prenex form. Fatal errors (0 for the step): moving  orall x out of the hypothesis as  orall x (it becomes \exists x); applying a passage law when the moving variable is free in \psi. [C2: Exit check: negations] 1. A sequence of functions f_n converges to f uniformly on A when  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists N \in 
N \;  orall n \in 
N \;  orall x \in A \;  igl( n \ge N 	o \abs{f_n(x) - f(x)} < \varepsilon  igr), where f_n(x) is a term in the two variables n and x. Negate this into positive form, citing the laws. 2. Using the negation of uniform continuity in @exm-negating-definitions (c), prove that f(x) = 1/x is not uniformly continuous on (0, 1). Give the witnesses that the negation asks for, each as a function of what is chosen before it, and check every condition. [Hint 1] For (b), the negation asks for one \varepsilon first. Near 0, the graph of 1/x is steep: two points close together have values far apart. [Hint 2] Take \varepsilon = 1 and let \delta > 0 be arbitrary. You must now find x, y \in (0, 1), depending on \delta, with \abs{x - y} < \delta and \abs{1/x - 1/y} \ge 1. (a) @prp-bounded-quantifier-negation four times, then @prp-negated-implication and the order fact: \exists \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall N \in 
N \; \exists n \in 
N \; \exists x \in A \;  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{f_n(x) - f(x)} \ge \varepsilon  igr). In words: for some \varepsilon > 0, however far out we start, some later f_n is at least \varepsilon away from f at some point of A. The point may change with n. (b) By @exm-negating-definitions (c), we must prove \exists \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall \delta > 0 \; \exists x \in (0, 1) \; \exists y \in (0, 1) \; \Bigl( \abs{x - y} < \delta \wedge \Bigl\lvert  rac1x -  rac1y \Bigrvert \ge \varepsilon \Bigr). Take \varepsilon = 1, which is positive. Let \delta > 0 be arbitrary, and let t \coloneqq \min(\delta, 	frac12), so 0 < t \le 	frac12 and t \le \delta; then take x \coloneqq t and y \coloneqq t/2, which depend on \delta. Check: - x, y \in (0, 1): 0 < t/2 < t \le 	frac12 < 1. - \abs{x - y} = t/2 < t \le \delta, since t > 0. - \abs{1/x - 1/y} = \abs{1/t - 2/t} = 1/t \ge 2 \ge 1 = \varepsilon, since t \le 	frac12. Since \delta > 0 was arbitrary, the negation of uniform continuity holds, so 1/x is not uniformly continuous on (0, 1). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) the negation, with every bound kept, \wedge in place of 	o, and the quantifiers in the order \exists \varepsilon\;  orall N\; \exists n\; \exists x \in A. - 2: (b) the witness \varepsilon, stated before \delta is given. - 2: for an arbitrary \delta > 0, points x and y given as functions of \delta. - 3: the three checks: x, y \in (0, 1); \abs{x - y} < \delta; \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \ge \varepsilon. A different correct choice earns full marks (for instance x = t, y = t/3); the scheme rewards the order of the choices and the checks. Fatal errors (0 for the step): \varepsilon chosen depending on \delta; points chosen before \delta is given, or not depending on it where they must; a bound negated instead of the quantifier (\exists \varepsilon \le 0, \exists n < N). [C3: “There exists” from “for every”] Suppose \exists were not a symbol of the language, and \exists x\, \varphi abbreviated 
eg orall x\, 
eg\varphi. 1. Show that ulename{\exists I} is then a derived step: from \varphi[t/x], with t free for x in \varphi, derive 
eg orall x\, 
eg\varphi. 2. Show that ulename{\exists E} is one too: if \Gamma, \varphi[x_0/x] \vdash \chi, where x_0 is a variable other than x that appears neither in \Gamma, nor in \chi, nor in \varphi, then \Gamma, 
eg orall x\, 
eg\varphi \vdash \chi. 3. Which of (a) and (b) uses a classical rule (ulename{RAA} or ulename{LEM})? [Hint 1] In (a) the goal is a negation: open a ulename{
eg I} box. [Hint 2] In (b) nothing in the premises can be taken apart; aim the clash at the premise 
eg orall x\, 
eg\varphi. (a) Five lines: Line 3 is ulename{ orall E} at t, which is free for x in 
eg\varphi because it is free for x in \varphi. (b) From the premises \Gamma and 
eg orall x\, 
eg\varphi: - assume 
eg\chi, for ulename{RAA}; - open a flagged box x_0, and in it assume \varphi[x_0/x], for ulename{
eg I}; - paste the given derivation of \chi, whose premises \Gamma are available. Its own flags are first renamed to names that appear nowhere else, as “The laws as one line” requires, so that the open assumption 
eg\chi cannot spoil its side conditions; - write  ot by ulename{
eg E} with 
eg\chi, and 
eg\varphi[x_0/x] by ulename{
eg I}; close the flagged box with  orall x\, 
eg\varphi by ulename{ orall I}. Here x_0 is in no premise, not in the open assumption 
eg\chi and not in  orall x\, 
eg\varphi; - write  ot by ulename{
eg E} with the premise 
eg orall x\, 
eg\varphi, and \chi by ulename{RAA}. (c) (b) uses one: ulename{RAA} at its last line (or ulename{LEM}, in a proof by cases); (a) uses neither. (Whether (b) could avoid a classical rule altogether is not asked.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a). - 2: (b)’s classical step (ulename{RAA}, or ulename{LEM} with a case split) and flagged box, in the right nesting. - 3: the side condition of the ulename{ orall I} line, including the renaming of the pasted flags. - 2: (c). Fatal errors (0 for the step): ulename{ orall I} on x_0 while \varphi[x_0/x] is still open; instantiating 
eg orall x\, 
eg\varphi by ulename{ orall E}.

title: 6.3 Finding First-Order Derivations
content:
Finding First-Order Derivations Chapter 5 added one step to the search method in each rule section, and Section 6.2 added laws. This section puts the steps into one method, puts in order the moves that do most of the work with quantifiers and names a third, admits the propositional step TAUT into derivations with quantifiers, and runs the four kinds of task of Section 3.2 again. The new difficulty is names: which term to instantiate at, when to open a box for a witness, and which names a line may mention when a box closes. [Looking back] Section 3.1 assembled the search method for the connectives, and Section 3.2 sorted the tasks it serves. Here both return with flags and witnesses. Backward from the goal and forward from the premises is unchanged; what is new is that a box may carry a name, and a closing line must not mention it. The search method, extended Section 3.1 put the moves for the connectives in order. Each of Sections 5.3–5.7 added a step. Here is the method with all of them. Searching for a derivation of \Gamma \vdash \varphi in predicate logic. 1. Set up. Write the premises \Gamma at the top and \varphi at the bottom, with one gap between. Translate any definition in words into a formula first, as in @exm-translate-limit. 2. Goal-directed step. Take the current goal’s main symbol and set up its introduction rule: - \wedge, 	o, 
eg, \leftrightarrow: as in Section 3.1; -  orall x\, \psi: open a flagged box with a fresh name x_0; the new goal, the box’s last line, is \psi[x_0/x] (Section 5.4). For  orall x \in A\; \psi, the box opens with the assumption x_0 \in A; - \vee: postpone, as in Section 3.1; - \exists x\, \psi: postpone; work on the premises until an available line shows a term t with \psi[t/x], then use ulename{\exists I} (Section 5.5). For \exists x \in A\; \psi, the line t \in A is needed too. Repeat while the goal is \wedge, 	o, 
eg, \leftrightarrow, or  orall. 3. Premise-directed step. Take the main symbol of a resource and apply its elimination rule: - \wedge, 	o, \vee, \leftrightarrow, and the derived rules: as in Section 3.1; - \exists x\, \psi: open the ulename{\exists E} box early, as soon as the line is available, with a fresh witness x_0, and make its last line the current goal, which must not mention x_0 (Section 5.6). An early box lets the witness serve the goals that come later; -  orall x\, \psi: do not instantiate blindly; instantiate at the term that the goal, or another resource, mentions (Section 5.3). For  orall x \in A\; \psi, the line t \in A is needed too; - an equation t_1 = t_2: use ulename{{=}E} with a \varphi chosen so that one substitution turns an available line into the goal, turning the equation round first if needed (Section 5.7). 4. Clash. As in Section 3.1: for the goal  ot, find or manufacture a pair \chi, 
eg\chi; an impossible case closes itself by ulename{ ot E}. 5. Stuck. As in Section 3.1: ulename{RAA} on the current goal, or ulename{LEM} on a well-chosen statement. When no gap is left, number the lines and check the derivation as @def-derivation, extended in Section 5.4, says: every citation is available, and every side condition holds (t free for x at ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists I}, bounded or not; t_1 and t_2 free for x at ulename{{=}E}; a fresh name at each line that closes a flagged box). Two of the new steps deserve a word on their place in the order. The goal step for  orall is safe in the same way as the goal steps for 	o and 
eg (Section 3.1): if  orall x\, \psi is derivable at all, then so is \psi[x_0/x] for a fresh x_0, by one more ulename{ orall E}; so opening the box loses nothing. The goal step for \exists is unsafe in the same way as the one for \vee: a witness chosen too early may be the wrong one, as in @exm-existential-introduction-derivations, where “take y = c” stalled. That is why \exists is postponed and the ulename{\exists E} boxes of the premises are opened early: the witnesses they supply are often the terms the postponed goal is waiting for, as N_0 was in the limit derivation of Section 6.1. Three moves for quantifiers Most first-order searches turn on three moves. The first two carry the names Chapter 5 gave them; what is new here is their order, which the method above already follows. Name the witness early (Section 5.6). When an \exists line is among the resources, open its box at once, with a fresh witness, and make the box’s last line the current goal. The witness costs nothing to name, and it is often the very term that a  orall line or the goal is waiting for. Instantiate at the term you need (Section 5.3), and so not before that term is known. A  orall line can be instantiated at any term at all, which is exactly why instantiating it before the goal or a witness names the term is a blind choice. Wait for the witnesses, then instantiate at them. The propositional core. Once the boxes are open and the  orall lines are instantiated, what is left is often a step that holds for propositional reasons alone. The subsection “The propositional core” below names this move and gives it a one-line step. Two pairs of steps recur: ulename{ orall E} followed by ulename{{	o}E}, which applies a general law at one point, and ulename{\exists E} followed, inside its box, by ulename{\exists I} with a term built from the names in hand. The next move, read off the goal and the lines in hand: The last edge reads “no”, not “impossible”: the chart is a guide to the next move, and it makes no claim that every derivable sequent is found by following it. It leaves out the premise-directed connective steps, the clash and the propositional core (TAUT, below); for those, follow the method above. [A search that waits for its witnesses] Show that  orall x\, (P(x) 	o \exists y\, R(x, y)), \  orall x\,  orall y\, (R(x, y) 	o Q(y)), \ \exists x\, P(x) \vdash \exists y\, Q(y). The goal is an \exists: postpone it. Premise 3 is an \exists: open its box now, with witness x_0 (left). Premise 1 is a  orall, and x_0 is now the term it needs: ulename{ orall E} then ulename{{	o}E} gives an \exists y line. Open that box at once, with witness y_0 (right). Premise 2 needs two terms, and both are in hand: x_0, then y_0. The postponed goal gets its witness, y_0. In the left snapshot the gap’s goal is still \exists y\, Q(y): an ulename{\exists E} box keeps the goal it was opened for, and its assumption, line 4, says “P(x_0)” and nothing more. In the right snapshot the same goal has moved one box further in, and line 7 is now the only line that asserts R of particular terms. At line 12, y_0 is not in line 12, in line 6, in the premises, or in the open assumption on line 4. At line 13, x_0 is not in line 13, in line 3, or in the premises, and no assumption is open. Read over 
Z, with P(x) as “x > 0”, R(x, y) as “y = 2x + 1” and Q(y) as “y is odd”: every positive integer has a 2x + 1; every number of the form 2x + 1 is odd; some integer is positive; so some integer is odd. Compare a search that starts with premise 1, before any witness is named. It must instantiate at some term, a variable or a constant that nothing mentions, say c; the line P(c) 	o \exists y\, R(c, y) then waits for P(c), which no premise gives. The box of premise 3 supplies the term that makes premise 1 usable. Why is line 8 an instance at x_0, and not at some other term? Line 7, the only line that asserts R of particular terms, mentions x_0 and y_0. Premise 2 is useful only at the terms that line names. This is the move “instantiate at the term you need”: the terms were known only once the witnesses were named. Steps that are right for propositional reasons Inside the boxes of a first-order derivation, many steps are propositional: ulename{\wedge E}, ulename{{	o}E}, a contrapositive, a case split. Section 4.8 let a propositional derivation take such steps in one line, as TAUT. With quantifiers the step must not look inside a quantifier, and the next definition says exactly what it may look at. [Propositional Skeleton] Call a first-order formula prime if it is atomic and not  ot, or begins with a quantifier, bounded or not. Assign to each prime formula a propositional atom, the same atom to two prime formulas exactly when one can be turned into the other by finitely many renamings of bound variables (Section 5.2), in either direction; this is an equivalence relation, so the assignment is well defined. The propositional skeleton \mathrm{sk}(\varphi) of a formula \varphi is defined by recursion: \mathrm{sk}( ot) =  ot; \mathrm{sk}(\pi) is the atom of \pi for a prime formula \pi; \mathrm{sk}(
eg\varphi) = 
eg\,\mathrm{sk}(\varphi); and \mathrm{sk}(\varphi \circ \psi) = \mathrm{sk}(\varphi) \circ \mathrm{sk}(\psi) for each of \wedge, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow. The formulas of one list take their skeletons from one assignment. The skeleton keeps the connectives outside every quantifier and hides everything else; this is not the skeleton of a derivation that Section 3.1 reads off the goal, and wherever the two could be confused, the book says “propositional skeleton” for this one. For example, \mathrm{sk} igl(  orall x\, P(x) 	o (\exists y\, R(y, c) \vee 
eg orall z\, P(z))  igr) = p 	o (q \vee 
eg p), since  orall x\, P(x) and  orall z\, P(z) differ only by renaming and so share the atom p. Why only renaming? The formulas  orall x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) and  orall x\, P(x) \wedge  orall x\, Q(x) are provably equivalent (@prp-quantifier-distribution (a)), yet the first is prime and the second is a conjunction of two prime formulas. If provable equivalence were allowed to merge atoms, the skeleton would depend on what has been derived, and a TAUT line could hide a quantifier step inside a table. Renaming is different: whether two formulas differ only by renaming bound variables can be seen by comparing them symbol by symbol, so anyone can compute the skeleton without a derivation. And  ot is kept as itself, not given an atom, so that 
eg ot is a tautology and a cited line  ot entails every skeleton, as ulename{ ot E} says it should; an atom would have neither property. [Tautological Steps on the Skeleton] Let \Gamma be a list of first-order formulas and \psi a formula, with skeletons taken from one assignment. If the skeletons of \Gamma semantically entail \mathrm{sk}(\psi) (@def-valid-argument), then \Gamma \vdash \psi. If no two different prime formulas occurring outside all quantifiers in \Gamma and \psi share an atom, the derivation uses only the rules of Chapters 1 and 2. In words: a step that is right for propositional reasons alone is derivable, with the quantified parts carried along untouched. The proof takes the propositional derivation that completeness provides and puts the prime formulas back in place of their atoms; it is in the fold below. Step 1: no two different prime formulas outside all quantifiers share an atom. By @cor-derivable-iff-valid (completeness, Section 4.8) there is a derivation D of \mathrm{sk}(\Gamma) \vdash \mathrm{sk}(\psi) with the rules of Chapters 1 and 2; its lines are propositional formulas. Replace, in every line of D, each atom of \mathrm{sk}(\Gamma), \mathrm{sk}(\psi) by the prime formula of \Gamma, \psi to which it was assigned, and any other atom by  ot. This is the substitution of formulas for atoms that @def-derived-rule makes for letters, and that @lem-substitution makes for meaning. Every rule of Chapters 1 and 2 is a schema in formulas, and the replacement commutes with each connective and leaves  ot alone. So each line keeps its rule and its citations, and each box keeps its extent and its assumption; this holds for ulename{RAA}, ulename{LEM} and ulename{ ot E} as for the others. D has no flagged box, so no side condition about names arises. Each premise \mathrm{sk}(\gamma) becomes \gamma, and the last line becomes \psi. So the result is a first-order derivation of \Gamma \vdash \psi (@def-derivation, as Section 5.4 extended it), and it uses only the rules of Chapters 1 and 2. This is the second sentence of the statement. Step 2: the general case. Choose one prime formula for each atom, and let \gamma^* be \gamma with every prime formula occurring outside all quantifiers (the occurrences the skeleton sees) replaced by the chosen one of its atom. Prime formulas with one atom differ only by renaming. A renaming is a provable equivalence whose closure is derivable (the renaming sentence after @prp-replacement), so @prp-replacement, applied one occurrence and one renaming step at a time (through a letter new to the formula where needed), with the steps chained by @lem-weakening-cut (c), gives \gamma \dashv\vdash \gamma^* for each formula \gamma of the list, and \psi \dashv\vdash \psi^*. The formulas \Gamma^* and \psi^* have the same skeletons as \Gamma and \psi, and in them no two different prime formulas outside all quantifiers share an atom, so Step 1 gives \Gamma^* \vdash \psi^*. Now @lem-weakening-cut (Section 2.3) chains \Gamma \vdash \gamma^* for each \gamma, then \Gamma^* \vdash \psi^*, then \psi^* \vdash \psi. Each pasted block’s flags are first renamed to names new to the whole derivation, as “The laws as one line” (Section 6.2) argues. Then no flag of a pasted block occurs in a premise or an open assumption of the derivation it is pasted into, so every ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} side condition of the block still holds, and @lem-weakening-cut (c) holds for these first-order derivations by the same pasting. So \Gamma \vdash \psi. TAUT on the skeleton. From now on, a line of a derivation may be justified ulename{TAUT}, citing available lines, when their skeletons semantically entail its skeleton (@def-valid-argument), all from one assignment; with no cited lines, when its skeleton is a tautology. This is @def-rule-taut of Section 4.8, applied to skeletons. By @prp-taut-skeleton the line abbreviates a block of primitive steps, pasted in with any flags renamed to names new to the whole derivation, as “The laws as one line” (Section 6.2) allows. As in Section 4.8, use TAUT only for a step a written proof would leave unsaid. These are TAUT steps: - from 
eg(\exists x\, P(x) \wedge Q(c)) and Q(c) to 
eg\exists x\, P(x), since 
eg(p \wedge q), q \models 
eg p; - from  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) 	o R and 
eg R to 
eg orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)): modus tollens on the skeleton, p 	o r, 
eg r \models 
eg p. These are not: - from  orall x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) to  orall y\,  orall x\, R(x, y): the two prime formulas do not differ by renaming, so the skeletons are p and q, and p 
ot\models q. The step is derivable, by @exm-universal-introduction-derivations (c), and that derivation looks inside the quantifiers; - from  orall x\, P(x) to P(c): the skeletons are p and q; this is ulename{ orall E}; - x = x: the skeleton is one atom, not a tautology; this is ulename{{=}I}. Which are TAUT steps? (a) From \exists x\, P(x) \wedge  orall y\, Q(y) to  orall y\, Q(y) \wedge \exists x\, P(x). (b) From  orall x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) to  orall x\, P(x). (c) From 
eg orall x\, P(x) to \exists x\, 
eg P(x). (a) Yes: p \wedge q \models q \wedge p. (b) No: the skeletons are two different atoms; the step is @prp-quantifier-distribution (a), which looks inside  orall x. (c) No: the skeletons are 
eg p and q; the step is QN (a) of Section 6.2, which needs the quantifier rules and ulename{RAA}. [Not allowed: TAUT] - From  orall x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) to  orall x\, Q(x). Looks inside a quantifier; needs a flagged box. - From  orall x\, P(x) to P(f(c)). An instance, not an entailment of skeletons; needs ulename{ orall E}. - From P(c) to \exists x\, P(x). Needs ulename{\exists I}. - From s = t and P(s) to P(t). The skeleton is p, q \models r, which fails; needs ulename{{=}E}. - Citing a line inside a box that has closed. Not available, whatever the table says (@def-derivation). The propositional core Many first-order derivations have the same shape. Open the boxes the goal asks for, instantiate every  orall line at the names in play, then finish with a step that is propositional. The quantifiers frame the derivation, and its core is a truth-table fact. [A propositional core inside a flagged box] Show that  orall x\, (P(x) 	o (Q(x) \vee R(x))), \  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) \vdash  orall x\, (P(x) 	o R(x)). The skeleton of line 5’s step is p 	o (q \vee r), 
eg q \models p 	o r. At line 6, x_0 is not in a premise or in line 6, and no assumption is open. Read over 
Z, with P(n) as “n > 1”, Q(n) as “n^2 = 2” and R(n) as “n > 0”. The first premise says “if n > 1, then n^2 = 2 or n > 0”, true since n > 1 gives n > 0; the second says that no integer squares to 2. Both premises are true under this reading, and so is the conclusion, which says that every integer greater than 1 is positive. The quantifier part of the derivation is two instantiations and one generalization, and its core is propositional. The order of the steps is the point. TAUT could not have been applied to the premises themselves: their skeletons are two atoms p and q, and the goal’s is a third, r, and p, q 
ot\models r. Only after the flagged box is open and both premises are instantiated at its flag do the lines show the connectives that the table needs. So the move reads: boxes first, instances at the flag second, and the table last. Write out what line 5 abbreviates, with the rules of Chapters 1 and 2. Lines 5–13 below replace the one TAUT line: That is nine lines in place of one. A written proof would say “so R(x_0), since 
eg Q(x_0)”. Four kinds of task, with quantifiers Section 3.2 sorted propositional problems into four kinds, and the kind decides how the search begins. The same four come back. A theorem \vdash \varphi has no premises; an equivalence \varphi \dashv\vdash \psi needs two derivations; inconsistency of a list is a derivation of  ot from it (Section 3.2’s definition reads the same for first-order formulas, now with all the rules); and derive or break withholds the verdict. A claim is broken by a counter-reading, which makes every member of its counterexample set true (Section 7.2). [One pair of predicates, four tasks] 1. Theorem. Show that \vdash  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)). 2. Equivalence. Show that  orall x\, (P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x)) \dashv\vdash  orall x\, (Q(x) 	o 
eg P(x)). 3. Inconsistency. Show that the list  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \ \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge 
eg Q(x)) is inconsistent. 4. Derive or break. Decide  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) \vdash  orall x\, P(x) 	o  orall x\, Q(x) and its converse. (a) With no premises the search starts from the goal alone: an ulename{{	o}I} box, then the \exists goal waits for a line that shows an instance. Line 2 instantiates at the variable x itself, and line 4 uses ulename{\exists I} at x, as in @prp-forall-implies-exists. Any term would have done as the witness, since line 1 holds at every term; the variable x is simply the term at hand, and no constant has to be invented. (b) The E form of Section 6.2 says the same with its two predicates exchanged: “no P is Q” is “no Q is P”. An equivalence is two searches, and here the second is the first with the letters exchanged, so one search does the work of both. Each direction opens a flagged box, instantiates at its flag, takes one TAUT step and generalizes: The skeletons are p 	o 
eg q \models q 	o 
eg p and the same with p and q exchanged. (c) An A form and its O form (Section 6.2). The goal is  ot, so the clash step of the method applies, but no pair \chi, 
eg\chi is in sight among the premises: the clash lives at a witness. The \exists premise opens its box at once, the  orall premise is instantiated at the witness, and the clash is propositional: Line 5’s skeleton is p \wedge 
eg q, p 	o q \models  ot. (d) With the verdict withheld, spend a minute on each side before committing. For the first claim, a reading that makes the premise true and the conclusion false would need every P to be a Q, every element to be a P, and some element not a Q, which cannot happen; so try to derive it. For the converse, a false hypothesis  orall x\, P(x) makes the premise true cheaply, which suggests a break. The first claim derives. Lines 3–6 are @exm-universal-introduction-derivations (b), run inside the box of line 2: At line 6, x_0 is not in the premise, in line 6, or in the open assumption on line 2. The converse breaks. Over 
Z, read P as “even” and Q as “positive”. “Every integer is even” is false, so the premise “if every integer is even, then every integer is positive” is true; the conclusion “every even integer is positive” is false at 0. Test the subgoal by a counter-reading. Section 4.7 tested a propositional subgoal by a refuting row before chasing it. The first-order form of the move is the same. When a search produces a subgoal, look for a reading that makes the available lines true and the subgoal false before you chase it. If you find one, the subgoal is the wrong one: Section 7.2 states that such a reading rules out every derivation of it from those lines. Return to the step that produced it, and choose differently there: another term for a  orall E, a box opened earlier, or a different case split. A reading takes a minute to find, and it can save the search a long chase. A search for the limit derivation of Section 6.1 instantiates the premise at \varepsilon_0 instead of \varepsilon_0/2, and reaches the subgoal \abs{2 a_{n_0} - 2L} < \varepsilon_0 with \abs{a_{n_0} - L} < \varepsilon_0 available. Find a sequence and numbers that make every available line true and the subgoal false. Take \varepsilon_0 = 1; a_n = L for every n except a_{n_0} = L + 0.75; and N_0 = n_0. The premise holds, since the sequence is eventually constant at L. Every term is within 0.75 < 1 of L, so the instance of the premise at \varepsilon_0 and the box line  orall n \in 
N\; (n \ge N_0 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon_0) hold; n_0 \ge N_0 holds; and \abs{a_{n_0} - L} = 0.75 < 1. But \abs{2 a_{n_0} - 2L} = 1.5 \ge 1. The subgoal is the wrong one; go back to the choice of term. Which task is \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge 
eg P(x)) \vdash  ot, and how long is its derivation with TAUT? Inconsistency. Three lines below the premise: A library of first-order sequents Here is what the book has proved about quantifiers, grouped by use; a search that needs one of these can copy its derivation, with formulas in place of letters, rather than rediscover it. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Use Sequent Where ------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- exchange two like quantifiers  orall x\,  orall y\, \varphi \dashv\vdash  orall y\,  orall x\, \varphi @exm-universal-introduction-derivations (c) rename a bound variable  orall y\, \varphi \dashv\vdash  orall z\, \varphi[z/y], and the same for \exists Section 5.4 (the fold after @exm-universal-introduction-derivations); Section 5.6 every gives some  orall x\, \varphi \vdash \exists x\, \varphi @prp-forall-implies-exists some-all gives all-some \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \vdash  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) @prp-exists-forall-swap distribute  orall over \wedge and \exists over \vee both ways;  orall over \vee and \exists over \wedge one way @prp-quantifier-distribution (the instances for P, Q first in @prp-forall-and and @prp-exists-and) negate “not every” and “some not”; “none” and “every not”; a negated implication; bounded forms @prp-quantifier-negation, @prp-negated-implication, @prp-bounded-quantifier-negation move across a connective the passage laws @prp-quantifier-passage replace a part a provable equivalence, inside any formula @prp-replacement equality symmetric and transitive; equals share every property @prp-equality-symmetric-transitive, @prp-leibniz-law bounds in one step the bounded rules @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules propositional steps TAUT on the skeleton @prp-taut-skeleton --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The laws of Section 6.2 may already be used as one line, by “The laws as one line”; the other rows are patterns to copy. Either way, a row is used by matching its shape and then checking its conditions: the passage laws need the moved variable not free in the other side, a renaming needs a letter new to the formula, and an instance of a row’s letters must be free for the variables it replaces. [Looking ahead] Every claim this section broke, it broke by a counter-reading. Chapter 7 gives counter-readings an exact form, the counter-model, and states that a counter-model rules out every derivation. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. What is the propositional skeleton of 
eg\exists x\, P(x) \vee (Q(c) \wedge \exists y\, P(y))? Is it a tautology? 2. What is the propositional skeleton of \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \wedge 
eg\exists x\, (Q(x) \wedge P(x))? Can a TAUT step derive  ot from this formula? 3. Which are TAUT steps? (i) From  orall x\, P(x) and  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y) to \exists y\, Q(y). (ii) From  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) and P(c) to Q(c). (iii) From 
eg
eg\exists x\, P(x) to \exists x\, P(x). 4. In @exm-search-with-witnesses, why is the box on premise 3 opened before premise 1 is used? 5. A counter-reading makes the premises of a claim true and its conclusion false. What may you say now, and what will Section 7.2 add? (a) 
eg p \vee (q \wedge p): \exists x\, P(x) and \exists y\, P(y) differ only by renaming, so they share p. It is not a tautology: p true and q false make it false. (b) p \wedge 
eg q. The two prime formulas are not renamings of each other (P(x) \wedge Q(x) against Q(x) \wedge P(x)), so they get different atoms, and p \wedge 
eg q is true in a row: no.  ot is derivable all the same, by an ulename{\exists E} box on the first conjunct, a TAUT step inside it to Q(x_0) \wedge P(x_0), ulename{\exists I}, and a clash with the second conjunct. (c) (i) Yes: p, p 	o q \models q. (ii) No: p, q 
ot\models r; it is ulename{ orall E} at c, then ulename{{	o}E}. (iii) Yes: 
eg
eg p \models p. (d) Premise 1 is a  orall whose useful term is not yet known, and the box supplies it, x_0. These are the moves “name the witness early” and “instantiate at the term you need”, in that order. (e) Now: the claim breaks, and a search for it is abandoned. Section 7.2 states that such a claim has no derivation. B. Practice [B1: Derive or break, twelve claims] Derive each claim, with TAUT allowed, or break it by a reading over 
Z that makes every member of its counterexample set true. The groups say which move to try first; they do not say which claims hold. Claims 1–3: name the witness early. Claims 4 and 5: instantiate at the term you need. Claims 6–8: the propositional core. Claims 9–12: move a quantifier, or derive  ot. 1. \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)), \  orall x\, (P(x) 	o (Q(x) 	o R(f(x)))) \vdash \exists y\, R(y). 2. \exists x\, R(x, x) \vdash  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y). 3. \exists x\, P(x), \  orall x\, (P(x) 	o  orall y\, R(x, y)) \vdash  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y). 4.  orall x\,  orall y\, (R(x, y) 	o R(y, x)), \  orall x\, R(x, f(x)) \vdash  orall x\, R(f(x), x). 5.  orall x\, R(x, f(x)) \vdash  orall x\, R(f(x), x). 6.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \  orall x\, (Q(x) 	o R(x)) \vdash  orall x\, (
eg R(x) 	o 
eg P(x)). 7.  orall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)), \  orall x\, 
eg P(x) \vdash  orall x\, Q(x). 8.  orall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)), \ 
eg orall x\, P(x) \vdash  orall x\, Q(x). 9.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) \vdash \exists x\, P(x) 	o \exists x\, Q(x). 10.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) \vdash \exists x\, P(x) 	o  orall x\, Q(x). 11.  orall x\, (P(x) \leftrightarrow 
eg P(f(x))), \  orall x\, P(x) \vdash  ot. 12.  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y), \  orall x\,  orall y\, (R(x, y) 	o 
eg R(y, x)) \vdash  ot. 1. Derive. The box of the witness opens first; inside it, premise 2 is instantiated at x_0, and the postponed goal takes the compound witness f(x_0). Line 5’s skeleton is p \wedge q, p 	o (q 	o r) \models r. At line 7, x_0 is not in line 7, in line 1, or in a premise. 2. Breaks. Read R(x, y) as “x \cdot y = 1”. The premise is true, since 1 \cdot 1 = 1; the conclusion fails at x = 0, since 0 \cdot y = 0 for every y. 3. Derive. At line 8, y_0 is not in a premise, in the open assumption on line 3, or in line 8. At line 9, x_0 is not in line 9, in line 1, or in a premise. 4. Derive. The term premise 1 needs is f(x_0), and premise 2 names it. Line 5 instantiates at f(x_0), which is free for y. At line 7, x_0 is not in a premise or in line 7, and no assumption is open. 5. Breaks. Read f(x) as x + 1 and R as <. Every x < x + 1, so the premise is true; no x + 1 < x, so the conclusion is false. 6. Derive. Line 5’s skeleton is p 	o q, q 	o r \models 
eg r 	o 
eg p. 7. Derive. Line 5’s skeleton is p \vee q, 
eg p \models q. 8. Breaks. Read P as “even” and Q as “odd”. Every integer is even or odd; not every integer is even; and 0 is not odd, so “every integer is odd” is false. 9. Derive. At line 7, x_0 is not in line 7, in line 2, in the premise, or in an open assumption (line 2’s box is still open, and line 2 does not mention x_0). 10. Breaks. Read P(x) as “x = 0” and Q(x) as “x \cdot x = x”. The premise holds, since the only x with x = 0 has 0 \cdot 0 = 0. In the conclusion, \exists x\, (x = 0) is true and  orall x\, (x \cdot x = x) is false, since 2 \cdot 2 = 4; so the implication is false. 11. Derive. Premise 2 is instantiated twice, at y and at f(y), the two terms that premise 1 at y mentions. Line 6’s skeleton is p \leftrightarrow 
eg q, p, q \models  ot: no row makes all three true. 12. Breaks. Read R as <. Every integer has a larger one, and x < y excludes y < x. Both premises are true, and 
eg ot is true, so the whole counterexample set is true: the list is not shown inconsistent. Seven claims derive and five break. Four breaks sit beside a derivable look-alike: 5 beside 4, 8 beside 7, 10 beside 9, and 12 beside 11. Claim 2 weakens the premise of the derivable  orall x\, R(x, x) \vdash  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) of @exm-existential-introduction-derivations (c). Every break is a counter-reading (Section 7.2). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 4: the twelve verdicts, 	frac13 point for each correct one, rounded down. - 3: the seven derivations, each with every closing side condition checked and every TAUT line’s skeleton named. - 3: the five readings, each with every premise and the conclusion evaluated. Fatal errors (0 for the claim): a TAUT line that looks inside a quantifier; a “break” with a premise false. [B2: Two witnesses in a row] The premises are 1  orall x\, (P(x) 	o \exists y\, R(x, y)), 2  orall x\,  orall y\, (R(x, y) 	o P(y)) and 3 P(c); the goal is \exists y\, \exists z\, (R(c, y) \wedge R(y, z)). Here is a partial derivation: Name the move, then complete it. The move is “name the witness early”, twice, with each  orall line instantiated only at the terms in hand: c (premise 3) first, then the witness y_0. Lines 4 and 7 instantiate at c, and lines 8 and 10 at y_0; line 15 is ulename{\exists I} at y_0, which is free for y. At line 16, z_0 is not in line 16, in line 11, in the premises, or in the open assumption on line 6. At line 17, y_0 is not in line 17, in line 5, or in the premises. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: names the move. - 3: opens the two boxes as soon as their \exists lines exist. - 3: the ulename{ orall E} lines at c, c, y_0 and y_0, the terms read off the lines in hand. - 2: the two side conditions. Fatal error (0 for the step): ulename{\exists I} on line 15 before line 14, so that the witness z_0 appears in the box’s last line. [B3: How much TAUT saves] 1. Derive  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \  orall x\, (Q(x) 	o 
eg P(x)) \vdash  orall x\, 
eg P(x) twice: once without TAUT, once with exactly one TAUT line. Count the lines. 2. Is the step from  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) to  orall x\, (
eg Q(x) 	o 
eg P(x)) a TAUT step? (a) With TAUT, six lines (left); without it, ten (right): Line 5 on the left has the skeleton p 	o q, q 	o 
eg p \models 
eg p. (b) No: the two formulas are prime and not renamings of each other, so their skeletons are two different atoms. The step is derivable by instantiating, one TAUT line (p 	o q \models 
eg q 	o 
eg p) and generalizing, the pattern of @exm-four-tasks-with-quantifiers (b). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: the TAUT derivation, with the skeleton named. - 4: the derivation without TAUT. - 1: the count. - 2: (b), with the reason. Fatal error (0 for the step): a TAUT line citing the  orall lines directly to reach 
eg P(x_0). C. Going deeper [C1: Some index decides, used later] Let D(n) say “a_n > 0” for a sequence (a_n), over a domain of indices. 1. Derive \vdash \exists n\, (D(n) 	o  orall m\, D(m)), with ulename{LEM} on  orall m\, D(m). 2. Derive it again in two lines, from one TAUT line and one law of Section 6.2. 3. Say in two sentences which index the sentence promises, and why the derivations of (a) and (b) name none. [Hint 1] For (a): in the case 
eg orall m\, D(m), which law of Section 6.2 turns the negated  orall into an \exists? [Hint 2] For (b): the formula  orall n\, D(n) 	o  orall m\, D(m) has the skeleton p 	o p. Which passage law moves the  orall n out of the hypothesis of an implication, turning it into \exists n? (a) Line 6 is ulename{\exists I} at the variable n itself, as in the proof of passage law (d); as there, the step is sound because every domain is non-empty (Section 7.1). Line 11 is ulename{\exists I} at m_0. At line 12, m_0 is not in line 12, in line 8, or in the open assumption on line 7. (b) The two prime formulas of line 1 differ only by renaming, so the skeleton is p 	o p, a tautology. Line 2 is @prp-quantifier-passage (d), the direction \dashv, used as one line (“The laws as one line”), with \varphi the formula D(n) and \psi the formula  orall m\, D(m), in which n is not free. (c) If every term is positive, any index will do; if not, an index with a_n \le 0 does, since then the implication is vacuously true. The derivation splits on which case holds without deciding it (ulename{LEM} in (a), the classical direction of (d) in (b)), so it never names the index. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 4: (a), with the ulename{LEM} split, both cases closed, with the side condition of every line that closes a flagged box checked. - 3: (b), with the TAUT line justified by renaming, and law (d) with its condition checked. - 3: (c). Fatal errors (0 for the step): giving  orall n\, D(n) and  orall m\, D(m) different atoms and then claiming the TAUT line anyway; ulename{\exists I} at m_0 after its box has closed. [C2: Every M is P, every M is S, so some S is P?] 1. Break  orall x\, (M(x) 	o P(x)), \  orall x\, (M(x) 	o S(x)) \vdash \exists x\, (S(x) \wedge P(x)) by a reading over 
N. 2. Add the premise \exists x\, M(x) and derive the conclusion. 3. Which line of (b) needs the new premise, and what does Section 5.1’s existential import have to do with it? (a) Breaks. Read M(n) as “n is an even prime greater than 2”, which is true of no n; P(n) as “n is odd”; and S(n) as “n is even”. Both premises are vacuously true, since their hypothesis M(n) is false for every n, and “some even number is odd” is false (Section 7.2). (b) Line 7’s skeleton is m, m 	o p, m 	o s \models s \wedge p. At line 9, x_0 is not in line 9, in line 3, or in a premise. (c) Line 7: its TAUT needs M(x_0), line 4, which only the box of premise 3 supplies. Without it, ulename{\exists I} could still be applied at some term, but no line would say that term is S and P. A “for every” claims no instance, so the old reading of “every M is P” as also saying that there are Ms is not the book’s reading. With that reading the inference was valid; without it, the premise must be added. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a), with all three truth values justified. - 4: (b). - 3: (c). Fatal error (0 for the step): a “break” whose M is true of some number.

title: 6.4 Uniformly Continuous Implies Continuous, Rule by Rule
content:
Uniformly Continuous Implies Continuous, Rule by Rule Chapter 5 opened with a question. Continuity and uniform continuity differ only in where one quantifier stands; why does one imply the other in a few lines, while the converse is false? Section 5.1 gave the informal answer: a variable may depend on the variables quantified to its left, and only on them. @exr-translation-c1 of Section 6.1 asked for both translations into formulas, and Section 6.2 negated uniform continuity (@exm-negating-definitions (c)). This section answers the question with the rules. It derives “uniformly continuous implies continuous” in full, line by line, with the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules. It then reads off the derivation the one thing this section adds: which boxes are open where a constant is chosen, and what that says about what the constant may depend on. The same reading locates the exact lines at which the converse breaks down, and the function x^2 shows that the converse is not merely unproved but false. Two definitions that differ in one place Let A be a set of real numbers and f a function defined on A. We work over the domain 
R, with f a one-place function symbol, \in A a one-place predicate symbol (Section 5.2), and \abs{\cdot} the absolute value. Here the two definitions are only quantifier patterns, and nothing is used about f except that f(x) is a term. (A function symbol has a value at every real number; the values outside A are never used, because f is only applied to variables bounded by \in A, as with sequences in Section 5.1.) f is uniformly continuous on A (UC) when  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon  igr). f is continuous at every point of A (C) when  orall x \in A \;  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall y \in A \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon  igr). The two formulas have the same matrix and the same four bounded quantifiers. Only  orall x \in A has moved: in C it stands before \exists \delta > 0, in UC after it. In the game of Section 5.1, the defender chooses \delta in C after seeing x and \varepsilon, and in UC after seeing only \varepsilon. So in UC a single \delta must serve every point of A at once: that is what uniformly means. Swap the first two quantifiers of UC, to get \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \; ( \abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon ). What does the new formula say about two points of A closer than \delta? Does f(x) = x on 
R satisfy it? Now \delta is chosen before \varepsilon, so it must work for every \varepsilon > 0 at once. For two points x, y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta, this says \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0, and by @prp-arbitrarily-close-equal, f(x) = f(y). So the formula says: for some \delta > 0, any two points of A closer than \delta have the same value. The function f(x) = x on 
R fails it: whatever \delta > 0 is proposed, the points 0 and \delta/2 are closer than \delta and have different values. Yet f(x) = x is uniformly continuous, with \delta = \varepsilon. Swapping  orall \varepsilon and \exists \delta asks far too much. The skeleton first Hold \varepsilon fixed, and write K(x, \delta) for “\delta works at x”, the formula  orall y \in A\; (\abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon). Drop the bounds on \delta and x for a moment. Then UC at this \varepsilon says \exists \delta\,  orall x\, K(x, \delta), one \delta for every point, and C at this \varepsilon says  orall x\, \exists \delta\, K(x, \delta), a \delta for each point. The step from the first to the second is @prp-exists-forall-swap with other letters: Fix a point, obtain the one \delta that works everywhere, choose it for this point. The converse, from  orall x\, \exists \delta\, K to \exists \delta\,  orall x\, K, is the swap whose search stalled in Section 5.6. The rest of this section puts \varepsilon and the bounds back and writes K out. That costs five lines: the premise UC itself (line 1), the assumptions x_0 \in A, \varepsilon_0 > 0 and \delta_0 > 0 (lines 2, 3 and 5), and the line that closes the box of \varepsilon_0 (line 10). The skeleton’s line 1 becomes line 4 of the derivation below (UC at \varepsilon_0), its lines 2–5 become lines 6–9, and its line 6 becomes line 11, which closes the box of x_0. Why may line 5 of the skeleton close the box of \delta_0? \delta_0 does not appear in line 5, \exists \delta\, K(x_0, \delta), nor in the existential of line 1, which is also the only premise, and the one box still open, that of x_0, has no assumption. Every clause of ulename{\exists E} holds. The derivation [Uniformly continuous implies continuous] Derive C from UC, with the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules. Run the search method of Section 6.3. The goal C begins  orall x \in A, then  orall \varepsilon > 0: the goal-directed steps open two bounded ulename{ orall I} boxes, “let x_0 \in A” and “let \varepsilon_0 > 0”, and write the last two lines. The new goal begins \exists \delta > 0, and no witness is in sight, so it is postponed (Section 5.5). Turn to the premise UC. It begins  orall \varepsilon > 0, and the term the goal mentions is \varepsilon_0, whose bound \varepsilon_0 > 0 is on a line: ulename{ orall E} at \varepsilon_0 (Section 5.3). That gives an \exists \delta > 0 line, and its ulename{\exists E} box is opened at once, with a witness \delta_0 (Section 5.6), aiming for the postponed goal as its last line. Inside, the premise has become “\delta_0 works for all x, y \in A”; instantiate it at the point we have, x_0. Now the postponed goal has its witness: \delta_0 itself. Before reading on: which lines does the line introducing \delta_0 rest on, and does any of them mention x_0? Every line is tagged with its rule; lines 4, 7 and 8 are the one-line bounded rules, and lines 9, 10 and 11 close bounded boxes. The terms and the side conditions: - Line 4: ulename{ orall E} at \varepsilon_0, with its bound on line 3. The term \varepsilon_0 is a variable that does not appear in line 1, so it is free for \varepsilon. - Line 7: ulename{ orall E} at x_0, with its bound on line 2, which is available because the box of line 2 is still open. - Line 8: ulename{\exists I} with the witness \delta_0, its bound on line 5 and the instance on line 7. - Line 9 (ulename{\exists E}, flag \delta_0): \delta_0 does not appear in line 9 (the witness was forgotten at line 8), in line 4, in the premise, or in the assumptions still open at line 9, lines 2 and 3. - Line 10 (ulename{ orall I}, flag \varepsilon_0): \varepsilon_0 does not appear in the premise, in line 10, or in the assumption still open at line 10, line 2. - Line 11 (ulename{ orall I}, flag x_0): x_0 does not appear in the premise or in line 11, and no assumption is open. The answer to the prompt: line 5 is the assumption of the ulename{\exists E} box, so it rests on line 4, which rests on lines 1 and 3. None of the three mentions x_0.
