Both variants end in  orall \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall x \in A \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall y \in A \; (\dots), and C follows by exchanging the two bounded universal quantifiers (the swap of @exm-universal-introduction-derivations (c), with the bounded rules); sentence (iv), “since \varepsilon and x were arbitrary”, covers both steps in prose. Distractor (ii) introduces \delta as an arbitrary object, by ulename{ orall I}. But in “continuous at x” the \delta is under \exists: the proof must produce it, by a choice from the hypothesis, not receive it from a challenger. A proof that took \delta arbitrary would have to show that every \delta > 0 works, which is false in general. Distractor (vii) chooses \delta and only afterwards lets x be arbitrary. It looks legitimate, because when (vii) is read after (viii), x is already fixed, and continuity at x does allow \delta to depend on x. But the sentence reverses the order of the two steps: a \delta fitted to one particular x is followed by “let x be arbitrary”, which claims that the same \delta works for every x. In the rules: if \delta really was chosen for this x, its ulename{\exists E} box assumes a line that mentions x, and generalizing over x while that assumption is open breaks the side condition of ulename{ orall I}, the first blocked line of @exm-converse-fails. If \delta does not depend on x, as here, then “for this x” is idle and the sentence should be (vi). [B3: The square root] Prove that f(x) = \sqrt{x} is uniformly continuous on A = [0, \infty). You may use the school inequality \abs{\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{y}} \le \sqrt{\abs{x - y}} for all x, y \ge 0. State what your \delta depends on. Let \varepsilon > 0, and let \delta \coloneqq \varepsilon^2, which is positive and depends on \varepsilon only. Let x, y \in [0, \infty) with \abs{x - y} < \delta. Then, by the inequality given and because the square root is strictly increasing on [0, \infty), \abs{\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{y}} \le \sqrt{\abs{x - y}} < \sqrt{\varepsilon^2} = \varepsilon . Since x and y were arbitrary, this \delta works for all pairs of points; since \varepsilon was arbitrary, f is uniformly continuous on [0, \infty). The \delta was chosen before the points: in a derivation of this proof, its ulename{\exists I} line would lie inside the box of \varepsilon_0 only. [B4: Witness functions] For each function, give a witness function for uniform continuity on the set named, say what it depends on, and prove that it works. 1. f(x) = \abs{x} on 
R. 2. f(x) = x^2 on [0, 3]. 3. Say in one sentence why the formula of (b) gives no witness function on all of 
R. (a) \delta(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon, which depends on \varepsilon only. Let x, y \in 
R with \abs{x - y} < \varepsilon. By the triangle inequality (@exm-triangle-inequality-cases), \abs{x} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y} and \abs{y} \le \abs{y - x} + \abs{x}, so \abs{x} - \abs{y} \le \abs{x - y} and \abs{y} - \abs{x} \le \abs{x - y}; hence \abs{\abs{x} - \abs{y}} \le \abs{x - y} < \varepsilon. (b) \delta(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon/6. For x, y \in [0, 3], \abs{x + y} = x + y \le 6, so if \abs{x - y} < \varepsilon/6, then \abs{x^2 - y^2} = \abs{x - y} \cdot \abs{x + y} \le 6 \abs{x - y} < \varepsilon . It depends on \varepsilon and on the bound 3 of the set, and on no point. (c) On 
R, \abs{x + y} has no bound, so no constant can replace the 6, and @exm-square-not-uniform shows that no witness function exists there at all. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a), with \abs{\abs{x} - \abs{y}} \le \abs{x - y} proved (for instance by the triangle inequality twice). - 4: (b): 1 for the bound \abs{x + y} \le 6, 2 for the chain, 1 for the dependence. - 3: (c). Fatal error (0 for the step): a “witness” that mentions x or y. C. Going deeper [C1: Composition, half done] Let f be uniformly continuous on A, with f(x) \in B for every x \in A, and let g be uniformly continuous on B. Here is the start of a proof that the composite x \mapsto g(f(x)) is uniformly continuous on A: Fix \varepsilon > 0. By the uniform continuity of g, choose \eta > 0 such that \abs{u - v} < \eta implies \abs{g(u) - g(v)} < \varepsilon for all u, v \in B. The rest is blank. Name the move, then complete it. [Hint 1] The goal asks for a \delta. Which hypothesis can produce one, and at which positive number should it be applied? [Hint 2] “By the uniform continuity of f, applied to \eta, choose \delta > 0 such that …” The move is fix, obtain, choose: \varepsilon was fixed (ulename{ orall I}), \eta obtained from the hypothesis on g (ulename{ orall E} at \varepsilon, then ulename{\exists E}); now obtain \delta from the hypothesis on f at the term the goal needs, \eta (ulename{ orall E} at \eta, then ulename{\exists E}), and choose that \delta as the witness (ulename{\exists I}). Completion. Since \eta > 0, the uniform continuity of f, applied to \eta, gives \delta > 0 such that \abs{x - y} < \delta implies \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \eta for all x, y \in A; choose such a \delta. It depends on \eta, hence on \varepsilon, and on no point. Let x, y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta. Then \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \eta, and f(x), f(y) \in B, so the choice of \eta, applied to u = f(x) and v = f(y), gives \abs{g(f(x)) - g(f(y))} < \varepsilon. Since x, y were arbitrary, this \delta works for all pairs of points of A; since \varepsilon > 0 was arbitrary, x \mapsto g(f(x)) is uniformly continuous on A. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: names the move (fix, obtain, choose), or the rules ulename{ orall E} at \eta, ulename{\exists E}, ulename{\exists I}. - 3: applies the uniform continuity of f at \eta (not at \varepsilon), using \eta > 0, and chooses \delta before any point. - 3: for arbitrary x, y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta, gets \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \eta and then \abs{g(f(x)) - g(f(y))} < \varepsilon, using f(x), f(y) \in B. - 2: concludes with the quantifiers in the order \varepsilon, \delta, points, and says \delta depends on \varepsilon only. Fatal errors (0 for the step): \delta chosen after x or depending on x; the uniform continuity of g applied to points not known to lie in B. [C2: Gluing two sets] Let A and B be sets of real numbers and S the set of numbers that lie in A or in B. Suppose f is uniformly continuous on A and uniformly continuous on B. 1. Show that f need not be uniformly continuous on S: take A = (0, 1), B = (1, 2), and f(x) = 0 for x < 1, f(x) = 1 for x \ge 1. 2. Prove that f is uniformly continuous on S when A = [a, b] and B = [b, c] with a < b < c. [Hint 1] For (b), the two sets share the point b. Two points on opposite sides of b are each close to b. [Hint 2] For (b), apply the two hypotheses at \varepsilon/2 and take \delta = \min(\delta_1, \delta_2). (a) On A = (0, 1), f is constantly 0, so every \delta > 0 works for every \varepsilon > 0: \abs{f(x) - f(y)} = 0 < \varepsilon. The same holds on B = (1, 2), where f is constantly 1. On S we prove the negation of uniform continuity (@exm-negating-definitions (c)). Take \varepsilon = 1. Let \delta > 0, and let \eta \coloneqq \min(\delta/4, 	frac12), x \coloneqq 1 - \eta, y \coloneqq 1 + \eta. Then 	frac12 \le x < 1, so x \in A \subseteq S; 1 < y \le 	frac32, so y \in B \subseteq S; \abs{x - y} = 2\eta \le \delta/2 < \delta; and \abs{f(x) - f(y)} = \abs{0 - 1} = 1 \ge \varepsilon. So f is not uniformly continuous on S. The gluing fails because the two sets come arbitrarily close at 1 but have no point in common: points close to 1 on opposite sides are each controlled only by their own set, and no common point links them. (b) Let \varepsilon > 0. By the uniform continuity on A at \varepsilon/2, choose \delta_1 > 0 such that \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon/2 for all x, y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta_1; likewise choose \delta_2 > 0 for B. Let \delta \coloneqq \min(\delta_1, \delta_2) > 0, which depends on \varepsilon only. Let x, y \in S with \abs{x - y} < \delta. There are three cases. - Case 1: x, y \in A. Then \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon, since \abs{x - y} < \delta \le \delta_1. - Case 2: x, y \in B. The same, with \delta_2. - Case 3: one point in each set, say x \in A and y \in B (the other way round is the same with the letters exchanged). Then x \le b \le y, so \abs{x - b} = b - x \le y - x = \abs{x - y} < \delta \le \delta_1, and b \in A; hence \abs{f(x) - f(b)} < \varepsilon/2. Likewise \abs{b - y} \le \abs{x - y} < \delta_2 and b \in B, so \abs{f(b) - f(y)} < \varepsilon/2. By the triangle inequality (@exm-triangle-inequality-cases), \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \le \abs{f(x) - f(b)} + \abs{f(b) - f(y)} < \varepsilon . Every point of S lies in A or in B, so the cases cover all pairs. So f is uniformly continuous on S. The common point b is what (a) lacked: there, A and B came arbitrarily close at 1 but had no point in common. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) uniform continuity on A and on B checked, and the negation on S proved: \varepsilon first, then for arbitrary \delta two points depending on \delta, with all three conditions checked. - 2: (b) \delta_1 for A at some \varepsilon_1 > 0 and \delta_2 for B at some \varepsilon_2 > 0 with \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 \le \varepsilon (the solution takes \varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon/2), and \delta = \min(\delta_1, \delta_2), depending on \varepsilon only. - 2: the cases with both points in one set. - 3: the mixed case, through the point b, with \abs{x - b}, \abs{b - y} \le \abs{x - y} justified and the triangle inequality cited. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a \delta depending on x or y; the mixed case omitted; in (a), points chosen before \delta. [C3: Exit check: a quantifier derivation] 1. Give a full derivation of \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge  orall y\, R(x, y)  igr) \vdash  orall y\, \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge R(x, y)  igr), and check the side condition of every line that closes a flagged box. 2. For the converse,  orall y\, \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge R(x, y)  igr) \vdash \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge  orall y\, R(x, y)  igr), give a domain with two elements and a reading of P and R under which the premise is true and the conclusion false, checking both with the informal reading of Section 5.1. (a) The goal is a  orall: open a flagged box for y_0. The premise is an \exists: open its ulename{\exists E} box at once, with a witness x_0, aiming for the goal’s instance. Inside, take the conjunction apart, instantiate  orall y at y_0, and choose x_0 as the witness: - Line 8 (ulename{\exists E}, flag x_0): x_0 does not appear in line 8, in line 1 (the premise), or in any assumption still open at line 8 (there is none: the box of y_0 has no assumption). Line 7, the last line of the box of x_0, is a line of that box itself and is the formula \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge R(x, y_0)) that line 8 repeats (@def-rules-existential). - Line 9 (ulename{ orall I}, flag y_0): y_0 does not appear in the premise or in line 9, and no assumption is open. Line 8, the last line of the box of y_0, is the instance at y_0 of \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge R(x, y)). The other nesting, with the box of y_0 inside the box of x_0, works too: ulename{ orall I} at the end of the inner box (its name y_0 is in no open assumption, since the assumption on line 2 does not mention it), then ulename{\exists E} on a conclusion without x_0. (b) Take a domain with two elements a, b; let P be true of both, and let R(x, y) mean “x is y”. The premise is true: for y = a the witness x = a has P(a) and R(a, a), and for y = b the witness x = b works. The conclusion is false: x = a fails  orall y\, R(a, y) at y = b, and x = b fails it at y = a. The witness in the premise depends on y; the conclusion asks for one x that serves every y. (Section 7.2 makes this informal reading a structure, and shows that it proves the converse is not derivable.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: a flagged box with a fresh name y_0 for the ulename{ orall I}, closed correctly. - 3: an ulename{\exists E} box with a fresh witness x_0, whose conclusion does not contain x_0, with the side condition checked. - 2: ulename{\wedge E}, ulename{ orall E} at y_0 and ulename{\exists I} with the witness x_0, with the correct terms. - 3: the two-element reading: domain, meaning of P and R, the premise checked for each y and the conclusion refuted for each x. Either nesting of the two boxes earns full marks. Fatal errors (0 for the step): ulename{ orall I} on a name that appears in an open assumption; an ulename{\exists E} conclusion containing the witness. R. Review [R1] Derive  orall x\, (f(x) = x) \vdash  orall x\, (f(f(x)) = x). The goal is a  orall: open a flagged box. The premise is instantiated twice, at the flag and at the compound term f(x_0), the term the goal’s instance contains. Line 3 instantiates at f(x_0), which is free for x. Line 4 is transitivity, @prp-equality-symmetric-transitive (b), written as its one ulename{{=}E} step: the equation of line 2 rewrites the last f(x_0) of line 3. At line 5, x_0 is not in the premise or in line 5, and no assumption is open. The method is Section 5.3’s “instantiate at the term you need”, here a compound term, with the equality of Section 5.7. [R2] Show that the list P \leftrightarrow 
eg Q, \ Q \leftrightarrow 
eg R, \ R \leftrightarrow 
eg P is inconsistent. A list is inconsistent when  ot is derivable from it (@def-inconsistent-set). The derivation below uses no ulename{RAA}: three ulename{
eg I} boxes give 
eg R, 
eg P and 
eg Q, and each ulename{\leftrightarrow E} is used in whichever of its two forms (@def-rules-biconditional) the line needs. A TAUT line (Section 4.8) would do it in one step, since the three formulas have no row that makes them all true: an odd cycle of “is the negation of” is impossible. [R3] You have derived P \wedge (Q \vee R) \vdash (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R). Derive \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge (Q(x) \vee R(x))  igr) \vdash \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \vee \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge R(x)), and say which line is the propositional law. Line 3, justified by TAUT on the skeleton p \wedge (q \vee r) \models (p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge r), is the propositional law @prp-distributivity of Section 1.6; citing it as a derived rule (@def-derived-rule) gives the same line. At line 11, x_0 is not in line 11 or in line 1, the premise, and no assumption is open. The quantifier steps frame the law: this is the propositional core of Section 6.3.

title: Models and Theories
content:
Models and Theories The axioms of a partial order say that \le is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. Do they prove that any two elements are comparable,  orall x\,  orall y\, (x \le y \vee y \le x)? A search for a derivation stalls, and a stalled search proves nothing. Two dots settle it: a domain \{ a, b \} in which each element is \le itself and nothing else. All three axioms are true there and comparability is false, so, by a statement of Section 7.2, no derivation exists. What does “true there” mean, and why does one picture rule out every derivation? This chapter answers both, and then uses such pictures on whole theories: in Section 7.4, “is every group commutative?” is answered by the six symmetries of a triangle. How to read this chapter. First reading: Sections 7.1, 7.2 and 7.4, and Section 7.5 up to “Isomorphic structures”. Second pass: the rest of Section 7.5. Optional: Sections 7.3 and 7.6. The statement that a counter-model rules out every derivation is on the trunk, in Section 7.2; its proof is optional, in Section 7.3. Nothing on the first-reading list uses anything off it. Before you start: five tempting claims. Each is a claim this chapter corrects; decide each now, and check again at the section named. 1. “ orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) is true.” 2. “A search for a derivation of \Gamma \vdash \varphi stalled, so \Gamma 
vdash \varphi.” 3. “If \sigma is true in (
N, <), then \sigma is derivable.” 4. “Every group is commutative: the integers under addition are.” 5. “(
N, <) and the even numbers with < can be told apart by some sentence, since one is part of the other.” 1. Not until a structure is fixed: true in (
N, <), false in (\{ 1, 2, 3 \}, <) (Section 7.1). 2. No. A stalled search proves nothing; a counter-model does (Section 7.2). 3. No. Derivable sentences are true in every structure;  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) is true in (
N, <) and false in a three-element order (Section 7.2). 4. No. The six symmetries of a triangle form a group in which two motions done in the two orders differ (Section 7.4). 5. No. Doubling matches them element for element and order for order, and matched structures satisfy the same sentences (Section 7.5, second pass). What you need. Chapters 1–6, above all the semantics of Chapter 4 (rows, \models, soundness) and the quantifier rules of Chapter 5. Section 7.5’s second half uses functions and bijections in their everyday sense. Time. About 20 hours on the core track (Sections 7.1, 7.2, 7.4 and the first half of 7.5: all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 45 hours for everything. Minimum before Sets and Functions. Chapters 1–6 and 8, core; Sections 7.1–7.2 before its Section 4.1; Sections 7.4–7.5 recommended. Roadmap - Structures and Satisfaction. A domain and a meaning for every symbol, an assignment for the free variables, clauses that decide every formula; finite structures drawn; proofs by meaning. - Counter-models. Three pictures, a procedure for finding one, small domains by expansion, each side condition of Chapter 5 broken, and the statement that a counter-model rules out every derivation. - Soundness for Predicate Logic (optional). The proof of that statement, by Chapter 4’s induction. - Theories and Their Models. Axioms as sentences, consistency by a model, independence by two models. - Definability and Isomorphism. A formula defines a set; \exists is a projection. Second pass: isomorphic structures satisfy the same sentences; automorphisms move what is not definable. - What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say (optional). Completeness, compactness, non-standard numbers, undecidability, all stated without proof. Named moves - Refute with a model. One structure with the premises true and the conclusion false. (Section 7.2) - Prove by meaning, clause by clause. Unwind the premises and the conclusion through (S1)–(S7). (Section 7.1) - Search for a counter-model. Start from the counterexample set, meet the existential demands first, add only forced elements. (Section 7.2) - Expand over a small domain. On two or three elements a quantifier is a long \wedge or \vee. (Section 7.2) - Consistent by a model; independent by two models. (Section 7.4) - Define by a formula. (Section 7.5) - An automorphism moves what cannot be defined. (Section 7.5, second pass) Where this goes. Sets and Functions, Chapters 1 and 2 develop the sets, pairs and functions that Sections 7.1 and 7.5 use in their everyday sense, and its Chapter 6 builds a counter-model by Section 7.2’s procedure; its Chapter 5 studies the relations of Section 7.4. Summary A structure fixes a domain and a meaning for every symbol, an assignment fixes the free variables, and seven clauses decide every formula (@def-satisfaction); a sentence is true or false in a structure, never “true” alone. A counter-model makes the counterexample set true; by soundness for predicate logic (stated in Section 7.2, proved in the optional Section 7.3) it rules out every derivation: the stalled searches of Chapters 5 and 6 become theorems of non-derivability, and each side condition of the quantifier rules is shown needed. A theory is a set of axioms (@def-theory); a model shows it consistent (@prp-model-shows-consistency), and two models show a sentence independent of it (@prp-model-shows-independence), as the antichain does for comparability and the triangle for commutativity. Formulas define sets (@def-definable-set), and, on the second pass, isomorphic structures satisfy the same sentences (@thm-isomorphism-invariance). Proved: the semantics, and every non-derivability result the chapter gets from a counter-model, given the soundness statement. Stated without proof: the undecidability of derivability (Church and Turing; Section 7.2, again in 7.6) and the 2^k bound on counter-models of monadic claims (Section 7.2); in the optional Section 7.6, completeness (every consistent theory has a model), compactness, the Löwenheim–Skolem theorem and the decidability of monadic sentences; and, in the solution to Exercise R2 of Section 7.5, that P \wedge Q cannot be derived from its premise without ulename{RAA} (nothing depends on it). Beyond this volume: why no consistent theory whose axioms a procedure can list, and which derives the basic facts of arithmetic, decides every sentence about 
N (Gödel’s incompleteness theorem, named in Section 7.6). Chapter 8 turns derivations into the prose of mathematics. Terms - assignment: a value for each variable (@def-assignment). - automorphism: an isomorphism onto itself (@def-isomorphism-of-structures). - consistent, inconsistent theory: no finite list of axioms derives  ot (@def-inconsistent-theory). - counter-model: premises true, conclusion false (@def-first-order-entailment). - definable set: the elements where a formula holds (@def-definable-set). - domain: what a structure’s quantifiers range over (@def-structure). - independent sentence: neither derivable nor refutable (@prp-model-shows-independence). - isomorphism of structures: a bijection respecting every symbol (@def-isomorphism-of-structures). - model of a theory: a structure with every axiom true (@def-model-of-theory). - satisfaction,  M, \ell \models \varphi: the clauses (S1)–(S7) (@def-satisfaction). - semantic entailment, \Gamma \models \varphi: no counter-model (@def-first-order-entailment). - structure: a domain and a meaning for every symbol (@def-structure). - theory, T \vdash \sigma: a set of axioms; derivable from finitely many (@def-theory). - true in a structure,  M \models \sigma: satisfied under every assignment (Section 7.1).

title: 7.1 Structures and Satisfaction
content:
Structures and Satisfaction Sections 5.3 to 6.4 derived a good deal, and some searches stalled. The converse of @prp-exists-forall-swap could not be finished: every attempt ran into a side condition. The converse of @prp-exists-and stalled in the same way, and so did the search for \exists x\, P(x) \vdash P(c) in @exr-existential-introduction-c2. But a search that fails proves nothing, since a cleverer derivation might exist. Chapter 4 met the same problem for the connectives and solved it with meaning: a row of a truth table that makes the premises true and the conclusion false rules out every derivation at once (@cor-refuting-row). This section builds the meaning of a quantified formula: a model, a domain of objects with a meaning for every symbol. A model that makes the premises true and the conclusion false is a counter-model, the exact form of the counter-readings used since Section 5.3, and Section 7.2 uses it to settle the stalled searches. [Looking back] Section 4.4 gave each formula of Chapter 4 a truth value by recursion on the formula, one clause per connective, under a row. This section does the same for first-order formulas, with a structure and an assignment in place of a row. Clauses (S3)–(S5) below are Chapter 4’s clauses for  ot and the connectives, read as conditions for satisfaction instead of truth under a row; (S6) and (S7), for the quantifiers, are the new ones. Why a row is not enough Chapter 4’s semantics gave each atom a truth value and computed the rest. Try it on the stalled sequent of @prp-exists-forall-swap’s converse,  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) \vdash \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) . Neither side has a main connective among 
eg, \wedge, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow: each is a quantified formula, and a truth table would have to treat each as one atom. The sequent would become p \vdash q, refuted by the row p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F}. That “refutation” is worthless. The same reading refutes  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x), which is derivable (@prp-forall-implies-exists). Treating a quantified formula as an atom throws away exactly the structure that the quantifier rules use. So what does make  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) true or false? Section 5.1 read such sentences informally, over a domain: “for every y in the domain there is an x in the domain with R(x, y)”. To decide it we need three things. - A domain: the objects the variables range over. Over 
Z the sentence may be true and over a three-element set false. - A meaning for each symbol. R is a predicate symbol, a name with two slots and no meaning of its own (Section 5.2). Read as > on 
Z, the sentence says “every integer has an integer above it”, which is true; read as < on 
N, it says “every natural number has a natural number below it”, which is false at y = 0. - Values for the free variables, if there are any. The formula \exists y\, (y < x) is neither true nor false on 
N until we know which number x is. The first two together are a structure; the third is an assignment. A structure with an assignment decides every formula, by clauses that read the quantifiers as Section 5.1 read them. That is all this section does; Section 7.2 uses the result. Structures Situate the notion first. A formula is built from symbols: constants such as c and 0, function symbols such as f and +, predicate symbols such as P, R and <, each function and predicate symbol with its number of argument places, its arity (Section 5.2, @def-term and @def-first-order-formula). The symbol = is special: it is part of the logic, with rules of its own (@def-rules-equality), and it will always mean the same thing. A structure gives every other symbol a meaning. A structure is a non-empty set of objects together with a meaning for each symbol: an object for each constant, an operation for each function symbol, and a relation for each predicate symbol. [Structure] Fix a collection of constants, function symbols and predicate symbols, each function and predicate symbol with its arity n \ge 1. A structure  M (also called a model) for these symbols consists of 1. a non-empty set D, the domain of  M; 2. for each constant c, an element c^{ M} \in D; 3. for each function symbol f of arity n, a function f^{ M} \colon D^n 	o D, defined at every n-tuple of elements of D; 4. for each predicate symbol R of arity n, a set R^{ M} of n-tuples of elements of D. The symbol = is not interpreted by  M: in every structure it means identity, “is the same element of D as”. In words. (M1) says what the variables range over, and insists that there is at least one object. (M2) says which object each name names; two constants may name the same object. (M3) makes each function symbol an operation that can be applied to any objects of the domain and always returns an object of the domain. (M4) makes each predicate symbol a relation: R^{ M} is the set of tuples for which R “holds”. A one-place predicate symbol P becomes a subset P^{ M} \subseteq D, a two-place one a set of ordered pairs, and so on. Here D^n is the set of n-tuples (d_1, \dots, d_n) of elements of D; this section uses only their everyday meaning. We usually describe a structure in one line, naming the domain and the meaning of each symbol, and write “ M = (
Z, <)” for the structure with domain 
Z in which the symbol < means the usual order. When a symbol has its usual meaning on a familiar set, we say so and do not write <^{ M}. When the domain is followed by a list of symbols, a semicolon separates the domain from the list, as in (
R; 1, +, \cdot): each listed symbol has its usual meaning on that set, and only the listed symbols belong to the structure. With a single symbol we may also write a comma, as in (
Z, <). Examples, simplest first. - One element. D = \{ a \}, with P^{ M} = \{ a \}. This is the degenerate structure. Every variable must take the value a, so “for every element” and “there is an element” both mean “a”. It will reappear as a test case: a sentence true here and false in some other structure cannot be derivable (by the soundness statement in Section 7.2), and some of the chapter’s non-derivable sequents need at least two elements to refute. - Two elements, one relation. D = \{ a, b \}, with R^{ M} = \{ (a, a), (b, b) \}: the relation “is the same as”, written out as a set of pairs. A finite structure can be given completely by listing. - The integers with their order. D = 
Z, with R^{ M} = \{ (x, y) \in 
Z^2 : x > y \}. Here the relation is described by a condition rather than a list. - Arithmetic. D = 
R, with the constants 0 and 1 naming zero and one, the function symbols +, \cdot and two-place - meaning addition, multiplication and subtraction, the one-place symbols -, (\cdot)^2 and \abs{\cdot} meaning negation, squaring and absolute value, and <, \le, >, \ge the usual order. Extended by the other familiar symbols with their usual meanings (numerals, halving, the predicates \in A, division with its value at a zero denominator fixed arbitrarily as in the non-example below, and a function symbol for each sequence or function an example uses), this is the structure in which the analysis examples of Chapters 5 and 6 have been read all along. Non-example by minimal change. Take the arithmetic structure and add a one-place function symbol g, meant to be read as x \mapsto 1/x. This is not a structure: (M3) asks for a function defined at every element of D, and 1/0 is not defined. Everything else in the description is fine; exactly clause (M3) fails, at the single point 0. There are two repairs. Shrink the domain to (0, \infty), where 1/x is always defined; or keep 
R and give g any value at 0, say g^{ M}(0) \coloneqq 0. The second repair is the one this book uses for terms such as 1/n: the value at 0 is fixed arbitrarily and is never looked at, because such terms are used only under a bound n \in 
Z_{>0} (as in Exercise C3 of Section 7.2), exactly as a sequence a_n was read in Section 5.1 as a function symbol whose values off 
N are never used. The domain is non-empty because of @prp-forall-implies-exists; the subsection “Why domains are non-empty” explains why. - Total functions. Clause (M3) is what makes every term name an object: the term g(0) must have a value, or the formula g(0) = g(0), which ulename{{=}I} derives from nothing, would have no truth value. - Identity for =. The rule ulename{{=}E} replaces equals by equals everywhere. If a structure could read = as some other relation, ulename{{=}E} would fail. On 
Z, read x = y as “x and y have the same parity” and P as “is positive”: then -2 = 2 and P(2) would both hold, while P(-2), which ulename{{=}E} derives from them, fails. With = fixed as identity, no such reading exists. A structure must interpret every symbol that occurs in the formulas at hand. “Take D = 
Z” is not yet a structure for  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y): until R is given a meaning, the sentence has no truth value, and the same domain makes it true with R read as > and false with R read as “x \cdot x = y” (at y = 2). Always write the domain and the meaning of each symbol. Drawing a finite structure A finite structure whose symbols are one- and two-place predicate symbols can be drawn, as Section 5.1 drew its worlds. Each element is a dot. Beside a dot stand its name and the one-place predicates it satisfies. For a two-place relation R, an arrow runs from d to e for each pair (d, e) in R^{ M}, and a loop at d records the pair (d, d). Deciding a sentence in a drawn structure is then reading the picture, dot by dot. When the relation is a partial order \le, arrows crowd the picture, and a lighter drawing is used. Section 7.4 defines partial orders; here it is enough that \le is reflexive and transitive and never holds both ways between two different elements. The Hasse diagram of such a structure puts d below e when d \le e and d 
e e, and draws a line only for the pairs with nothing strictly between them. The loops, and the pairs that follow by chaining lines upwards, are understood. In the right picture below, 1 \le 6 holds although no line joins 1 and 6: the chain 1, 2, 6 runs upwards. A picture is a structure only when it says what every symbol means: the caption names the domain and each symbol. Figure F draws two structures. Left: D = \{ a, b, c \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, R^{ M} = \{ (a, b), (b, b), (c, a) \}. Right: D = \{ 1, 2, 3, 6 \}, with x \le y read as “x divides y”. Figure F. An arrow diagram (left) and a Hasse diagram (right). In the left structure of Figure F, decide  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) and \exists y\,  orall x\, R(x, y). The first is true: every dot has an arrow out of it (a 	o b, b 	o b, c 	o a). The second is false: no dot receives an arrow from all three. The dot b receives none from c, the dot a none from a or b, and the dot c none at all. Assignments and the value of a term A structure names the objects that constants stand for. Variables are different: their whole purpose is to range over the domain, so a structure gives them no fixed value. A separate object records what they stand for at a given moment. [Assignment] Let  M be a structure with domain D. An assignment in  M is a function \ell that gives every variable x a value \ell(x) \in D. For an assignment \ell, a variable x and an element d \in D, the assignment \ell[x \mapsto d] is the one that gives x the value d and every other variable the value \ell gives it: \ell[x \mapsto d](y) \coloneqq  egin{cases} d & 	ext{if } y 	ext{ is the variable } x, \ \ell(y) & 	ext{if } y 	ext{ is any other variable.} \end{cases} In words: an assignment is a choice of value for every variable at once, and \ell[x \mapsto d] changes that choice at the one variable x, leaving the others alone. The assignment \ell[x \mapsto d] is what the quantifiers will use: “for every x” will mean “for every d \in D, with x set to d”. Changes can be stacked: \ell[x \mapsto d][y \mapsto e] first sets x to d and then y to e. When x and y are different variables the order does not matter, since each change touches only its own variable; when they are the same variable, the later change wins. There are always assignments, because D is non-empty: pick any d_0 \in D and let every variable have the value d_0. Like a valuation in Chapter 4 (@def-valuation), an assignment fixes infinitely many values, and a formula will only ever look at finitely many of them. With a structure and an assignment, every term names an element of the domain. Terms are built by the clauses of @def-term, so the value is defined by recursion on terms, in the pattern of @thm-structural-recursion. The value of a term is computed from its variables and constants upwards, one function symbol at a time. For a structure  M and an assignment \ell, the value t^{ M, \ell} \in D of a term t is: - x^{ M, \ell} \coloneqq \ell(x) for a variable x; - c^{ M, \ell} \coloneqq c^{ M} for a constant c; - f(t_1, \dots, t_n)^{ M, \ell} \coloneqq f^{ M} igl( t_1^{ M, \ell}, \dots, t_n^{ M, \ell}  igr) for a function symbol f of arity n. The third clause is where (M3) is needed: f^{ M} must accept every tuple the terms t_1, \dots, t_n might produce. For example, in the arithmetic structure on 
R, let \ell(x) = 2 and \ell(y) = -3. The term x \cdot x + y, which is +(\cdot(x, x), y) written in the usual way, has value 2 \cdot 2 + (-3) = 1. Under \ell[y \mapsto 1] it has value 2 \cdot 2 + 1 = 5, and under \ell[x \mapsto 0] it has value -3. The term 1 + 1 has value 2 under every assignment, since it contains no variable. Satisfaction Now the central definition. We want to say when a structure and an assignment make a formula true. Formulas are built by the clauses of @def-first-order-formula, so we define it by recursion, one clause per way of building a formula, and each clause reads its connective or quantifier as Chapter 4 and Section 5.1 read it. A formula is satisfied when the objects its terms name stand in the relations its predicates name, combined by the connectives as in a truth table, with “for every x” and “there is an x” ranging over the domain. Satisfaction Let  M be a structure with domain D and \ell an assignment in  M. The relation  M, \ell \models \varphi, read “ M satisfies \varphi under \ell”, is defined by recursion on the formula \varphi: 1.  M, \ell \models R(t_1, \dots, t_n) if  igl( t_1^{ M, \ell}, \dots, t_n^{ M, \ell}  igr) \in R^{ M}; 2.  M, \ell \models t_1 = t_2 if t_1^{ M, \ell} and t_2^{ M, \ell} are the same element of D; 3.  M, \ell \models  ot never holds; 4.  M, \ell \models 
eg\varphi if  M, \ell \models \varphi does not hold; 5.  M, \ell \models \varphi \wedge \psi if both  M, \ell \models \varphi and  M, \ell \models \psi;  M, \ell \models \varphi \vee \psi if at least one of them holds;  M, \ell \models \varphi 	o \psi unless  M, \ell \models \varphi holds and  M, \ell \models \psi does not;  M, \ell \models \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi if both hold or neither does; 6.  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi if  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi for every d \in D; 7.  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi if  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi for at least one d \in D. When  M, \ell \models \varphi does not hold we write  M, \ell 
ot\models \varphi. For a list \Gamma of formulas,  M, \ell \models \Gamma means that  M, \ell \models \gamma for every formula \gamma of \Gamma. Read it clause by clause. (S1): an atomic formula is satisfied exactly when the values of its terms form a tuple in the relation that interprets its predicate symbol. (S2): an equation is satisfied when both sides name the same object; this is where “= means identity” enters. (S3)–(S5) are the  ot half of (V1) and clauses (V2)–(V6) of Chapter 4’s @def-truth-value, with “is true under v” replaced by “is satisfied by  M under \ell”:  ot is never satisfied, 
eg flips, \wedge needs both, \vee needs one, 	o fails only with a satisfied hypothesis and an unsatisfied conclusion, \leftrightarrow needs agreement. (S6) and (S7) are the new clauses. To decide  orall x\, \varphi, we run through the elements d of the domain, set x to d and leave every other variable alone, and ask whether \varphi is satisfied each time. For \exists x\, \varphi one success is enough. In symbols, for (S6) and (S7):  egin{aligned}  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi \quad &	ext{iff} \quad 	ext{for every } d \in D, \ \  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi , \  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi \quad &	ext{iff} \quad 	ext{there is } d \in D 	ext{ with }  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi . \end{aligned} A trace, step by step. Decide  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) in two structures, both with < the usual order:  M_1 with domain 
N, and  M_2 with domain \{ 1, 2, 3 \}. Let \ell be any assignment. In  M_1: by (S6) we must check, for every d \in 
N, that  M_1, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \exists y\, (x < y). Fix d. By (S7) it is enough to find one e \in 
N with  M_1, \ell[x \mapsto d][y \mapsto e] \models x < y. Take e = d + 1. Under \ell[x \mapsto d][y \mapsto d + 1] the terms x and y have the values d and d + 1, and d < d + 1, so (S1) holds. Hence the sentence is satisfied. Notice that the witness e = d + 1 depends on d: (S7) is checked inside (S6), once for each d. In  M_2: (S6) asks the same for d = 1, 2, 3. At d = 1 and d = 2 the witnesses e = 2 and e = 3 work. At d = 3 no e \in \{ 1, 2, 3 \} has 3 < e, so (S7) fails for \ell[x \mapsto 3], and (S6) fails. So  M_2 
ot\models  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y), and the failure has a name: the element 3 has nothing above it. The assignment matters for free variables. In  M_1 = (
N, <), with \le also read as usual, take the formula  orall y\, (x \le y), in which x is free. Under an assignment with \ell(x) = 0 it is satisfied, since every e \in 
N has 0 \le e (recall that 
N = \{ 0, 1, 2, \dots \}). Under an assignment with \ell(x) = 1 it is not: e = 0 gives 1 \le 0, which fails. The same formula in the same structure is satisfied under one assignment and not under another; it is a property of x, “x is least”, not a statement. Well defined. The clauses define, for each formula, which pairs ( M, \ell) satisfy it, by recursion on the formula: (S1)–(S3) settle the atomic formulas and  ot, and each of (S4)–(S7) settles a compound formula from its immediate parts. One point needs a word. Clauses (S6) and (S7) consult the immediate part \varphi under other assignments \ell[x \mapsto d], not under \ell. So the recursion must define satisfaction of each formula under all assignments at once, and then (S6) reads off the answer for \varphi at every \ell[x \mapsto d]. The recursion is still on the formula alone, and @thm-structural-recursion, applied to formulas built by the clauses of @def-first-order-formula, gives exactly one such relation. Degenerate cases. In the one-element structure D = \{ a \}, every assignment gives every variable the value a, so \ell[x \mapsto a] = \ell and (S6) and (S7) both reduce to “ M, \ell \models \varphi”. So  orall x\, \varphi and \exists x\, \varphi are satisfied together or not at all, and every equation x = y is satisfied. In any structure,  orall x\, (x = x) is satisfied, since every d is the same element as itself; and \exists x\, 
eg(x = x) never is. Satisfaction as a game. Section 5.1 read a sentence whose quantifiers all stand in front as a game between a challenger, who tries to make it false, and a defender, who tries to make it true. The clauses extend that game to every formula, one move per clause. At  orall x\, \varphi (S6) the challenger picks an element d \in D for x; at \exists x\, \varphi (S7) the defender picks. At \varphi \wedge \psi the challenger picks the side to be checked, and at \varphi \vee \psi the defender does; \varphi 	o \psi is played as 
eg\varphi \vee \psi, and \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi as the two implications joined by \wedge. At 
eg\varphi the players change roles (S4), since making 
eg\varphi true is making \varphi false. At an atomic formula the game ends, and the defender wins exactly when (S1) or (S2) holds; at  ot the defender never wins (S3). A sentence is true in  M exactly when the defender can answer every challenge and win: read clause by clause, that is what (S1)–(S7) say. In the trace above, the defender’s answer e = d + 1 to each challenge d is such a way of winning on 
N; on \{ 1, 2, 3 \} the challenge d = 3 has no answer. Play the game for \exists y\,  orall x\, (x \le y) on (
N, \le) and on (\{ 1, 2, 3 \}, \le). Who moves first, and who wins? The defender moves first, since \exists comes first: the order of the quantifiers is the order of the moves. On 
N, whatever e the defender names, the challenger answers x = e + 1 and wins, so the sentence is false. On \{ 1, 2, 3 \} the defender names 3, and every challenge x has x \le 3, so the sentence is true. Is  orall x\, \exists y\, (y \cdot y = x) satisfied in 
R, in [0, \infty), and in 
C, each with \cdot the usual product? In 
R, no: at d = -1, (S7) asks for a real e with e \cdot e = -1, and every real square is \ge 0. In [0, \infty), yes: for each d \ge 0, e = \sqrt{d} is in the domain and e \cdot e = d; and [0, \infty) with \cdot is a structure, since a product of non-negative reals is non-negative (M3). In 
C, yes: every complex number has a complex square root (school algebra of complex numbers: r(\cos	heta + i\sin	heta) with r \ge 0 has the square root \sqrt{r}\,(\cos rac{	heta}{2} + i\sin rac{	heta}{2})). The sentence is the same all three times; only the structure changes. Only the free variables matter The example of  orall y\, (x \le y) above showed \ell mattering. In the first example it did not: the verdict on  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) was reached for “any assignment \ell”. That is no accident. A sentence has no free variables (@def-sentence), and every variable it contains is bound, so every value \ell gives is overwritten by (S6) or (S7) before it is looked at. We prove the general fact, which is the first-order version of Chapter 4’s @lem-coincidence: satisfaction depends only on the values of the free variables. Say that two assignments \ell and \ell' agree on a set of variables if \ell(y) = \ell'(y) for every variable y in it. We need the free variables of a formula (@def-free-variable), in the recursive description given after that definition in Section 5.2: every variable occurring in an atomic formula is free there; 
eg\varphi has the free variables of \varphi; \varphi \circ \psi, for a binary connective \circ, has those of \varphi and those of \psi; and  orall x\, \varphi and \exists x\, \varphi have those of \varphi other than x. [Free Variables Coincidence Lemma] Let  M be a structure and \varphi a formula, and let \ell and \ell' be assignments in  M that agree on every free variable of \varphi. Then  M, \ell \models \varphi \quad 	ext{if and only if} \quad  M, \ell' \models \varphi . In words: to decide a formula, only the values of its free variables matter. Structural induction on \varphi, as for @lem-coincidence, after a first induction on terms: a term’s value depends only on the values of its variables. The connective cases are Chapter 4’s. The quantifier case is the only new one, and it explains why the property must be stated for all pairs of assignments: (S6) compares \ell[x \mapsto d] with \ell'[x \mapsto d], which are new assignments, so the induction hypothesis must apply to them. They agree at x, since both give it d, and at every other free variable of \varphi, since those are free in  orall x\, \varphi. Terms first. We show: if \ell and \ell' agree on every variable occurring in a term t, then t^{ M, \ell} = t^{ M, \ell'}. We use structural induction on terms (@def-term; the pattern of @thm-structural-induction). For a variable x, the variable x occurs in x, so x^{ M, \ell} = \ell(x) = \ell'(x) = x^{ M, \ell'}. For a constant c, both values are c^{ M}. For f(t_1, \dots, t_n), every variable of t_i occurs in f(t_1, \dots, t_n), so the hypothesis for t_i gives t_i^{ M, \ell} = t_i^{ M, \ell'} for each i; applying f^{ M} to equal tuples gives equal values. Formulas. We apply structural induction to the property C(\varphi): for all assignments \ell, \ell' in  M that agree on the free variables of \varphi,  M, \ell \models \varphi if and only if  M, \ell' \models \varphi. Atomic formulas. Let \varphi be R(t_1, \dots, t_n), and let \ell, \ell' agree on its free variables. Every variable occurring in \varphi is free in it (@def-free-variable), so \ell and \ell' agree on the variables of each t_i, and by the claim for terms t_i^{ M, \ell} = t_i^{ M, \ell'}. The two tuples in (S1) are equal, so one lies in R^{ M} exactly when the other does. The case t_1 = t_2 is the same with (S2). For  ot, neither side holds, by (S3). Connectives. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let \ell, \ell' agree on the free variables of \varphi \wedge \psi. These include the free variables of \varphi and those of \psi, so  M, \ell \models \varphi if and only if  M, \ell' \models \varphi, and likewise for \psi. By (S5), satisfaction of \varphi \wedge \psi is decided by these two answers through the same rule for \ell and for \ell', so C(\varphi \wedge \psi) holds. The cases 
eg\varphi, \varphi \vee \psi, \varphi 	o \psi, and \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi are the same argument with (S4) and the other parts of (S5), as in the proof of @lem-coincidence. Universal quantifier. Assume C(\varphi), let x be a variable, and let \ell, \ell' agree on the free variables of  orall x\, \varphi. Let d \in D. We claim that \ell[x \mapsto d] and \ell'[x \mapsto d] agree on the free variables of \varphi. At x, both give d. A free variable y of \varphi other than x is a free variable of  orall x\, \varphi (@def-free-variable), so \ell[x \mapsto d](y) = \ell(y) = \ell'(y) = \ell'[x \mapsto d](y). By C(\varphi), applied to these two assignments,  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi \quad 	ext{iff} \quad  M, \ell'[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi . This holds for every d \in D, so by (S6)  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi if and only if  M, \ell' \models  orall x\, \varphi. This proves C( orall x\, \varphi). Existential quantifier. The same argument, with (S7) in place of (S6): the displayed equivalence holds for each d, so there is a d making the left side hold exactly when there is one making the right side hold. Every clause of @def-first-order-formula has been covered, so C(\varphi) holds for every formula \varphi. This proves the lemma. In (
N, \le), does whether \ell satisfies  orall y\, (x \le y) depend on \ell(y)? No: y is not free in the formula, so by the lemma only \ell(x) matters. The formula holds exactly when \ell(x) = 0. The lemma has a consequence that the rest of the section uses constantly. Sentences. If \varphi is a sentence, it has no free variables, so any two assignments agree on its free variables, and the lemma says that  M, \ell \models \varphi either holds for every assignment \ell or for none. We then write  M \models \varphi, and say that \varphi is true in  M (or that  M is a model of \varphi), in the first case, and  M 
ot\models \varphi, \varphi is false in  M, in the second. At least one assignment exists because D is non-empty, so a sentence is always exactly one of true and false in  M. This is the precise form of Section 5.1’s informal “true over a domain”. Only finitely many values matter. A formula has finitely many free variables. To decide  M, \ell \models \varphi, it is enough to know \ell on those. So we describe an assignment by the values that matter (“\ell(x) = 2”), exactly as Chapter 4 described a valuation by the values of a few atoms. The same sentence can be true in one structure and false in another, and “true” without a structure means nothing.  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) is true in (
N, <) and false in (\{ 1, 2, 3 \}, <), as traced above. A sentence of predicate logic is like a formula of Chapter 4 with atoms: it has a truth value only once the meaning of its symbols has been fixed. Semantic entailment Chapter 4 said that \Gamma entails \psi when every row that makes \Gamma true makes \psi true (@def-valid-argument). The row is now a structure with an assignment. An argument is valid when every structure, under every assignment, that satisfies all the premises also satisfies the conclusion. [Semantic Entailment in Predicate Logic] Let \Gamma be a list of formulas and \varphi a formula. We say \Gamma semantically entails \varphi, and write \Gamma \models \varphi, if for every structure  M for the symbols occurring in \Gamma and \varphi, and every assignment \ell in  M,  M, \ell \models \Gamma \quad \Rightarrow \quad  M, \ell \models \varphi . We write \models \varphi when \Gamma is empty. If \Gamma \models \varphi fails, we write \Gamma 
ot\models \varphi; a structure  M with an assignment \ell such that  M, \ell \models \Gamma and  M, \ell 
ot\models \varphi is a counter-model to \Gamma \models \varphi. In words: “every structure” means every domain and every meaning of the symbols, so an entailment holds for reasons of form and not because of what R happens to mean. “Every assignment” covers every value of the free variables; when \Gamma and \varphi are sentences, the assignment makes no difference, by @lem-free-coincidence. And a counter-model is the analogue of Chapter 4’s refuting row: one structure, with one assignment, where the premises hold and the conclusion does not. The symbol \models is the one of Chapter 4, and the context always shows which is meant: a sequent of formulas with quantifiers or predicate symbols is read with this definition. A structure may interpret symbols that do not occur in \Gamma or \varphi. The clauses of @def-satisfaction consult only the symbols of the formula at hand, so such extra meanings change nothing. First examples of entailment. The argument Section 5.1 opened with, “every positive real has a square root; 2 is positive; so 2 has a square root”, is  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \ P(c) \vdash Q(c), derived in Section 5.3. Truth tables called it invalid, since they saw three unrelated atoms. It is valid in the new sense:  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \ P(c) \models Q(c) . Let  M, \ell satisfy both premises, and let a = c^{ M}. By (S6) for the first premise, with d = a, we get  M, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models P(x) 	o Q(x). Under \ell[x \mapsto a] the term x has value a, and under \ell the term c has value a; so by (S1),  M, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models P(x) holds if and only if a \in P^{ M} if and only if  M, \ell \models P(c), which is the second premise. So by (S5)  M, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models Q(x), that is, a \in Q^{ M}, and by (S1) again  M, \ell \models Q(c). Chapter 4’s objection to this argument is gone. Proving an entailment by meaning To show \Gamma \models \varphi, fix an arbitrary structure and assignment satisfying \Gamma, and show that they satisfy \varphi. The first proof below writes every step with the clause that licenses it; the second condenses it to what a mathematician writes. [A Semantic Proof, Clause by Clause] Show that \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \models  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y). Each step ends with the clause that licenses it. 1. Let  M be a structure with domain D and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) (@def-first-order-entailment). 2. There is d \in D with  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models  orall y\, R(x, y) (S7). 3. To show  M, \ell \models  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y), let e \in D; we must show  M, \ell[y \mapsto e] \models \exists x\, R(x, y) (S6). 4. From item 2, with this e:  M, \ell[x \mapsto d][y \mapsto e] \models R(x, y) (S6). 5. Under \ell[x \mapsto d][y \mapsto e] the terms x, y have the values d, e, so (d, e) \in R^{ M} (S1). 6. Take the witness d for x: under \ell[y \mapsto e][x \mapsto d] the values are again d, e, so  M, \ell[y \mapsto e][x \mapsto d] \models R(x, y) by item 5 (S1), and so  M, \ell[y \mapsto e] \models \exists x\, R(x, y) (S7). 7. Since e was arbitrary,  M, \ell \models  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) (S6). Condensed. Suppose some d is R-related to everything. Then for each e, the element d itself is related to e, so each e has something related to it. Section 5.6 derived the same sequent (@prp-exists-forall-swap); this is its meaning. The converse fails, and Section 7.2 draws why. In item 6, why are \ell[y \mapsto e][x \mapsto d] and \ell[x \mapsto d][y \mapsto e] the same assignment? The variables x and y are different, and each change touches only its own variable, so the order of the two changes does not matter (the paragraph after @def-assignment). [The Drinker Sentence, by Meaning] Show that \models \exists x\,  igl( P(x) 	o  orall y\, P(y)  igr): in every structure, some element has the property that if it has P, everything has P. Let  M and \ell be given, with domain D. Case 1: P^{ M} = D. Choose any d \in D, which exists because D is non-empty (M1). Under \ell[x \mapsto d] the formula  orall y\, P(y) is satisfied, by (S6), so the implication is satisfied, by (S5); hence the sentence holds, by (S7). Case 2: some d \in D is not in P^{ M}. Under \ell[x \mapsto d] the hypothesis P(x) fails (S1), so the implication is satisfied (S5), and (S7) gives the sentence. The case split is on a question about the whole structure, whether P^{ M} = D, and the witness depends on its answer; this is why no witness can be named in advance, and why a derivation needs a detour (Section 6.3 derived it, with D, n, m in place of P, x, y, @exr-first-order-search-c1). Case 1 is where the non-empty domain is used, as in the next subsection. Why domains are non-empty Clause (M1) of @def-structure demands a non-empty domain. Here is the reason. @prp-forall-implies-exists derives  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x) in three lines: ulename{ orall E} at the variable x, then ulename{\exists I}. The matching entailment holds for our structures:  orall x\, P(x) \models \exists x\, P(x) . Let  M, \ell \models  orall x\, P(x). Since D is non-empty, choose some d \in D. By (S6),  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models P(x), and this d is the one element (S7) asks for, so  M, \ell \models \exists x\, P(x). Now suppose empty domains were allowed. In a structure with D = \emptyset, (S6) says  orall x\, P(x) is satisfied, since “for every d \in \emptyset” has nothing to check; and (S7) says \exists x\, P(x) is not, since there is no d at all. So the sequent would be derivable and yet fail in a structure, and the rules would lead from a true premise to a false conclusion. (Worse, no assignment into an empty domain exists, so even the clauses could not be applied as written.) One of two things had to give: the rule ulename{ orall E} at a variable, or empty domains. The book, like most of mathematics, keeps the rules and makes domains non-empty. Nothing is lost. Statements about an empty set are handled by the bounded quantifiers of @def-bounded-quantifier, inside a non-empty domain. The bounded forms  orall x \in \emptyset\ \varphi and \exists x \in \emptyset\ \varphi abbreviate  orall x\, (x \in \emptyset 	o \varphi) and \exists x\, (x \in \emptyset \wedge \varphi), and in a structure with domain 
R in which the one-place predicate symbol \in \emptyset (Section 5.2) is interpreted, by (M4), as the empty subset of 
R, the first is true (every hypothesis d \in \emptyset is false) and the second is false (no d is in \emptyset). Vacuous truth lives in the bound, not in the domain. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let  M_{
N},  M_{
Z},  M_{
Q} be the structures with domains 
N,

eg(y < x), (iii)  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( x < y 	o \exists z\, (x < z \wedge z < y)  igr) and (iv)  orall x\, \exists y\, (y < x), say in which of the three structures it is true, with a witness or a failing element for each verdict. 2. True or false: if a sentence is true in some structure, it is true in every structure for its symbols. 3. Why must the domain of a structure be non-empty? In an empty domain  orall x\, P(x) would be true, with nothing to check, and \exists x\, P(x) false, with no witness; so the rules would lead from a true premise to a false conclusion. (There would also be no assignments at all.) (d) (S7), applied to the premise in item 2. The element d is fixed before any e is chosen, and item 2 says that d is related to every e, by (S6); so item 6 may use d whatever e item 3 picked. [A2: Drill] Each part takes a line or two. Parts (a)–(d) read a structure or a clause, (e)–(i) decide a formula in a given structure, with a witness or a failing element, (j) and (k) judge, and (l) builds a structure. 1. Let D = \{ a, b \} and P^{ M} = \{ a \}. Is  orall x\, P(x) true in  M? 2. In the same structure, is \exists x\,

By @lem-free-coincidence, the values of which variables can matter to the truth of  orall y\, (x \le y) \wedge z = z in a given structure? Do they all matter? 5. In (\{ 0, 1, 2 \}, \le), is \exists x\,  orall y\, (x \le y) true? 6. In (
N, <), under an assignment with \ell(x) = 3, is \exists y\, (y < x) satisfied? And with \ell(x) = 0? 7. In the left structure of Figure F, is  orall x\, (P(x) 	o \exists y\, R(y, x)) true? 8. Decide  orall x\,  orall y\, (x \le y \vee y \le x) in (

(c) (-2) \cdot (-2) + 1 = 5. (d) At most x and z, its free variables; not y. Not always: z never matters, since z = z holds under every assignment, and whether x matters depends on the structure. In (
N, \le) it does (true with \ell(x) = 0, false with \ell(x) = 1); if \le^{ M} is empty it does not. The lemma gives an upper bound, not the exact set. (e) Yes, with x = 0. (f) Yes, with y = 0. With \ell(x) = 0, no: nothing in 
N is below 0. (g) Yes: the only element with P is a, and the arrow c 	o a enters it; at b and c the hypothesis fails. (h) True in

otin 
N. (k) Both true: the first because its hypothesis fails at a; the second because both sides are true. (l) R^{ M} = \{ (1, 2), (2, 1) \}: no loops, and each element has an arrow out. B. Practice [B1: One sentence, two pictures] Two structures for the one symbol \le are drawn below. On the left,  M_1: the domain D_1 = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 \}, with x \le y read as “x divides y”, as a Hasse diagram. On the right,  M_2 = (\{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 \}, \le), with the usual order, as a vertical chain. Decide each sentence in each structure, with a witness or a failing pair: 1. \exists x\,  orall y\, (x \le y); 2. \exists x\,  orall y\, (y \le x); 3.  orall x\,  orall y\, (x \le y \vee y \le x); 4.  orall x\,  orall y\, \exists z\, (x \le z \wedge y \le z). Which of them tell the two structures apart? (i) True in both: x = 1 in each, since 1 divides every element of D_1 and is the least element of  M_2. (ii) True in both: x = 12 in  M_1, since every element of D_1 divides 12; x = 6 in  M_2. (iii) False in  M_1, at x = 2, y = 3: neither divides the other. True in  M_2: of two numbers, one is at most the other. (iv) True in both: z = 12 in  M_1, and z = 6 in  M_2 (or z the larger of x and y). Only (iii) separates them. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 8: 2 for each of (i)–(iv) in both structures, 1 for the verdicts and 1 for a named witness or failing pair for every verdict. - 2: naming (iii) as the only separating sentence. Fatal errors (0 for the part): a verdict on  M_1 that reads \le as the usual order of numbers. [B2: A model on three elements] Give an example of a structure with exactly three elements in which both  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad  orall x\, 
eg R(x, x) are true. Check both sentences. Which properties must every such structure have? Take D = \{ 0, 1, 2 \} and R^{ M} = \{ (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0) \}: each element is related to the next one around a circle. First sentence: for d = 0, 1, 2, the witnesses e = 1, 2, 0 give pairs in R^{ M}. Second sentence: none of (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2) is in R^{ M}, so 
eg R(x, x) is satisfied under \ell[x \mapsto d] for each d. The properties every answer must have: the domain has three elements; every element d has some e with (d, e) \in R^{ M}; and no pair (d, d) is in R^{ M}, so that e is always different from d. Any R^{ M} meeting these works, for instance \{ (0, 1), (1, 0), (2, 0) \} or the set of all pairs (d, e) with d 
e e. [B3: Is it a structure?] For each description, say whether it is a structure for the symbols named. If not, name the clause of @def-structure that fails, and repair it with as small a change as you can. 1. D = 
Q, with a one-place function symbol f read as x \mapsto 1/x for x 
e 0 and f(0) = 0. 2. D = 
N, with f read as x \mapsto x - 1. 3. D = \emptyset, with P read as the empty set. 4. D = 
Z, with a constant c naming 	frac12. 5. D = 
R, with a two-place predicate symbol R read as \{ (x, y) : y = \sqrt{x} \}. 6. D = 
R, with a one-place function symbol g read as x \mapsto \sqrt{x}. (i) Yes: every element has a value in 
Q. (ii) No: (M3) fails, since f(0) = -1 
otin 
N. Repair: f(0) \coloneqq 0. (iii) No: (M1) fails. Repair: any non-empty domain. (iv) No: (M2) fails, since 	frac12 
otin 
Z. Repair: D = 
Q, or let c name an integer. (v) Yes: (M4) asks only for a set of pairs, and nothing requires a relation to hold for every first element. (vi) No: (M3) fails, since \sqrt{-1} is not real. Repair: D = [0, \infty), or fix g(x) \coloneqq 0 for x < 0. Descriptions (v) and (vi) carry the same information, and only the function symbol must be total. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 6: 1 for each verdict. - 2: the clause named at each “no” (all four right). - 2: repairs that are minimal and correct. Fatal errors (0 for the part): calling (v) a non-structure because \sqrt{x} is undefined for x < 0. C. Going deeper [C1: Proofs by meaning] 1. Prove  orall x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \models  orall x\, P(x) \wedge  orall x\, Q(x) clause by clause, as in @exm-clause-by-clause. 2. Prove  orall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)) \models  orall x\, P(x) \vee \exists x\, Q(x), condensed. 3. Prove \exists x\, (P(x) 	o Q(c)) \models  orall x\, P(x) 	o Q(c), condensed, and say where your proof uses the existential premise. (a) Let  M, \ell \models  orall x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)). By (S5) it suffices to show each conjunct. For  orall x\, P(x), let d \in D (S6). By (S6) for the premise,  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models P(x) \wedge Q(x); by (S5),  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models P(x). Since d was arbitrary,  M, \ell \models  orall x\, P(x) (S6). Likewise  M, \ell \models  orall x\, Q(x), with the other half of (S5). (b) If P^{ M} = D, the left disjunct holds. Otherwise some d \in D is not in P^{ M}. The premise at d gives d \in P^{ M} or d \in Q^{ M}, so d \in Q^{ M}, and \exists x\, Q(x) holds. Either way the disjunction holds. (c) Let d be the premise’s witness: if d \in P^{ M}, then c^{ M} \in Q^{ M}. Suppose  orall x\, P(x) holds; then d \in P^{ M}, so Q(c) holds. The witness d is where the existential premise is used: the hypothesis  orall x\, P(x) is applied at it. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 4: (a), with every step’s clause named, and (S6) used both to fix d and on the premise. - 3: (b), split on whether P^{ M} = D (or on a failing element), with the premise used at that element. - 3: (c), taking the premise’s witness d and applying the hypothesis  orall x\, P(x) at d (in either order). Fatal errors (0 for the part): in (a), a proof in which d is a particular element (for example a constant’s value, or an element chosen to lie in P^{ M}) rather than an arbitrary d \in D, so that the closing (S6) step for  orall x\, P(x) is unjustified. [C2: Challenge: only the symbols that occur matter] Let  M and  N be structures with the same domain D that give the same meaning to every symbol occurring in a formula \varphi. Prove that for every assignment \ell,  M, \ell \models \varphi if and only if  N, \ell \models \varphi. (This is the claim after @def-first-order-entailment that extra meanings change nothing.) [Hint 1] Terms first, as in the proof of @lem-free-coincidence. [Hint 2] Prove, by structural induction on \varphi, the property: for every assignment \ell, …; the quantifier case needs it at \ell[x \mapsto d]. Terms. For every term t whose symbols  M and  N interpret alike, t^{ M, \ell} = t^{ N, \ell} for every \ell, by structural induction on t. For a variable x, both values are \ell(x). For a constant c, they are c^{ M} = c^{ N}. For f(t_1, \dots, t_n), the hypothesis gives equal values of the t_i, and f^{ M} = f^{ N} applied to equal tuples gives equal values. Formulas. Let A(\varphi) be the property: for every assignment \ell,  M, \ell \models \varphi if and only if  N, \ell \models \varphi, for formulas \varphi whose symbols  M and  N interpret alike. Atomic formulas: the tuples of values are equal by the claim for terms, and R^{ M} = R^{ N}, so (S1) gives the same answer; equations likewise by (S2);  ot by (S3). Connectives: (S4) and (S5) combine equal answers into equal answers. For  orall x\, \varphi: the two structures have the same domain, so d ranges over the same elements in both; for each d, A(\varphi) at the assignment \ell[x \mapsto d] gives equal answers, and (S6) gives A( orall x\, \varphi). For \exists x\, \varphi, the same with (S7). Every clause of @def-first-order-formula has been covered, so A(\varphi) holds for every formula. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the claim for terms, by induction. - 2: the atomic cases, with (S1) and (S2). - 2: the connective cases. - 3: the quantifier case, using the property at the changed assignments and the shared domain. - 1: naming where “same domain” is used. Fatal errors (0 for the step): an induction hypothesis stated for one fixed \ell only.

title: 7.2 Counter-models
content:
Counter-models Section 7.1 gave every formula a meaning in a structure. This section uses it to answer the question Chapters 5 and 6 left open: when a search for a derivation stalls, is there no derivation, or only no derivation found yet? The answer is a counter-model, a structure with an assignment in which the premises are true and the conclusion false (@def-first-order-entailment), together with one statement, soundness for predicate logic, that turns it into a proof that no derivation exists. [Looking back] Sections 4.5 and 4.6 refuted a propositional claim by a row that made its counterexample set true, and searched for that row systematically; Section 4.7 proved that a refuting row rules out every derivation. This section does the same with structures: the counter-model is the row, the procedure below is the search, and the side-condition table plays the part of Section 4.7’s rule-by-rule table. Three pictures Section 5.3 called a reading in which the premises are true and the conclusion false a counter-reading. Here are three, drawn as in Section 7.1. Three counter-readings. (A) P holds at a and Q at b: \exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, Q(x) is true, with the witnesses a and b, and \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) is false, since no dot has both labels; so the converse of @prp-exists-and does not follow (Section 5.6 asked). (B) The integers, with R(x, y) read as x > y. Only the arrows to the next integer down are drawn; R is the whole order >, so R(x, y) holds whenever a chain of arrows leads from x to y.  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) is true, since every integer y has y + 1 above it, and \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) is false, since an integer above every integer would be above itself; so the converse of @prp-exists-forall-swap does not follow. (C) P holds at b, and the constant c names a: \exists x\, P(x) is true, at b, and P(c) is false (@exr-existential-introduction-c2 asked why no derivation was found). Each picture is a structure in the sense of Section 7.1: a domain with a meaning for every symbol. The rest of this section checks such pictures by the clauses, finds them by a procedure, and shows why one of them rules out every derivation. Draw two dots that make  orall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)) true and  orall x\, P(x) \vee  orall x\, Q(x) false. Picture (A) again: each dot has P or Q;  orall x\, P(x) fails at b, and  orall x\, Q(x) fails at a. In picture (C), which clauses of @def-satisfaction decide \exists x\, P(x), and at which element? (S7) asks for some d \in D with  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models P(x); at d = b, (S1) asks whether b \in P^{ M}, and it is. Counter-models A counter-model is found the way a refuting row was found in Chapter 4, by working backwards from what must fail. The conclusion must be false, so read off what that demands; the premises must be true, so read off what they demand; and then build the smallest structure meeting both. The worked examples that follow (the swap, the converses of @prp-exists-and and of the  orall/\vee law, \exists x\, P(x) \vdash P(c), and P(x_0) \vdash  orall x\, P(x)) are sequents whose derivations stalled or were blocked in earlier sections. [The swap of \exists and  orall] Show that  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) 
ot\models \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) , first by a structure on 
Z, then by a structure with two elements. Both formulas are sentences, so by @lem-free-coincidence we need only a structure; any assignment will do. A structure on 
Z. Let  M have domain 
Z and R^{ M} = \{ (x, y) : x > y \}, so that R(x, y) says “x > y”. The premise says “every integer has an integer above it”. To check it by (S6) and (S7): for each e \in 
Z we need some d \in 
Z with (d, e) \in R^{ M}, that is, d > e; d = e + 1 works. The conclusion says “some integer is above every integer”. By (S7) and (S6) it would need a d \in 
Z with d > e for every e \in 
Z; but e = d gives d > d, which is false. So  M \models  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) and  M 
ot\models \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y). A structure with two elements. Let D = \{ a, b \} and R^{ M} = \{ (a, a), (b, b) \}, so that R(x, y) says “x is y”. Premise: for e = a take d = a, and for e = b take d = b; both pairs are in R^{ M}. Conclusion: d = a fails at e = b, since (a, b) 
otin R^{ M}, and d = b fails at e = a. So the premise is true and the conclusion false. The pattern is the one Section 5.1 read as a game. In the premise the witness x is chosen after y and may depend on it (x = y + 1, or x = y); the conclusion asks for one x that works for every y in advance. A one-element structure cannot separate the two sentences: with D = \{ a \}, both are true if (a, a) \in R^{ M} and both false otherwise. Two elements are the least that will do. The two-element structure is the 
Z structure’s idea at its smallest: each element is related to something, and nothing is related to everything. Picture (A), checked by the clauses. With D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, Q^{ M} = \{ b \}, the premise of the converse of @prp-exists-and holds by (S5) and (S7), with witnesses a and b, and the conclusion fails, since a 
otin Q^{ M} and b 
otin P^{ M}: \exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, Q(x) 
ot\models \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) . The same structure refutes the converse of the  orall/\vee law of @prp-quantifier-distribution, since each element is in P^{ M} or in Q^{ M}, and neither set is all of D:  orall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)) 
ot\models  orall x\, P(x) \vee  orall x\, Q(x) . Picture (C): with c^{ M} = a and P^{ M} = \{ b \}, \exists x\, P(x) holds with the witness b, and P(c) fails, since a 
otin P^{ M}. So \exists x\, P(x) 
ot\models P(c). In 
Z, with P and Q read as “even” and “odd”: some integer is even and some integer is odd, but no integer is both; and every integer is even or odd, but it is false that every integer is even, and false that every integer is odd. The assignment is part of a counter-model. Section 5.4 showed why ulename{ orall I} may not generalize over a name in a premise: from P(x_0) one would “derive”  orall x\, P(x). Here x_0 is a variable, free in the premise, so a counter-model needs an assignment as well as a structure. Let  M have domain 
Z with P^{ M} the set of even integers, and let \ell(x_0) = 2. Then  M, \ell \models P(x_0), since 2 is even, and  M, \ell 
ot\models  orall x\, P(x), since (S6) fails at d = 1. So P(x_0) 
ot\models  orall x\, P(x). Under the assignment with \ell(x_0) = 1 the premise is false, and that assignment refutes nothing; the counter-model is the structure with \ell(x_0) = 2. A “counter-model” that falsifies a premise refutes nothing. For  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) \vdash \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y), the structure (
N, <), with R(x, y) read as “x < y”, makes the conclusion false, since no natural number is below every natural number; but it also makes the premise false, since nothing in 
N is below y = 0. It is not a counter-model, and it proves nothing about the sequent. As with rows in Chapter 4, check the premises first. A model of a list of sentences. Counter-models are one use of structures; describing a whole kind of object is another. Consider the three sentences  egin{aligned} & orall x\, 
eg(x < x), \ & orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( (x < y \wedge y < z) 	o x < z  igr), \ & orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y), \end{aligned} which say that < is a strict order (never x < x; x < y and y < z give x < z) with no largest element. The structure (
N, <) is a model of all three: no number is less than itself, the order is transitive, and d + 1 > d is a witness for the third sentence. It is the one the sentences were written with in mind, but not the only one: in (
Z, <) and (
Q, <) all three are true, by the same checks. Finite counter-models are convenient because every clause can be checked by listing. They are not always available: Exercise C1 below gives a sentence that is true in every finite structure and false in an infinite one, and Exercise C2 a sentence with only infinite models. These models differ in ways the three sentences cannot see: 
Z has no least element, and 
Q has a third element between any two. And the one-element structure D = \{ a \} is not a model of the three sentences: if (a, a) \in <^{ M} the first sentence fails, and if not, the third fails at d = a. Exercise C2 shows that no finite structure is a model of them. Give a counter-model to  orall x\, P(x) 	o  orall x\, Q(x) \models  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)). (Think about what makes an implication with a universal hypothesis true cheaply.) Take D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, Q^{ M} = \emptyset. The premise is an implication whose hypothesis  orall x\, P(x) is false (it fails at b), so by (S5) the premise is true. The conclusion fails at d = a: a \in P^{ M} and a 
otin Q^{ M}, so P(x) 	o Q(x) is not satisfied under \ell[x \mapsto a]. (Any structure with P^{ M} 
e D and some element in P^{ M} but not in Q^{ M} works.) Finding a counter-model A counter-model is a structure with an assignment under which every member of the counterexample set \Gamma,
