ot\models  orall x\, P(x). 2.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) 
ot\models \exists x\, P(x) 	o  orall x\, Q(x). 3. 
ot\models \exists x\, P(x) 	o P(x). (Here x is free in the last P(x); the assignment is part of the answer.) (i) Take D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}. The premise holds by (S7) with d = a. The conclusion fails by (S6) at d = b, since b 
otin P^{ M}. (ii) Take D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = Q^{ M} = \{ a \}. Premise: at d = a, P(x) and Q(x) are both satisfied, so P(x) 	o Q(x) is; at d = b, P(x) is not satisfied, so P(x) 	o Q(x) is, by (S5). Hence the premise holds by (S6). Conclusion: \exists x\, P(x) holds (d = a) and  orall x\, Q(x) fails (at d = b), so by (S5) the implication fails. In words: whatever has P has Q, and something has P; that does not make everything have Q. (iii) Take D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, and an assignment with \ell(x) = b. The hypothesis \exists x\, P(x) holds by (S7) with d = a; its x is bound, and the value \ell(x) is overwritten. The conclusion P(x) has x free, with value \ell(x) = b 
otin P^{ M}, so it fails. By (S5) the implication fails under \ell. Under an assignment with \ell(x) = a the implication holds; so the formula is satisfied under some assignments and not others, and a counter-model must name \ell. Now take \varphi and \psi both to be P(x). The formula  orall x\, (P(x) 	o P(x)) is satisfied in every structure under every assignment, since P(x) 	o P(x) is satisfied at every d by (S5) and (S6). So this structure, with \ell, is a counter-model to  orall x\, (P(x) 	o P(x)) \models \exists x\, P(x) 	o P(x), and by the soundness statement of this section that sequent is not derivable. This is why the passage law  orall x\, (\varphi 	o \psi) \dashv\vdash \exists x\, \varphi 	o \psi of @prp-quantifier-passage needs x not free in \psi. [B2: Prove it or break it] For each claim \Gamma \models \varphi, either prove it by meaning (clause by clause or condensed) or give a counter-model, and state what follows about \Gamma \vdash \varphi. For (a) and (c), if the claim holds, also give a derivation. 1.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) \models  orall x\, 
eg P(x). 2.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \ \exists x\, 
eg P(x) \models \exists x\, 
eg Q(x). 3. \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \models \exists x\, R(x, x). 4.  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) \models  orall x\, \exists y\, R(y, x). 5.  orall x\,  igl( P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y)  igr) \models \exists x\, P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y). 6. \exists x\, P(x) 	o  orall y\, Q(y) \models  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)). 7.  orall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)), \ \exists x\, 
eg P(x) \models  orall x\, Q(x). 8.  orall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)), \  orall x\, 
eg P(x) \models  orall x\, Q(x). (a) Holds. If some d were in P^{ M}, then d \in Q^{ M} by the first premise, against the second; so no d is in P^{ M}. A derivation: So \Gamma \vdash \varphi. (b) Fails. D = \{ a \}, P^{ M} = \emptyset, Q^{ M} = \{ a \}: the first premise holds since its hypothesis is false at a, the second holds at a, and the conclusion fails since a \in Q^{ M}. So \Gamma 
vdash \varphi, by the soundness statement. (c) Holds. The premise’s witness d has (d, e) \in R^{ M} for every e, in particular for e = d. A derivation: (d) Fails. D = \{ a, b \}, R^{ M} = \{ (a, b), (b, b) \}: each element has an arrow out, and a has none in. So \Gamma 
vdash \varphi. (e) Holds. If \exists x\, P(x) is true, with witness d, the premise at d gives \exists y\, Q(y); if it is false, the conclusion is true by (S5). (f) Holds. If d \in P^{ M}, then \exists x\, P(x) holds, so  orall y\, Q(y) holds by the premise, so d \in Q^{ M}. (g) Fails. D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, Q^{ M} = \{ b \}: every element is in P^{ M} or Q^{ M}, b 
otin P^{ M}, and a 
otin Q^{ M}. So \Gamma 
vdash \varphi. (h) Holds. Each d is in P^{ M} or Q^{ M}, and not in P^{ M}; so it is in Q^{ M}. A proof by meaning shows \Gamma \models \varphi, not \Gamma \vdash \varphi. The derivations of (a) and (c) show \vdash; for (e), (f) and (h) the matching derivations exist but are not asked for (each is a short exercise with Chapter 5’s rules). The pairs (a) and (b), and (g) and (h), are look-alikes; so are (c) and (d), with opposite prefixes: an \exists orall premise gives a loop, while a  orall\exists premise does not even give every element an incoming arrow. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 8: 1 per part (a)–(h): the correct verdict with its justification, either a proof by meaning that covers every premise, or a counter-model with the premises checked true and the conclusion checked false. A bare verdict scores 0. - 1: the two derivations of (a) and (c), checked rule by rule (both needed). - 1: stating, at a failing claim, that the counter-model gives \Gamma 
vdash \varphi by the soundness statement. Fatal errors (0 for that part): a “counter-model” that falsifies a premise; a proof by meaning offered as a derivation; a verdict given without a justification. [B3: The converse from Section 5.4] @exr-universal-introduction-b2 derived  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) \vdash  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) 	o  orall x\, 
eg P(x), and its search for the converse stalled; this section settled that converse above, in “What this certifies”, with an infinite structure. Find a counter-model to  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) 	o  orall x\, 
eg P(x) \models  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) with exactly two elements, working backwards from the conclusion: say which element breaks the conclusion and how the premise is made true most cheaply. Work backwards. The conclusion fails when some d has d \in P^{ M} and d 
otin Q^{ M}. The premise is cheapest to make true through a false hypothesis: make  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) false by putting some element in Q^{ M}. Take D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, Q^{ M} = \{ b \}. Premise:  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) fails at d = b, since b \in Q^{ M}; so the implication holds by (S5). Conclusion: at d = a, a \in P^{ M} and a 
otin Q^{ M}, so P(x) 	o Q(x) fails under \ell[x \mapsto a], and (S6) fails. By the soundness statement of this section, the converse is not derivable, and the stalled search could not have succeeded. [B4: Each side condition earns its place] Each derivation below breaks a side condition. For (a)–(c), name the line that breaks a side condition and the condition it breaks, give a counter-model to the sequent of its last line, and, where you can, repair the derivation so that it reaches a correct conclusion. For (d), say whether the conclusion is true (follows from the premise) and whether the derivation proves it. (a) (b) (c) (d) (a) Line 3: x_0 appears in the assumption on line 1, which is open at line 3. Line 5 is a legal ulename{ orall I}: no premise, no open assumption, and x_0 is not in the conclusion. (This is the same-name nesting of Section 5.4’s fold “The same error, as a false sentence”, read there over 
Z with x > 0; here P is left open.) Counter-model to \models  orall y\, (P(y) 	o  orall x\, P(x)): D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}. At y = a, P(a) holds and  orall x\, P(x) fails at b. No derivation reaches this conclusion: the counter-model shows it. A repair to a correct conclusion drops the inner box and uses ulename{\exists I} in place of the illegal ulename{ orall I}: This is the RIGHT entry of the second row of the side-condition table, generalized. (b) Line 2: in \varphi =  orall y\, (x = y) the term y is not free for x, since it would be captured by  orall y. Counter-model: any domain with two elements; the premise holds, and no element equals both. Repairs: \exists x\,  orall y\, (y = y) by ulename{\exists I} from line 1, with x not in \varphi; or z = z by ulename{ orall E} at z, then \exists x\, (x = z) by ulename{\exists I}. (c) Line 6: x_0 appears in \chi = Q(x_0). The last line has x_0 free, so the counter-model needs an assignment: D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = Q^{ M} = \{ a \}, \ell(x_0) = b. Both premises hold, and Q(x_0) fails. Repair: forget the witness before the box closes. (d) The conclusion is true: it follows from the premise, and is derived correctly in one line,  orall x\, P(x) by ulename{\wedge E} from line 1; so the sequent has no counter-model. The derivation does not prove it: line 3 breaks “the flag appears in no premise”, since x_0 is in line 1. The counterexample is to the step, not to the conclusion: the same step takes P(x_0) to  orall x\, P(x), and 
Z, with P read as “even” and \ell(x_0) = 2, makes P(x_0) true and  orall x\, P(x) false (the second row of the side-condition table). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 6: (a)–(c), 1 each for the line with its condition, and 1 each for a checked counter-model. - 1: the repairs of (a)–(c), and the remark that (a)’s original conclusion is unreachable. - 3: (d): the conclusion judged true, with the one-line derivation (1); the illegal line and its condition named (1); a counter-model to the step pattern rather than to the conclusion (1). Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (c), a counter-model with the assignment omitted, although the last line has a free variable; in (d), a claimed counter-model to the conclusion. C. Going deeper [C1: True in every finite model, used later] Let f be a one-place function symbol, and let \sigma be the sentence  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( f(x) = f(y) 	o x = y  igr) 	o  orall y\, \exists x\,  igl( f(x) = y  igr) , “if f is injective, then f is surjective”. 1. Prove that \sigma is true in every structure whose domain is finite. 2. Give a structure with an infinite domain in which \sigma is false. 3. Deduce that \sigma is not derivable, although no finite structure is a counter-model. [Hint 1] For (a), suppose f^{ M} is injective on a finite D with n elements, and count the elements of its image. [Hint 2] For (b), look for an operation on 
N that never repeats a value but misses a value. (a) Let  M have a finite domain D with n \ge 1 elements. If the hypothesis of \sigma is false in  M, then \sigma is true by (S5). So suppose it is true: by (S6), (S5) and (S2), for all d, e \in D, f^{ M}(d) = f^{ M}(e) implies d = e; that is, f^{ M} takes different values at different elements. Then the n elements of D have n different values, so the set of values \{ f^{ M}(d) : d \in D \} is a subset of D with n elements. A subset of an n-element set with n elements is the whole set (a counting fact from school, proved in Sets and Functions, Section 4.1). So every e \in D is f^{ M}(d) for some d, which is the conclusion of \sigma by (S6), (S7) and (S2). Hence \sigma is true in  M. (b) Take D = 
N and f^{ M}(d) = d + 1. The hypothesis holds: d + 1 = e + 1 gives d = e. The conclusion fails at y = 0: there is no d \in 
N with d + 1 = 0, since d \ge 0 gives d + 1 \ge 1. So \sigma is false in  M. (c) The structure of (b) is a counter-model to \models \sigma (with \Gamma empty). By the soundness statement of this section, \sigma is not derivable. By (a), no finite structure could have shown this: a search for counter-models that lists finite structures of size 1, 2, 3, … would never stop. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: (a) disposes of the case where the hypothesis of \sigma is false, by the clause for 	o. - 3: (a) reads the hypothesis as injectivity of f^{ M} and uses finiteness to get surjectivity, naming the counting fact. - 3: (b) a structure with infinite domain, with the hypothesis checked and the conclusion refuted at a named element. - 3: (c) concludes non-derivability through soundness and says why finite structures could not have done it. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (b), a “counter-model” in which f^{ M} is not injective; in (a), an argument that never uses finiteness. [C2: A sentence with no finite model, used later] Let 	au be the conjunction of the three sentences of the text saying that < is a strict order with no largest element:  orall x\, 
eg(x < x) \ \wedge \  orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( (x < y \wedge y < z) 	o x < z  igr) \ \wedge \  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) . Prove that every model of 	au has an infinite domain. Where does your proof use that domains are non-empty? [Hint 1] Start from one element and keep climbing with the third conjunct. [Hint 2] Prove by induction on k that there are elements d_1 < d_2 < \dots < d_k of D with d_i < d_j whenever i < j. Let  M be a model of 	au, with domain D, and write d < e for (d, e) \in <^{ M}. We prove, for every k \ge 1, the statement A(k): there are elements d_1, \dots, d_k of D with d_i < d_j whenever 1 \le i < j \le k. We use @ax-induction, applied to the property A(m + 1) of m \in 
N, so that the base case is A(1). Base. D is non-empty (@def-structure, (M1)), so there is some d_1 \in D, and A(1) holds, with no pairs i < j to check. This is the one place the proof uses non-emptiness. If an empty domain were allowed, with “for every d \in \emptyset” read as having nothing to check, all three conjuncts would hold in it (each begins with  orall), and it has no elements at all: the statement “every model is infinite” would fail. Step. Suppose d_1, \dots, d_k are as in A(k). By the third conjunct and (S6), (S7), there is d_{k+1} \in D with d_k < d_{k+1}. For i < k, we have d_i < d_k by A(k), and then d_i < d_{k+1} by the second conjunct (transitivity). So A(k + 1) holds. Now the elements d_1, \dots, d_k are all different: if d_i = d_j with i < j, then d_i < d_j says d_i < d_i, which the first conjunct forbids. So for every k \ge 1, the domain contains k different elements. A finite set with n elements does not contain n + 1 different elements, so D is not finite. Since (
N, <) is a model of 	au (as the text checked), 	au has models, and all of them are infinite. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: names the non-empty domain as the start of the construction, and says what fails without it. - 3: an induction producing, for every k, a chain of k elements, using the third conjunct for the step. - 2: uses transitivity to keep the whole chain increasing, not only neighbors. - 3: uses irreflexivity to show the elements are different, and concludes that D is infinite. A second route: a proof that every non-empty finite subset of D has a <-maximal element (induction on its size, with irreflexivity in the base and transitivity in the step), applied to D, which is non-empty, and contradicted by the third conjunct, earns 2 for using D non-empty, 3 for the induction, 2 for transitivity in the step, and 3 for irreflexivity plus the contradiction with the third conjunct. Fatal errors (0 for the step): building the chain without showing its elements are distinct; an “infinite chain” asserted without an induction or a recursion. [C3: Exit check: formalize, negate, decide] Work over the domain 
R, with n \in 
Z_{>0} as a bound as in Section 5.1, and 1/n as a term. 1. Formalize, with bounded quantifiers: “for every \varepsilon > 0 there is N \in 
Z_{>0} such that 1/n < \varepsilon for every n \in 
Z_{>0} with n \ge N.” 2. Formalize the sentence obtained from (a) by moving “there is N \in 
Z_{>0}” to the front. 3. Negate each of (a) and (b) into positive form: no 
eg left in front of a quantifier or an implication, and 
eg(s < t) written as s \ge t. 4. Decide which of (a) and (b) is true in 
R. For the true sentence give a proof, saying what each chosen number depends on; for the false one, prove its negation, giving the witnesses it asks for. You may use that for every real number there is a natural number larger than it. A remark on the term 1/n. In the structure 
R, the symbol / must be a function on all of 
R^2 (@def-structure, (M3)); give x/0 a value for every x \in 
R, say x/0 \coloneqq 0. The bound n \in 
Z_{>0} keeps n \ge 1, so those values are never used. (a)  orall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists N \in 
Z_{>0}\  orall n \in 
Z_{>0}\  igl( n \ge N 	o 1/n < \varepsilon  igr). (b) \exists N \in 
Z_{>0}\  orall \varepsilon > 0\  orall n \in 
Z_{>0}\  igl( n \ge N 	o 1/n < \varepsilon  igr). (c) Push 
eg inward one quantifier at a time, keeping each bound (@prp-bounded-quantifier-negation), then negate the implication (@prp-negated-implication):  egin{aligned} 
eg(a): &\quad \exists \varepsilon > 0\  orall N \in 
Z_{>0}\ \exists n \in 
Z_{>0}\  igl( n \ge N \wedge 1/n \ge \varepsilon  igr), \ 
eg(b): &\quad  orall N \in 
Z_{>0}\ \exists \varepsilon > 0\ \exists n \in 
Z_{>0}\  igl( n \ge N \wedge 1/n \ge \varepsilon  igr). \end{aligned} (d) (a) is true. Let \varepsilon > 0. Choose a natural number N with N > 1/\varepsilon, by the fact allowed in the problem; since 1/\varepsilon > 0, N \in 
Z_{>0}, and N depends on \varepsilon. Let n \in 
Z_{>0} with n \ge N. Then n \ge N > 1/\varepsilon > 0, and multiplying n > 1/\varepsilon by the positive number \varepsilon / n gives \varepsilon > 1/n. Since n was arbitrary, and then \varepsilon, (a) holds. (b) is false; its negation is true. Let N \in 
Z_{>0}. Take \varepsilon = 1/N, which is positive, and n = N, which is in 
Z_{>0} with n \ge N. Then 1/n = 1/N \ge 1/N = \varepsilon. Both witnesses depend on N, as the order  orall N\ \exists \varepsilon\ \exists n allows. Since N was arbitrary, 
eg(b) holds, so (b) is false. In words: no single N works for every \varepsilon, because \varepsilon = 1/N defeats that N. The two sentences differ only in the order of  orall \varepsilon and \exists N. In (a) the N is chosen after \varepsilon and may depend on it; in (b) it must be chosen first, which is the swap of @exm-counter-model-swap in an analysis setting. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: both formalizations, with the bounds \varepsilon > 0, N \in 
Z_{>0}, n \in 
Z_{>0} attached to the right quantifiers and 	o under the  orall n. - 3: both negations in positive form, with every bound kept, the quantifier order of each preserved, and \wedge under the \exists n. - 2: verdict “true” for (a), with a proof in which N is chosen after \varepsilon and said to depend on it. - 3: verdict “false” for (b), with \varepsilon and n given as functions of N and the three facts \varepsilon > 0, n \ge N, 1/n \ge \varepsilon checked. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in the negation of (b), \varepsilon chosen before N (a single \varepsilon for all N); a bound negated instead of the quantifier (\exists \varepsilon \le 0, or \exists n < N). [C4: The least size of a counter-model] For each claim, find the least size of a counter-model, and prove by expansion that no smaller one exists. 1. \exists x\, P(x), \ \exists x\, Q(x), \ \exists x\, R(x) \models \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \vee \exists x\, (Q(x) \wedge R(x)) \vee \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge R(x)). 2.  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y), \  orall x\, 
eg R(x, x) \models \exists x\, \exists y\,  igl( R(x, y) \wedge R(y, x)  igr). 3. \exists x\, P(x), \ \exists x\, 
eg P(x), \ \exists x\, Q(x), \ \exists x\, 
eg Q(x) \models \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \vee \exists x\, (
eg P(x) \wedge 
eg Q(x)). [Hint] In each part, the premises demand witnesses. Count how many of them can share an element before the conclusion becomes true. (a) Least size 3: D = \{ a, b, c \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, Q^{ M} = \{ b \}, R^{ M} = \{ c \}. The premises hold with the witnesses a, b, c, and no element has two of the three predicates, so each disjunct of the conclusion fails. With at most two elements, the three witnesses for P, Q, R lie among two elements, so one element is a witness for two of them, and the matching disjunct holds. (Over \{ a, b \}: the premises expand to P(a) \vee P(b), Q(a) \vee Q(b), R(a) \vee R(b); of the three letters chosen, two fall on the same element.) (b) Least size 3: D = \{ a, b, c \}, R^{ M} = \{ (a, b), (b, c), (c, a) \}, a three-cycle: every element has an arrow out, none has a loop, and no two elements have arrows both ways. Size 1: the first premise expands to R(a, a), against the second. Size 2: the second premise gives 
eg R(a, a) \wedge 
eg R(b, b), so the first, (R(a, a) \vee R(a, b)) \wedge (R(b, a) \vee R(b, b)), forces R(a, b) and R(b, a), and the conclusion holds at x = a, y = b. (c) Least size 2: D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, Q^{ M} = \{ b \}: each element has exactly one of P, Q, so neither disjunct of the conclusion holds. Size 1: \exists x\, P(x) and \exists x\, 
eg P(x) expand to P(a) and 
eg P(a), which cannot both hold. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 4: (a): the counter-model checked (2); the counting argument for size 2 (2). - 4: (b): the counter-model (1); size 1 (1); size 2 by expansion (2). - 2: (c). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a size claim without the proof that every smaller structure fails.

title: 7.3 Soundness for Predicate Logic
content:
Soundness for Predicate Logic This section is optional, and nothing outside it depends on it: Section 7.2 stated soundness for predicate logic without proof, and the rest of the book uses that statement. The results below build on one another, so they carry no optional marker of their own; the section as a whole is the unit a reader may skip. Here is the proof. It is Chapter 4’s proof of @thm-soundness with six new cases, one for each quantifier and equality rule, and it is worth reading for one reason above all: each side condition of Sections 5.3 to 5.7 is used in the case of its own rule, and there one can see what would go wrong without it. The section proves a lemma about substitution and its corollary on renaming bound variables, then the theorem, then the corollary that turns every counter-model of Section 7.2 into a proof that no derivation exists. What carries over, and what is new Chapter 4 proved that whatever the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 derive is true in every row where the premises are true. The proof had four steps (Steps 1–4 of the proof of @thm-soundness). It reduced to derivations in the primitive rules; it proved a claim for every line, not only the last, namely \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k, where \Gamma_k is the context of line k; it did so by strong induction on k, one case per rule; and it read off the claim for the last line. We follow the same four steps. Step 2 is an induction, and the checklist of Section 4.2 applies to it as it applied to Chapter 4’s: the claim stated for every line, the cases, and what each case may use. Three things change. The formulas. Lines now carry first-order formulas (@def-first-order-formula), and \models is the entailment of @def-first-order-entailment: \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k says that every structure  M and assignment \ell with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k satisfy \varphi_k. Assignments are not optional here. Lines inside a flagged box can mention the box’s name, a variable such as x_0, free; such a line is then not a sentence, and its truth depends on the value of x_0. This is why Section 5.4 insisted that fresh names are always variables, never constants: the proof below changes their values. The rules. The primitive rules are the thirteen of Chapter 4’s list (Section 4.7) and six new ones: ulename{ orall E} (@def-rule-universal-elimination), ulename{ orall I} (@def-rules-universal), ulename{\exists I} (@def-rule-existential-introduction), ulename{\exists E} (@def-rules-existential), ulename{{=}I} and ulename{{=}E} (@def-rules-equality). Two of the new rules cite a box, the flagged box of ulename{ orall I} and the ulename{\exists E} box, so the box rules are now seven: Chapter 4’s five, and ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E}. The other four new rules cite only lines and join the one-step rules. Derived rules and “arith”. As in Step 1 of @thm-soundness, a line citing a derived rule abbreviates a pasted derivation in primitive rules. This covers Chapter 2’s derived rules (@def-derived-rule), whose derivations have no flagged boxes and apply to first-order formulas as they stand, and the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules, each of which Section 6.1 expanded into a displayed block of unbounded steps whose side conditions hold whenever the bounded ones do, and the one-line “(sym)” and “(trans)” of Section 5.7 (@prp-equality-symmetric-transitive), each of which abbreviates its three-line derivation from ulename{{=}I} and ulename{{=}E} with the given terms pasted in. Those derivations have no boxes, and each \varphi they use is an equation, with no quantifier, so every term is free for its variable and the side conditions of @def-rules-equality hold. It also covers the shortcuts of Chapter 6. A law of Section 6.2 used as one line (QN, NIm, VI, the passage and distribution laws), and a derivable formula written as a line, abbreviate their printed derivations, pasted in with each flag renamed to a name new to the whole derivation, as “The laws as one line” (Section 6.2, after @prp-quantifier-negation) argues. A ulename{TAUT} line abbreviates the block of primitive steps that @prp-taut-skeleton provides, pasted in the same way (Section 6.3). In each case the side conditions of ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} still hold inside the pasted block. A line justified “arith” is not a rule at all: it records an arithmetic fact. Written out, it is a universally quantified arithmetic sentence taken as an extra premise, whose bound variables are distinct and appear nowhere else in the derivation, instantiated by ulename{ orall E} at the terms on the line and applied by ulename{{	o}E}, as Section 5.4 did explicitly when it turned the premises of a Chapter 1 derivation into universal statements. That choice of bound variables means that no fresh name of the derivation appears in the new premise, so the side conditions of ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} still hold, and that every term on the line is free for the variable it replaces at each ulename{ orall E} step. So a derivation with “arith” lines is a derivation in primitive rules from its premises together with those arithmetic sentences, and soundness speaks about that derivation. Renaming. Section 5.2 took, as a convention, that formulas differing only by renaming bound variables say the same thing, so a derivation may write a line, or apply a rule to a cited line, in a renamed form. This is not a rule either. @cor-renaming-bound-variables below shows that a formula and any renamed form of it are satisfied by exactly the same structures and assignments, so such a step changes nothing in the proof, which may take every line in the form its rule displays. Contexts, once more The context \Gamma_k of line k is still the list of the premises together with the assumptions of every box containing line k (Section 4.7, before @lem-context-inclusion). A flagged box of ulename{ orall I} has no assumption, so it adds nothing to the context of the lines inside it. The ulename{\exists E} box opens with its assumption \varphi[x_0/x], which does join the context. Section 5.4 extended @def-derivation to flagged boxes and kept its scope rule and its notion of availability word for word; two boxes are still disjoint or one inside the other. So @lem-context-inclusion (a), whose proof uses only the scope rule, holds as it stands: if line i is available at line k, then \Gamma_i \subseteq \Gamma_k. Part (b) needs one extension, since its statement names “the assumption of that box”. It becomes: if line k is justified by a box rule citing the box from line a to line b, then \Gamma_b is \Gamma_k together with the assumption of that box if it has one, and \Gamma_b is \Gamma_k if it is a flagged box without an assumption. The proof of (b) in Section 4.7 is unchanged. It showed that the boxes containing line b are exactly the cited box and the boxes containing line k, and for that it used one fact about box rules: the last line of the cited box is a line of that box itself, not of a box inside it. The two new box rules demand the same: ulename{ orall I} requires \varphi[x_0/x] to be the last line of the flagged box, a line of that box itself (@def-rules-universal), and ulename{\exists E} requires \chi to be the last line of the box itself (@def-rules-existential). So the boxes containing line b are the cited box and those containing line k, and the context of line b adds to \Gamma_k only the cited box’s assumption, if any. When a flagged box immediately contains another box and is cited from the first line of that inner box, as the citation convention of Section 5.4 says, the argument is the same: the cited box runs from that line to its last line, and its last line lies in no box inside it. Substitution and satisfaction Five of the six new rules write a substitution: ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists I} write \varphi[t/x] for a term t, in their conclusion or premise; ulename{{=}E} writes one in both; and ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} write \varphi[x_0/x] for the fresh name. To handle them we need to know what \varphi[t/x] means in a structure. The natural guess is that substituting the term t for x has the same effect as giving x the value of t. Section 5.2 showed that this can fail: in \exists y\, (y > x), putting y + 1 for x blindly gives \exists y\, (y > y + 1), which is false in 
Z, while giving x the value of y + 1, whatever it is, leaves \exists y\, (y > x) true. The y of the term was captured. The lemma says that capture is the only thing that can go wrong. [Substitution Lemma] Let  M be a structure, \ell an assignment in  M, \varphi a formula, x a variable, and t a term that is free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for). Write a \coloneqq t^{ M, \ell}. Then  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x] \quad 	ext{if and only if} \quad  M, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models \varphi . First terms: substituting t for x in a term s and then evaluating is the same as evaluating s with x set to the value of t. Then structural induction on \varphi, for all assignments at once, since the quantifier clauses change the assignment. Atomic formulas follow from the claim for terms, and connectives pass straight through. The only real case is  orall y\, \varphi with x free in it. The substitution goes inside, and (S6) sets y to each d in turn. For the induction hypothesis to help, the value of t must not change when y does, and that is exactly what “free for” guarantees: y does not occur in t. Fix  M, x and t. For an assignment \ell, write a_\ell \coloneqq t^{ M, \ell}. Terms. We show, for every term s and every assignment \ell, that (s[t/x])^{ M, \ell} = s^{ M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell]}, by structural induction on s (@def-term). If s is the variable x, then s[t/x] is t, with value a_\ell, and s^{ M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell]} = \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell](x) = a_\ell (@def-assignment). If s is another variable y, then s[t/x] is y, and both sides are \ell(y), since \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] changes only x. If s is a constant c, both sides are c^{ M}. If s is f(s_1, \dots, s_n), then s[t/x] is f(s_1[t/x], \dots, s_n[t/x]) (@def-substitution), and applying f^{ M} to the values, which agree by the hypothesis for s_1, \dots, s_n, gives equal results. Formulas. We prove, by structural induction on \varphi, the property B(\varphi): if t is free for x in \varphi, then for every assignment \ell,  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x] if and only if  M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] \models \varphi. Two facts are used throughout. If t is free for x in 
eg\varphi or in \varphi \circ \psi, it is free for x in the parts, by the recursive description of “free for” after @def-free-for in Section 5.2. And by @def-substitution, substitution passes through connectives: (
eg\varphi)[t/x] is

By the claim for terms, the tuple of values of the s_i[t/x] under \ell is the tuple of values of the s_i under \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell], so (S1) of @def-satisfaction gives the same answer on both sides. Equations s_1 = s_2 are the same with (S2). For  ot,  ot[t/x] is  ot, and neither side holds (S3). Connectives. For \varphi \wedge \psi: by B(\varphi) and B(\psi),  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x] if and only if  M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] \models \varphi, and likewise for \psi; (S5) combines the two answers in the same way on both sides. The cases 
eg, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow are the same with (S4) and the other parts of (S5). Universal quantifier, x not free in  orall y\, \varphi. This happens when y is the variable x, or when x is not free in \varphi. Then ( orall y\, \varphi)[t/x] is  orall y\, \varphi itself, since there is no free occurrence of x to replace (Section 5.2 proved that \psi[t/x] = \psi whenever x is not free in \psi). The assignments \ell and \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] differ at most at x, which is not free in  orall y\, \varphi; so by @lem-free-coincidence,  M, \ell \models  orall y\, \varphi if and only if  M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] \models  orall y\, \varphi, which is B( orall y\, \varphi). Universal quantifier, x free in  orall y\, \varphi. Then y is not x, and x is free in \varphi. Every free occurrence of x in  orall y\, \varphi lies in the scope of  orall y, so, as t is free for x in  orall y\, \varphi, the variable y does not occur in t, and t is free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for, and its recursive description in Section 5.2). By @def-substitution, ( orall y\, \varphi)[t/x] is  orall y\, (\varphi[t/x]). Let d \in D. Since y does not occur in t, the assignments \ell and \ell[y \mapsto d] agree on every variable of t, so a_{\ell[y \mapsto d]} = a_\ell, by the claim for terms in the proof of @lem-free-coincidence. Since x and y are different variables, \ell[y \mapsto d][x \mapsto a_\ell] = \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell][y \mapsto d]. Hence, using B(\varphi) for the assignment \ell[y \mapsto d] in the second step,  egin{aligned}  M, \ell \models  orall y\, (\varphi[t/x]) &\iff 	ext{for every } d \in D, \  M, \ell[y \mapsto d] \models \varphi[t/x] \ &\iff 	ext{for every } d \in D, \  M, \ell[y \mapsto d][x \mapsto a_\ell] \models \varphi \ &\iff 	ext{for every } d \in D, \  M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell][y \mapsto d] \models \varphi \ &\iff  M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] \models  orall y\, \varphi , \end{aligned} where the first and last steps are (S6). This is B( orall y\, \varphi). Existential quantifier. The same two subcases, with (S7) in place of (S6) and “for some d” in place of “for every d”. Every clause of @def-first-order-formula is covered, so B(\varphi) holds for every formula. This proves the lemma. The hypothesis “free for” was used once, in the second quantifier case, to get a_{\ell[y \mapsto d]} = a_\ell. The capture example shows what happens without it. In the structure on 
Z with >, +, and 1 as usual, take \varphi = \exists y\, (y > x) and t = y + 1, which is not free for x in \varphi. The blind substitution is \exists y\, (y > y + 1), false under every assignment. But  M, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models \exists y\, (y > x) holds for every a \in 
Z, with witness a + 1. The two sides of the lemma disagree, and the reason is visible in the displayed chain: when (S7) sets y to a new value, the value of y + 1 moves with it. Let  M be the structure on 
Z with <, +, and 1 as usual, \varphi =  orall z\, (x < z 	o y < z), t = y + 1, and let \ell(x) = 3, \ell(y) = 5. Is t free for x in \varphi? Compute both sides of @lem-term-substitution. Yes: the only quantifier in \varphi is  orall z, and z does not occur in y + 1. Here a = t^{ M, \ell} = 6. The right side asks whether  M, \ell[x \mapsto 6] \models \varphi: every z > 6 is > 5, so yes. The left side is \varphi[t/x] =  orall z\, (y + 1 < z 	o y < z) under \ell: every z > 6 is > 5, so yes. Both sides hold, as the lemma says. (Under \ell itself, \varphi is false: z = 4 has 3 < 4 and not 5 < 4. The lemma compares \varphi[t/x] with \varphi at the new value of x, not at the old one.) The lemma also pays a debt of Section 5.2, which took renaming of bound variables inside a formula as a convention and left its justification in terms of meaning to this section. [Renaming Keeps Meaning] Let \varphi be a formula and y, z variables, with z not appearing in \varphi (Section 5.2). Let  M be a structure for the symbols of \varphi, with domain D. 1. For every assignment \ell,  M, \ell \models  orall y\, \varphi if and only if  M, \ell \models  orall z\, \varphi[z/y], and  M, \ell \models \exists y\, \varphi if and only if  M, \ell \models \exists z\, \varphi[z/y]. 2. If \psi' arises from a formula \psi by such a renaming of one quantifier anywhere inside \psi (Section 5.2), then for every structure  M for the symbols of \psi and every assignment \ell in it,  M, \ell \models \psi if and only if  M, \ell \models \psi'. (a) If z is y, then \varphi[y/y] is \varphi and there is nothing to prove. Let z be a variable other than y. Since z does not appear in \varphi, no quantifier of \varphi is on z, so z is free for y in \varphi (@def-free-for). Let d \in D. Under \ell[z \mapsto d] the term z has value d, so @lem-term-substitution gives:  M, \ell[z \mapsto d] \models \varphi[z/y] if and only if  M, \ell[z \mapsto d][y \mapsto d] \models \varphi. The assignments \ell[z \mapsto d][y \mapsto d] and \ell[y \mapsto d] differ at most at z, which does not appear in \varphi; by @lem-free-coincidence, the last statement holds if and only if  M, \ell[y \mapsto d] \models \varphi. So  M, \ell[z \mapsto d] \models \varphi[z/y] if and only if  M, \ell[y \mapsto d] \models \varphi, for every d \in D. Now (S6) gives the statement for  orall, and (S7) the statement for \exists. (b) By structural induction on \psi, for all assignments at once, since the quantifier clauses change the assignment. If the renamed quantifier is the outermost symbol of \psi, this is (a). Otherwise \psi is not atomic, and the renaming takes place inside one immediate part of \psi, which it turns into a formula satisfied by the same assignments, by the induction hypothesis; the other parts are unchanged. If \psi is 
eg\alpha or \alpha \circ  eta, (S4) or (S5) then gives the same answer for \psi and \psi' under every \ell. If \psi is  orall w\, \alpha or \exists w\, \alpha, with the renaming inside \alpha, then \psi' is  orall w\, \alpha' or \exists w\, \alpha', and \alpha, \alpha' are satisfied by the same assignments \ell[w \mapsto d], so (S6) or (S7) gives the same answer for \psi and \psi'. Several renamings one after another are covered by applying (b) once for each. The soundness theorem We can now state the theorem that Section 7.2 took on trust. Soundness for Predicate Logic Let \Gamma be a list of formulas and \psi a formula. If \Gamma \vdash \psi with the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 and the quantifier and equality rules of Sections 5.3 to 5.7, then \Gamma \models \psi (@def-first-order-entailment). The steps are those of Chapter 4’s proof (Steps 1–4 of @thm-soundness). ① Reduce to derivations in the primitive rules. ② Prove \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k for every line k, by strong induction on k (@thm-strong-induction): fix a structure  M and an assignment \ell satisfying \Gamma_k, and show that they satisfy \varphi_k. ③ The cases. Premises, assumptions, and the thirteen propositional rules go through word for word, because (S3)–(S5) are Chapter 4’s clauses. ulename{ orall E}, ulename{\exists I}, and ulename{{=}E} are @lem-term-substitution, used once or twice. ulename{{=}I} is (S2). The two box rules are the heart of the proof, and they both use the same trick: change the value of the fresh name. In ulename{ orall I}, to show  orall x\, \varphi under \ell, take any d, and set x_0 to d; the context does not notice, because x_0 is not in it, so the box’s last line \varphi[x_0/x] holds there, and moving d from x_0 to x gives \varphi under \ell[x \mapsto d]. In ulename{\exists E}, set x_0 to the witness d that \exists x\, \varphi provides; the box’s assumption holds there, so its last line \chi holds there, and since \chi does not mention x_0, it holds under \ell as well. ④ The last line lies in no box, so its context is the premises. Before reading on: in the ulename{ orall I} case below, the assignment \ell[x_0 \mapsto d] must still satisfy the context \Gamma_k, and at the end the conclusion must come back from \ell[x_0 \mapsto d][x \mapsto d] to \ell[x \mapsto d]. Which clause of the side condition of ulename{ orall I} does each step use? Step 1 (reduction). Suppose \Gamma \vdash \psi. By the subsection “What carries over, and what is new”, there is a derivation of \psi in the primitive rules whose premises all belong to \Gamma. (A derivation with “arith” lines is of this kind only for the list of its premises together with the arithmetic sentences A those lines stand for, as explained there. The theorem applies to it with the list \Gamma, A in place of \Gamma, and gives \Gamma, A \models \psi: truth in every structure that satisfies \Gamma and A. The sentences A hold, for instance, when the arithmetic symbols have their usual meaning on 
R, as in Section 7.1.) Fix one, with lines 1, \dots, n, formulas \varphi_k, and contexts \Gamma_k. Let \Sigma be the finite set of constants, function symbols and predicate symbols that occur in some line of it. A line may contain symbols that occur neither in \Gamma nor in \psi, as c does in the line P(c) between  orall x\, P(x) and \exists x\, P(x); so the induction is run over structures that interpret every symbol of \Sigma, and Step 4 returns to the structures of @def-first-order-entailment. Step 2 (the induction). For k \in 
N, let S(k) be: if 1 \le k \le n, then every structure  M that interprets every symbol of \Sigma and every assignment \ell in  M with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k satisfy  M, \ell \models \varphi_k. In Steps 2 and 3, “structure” means a structure that interprets every symbol of \Sigma, and possibly more. We prove S(k) for all k by @thm-strong-induction. For k = 0 and k > n, S(k) holds vacuously. Let 1 \le k \le n and assume S(j) for every j < k. Every line and box that line k cites is available at line k, so lies before it (@def-derivation); hence the hypothesis holds for every cited line and for the last line of every cited box. Let  M be a structure, with domain D, and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k. We show  M, \ell \models \varphi_k. Two consequences of the hypothesis do the bookkeeping, as in the proof of @thm-soundness. If line k cites line i, then \Gamma_i \subseteq \Gamma_k by @lem-context-inclusion (a), so  M, \ell \models \Gamma_i, and S(i) gives  M, \ell \models \varphi_i \quad 	ext{for every line } i 	ext{ cited by line } k . 	ag{$\ast$} If line k cites, by a box rule, the box from line a to line b, then by @lem-context-inclusion (b), extended in the subsection “Contexts, once more”, and S(b): 	ext{every structure and assignment satisfying } \Gamma_k 	ext{ and the box's assumption, if any, satisfy } \varphi_b . 	ag{$\ast\ast$} Step 3 (the cases). If line k is a premise, an assumption, or justified by one of the thirteen primitive rules of Chapters 1 and 2, then  M, \ell \models \varphi_k. Claims 1–3 in the proof of @thm-soundness treat these cases. Each step there uses only (\ast), (\ast\ast), the fact that a premise or an assumption belongs to its own context, and the clauses (V1)–(V6) of @def-truth-value. Clauses (S3)–(S5) of @def-satisfaction are (V1)–(V6) with “v makes \varphi true” replaced by “ M, \ell \models \varphi”. Making that replacement throughout, the proofs of those claims prove this one, case by case. If line k is justified by ulename{ orall E}, ulename{\exists I}, ulename{{=}I}, or ulename{{=}E}, then  M, \ell \models \varphi_k. ulename{ orall E}. Line k is \varphi[t/x], citing a line holding  orall x\, \varphi, with t free for x in \varphi. By (\ast),  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi, so by (S6),  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi for every d \in D, in particular for d = t^{ M, \ell}. By @lem-term-substitution, which applies because t is free for x in \varphi,  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x]. ulename{\exists I}. Line k is \exists x\, \varphi, citing a line holding \varphi[t/x], with t free for x in \varphi. By (\ast),  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x]. By @lem-term-substitution,  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi with d = t^{ M, \ell} \in D. So d is the element (S7) asks for, and  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi. ulename{{=}I}. Line k is t = t. The two sides have the same value t^{ M, \ell}, so (S2) holds. ulename{{=}E}. Line k is \varphi[t_2/x], citing lines holding t_1 = t_2 and \varphi[t_1/x], with t_1 and t_2 free for x in \varphi. By (\ast) and (S2), t_1^{ M, \ell} and t_2^{ M, \ell} are the same element d; and  M, \ell \models \varphi[t_1/x]. By @lem-term-substitution for t_1,  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. By @lem-term-substitution for t_2, read from right to left,  M, \ell \models \varphi[t_2/x]. If line k is justified by ulename{ orall I} or ulename{\exists E}, then  M, \ell \models \varphi_k. ulename{ orall I}. Line k is  orall x\, \varphi, citing a flagged box with name x_0 and no assumption, whose last line b holds \varphi[x_0/x]. The side condition of @def-rules-universal says that at line k the name x_0 appears in no premise and in no assumption of a box still open at line k, and not in  orall x\, \varphi. The premises and the assumptions of the boxes open at line k are exactly the formulas of \Gamma_k, so (i) x_0 appears in no formula of \Gamma_k; and (ii) x_0 does not appear in  orall x\, \varphi, so x_0 is not the variable x, and x_0 does not appear in \varphi. The flagged box has no assumption, so (\ast\ast) says: every structure and assignment satisfying \Gamma_k satisfy \varphi[x_0/x]. Let d \in D; we show  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. Put \ell' \coloneqq \ell[x_0 \mapsto d]. It differs from \ell at most at x_0, which by (i) is free in no formula of \Gamma_k; so by @lem-free-coincidence,  M, \ell' \models \Gamma_k. This is where the fresh-name condition is used: changing the value of x_0 cannot disturb anything we assumed. By (\ast\ast),  M, \ell' \models \varphi[x_0/x]. By (ii), x_0 does not appear in \varphi, so no quantifier of \varphi is on x_0, and the term x_0 is free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for). Its value under \ell' is d, so @lem-term-substitution gives  M, \ell[x_0 \mapsto d][x \mapsto d] \models \varphi . The assignments \ell[x_0 \mapsto d][x \mapsto d] and \ell[x \mapsto d] agree at x, where both give d, and at every variable other than x and x_0, where both give the value \ell gives. They can differ only at x_0, which by (ii) does not appear in \varphi. By @lem-free-coincidence,  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. Since d \in D was arbitrary, (S6) gives  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi. ulename{\exists E}. Line k is \chi, citing a line h holding \exists x\, \varphi and a box with name x_0 that opens with the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] and ends with \chi. The side condition of @def-rules-existential says that x_0 appears neither in \chi, nor in \exists x\, \varphi, nor in any premise, nor in any assumption of a box still open at line k. So (i) x_0 appears in no formula of \Gamma_k; (ii) x_0 is not x, and does not appear in \varphi; (iii) x_0 does not appear in \chi. By (\ast\ast), every structure and assignment satisfying \Gamma_k and \varphi[x_0/x] satisfy \chi. By (\ast) for line h,  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi; by (S7), choose d \in D with  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. Put \ell' \coloneqq \ell[x_0 \mapsto d]. First,  M, \ell' \models \Gamma_k, by (i) and @lem-free-coincidence, as in the ulename{ orall I} case. Second,  M, \ell' \models \varphi[x_0/x]. Indeed, \ell'[x \mapsto d] = \ell[x_0 \mapsto d][x \mapsto d] and \ell[x \mapsto d] differ at most at x_0, which by (ii) does not appear in \varphi, so  M, \ell'[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi by @lem-free-coincidence; the term x_0 is free for x in \varphi by (ii), and has value d under \ell', so @lem-term-substitution gives  M, \ell' \models \varphi[x_0/x]. This is where “x_0 not in \exists x\, \varphi” is used. By (\ast\ast),  M, \ell' \models \chi. Finally, \ell' and \ell differ at most at x_0, which by (iii) does not appear in \chi, so  M, \ell \models \chi by @lem-free-coincidence. This is where “x_0 not in \chi” is used. The three claims cover every way a line can be justified, so S(k) holds, and by @thm-strong-induction S(k) holds for every line k of the derivation. Step 4 (the last line). The last line n lies in no box (@def-derivation), so \Gamma_n consists of premises only, and \varphi_n = \psi. Let  M be a structure for the symbols occurring in \Gamma and \psi, with domain D, and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \Gamma. Then \ell is an assignment in  M', and by the remark after @def-first-order-entailment (the clauses of @def-satisfaction consult only the symbols of the formula at hand), each formula of \Gamma, and \psi, is satisfied by  M', \ell exactly when it is satisfied by  M, \ell. Every premise belongs to \Gamma, so  M', \ell \models \Gamma_n; by S(n),  M', \ell \models \psi; and so  M, \ell \models \psi. This proves \Gamma \models \psi. The answer to the prompt: the first step uses the clauses “no premise” and “no open assumption”, which together say that x_0 is not in \Gamma_k; the second uses “not in  orall x\, \varphi”. The last line \varphi[x_0/x] of the box, which may mention x_0 as often as it likes, plays no part in either. That is the precise sense in which “let x_0 be arbitrary” works: whatever value x_0 is given, what we know still holds, so what we proved about x_0 holds at that value. The ulename{\exists E} case uses the same move with the opposite purpose. There the value of x_0 is not arbitrary; it is set to the witness d. What makes that legitimate is that nothing else knows about x_0 (condition (i)), that the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] then holds at the witness (condition (ii)), and that the result \chi forgets it again (condition (iii)). Counter-models prove non-derivability The corollary is the one Section 7.2 used, now with a proof. [Counter-models] Let \Gamma be a list of formulas and \psi a formula. If some structure  M and assignment \ell satisfy every formula of \Gamma and do not satisfy \psi, then \Gamma 
vdash \psi. The pair  M, \ell shows that \Gamma \models \psi fails (@def-first-order-entailment). If \Gamma \vdash \psi held, @thm-first-order-soundness would give \Gamma \models \psi. So \Gamma \vdash \psi does not hold. If the derivations in question may use “arith” lines, a counter-model must also satisfy the arithmetic sentences those lines stand for (Step 1 of the proof of @thm-first-order-soundness), for instance by giving the arithmetic symbols their usual meaning. Every counter-model of Section 7.2 is now a proof that no derivation exists. - By @exm-counter-model-swap,  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) 
vdash \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y). The converse search of @prp-exists-forall-swap stalled at two lines, a ulename{ orall I} blocked by an open assumption and an ulename{\exists E} blocked by its conclusion; now we know that no other route could have succeeded. - The two-element structure with P^{ M} = \{ a \}, Q^{ M} = \{ b \} gives \exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, Q(x) 
vdash \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) and  orall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)) 
vdash  orall x\, P(x) \vee  orall x\, Q(x): the one-way laws of @prp-quantifier-distribution are one-way. - \exists x\, P(x) 
vdash P(c), which @exr-existential-introduction-c2 could only explain informally. - P(x_0) 
vdash  orall x\, P(x), by the structure on 
Z with P^{ M} the even integers and \ell(x_0) = 2: generalizing over a name in a premise is not merely forbidden, it would be unsound. - The passage laws of @prp-quantifier-passage need x not free in \psi: with x free, 
vdash \exists x\, P(x) 	o P(x), by the counter-model of @exr-models-b1 (iii), which names an assignment. The converse of @thm-first-order-soundness is also true: if \Gamma \models \psi, then \Gamma \vdash \psi. This is the completeness theorem for predicate logic, proved by Gödel in 1929. Its proof needs to build a structure out of the formulas themselves, and it is beyond this book; nothing here depends on it. One difference from Chapter 4 remains even with completeness: there is no truth table to check. Whether a sentence of predicate logic is derivable cannot, in general, be decided by any mechanical procedure (Church and Turing, 1936). A failed search and a missing counter-model can both go on for ever. Every side condition is a case of the proof The side conditions of Sections 5.3 to 5.7 were introduced one at a time, each with a counterexample. The proof above shows that they are all the same kind of thing: each is used in the case of its own rule, and dropping it breaks a step of that case. Each counterexample of Sections 5.3 to 5.7 can be read as a failed case: - generalizing over a name in a premise, as in “P(x_0) \vdash  orall x\, P(x)” (Section 5.4): the ulename{ orall I} case fails at “ M, \ell[x_0 \mapsto d] \models \Gamma_k”, since changing x_0 changes the premise P(x_0); - generalizing over a name in an open assumption, as in “from x_0 > 0,  orall x\, (x > 0)” (Section 5.4): the same step, with the assumption x_0 > 0 in \Gamma_k; - a name that leaks into the conclusion of ulename{ orall I}, as in @exr-existential-introduction-c1: the last step of the ulename{ orall I} case, since x_0 now occurs in \varphi; - treating the witness as arbitrary, by ulename{ orall I} over its name inside its ulename{\exists E} box (Section 5.6): the ulename{ orall I} case again, since the box’s assumption is in \Gamma_k; - letting the witness escape its box, or giving a second witness a name already in an open assumption (Section 5.6): the ulename{\exists E} case, at condition (iii) or (i); - a capture in ulename{ orall E} (Section 5.3) or ulename{\exists I} (Section 5.5): the ulename{ orall E} or ulename{\exists I} case, where @lem-term-substitution does not apply; Exercise C2 and the solution to Exercise B1 give false conclusions; - a capture in ulename{{=}E}, as in a = y, \ \exists y\, (y < a) \vdash \exists y\, (y < y) (Section 5.7): the ulename{{=}E} case, where @lem-term-substitution does not apply to t_2. A side condition is not mere bookkeeping: a derivation that breaks one is not covered by @thm-first-order-soundness, and it can reach a false line, as the counter-model to P(x_0) \vdash  orall x\, P(x) in the previous subsection shows for the first item of the list. @exr-existential-elimination-c2 gives a derivation of \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \vdash \exists x\, P(x) whose ulename{\exists E} box ends in P(x_0); the line after the box is P(x_0) by ulename{\exists E}, and the last line is \exists x\, P(x) by ulename{\exists I}. Which case of the proof of @thm-first-order-soundness fails, at which step, and for which line? Give a structure and an assignment showing that the claim \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k is false for that line. The ulename{\exists E} case fails, at its last step: \chi = P(x_0) contains x_0, so condition (iii) is false, and “ M, \ell' \models \chi” cannot be carried back from \ell' = \ell[x_0 \mapsto d] to \ell. The line concerned is the illegal ulename{\exists E} line P(x_0), whose context is the premise alone. Take D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = Q^{ M} = \{ a \} and \ell(x_0) = b: the premise \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) holds (witness a), and P(x_0) fails, since b 
otin P^{ M}. The final conclusion \exists x\, P(x) is still true in this structure, as it is in every structure satisfying the premise; the fault is in the line before it. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These parts are about the proof of @thm-first-order-soundness. 1. In the ulename{ orall I} case, name the two places where the side condition of ulename{ orall I} is used, and say which clause each uses. 2. The derivation below breaks the side condition of ulename{\exists E}: its conclusion P(x_0) contains the fresh name. Which step of the ulename{\exists E} case fails? Give a structure and an assignment in which the premise holds and line 3 does not. 3. Give the idea of the proof in two sentences. 4. Why does the claim \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k quantify over assignments, and not only over structures? Point to a line of the derivation of @prp-exists-forall-swap printed in this section. (a) First, to show that \ell[x_0 \mapsto d] still satisfies \Gamma_k: this uses “x_0 appears in no premise and in no assumption of a box open at line k”, which together say that x_0 is in no formula of \Gamma_k, so @lem-free-coincidence applies. Second, to pass from \ell[x_0 \mapsto d][x \mapsto d] to \ell[x \mapsto d] (and, before that, to know that x_0 is free for x in \varphi): this uses “x_0 does not appear in  orall x\, \varphi”. (b) The last step: from  M, \ell[x_0 \mapsto d] \models \chi to  M, \ell \models \chi, which needs x_0 not in \chi. Take D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, \ell(x_0) = b. The premise \exists x\, P(x) holds, with witness a; line 3, P(x_0), fails, since \ell(x_0) = b 
otin P^{ M}. Inside the box, under \ell[x_0 \mapsto a], line 2 holds; the proof would carry it back to \ell, and that is exactly what fails. (c) Every line of a derivation is satisfied by every structure and assignment that satisfy its context, by strong induction on the line, with one case per rule. The quantifier box rules are handled by changing the value of the fresh name, which the side conditions guarantee the context and the conclusion cannot notice. (d) Lines inside boxes contain free variables, the fresh names, and their truth depends on the values of those variables. Line 3, R(x_0, y_0), is not a sentence: in the structure on 
Z with R read as <, it is satisfied when \ell(x_0) = 1, \ell(y_0) = 2, and not when \ell(x_0) = 2, \ell(y_0) = 1. The ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} cases work precisely by changing such values. B. Practice [B1: The ulename{\exists I} case] Write out the ulename{\exists I} case of the proof of @thm-first-order-soundness in full: state what is known about the cited line, and show  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi, naming the reason for each step. Where is “t free for x in \varphi” used? Line k is \exists x\, \varphi, by ulename{\exists I} citing a line i holding \varphi[t/x], where t is free for x in \varphi (@def-rule-existential-introduction). Let  M be a structure interpreting every symbol of the derivation (as in Step 2), with domain D, and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k. Line i is available at line k, so \Gamma_i \subseteq \Gamma_k by @lem-context-inclusion (a), and  M, \ell \models \Gamma_i. Since i < k, the induction hypothesis S(i) gives  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x]. Let d \coloneqq t^{ M, \ell}, an element of D. Because t is free for x in \varphi, @lem-term-substitution applies and gives  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. By (S7) of @def-satisfaction, with the element d,  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi. “Free for” is used exactly once, to apply @lem-term-substitution. Without it the step fails: from  orall y\, R(y, y), read as ( orall y\, R(x, y))[y/x], an “ulename{\exists I}” would give \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y), and in the structure on 
Z with R read as \le the first is true and the second (“there is a least integer”) false. [B2: Three non-derivability results] Use the following counter-models from Section 7.2 to state three non-derivability results, citing @cor-counter-model, and check in each case that the structure (and assignment) satisfy every premise and not the conclusion. 1. The two-element structure of @exm-counter-model-swap. 2. The counter-model of @exr-models-b3. 3. The counter-model of @exr-models-b1 (iii). (a) D = \{ a, b \}, R^{ M} = \{ (a, a), (b, b) \}. The premise  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) holds (for y = a take x = a, for y = b take x = b); the conclusion \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) fails (x = a fails at y = b, x = b at y = a). Both are sentences, so any assignment will do. By @cor-counter-model,  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) 
vdash \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y). (b) D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, Q^{ M} = \{ b \}. The premise  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) 	o  orall x\, 
eg P(x) holds, since its hypothesis fails at b; the conclusion  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) fails at a. By @cor-counter-model,  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) 	o  orall x\, 
eg P(x) 
vdash  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)). (c) D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, with an assignment \ell(x) = b. There are no premises, so the condition on premises holds trivially. The formula \exists x\, P(x) 	o P(x) fails under \ell: its hypothesis holds (witness a) and its conclusion, with x free, has value b 
otin P^{ M}. By @cor-counter-model, with \Gamma empty, 
vdash \exists x\, P(x) 	o P(x). Here the assignment is essential: under \ell(x) = a the formula holds, and the structure alone would not have been a counter-model. C. Going deeper [C1: The ulename{\exists E} case] Write out the ulename{\exists E} case of the proof of @thm-first-order-soundness in full, from memory: the data of line k, the side condition, what the induction hypothesis gives for the cited line and the cited box, and the argument, naming at each step which clause of the side condition it uses. [Hint 1] The tool is the assignment \ell[x_0 \mapsto d], where d is a witness for \exists x\, \varphi under \ell. You will need @lem-free-coincidence three times and @lem-term-substitution once. [Hint 2] Start: “Let  M be a structure interpreting every symbol of the derivation, with domain D, and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k. By the induction hypothesis for line h and @lem-context-inclusion (a),  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi, so choose d \in D with  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi.” Data. Line k is \chi, by ulename{\exists E} citing a line h holding \exists x\, \varphi and a box with name x_0, from line a (the assumption \varphi[x_0/x]) to line b (the formula \chi). Side condition (@def-rules-existential): x_0 appears neither in \chi, nor in \exists x\, \varphi, nor in a premise, nor in an assumption of a box still open at line k. What the hypothesis gives. Line h is available at line k, so \Gamma_h \subseteq \Gamma_k (@lem-context-inclusion (a)), and S(h) holds: every structure interpreting every symbol of the derivation, and every assignment satisfying \Gamma_h, satisfy \exists x\, \varphi. The box is cited by a box rule, so its last line has context \Gamma_k, \varphi[x_0/x] (@lem-context-inclusion (b), extended in the subsection “Contexts, once more”), and S(b) says that every such structure and assignment satisfying \Gamma_k and \varphi[x_0/x] satisfy \chi. The argument. Let  M be a structure interpreting every symbol of the derivation (as in Step 2), with domain D, and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k. Then  M, \ell \models \Gamma_h, so  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi; by (S7), choose d \in D with  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. Let \ell' \coloneqq \ell[x_0 \mapsto d]. 1.  M, \ell' \models \Gamma_k. The formulas of \Gamma_k are the premises and the assumptions of the boxes open at line k; by the side condition, x_0 appears in none of them. \ell' differs from \ell only at x_0, so @lem-free-coincidence applies to each formula of \Gamma_k. 2.  M, \ell' \models \varphi[x_0/x]. Since x_0 does not appear in \exists x\, \varphi, it is not x and does not appear in \varphi. So \ell'[x \mapsto d] and \ell[x \mapsto d] differ at most at x_0, which is not in \varphi, and  M, \ell'[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi by @lem-free-coincidence. The term x_0 is free for x in \varphi, as no quantifier of \varphi is on x_0, and x_0^{ M, \ell'} = d; so @lem-term-substitution gives  M, \ell' \models \varphi[x_0/x]. 3. By 1, 2 and the hypothesis for the box,  M, \ell' \models \chi. 4. \ell' and \ell differ only at x_0, which does not appear in \chi; by @lem-free-coincidence,  M, \ell \models \chi. Since  M and \ell were arbitrary, this proves S(k). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: states the data and the full side condition, and the context \Gamma_k, \varphi[x_0/x] of the box’s last line. - 2: obtains a witness d from the cited line through the induction hypothesis and (S7), and sets x_0 to d. - 2: shows the new assignment still satisfies \Gamma_k, using “x_0 in no premise and no open assumption”. - 2: shows the new assignment satisfies \varphi[x_0/x], using “x_0 not in \exists x\, \varphi” and the substitution lemma. - 2: applies the hypothesis for the box, and returns to \ell using “x_0 not in \chi”. A proof that treats the box’s assumption and the context in the other order earns the same points. Fatal errors (0 for the step): setting x_0 to an arbitrary element rather than the witness; concluding  M, \ell \models \chi directly from  M, \ell' \models \chi without the condition on \chi. [C2: “Free for” is needed] Show that the side condition “t is free for x in \varphi” of ulename{ orall E} cannot be dropped. Give a two-line “derivation” that uses ulename{ orall E} with a term that is not free for x, a structure in which its premise is true and its conclusion false, and the step of the proof of @lem-term-substitution that fails. [Hint 1] Look for a premise  orall x\, \varphi in which \varphi contains a quantifier  orall y and x occurs free inside its scope; instantiate at t = y. [Hint 2] Try \varphi = 
eg orall y\, (y \le x), “x is not an upper bound of everything”, in a structure with no largest element. Take \varphi = 
eg orall y\, (y \le x) and t = y. The free occurrence of x in \varphi lies in the scope of  orall y, and y occurs in t, so t is not free for x in \varphi. Ignoring this, ulename{ orall E} would allow: In (
Z, \le), the premise says “for every integer x, not every integer y is \le x”, that is, no integer is largest: for each x, the integer x + 1 is not \le x. It is true. The conclusion says “not every integer y has y \le y”, which is false, since \le is reflexive. So the premise is true and the conclusion false, and a rule allowing this step would be unsound. The step of @lem-term-substitution that fails is the second quantifier case, applied to  orall y\, (y \le x): it needs y not in t, so that the value of t does not change when (S6) sets y to each d. Here t = y, and its value is the new d each time:  orall y\, (y \le y) compares each d with itself, while  orall y\, (y \le x) at the value a of t compares each d with the fixed a. The legal route renames first (Section 5.2):  orall x\, 
eg orall z\, (z \le x), and then ulename{ orall E} at y gives 
eg orall z\, (z \le y), which is true in (
Z, \le) under every assignment. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: a premise and a ulename{ orall E} step at a term that is not free for x, with the capture identified. - 4: a structure, with the premise checked true and the conclusion checked false. - 3: names the quantifier case of @lem-term-substitution and the fact it needs (y not in t). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a “counter-model” in which the premise is false; a step in which t is in fact free for x.

title: 7.4 Theories and Their Models
content:
Theories and Their Models Section 7.2 called a structure in which three sentences are true a model of them. Mathematics works this way all the time: a list of axioms describes a kind of structure, and a theorem about that kind is whatever follows from the axioms. This section makes that precise, and answers the chapter’s first question: the axioms of a partial order do not prove that any two elements are comparable. The plan has five steps. First, theories and their models are defined. A gallery follows: equivalence relations, orders, groups and fields, each written as axioms, each with a model and a non-model. Then one theorem is derived from the group axioms, to show what a theorem of a theory is. Then comes consistency, which a single model proves. Last comes independence, which two models prove. Theories and their models Fix the symbols (constants, function and predicate symbols) that the axioms will use, as in @def-structure. A theory is a collection of sentences taken as axioms; its theorems are what can be derived from finitely many of them. [Theory] A theory T is a set of sentences in the chosen symbols, called its axioms; the set may be finite or infinite. A sentence \sigma is derivable from T, written T \vdash \sigma, if \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \vdash \sigma for some finite list \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n of axioms of T (n \ge 0); such a \sigma is a theorem of T. In words: a derivation is finite, so it uses finitely many axioms, even when T has infinitely many. So “T \vdash \sigma” reads @def-derivable through a finite list, and needs nothing new. The case n = 0 says that a sentence derivable from no premises at all is a theorem of every theory. At the other end, each axiom is a theorem of its own theory: the derivation whose only line is the axiom, as a premise, has it as its last line. The theorems are everything in between: what the axioms, used finitely often, force. A model of a theory is a structure in which every axiom is true. [Model of a Theory] A structure  M for the symbols of T is a model of T, written  M \models T, if every axiom of T is true in  M. A sentence \sigma is a semantic consequence of T, written T \models \sigma, if \sigma is true in every model of T. The axioms are sentences, so no assignment is needed: by @lem-free-coincidence each axiom is true or false in  M outright. And “every model of T” is the theory’s version of “every structure satisfying \Gamma” in @def-first-order-entailment. Let T be the three sentences of the strict order with no largest element (Section 7.2). Is (\{ 0 \}, <) a model of T? Is the set 
Q_{>0} of positive rationals with <? Not the first:  orall x\, 
eg(x < x) and transitivity hold, but  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) fails at 0, since nothing is above it. The second is a model: no rational is below itself, < is transitive, and for each positive d the witness d + 1 is again positive and above d. A gallery of theories Each theory below is given by its axioms, written as sentences and named, with a model and a non-model. A non-model is checked by naming the axiom that fails and where. The names in parentheses are local to this chapter, except the field clauses (F1)–(F9), which keep their series-wide numbering; none of them is one of the clauses (S1)–(S7) of @def-satisfaction. [Axioms, Models and Non-models] Equivalence relations. One two-place predicate symbol R, and three axioms:  egin{aligned} &	ext{(Refl)} &&  orall x\, R(x, x), \ &	ext{(Sym)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\, (R(x, y) 	o R(y, x)), \ &	ext{(Trans)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( (R(x, y) \wedge R(y, z)) 	o R(x, z)  igr). \end{aligned} A model: D = \{ a, b, c \}, with R^{ M} relating a and b both ways and every element to itself (Figure A, left). Each loop gives (Refl); the only pairs of different elements are (a, b) and (b, a), which give (Sym); and every chain of two arrows ends where a loop or one of these pairs already is, which gives (Trans). In numbers: “x and y have the same parity” on 
Z. A non-model: on 
Z, read R(x, y) as \abs{x - y} \le 1. It is reflexive and symmetric, and (Trans) fails at 0, 1, 2: \abs{0 - 1} \le 1 and \abs{1 - 2} \le 1, but \abs{0 - 2} = 2. Partial and linear orders. One two-place symbol \le. The axioms (Refl) and (Trans), written with \le, together with 	ext{(Antisym)} \quad  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( (x \le y \wedge y \le x) 	o x = y  igr), make the theory of a partial order. Adding 	ext{(Conn)} \quad  orall x\,  orall y\, (x \le y \vee y \le x) gives the theory of a linear order. A model of the first and not the second: divisibility on \{ 1, 2, 3, 6 \} (the right panel of Figure F in Section 7.1), where 2 and 3 are incomparable, so (Conn) fails at (2, 3). A model of both: (
N, \le). Smallest of all, the antichain D = \{ a, b \} with \le^{ M} = \{ (a, a), (b, b) \} (Figure A, right) is a partial order: the loops give (Refl), and (Antisym) and (Trans) only ever meet pairs (d, d). (Conn) fails at (a, b). Strict and dense orders. One two-place symbol <. The axioms  egin{aligned} &	ext{(Irrefl)} &&  orall x\, 
eg(x < x), \ &	ext{(Trans)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( (x < y \wedge y < z) 	o x < z  igr) \end{aligned} make a strict order; with 	ext{(Tri)} \quad  orall x\,  orall y\, (x < y \vee x = y \vee y < x) a strict linear order; and with 	ext{(Dense)} \quad  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( x < y 	o \exists z\, (x < z \wedge z < y)  igr) a dense one. A model of all four: (
Q, <), where (p + q)/2 lies between p < q. A non-model of (Dense): (
Z, <), at 0 < 1, since no integer lies strictly between. Groups. A two-place function symbol \cdot and a constant e, with  egin{aligned} &	ext{(Assoc)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( (x \cdot y) \cdot z = x \cdot (y \cdot z)  igr), \ &	ext{(Id)} &&  orall x\, (x \cdot e = x \wedge e \cdot x = x), \ &	ext{(Inv)} &&  orall x\, \exists y\, (x \cdot y = e \wedge y \cdot x = e). \end{aligned} A model: (
Z; +, 0), with \cdot read as + and e as 0; the inverse of d is -d. A non-model: (
N; +, 0), where (Inv) fails at 1, since no natural number added to 1 gives 0. Commutativity, 	ext{(Comm)} \quad  orall x\,  orall y\, (x \cdot y = y \cdot x), is not an axiom; the next example shows why. Fields. Constants 0, 1 and two-place function symbols +, \cdot, with ten axioms, the nine (F1)–(F9), numbered as in the field axioms used throughout this series, and (1 
e 0):  egin{aligned} &	ext{(F1)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\, (x + y = y + x), &&	ext{(F2)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( (x + y) + z = x + (y + z)  igr), \ &	ext{(F3)} &&  orall x\, (x + 0 = x), &&	ext{(F4)} &&  orall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 0), \ &	ext{(F5)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( (x \cdot y) \cdot z = x \cdot (y \cdot z)  igr), &&	ext{(F6)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\, (x \cdot y = y \cdot x), \ &	ext{(F7)} &&  orall x\, (x \cdot 1 = x), &&	ext{(F8)} &&  orall x\,  igl( 
eg(x = 0) 	o \exists y\, (x \cdot y = 1)  igr), \ &	ext{(F9)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( x \cdot (y + z) = x \cdot y + x \cdot z  igr), &&(1 
e 0) &&
