The plan: fix x_0, y_0, assume both are least, instantiate each at the other, and let a TAUT step combine the two disjunctions with (Irrefl) and (Trans) at x_0, y_0. Line 14 is ulename{{=}E} with \varphi the formula z = y_0: line 13 is \varphi[y_0 / z], and line 12 says y_0 = x_0, so the rule gives \varphi[x_0 / z]. The TAUT step on line 16 reads the skeleton with the letters A for x_0 = y_0, B for x_0 < y_0, C for y_0 = x_0, D for y_0 < x_0 and E for x_0 < x_0. From A \vee B, C \vee D, 
eg E, (B \wedge D) 	o E and C 	o A, the letter A follows in every row: if A is false, then B is true; C 	o A makes C false, so D is true; then E is true, against 
eg E. At line 18, y_0 is in no premise, no assumption is open outside its box, and y_0 is not in line 18; at line 19 the same holds for x_0. Only (Irrefl) and (Trans) were used. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a), a model with every axiom checked. - 3: (b), two models of T (the axioms checked for the new one), with (Dense) checked in each. - 4: (c), the derivation: the case y_0 = x_0 closed, by symmetry of = via ulename{{=}I} and ulename{{=}E} or by ulename{{=}E} into x_0 < y_0 (1), the instance of (Trans) at x_0, y_0, x_0, reached by three ulename{ orall E} steps (1), the cases combined, by a TAUT step whose skeleton is a tautology or by an equivalent ulename{\vee E} and ulename{ ot E} case analysis (1), the ulename{ orall I} side conditions (1). - 1: names the axioms used. Fatal error (0 for (c)): a TAUT step that needs y_0 = x_0 and x_0 = y_0 to be the same letter (they are not).

title: 7.5 Definability and Isomorphism
content:
Definability and Isomorphism A sentence is true or false in a structure. A formula with one free variable is different: it is true of some elements of a structure and false of others, so it picks out a set. In (
N; +) the formula \exists y\, (x = y + y) is true of 0, 2, 4, \dots and false of the odd numbers, so it picks out the even numbers, although the structure has no symbol for “even”. This section asks which sets a structure’s language can pick out. Its first half writes formulas for sets: points, intervals, orders, the primes, a supremum. Its second half, for a second reading, asks why some sets cannot be picked out at all, and answers with a map that moves the elements of a structure without changing anything a formula can see. [Looking back] Section 4.9 asked what the connectives can say, and answered: every truth function, by a normal form. This section asks the same question of a first-order language inside one structure. There the answer was “everything”; here it depends on the structure, and a set that one structure’s formulas define, another’s cannot. Formulas define sets A formula defines the set of elements (or tuples of elements) that make it true. [Definable Set] Let  M be a structure with domain D, and \varphi a formula whose free variables are among x_1, \dots, x_n, all different. The set defined by \varphi in  M is \{ (d_1, \dots, d_n) \in D^n :  M, \ell[x_1 \mapsto d_1] \cdots [x_n \mapsto d_n] \models \varphi \} , for any assignment \ell. A set S \subseteq D^n is definable in  M if some formula defines it. By @lem-free-coincidence the set does not depend on \ell: the assignments \ell[x_1 \mapsto d_1] \cdots [x_n \mapsto d_n], for different \ell, agree on x_1, \dots, x_n, and only the values of the free variables matter. For n = 1 the set is a set of elements, and we write it in set-builder form, \{ x \in D : \varphi \}. Set-builder notation, used since school, is exactly this: the reading of a formula in a structure. Two remarks on the definition. The structure is part of the question: the same formula defines different sets in different structures, and a set is definable in  M, never definable outright. And the formula may use only the symbols of  M: to define a set in (
N; +) we may write +, =, connectives and quantifiers, and nothing else, not even 0 or <. The connectives act on defined sets as the set operations do. If \varphi and \psi define S and T (with the same free variable x), then by (S4) and (S5) the formula \varphi \wedge \psi defines S \cap T, \varphi \vee \psi defines S \cup T, and 
eg\varphi defines D \setminus S, the elements not in S. So the definable sets of a structure are closed under intersection, union and complement, and a set built from definable sets by these operations is definable without further work. [Sets Defined by Formulas] Each formula is read back in words. 1. In (
R; +, \cdot), the formula \exists y\, (x = y \cdot y), “x is a square”, defines [0, \infty): a real number is the square of a real number exactly when it is non-negative. 2. In (
N; +), the formula x + x = x, “x added to itself gives itself”, defines \{ 0 \}, since d + d = d forces d = 0. The formula \exists z\, (
eg(z + z = z) \wedge x + z = y), “y is x plus something non-zero”, defines the set of pairs (d, e) with d < e. 3. In (
N; \cdot), write U(x) for the formula  orall y\, (x \cdot y = y), “multiplying by x changes nothing”. It defines \{ 1 \}: at x = 0 the instance y = 1 fails, since 0 \cdot 1 = 0; at x \ge 2 the instance y = 1 fails too, since x \cdot 1 = x 
e 1; and at x = 1 every instance holds. 4. In (
N; \cdot), the formula 
eg U(x) \wedge  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( y \cdot z = x 	o (U(y) \vee U(z))  igr) , “x is not 1, and whenever x is a product, one factor is 1”, defines the primes. At x = 0 the instance y = z = 0 fails (0 \cdot 0 = 0, and neither factor is 1); at x = 1 the first conjunct fails; at a composite x = yz with y, z \ge 2 the instance at that y, z fails; at a prime, every factorization has a factor 1. Each definition builds on the last: 0 and 1 are not symbols of these structures, yet the language can name them, and once 1 is defined, “prime” can be written with it. In (d), U(y) is the formula U(x) with y for x and its bound y renamed, say  orall w\, (y \cdot w = w), so that the substituted letter is not captured. To check that a formula defines a given set, check two directions, as for any equality of sets: every element of the set satisfies the formula, and every element that satisfies the formula is in the set. In (d) the cases x = 0, x = 1 and “x composite” are the second direction, and “at a prime” is the first. Leave out a case and a definition can be wrong at one point. Delete the conjunct 
eg U(x) from (d): at x = 1 every factorization y \cdot z = 1 has y = z = 1, so the remaining formula is true of 1, and it defines the primes together with 1. Exactly one element changed sides. What does \exists y\, (x = y + y) define in (
Z; +)? In (
Q; +)? In (
Z; +), the even integers. In (
Q; +), all of 
Q: every rational x is y + y for y = x/2, which is again rational. Same formula, two structures, two sets. \exists is a projection A formula with two free variables defines a set of pairs, and a set of pairs of reals can be drawn. In (
R; \cdot), the formula y \cdot y = x defines \{ (d, e) : e^2 = d \}, a parabola lying on its side. The formula \exists y\, (y \cdot y = x) has the one free variable x, and by (S7) it is true of d exactly when some e puts the point (d, e) on the parabola. So it defines the set of first coordinates of the points of the parabola: its shadow on the x-axis, [0, \infty). The dashed segments drop two points, (1, 1) and (1, -1), and the point (4, 2), onto their shadows 1 and 4. No point of the parabola lies above a negative x, so no negative number is in the shadow. In general, \exists y\, \varphi defines the projection of the set that \varphi defines: d is in it exactly when some e puts (d, e) in \varphi’s set, by (S7). Dually,  orall y\, \varphi keeps the d whose whole vertical line lies in \varphi’s set, by (S6). This is the picture behind every \exists in a definition: to show a set definable, it is often easiest to describe a set of pairs and project. The two readings are tied by negation. By (S4), (S6) and (S7),  orall y\, \varphi is satisfied exactly when \exists y\, 
eg\varphi is not, so the set defined by  orall y\, \varphi is the complement of the projection of the complement of \varphi’s set: remove \varphi’s set from the plane, take the shadow of what is left, and keep the points of the axis that are not in that shadow. In (
R; \le, \cdot), which set does  orall y\, (x \le y \cdot y) define? (-\infty, 0]. The least value of y \cdot y is 0, at y = 0, so x \le y^2 holds for every y exactly when x \le 0. In the picture: the vertical line at x lies wholly in the region x \le y^2 when x \le 0, and the line at a positive x leaves it near y = 0. Define it by a formula A common task in mathematics is to turn a notion described in words into a formula, and the skill is the reverse of reading back. The notion must be said using only the symbols of the structure, and every variable that is not the defined set’s own must be bound. [Maximum, Maximal, Supremum] 1. In a structure with one two-place symbol \le read as a partial order: “x is a greatest element” is  orall y\, (y \le x), “everything is below x”. “x is a maximal element” is  orall y\, (x \le y 	o y = x), “nothing is above x except x itself”. In the divisibility order on \{ 1, 2, 3 \} (d \le e when d divides e), 2 and 3 are maximal, and there is no greatest element, since 2 does not divide 3 nor 3 divide 2. On \{ 1, 2, 3, 6 \}, 6 is both maximal and greatest. 2. Add a one-place symbol A for a set of reals, and work in (
R; \le, A). “x is an upper bound of A” is the formula B(x):  orall y\, (A(y) 	o y \le x), “every element of A is at most x”. “x is the supremum of A” is B(x) \wedge  orall z\, (B(z) 	o x \le z), “x is an upper bound, and below every upper bound”. For A = [0, 1), the supremum is 1: it is an upper bound, and any z < 1 is exceeded by an element of [0, 1), such as the larger of 0 and (z + 1)/2, so z is not one. No element of A is greatest. 3. “A has a greatest element” is the sentence \exists x\, (A(x) \wedge B(x)), “some element of A is an upper bound of A”. It is false for A = [0, 1) and true for A = [0, 1]. In (c) the formula B(x) is used inside a larger formula, as a word is used in a sentence. This is how definitions accumulate: each defined notion is an abbreviation, and the full formula is the abbreviation written out. Defining a notion goes in three steps. First, say the notion in words that use only the structure’s symbols: “upper bound” becomes “every element of A is at most x”. Second, write each auxiliary notion as a formula with its own free variable, and substitute it where it is used, renaming bound variables so that nothing is captured. Third, check both directions on a small case. The commonest slip is a variable left free. Written without its  orall y, the formula A(y) 	o y \le x has two free variables and defines a set of pairs, those (d, e) with d 
otin A or d \le e; it is not a property of x at all. A defined notion can also be given its own symbol, as “even” and “the supremum of A” are in ordinary mathematics. Section 5.8 showed (@prp-definitional-extension) that such a definition is safe: introducing a predicate symbol by  orall x\, (P(x) \leftrightarrow \varphi), or a constant for an element that \varphi is proved to have, proves nothing new about the old symbols. Definability says which notions can be so introduced in a given structure: exactly those some formula of its language defines. Greatest is not maximal. A maximal element has nothing strictly above it; a greatest element is above everything. In the divisibility order on \{ 1, 2, 3 \}, 2 is maximal and not greatest. Writing  orall y\, (y \le x) for “maximal” defines the wrong set: in that order it defines \emptyset, while the maximal elements are 2 and 3. In the divisibility order on \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 \}, which elements are maximal? Is there a greatest element? 4 and 6: neither divides any other element of the set. There is no greatest element: 4 does not divide 6, and 6 does not divide 4. Isomorphic structures (second pass) This half of the section is for a second reading. It asks when two structures are the same except for the names of their elements, and proves that such structures satisfy the same sentences. From that comes a way to show that a set is not definable. It uses functions and bijections in their everyday sense: a rule that sends each element to one element, and, for a bijection, one that matches the two domains one to one, every element of the second domain hit exactly once. [Isomorphism of Structures] Let  M and  N be structures for the same symbols, with domains D and E. An isomorphism h \colon  M 	o  N is a bijection h \colon D 	o E such that 1. h(c^{ M}) = c^{ N} for each constant c; 2. h igl( f^{ M}(d_1, \dots, d_n)  igr) = f^{ N} igl( h(d_1), \dots, h(d_n)  igr) for each function symbol f of arity n and all d_1, \dots, d_n \in D; 3. (d_1, \dots, d_n) \in R^{ M} if and only if  igl( h(d_1), \dots, h(d_n)  igr) \in R^{ N}, for each predicate symbol R of arity n and all d_1, \dots, d_n \in D. An isomorphism  M 	o  M is an automorphism of  M.  M and  N are isomorphic if an isomorphism  M 	o  N exists. In words: h renames every element, and the renaming carries each constant to the corresponding constant, each operation to the corresponding operation, and each relation onto the corresponding relation, in both directions. Clause (iii) is needed in both directions. The identity map 1 \mapsto 1, 2 \mapsto 2, from \{ 1, 2 \} with R empty to \{ 1, 2 \} with R = \{ (1, 2) \}, is a bijection, and it sends every pair in the first relation into the second, since there are none. Yet the sentence \exists x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) is false in the first structure and true in the second. The converse half of (iii) fails at (1, 2), and with it the map is not an isomorphism. Examples. (
N, <) and the even numbers with < are isomorphic, by h(d) = 2d: every even number is 2d for exactly one d, and d < e if and only if 2d < 2e. A finite example, with the bijection as a table: On the left,  M has D = \{ a, b, c \} and R^{ M} = \{ (a, b), (b, c), (a, c) \}; on the right is (\{ 1, 2, 3 \}, <), with an arrow from d to e when d < e. The table is a bijection, and it sends the three arrows on the left exactly onto the three on the right. A non-example: d \mapsto d + 1, from (
N, <) to itself, preserves < in both directions and is one to one, but it is not onto: nothing is sent to 0. So it is not an automorphism. [Isomorphic Structures Satisfy the Same Sentences] Let h \colon  M 	o  N be an isomorphism. For every formula \varphi and every assignment \ell in  M,  M, \ell \models \varphi \quad 	ext{if and only if} \quad  N, h \circ \ell \models \varphi , where h \circ \ell gives each variable x the value h(\ell(x)). In particular,  M \models \sigma if and only if  N \models \sigma, for every sentence \sigma. In words: renaming the elements, consistently, changes the truth of nothing. The theorem is most often used backwards: a sentence true in one structure and false in another shows that the two are not isomorphic. The sentence  orall x\, \exists y\, (y + y = x), “every element is a sum of two equal ones”, is true in (
Q; +) (take y = x/2) and false in (
Z; +) (at x = 1), so no bijection 
Q 	o 
Z carries addition to addition, although bijections 
Q 	o 
Z exist (Sets and Functions, Chapter 4). The converse of the theorem fails: two structures can satisfy the same sentences without being isomorphic, and the optional Section 7.6 meets such a pair. The proof is in the fold below. An induction on terms and then on formulas, of the kind Section 7.1 gave for @lem-free-coincidence. Each clause of the definition of isomorphism carries one kind of atomic formula across; injectivity carries equations back; and in the quantifier cases, as d runs over D, its image h(d) must run over all of E, which is what “onto” gives. Terms. First, h(t^{ M, \ell}) = t^{ N, h \circ \ell} for every term t, by induction on t. For a variable x, both sides are h(\ell(x)), by the definition of h \circ \ell. For a constant, this is clause (i). For t = f(t_1, \dots, t_n), clause (ii) and the hypothesis for t_1, \dots, t_n give h igl( f^{ M}(t_1^{ M, \ell}, \dots, t_n^{ M, \ell})  igr) = f^{ N} igl( h(t_1^{ M, \ell}), \dots, h(t_n^{ M, \ell})  igr) = f^{ N} igl( t_1^{ N, h \circ \ell}, \dots, t_n^{ N, h \circ \ell}  igr) . Formulas. Structural induction on \varphi, with the claim stated for all assignments \ell at once, since the quantifier clauses change the assignment. Atomic. By (S1),  M, \ell \models R(t_1, \dots, t_n) means that the tuple of the values t_i^{ M, \ell} is in R^{ M}. By clause (iii) that holds exactly when the tuple of their images is in R^{ N}, and by the claim for terms the images are the values t_i^{ N, h \circ \ell}: this is (S1) for  N, h \circ \ell. Equations. t_1^{ M, \ell} = t_2^{ M, \ell} implies h(t_1^{ M, \ell}) = h(t_2^{ M, \ell}); the converse holds because h is injective. With the claim for terms, this is (S2) on both sides.  ot is satisfied on neither side, by (S3). Connectives. The answers for \varphi and \psi agree on the two sides by hypothesis, and (S4), (S5) combine them by the same rule on both sides. Universal quantifier.  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi holds if and only if  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi for every d \in D, by (S6); by the hypothesis, applied to the assignment \ell[x \mapsto d], if and only if  N, h \circ (\ell[x \mapsto d]) \models \varphi for every d \in D. Now h \circ (\ell[x \mapsto d]) = (h \circ \ell)[x \mapsto h(d)]: both give x the value h(d) and every other variable y the value h(\ell(y)). As d runs over D, h(d) runs over all of E, because h is onto. So the condition says that  N, (h \circ \ell)[x \mapsto e] \models \varphi for every e \in E, which is (S6) for  N, h \circ \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi. Existential quantifier. The same, with (S7): some d \in D works on the left exactly when some e = h(d) \in E works on the right, and every e \in E is such an h(d), since h is onto. For a sentence, @lem-free-coincidence makes the assignment irrelevant on both sides, which gives the last sentence of the statement. Why can no sentence in the symbol < tell (
N, <) from the even numbers with <? Doubling is an isomorphism between them, so by @thm-isomorphism-invariance they satisfy the same sentences. What an automorphism cannot move (second pass) An automorphism is a renaming of a structure onto itself. By the theorem, a formula cannot tell an element from its image. [Automorphisms Preserve Definable Sets] If h is an automorphism of  M and S \subseteq D is definable in  M, then for every d \in D, d \in S if and only if h(d) \in S. Let \varphi, with free variable x, define S, and let \ell be an assignment with \ell(x) = d. By @thm-isomorphism-invariance with  N =  M,  M, \ell \models \varphi if and only if  M, h \circ \ell \models \varphi. The first says d \in S; since (h \circ \ell)(x) = h(d), the second says h(d) \in S. So to show that a set is not definable, find an automorphism that moves an element of it to an element outside it. [Zero Cannot Be Defined from the Order of the Integers] In (
Z, <), the shift h(d) = d + 1 is an automorphism: it is a bijection, with inverse d \mapsto d - 1, and d < e if and only if d + 1 < e + 1. It sends 0 to 1, and 1 
otin \{ 0 \}. By @cor-automorphisms-fix-definable-sets, \{ 0 \} is not definable in (
Z, <): no formula in < alone singles out zero among the integers. Contrast (
N, <). There \{ 0 \} is definable, by  orall y\, 
eg(y < x), “nothing is below x”. The corollary is not contradicted, since d \mapsto d + 1 is not an automorphism of (
N, <): it is not onto. A finite picture: the four-cycle below, with D = \{ a, b, c, d \} and R the four arrows a 	o b 	o c 	o d 	o a. The rotation a \mapsto b, b \mapsto c, c \mapsto d, d \mapsto a is a bijection that sends each arrow to an arrow and each non-arrow to a non-arrow, so it is an automorphism. Applied once, twice or three times, it moves any element to any other, so no single element is definable. A minimal change makes one element definable again. Add the loop (a, a) to R. Now R(x, x) defines \{ a \}, and the rotation is no longer an automorphism, since it sends the arrow (a, a) to (b, b), which is not an arrow. The method can only use the automorphisms a structure has; each of the three non-trivial rotations sends the loop (a, a) to a loop at b, c or d, so adding one arrow removed all three. An automorphism shows that a set is not definable; it never shows that one is. That no automorphism moves a set is not evidence that a formula defines it. To show a set definable, write the formula. In the four-cycle, where does the rotation send the set \{ a, c \}? Could \{ a, c \} be definable? The rotation sends a to b and c to d, so it moves a \in \{ a, c \} to b 
otin \{ a, c \}. By @cor-automorphisms-fix-definable-sets, \{ a, c \} is not definable. Its complement \{ b, d \} is not definable either, by the same rotation. [Looking ahead] Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 6, proves that any two complete ordered fields are isomorphic, by an isomorphism built from the rationals below each element; by this section, they then satisfy the same sentences. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define “S \subseteq D is definable in  M”. 2. Write formulas defining, in (
N; +), the even numbers and the set \{ 0 \}. 3. Why does a formula with two free variables define a set of pairs, and not a set of elements? 4. (Second pass.) State @thm-isomorphism-invariance. 5. (Second pass; key proof.) Where does the proof of @thm-isomorphism-invariance use that h is onto, and where that it is injective? What goes wrong for d \mapsto d + 1 on (
N, <)? 6. (Second pass.) Why does x \mapsto x + 1 show \{ 0 \} undefinable in (
Z, <) but not in (
N, <)? (a) Some formula \varphi with free variable x (at most) defines it: S = \{ d \in D :  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi \}, for any assignment \ell (@def-definable-set). (b) \exists y\, (x = y + y), “x is a sum of two equal numbers”; x + x = x, “x added to itself is itself”. (c) Its truth depends on the values of both variables (and, by @lem-free-coincidence, on nothing else), so it is true or false of pairs of values. (d) If h \colon  M 	o  N is an isomorphism, then  M, \ell \models \varphi if and only if  N, h \circ \ell \models \varphi, for every formula \varphi and every assignment \ell in  M; in particular  M and  N satisfy the same sentences. (e) Onto: in the  orall and \exists cases, so that h(d) runs over all of E as d runs over D. Injective: in the equation case, to go from h(t_1^{ M, \ell}) = h(t_2^{ M, \ell}) back to t_1^{ M, \ell} = t_2^{ M, \ell}. The map d \mapsto d + 1 is not onto, and the  orall case fails:  orall y\, 
eg(y < x) is satisfied when x has the value 0, and not when x has the value h(0) = 1, because the element 0 below 1 is exactly the one the map never reaches. (f) It is an automorphism of (
Z, <) and moves 0; it is not an automorphism of (
N, <) (not onto), and in (
N, <) the set \{ 0 \} is in fact definable, by  orall y\, 
eg(y < x). [A2: Drill] Each part takes a line or two. Parts (a)–(f) belong to the first half of the section; parts (g)–(l) to the second half (second pass). They run from reading a formula, through writing one, to judging maps and using them. 1. What subset of 
Z does \exists y\, (x = y + y + y) define in (
Z; +)? 2. Define \{ 0 \} in (
Z; +). 3. Define the pairs with x \le y in (
N; +). 4. In (\{ 1, 2, 3 \}, <), which set does  orall y\, 
eg(y < x) define? In (
Z, <)? 5. Write “x is maximal” and “x is greatest” for a partial order \le. 6. In (
R; 1, +, \cdot), \varphi is x \cdot x + y \cdot y = 1. What does \exists y\, \varphi define? 7. Is h(d) = 2d an isomorphism from (
Z, <) to the even integers with <? 8. Is h(d) = -d an automorphism of (
Z, <)? Of (
Z; +)? 9. Using (h), is \{ 1 \} definable in (
Z; +)? 10. Is that consistent with (b)? 11.  M has D = \{ a, b, c \} and R^{ M} = \{ (a, c), (b, c) \}. Which singletons are definable? 12. Are (
N, <) and (
Z, <) isomorphic? Give a sentence that shows it. (a) The multiples of 3. (b) x + x = x. (c) \exists z\, (x + z = y), “y is x plus something”. (d) \{ 1 \}, “nothing is below x”; \emptyset, since every integer has a smaller one. (e)  orall y\, (x \le y 	o y = x);  orall y\, (y \le x). (f) [-1, 1], the shadow of the unit circle on the x-axis. (g) Yes: a bijection onto the evens, and d < e if and only if 2d < 2e. (h) Not of (
Z, <): 0 < 1, but -0 = 0 > -1. Yes of (
Z; +): it is a bijection (its own inverse), and -(d + e) = (-d) + (-e). (i) No: the automorphism d \mapsto -d sends 1 to -1 
otin \{ 1 \}. (j) Yes: d \mapsto -d sends 0 to 0, so it does not move \{ 0 \}. (k) \{ c \}, by \exists y\, R(y, x), “something points to x”. Not \{ a \} or \{ b \}: swapping a and b (and fixing c) is an automorphism. (l) No. \exists x\,  orall y\, 
eg(y < x), “there is a least element”, is true in (
N, <) and false in (
Z, <); isomorphic structures would agree on it. B. Practice [B1: Define it by a formula] Define by a formula, and read each formula back in words. Parts (i)–(iii) are in (
N; \cdot); parts (iv) and (v) are in (
R; \le, A), with A a one-place symbol. 1. “x divides y”. 2. “x is a square”. 3. “x and y have no common divisor except 1”. 4. “A is bounded above”. 5. “A has a supremum that is not in A”. (i) \exists z\, (x \cdot z = y): “y is x times something”. (ii) \exists y\, (y \cdot y = x): “x is something times itself”. (iii)  orall z\,  igl( (\exists u\, (z \cdot u = x) \wedge \exists v\, (z \cdot v = y)) 	o  orall w\, (z \cdot w = w)  igr): “every common divisor z of x and y is 1”. The consequent is U(z) of @exm-definable-sets (c), with its bound variable renamed to w: written with the bound y of U, it would capture the free y. (At x = y = 0 every z is a common divisor, so the formula fails, as it should.) Find every automorphism of  M: D = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4 \}, R^{ M} = \{ (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) \}, the answer given to @exr-theories-and-models-b1 (ii). 2. Which singletons and which two-element subsets of D does that leave possibly definable? Define those that are. 3. Is d \mapsto d + 1 an automorphism of (

That leaves 1 and 2, which may stay or be swapped, and both choices preserve R. So there are two automorphisms: the identity, and the swap of 1 and 2. eg\exists y\, (R(x, y) \wedge

(c) No: it sends the value 0 of the constant to 1, and clause (i) of @def-isomorphism-of-structures asks h(0) = 0. Marking scheme. (10 points) 4 for (a): both automorphisms, with the argument that 3 and 4 are fixed. 4 for (b): each definable set with its formula, and each other set with the automorphism that moves it. 2 for (c). Fatal error (0 for (b)): claiming a set definable because no automorphism moving it was found. C. Going deeper [C1: The definable subsets of (
Z, <)] (Second pass.) 1. Prove that the only subsets of

Z. 2. Show that the relation “y = x + 1” is definable in (

Z. (b) x < y \wedge 
eg\exists z\, (x < z \wedge z < y), “y is above x with nothing in between”. In

(c) The corollary, and the argument of (a), concern sets of elements. “y = x + 1” defines a set of pairs, and a shift moves each pair (n, n + 1) to another pair (m, m + 1) of the same set, so the set of pairs is not moved. What (a) forbids is a formula singling out some integers and not others; (b) singles out a relation that every integer has to its successor. Marking scheme. (10 points) 5 for (a): the shift shown to be an automorphism (bijective and order-preserving), then the corollary applied. 3 for (b), with both directions checked in 
Z. 2 for (c). Fatal error (0 for (a)): using d \mapsto -d, which does not preserve <. [C2: Challenge: the automorphisms of (
Q, <)] (Second pass.) 1. Show that x \mapsto 2x, and x \mapsto x + q for each rational q, are automorphisms of (
Q, <). 2. Deduce that the only subsets of 
Q definable in (
Q, <) by a formula with one free variable are \emptyset and 
Q. 3. Show that \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0 \} is definable in (
Q; <, 0), with 0 a constant, but not in (
Q, <). (a) Both are bijections of 
Q, with inverses x \mapsto x/2 and x \mapsto x - q, and both preserve < in both directions: x < y if and only if 2x < 2y, if and only if x + q < y + q. (b) The translations alone suffice: given p in a non-empty definable set S and any p' \in 
Q, the automorphism x \mapsto x + (p' - p) sends p to p', so p' \in S by @cor-automorphisms-fix-definable-sets. As in C1, S = 
Q. (c) In (
Q; <, 0) the formula 0 < x defines it. In (
Q, <) it is neither \emptyset nor 
Q, so by (b) it is not definable. Marking scheme. (10 points) 3 for (a), 4 for (b), 3 for (c). Fatal error (0 for (b)): an argument with x \mapsto 2x alone, which fixes 0 and so cannot move 0 to anything else. R. Review [R1] Decide whether each sequent is derivable, and justify your answer. 1. (p 	o q) 	o r \vdash p 	o r. 2. (p 	o q) 	o r \vdash q 	o r. (a) Not derivable. Look for a refuting row, backwards from the conclusion: p 	o r is false only when p = \mathrm{T} and r = \mathrm{F}. The premise must then be true, so its hypothesis p 	o q must be false, which needs q = \mathrm{F}. In the row p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F}, r = \mathrm{F}, the premise is \mathrm{F} 	o \mathrm{F}, true, and the conclusion is \mathrm{T} 	o \mathrm{F}, false. By @cor-refuting-row there is no derivation. (b) Derivable. The goal is an implication, so open a box on q; the premise is waiting for p 	o q, which a box on p produces by repeating q (the goal-directed and premise-directed steps of the search method of Section 3.1). The row method of (a) could not settle (b): no row refutes it, and only a derivation (or @thm-completeness) shows it is derivable. [R2] Derive 
eg(P 	o 
eg Q) \vdash 
eg
eg P \wedge 
eg
eg Q without ulename{RAA} and without derived rules that use it. Which rule would you need to derive P \wedge Q itself? The goal is a conjunction, so derive each conjunct. Each is a negation, so each gets a ulename{
eg I} box, whose goal is  ot. The only way to use the premise 
eg(P 	o 
eg Q) is to clash with it, so inside each box we build P 	o 
eg Q. In the first box, from 
eg P: a ulename{{	o}I} box on P clashes P with 
eg P and uses ulename{ ot E} (the pattern of @prp-vacuous-implication). In the second, from 
eg Q: a ulename{{	o}I} box on P simply repeats 
eg Q. These are the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 (@def-rules-negation, @def-rules-contradiction, @def-rules-implication). No ulename{RAA} is used. To reach P \wedge Q we would need P from 
eg
eg P and Q from 
eg
eg Q, that is, ulename{
eg
eg E}, which is derived with ulename{RAA} (@prp-double-negation), or an ulename{RAA} box directly (@def-rule-raa). The look-alike is @exr-finding-derivations-b1 (b), 
eg(P 	o Q) \vdash P \wedge 
eg Q: there the conjunct P needed ulename{RAA}, while 
eg Q came by ulename{
eg I} alone. Here both conjuncts stop at a double negation. That no derivation of P (or of P \wedge Q) from the premise avoids ulename{RAA} is true, but we state it without proof, and nothing depends on it. [R3] Derive 
eg\exists x\, (P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x)) \vdash  orall x\,  igl( 
eg
eg P(x) \wedge 
eg
eg Q(x)  igr) without ulename{RAA}. The goal is  orall x, so open a flagged box with a fresh name x_0 (@def-rules-universal); the new goal is 
eg
eg P(x_0) \wedge 
eg
eg Q(x_0). Inside, run the derivation of R2 (@exr-models-r2) with P(x_0) and Q(x_0) in place of P and Q. One change: the premise is now 
eg\exists x\, (P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x)), not 
eg(P 	o 
eg Q), so each clash first turns P(x_0) 	o 
eg Q(x_0) into \exists x\, (P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x)) by ulename{\exists I} at x_0 (@def-rule-existential-introduction). The side condition of ulename{ orall I} at line 18: x_0 does not appear in the premise on line 1, no box is open at line 18, and x_0 does not appear in the conclusion. The flagged box immediately contains the ulename{
eg I} box of line 2, so it is cited from line 2, the first line of that inner box. Lines 7 and 14 are legal ulename{\exists I} steps: P(x_0) 	o 
eg Q(x_0) is (P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x))[x_0/x]. The whole derivation is R2’s, run inside a flagged box, with an ulename{\exists I} before each clash. [R4] Is the sentence  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) 	o \exists y\,  orall x\, (x < y) true in (
N, <)? Is it derivable? True in (
N, <)? No. The hypothesis  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) is true in (
N, <): each d has d + 1 above it. The conclusion \exists y\,  orall x\, (x < y) is false: a candidate e fails at x = e, since e < e is false. By (S5) of @def-satisfaction, an implication with a true hypothesis and a false conclusion is false. Derivable? No. By the soundness statement of Section 7.2, a derivable sentence is true in every structure; this one is false in (
N, <), so no derivation exists. Why these tools. A structure settles the question in two lines, while a derivation search could only fail, and a failed search proves nothing. A truth table is the wrong look-alike: it reads the sentence as p 	o q with two atoms, and a refuting row for p 	o q says nothing here, since the sentence  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists x\, P(x) has the same shape and is derivable (@prp-forall-implies-exists, then ulename{{	o}I}). The soundness statement used here is proved in Section 7.3.

title: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content:
What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say This section is optional, and nothing outside it depends on it. Every theorem in it is stated without proof, except where a short argument from a stated theorem is given and marked as such; its results carry no optional marker of their own, and the section as a whole is the unit a reader may skip. Section 7.4 asked of a theory two questions that sound different: is it consistent, that is, does no finite list of its axioms derive  ot? And has it a model? A model answers the first question (@prp-model-shows-consistency), but nothing so far says that a consistent theory must have one. This section states the theorem that says so, Gödel’s completeness theorem, and then follows its consequences. The first is compactness: a theory has a model as soon as each finite part of it has one. From compactness come the surprises. A first-order theory cannot fix the size of its infinite models; the true sentences about 
N have a model with an element larger than every number; and the property “finite” cannot be written as a sentence. The section ends with what can and cannot be decided by a mechanical procedure, and names the incompleteness theorem, which is a different matter from completeness. [Looking back] Section 4.8 proved that every valid propositional claim is derivable, and the optional Section 4.10 proved compactness for propositional logic. Both hold for predicate logic too; this section states them, and then shows what they cost: a first-order language cannot pin down the natural numbers. Completeness The soundness statement of Section 7.2 runs from derivations to truth: whatever a list of premises derives is true in every structure where the premises are true. The completeness theorem runs back. [Gödel’s Completeness Theorem] For every theory T and sentence \sigma: T \vdash \sigma if and only if T \models \sigma. Equivalently, a theory is consistent if and only if it has a model. This theorem is stated without proof. One direction is the soundness statement of Section 7.2; the other is new. Here T \vdash \sigma and T \models \sigma are those of @def-theory and @def-model-of-theory: some finite list of axioms derives \sigma, and \sigma is true in every model of T. The two forms say the same thing. Take \sigma =  ot: T \vdash  ot says that T is inconsistent (@def-inconsistent-theory), and T \models  ot says that no model of T exists, since  ot is true in no structure. In the other direction, T \models \sigma means that the theory T with 
eg\sigma added, the counterexample set of the claim, has no model; and T \vdash \sigma means that this theory is inconsistent, by ulename{
eg E} in one direction and ulename{RAA} in the other. What the theorem means for this chapter is best said with its two halves side by side. Faced with a claim T \vdash \sigma, Chapters 5 and 6 searched for a derivation, and this chapter searched for a counter-model, a model of T in which \sigma is false. Soundness says that both cannot succeed. Completeness says that one of them must: a stalled derivation search and a missing counter-model cannot both be real. The words “consistent” and “has a model”, which Section 7.4 kept apart and never swapped, are now known to coincide, but only here, and with a theorem stated and not proved. Nothing outside this section uses the coincidence. Section 7.4’s group axioms show both outcomes. They derive that the identity is unique (@prp-group-identity-unique), and that settles one claim by a derivation. They do not derive (Comm), and the triangle group of @exm-triangle-group, a model of the axioms in which (Comm) is false, settles that claim by a counter-model. Completeness says that every claim about groups is settled in one of these two ways, though it does not say which, or how long the search for either will take. The theorem says nothing about how to find the derivation or the model, and the last part of this section states, without proof, that no method finds one of them in every case. This is a sketch, not a proof. It follows the route of Section 4.10’s proof of propositional compactness through Lindenbaum’s lemma (@lem-lindenbaum). Start from a consistent theory T; we want a model. The idea is to build the model out of the language itself, with the closed terms as its elements. Two difficulties arise, and each has a remedy. Witnesses. A sentence \exists x\, \varphi of the theory may hold with no closed term to show for it. So add new constants, and for each sentence \exists x\, \varphi a witness axiom \exists x\, \varphi 	o \varphi[c/x], with c a constant new to everything so far. Adding it keeps the theory consistent, for the same reason the name in an ulename{\exists E} box must be fresh: an old name already carries information, and a new one carries none, so assuming that it names a witness can lead to no contradiction that the bare \exists x\, \varphi did not already give. This is repeated, since the new constants make new sentences, each with its own witness. Deciding every sentence. A consistent theory may leave a sentence undecided, and a structure cannot. So extend the theory, one sentence at a time, to a maximal consistent set: list all sentences, and add each one if the result stays consistent. As in Lindenbaum’s lemma, the result decides every sentence, containing it or its negation. The structure. Its elements are the closed terms, with two terms identified when the set contains their equation; a constant names itself, a function symbol builds the longer term, and a predicate holds of the terms for which the set says it holds. An induction on sentences, the propositional one of Section 4.10 with a case for each quantifier, where the witness axioms do their work, shows that this structure satisfies exactly the sentences of the set. It satisfies T in particular. The details, for countably many symbols, fill a chapter of a logic text; this book stops at the outline. Compactness Completeness ties models to derivations, and a derivation uses only finitely many premises. That one fact has a consequence about models alone. [Compactness Theorem] If every finite subset of a theory T has a model, then T has a model. A short argument from completeness. Suppose T had no model. Then T is inconsistent, by @thm-first-order-completeness, so some finite list of its axioms derives  ot (@def-inconsistent-theory). The finite subset made of those axioms is then itself an inconsistent theory, so by @prp-model-shows-consistency it has no model, against the hypothesis. “Every finite subset has a model” is not “has a finite model”. The finite subsets are finite lists of axioms; the models that satisfy them may be infinite, and the model the theorem gives may be infinite even when every finite subset has a finite model. Compactness never makes a structure smaller. Read the theorem from the side of what a theory forbids. A structure fails to be a model of T when some axiom is false in it. The theorem says that a property needing infinitely many axioms at once to fail is never enforced by first-order sentences: whatever a theory forbids, some finite part of it already forbids. That is the source of everything below. The standard tool is a list of sentences that count. For n \ge 2, let \sigma_n be the sentence “there are at least n elements”: n variables bound by \exists, followed by the conjunction of 
eg(x_i = x_j) for all i < j. It is true in a structure exactly when the domain has n or more elements. Any finite set of the \sigma_n is true in a large enough finite structure; all of them together are true only in an infinite one. Every use of compactness below follows one pattern: add infinitely many axioms that no single intended structure satisfies all at once, check that each finite part of the result has a model, and conclude that the whole has one. The model it gives is then a new structure, with properties the intended ones lack. Let \sigma_n say “there are at least n elements”. Write \sigma_3. \exists x\, \exists y\, \exists z\,  igl( 
eg(x = y) \wedge 
eg(x = z) \wedge 
eg(y = z)  igr). Does compactness hold for propositional logic? Yes: the optional Section 4.10 proved it; this section states the first-order version. Large models and small ones A set can be listed if its elements can be written as a sequence d_0, d_1, d_2, \dots in which every element appears; 
N, 
Z and 
Q can, and so can every non-empty finite set (repeat its last element forever). “Listed” here has its everyday meaning. [Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem] Let T be a theory in countably many symbols (the symbols can be listed s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots). If T has an infinite model, then it has a model whose domain can be listed as d_0, d_1, d_2, \dots, and also a model whose domain cannot be so listed. This theorem is stated without proof. Two consequences show its force. First, take for T all the sentences true in (
R; 0, 1, +, \cdot, <). The theorem gives a structure that satisfies every one of them and whose elements can be listed, although the elements of 
R cannot be (a fact stated here, not proved). Every first-order property of the real numbers holds in that structure, so the property that separates 
R from a listable set is not first-order. Second, take for T the sentences true in (
N; 0, S, +, \cdot, <), with S the successor. The theorem gives a model of all of them that cannot be listed: far too large to be 
N under other names. So no first-order theory with an infinite model fixes the size of its models. Section 7.5 showed that isomorphic structures satisfy the same sentences; here are structures that satisfy the same sentences and are not isomorphic, since one can be listed and the other cannot. How can a listable structure satisfy every first-order sentence true in 
R, when 
R is “complete”: every non-empty set of reals bounded above has a supremum? The answer is the one the next two subsections give for 
N. Completeness of 
R speaks of all sets of reals. A first-order sentence can speak only of sets defined by formulas (Section 7.5): for each formula there is a sentence “if the set this formula defines is non-empty and bounded above, it has a supremum”, and each of these is true in 
R. The listable model satisfies all of them, and fails the statement about all sets, which is not a first-order sentence. It must fail it: the listable model is an ordered field, as 
R is, and any two complete ordered fields are isomorphic (Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 6), so a complete listable model would make 
R listable, and 
R cannot be listed. A theory T in countably many symbols has the model (
Q, <). Must it also have a model whose domain cannot be listed? Yes: (
Q, <) is an infinite model, so by @thm-lowenheim-skolem T also has a model that cannot be listed. For the strict order axioms, (
R, <) is one. Numbers that are not numerals The symbols of arithmetic are 0, the one-place S for successor, +, \cdot and <, read in 
N as usual. The numeral \underline{n} is the closed term S(S(\cdots S(0) \cdots)) with n letters S; its value in 
N is n. [A Model of Arithmetic with an Infinite Number] Let T be the set of all sentences in 0, S, +, \cdot, < that are true in 
N. Add a new constant c, and to T add the axioms \underline{0} < c, \quad \underline{1} < c, \quad \underline{2} < c, \quad \dots , one for each n \in 
N. Call the result T'. Every finite subset of T' has a model. A finite subset contains finitely many sentences of T and finitely many axioms \underline{n} < c; let N be the largest n among them (or 0 if there is none). Read the symbols in 
N as usual and c as N + 1. The sentences of T do not mention c, and they are true in 
N; each \underline{n} < c in the subset says n < N + 1, which is true. So T' has a model. By @thm-first-order-compactness there is a structure  M in which every sentence of T' is true. In  M every sentence true in 
N is true, and c^{ M} is above the value in  M of every numeral. It differs from each of them: if c^{ M} were the value of \underline{n}, the axiom \underline{n} < c would put an element below itself, while  orall x\, 
eg(x < x) is true in 
N, so in T, so in  M. An element of  M that is the value of no numeral is called non-standard; the values of numerals are the standard elements.  M satisfies every first-order sentence that 
N satisfies, and still has an element that no numeral names. Its standard elements lie at the bottom: the sentences  orall x\, (x < \underline{n + 1} 	o x = \underline{0} \vee \dots \vee x = \underline{n}), one for each n, together with  orall x\, 
eg(x < \underline{0}), are true in 
N and so in  M, and they say that nothing non-standard lies below a standard element; since  orall x\,  orall y\, (x < y \vee x = y \vee y < x) is also true in 
N and so in  M, every standard element lies below every non-standard one. The model  M is not 
N under another name. In 
N itself, read as usual, no value of c works for the whole of T': if c is read as the number n, the axiom \underline{n} < c says n < n. Each finite part of T' is satisfied by 
N, each with its own value for c; the whole set is satisfied only by a structure that compactness supplies, and that structure has elements 
N lacks. Since  M satisfies the same sentences in 0, S, +, \cdot, < as 
N, no first-order sentence about arithmetic can tell the two apart; yet they are not isomorphic, since an isomorphism would send each numeral’s value to the same numeral’s value, and c^{ M} to an element of 
N above every number, and there is none. Is c^{ M} = S^{ M}(d) for some element d of  M? Yes. The sentence  orall x\, (
eg(x = 0) 	o \exists y\, (S(y) = x)) is true in 
N, so it is true in  M; and c^{ M} 
e 0^{ M}, since \underline{0} < c is an axiom and  orall x\, 
eg(x < x) holds in  M. Induction: a schema and an axiom How can  M satisfy induction, when its standard elements contain 0, are closed under successor, and are not everything? The answer turns on what first-order induction says. The induction schema of first-order arithmetic is one sentence for each formula \varphi with free variable x:  igl( \varphi[0/x] \wedge  orall x\, (\varphi 	o \varphi[S(x)/x])  igr) 	o  orall x\, \varphi , with its other free variables, if any, bound by  orall in front. Each instance is true in 
N, by induction, so each is in T and true in the model  M of @exm-non-standard-naturals. Yet the set of standard elements of  M contains 0^{ M} and is closed under S^{ M}, and is not all of the domain. There is no contradiction: the schema speaks only about sets defined by formulas (Section 7.5), with any other free variables fixed at elements of the domain, and the standard elements are not such a set. The argument is short. Suppose a formula \varphi, with free variable x and its other free variables z_1, \dots, z_k (if any) fixed at elements e_1, \dots, e_k of  M, defined the standard elements in  M; every assignment below sends each z_i to e_i. By @lem-term-substitution (Section 7.3; 0 is closed, and S(x) is free for x in \varphi), \varphi[0/x] holds in  M exactly when \varphi holds of 0^{ M}, and \varphi[S(x)/x] holds under an assignment \ell exactly when \varphi holds of S^{ M}(\ell(x)). Then \varphi[0/x] holds in  M, since 0^{ M} is standard, and  orall x\, (\varphi 	o \varphi[S(x)/x]) holds, since the successor of a standard element is standard. The induction instance for \varphi is a sentence true in 
N, so it is in T and true in  M; read with each z_i at e_i, it gives  orall x\, \varphi in  M, so every element would be standard, against c^{ M}. (Exercise C2 reaches the same conclusion another way, by least elements.) The induction principle of Section 4.2 (@ax-induction) is stated for every property of natural numbers. Read in a structure, that is a statement about all subsets of the domain, not only the definable ones: it quantifies over sets, and is a second-order statement. Applied to the set of standard elements, it would rule out non-standard elements at once, and so a structure satisfying it, with 0 and successor read as usual, has no room for c^{ M}. First-order logic can state the schema, not the axiom; compactness is the price of its completeness. What can be decided A question about sentences is decidable if a mechanical procedure answers it, correctly and in finitely many steps, for every sentence. Three facts, each stated without proof here, mark the boundary. Decidable: propositional logic. Chapter 4’s search tree decides every propositional claim in finitely many steps (@prp-search-decides): it either closes, and the claim is valid, or it leaves an open branch, which gives a refuting row. Undecidable: predicate logic (Church and Turing, 1936). No mechanical procedure decides, for every first-order sentence, whether it is derivable. With completeness, the boundary can be said exactly: listing all derivations, shortest first, finds one when one exists; what no procedure can do is announce, in every case, that none exists. A stalled search, the situation of Chapter 6, is the normal state of affairs and not a sign that more cleverness was needed. Decidable: the monadic fragment. For sentences with only one-place predicate symbols and no constants, function symbols or =, the bound of Section 7.2’s remark makes the counter-model search finite: if such a sentence has a counter-model at all, it has one of bounded size, and there are finitely many structures of each size to try. Incompleteness, named. Gödel showed in 1931 that no consistent theory whose axioms a mechanical procedure can list, and which derives the basic facts of arithmetic, derives every sentence true in 
N. Completeness says every sentence true in all models of a theory is derivable from it; incompleteness says that the sentences true in the intended model 
N are not all true in all models of any such theory. The two theorems do not conflict: the non-standard models are where they part. A sentence \sigma is true in 
N and false in some model of a theory T of arithmetic. Can T \vdash \sigma? No: by the soundness statement of Section 7.2, T \vdash \sigma would make \sigma true in every model of T. [Looking ahead] Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 1, takes the second-order induction principle as clause (P5) of a Peano system and proves that any two Peano systems are isomorphic; this section explains why no first-order list of axioms could do the same. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State @thm-first-order-completeness in its two forms. 2. State @thm-first-order-compactness, and give the short argument from completeness in three sentences. 3. What is a non-standard element of a model of arithmetic? 4. Why does the induction schema not rule non-standard elements out? 5. Name one decidable and one undecidable question about sentences. (a) For every theory T and sentence \sigma, T \vdash \sigma if and only if T \models \sigma. Equivalently, a theory is consistent if and only if it has a model. (b) If every finite subset of T has a model, so has T. If T had no model, it would be inconsistent by completeness, so a finite list of its axioms would derive  ot. That finite subset would be inconsistent, and so, by @prp-model-shows-consistency, without a model, against the hypothesis. (c) An element that is not the value of any numeral \underline{n}. (d) Each instance speaks of a set defined by a formula, and the standard elements are not such a set (the argument in “Induction: a schema and an axiom”). (e) Decidable: validity of a propositional claim (or of a monadic sentence). Undecidable: derivability of a first-order sentence. [A2: Drill] Each part takes a line or two. The parts run from writing a counting sentence, through naming the theorem that answers a question, to judging what a theorem does and does not say. 1. Write \sigma_2, “there are at least two elements”. 2. Write “there are at most two elements”. 3. Which theorem says “every consistent theory has a model”? 4. Which says “if every finite part of T has a model, T has one”? 5. True or false: completeness says that every sentence true in (
N; 0, S, +, \cdot, <) is derivable with no premises. 6. True or false: a theory with models of every finite size has an infinite model. 7. Is “the domain is finite” expressible by one sentence? 8. True or false: in a model of all sentences true in 
N, every element is the value of a numeral. 9. Over what does the second-order induction principle quantify that the schema does not? 10. Is derivability of a propositional claim decidable? Of a monadic first-order sentence (one-place predicate symbols only; no constants, function symbols or =)? Of a first-order sentence in general? 11. Does (
R; 0, 1, +, \cdot, <) have a model of the same sentences whose domain can be listed? 12. Why is a theory whose models are exactly the structures of size 3 possible, and one whose models are exactly the finite structures not? (a) \exists x\, \exists y\, 
eg(x = y). (b)  orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\, (x = y \vee x = z \vee y = z). (c) Completeness, in its second form. (d) Compactness. (e) False: with no premises, completeness makes derivable only the sentences true in every structure.  orall x\, 
eg(S(x) = 0) is true in 
N and false in a one-element structure (Section 7.2). (f) True, by compactness, as in B1. (g) No (C1). (h) False: @exm-non-standard-naturals gives such a model with a non-standard element. (i) All sets (properties) of elements, not only those defined by formulas. (j) Yes; yes; no. (k) Yes, by @thm-lowenheim-skolem. (l) “At least 3 and at most 3 elements” is one sentence, \sigma_3 with the “at most” sentence. No theory can do it for “finite”: such a theory would have a model of every finite size (the structures built in the solution of C1), so by @exr-limits-of-first-order-logic-b1 it would have an infinite model, which is not finite. B. Practice [B1: Arbitrarily large finite models] Prove: if a theory T has, for every n, a finite model with at least n elements, then T has an infinite model. Apply it to the theory of an equivalence relation R in which every class has exactly two elements, with that last condition written as one sentence. Let T' be T with every \sigma_n, n \ge 2, added. A finite subset of T' contains only finitely many \sigma_n; let N be the largest such n (or 2 if there is none). By hypothesis T has a finite model with at least N elements, and it satisfies every \sigma_n with n \le N, so it is a model of the finite subset. By @thm-first-order-compactness T' has a model. It satisfies every \sigma_n, so it has at least n elements for every n: it is infinite. And it is a model of T. Application. The axioms are (Refl), (Sym), (Trans) for R and  orall x\, \exists y\,  igl( 
eg(x = y) \wedge R(x, y) \wedge  orall z\, (R(x, z) 	o (z = x \vee z = y))  igr) , “each x is related to exactly one element besides itself”. For each k \ge 1, a set of 2k elements split into k pairs, with R “in the same pair”, is a model, so there are models with at least n elements for every n. So an infinite model exists; 
Z with R(x, y) read as “x and y lie in the same pair \{2m, 2m + 1\} for some m \in 
Z” is one. Marking scheme. (10 points) 3 for T' defined by adding axioms that force infinitely many elements (the \sigma_n, or distinct new constants c_i, the model then cut back to T’s symbols). 3 for every finite subset having a model, with the size argument. 2 for compactness applied and the model shown infinite. 2 for the application’s sentence and models. Fatal error (0 for the proof): applying compactness to T' without checking its finite subsets. [B2: Which theorem settles it?] For each question, say which statement of this section or of Section 7.2 settles it (or that none does), and answer it. 1. \models \sigma is known. Is \vdash \sigma? 2. T 
vdash  ot. Has T a model? 3. \sigma is true in every finite structure. Is \sigma valid? 4. Is there a structure satisfying every sentence true in 
N, with an element above the value of every numeral? 5. Is there a procedure that decides validity for sentences built from one-place predicate symbols only (no constants, function symbols or =)? (i) Completeness: yes. (ii) Completeness, second form: yes. (iii) No theorem makes it so, and it need not be: the sentence of @exr-models-c1 is true in every finite structure and false in 
N with f read as the successor, so it is not valid. (iv) Compactness: yes (@exm-non-standard-naturals). (v) The monadic remark: yes. Marking scheme. (10 points) 2 for each part: 1 for the statement named (in (iii), for saying that no statement settles it), 1 for the answer (in (iii), “no”, with a counter-model). Fatal error (0 for (iii)): answering “yes, by completeness”. C. Going deeper [C1: “Finite” is not first-order] Prove that no sentence \varphi is true in exactly the finite structures for its symbols. [Hint 1] Use @exr-limits-of-first-order-logic-b1. [Hint 2] Suppose \varphi were one, and consider the theory T = \{ \varphi \}. Suppose \varphi is true in every finite structure for its symbols and in no infinite one. For each n \ge 1 there is a structure of size n for the symbols of \varphi: take any n-element set, read each constant as one fixed element a of it, each function symbol as the function with the constant value a, and each predicate symbol as the empty relation. It is finite, so \varphi is true in it. So T = \{ \varphi \} has finite models of every size, and by @exr-limits-of-first-order-logic-b1 it has an infinite model, in which \varphi is true: a contradiction. Marking scheme. (10 points) 3 for the supposition stated precisely. 4 for models of every finite size exhibited. 3 for B1 (or compactness directly) applied, and the contradiction named. Fatal error (0 for the proof): a “proof” that only shows that one particular sentence fails. [C2: Challenge: least elements in a non-standard model] Let  M be the model of @exm-non-standard-naturals. 1. For a formula \psi with free variable x, write a sentence saying “if some element satisfies \psi, some least element satisfies \psi”, and explain why it is true in  M. 2. Take \psi = 
eg\varphi, where \varphi is a formula supposed to define the standard elements in  M. The sentence of (a) then names a least non-standard element e. Choose an element below e that is also non-standard, and conclude, without using the induction argument of this section, that no such \varphi exists. (a) Choose a variable y that does not occur in \psi, free or bound; no quantifier of \psi is on y, so y is free for x in \psi (@def-free-for). The sentence is \exists x\, \psi 	o \exists x\,  igl( \psi \wedge  orall y\, (y < x 	o 
eg\psi[y/x])  igr) , with any other free variables of \psi bound by  orall in front. By @lem-term-substitution (Section 7.3; y is free for x), 
eg\psi[y/x] is satisfied under \ell exactly when \psi fails of \ell(y), so the sentence says what (a) asks, in 
N and in  M alike. It is true in 
N by the least-number principle (every non-empty set of natural numbers has a least element), whatever set \psi defines there. So it belongs to T, and it is true in  M. (b) 
eg\varphi is satisfied by c^{ M}, which is non-standard, so (a) gives a least e satisfying 
eg\varphi: a least non-standard element. e 
e 0^{ M}, since 0^{ M} is standard; and  orall x\, (
eg(x = 0) 	o \exists y\, (S(y) = x)) is true in 
N, so in  M. Choose d with S^{ M}(d) = e. Then d < e in  M, since  orall y\, (y < S(y)) is true in 
N. And d is non-standard: if d were the value of \underline{n}, then e = S^{ M}(d) would be the value of \underline{n + 1}. So d satisfies 
eg\varphi and lies below e, against the choice of e. Marking scheme. (10 points) 4 for (a): the sentence, with y chosen not to occur in \psi, so that it is free for x, and the reading of 
eg\psi[y/x] by @lem-term-substitution, its truth in 
N by the least-number principle, and the transfer to  M through T. 4 for (b): the predecessor d obtained from a sentence true in 
N, with d < e and d non-standard both argued. 2 for the contradiction named. Fatal error (0 for (a)): the least-number principle used for an arbitrary subset of  M rather than through a sentence of T.

title: From Derivations to Mathematical Prose
8.1 The Connective Rules in Prose
8.2 The Quantifier Rules in Prose
content:
The Quantifier Rules in Prose Section 8.1 read the connective rules in the sentences of written proofs. The statements of analysis, though, are made of “for every” and “there exists”, and most of the words in an analysis proof carry a quantifier rule: “let”, “fix”, “choose”, “take”, “will do”. This section completes the dictionary with the rows for the quantifiers, equality and unique existence, for definitions, “the” and double inclusion, and for the patterns that are not single rules but are written as if they were: the lemma (“it suffices to show”) and its two “stronger” cases, induction, and symmetry (“without loss of generality”). It also makes exact one habit of analysis prose, the parenthesis “(depending on \varepsilon)”. Three sentences, three rules Section 6.1 derived “if a_n 	o L, then 2a_n 	o 2L” in sixteen lines. Written the way a mathematician writes it, the same argument takes three sentences: Let \varepsilon > 0. Since a_n 	o L and \varepsilon/2 > 0, we may choose N \in 
N (depending on \varepsilon) such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N. Then for every n \ge N, \abs{2a_n - 2L} = 2\abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon. Here is the derivation of Section 6.1 again, with the same line numbers. To keep its lines short, write A(n, \varepsilon) for \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon and B(n, \varepsilon) for \abs{2a_n - 2L} < \varepsilon. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Sentence Lines --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------- “Let \varepsilon > 0.” opens the box 2–15; its closing line 16 is not written “Since a_n 	o L and \varepsilon/2 > 0, we may choose N …” 3 and 4, then opens the box 5–14 “Then for every n \ge N, \abs{2a_n - 2L} = 2\abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon.” 7–13 (the paragraph ends) 14, 15, 16 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Each sentence opens a box, and the boxes are nested in the order of the sentences. - “Let \varepsilon > 0” opens the bounded ulename{ orall I} box of lines 2–15 in the derivation above, with the fresh name \varepsilon_0. Its closing line, line 16, is not written: the paragraph simply ends, and a reader who heard “let” knows that the box closes there. - “Choose N …” is two rules. The words “since a_n 	o L and \varepsilon/2 > 0” are the ulename{ orall E} of line 4, at the term \varepsilon_0/2, with its bound from line 3. The word “choose” opens the ulename{\exists E} box of lines 5–14, with the fresh name N_0. - “Then for every n \ge N” opens the ulename{ orall I} box of n_0 and the ulename{{	o}I} box of n_0 \ge N_0 (lines 7 and 9), and the computation is lines 8, 10 and 11. The words “for every n \ge N” also announce the lines that close these two boxes, 12 and 13. - The ulename{\exists I} of line 14, which writes “some N works” from “this N works”, and the closing line 15 of the ulename{\exists E} box, are silent. They are the end of the paragraph. The one word in the paragraph that no rule asks for is the parenthesis “(depending on \varepsilon)”. It is the subject of a subsection below. First, the rows. The quantifier rows --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule Phrases Silent in plain prose? ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------- ulename{ orall I} “let x \in A”; “fix \varepsilon > 0”; “let \varepsilon > 0 be given”; “since x was arbitrary” never the introduction; “since x was arbitrary” may be silent ulename{ orall E} “in particular, for x = \dots”; “applying … with \varepsilon/2 in place of \varepsilon” the instance must be named when it is not the obvious one ulename{\exists I} “take N = \dots”; “let \delta \coloneqq \dots; then …”; “… will do” never; its dependencies are stated ulename{\exists E} “choose N such that”; “by hypothesis there is k with n = 2k”; “let x_0 be such a point” never; the name must be fresh --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The phrases in the table are mostly the bounded forms of the rules (@prp-bounded-quantifier-rules): “let x \in A” opens a ulename{ orall I} box whose assumption is x \in A, and “choose N \in 
N such that …” opens an ulename{\exists E} box with the two assumptions N \in 
N and “…”. A bound is part of the phrase: “let \varepsilon > 0” is one step, not “let \varepsilon” followed by “suppose \varepsilon > 0”. In analysis, ulename{ orall I} is the first sentence of every limit proof: “Let \varepsilon > 0.” ulename{ orall E} is “apply the definition of a_n 	o L with \varepsilon/2”: the instance \varepsilon/2 is not the obvious one, so it is named. ulename{\exists I} is the line that places a constant, “let \delta \coloneqq \min\{1, \varepsilon/10\}”, written before the computation that shows it works. ulename{\exists E} is “choose N (depending on \varepsilon) such that …”, in which the name N has not been used before in the proof. [A constant sequence] Let c be a real number and let a_n \coloneqq c for every n \in 
N. Prove that a_n 	o c, and annotate each phrase with its rule. Let \varepsilon > 0 [ulename{ orall I}, opening]. Take N \coloneqq 0 [ulename{\exists I}]. Let n \in 
N with n \ge N [ulename{ orall I}, ulename{{	o}I}, opening]. Then \abs{a_n - c} = \abs{c - c} = 0 < \varepsilon , where the first equality substitutes a_n = c [ulename{{=}E}] and the last step uses \varepsilon > 0, the assumption of the first box. This proves a_n 	o c. The last sentence stands for three closing lines, all silent: the ulename{{	o}I} and ulename{ orall I} for n (“for every n \ge N”), and the ulename{ orall I} for \varepsilon (“since \varepsilon was arbitrary”). The witness “take N \coloneqq 0” is placed before the work that justifies it. Two things here are degenerate, and both are worth seeing once. The witness N depends on nothing: any N \in 
N works. And the assumption n \ge N is never used. The box is still opened, because the goal  orall n \in 
N\; (n \ge N 	o \dots) asks for it; without “let n \ge N”, the line “\abs{a_n - c} = 0” would not say which n it is about. The dependency parenthesis In the paragraph that opened this section, N was chosen “(depending on \varepsilon)”. Section 6.4 read off a derivation the rule behind the parenthesis: A constant chosen in a box may depend on the names of the boxes open around that box, and it does depend only on the names in the line it comes from. In the derivation of Section 6.1, the witness N_0 is obtained at line 5 from line 4, which mentions \varepsilon_0, inside the box of \varepsilon_0 only. So N_0 may depend on \varepsilon_0, and it does. In the derivation of @exm-uniform-implies-continuous, the witness \delta_0 is obtained inside the boxes of x_0 and \varepsilon_0, so it may depend on both; but it comes from a line that mentions \varepsilon_0 alone, so it does depend only on \varepsilon_0, and that is uniformity. A chosen constant may depend on the names of the boxes it sits in, and does depend only on the names in the line it comes from (the solid arrows). Numbers show why the arrows matter. Take f(x) = x^2 and \varepsilon = 1. At the point a \ge 0, the largest \delta with \abs{x^2 - a^2} < 1 for every x with \abs{x - a} < \delta is \sqrt{a^2 + 1} - a: about 0.41 at a = 1, and about 0.005 at a = 100. No single \delta serves every point, so \delta must depend on the point as well as on \varepsilon: panel (a). For f(x) = 3x + 1, \abs{f(x) - f(a)} = 3\abs{x - a}, so \delta = \varepsilon/3 works at every point at once: \delta depends on \varepsilon only, panel (b). The parenthesis is the prose record of this. “Choose N (depending on \varepsilon)” says: the boxes open here are those of \varepsilon (besides the data of the theorem, such as the sequence), and the line from which N comes mentions \varepsilon. “Choose \delta (depending on \varepsilon and on x)” says that \delta came from a line mentioning both, inside both boxes. A witness that came from a line mentioning neither is a constant, and the proof may say “(depending on neither)” or simply “a fixed \delta”. This is why proofs in analysis say what each chosen constant depends on. A missing parenthesis is not a wrong step, but it hides the one fact a reader most needs in order to check the quantifier order, and many false proofs in analysis go wrong exactly there. For f(x) = x^2 and \varepsilon = 1, does \delta = 0.1 work at the point a = 2? At a = 10? At a = 2, yes, since 0.1 < \sqrt 5 - 2 \approx 0.236. At a = 10, no: x = 10.06 has \abs{x - 10} = 0.06 < 0.1 and x^2 - 100 = 1.2036 \ge 1. [The reciprocals tend to zero] Prove that 1/n 	o 0, for the sequence (1/n)_{n \ge 1}. Annotate each phrase with its rule, and state what the chosen constant depends on. The sequence starts at n = 1, so in the definition of Section 6.1 the numbers N and n range over the positive integers 
Z_{>0}. We use one school fact about the real numbers: for every real number u there is an integer greater than u. (It follows from the axioms for the real numbers; here we take it as known.) Let \varepsilon > 0 [ulename{ orall I}, opening]. It suffices to find N \in 
Z_{>0} with  rac{1}{N} < \varepsilon , 	ag{$\ast$} since then every n \in 
Z_{>0} with n \ge N has 0 < 1/n \le 1/N < \varepsilon, so \abs{1/n - 0} < \varepsilon [it suffices: the claim (\ast) displayed, then used]. By the school fact, applied to u = 1/\varepsilon [ulename{ orall E}], there is an integer greater than 1/\varepsilon; choose such an integer N [ulename{\exists E}], which depends on \varepsilon. Since \varepsilon > 0, we have 1/\varepsilon > 0, so N > 0 and N \in 
Z_{>0}. From N > 1/\varepsilon > 0, taking reciprocals reverses the inequality: 1/N < \varepsilon, which is (\ast). So this N will do [ulename{\exists I}], and 1/n 	o 0. Read the proof as a skeleton. The first sentence opens the box of \varepsilon. The second is an “it suffices to show”, in the sense of the row below: it states a simpler claim (\ast), shows on the spot that (\ast) is enough, and leaves (\ast) to be proved. The next paragraph proves (\ast). It contains two different quantifier steps that both concern N: “choose” is the ulename{\exists E} on the school fact, which hands over some integer beyond 1/\varepsilon and calls it N; “will do” is the ulename{\exists I} that offers this N as the witness the definition asks for. Between them, the clause “so N > 0 and N \in 
Z_{>0}” checks the bound N \in 
Z_{>0} of the witness, which the bounded ulename{\exists I} needs as a line. The constant N depends on \varepsilon only: it came from the school fact at 1/\varepsilon, inside the box of \varepsilon. For instance, \varepsilon = 0.03 has 1/\varepsilon = 33.3\ldots, and N = 34 is a choice that works; so is any larger integer. “For every \varepsilon > 0, \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for all large n.” Where is the hidden \exists N, and between which two quantifiers does it stand? “For all large n” is “there is an N such that for every n \ge N” (Section 6.1): the hidden \exists N stands after  orall \varepsilon > 0 and before  orall n \ge N. Written out, the sentence is  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists N \in 
N \;  orall n \in 
N \; (n \ge N 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon), the definition of a_n 	o L. Since \exists N comes after  orall \varepsilon, the N may depend on \varepsilon. Equality and unique existence ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Rule Phrases Silent in plain prose? ---------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------ ulename{{=}I}, ulename{{=}E} “substituting”; chains “\dots = \dots = \dots”; “by (1)” yes, inside chains \exists! “there is exactly one”; “existence … uniqueness …”; “suppose y also …” never either half ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ In analysis, ulename{{=}E} is at work in every chain of equalities and inequalities, such as \abs{x^2 - 4} = \abs{x - 2}\, \abs{x + 2} \le 5 \abs{x - 2} \quad 	ext{for } \abs{x - 2} < 1 , where each = link substitutes equals for equals and each inequality link applies one fact about order (Section 5.7). (Here \abs{x - 2} < 1 gives 1 < x < 3, so 3 < x + 2 < 5.) The ulename{{=}I} lines t = t that such chains rest on are never written. Unique existence (@def-unique-existence) has two halves, which @prp-unique-existence-use separates: “2x + 3 = 7 has exactly one real solution: x = 2 is one, and if 2y + 3 = 7, then y = 2”. The first clause is existence, by ulename{\exists I}; the second is uniqueness, a ulename{ orall I} and ulename{{	o}I} box on a second candidate. Neither half implies the other, so neither may be silent. The uniqueness half often stands alone, when existence is not claimed or is proved elsewhere. Uniqueness of limits is a case of this kind. [A sequence has at most one limit] Let (a_n) be a sequence of real numbers with a_n 	o L and a_n 	o M. Prove that L = M, and annotate each phrase with its rule. Let \varepsilon > 0 [ulename{ orall I}, opening]. Then \varepsilon/2 > 0, so, applying the definition of a_n 	o L with \varepsilon/2 in place of \varepsilon [ulename{ orall E}], we may choose N_1 \in 
N (depending on \varepsilon) such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_1 [ulename{\exists E}, fresh name N_1]. Likewise, from a_n 	o M, choose N_2 \in 
N (depending on \varepsilon) such that \abs{a_n - M} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_2 [ulename{ orall E}, ulename{\exists E}, fresh name N_2]. Let n \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}. Then n \in 
N, n \ge N_1 and n \ge N_2, so both bounds apply at n [ulename{ orall E} at n, twice, with ulename{{	o}E}], and  egin{aligned} \abs{L - M} &= \abs{(L - a_n) + (a_n - M)} \ &\le \abs{a_n - L} + \abs{a_n - M} <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon , \end{aligned} where the inequality is the triangle inequality of @exm-triangle-inequality-cases, with \abs{L - a_n} = \abs{a_n - L}. Since \varepsilon > 0 was arbitrary, \abs{L - M} < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0 [ulename{ orall I}, closing], and @prp-arbitrarily-close-equal gives L = M [ulename{{	o}E}, citing it]. Four things in this proof are never silent, and each is visible. The instance \varepsilon/2 is named twice, because it is not the obvious instance. The two witnesses get two names, N_1 and N_2: the hypotheses promise a threshold for L and a threshold for M, and nothing says they are the same number, so calling both N would assert an equality nobody proved (Section 8.6 catalogues the error). The point n = \max\{N_1, N_2\} is named, since the bounds are applied at it. And the closing result is cited by name. What is silent is the bookkeeping of the two ulename{\exists E} boxes. The line \abs{L - M} < \varepsilon mentions neither N_1, N_2 nor n, so the side condition of ulename{\exists E} lets it leave both boxes, and then the box of \varepsilon closes on it. The calculation chain hides its ulename{{=}E} steps, as the row allows. The proof shows that a sequence has at most one limit: the uniqueness half of \exists!. Whether a given sequence has a limit at all is a separate question, which this proof does not touch. What the sentence does not say Some quantifiers in mathematical English are not written at all, and some are written where they do not apply. Four habits of mathematical English cover most of them. The hidden universal closure. A theorem stated as “if n is even, then n^2 is even” means “for every integer n, if n is even, then n^2 is even”. Section 5.1 introduced this convention: a letter that is not introduced anywhere, in the statement of a theorem, is read with a “for every” in front of the whole statement. It applies to the statement of a theorem, lemma or exercise, not to a line inside a proof: inside a proof every letter has been introduced by a “let” or a “choose”, and its box tells the reader which. The proof of such a theorem begins by opening the hidden box: “let n be an integer”. “For all large n” hides an \exists N and a bound, as the Quick check above found. “Eventually” means the same. The negation of “P(n) for all large n” is “for every N there is an n \ge N for which P(n) fails”, usually said “P(n) fails for infinitely many n”. “Any” can mean “every” or “some”, and only the rest of the sentence decides (Section 5.1). “Any x \in A is positive” means every element of A is positive. “If any x \in A is positive, then A is non-empty” means: if some element of A is positive. When “any” appears, rewrite the sentence once with “every” and once with “some”, and keep the one that was meant. Quantifiers at the end of a sentence. English lets a writer put “for some x” or “for all y” after the formula they govern, and then the order of two such phrases is unclear. “x^2 > y for some x for all y”, over 
R, has two readings:  orall y\, \exists x\; (x^2 > y) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad \exists x\,  orall y\; (x^2 > y) . The first is true (for y \ge 0 take x = y + 1, since (y + 1)^2 = y^2 + 2y + 1 > y; for y < 0 take x = 0). The second is false (whatever x is proposed, y = x^2 refutes it). The remedy is to write the quantifiers of such a statement in front, in the order in which they apply. A trailing phrase such as “for every n \ge N” is safe only when it is the last quantifier of the sentence, as in the definition of a_n 	o L. (10 points) - 2: (\subseteq), with k chosen and both witnesses written. - 4: (\supseteq): two choices with distinct names (1); the computation b = 2(a - b), or another valid route to an integer c with n = 6c (2); the witness named (1). - 2: the double-inclusion frame: both inclusions, each opened by “let n \in \dots”, and the conclusion A = B by extensionality, cited. - 2: the tags: ulename{ orall I}, ulename{\exists E} with fresh names, ulename{\exists I}.
