Fatal errors (0 for the step): one name for both witnesses; “2 \mid n and 3 \mid n, so 6 \mid n” asserted without an argument (N9). C. Going deeper [C1: When “similarly” is honest] 1. Prove that \max\{x, y\} + \min\{x, y\} = x + y for all real x and y, with a “without loss of generality”. Then write out the ulename{\vee E} it abbreviates, and check that its second box is the first with the letters exchanged. 2. Let x \ge 0 and y be real numbers. A student proves x \max\{x, y\} \ge xy as follows: “Without loss of generality x \le y. Then \max\{x, y\} = y, and xy \ge xy.” Explain why “without loss of generality” is not legitimate here, prove the case the student skipped, and show by an example that the hypothesis x \ge 0 cannot be dropped from the statement. [Hint 1] In (b), exchange x and y in the statement and in the hypothesis, and compare with the original. [Hint 2] In the case y \le x, \max\{x, y\} = x, and the claim becomes x^2 \ge xy. (a) Without loss of generality x \le y. Then \max\{x, y\} = y and \min\{x, y\} = x, so \max\{x, y\} + \min\{x, y\} = y + x = x + y. The phrase abbreviates ulename{\vee E} on “x \le y or y \le x”, true for all real x, y by trichotomy. Box 1, on x \le y, is the paragraph above. Box 2, on y \le x: then \max\{x, y\} = x and \min\{x, y\} = y, so \max\{x, y\} + \min\{x, y\} = x + y. Exchanging x and y in box 1 gives “y \le x; \max\{y, x\} = x, \min\{y, x\} = y; \max\{y, x\} + \min\{y, x\} = x + y = y + x”, which is box 2 read through \max\{y, x\} = \max\{x, y\}, \min\{y, x\} = \min\{x, y\} and y + x = x + y. These identities say that the statement is unchanged by the exchange, and there are no hypotheses, so the swap is exact. (b) Exchanging x and y changes both the hypothesis and the claim: it gives “y \ge 0, and y \max\{y, x\} \ge yx”, which is not the original statement. So the case y \le x is not the case x \le y in disguise, and it needs its own argument. Case y \le x. Then \max\{x, y\} = x, and multiplying x \ge y by x \ge 0 gives x \max\{x, y\} = x^2 \ge xy. With the student’s case (x \le y: x \max\{x, y\} = xy \ge xy), this proves the claim in either case. The hypothesis x \ge 0 is used only in the skipped case. It cannot be dropped: x = -1, y = -2 has \max\{x, y\} = -1, so x \max\{x, y\} = 1, while xy = 2, and 1 \ge 2 is false. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) a correct computation in the case x \le y. - 3: (a) the ulename{\vee E} written out, with its disjunction justified, and the exchange checked against the statement. - 2: (b) the reason: the exchange changes the hypothesis and the claim. - 2: (b) the case y \le x proved, using x \ge 0. - 1: (b) a counterexample without x \ge 0, checked. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (b), “the other case is similar” without computing it; a counterexample that satisfies x \ge 0. [C2: Moving a quantifier changes the meaning] Give an example of a sentence of analysis, in English, that begins “for every x …”, whose meaning changes when the phrase “for every x” is moved to the end of the sentence. Write both readings in symbols and show that one is true and the other false. An example. “For every real x > 0, there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < x.” Moved: “There is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < x, for every real x > 0.” The readings are  orall x > 0\; \exists n \in 
Z_{>0}\; (1/n < x) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad \exists n \in 
Z_{>0}\;  orall x > 0\; (1/n < x) . The first is true: given x > 0, there is an integer n > 1/x (the school fact of @exm-rhetoric-existential), and n > 1/x > 0 gives n \in 
Z_{>0} and 1/n < x. The second is false: whatever n \in 
Z_{>0} is proposed, x = 1/n is positive and 1/n < x fails. (It is natural to read the moved sentence as the second formula, since its “for every x” now comes after “there is n”; whichever reading a reader picks, the sentence no longer says one thing.) What a different answer must have, so that it can be checked against this one: - the sentence contains “for every x” and at least one existential quantifier (“there is”, “for some”) whose scope contains a formula mentioning x; - moved to the end, “for every x” can be read as coming after the existential quantifier, so that the witness may no longer depend on x; - both readings are written in symbols with all quantifiers in front, and there is a specific interpretation (here 
R with its usual order) in which one reading is true and the other false, each claim checked; - the false reading is refuted by naming, for each candidate witness, a value of x that defeats it. Another correct answer, for f(x) = x^2 on 
R, is “for every x, for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon whenever \abs{x - y} < \delta” (continuity, true); with “for every x” moved to the end, it becomes the sentence of the warning, whose uniform-continuity reading @exm-square-not-uniform refutes.

title: 8.3 Four Levels of One Proof
8.4 Reading a Proof: Self-Explanation
content:
Reading a Proof: Self-Explanation Section 8.3 showed that a level-3 proof leaves steps unsaid by a fixed convention, and that any doubtful stretch can be expanded and checked. That presupposes a reader who notices the doubtful stretch. This section is about becoming that reader. It teaches one habit, self-explanation: for each line of a proof, say what makes it true. The habit is taught here once, on one short proof, and the rest of the book relies on it. When a later proof ends its Idea with “Before reading on: …” or “Self-explain lines 3–5”, this is the passage it means. Two readers of one proof Two people read the same proof, line by line, to the end. Both say they understood it. Asked afterwards whether it was correct, one can answer and point to the reason each line holds; the other can only repeat the proof in other words. What separates them is not intelligence or background. It is what each did at every line. The first asked, at each line, what makes this true? and answered by pointing: to earlier lines, to a definition, to a named result, and to the rule that combines them. The second asked what does this say? and answered by restating it. Only the first answer can come out wrong, and that is exactly why it is useful. A restatement always succeeds, so it tests nothing. To self-explain a line is to name its warrant: the earlier lines, definitions and results it comes from, and the rule that gets it from them. The answer has the shape of a justification column in a derivation. In the derivations of Chapters 1–7 that column was printed beside every line. In level-3 prose it is gone, and self-explanation is the reader writing it back in, at level 1 or 2 of @def-levels-of-proof, one line at a time. The training passage Here is a short proof. Read it once, then read the two explanations that follow. [Explaining a proof, well and badly] Claim. For every real number x > 0, x + 1/x \ge 2. Proof. Let x > 0. 1. (x - 1)^2 \ge 0. 2. So x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0. 3. Dividing by x, x - 2 + 1/x \ge 0. 4. Hence x + 1/x \ge 2. Self-explain each line of the proof. Explained well. - The opening. “Let x > 0” opens a box for an arbitrary x with the assumption x > 0: the claim is  orall x > 0 \; (x + 1/x \ge 2), and this is its bounded ulename{ orall I}. Everything below may use x > 0; so far nothing has. - Line 1 is an instance of the school fact that the square of every real number is at least 0, at the term x - 1 (a ulename{ orall E}). It uses no earlier line, and in particular not x > 0: it holds for every real x. - Line 2 follows from line 1 because (x - 1)^2 and x^2 - 2x + 1 are the same number, by expanding the square; one is replaced by the other (ulename{{=}E}). - Line 3 follows from line 2 by dividing both sides by x. Two things need x > 0 here. Dividing by x needs x 
e 0, and dividing both sides of an inequality by a number is guaranteed to keep its direction only when that number is positive. Both come from the assumption x > 0, and this is the only place in the proof where the assumption is used. The left side becomes (x^2 - 2x + 1)/x = x - 2 + 1/x, and the right side 0/x = 0. - Line 4 follows from line 3 by adding 2 to both sides, which keeps any inequality. It is the claim for this x; since x was arbitrary, the claim holds for every x > 0 (the closing ulename{ orall I}, silent in the proof as written). Explained badly. - Line 1: we start with a square, which is positive. - Line 2: multiply it out. - Line 3: now we divide by x and it still works. - Line 4: rearranging gives the answer. Both explanations follow the order of the proof, and the second is not even wrong everywhere; it is shorter, and every sentence after the first describes what happened (the first we return to below). But compare what each one did with line 3. The first says why the inequality survives the division, and in saying it, finds the one place where the hypothesis x > 0 earns its keep. The second says “it still works”, which is a description of the outcome, not a reason. The difference shows as soon as the proof is wrong. Change the claim to “for every real x 
e 0, x + 1/x \ge 2”, and keep all four lines. The bad explanation reads the new proof exactly as happily as the old one: we start with a square, multiply out, divide by x and it still works, rearrange. The good explanation stops at line 3. It needs “the inequality keeps its direction because x > 0”, and the hypothesis now says only x 
e 0; for negative x, division by x reverses the inequality, and line 3 does not follow. The claim is in fact false: at x = -1, x + 1/x = -2 < 2. A reader who explains warrants finds the gap; a reader who paraphrases cannot, because a paraphrase of a wrong step reads exactly like a paraphrase of a right one. The bad explanation also slipped in its first line. A square is not always positive, only at least 0: (x - 1)^2 = 0 at x = 1, where the claim holds with equality. Restating invites such slips, because nothing is being checked. Explaining a warrant forces the exact fact, “every square is at least 0”, because the explanation has to cite it. So the first kind of reading does three things the second does not. It checks each step, since a warrant can fail to exist. It locates the hypotheses, since every use of a hypothesis is a warrant. And it prepares the reader to reuse the proof, since the warrants, not the restatements, are what transfer to the next problem. How to explain a line For each line, ask four questions, in this order. 1. What kind of line is it? An assumption that opens a box (“let”, “suppose”, “choose … such that”), a line derived from earlier ones, or the closing of a box (“hence”, “so”, “since x was arbitrary”). In a derivation the annotation answers it: “asm, for ulename{{	o}I}” beside an assumption names the rule that will close its box (Section 8.1). 2. Where does it come from? Name the earlier lines, the definitions and the results it uses. “Line 2”, “the definition of even”, “@thm-square-even-implies-even”, “the hypothesis x > 0”. A result is named, not paraphrased. 3. By which step? A rule of Chapters 1–7, or a piece of arithmetic that you can say in one clause (“divide both sides by x”, “expand the square”). 4. Is it legitimate here? Is every cited line still available, inside the boxes that are open (@def-derivation)? Is a chosen name fresh? Does a division have a non-zero divisor, and does an inequality keep its direction? You do not need to write out a derivation; a phrase per line is enough, at the level of the “explained well” column above. When you cannot answer one of the four questions, you have found what to look at: either a step you do not yet understand, or a gap in the proof. Section 8.3 says what to do next: expand that stretch to level 1. Which of the four questions does the bad explanation of line 3 in @exm-self-explanation fail to answer? The fourth, whether the step is legitimate here: does dividing by x keep the direction of the inequality? With it the second fails too, since the warrant x > 0 is never named. Self-explanation is not re-reading, and not summarizing. Reading a proof twice more makes it familiar, not checked: familiarity is what makes the bad explanation of @exm-self-explanation feel adequate. A summary (“the proof expands a square and divides by x”) is useful afterwards, but it skips exactly the warrants that matter, such as why the division by x is allowed and keeps the inequality’s direction. Self-explanation is local and backward-looking: each line, against what came before it. Here is a six-line proof that for real numbers x and y, if x + y > 2, then x > 1 or y > 1. 1. We prove the contrapositive: if it is not the case that x > 1 or y > 1, then x + y > 2 fails. 2. Suppose it is not the case that x > 1 or y > 1. 3. Then x \le 1 and y \le 1. 4. Adding these, x + y \le 2. 5. So x + y > 2 fails. 6. This proves the contrapositive, and hence the claim. Self-explain lines 2–4. Line 2 is an assumption: it opens the ulename{{	o}I} box for the contrapositive announced in line 1, whose hypothesis is 
eg(x > 1 \vee y > 1). Line 3 comes from line 2 in two steps. First @prp-de-morgan (a), 
eg(P \vee Q) \vdash 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q, gives “not x > 1, and not y > 1”. Then the order fact that 
eg(u > 1) means u \le 1, for every real u, turns each conjunct into the form written. Line 4 uses both conjuncts of line 3 (ulename{\wedge E}, twice) and the order fact that inequalities may be added: x \le 1 and y \le 1 give x + y \le 1 + y \le 1 + 1 = 2. (For the record: line 5 is the order fact x + y \le 2 means 
eg(x + y > 2); line 6 closes the box by ulename{{	o}I} and then passes from the contrapositive to the claim by @prp-contrapositive-converse, a classical step.) Naming the unstated fact Section 3.3 turned a paragraph of argument into a sequent: its conclusion, its stated premises, and the unstated facts that close its gaps. A proof is read the same way, one line at a time. Often the second question, where does it come from?, has an answer the writer did not write: a fact used but not stated. Self-explaining the line means naming that fact, and the fact then turns out to be one of three things. It may be a school fact or a definition: name it. It may be an earlier result: cite it. Or it may be false, and then the line fails. Two lines that look alike: - “Since n^2 is a multiple of 3, so is n.” The unstated fact, “if 3 \mid n^2, then 3 \mid n”, is true. A careful proof proves it, by cases on the remainder of n on division by 3. - “Since n^2 is a multiple of 4, so is n.” The unstated fact, “if 4 \mid n^2, then 4 \mid n”, is false at n = 2. Chapter 1 met it as a missing premise (@exr-using-an-implication-b5). A reader who only paraphrases reads both lines alike. In “Since x > 1, x^2 > x”, name the unstated fact and the hypothesis it needs. Multiplying both sides of x > 1 by x keeps the direction of the inequality because x > 0; and x > 0 follows from x > 1 > 0. Strategies of good readers Self-explanation is the habit for single lines. Readers who are good at proofs also do a few things with a proof as a whole. Here are five, shown on one short proof. Claim. For real numbers x > 0 and y > 0, \sqrt{xy} \le (x + y)/2. Proof. Let x > 0 and y > 0. Since x = (\sqrt x)^2, y = (\sqrt y)^2 and \sqrt{xy} = \sqrt x \, \sqrt y, x + y - 2\sqrt{xy} = (\sqrt x - \sqrt y)^2 \ge 0 . Hence 2\sqrt{xy} \le x + y, and dividing by 2 gives the claim. 1. Try it first. Before reading the proof, spend a few minutes on the claim yourself. A natural attempt squares both sides: xy \le (x + y)^2/4 is 4xy \le x^2 + 2xy + y^2, that is, 0 \le (x - y)^2, which is true. Already you know what the difficulty is (the square root) and what your attempt rests on (that a square is at least 0). 2. Identify the framework. Find the skeleton, level 1 of @def-levels-of-proof. Here: a bounded ulename{ orall I} on x and y (opened by “Let”, closed silently) with the bounds x > 0, y > 0, then a direct chain. There is no case split, no contradiction, and no chosen witness. Knowing that tells you where to look: every line is a computation, so every warrant is an algebraic fact. 3. Break it into sub-proofs. The proof has one claim inside it, the displayed identity, and then a short finish. A claim inside a proof is proved once and then used, as with a lemma in Section 8.2 (“It suffices to show”). Read the claim on its own: it needs \sqrt{xy} = \sqrt x \sqrt y (true for x, y \ge 0) and (\sqrt x)^2 = x. 4. Illustrate a hard line with an example. If the identity is not clear, try numbers. With x = 1 and y = 4: the left side is 1 + 4 - 2 \cdot 2 = 1, the right side (1 - 2)^2 = 1. An example checks nothing in general, but it shows what the line claims. 5. Compare with your own attempt. Your squaring route proves the claim too, and it hides a warrant the given proof avoids: passing back from xy \le (x + y)^2/4 to \sqrt{xy} \le (x + y)/2 uses the converse of “squaring preserves order”: from a^2 \le b^2 conclude a \le b. This holds when b \ge 0, because then \abs{a} \le b; here b = (x + y)/2 > 0. Without that hypothesis it fails: a = 1, b = -2. Comparing the two routes shows why the given proof introduces \sqrt x and \sqrt y: it never has to undo a squaring. The comparison also links this claim to @exm-self-explanation: put y = 1/x, and \sqrt{xy} = 1, so the claim becomes x + 1/x \ge 2. The five strategies work at the level of the whole proof and self-explanation at the level of the line, and they support each other. Trying first tells you which line will be the hard one; the framework tells you which boxes are open at each line, which is what the fourth question of self-explanation needs. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Here is a proof that if a > 0, b > 0 and a^2 = b^2, then a = b. (1) a^2 - b^2 = 0. (2) (a - b)(a + b) = 0. (3) a + b > 0. (4) Hence a - b = 0, that is, a = b. Classify each explanation as one that justifies its line or one that paraphrases it. 1. “Line 1 follows from the hypothesis a^2 = b^2 by subtracting b^2 from both sides.” 2. “Line 2: then the factored form is zero as well.” 3. “Line 2 is line 1 rewritten with the identity u^2 - v^2 = (u - v)(u + v), at u = a and v = b.” 4. “Line 3: now we know that a + b is positive.” 5. “Line 3 holds because a > 0 and b > 0 are hypotheses, and a sum of two positive numbers is positive.” 6. “Line 4: so a - b is zero, which is what we wanted.” (a) Justifies: it names the source (the hypothesis) and the step (subtracting b^2). (b) Paraphrases: “is zero as well” restates line 2 without saying why the product equals the left side of line 1. (c) Justifies: it names the identity and the instance. (d) Paraphrases: it restates line 3 and gives no reason. (e) Justifies: it names both hypotheses and the fact that combines them. (f) Paraphrases: it gives no warrant. A justification would say: by line 2 a product is zero, so one of its factors is zero; line 3 says the factor a + b is not zero, being positive; so a - b = 0 (@prp-disjunctive-syllogism, applied to “a + b = 0 or a - b = 0” and a + b 
e 0). [A2: Drill] Answer each part in a phrase. (a) and (b) ask whether an explanation justifies or paraphrases; (c) and (d) which of the four questions is at work; (e) and (f) what kind of line it is; (g)–(i) name the unstated fact; (k) locates a hypothesis; (j) and (l) are about the habits of good readers. 1. A line: “Since n is even, n^2 is even.” An explanation: “With n = 2k, n^2 = 2(2k^2), and 2k^2 is an integer.” Does it justify or paraphrase? 2. A line: “x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1).” An explanation: “We factor it.” Justify or paraphrase? 3. Which of the four questions asks “May we divide by x - 1 here?” 4. Which question does the answer “this line opens a box” answer? 5. What kind of line is “Choose \delta > 0 such that …”, and what does its derivation print beside it? 6. What kind of line is “Since \varepsilon was arbitrary, …”? 7. Name the unstated fact: “Since 0 < a < b, a^2 < b^2.” 8. Name the unstated fact: “\abs{x - 2} < 1, so x > 1.” 9. Name the unstated facts: “x^2 = 9 and x > 0, so x = 3.” 10. After three readings, a proof feels clear. Has the reader self-explained it? 11. “Let x < 0. Then 1/x < 0.” Which hypothesis is used, and how? 12. “Before reading the proof, I tried the claim myself by squaring both sides.” Which strategy is this? (a) It justifies: it names the definition of even, the witness and the algebra. (b) Paraphrase. It says what happened, not which identity makes the line true (u^2 - v^2 = (u - v)(u + v) at u = x, v = 1). (c) The fourth: is the step legitimate here (is x - 1 
e 0)? (d) The first: what kind of line it is. (e) An assumption that opens an ulename{\exists E} box with a fresh name; “asm, for ulename{\exists E}”. (f) The closing of a ulename{ orall I} box. (g) Multiplying an inequality by a positive number keeps it: a \cdot a < a \cdot b (multiply a < b by a > 0) and a \cdot b < b \cdot b (multiply by b > 0). (h) \abs{u} < r holds exactly when -r < u < r; here -1 < x - 2. (i) x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3), and a product of real numbers is 0 only if a factor is, so x = 3 or x = -3; then x > 0 rules out -3 (ulename{DS}). (j) Not necessarily: familiarity is not a warrant checked line by line (the warning “Self-explanation is not re-reading”). (k) x < 0. It gives x 
e 0, so 1/x exists; and x \cdot (1/x) = 1 > 0, so 1/x has the sign of x. (l) Try it first. B. Practice [B1: Self-explain a counterexample] Here, with its lines numbered, is the half of @exm-square-not-uniform that shows f(x) = x^2 is not uniformly continuous on 
R. (1) By the negation of uniform continuity, with the bounds x \in 
R and y \in 
R dropped because they always hold, we must show \exists \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall \delta > 0 \; \exists x \; \exists y \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta \wedge \abs{x^2 - y^2} \ge \varepsilon  igr). (2) Take \varepsilon = 1. (3) Let \delta > 0 be arbitrary, and take x \coloneqq 1/\delta and y \coloneqq 1/\delta + \delta/2, which depend on \delta. (4) Then \abs{x - y} = \delta/2 < \delta, (5) and, since y > x > 0, \abs{x^2 - y^2} = (y - x)(y + x) =  rac{\delta}{2} \Bigl(  rac{2}{\delta} +  rac{\delta}{2} \Bigr) = 1 +  rac{\delta^2}{4} \ge 1 . (3) Since \delta was arbitrary, uniform continuity fails. Self-explain each line, citing labels where a line uses an earlier result. Say at which lines \delta > 0 is used. (1) The goal “not uniformly continuous” is replaced by the displayed formula: the negation of uniform continuity with no 
eg in front of a quantifier (Section 6.2’s recipe, @exm-negating-definitions (c)). The proof now proves that formula. (2) 1 is the witness for “there is \varepsilon > 0”, and 1 > 0. It is written first and justified by the end. (3) \delta > 0 is arbitrary: what follows must work for every \delta. The numbers x and y are built from \delta, which is allowed because \delta is already given; 1/\delta exists because \delta 
e 0. (4) y - x = \delta/2 > 0, so \abs{x - y} = \delta/2, and \delta/2 < \delta because \delta > 0. (5) Both numbers are positive and y > x, so \abs{x^2 - y^2} = y^2 - x^2 = (y - x)(y + x); multiplying out gives 1 + \delta^2/4, at least 1 because a square is at least 0. (6) \delta was arbitrary, so the displayed formula holds with \varepsilon = 1, and uniform continuity fails. \delta > 0 is used in (3), in (4) twice, and in (5). (1) A cut: the goal “f is not uniformly continuous” is replaced by the displayed formula, and the proof then proves the formula. The formula is the positive form of the negation of uniform continuity, @exm-negating-definitions (c), read with A = 
R; there the two are shown interderivable, by @prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @prp-negated-implication and the order fact 
eg(u < \varepsilon) iff u \ge \varepsilon. The direction used here is from the displayed formula to the negation. The bounds can be dropped because a bounded quantifier \exists x \in 
R abbreviates \exists x\, (x \in 
R \wedge \dots) (@def-bounded-quantifier), and over the domain 
R the conjunct x \in 
R always holds. (2) The witness for \exists \varepsilon > 0: a bounded ulename{\exists I} at the term 1, with its bound 1 > 0. It is written first, but as a rule it is applied last: the instance it needs, the formula after \exists \varepsilon > 0 with 1 for \varepsilon, is what lines (3)–(6) prove. (3) “Let \delta > 0 be arbitrary” opens a bounded ulename{ orall I} box flagged \delta_0 with the assumption \delta_0 > 0. As in Section 5.4, the prose uses the letter \delta both for the flag and for the bound variable; below, \delta in the arithmetic is the flag \delta_0. The terms 1/\delta and 1/\delta + \delta/2 are the witnesses for \exists x and \exists y (two ulename{\exists I}, applied at the end of the box). They may mention \delta because \delta’s box is open; the clause “which depend on \delta” records this. The term 1/\delta exists because \delta 
e 0, from \delta > 0. (4) Arithmetic: y - x = \delta/2, which is positive since \delta > 0, so \abs{x - y} = \delta/2; and \delta/2 < \delta since \delta > 0. This is the first conjunct. (5) Arithmetic. Since \delta > 0, x = 1/\delta > 0 and y = x + \delta/2 > x. Then x^2 < y^2, so \abs{x^2 - y^2} = y^2 - x^2 = (y - x)(y + x), with y - x = \delta/2 and y + x = 2/\delta + \delta/2; multiplying out gives 1 + \delta^2/4, which is at least 1 because \delta^2/4 \ge 0. This is the second conjunct; with (4) it gives the conjunction (ulename{\wedge I}), and the two ulename{\exists I} of (3) then give \exists x\, \exists y\, (\dots). (6) The closing line of the bounded ulename{ orall I} box flagged \delta_0 (@prp-bounded-quantifier-rules). The side condition holds: the proof has no premises; the only assumption mentioning \delta_0 is \delta_0 > 0, the assumption of the box this line closes, and no outer box is open; and \delta_0 does not appear in the conclusion  orall \delta > 0\, \exists x\, \exists y\, (\dots), whose \delta is a bound variable different from the flag. With (2) this proves the displayed formula, and by the cut (1) uniform continuity fails. \delta > 0 is used in (3) (so that 1/\delta exists), in (4) (twice) and in (5) (for y > x > 0). [B2: The unjustified line] Here is a proof that for real numbers x < y, x^3 < y^3. (1) Let x < y. (2) Then y^3 - x^3 = (y - x)(y^2 + xy + x^2). (3) Since x < y, y - x > 0. (4) Also y^2 + xy + x^2 > 0. (5) So y^3 - x^3 > 0, as a product of two positive numbers. (6) Hence x^3 < y^3. Every line is true. Line 1 opens the box; of the rest, all but one are instances of a routine algebra or order fact, cited or not; one line is not an instance of any fact stated so far, and it needs an argument of its own. Self-explain the proof line by line to find it, and supply that argument as its warrant. Line 1 opens the box, with the assumption x < y. Line 2 is the identity (y - x)(y^2 + xy + x^2) = y^3 - x^3, checked by multiplying out. Line 3 cites line 1 and the order fact u < v iff v - u > 0. Line 5 cites lines 2, 3 and 4 and the fact that a product of two positive numbers is positive. Line 6 is line 5 rearranged by the same order fact. Line 4 is the one without a warrant: it cites nothing, and it is not an instance of any fact stated so far. It is not obvious either, since xy can be negative. A warrant: complete the square, y^2 + xy + x^2 = \Bigl( y +  rac{x}{2} \Bigr)^2 +  rac{3x^2}{4} \ge 0 , with equality only if x = 0 and y + x/2 = 0, that is, only if x = y = 0. Line 1 rules that out, since x < y gives x 
e y. So y^2 + xy + x^2 > 0. The repaired line 4 uses the hypothesis x < y a second time, which the proof as printed hides; a reader who explains only “the bracket is positive” has paraphrased line 4 and missed this. [B3: Name the unstated facts] Here is a proof. Claim. For every real x \ge 0, x^3 + 2 \ge 3x. (1) x^3 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)^2 (x + 2). (2) (x - 1)^2 \ge 0. (3) x + 2 > 0. (4) So x^3 - 3x + 2 \ge 0, (5) that is, x^3 + 2 \ge 3x. 1. Name the unstated fact behind each line. 2. Which line uses the hypothesis x \ge 0, and how? 3. Find the least c such that the same proof, with at most two lines reworded, proves the claim for every x \ge c. Show that the claim fails at x = -3. (a) - (1) A polynomial identity, checked by expanding: (x^2 - 2x + 1)(x + 2) = x^3 + 2x^2 - 2x^2 - 4x + x + 2 = x^3 - 3x + 2. - (2) Every square is at least 0. - (3) x \ge 0 gives x + 2 \ge 2 > 0. - (4) A product of a non-negative and a positive number is non-negative, applied to (2) and (3), then (1) substituted (ulename{{=}E}). - (5) Adding 3x to both sides keeps the inequality. (b) Line (3), and only there: x \ge 0 gives x + 2 \ge 2 > 0, which line (4) needs as the positive factor. (c) c = -2. For x \ge -2, line (3) becomes “x + 2 \ge 0”, and line (4) uses “a product of two non-negative numbers is non-negative”; every other line stands. Below -2 the claim is false. At x = -3: (-3)^3 + 2 = -25, while 3x = -9, and -25 \ge -9 fails. (For every x < -2, (x - 1)^2 > 0 and x + 2 < 0, so the product is negative.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 5: (a), one per line, each naming the fact (not restating the line). - 2: (b) line (3), with how x \ge 0 enters. - 2: (c) c = -2, with the reworded lines (3) and (4). - 1: the failure at x = -3 computed. Fatal errors (0 for the step): explanations that restate the lines; in (c), “the hypothesis can be dropped”. C. Going deeper [C1: A longer proof] Here is a proof that a sequence has at most one limit, with its lines numbered. Claim. If a_n 	o L and a_n 	o M, then L = M. (1) Suppose a_n 	o L and a_n 	o M, and suppose, for a contradiction, that L 
e M. (2) Let \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{L - M}/2. Then \varepsilon > 0. (3) Choose N_1 \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_1, and N_2 \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - M} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_2. (4) Let n \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}. (5) Then \abs{L - M} \le \abs{L - a_n} + \abs{a_n - M} < \varepsilon + \varepsilon = \abs{L - M}. (6) So \abs{L - M} < \abs{L - M}, which is impossible. (7) Hence L = M. Self-explain each line, citing labels where a line uses an earlier result. Say where the assumption L 
e M is used, and which rule closes the box it opens. [Hint 1] Line (3) applies the definition of a limit at \varepsilon. What does that need, and which line supplies it? [Hint 2] Line (5) uses one named result and two lines of (3). Which? (1) Two openings: the ulename{{	o}I} box with the two hypotheses, and inside it a box on L 
e M, that is, 
eg(L = M); the goal L = M is positive, so this is an ulename{RAA} box. (2) A constant, defined from L and M. It is positive because L 
e M gives \abs{L - M} > 0: the one use of the assumption. (3) The definition of a_n 	o L (as in @exm-negating-definitions (a)) applied at \varepsilon (ulename{ orall E} at a term that is not the obvious one, with its bound \varepsilon > 0 from (2)), then ulename{\exists E} with the fresh name N_1; the same for M, with a second fresh name N_2 (one name for both would be (N4) of Section 8.6). (4) A constant: the larger of two natural numbers, so n \ge N_1 and n \ge N_2. (5) The triangle inequality (@exm-triangle-inequality-cases), with \abs{L - a_n} = \abs{a_n - L}; then the two bounds of (3) at this n (ulename{ orall E} at n, ulename{{	o}E} with n \ge N_1 and with n \ge N_2); then \varepsilon + \varepsilon = \abs{L - M} by (2). (6) The clash: \abs{L - M} < \abs{L - M} against the fact that no number is less than itself (ulename{
eg E}). The line does not mention N_1 or N_2, so the two ulename{\exists E} boxes close on it. (7) ulename{RAA}: the box assumed 
eg(L = M) and the line written after it is L = M. The closing of the ulename{{	o}I} box is silent. The assumption is used once, at (2), and it does work there, so the proof is not in costume; Section 8.2 proved the same claim without opening this box (@exm-rhetoric-equality). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (1) and (7), the two boxes and ulename{RAA} as the closing rule (not ulename{
eg I}). - 2: (2), \varepsilon > 0 from L 
e M, named as the use of the assumption. - 2: (3), the instance named, two fresh names. - 2: (5), the triangle inequality cited and both bounds applied at n \ge N_1, N_2. - 2: (6), the clash named, and the ulename{\exists E} boxes closing because  ot does not mention N_1, N_2. Fatal errors (0 for the step): calling (7) ulename{
eg I}; applying the definition at \varepsilon without its positivity. [C2: Challenge: A proof about derivations] Self-explain the proof of @lem-atom-splitting in Section 4.8: for each of its five numbered steps, and for each claim in the paragraph that follows them, say what it uses and why that is legitimate. Then state the idea of the proof in two sentences. [Hint 1] Keep @def-derivation open beside you: the paragraph after the five steps checks, in turn, the premises, the scope rule for the transplanted citations, the rule schemas, the last line of each box, and the availability of what the last line cites. [Hint 2] Start with step 2. Which result supplies p \vee 
eg p, what is substituted for its letter, and why may that line cite nothing? Step 1. The premises of the new list are the members of \Delta that D or E uses. Clause (D1) of @def-derivation places premises first, above every box, and puts no restriction on which statements they are. The conclusion will be \Delta \vdash \psi, so only members of \Delta are taken. The premises p, 
eg p of D and E are therefore left out, unless they also belong to \Delta, which does no harm. Step 2. The line p \vee 
eg p is @prp-excluded-middle with the atom p for the letter P, used as a derived rule (@def-derived-rule) with no premises, so it cites nothing. This is the one classical step, through ulename{LEM}. Step 3. The box opened by p contains the non-premise lines of D with their own boxes; every citation of the premise p is redirected to the assumption, and every citation of a premise in \Delta to the premise line of step 1. The two degenerate cases (the last line of D is a premise) are handled separately so that the box still ends in \psi, by repetition (ulename{R}, clause (D3)) where needed. Step 4. The same, for E with the assumption 
eg p. Step 5. The last line \psi is ulename{\vee E} (@def-rules-disjunction), citing the disjunction of step 2 and the two boxes, each opened by one disjunct and ending in \psi. The verification paragraph. It checks that the list is a derivation. (i) Premises are first and in no box, so they are available everywhere. (ii) Inside each new box, a line of D cites the same lines and boxes as before, renumbered, or a premise line, or the assumption, and each of those is available by the scope rule of @def-derivation: the old boxes have simply been placed inside one new box, which contains both the citing line and the cited one. (iii) Each line is still an instance of its rule’s schema, since its statement and the statements it cites are unchanged, as in the proof of @lem-weakening-cut. (iv) The last line of each new box is \psi, as a line of that box itself, which ulename{\vee E} requires. (v) The disjunction and the two boxes are available at the last line, which lies in no box. So the last line is a correct ulename{\vee E}, and \Delta \vdash \psi. The idea in two sentences. The lemma is proof by cases on p \vee 
eg p: excluded middle supplies the disjunction, and the two given derivations, with their premise p or 
eg p turned into the assumption of a box, are the two cases of ulename{\vee E}. All the work is in checking that the transplanted lines still cite only available lines. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: step 2 explained: @prp-excluded-middle as a derived rule at the atom p, citing nothing, and identified as the classical step. - 2: steps 3 and 4 explained: the redirection of citations of p (or 
eg p) to the assumption and of members of \Delta to the premise lines, and the degenerate cases. - 1: step 5 named as ulename{\vee E} with its three citations. - 3: the verification paragraph explained against @def-derivation: availability by the scope rule, schemas unchanged, each box ending in \psi as its own line. - 2: an idea in two sentences that names both the case split on p \vee 
eg p and the transplanting of D and E into the two boxes. Fatal errors (0 for the step): explanations that restate the steps without naming what they use; calling the case split ulename{
eg I} or ulename{RAA}.

title: 8.5 Writing a Proof
content: Writing a Proof Section 8.4 trained a reader to say what licenses each line of a proof, as @exm-self-explanation did line by line. This section turns to the writer. A proof is written for a reader who will check it in exactly that way, so the writer’s job is to make each line’s warrant visible. The section gives a procedure that leads from a statement to plain prose, the conventions of written mathematics, each a rule of Chapters 1–7 made audible, and four worked examples. A procedure A reader checks a proof forwards, one line at a time. A writer finds a proof mostly backwards, from the goal. The two directions are not in conflict: Section 3.1 showed that the search for a derivation is goal-directed, and @def-derivation says that the derivation found is a list in which each line cites only lines above it. The procedure below keeps both, the search in scratch work and the derivation on the page. Its steps 3 and 6 use the levels of @def-levels-of-proof and the convention of @def-silent-steps from Section 8.3. Writing a proof of a statement. 1. Write the goal in symbols. Translate the statement, its hypotheses and its conclusion into a formula, as in Section 6.1, with every quantifier and its bound. Read a letter that is not introduced as universally quantified (Section 5.1). Set up the Givens/Goal table: the hypotheses on the left, the goal on the right. 2. Unwind the definitions. Replace each defined word (“bounded”, “converges”, “irrational”, “\subseteq”) by its definition, in the hypotheses and in the goal. This is \rulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} on a definition. 3. Read the skeleton off the goal (Section 3.1, extended in Section 6.3), and write it at level 1: the boxes, their first lines and their last lines. Open the \rulename{\exists E} boxes of existential hypotheses early. 4. Fill the boxes: backwards in scratch, forwards on the page. The search runs from the goal; the written proof runs from the hypotheses, each line citing lines above it. What the search found goes into the Idea, not into the Proof. 5. Choose constants last in the search, and write them first on the page, each with what it depends on. 6. Write level 3, leaving silent exactly the steps that @def-silent-steps allows, and no others. 7. Reread as a checker: for each line, is it true, and by which rule does it follow from which available lines? (Section 8.6 makes this a two-column check.) Steps 1–3 involve no mathematics, only logical form, and they fix the first and last sentence of every box before anything is invented (“skeleton first”). A picture after the next example shows steps 4 and 5. Which step of the procedure produces the sentence “Let \varepsilon > 0” at the start of a proof that a_n \to L, and which step keeps it at level 3? Step 3. Unwound in step 2, the goal begins \forall \varepsilon > 0, so its skeleton is a bounded \rulename{\forall I} box whose assumption is \varepsilon_0 > 0; “Let \varepsilon > 0” is the first line of that box. Step 6 keeps it, because the opening of a \rulename{\forall I} box is never silent (@def-silent-steps). The closing “since \varepsilon was arbitrary” may be silent. The procedure, run once This example runs all seven steps on a statement not seen before. Sets of reals are used here as Chapter 5 used them, with “a \in A” a one-place predicate and A \subseteq B read as “every element of A is an element of B”. [A subset of a bounded set] Let A and B be sets of real numbers with A \subseteq B. Prove that if B is bounded above, then A is bounded above. Steps 1 and 2: the goal in symbols, unwound. Over the domain \nR, “B is bounded above” is \exists M \; \forall b \in B \; (b \le M) (Section 6.1), and A \subseteq B is \forall x \in A \; (x \in B). The statement is an implication, so the derivation below is the inside of a \rulename{{\to}I} box: its assumption is the first formula (line 2), the hypothesis is the second, and its goal is \exists M \; \forall a \in A \; (a \le M). ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------ A \subseteq B; B bounded above A bounded above \forall x \in A \; (x \in B); \exists M \; \forall b \in B \; (b \le M) \exists M \; \forall a \in A \; (a \le M) \forall x \in A \; (x \in B); \forall b \in B \; (b \le M_0) (\rulename{\exists E}, M_0 fresh) \exists M \; \forall a \in A \; (a \le M) the same \forall a \in A \; (a \le M_0) (try the witness M_0) the same, and a_0 \in A (\rulename{\forall I}, a_0 fresh) a_0 \le M_0 the same, and a_0 \in B (\rulename{\forall E} at a_0) a_0 \le M_0 ✓ (\rulename{\forall E} at a_0) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The second row is step 2; each later row is one move of steps 3 and 4; the table’s last row is where the search ends. Step 3: the skeleton. The goal is an existential, so it is postponed: no witness is in sight yet. The assumption “B is bounded above” (line 2) is an existential, so its \rulename{\exists E} box opens at once, with a fresh name M_0 and the assumption \forall b \in B \; (b \le M_0); the box’s last line is the goal. Step 4: filling the box. Backwards: the goal needs a witness M and a proof of \forall a \in A \; (a \le M). The only bound in sight is M_0, so try it. Then the new goal is a bounded universal: a box “let a_0 \in A” whose last line is a_0 \le M_0. That line comes from the bound on B, instantiated at a_0, which needs a_0 \in B; and a_0 \in B comes from A \subseteq B instantiated at a_0. Forwards, the same lines in the order of the list are the derivation below (with the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules; each bounded \rulename{\forall E} abbreviates a \rulename{\forall E} and a \rulename{{\to}E}, and the bounded \rulename{\forall I} box a \rulename{\forall I} box with a \rulename{{\to}I} box inside). The side conditions hold: a_0 appears in neither line 1 nor line 2, not in line 7 and not in the open assumption on line 3; M_0 appears in none of lines 1, 2 and 9. Step 5: the constant. The witness for the goal is the bound M_0. The search could choose it only once the \rulename{\exists E} box supplied M_0, and confirm it only at line 6; the page writes it first, in the sentence that chooses it. It depends on B only: its box is opened before the box of a_0, so it cannot depend on a_0, and it must not, because a single bound has to serve every element of A. Step 6: level 3. Suppose B is bounded above, and choose an upper bound M of B (depending on B only). Let a \in A. Since A \subseteq B, we have a \in B, and so a \le M. Hence M is an upper bound of A, and A is bounded above. The two instances of \rulename{\forall E} (lines 5 and 6) are at the obvious term a, and each appears only as the citation that licenses it (“since A \subseteq B”, “so”, which cites the choice of M). The closing of the \rulename{\forall I} box, “since a was arbitrary”, is silent. Two steps that are never silent are on the page: the \rulename{\exists E} with its fresh name (“choose an upper bound M”), and the \rulename{\exists I} with its witness and dependence (“M is an upper bound of A”; “depending on B only”). “Suppose B is bounded above” opens the \rulename{{\to}I} box; its closing is silent. Step 7: reread. The order of the first two sentences matters. With “let a \in A” first and M chosen inside, the \rulename{\exists I} would fall inside the box of a_0, giving only \forall a \in A \; \exists M \; (a \le M), which says nothing. The example used A \subseteq B once, at line 5, and “B is bounded above” once, at line 9, by \rulename{\exists E}, whose box assumption is used at line 6. The two warnings below concern steps 4 and 5. Scratch paper and the page Steps 4 and 5 say that the search runs backwards and the page runs forwards. Here is the example’s search beside its page. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Scratch paper (from the goal, backwards) The page (from the hypotheses, forwards) ------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------ 1. Goal: an M with a \le M for every a \in A. 1. Suppose B is bounded above, and choose an upper bound M of B. 2. B bounded above gives some bound M: try it. 2. Let a \in A. 3. Need a \le M for an arbitrary a \in A. 3. Since A \subseteq B, a \in B. 4. That needs a \in B. 4. So a \le M. 5. a \in B comes from A \subseteq B. ✓ 5. Hence M is an upper bound of A. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Read the scratch column from the bottom up and it is the page, except for the constant: M is found at scratch line 2, after the goal has been read, but on the page it is chosen in the first sentence, before anything uses it. Step 4 as a logical fact. The search of Section 3.1 opens a box for the goal before it knows how the box will be filled, and it postpones an existential goal until a witness appears; that is why it works backwards. But a derivation is a list in which line k cites only lines available at k (@def-derivation), and a written proof is that list in sentences. So the order of the page is forced by the rules, not by taste: “\abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon holds if \abs{x - a} < \varepsilon/2” points from a later line to an earlier one. The backward reasoning lives in the Idea block. Step 5 as a logical fact. A chosen constant, such as “let \delta \coloneqq \varepsilon/2”, is the witness of an \rulename{\exists I} line. The search finds it last, because only the end of the search shows what it must do. On the page it comes first, right after the names it is built from, because later lines use it. Those names are its dependencies; they must be among the names of the boxes open where it is chosen (Section 6.4). The search is not the proof. A page that reads “we want x^2 < 4; this holds if x < 2; so let x < 2” has copied the search, and each “holds if” points backwards. A backward step can be false, and the page hides it: “x < 2 implies x^2 < 4” fails at x = -3. In scratch work every backward step must be checked as an implication pointing forwards; on the page only the forward chain appears, each line citing lines above it. A constant without its dependencies is a claim nobody can check. In a proof that x^2 is uniformly continuous on \nR, the sentence “let \delta \coloneqq \min\{1, \varepsilon/(2\abs{x} + 1)\}” looks innocent. Asked “what does \delta depend on?”, the formula answers: on \varepsilon and on x, so the \delta was chosen inside the box of x, and the proof shows only continuity at every point. Uniform continuity is false here (@exm-square-not-uniform). Writing “(depending on \varepsilon only)” after the constant is what lets a reader catch the error. On the page, which sentence carries the witness of the final \rulename{\exists I}, and why can the choice of M not come after “Let a \in A”? “Hence M is an upper bound of A” offers M as the witness; it was chosen in sentence 1. Chosen after “Let a \in A”, M would sit inside the box of a, and the proof would give only \forall a \in A \; \exists M \; (a \le M), which says nothing (step 7 of the example). A writer’s scratch paper reads: “want \abs{3x - 6} < \varepsilon when \abs{x - 2} < \delta; \abs{3x - 6} = 3\abs{x - 2}; so \delta = \varepsilon/3.” Write the first two sentences of the page. “Let \varepsilon > 0, and let \delta \coloneqq \varepsilon/3, which is positive and depends on \varepsilon only. Let x be a real number with \abs{x - 2} < \delta.” Conventions of written mathematics A handful of conventions make a proof checkable. Each is a rule of Chapters 1–7 heard in a sentence. - Announce the skeleton. “We prove the contrapositive”, “by induction on n”, “we consider two cases”, “suppose, for a contradiction, that …”. An announcement tells the reader which box is opening, and so what its last line must be. - Name every object when it is introduced, by “let” (an arbitrary object, \rulename{\forall I}), “choose” (a witness, \rulename{\exists E}, with a fresh name), or “let … \coloneqq …” (a constant, the witness of \rulename{\exists I}), and say what a chosen object depends on. - One claim per sentence. A sentence carries one line, or a short chain of lines joined by “so”, each step of which the reader can name. Two unrelated claims joined by “and” hide which one is used later. - End with what was shown. The last sentence of a proof states the goal, or the last line before only closings that @def-silent-steps lets be silent. If it is not the statement to be proved, the reader should be told how the two are related. - Label displayed claims that will be cited, (\ast) or (1), and cite them by the label. A citation is a line number in prose. None of these is a matter of style. An object used without being introduced is a line citing nothing, and an announcement that does not match its box (assuming the conclusion of an implication) proves the converse; these are entries (N9) and (N5) of the catalogue in Section 8.6. Matching sentences and rules The next two examples go in opposite directions. [Label every sentence] Here is a short proof. Label each sentence with the rule it uses. Claim. For a real number x, if \abs{x - 1} < 1, then x > 0. Proof. (1) Assume \abs{x - 1} < 1. (2) Every real number is at least 1 or below it, so either x \ge 1 or x < 1. (3) Suppose first that x \ge 1. (4) Then x \ge 1 > 0. (5) Suppose instead that x < 1. (6) Then x - 1 < 0, so \abs{x - 1} = 1 - x. (7) Hence 1 - x < 1, that is, x > 0. (8) In either case x > 0, which proves the claim. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Sentence What it does Rule ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------- (1) opens a box with the hypothesis assumption for \rulename{{\to}I} (2) states the disjunction the split needs a fact about real numbers (3) opens the first case assumption for \rulename{\vee E} (4) algebra (5) opens the second case assumption for \rulename{\vee E} (6) algebra (7) uses the assumption of (1), whose box is still open algebra (8) combines the cases, then closes the outer box \rulename{\vee E} on (2), (3)–(4), (5)–(7); then \rulename{{\to}I} -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Sentence (7) uses the assumption made in (1), and it may: that box is still open. Measured against @def-silent-steps, nothing that must be written is missing: the split is on the page with a disjunction that covers every real x, each case opens with its assumption, and what is left out may be silent. Labeling also shows where the work is: the case split exists only because \abs{\cdot} is defined by cases, and the school fact -\abs{u} \le u, used with u = x - 1, gives -1 < x - 1 in one step, with no \rulename{\vee E} at all. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Sentence What it does Rule ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (1) opens a box with the hypothesis assumption for \rulename{{\to}I} (2) states a fact about real numbers a school fact, entered as a line (3) opens the first case box assumption for \rulename{\vee E} (4) x \ge 1 and 1 > 0 give x > 0 \rulename{{\to}E}, with the fact “a \ge b and b > c imply a > c” (5) opens the second case box assumption for \rulename{\vee E} (6) computes \abs{x - 1} \rulename{{\to}E} twice, with the facts “x < 1 implies x - 1 < 0” and “a < 0 implies \abs{a} = -a” (7) uses the assumption of (1) \rulename{{=}E}, putting (6) into (1), then \rulename{{\to}E} with “1 - x < 1 implies x > 0” (8) combines the cases, then closes the outer box \rulename{\vee E} on (2), (3)–(4), (5)–(7); then \rulename{{\to}I} on (1)–(8) ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The facts of school algebra enter as implications, each used by \rulename{{\to}E}. Sentence (8) closes two boxes, which is normal. Measured against @def-silent-steps, the proof leaves out nothing that must be written: the split in (2) is on the page, and the disjunction it splits is a school fact (every real number is at least 1 or below it), so it covers every case; each case box opens with its assumption; and every step it leaves unwritten is of a kind that may be silent, for instance the \rulename{\forall E} instances of the school facts at the obvious terms, the conclusion x > 0 of case 1, which is left to the chain x \ge 1 > 0 of (4), the \rulename{\wedge I} behind (4), whose conjuncts are displayed, the \rulename{{=}E} of (7), and the closing of the \rulename{{\to}I} box, for which “which proves the claim” stands. Labeling also shows where the work is. The case split exists only because \abs{\cdot} is defined by cases (Chapter 1); the school fact -\abs{u} \le u, used with u = x - 1, gives -1 < x - 1 in one step, and a proof written that way would have no \rulename{\vee E} at all. The second direction starts from a derivation whose premises are facts about integers. [From a derivation to a paragraph] Let n be an integer. Write E for “n is even”, O for “n is odd”, F for “n + 1 is even”, and G for “n(n + 1) is even”. The derivation below uses four facts about integers as premises. Write the paragraph a mathematician would write for it. Every integer is even or odd, so we consider two cases. If n is even, then n(n + 1) has an even factor, and so it is even. If n is odd, then n + 1 is even, since an odd number plus one is even; so again n(n + 1) has an even factor and is even. In either case n(n + 1) is even. Compare the two. The paragraph keeps one sentence for each box and each rule that matters: line 1 becomes “we consider two cases”, with its reason; the two boxes become the two “if” sentences; line 10 becomes “in either case”. It drops the line numbers and the rule names, and it merges the two \rulename{{\to}E} steps of lines 8 and 9 into one sentence joined by “so”. It never skips a box: the reader still sees both cases and sees them combined. By @def-silent-steps, the closing “in either case …” could be dropped at level 3; the split of line 1, with the reason it covers every integer, could not. The paragraph leaves the premises unproved. Premises 2–4 are one line of algebra each (for instance, n = 2k gives n(n + 1) = 2\bigl(k(n + 1)\bigr)), and a careful write-up includes them; premise 1, that every integer is even or odd, is the fact (E1) that this volume takes as known. Generalizing a proof A proof written about one object sometimes proves much more. To generalize it, replace the object by a fresh name, the move of \rulename{\forall I} (Section 5.4), and read every line again. A line that uses only what the new name’s box assumes stays. A line that uses a property of the particular object must be proved again, or the generalization fails. [One of three, generalized] Here are two proofs that one of 17, 18, 19 is a multiple of 3. (P1) 18 = 3 \cdot 6. (P2) 17 = 3 \cdot 5 + 2, so 17 + 1 = 3 \cdot 6. Which one generalizes to “for every integer n, one of n, n + 1, n + 2 is a multiple of 3”? Write the general proof. (P1) does not generalize: it uses a fact about 18 alone. (P2) does, once its one particular fact, 17 = 3 \cdot 5 + 2, is replaced by what every integer has: n = 3k, n = 3k + 1 or n = 3k + 2 for an integer k, a school fact. Let n be an integer [assumption for \rulename{\forall I}]. Dividing by 3, there is an integer k with n = 3k, n = 3k + 1 or n = 3k + 2; choose such a k [\rulename{\exists E}]. If n = 3k, n is a multiple of 3. If n = 3k + 1, then n + 2 = 3(k + 1). If n = 3k + 2, then n + 1 = 3(k + 1). In every case one of the three is a multiple of 3 [\rulename{\vee E}]. Since n was arbitrary, this holds for every integer [\rulename{\forall I}]. (P2) was the third case, with k = 5. The test: after renaming, can every line still be justified from what the box of n assumes? A line that computes with the particular number fails the test. A proof that 7^2 - 1 is divisible by 8 reads “7^2 - 1 = 48 = 8 \cdot 6”. Does it generalize to every odd n? What would? No: it computes with 7. A general proof writes n = 2k + 1, so n^2 - 1 = 4k(k + 1), and shows that k(k + 1) is even, since one of k, k + 1 is even. That is the proof of @exr-levels-of-abbreviation-b2. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Here is a proof. Claim. For real numbers x and y, if x + y > 2, then x > 1 or y > 1. (1) Assume x + y > 2. (2) Suppose, for a contradiction, that it is not the case that x > 1 or y > 1. (3) Then x > 1 fails and y > 1 fails. (4) So x \le 1 and y \le 1. (5) Adding, x + y \le 2. (6) This contradicts x + y > 2. (7) Hence x > 1 or y > 1, which proves the claim. 1. Label each sentence with the rule it uses, as in @exm-annotate-abs. 2. Which sentence closes an \rulename{RAA} box, and which uses one of De Morgan’s laws (@prp-de-morgan)? Which law? 3. Everything inside the box of (2) follows from (2) alone, until the clash in (6). Which face of “by contradiction” (Section 8.1) does the proof wear, and which face is it really? Write the first sentence of the rewritten proof. 4. Sentence (7) closes two boxes. Which of the two closings may be silent at level 3, by @def-silent-steps? (a) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Sentence Rule ----------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (1) assumption, opening the \rulename{{\to}I} box (2) assumption \neg(x > 1 \vee y > 1), opening an \rulename{RAA} box (3) @prp-de-morgan (a), \neg(P \vee Q) \vdash \neg P \wedge \neg Q, applied to (2) (4) \rulename{\wedge E} on (3), twice; \rulename{{\to}E} with the order fact “\neg(a > 1) implies a \le 1”, twice; then \rulename{\wedge I} (5) \rulename{\wedge E} on (4), then \rulename{{\to}E} with “a \le 1 and b \le 1 imply a + b \le 2” (6) \rulename{{\to}E} with the order fact “a \le 2 implies \neg(a > 2)” on (5), then \rulename{\neg E} on (1) and the result (7) \rulename{RAA} on the box (2)–(6); then \rulename{{\to}I} on (1)–(7) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (b) Sentence (7) closes the \rulename{RAA} box: the box opened with the negation of the goal x > 1 \vee y > 1 and closes with the goal itself. Sentence (3) uses De Morgan’s law (a), a direction derived without \rulename{RAA}. (c) It wears face (iii), genuine \rulename{RAA}, but it is a contrapositive in costume, as in @exm-costume-contrapositive: the hypothesis (1) is used only at the clash, and everything else derives x + y \le 2 from x \le 1 and y \le 1. The rewrite opens: “We prove the contrapositive: if x \le 1 and y \le 1, then x + y \le 2.” The rewrite is clearer, but it does not remove the classical step: passing from the contrapositive back to the claim is @prp-contrapositive-converse, which uses \rulename{RAA}. (d) The closing of the \rulename{{\to}I} box (“so if x + y > 2, then …”) may be silent. The conclusion of the \rulename{RAA} box, “hence x > 1 or y > 1”, may not. [A2: Drill] Answer each part in a line. The parts follow the procedure: (a)–(b) symbols and unwinding, (c)–(d) the skeleton, (e) the order on the page, (f), (g), (i) the conventions, (h) the search and the page, (j)–(k) generalizing, (l) the Givens/Goal table. 1. Write in symbols, with every quantifier and bound: “the square of every odd integer is odd” (domain \nZ). 2. Unwind “the sequence (a_n) is bounded” (Section 5.6). 3. The goal is \forall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \; \forall x \; (\abs{x - a} < \delta \to \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon). What are the first and the last line of the outer box? 4. A hypothesis says “some integer k has n = 2k + 1”. When does its box open? 5. On the page, which comes first: “let \delta \coloneqq \varepsilon/4” or “let x be a real number with \abs{x - 1} < \delta”? 6. “x is positive and y is negative, and so xy < 0 and x - y > 0.” Which convention does this break? 7. A proof uses c in its fourth sentence, and c appears nowhere before. Which convention, and which entry of Section 8.6? 8. Is “this holds if x < 2” a sentence of the page? 9. Claim: x^2 - 4x + 3 < 0 for 1 < x < 3. A proof ends “… so x^2 - 4x + 3 = (x - 1)(x - 3).” What is missing? 10. A proof about the number 12 uses only “12 is a multiple of 4”. For which integers does the same proof prove the same claim? 11. A proof about “an arbitrary odd n” uses n > 0 in one line. What does it prove? 12. Givens \forall x \in A \; (x \in B) and \forall x \in B \; (x \in C); Goal \forall x \in A \; (x \in C). Write the next row of the Givens/Goal table. (a) \forall n \, \bigl( \exists k \, (n = 2k + 1) \to \exists j \, (n^2 = 2j + 1) \bigr). (b) \exists M \in \nR \; \forall n \in \nN \; (\abs{a_n} \le M). (c) First: the assumption \varepsilon_0 > 0, “Let \varepsilon > 0” (assumption for \rulename{\forall I}). Last: \exists \delta > 0 \; \forall x \; (\abs{x - a} < \delta \to \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon_0), by \rulename{\exists I} with the chosen \delta. (d) At once (step 3): an \rulename{\exists E} box with a fresh name k. (e) The constant (step 5). The box of x needs \delta; chosen after x, \delta could depend on x. (f) One claim per sentence: two claims joined by “and” hide which one is used later. (g) Name every object when it is introduced; (N9), a line that cites nothing. (h) No. It points backwards, from the goal, and belongs to scratch work or the Idea (step 4). (i) The end: x - 1 > 0 and x - 3 < 0, so the product is negative. The last sentence must be the claim (end with what was shown). (j) For every multiple of 4: rename 12 to a fresh n, with the assumption 4 \mid n. (k) Only the claim for positive odd n. For all odd n, the box would have to assume no more than oddness, so that line must be proved again without n > 0. (l) Givens: the same, and a_0 \in A (\rulename{\forall I}, a_0 fresh). Goal: a_0 \in C. B. Practice [B1: From skeleton to prose] Each part gives a statement and a level-1 skeleton of its proof. Write the proof at level 3, keeping every step that @def-silent-steps says is never silent. 1. For every integer n, if n is odd, then 3n + 5 is even. (Domain \nZ.) 2. No real number x satisfies x^2 + 1 = 2x - 1. (Domain \nR.) 3. For a real number x: x^3 = x if and only if x = -1, x = 0 or x = 1. (Here x is fixed; “or” chains group to the right.) Hint: line 3 of (c) uses the school fact that a product of real numbers is zero only if one of its factors is zero. (a) Let n be an integer, and suppose n is odd. Choose an integer k with n = 2k + 1. Then 3n + 5 = 6k + 3 + 5 = 2(3k + 4), and 3k + 4 is an integer, so 3n + 5 is even. “Choose an integer k” is the \rulename{\exists E} box, with a fresh name; the witness 3k + 4 of line 4 is on the page, and it depends on k, hence on n. Lines 5, 6 and 7 close boxes and are silent. (b) Suppose, to the contrary, that some real x satisfies x^2 + 1 = 2x - 1, and fix such an x. Rearranging, x^2 - 2x + 2 = 0, that is, (x - 1)^2 + 1 = 0. But (x - 1)^2 \ge 0, since a square is non-negative, so 1 \le 0, which is false. Hence no real x satisfies the equation. “Suppose, to the contrary” opens the \rulename{\neg I} box of line 1 (the goal is a negation, so no classical rule is used), and “fix such an x” the \rulename{\exists E} box. The clash of lines 5–7 is named, and the conclusion of the \rulename{\neg I} box is written; line 8 is silent. (c) Let x be real. (\Rightarrow) Suppose x^3 = x. Then (x + 1)\,x\,(x - 1) = x^3 - x = 0. A product of real numbers is zero only if a factor is zero, so x + 1 = 0, x = 0 or x - 1 = 0; that is, x = -1, x = 0 or x = 1. (\Leftarrow) Suppose x = -1, x = 0 or x = 1. In the three cases, x^3 = -1 = x, x^3 = 0 = x and x^3 = 1 = x. This proves the equivalence. Both directions are written, and the citation in line 3 is visible. The two splits of (\Leftarrow) are merged into “in the three cases”; the disjunction split is the hypothesis itself, and the closing lines 12 and 13 are silent. [B2: Put the proof in order] Let (a_n) and (b_n) be sequences of real numbers with a_n \to L and b_n \to M, where “a_n \to L” is the pattern of Section 6.1: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is N \in \nN such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N. Eight of the ten sentences below, in a suitable order, form a level-3 proof that a_n + b_n \to L + M; two are distractors. Write down an order for the eight, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each distractor is wrong. 1. Let n \in \nN with n \ge N. 2. Since b_n \to M and \varepsilon/2 > 0, choose N_2 \in \nN (depending on \varepsilon) such that \abs{b_n - M} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_2. 3. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}, where N_1 and N_2 serve every \varepsilon at once. 4. Then n \ge N_1 and n \ge N_2. 5. Let \varepsilon > 0. 6. Since n \ge N and \varepsilon > 0 were arbitrary, a_n + b_n \to L + M. 7. Choose N_1 \in \nN such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_1. 8. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}. 9. So \abs{(a_n + b_n) - (L + M)} \le \abs{a_n - L} + \abs{b_n - M} < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon. 10. Since a_n \to L and \varepsilon/2 > 0, choose N_1 \in \nN (depending on \varepsilon) such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_1. An admissible order: (v), (x), (ii), (viii), (i), (iv), (ix), (vi). The only other admissible order swaps (x) and (ii), which use only \varepsilon and one hypothesis each. Nothing else moves: (viii) uses N_1 and N_2; (i) uses N; (iv) uses n \ge N and the definition of N; (ix) uses (iv), (x) and (ii) at this n, and the triangle inequality (@exm-triangle-inequality-cases); (vi) closes the boxes of n and \varepsilon, with the \rulename{\exists I} of the witness N inside “a_n + b_n \to L + M”. The maximum exists because there are finitely many numbers. Distractor (iii) claims that N_1 and N_2 serve every \varepsilon at once. They were chosen from \forall \varepsilon \, \exists N, inside the box of \varepsilon, so they depend on \varepsilon and serve only the \varepsilon they were chosen for; a uniform N would need \exists N \, \forall \varepsilon, which the hypothesis does not give. This is the error that Section 8.6 catalogues as (N2). For a_n = 1/(n + 1), L = 0, no single N_1 serves every \varepsilon > 0: at \varepsilon = 1/(N_1 + 2) the term a_{N_1} = 1/(N_1 + 1) is too far from 0. Distractor (vii) applies the hypothesis at \varepsilon instead of \varepsilon/2. It is a legal step, but with it in place of (x), the bound in (ix) becomes \abs{(a_n + b_n) - (L + M)} < \varepsilon + \varepsilon/2, not < \varepsilon, so (ix) would no longer follow. It is an \varepsilon of the wrong kind for the goal. [B3: The last step] Here is a level-1 skeleton for the statement “for real numbers x and y, if x is rational and y is irrational, then x + y is irrational”, with x and y fixed: and its level-3 prose, with the closing sentence of the \rulename{\neg I} box left blank: Let x be rational and y irrational. Suppose x + y is rational. Then y = (x + y) - x is a difference of two rational numbers, so y is rational. This contradicts the irrationality of y. \underline{\qquad\qquad} Name the move, then complete it. The move is skeleton first: the blank is line 8, the line written after the \rulename{\neg I} box of lines 4–7 closes, a line the skeleton fixes before any arithmetic. That box assumed “x + y is rational” and reached \bot at line 7, so line 8 concludes its negation. It is the first face of “by contradiction” (Section 8.1), proof of a negative statement, and uses no classical rule: “irrational” means “not rational”, so the goal of the outer box, line 8, is a negation, and the inner box is opened on x + y \in \nQ with goal \bot. Completion. “Hence x + y is not rational, that is, x + y is irrational.” The conclusion of a \rulename{\neg I} box is never silent (@def-silent-steps), so this sentence must be written even though the reader can guess it. Line 9, the closing of the \rulename{{\to}I} box, may stay silent. The sentence before the blank, “this contradicts the irrationality of y”, is line 7, the clash of \rulename{\neg E}, which names both lines it cites. [B4: Which proof generalizes?] Two proofs that 6 divides 7^3 - 7 = 336: (P1) “336 = 6 \cdot 56.” (P2) “7^3 - 7 = 6 \cdot 7 \cdot 8, a product of three consecutive integers; one of them is even and one is a multiple of 3, so 6 divides the product.” 1. Which proof generalizes to “for every integer n, 6 \mid n^3 - n”, and why does the other not? 2. Write the general proof at level 3, with its fresh name and every fact it uses. 3. Which fact about 6 does (P2) leave unstated? (a) (P2) generalizes; (P1) computes with 7 and says nothing about another n. (b) Let n be an integer. Then n^3 - n = (n - 1)\, n\, (n + 1), a product of three consecutive integers. By @exm-generalise-proof, applied to n - 1, one of n - 1, n, n + 1 is a multiple of 3, so 3 \mid n^3 - n (a product with a factor divisible by d is divisible by d: if a = dc, then ab = d(cb)). By (E1), n is even or odd: if n is even, the factor n is even; if odd, n - 1 is even. So one factor is even, and 2 \mid n^3 - n. Since 2 and 3 divide it, so does 6 (by @exr-quantifier-rhetoric-b3, the inclusion \supseteq: if m = 2a = 3b, then b = 2(a - b) and m = 6(a - b)). (c) “If 2 \mid m and 3 \mid m, then 6 \mid m”, the fact of @exr-quantifier-rhetoric-b3. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) (P2), with the reason (P1) fails. - 2: (b) the factorization and the fresh name. - 2: (b) a multiple of 3 among the factors, cited or proved. - 2: (b) an even factor, from (E1). - 1: (b) the step from 2 and 3 to 6, proved or cited. - 1: (c) the fact named. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a proof that checks finitely many n (N1); “2 \mid m and 3 \mid m, so 6 \mid m” with neither proof nor citation (N9). C. Going deeper [C1: A constant found backwards] Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and let a be a fixed real number. Prove that for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon for every real x with \abs{x - a} < \delta. Write your answer as an Idea, which finds \delta backwards, followed by a Proof, which runs forwards. Say what \delta depends on. [Hint 1] Compute \abs{f(x) - f(a)} in terms of \abs{x - a} before choosing anything. [Hint 2] The Proof begins: “Let \varepsilon > 0, and let \delta \coloneqq …”. Idea. We want \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon. Compute: f(x) - f(a) = (2x + 3) - (2a + 3) = 2(x - a), so \abs{f(x) - f(a)} = 2\abs{x - a}. This is below \varepsilon exactly when \abs{x - a} < \varepsilon/2. So \delta = \varepsilon/2 should work, and it does not involve x or a. Proof. Let \varepsilon > 0, and let \delta \coloneqq \varepsilon/2, which is positive and depends on \varepsilon only. Let x be a real number with \abs{x - a} < \delta. Then \abs{f(x) - f(a)} = \abs{2(x - a)} = 2\abs{x - a} < 2\delta = \varepsilon . Since x was arbitrary, \delta works for \varepsilon; since \varepsilon > 0 was arbitrary, this proves the claim. The Idea reads the computation from the goal back to \abs{x - a}; the Proof places \delta right after \varepsilon, before any x appears, and justifies it by the final display. Because \delta does not depend on a either, the same proof shows that one \delta serves every point: f is uniformly continuous on \nR, in the sense of Section 6.4. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: an Idea that computes \abs{f(x) - f(a)} = 2\abs{x - a} and reads off \delta from the goal. - 2: the Proof opens with \varepsilon > 0 arbitrary and introduces \delta before any x, with \delta > 0 checked. - 2: says what \delta depends on (\varepsilon only, or \varepsilon and a if the choice involves a). - 3: for arbitrary x with \abs{x - a} < \delta, the forward chain to \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon, each step justified. - 1: a closing sentence with the quantifiers in the order \varepsilon, \delta, x. Any \delta with 0 < \delta \le \varepsilon/2 earns full marks. Fatal errors (0 for the step): \delta depending on x; a Proof that runs backwards (“this holds if …”). [C2: Rewrite it properly] A sequence (a_n) is bounded if there is M \in \nR with \abs{a_n} \le M for every n \in \nN (Section 5.6). The following proof that a sequence (a_n) with a_n \to L is bounded is correct in substance but badly written. We want some M with \abs{a_n} \le M. For big n, a_n is near L, so \abs{a_n} is less than \abs{L} + 1 if we use 1 for \varepsilon. The small n are only finitely many, so take the biggest. So M is the max of all of them and it works. 1. Name three faults of the text, each by the convention it breaks (this section) or the step that is not written. 2. Rewrite the proof at level 3. [Hint 1] Which objects does the text use without introducing them, and what does each depend on? [Hint 2] The rewrite begins: “Apply the definition of a_n \to L with \varepsilon = 1, and choose N \in \nN such that …”. (a) (i) It writes the search: “we want some M” and “if we use 1 for \varepsilon” describe what is being looked for, not lines that follow. (ii) It uses objects without introducing them: “big n” hides an N, obtained from the hypothesis at \varepsilon = 1 by \rulename{\forall E} and \rulename{\exists E}, which is never named; “the biggest” does not say of which numbers. (iii) It never says what M is or what it depends on: M is built from the finitely many terms before N, so it depends on N. (Also acceptable: the split into small and big n has no stated reason; the last sentence does not say what was shown.) (b) Apply the definition of a_n \to L with \varepsilon = 1, and choose N \in \nN such that \abs{a_n - L} < 1 for every n \ge N. Let M \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{a_0}, \abs{a_1}, \dots, \abs{a_{N-1}}, \abs{L} + 1 \}, the largest of finitely many numbers, so it exists; it depends on N (when N = 0 the list is just \abs{L} + 1). Let n \in \nN. Either n < N or n \ge N, since every natural number is one or the other. If n < N, then \abs{a_n} is in the list, so \abs{a_n} \le M. If n \ge N, then by the triangle inequality (@exm-triangle-inequality-cases) \abs{a_n} = \abs{(a_n - L) + L} \le \abs{a_n - L} + \abs{L} < 1 + \abs{L} \le M . In either case \abs{a_n} \le M. Hence (a_n) is bounded. The \rulename{\forall E} instance \varepsilon = 1 is named, because it is not the obvious one; the witness M of the final \rulename{\exists I} is defined before it is used, with its dependence; the split on n < N or n \ge N carries its reason (every natural number is one or the other). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) three genuine faults, each tied to a convention or an unwritten step (1 each). - 2: (b) applies the hypothesis at a named positive \varepsilon and chooses N from it. - 2: defines M before using it, with its dependence on N, bounding the early terms and \abs{L} + \varepsilon (a maximum or a sum). - 2: the two cases n < N and n \ge N, the second by the triangle inequality (cited) or an equivalent estimate from \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon, such as L - \varepsilon < a_n < L + \varepsilon and a split on the sign of a_n. - 1: ends with what was shown. Fatal errors (0 for the step): M chosen before N or as a maximum or sum of infinitely many numbers; the early terms omitted. [C3: From \sqrt 2 to \sqrt 3, and not to \sqrt 4] The level-3 proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational in @exm-sqrt2-four-levels uses (L) and @thm-square-even-implies-even. 1. Rewrite it as a proof that no rational number has square 3. You may use (\mathrm{L}_3): every rational number is p/q with integers p, q, q \ne 0, not both multiples of 3. Prove the lemma your proof needs in place of @thm-square-even-implies-even. 2. Rewrite it once more for 4, with (\mathrm{L}_4): every rational number is p/q with integers p, q, q \ne 0, not both multiples of 4, which is true. Which line fails? Why must some line fail? 3. Say in one sentence what a generalization keeps and what it must prove again. [Hint 1] The lemma is “if 3 \mid n^2, then 3 \mid n”. Split on the remainder of n on division by 3. [Hint 2] Let r be rational, and suppose r^2 = 3. By (\mathrm{L}_3), write r = p/q with integers p, q, not both multiples of 3. (a) Lemma: if 3 \mid n^2, then 3 \mid n. Write n = 3k, 3k + 1 or 3k + 2. In the first case 3 \mid n. Otherwise n^2 = 3(3k^2 + 2k) + 1 or n^2 = 3(3k^2 + 4k + 1) + 1, and a number 3j + 1 is not a multiple of 3: from 3j + 1 = 3t we get 3(t - j) = 1, and no integer is \tfrac13. So those cases clash with 3 \mid n^2, and 3 \mid n holds in each by \rulename{\bot E}. The proof. “Let r be rational, and suppose r^2 = 3. By (\mathrm{L}_3), write r = p/q with integers p, q, not both multiples of 3. Then p^2 = 3q^2, so 3 \mid p^2, and by the lemma 3 \mid p. Writing p = 3m gives 9m^2 = 3q^2, so q^2 = 3m^2, and by the lemma 3 \mid q. So p and q are both multiples of 3, a contradiction; hence r^2 \ne 3.” (b) The line “p^2 = 4q^2, so 4 \mid p^2, and by the lemma 4 \mid p” fails: “if 4 \mid n^2, then 4 \mid n” is false at n = 2. Some line must fail, because the claim is false: 4 = (2/1)^2, and p = 2, q = 1 satisfy (\mathrm{L}_4). Lines that are all licensed, from true premises, cannot reach a false conclusion (soundness: @thm-soundness, and the statement of Section 7.2 under “From counter-models to non-derivability” for the quantifier steps). (c) A generalization keeps the skeleton (the boxes, the choices, the clash) and every line that used only properties shared by the new object; it must prove again each line that used a property of the old one, here the lemma. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) the lemma proved by the residues mod 3, with the clash 3j + 1 \ne 3t justified. - 2: (a) the rest of the proof, with (\mathrm{L}_3) and the lemma used twice. - 2: (b) the failing line named, with the counterexample n = 2. - 1: (b) why a line must fail (\sqrt 4 = 2 is rational). - 2: (c) skeleton kept, particular lines re-proved. Fatal errors (0 for the step): the lemma asserted without proof (N9); in (b), blaming (\mathrm{L}_4).

title: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content:
Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed A reader working alone must judge proofs, including their own, and is the person least able to do it. The remedy is procedural. This section gives two questions to ask of every line and a catalogue of the errors that recur, each tied to the rule of Chapters 1–7 that it breaks, and then checks four short proofs line by line.
