Two questions for every line A proof is correct when every line is licensed: by @def-derivation, each line is a premise (a hypothesis, a proved result or a true school fact), an assumption, or one rule applied to available lines. So checking a proof means asking two questions of every line, with the answers in two columns. - Is it true? Is the line correct whenever the hypotheses and the assumptions of the open boxes are true? - Does it follow, and by which rule? From which available lines, and by which rule? The first column finds where to look; the second decides. The two questions are different. A line can be true and not follow: a correct fact the proof has not earned. This is the dangerous case, because nothing about the line looks wrong. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- It follows It does not follow ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ It is true the normal case: “n = 2k, so n^2 = 2(2k^2)”, in a proof that n^2 is even when n is the dangerous case: Proof B’s last line, “if n^2 is even, then n is even”, true and not earned It is false the fault is higher up: from the false line “every real x has x \ge 1 or x \le 0”, ulename{ orall E} at 	frac12 gives “	frac12 \ge 1 or 	frac12 \le 0”, which follows and is false “x < 1, so x^2 < 1”: false at x = -2 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- “False” means false in some situation where the hypotheses and the open assumptions are true. When a line follows and is false, some line it rests on, neither a hypothesis nor an open assumption, is false there too, because the rules never lead from true lines to a false one (@thm-soundness); follow it back until the second column fails. The two columns, as a procedure for one line: A “no” in the first column marks a line to look at first; only the second column decides. The silent steps are those of @def-silent-steps. The same holds for derivations with quantifiers and equality, by the soundness statement for predicate logic in Section 7.2 (“From counter-models to non-derivability”). (Proof C’s “1 is even” is true given its box’s assumption.) A proof that n^2 \ge n for every integer n opens with the line “n^2 - n = n(n - 1) \ge 0”. Is the line true? Does it follow? Would the answers change if n ranged over the reals? For an integer n the line is true: no integer lies strictly between 0 and 1, so n \le 0 (both factors \le 0) or n \ge 1 (both \ge 0). But as written it follows from nothing: it is the goal rearranged, without the case split that makes it true. For real n it is false at n = 1/2, where n(n - 1) = -1/4. The first column depends on the situation; the second fails in both. The catalogue Most wrong proofs fail in one of a few ways, each breaking a particular rule. Citing a line that is not available: the goal itself (circular reasoning), a result proved later, or a general “fact” neither proved nor a true school fact (a false “fact” never qualifies). Breaks @def-derivation: every line is a premise, an assumption, or a rule applied to available lines (Section 1.4). Instances: “if n^2 is even, then n is even: suppose n^2 is even; since n is even, …” (true, and circular); “x < 1, so x^2 < 1, since squaring preserves <” (false: x = -2). 10. Using an assumption after its box has closed. Breaks the scope rule of @def-derivation (Section 1.4). Instance: “Suppose n is even, say n = 2k; then n^2 = 4k^2. Hence if n is even, 4 \mid n^2. Instance: “if x^2 > 9 and x > 0, then x > 3: suppose, for a contradiction, that x < 3; then 0 < x < 3 gives x^2 < 9, against x^2 > 9; hence x > 3” (true: the box should open with x \le 3, and the case x = 3 is never examined). - (b) A bound negated instead of a quantifier (@prp-bounded-quantifier-negation). Instance: “a_n = 0 does not converge to 0, since some \varepsilon \le 0 has \abs{a_n - 0} \ge \varepsilon for all n” (false). - (c) The negation of \varphi 	o \psi written as an implication,

eg\psi (@prp-negated-implication). Instance: “if x > 2, then x^2 > 4” is “refuted” because “if x \le 2, then x^2 \le 4” holds at x = 0 (false: both are true at x = 0, so one is not the negation of the other). 12. Distinct letters taken for distinct objects. Two names introduced separately are treated as naming different objects, though no line says they differ. Breaks ulename{ orall I}: a box opened for two arbitrary names must cover every pair, including the pairs in which both name one object (ulename{ orall E} may put the same term for both, @def-rule-universal-elimination). Instance: “if a and b are roots of x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0, then a + b = 5: the two roots give x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - a)(x - b), and comparing coefficients, a + b = 5”. False: a = b = 2 are roots, and 2 + 2 = 4. 13. An “and so on” with nothing behind it. A step is repeated “and so on”, and its outcome is used for every stage, but the passage from each stage to the next, or the reason the process ends, is never proved. Breaks @ax-induction (or @thm-strong-induction): ulename{{	o}E} on the axiom needs its step as a line, and “and so on” is not that line. Instance: “a non-empty set A of positive rational numbers has a least element: take a_1 \in A; if it is not least, take a_2 \in A with a_2 < a_1, and so on, until the least element is reached” (false: \{ 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} has no least element, and the process never ends). 14. An object named before it is shown to exist. A step names an object, with “the …” or “let … be the …”, and so presupposes that such an object exists (for “the”, exactly one), though no line states or proves it. In (N9) the step asserts a fact that is not available; here the missing premise is never asserted at all, because it hides inside a name. Breaks ulename{\exists E}, which opens its box only by citing a line \exists x \, \varphi (@def-rules-existential), and the use of “the” (Section 5.8), which needs existence and uniqueness. Instance: “let N be the largest natural number; then N + 1 \le N, so 1 \le 0” (false: the presupposed premise, that a largest natural number exists, is false). Both new kinds of error can reach a true conclusion. The words of (N13)’s instance, said of a non-empty set of natural numbers, reach a true conclusion, but they leave out why the process ends: a strictly decreasing list of natural numbers that starts at a_1 has at most a_1 + 1 terms, which needs an induction. “Let m be the least positive integer with m^2 > 50; since 7^2 = 49 and 8^2 = 64, m = 8” reaches a true conclusion too, but the existence of a least such integer is a premise the proof must state: it is (N14). The barber who shaves exactly the villagers who do not shave themselves is (N14) as well; Section 5.6 shows that no such barber can exist (@thm-barber). An entry diagnoses a step, not the conclusion: a false instance shows the step leading from true premises to a false conclusion, and a true one that a correct conclusion does not excuse it. Some entries name errors met before: (N1) is the first error of Section 5.4’s list, and parts (b) and (c) of (N11) are warnings of Section 6.2. The catalogue lists steps that can lead from true lines to a false one. A step can also be valid but improper. “For all reals a and b, a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab; so for all reals b and a, a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab”, taken as one line, never leads from truth to falsehood, but no rule of the book writes it in one line, TAUT included (Section 8.3). That is a matter of level (@def-levels-of-proof), not an error: at level 0 it is ulename{ orall E} twice and ulename{ orall I} twice, and in prose it needs no words. Older books name some of these errors as fallacies: Traditional name Entry -------------------------------------------------- ------- hasty generalization (N1) equivocation: one name for two things (N4) affirming the consequent; denying the antecedent (N6) false dichotomy (N8) begging the question (N9) a presupposition (“the …”) (N14) Affirming a disjunct is a common error of Section 1.6. Which family, and which entry, does this belong to: “Some integer n has n^2 = n + 6; fix such an n. Since n was arbitrary, every integer n satisfies n^2 = n + 6”? A “for all” error, (N3): a name chosen by ulename{\exists E} is not arbitrary. The premise holds at n = 3; the conclusion fails at n = 0. Which entry does the sentence “choose N larger than every N_\varepsilon, one for each \varepsilon > 0” commit, and when is the same move not an error? (N2). Each N_\varepsilon comes from  orall \varepsilon \, \exists N, inside the box of its own \varepsilon; one N above all of them would be uniform, as if the hypothesis were \exists N \,  orall \varepsilon, and usually none exists, since the N_\varepsilon can grow without bound as \varepsilon shrinks. The move is legitimate when \varepsilon ranges over finitely many values \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_k: then \max\{N_{\varepsilon_1}, \dots, N_{\varepsilon_k}\} exists, because a finite set of natural numbers has a maximum. A true conclusion does not make a proof correct. “I know the result is true” answers the first column for the last line and nothing else. Argument B of Section 1.1 has a true conclusion and only true sentences, and it is wrong (Proof B below). Four proofs, checked Here are four short proofs as a student might write them; two are correct and two are not. [Proof A] Claim. For a real number x, if x^2 - 3x + 2 < 0, then 1 < x < 2. (1) Assume x^2 - 3x + 2 < 0. (2) Then (x - 1)(x - 2) < 0. (3) A product of two real numbers is negative only when one factor is positive and the other negative, so either x - 1 > 0 and x - 2 < 0, or x - 1 < 0 and x - 2 > 0. (4) In the first case, 1 < x < 2. (5) In the second case, x < 1 and x > 2, which is impossible. (6) Hence 1 < x < 2. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line True? By which rule? ----------------------- ------------------------ ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (1) assumption opens the ulename{{	o}I} box (2) assumption opens a box with “x > 1”, announced as ulename{RAA} (3) yes, given (2) ulename{{	o}E} with order facts (4) yes (3) gives 
eg(x^2 < 1) by order facts; ulename{
eg E} on (1) and that line (5) true, given (1), but … does not follow: the box assumed x > 1, which is not the negation of x < 1; ulename{
eg I} on it gives only 
eg(x > 1), that is, x \le 1 ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Verdict: wrong; line (5) fails, because the box of line (2) opened with the wrong statement; entry (N11). The negation of x < 1 is x \ge 1, and the case x = 1 is never examined: x = 1 has 
eg(x > 1) and not x < 1, a counterexample to the step. The claim is true. Repair: suppose, for a contradiction, that x \ge 1; then x^2 = x \cdot x \ge x \ge 1, which contradicts x^2 < 1; hence x < 1. [B2: Find the error] Find the error in the following proof, name its catalogue entry, and decide whether the claim is true. Claim. For all real numbers x and y, \abs{x} + \abs{y} = \abs{x + y}. (1) Let x and y be real numbers. (2) Either x and y are both \ge 0, or they are both < 0. (3) If both are \ge 0, then x + y \ge 0, so \abs{x} + \abs{y} = x + y = \abs{x + y}. (4) If both are < 0, then x + y < 0, so \abs{x} + \abs{y} = -x - y = -(x + y) = \abs{x + y}. (5) In either case \abs{x} + \abs{y} = \abs{x + y}. Line (2) fails. Its disjunction is not derived, and it is false when x and y have opposite signs, so line (5) combines cases that do not exhaust: entry (N8) of @exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Lines (3) and (4) are correct in their cases. The claim is false: for x = 1, y = -1, \abs{x} + \abs{y} = 2 and \abs{x + y} = 0; this pair satisfies neither case of line (2). What is true is \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y} (@exm-triangle-inequality-cases). [B3: Correct, or which entry?] Each proof below is correct, or commits one of (N12), (N13), (N14); you are not told how many of each. For a correct proof, name its most delicate step. For a wrong one, name the entry, say whether the claim is true, and give a counterexample to the claim or a repair of the proof. 1. Claim: for all integers m, n, if m and n are odd, then mn is odd. Proof: write m = 2k + 1 and n = 2l + 1 with integers k, l; then mn = 4kl + 2k + 2l + 1 = 2(2kl + k + l) + 1. 2. Claim: for all real a, b, if a^2 = b^2, then a = b or a = -b. Proof: (a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2 = 0, and a product of real numbers is 0 only if a factor is. 3. Claim: for all integers m, n, m^2 + n^2 \ge 1. Proof: two different integers are not both 0, so one of m^2, n^2 is at least 1. 4. Claim: every integer n \ge 2 is a product of primes. Proof: if n is prime, it is a product of one prime. If not, n = ab with 1 < a, b < n; split a and b in the same way, and so on, until only primes remain. 5. Claim: 1 is a solution of x^2 + x + 1 = 0. Proof: let x be the real solution. Then x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1) = 0, so x^3 = 1, and since x is real, x = 1. (i) Correct. The delicate step is the second ulename{\exists E}, which uses a second name l. The case m = n is covered, since nothing stops k = l: the names are distinct, the objects need not be. (ii) Correct. The delicate step is the product fact. It gives “a - b = 0 or a + b = 0” (ulename{{	o}E}, citing it), which is the claim, and no distinctness is assumed. (iii) (N12); the claim is false: m = n = 0 gives 0. The proof took m and n to be different integers. (iv) (N13); the claim is true. The “and so on” hides why the splitting ends: each factor is at least 2 and smaller than the number split. Repair by strong induction (@thm-strong-induction): if every k with 2 \le k < n is a product of primes, so is n, being prime or ab with a, b in that range. (v) (N14); the claim is false: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 
e 0. The presupposed premise “x^2 + x + 1 = 0 has a real solution” is false, since x^2 + x + 1 = (x + 	frac12)^2 + 	frac34 > 0. Look-alikes: (i) and (iii) both use two letters; only (iii) assumes the letters differ. Marking scheme. (10 points: 2 per part) - 1: the verdict. - 1: for a correct proof, the delicate step named; for a wrong one, the entry with a counterexample (iii, v) or a repair (iv). Fatal errors (0 for that part): calling (i) an instance of (N12) because k and l might be equal; calling (iv) correct. C. Going deeper [C1: The second half] Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R be continuous at a, as the quantifier pattern of Section 6.1: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon for every real x with \abs{x - a} < \delta. Suppose f(a) > 0. Here is a level-1 skeleton for the statement “there is \delta > 0 such that f(x) > 0 for every x with \abs{x - a} < \delta”: Its level-3 prose begins: Since f(a) > 0, the number f(a)/2 is positive. By the continuity of f at a, applied with \varepsilon = f(a)/2, choose \delta > 0 such that \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < f(a)/2 for every real x with \abs{x - a} < \delta. The rest is blank. Name the move, then complete it. Say which skeleton lines your sentences carry, and what \delta depends on. [Hint 1] What is left is the box of x_0 and the witness. [Hint 2] “Let x be a real number with \abs{x - a} < \delta. Then …” The move: skeleton first: the goal fixes the ulename{\exists I} of line 13 and the box of x_0. Filling it: ulename{ orall E} at the non-obvious instance \varepsilon = f(a)/2 (line 4), ulename{\exists E} on its \delta (line 5), and that \delta as the witness. Completion. Let x be a real number with \abs{x - a} < \delta. Then \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < f(a)/2, so, as -\abs{u} \le u, f(x) - f(a) > -f(a)/2, that is, f(x) > f(a)/2 > 0. So this \delta, which depends only on a, is as required. “Let x … with \abs{x - a} < \delta” opens the two boxes at line 7; “then \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < f(a)/2” is lines 8–9, the ulename{ orall E} at the obvious term x silent; “so … f(x) > f(a)/2 > 0” is line 10, which uses line 2. Lines 11 and 12 are silent closings, and the last sentence is lines 13–14, with the \delta already chosen as witness. It depends on a (through f(a) and the continuity at a) and on no x: the box of \delta_0 encloses the box of x_0. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: names the move (skeleton first; a hypothesis applied at a chosen \varepsilon, then its \delta reused as the witness), or the rules ulename{ orall E}, ulename{\exists E}, ulename{\exists I}. - 3: for an arbitrary x with \abs{x - a} < \delta, derives f(x) > f(a)/2, with the step from \abs{u} < r to u > -r justified. - 2: concludes f(x) > 0 using f(a) > 0, and states the conclusion with \delta before x. - 2: matches the sentences to the skeleton’s lines. - 1: says \delta depends on a and not on x. Second route: refuting f(x) \le 0 by \abs{f(x) - f(a)} \ge f(a) - f(x) \ge f(a) > f(a)/2 earns the second line and the f(x) > 0 part of the third. Fatal errors (0 for the step): choosing \delta after x; applying continuity at an \varepsilon not shown to be positive. [C2: A true conclusion] Here is a proof that \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 is irrational, a true conclusion. Find the line that fails and its catalogue entry, give a counterexample to the illegal step, and write a correct proof. (1) Suppose \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 = r for some rational number r. (2) Squaring, r^2 = 2 + 2\sqrt 6 + 3 = 5 + 2\sqrt 6. (3) Hence \sqrt 6 = (r^2 - 5)/2, which is rational, since r is. (4) But \sqrt 6 = \sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 3 is irrational, being a product of two irrational numbers. (5) This contradiction shows that \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 is irrational. [Hint 1] Run the second column on every line. [Hint 2] For a correct proof, isolate \sqrt 3 = r - \sqrt 2 before squaring. The failing line is (4). Its first half is true, \sqrt 6 = \sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 3, but its reason is not available. “A product of two irrational numbers is irrational” is neither proved nor a school fact: it is false, since \sqrt 2 is irrational (@thm-sqrt2-irrational), and \sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 = 2 is rational. So the line cites nothing: entry (N9) of @exm-not-allowed-catalogue. The product \sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 = 2 is a counterexample to the illegal step; there is none to the conclusion, which is true. Lines (1)–(3) and (5), and the ulename{
eg I} skeleton, are correct. A correct proof. Suppose \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 = r with r rational. Then r > 0, since both square roots are positive. Isolating, \sqrt 3 = r - \sqrt 2, and squaring, 3 = r^2 - 2r\sqrt 2 + 2, \qquad	ext{so}\qquad \sqrt 2 =  rac{r^2 - 1}{2r}, where dividing by 2r is legitimate because r > 0. The right-hand side is rational, which contradicts @thm-sqrt2-irrational. Hence \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 is irrational. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: names line (4) as the failing line, and the illegal step as the unproved general “fact”, entry (N9). - 2: a counterexample to that step (\sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 = 2, or another product of two irrationals that is rational). - 1: says the conclusion is true, so no counterexample to it exists. - 4: a correct proof: the ulename{
eg I} box on “r rational”, the algebra, the division justified by r 
e 0, and the clash with @thm-sqrt2-irrational (or with \sqrt 3 or \sqrt 6, its irrationality proved). Fatal errors (0 for the step): “correcting” line (4) by another unproved fact; dividing by r without r 
e 0. [C3: Exit check: four student proofs] Judge each proof. If it is wrong, give the line that fails, its entry in @exm-not-allowed-catalogue, and a counterexample to the illegal step. If it is correct, name the rule of its most delicate step and check that step. 1. Claim. For every integer n, if n is a multiple of 4 or a multiple of 6, then n is even. (1) Let n be an integer that is a multiple of 4 or of 6. (2) Case 1: n is a multiple of 4. Choose an integer k with n = 4k; then n = 2(2k), so n is even. (3) Case 2: n is a multiple of 6. Choose an integer k with n = 6k; then n = 2(3k), so n is even. (4) In either case, n is even. 2. Claim. For integers m and n, if m and n are even, then mn is divisible by 4. (1) Assume m and n are even. (2) Then m = 2k and n = 2k for an integer k. (3) So mn = 4k^2, which is divisible by 4. 3. Claim. For every real x, \abs{x - 1} \le \abs{x} + 1. (1) Either x \ge 1 or x \le 0. (2) If x \ge 1, then \abs{x - 1} = x - 1 \le x + 1 = \abs{x} + 1. (3) If x \le 0, then \abs{x - 1} = 1 - x = 1 + \abs{x}. (4) In either case, \abs{x - 1} \le \abs{x} + 1. 4. Claim. For every real x, if x^2 = 2x, then x = 2. (1) Assume x^2 = 2x. (2) Canceling x from both sides, x = 2. (3) Hence if x^2 = 2x, then x = 2. [Hint 1] Run the two-column check on every line, and keep the two questions apart: a true claim can have a wrong proof. [Hint 2] In (1), ask which boxes are open when the second k is chosen. In (3), ask what ulename{\vee E} needs from line (1). (1) Correct. The skeleton is ulename{ orall I} and ulename{{	o}I}, then ulename{\vee E} on the hypothesis itself, so the cases exhaust. The delicate step is the second “choose an integer k”, an ulename{\exists E} reusing a name. It is legal: the first box of k lies inside Case 1, which closed before Case 2 opened, so k appears in no open assumption, not in the existential and not in the conclusion. Sibling boxes may share a name (Section 5.6); (N4) forbids only a name still in use. (2) Wrong; line (2) fails; entry (N4) of @exm-not-allowed-catalogue. The second witness is named k while the box of m = 2k is open. Counterexample to the step: m = 2, n = 4; no integer k has 2 = 2k and 4 = 2k. The conclusion is true: with m = 2k and n = 2l, mn = 4kl. (3) Wrong; line (1) fails; entry (N8). “Either x \ge 1 or x \le 0” is not derived, and is false at x = 1/2, a counterexample to the step. The conclusion is true; the missing case repairs the proof: if 0 < x < 1, then \abs{x - 1} = 1 - x < 1 < \abs{x} + 1. (4) Wrong; line (2) fails; entry (N9); the claim is false. Canceling uses the “fact” “if ax = bx, then a = b”, which is neither proved nor a school fact, and is false: a = 1, b = 2, x = 0. It needs x 
e 0, which no line provides. The claim fails at x = 0; what is true is “x = 0 or x = 2”, from x(x - 2) = 0. Marking scheme. (10 points: 2.5 per proof) - For each of (2), (3), (4): the verdict “wrong” (1); the failing line and its entry, (N4), (N8), (N9) (1); a counterexample to the illegal step (0.5). - For (1): the verdict “correct” (1); the delicate step named as an ulename{\exists E} reusing a name in a sibling box (or as the ulename{\vee E} on the hypothesis) (1); that step checked against the side condition (0.5). For (4), “ulename{{	o}E} without its antecedent x 
e 0” is also accepted. Fatal errors (0 for that proof): calling proof (1) wrong as an instance of (N4) because the name k recurs; judging (2) or (3) correct because its conclusion is true. R. Review [R1: A dialogue] Two students discuss a claim. Ana: For every integer n, n^2 + n is even. Ben: Why? Ana: Take n = 3: 9 + 3 = 12. Take n = 4: 16 + 4 = 20. It always works. Ben: That is two numbers. Ana: All right. n^2 + n = n(n + 1). If n is even, the product has an even factor. If n is odd, n + 1 is even, so again it has an even factor. Either way n^2 + n is even. Ben: You only did positive numbers. Ana: I never used that n is positive. 1. Which entry of @exm-not-allowed-catalogue does Ana’s first argument commit? 2. Write her second argument as a level-3 proof, and name the rule each sentence carries. 3. Is Ben’s last objection right? 4. On which fact does the case split rest, and where was it stated? (a) (N1) of @exm-not-allowed-catalogue: two instances, then “always”. (b) “Let n be an integer [ulename{ orall I}]. Then n^2 + n = n(n + 1) [algebra]. By (E1), n is even or odd [ulename{\vee E}, with the reason the cases exhaust]. If n is even, say n = 2k [ulename{\exists E}], then n(n + 1) = 2 igl(k(n + 1) igr) is even [ulename{\exists I}, witness k(n + 1)]. If n is odd, say n = 2k + 1, then n + 1 = 2(k + 1), and n(n + 1) = 2 igl(n(k + 1) igr) is even [ulename{\exists E}, ulename{\exists I}]. In either case n^2 + n is even [ulename{\vee E}, closing; silent at level 3].” (c) No. The box of n assumed only that n is an integer, and no line used more, so ulename{ orall I} (@def-rules-universal, Section 5.4) gives the claim for every integer: n is in no premise, and the conclusion is about the bound variable. A proof that used n > 0 would have had to assume it in the box. (d) (E1), “every integer is even or odd”, stated in Section 2.1 as a school fact, before @thm-square-even-implies-even.

title: 8.7 The Dispute over Excluded Middle
content:
The Dispute over Excluded Middle Here is a proof that two numbers with a certain property exist which, when it is finished, still does not tell you what the numbers are. It is correct by the rules of this book. Some mathematicians, called intuitionists, reject it, for a century now and for reasons that are mathematical rather than merely fussy. This section shows the proof, says what those mathematicians ask of a proof, finds the one rule that fails to provide it, and asks what can be proved without that rule and what analysis would lose. Irrational powers, with and without a witness Here is the standard example of a proof that establishes existence without saying what exists. [An Irrational Power of an Irrational Number Can Be Rational] There are irrational numbers a and b such that a^b is rational. Try it first (ten minutes): find such a and b explicitly, and prove that your a and b are irrational and that a^b is rational. The first candidates anyone tries are a = b = \sqrt 2. Then the question is whether \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2} is rational, and the attempt stalls there: nothing in this book decides it. There are two ways out. The classical one splits on the undecided question with ulename{LEM}. If \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2} is rational, the first candidates work. If not, use it as the new a and raise it to \sqrt 2 once more, which turns the exponent into \sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 = 2. The proof below takes this way. The other way chooses an exponent that undoes the square root, and the proposition after the proof takes it. Let s \coloneqq \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2}, a positive real number. By excluded middle, s is rational or s is not rational [ulename{LEM}], and we argue by cases [ulename{\vee E}]. Case 1: s is rational. Take a \coloneqq \sqrt 2 and b \coloneqq \sqrt 2. Both are irrational by @thm-sqrt2-irrational, and a^b = s is rational [ulename{\exists I}]. Case 2: s is not rational. Take a \coloneqq s and b \coloneqq \sqrt 2. Then a is irrational by the case assumption and b by @thm-sqrt2-irrational, and a^b =  igl( \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2}  igr)^{\sqrt 2} = \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2} = \sqrt 2^{\,2} = 2, which is rational [ulename{\exists I}]. In either case there are irrational a and b with a^b rational. This proves the theorem. The classical step is the first line, ulename{LEM} on the statement “s is rational”. Every other step uses only rules other than ulename{RAA}. The proof does not tell us which pair works. It hands over two candidate pairs, (\sqrt 2, \sqrt 2) and (\sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2}, \sqrt 2), and a guarantee that one of them succeeds. The next subsection says why some mathematicians do not accept such a proof. Section 2.5 described excluded middle as making a decision; here the decision about “s is rational” is made, and nobody learns its outcome. In fact the second case holds: \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2} is transcendental, so in particular irrational, by the Gelfond–Schneider theorem, proved independently by Gelfond and by Schneider in 1934. That theorem lies far beyond this book, and nothing here uses it. It also does not repair the proof above, which never needed to know the answer. The other way out finds the witness. Since \sqrt 2^{\,b} = 2^{b/2}, the exponent b = 2\log_2 m = \log_2(m^2) gives \sqrt 2^{\,b} = m for every integer m \ge 2. The choice m = 2 gives b = 2, which is rational, so m must avoid the powers of 2; the first choice left is m = 3. [A Witness for an Irrational Power] The number \log_2 9 is irrational. Consequently a \coloneqq \sqrt 2 and b \coloneqq \log_2 9 are irrational numbers with a^b = 3. The irrationality goes as for \sqrt 2: suppose \log_2 9 is a fraction p/q, clear the denominator, and look at parity. Here the clash is quicker than for \sqrt 2: a power of 2 would equal a power of 9, and one is even while the other is odd. The positivity of \log_2 9 is what makes the power of 2 even. Suppose that \log_2 9 = p/q for integers p and q with q 
e 0; replacing p, q by -p, -q if necessary, we may take q \ge 1. Since 2^0 = 1 < 9 and t \mapsto 2^t is increasing, \log_2 9 > 0, so p > 0, that is, p \ge 1. From 2^{p/q} = 9, raising both sides to the power q gives 2^p = 9^q . The left side is even, since 2^p = 2 \cdot 2^{p-1} with p - 1 \ge 0. The right side is odd, being a product of q odd factors. No integer is both even and odd, by (E2) of Section 2.1, so this is a contradiction. Hence \log_2 9 is not rational [ulename{
eg I}]. For the consequence, a = \sqrt 2 is irrational by @thm-sqrt2-irrational, and b = \log_2 9 is irrational by what was just shown. Since \log_2 9 = \log_2 (3^2) = 2\log_2 3, a^b =  igl( 2^{1/2}  igr)^{\log_2 9} = 2^{(\log_2 9)/2} = 2^{\log_2 3} = 3 . This proves the proposition. This proof uses no classical rule. The irrationality of \log_2 9 is a negative statement, “no fraction equals \log_2 9”, and its box closes by ulename{
eg I}, like the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational. The witness (\sqrt 2, \log_2 9) is written down. So @prp-log2-9-irrational gives a second proof of @thm-irrational-power-rational, and this one names its witness. (The exponent laws for real exponents are school facts here.) Does the proof of @prp-log2-9-irrational use a classical rule? Does it name its witness? No classical rule: its box assumes \log_2 9 = p/q and concludes the negation, by ulename{
eg I}. And yes, the witness (\sqrt 2, \log_2 9) is written down. What a proof provides Chapter 4 gave the connectives a meaning through truth values: every letter is true or false, and a table computes the rest. That semantics already takes a side, since a row decides every letter. The intuitionist explains a statement instead by saying what counts as a proof of it. The resulting clauses are called the BHK reading, after Brouwer, Heyting, and Kolmogorov. To know a statement is to have a proof of it, and a proof of a compound statement is built from proofs of its parts. - There is no proof of  ot. - A proof of P \wedge Q is a pair: a proof of P and a proof of Q. - A proof of P \vee Q is a proof of P or a proof of Q, with a label saying which. - A proof of P 	o Q is a method that takes any proof of P and returns a proof of Q. - A proof of 
eg P is a method that takes any proof of P and returns a proof of  ot. So 
eg P is read as P 	o  ot, exactly the reading that the table in Section 2.2, after @def-rules-negation, found row by row. - A proof of \exists x\, \varphi is an object t together with a proof of \varphi[t/x]. - A proof of  orall x\, \varphi is a method that produces, for every object t, a proof of \varphi[t/x]. In words: a disjunction must say which side, an existence claim must name the object, and an implication or a universal statement must come with a method that works on every input. A proof of a negation provides no object at all; it is a guarantee that no proof of the negated statement will ever arrive. Each rule other than ulename{RAA} builds exactly what its clause asks for. ulename{\vee I} writes P \vee Q from a line P, so it knows which side it used. ulename{\exists I} writes \exists x\, \varphi from an instance \varphi[t/x], so the witness t is on the page. A ulename{{	o}I} box is a method: given the assumption, it produces the conclusion. ulename{RAA} is the exception. Its box shows that 
eg\varphi leads to  ot, which is a proof of 
eg
eg\varphi, and then it writes \varphi. Under the BHK reading a method for refuting every refutation of \varphi is not a proof of \varphi. Excluded middle under BHK. A proof of P \vee 
eg P for every statement P would be a single method that decides each statement, says which side holds, and proves that side. Nobody has such a method. Take Goldbach’s conjecture, that every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two primes: nobody has proved it and nobody has refuted it, so nobody can produce a labeled proof of “Goldbach’s conjecture or its negation”. The proof of @thm-irrational-power-rational is of this kind: it splits on “s is rational or not” by ulename{LEM}, and so never says which pair works. Not every, and some not. Chapter 6 derived 
eg orall x\, \varphi \vdash \exists x\, 
eg\varphi (@prp-quantifier-negation (a)) with two ulename{RAA} boxes, and noted that the derivation never says which x fails \varphi. The BHK reading says why that matters. A proof of the premise is a method that refutes every proof of  orall x\, \varphi; a proof of the conclusion must name an object. Nothing in the first produces the second, and the derivation does not try: its conclusion comes from ulename{RAA}, not from an ulename{\exists I} applied to an available instance. Classical mathematics accepts the step. A constructive mathematician accepts that conclusion only with an object in hand. Describe a BHK proof of 
eg(P \wedge 
eg P). Does it decide whether P holds? We need a method that takes any proof of P \wedge 
eg P and returns a proof of  ot. A proof of P \wedge 
eg P is a pair: a proof p of P and a method f turning proofs of P into proofs of  ot. Apply f to p. That is the whole method, and it never decides P: it only uses a pair that someone else supplies. (It is the BHK reading of a ulename{
eg I} box on P \wedge 
eg P whose clash is ulename{
eg E} on its two halves.) One extra rule Chapter 2 found that one rule stands apart. ulename{RAA} belongs to no connective, and over the other primitive rules it derives ulename{
eg
eg E} and ulename{LEM} and is derived by each of them (@thm-classical-rules-interderivable). Chapter 4’s optional @thm-raa-independent showed that the other propositional rules cannot derive it. Recall what Section 2.5 established. Over the primitive rules other than ulename{RAA}, the three rules ulename{RAA}, ulename{
eg
eg E}, and ulename{LEM} each derive the other two, so adding any one of them gives the same derivable sequents. There is one classical principle, and it has three faces. Nothing needs re-proving here; what is new is the decision to leave the principle out and see what remains. Call a derivation intuitionistic if no line is justified by ulename{RAA} and no line uses a derived rule or a cited result whose own derivation uses ulename{RAA}. Intuitionistic logic is the system of these derivations. Its rules are the introduction and elimination rules for \wedge, 	o, and \vee (Chapter 1); ulename{
eg I}, ulename{
eg E}, ulename{ ot E}, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}, and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} (Chapter 2); the rules for  orall, \exists, and = (Chapter 5); and repetition. Classical logic, the logic of Chapters 1–7, is the same list with ulename{RAA} added. TAUT (Section 4.8) is not among these rules: it is licensed by @cor-derivable-iff-valid, that is, by the completeness theorem, whose proof splits on atoms by ulename{LEM} (@lem-atom-splitting), so a line justified by TAUT, on a formula or on a propositional skeleton (Section 6.3), uses ulename{RAA} in the sense just defined. This is why Chapter 2 kept ulename{ ot E} as a primitive rule although ulename{RAA} and repetition derive it (the remark in the second-reading fold after @thm-classical-rules-interderivable). She may when Q is itself a negation, by Section 2.5’s fold “RAA is never needed to finish a negation”, which Section 8.1 applies to the contrapositive. A short history The dispute has dates. In 1908 L. E. J. Brouwer published “De onbetrouwbaarheid der logische principes” (“The unreliability of the logical principles”) in the Tijdschrift voor Wijsbegeerte. His point was that excluded middle had been abstracted from reasoning about finite collections, where every case can in principle be checked, and then applied without justification to infinite ones, where it cannot. Over the next two decades he rebuilt parts of analysis on this view, and the movement took the name intuitionism. In 1925 A. N. Kolmogorov showed that classical reasoning can be imitated inside a logic without excluded middle by putting a double negation in front of every subformula: the first double-negation translation (Exercise C2 below checks one step of it). In July 1927 David Hilbert lectured in Hamburg on “Die Grundlagen der Mathematik”, printed in 1928. He defended excluded middle in a much-repeated comparison: to take it from the mathematician would be like forbidding the astronomer the telescope or the boxer the use of his fists. The quarrel between his program and Brouwer’s became known as the Grundlagenstreit, the dispute over foundations. It turned personal in 1928, when Hilbert had Brouwer removed from the editorial board of the Mathematische Annalen; the board was then dissolved and re-formed without him. In 1929 V. Glivenko proved the theorem of the remark above: classical propositional logic sits inside intuitionistic logic behind a double negation. In 1930 Arend Heyting published “Die formalen Regeln der intuitionistischen Logik” in the Sitzungsberichte der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften. It wrote down rules for intuitionistic logic, in a format different from ours, and from then on the logic could be studied as a formal system like any other. In 1933 Kurt Gödel published a double-negation translation of arithmetic, which shows that classical arithmetic is consistent if intuitionistic arithmetic is. Gerhard Gentzen had found an equivalent translation independently and withdrew his paper of 1933 when Gödel’s appeared. In 1967 Errett Bishop published Foundations of Constructive Analysis. It developed a large part of analysis without excluded middle, and also without Brouwer’s philosophy and his special axioms about the real numbers. Most of what is now called constructive analysis descends from it. Excluded middle is not the only rule that has been questioned. Chapter 1 read P 	o Q as a promise that is broken only when P holds and Q fails, so a true Q makes P 	o Q true whatever P says, and \vdash P 	o (Q 	o P). Some logicians find that too generous: an “if” should connect its two parts. Logics built on that view, called relevance logics, reject P 	o (Q 	o P). This book keeps Chapter 1’s reading, which is the one mathematics uses. What analysis would lose What does analysis look like without the rule? Here are four previews, stated informally and without proof. Classical analysis takes the first as an axiom and proves the other three; each is a place where classical reasoning, by the rule or by an axiom, does work that a constructive proof cannot. - The supremum. Classical analysis takes as an axiom that every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a supremum. Constructively, a non-empty set A bounded above has a supremum if and only if it is order-located: for all real numbers x < y, either y is an upper bound of A or some element of A exceeds x (Bishop’s form of the least upper bound principle). The classical axiom asserts the supremum without requiring anyone to make these decisions. - Monotone sequences. E. Specker (1949) gave an increasing, bounded sequence of rational numbers that a computer program can list term by term, but whose limit is not a computable real number: no program can print its decimal digits. So the convergence of bounded monotone sequences, which classical analysis proves from that axiom, cannot come with a method for computing the limit. - The intermediate value theorem. Let f be continuous on [a, b] with f(a) < 0 < f(b). Classically, one proves that f(x) = 0 for some x \in [a, b]. Constructively, what holds in general is the approximate version: for every \varepsilon > 0 some x \in [a, b] has \abs{f(x)} < \varepsilon. The exact version holds under extra hypotheses, for example when f is strictly increasing. A bisection needs the sign of f at a midpoint m, and finitely many digits of f(m) cannot always tell whether f(m) is negative, zero, or positive: the digits of a value equal to 0 begin like those of a tiny positive or negative one. - Bolzano–Weierstrass. A bisection proof of the theorem says: one of the two halves of an interval contains infinitely many terms of the sequence; continue with that half. That step is ulename{LEM} on “the left half contains infinitely many terms”, a statement that nobody can decide in general, and the proof does not say which half. Proofs as programs The BHK clauses read like the description of a programming language. A proof of P \wedge Q is a pair; a proof of P \vee Q is a value tagged “left” or “right”; a proof of P 	o Q is a function; a proof of \exists x\, \varphi is a pair of an object and a proof; a proof of  orall x\, \varphi is a function that accepts any object. This match between propositions and types, and between proofs and programs, is the Curry–Howard correspondence. It is what a proof assistant such as Lean is built on: checking a proof is checking that a program has the right type. Intuitionistic logic fits this picture exactly. ulename{LEM} does not, since no program decides every proposition. Lean adds classical logic by an axiom, Classical.choice, a form of the axiom of choice. Excluded middle, Classical.em, is then a theorem, derived from choice together with two extensionality principles by Diaconescu’s theorem. Lean draws one line with care. A definition that uses classical logic to produce data, for instance a number chosen by deciding an arbitrary proposition, must be marked noncomputable, since no program computes it. A proof that uses Classical.em needs no mark, because proofs carry no data. -- excluded middle is a theorem, proved from the axiom of choice example (p : Prop) : Or p (Not p) := Classical.em p -- a number defined by deciding an arbitrary proposition open Classical in noncomputable def indicator (p : Prop) : Nat := if p then 1 else 0 “Constructive” does not mean “computable in practice”. A constructive proof provides a method, and the method may be hopeless. Deciding whether a whole number is prime by trying every smaller divisor is constructive, and for a number with a thousand digits no computer could finish it. Constructive mathematics asks whether a method exists, not whether it is fast. The book’s position The main line of this book stays classical. The decision is made once, in the axioms for the real numbers, which include trichotomy: for real numbers a and b, exactly one of a < b, a = b, b < a holds. Constructive analysis does not accept trichotomy for real numbers, because it would decide the sign of every real number. So a case split such as “x \ge 0 or x < 0” rests on an axiom, and the book does not flag it. What the book does flag is a genuinely non-constructive step of the kind discussed above, such as the bisection step of Bolzano–Weierstrass, and every use of the axiom of choice. One clause says so, and nothing more. Such a step is never silent anyway: by @def-silent-steps, a ulename{

title: 8.8 Stages of Knowledge: Kripke Models
content:
Stages of Knowledge: Kripke Models This section is optional, and nothing outside it depends on it. Section 8.7 named several classical laws that have no derivation without ulename{RAA}. For two of them, excluded middle and double-negation elimination, Chapter 4’s optional @thm-raa-independent gave a proof by a three-valued reading; for the rest, Section 8.7 states the fact and points here. Truth tables cannot show it: every row makes p \vee 
eg p true. Here is a reading that covers them all. A statement is not true or false once and for all, but known or not yet known at a stage of an inquiry that grows. The rules without ulename{RAA} are sound for this reading, and ulename{RAA} is not; two or three stages then suffice to show which laws need it. Stages of knowledge An inquiry passes through stages. At each stage some atomic statements are known: established, never to be withdrawn. From a stage, the inquiry may go on in several ways, to later stages where more is known. Nobody knows which way it will go. The atomic statements are the letters of Chapter 4’s formulas (@def-formula), its atoms, and the formulas of this section are those formulas: letters,  ot, and the connectives 
eg, \wedge, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow. [Kripke Model] A Kripke model consists of: - a finite non-empty set of stages; - for each stage w, a set of stages reachable from w (written w \le w'), such that w \le w for every stage, and w \le w' and w' \le w'' give w \le w''; - for each stage w, a set of letters known at w, such that a letter known at w is known at every stage reachable from w. We draw a model as dots for the stages, with an arrow from a stage to each stage that comes directly after it. A stage is reachable from w when it can be reached by following arrows, none or several; so w reaches itself, and arrows are never drawn for that. Beside each dot stands the set of letters known there. The model M_1: at w_0 nothing is known yet; at the later stage w_1, p is known. Forcing What a stage knows about a compound formula is computed from its parts, as a row computes a truth value, except that some connectives look ahead to later stages. Forcing Let w be a stage of a Kripke model. w forces a formula \varphi, written w \Vdash \varphi, as follows; w 
Vdash \varphi says that it does not. The definition is a recursion on \varphi (@thm-structural-recursion) that defines, for each formula, the set of stages that force it; clauses (K5) and (K6) need the sets of its parts, at other stages. 1. w \Vdash p, for a letter p, if p is known at w; 2. w \Vdash  ot never; 3. w \Vdash \varphi \wedge \psi if w \Vdash \varphi and w \Vdash \psi; 4. w \Vdash \varphi \vee \psi if w \Vdash \varphi or w \Vdash \psi; 5. w \Vdash \varphi 	o \psi if every stage w' reachable from w with w' \Vdash \varphi has w' \Vdash \psi; 6. w \Vdash 
eg\varphi if no stage reachable from w forces \varphi; 7. w \Vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi if w \Vdash \varphi 	o \psi and w \Vdash \psi 	o \varphi. A stage refutes a sequent \Gamma \vdash \psi if it forces every formula of \Gamma and does not force \psi. In words: a conjunction or a disjunction is decided at the stage itself, and a disjunction is forced only when one of its sides is: the inquiry must already know which. An implication and a negation look ahead. To force \varphi 	o \psi is to know that, however the inquiry goes on, \psi will be known whenever \varphi is. To force 
eg\varphi is to know that \varphi will never be known. Not forcing \varphi is weaker than forcing 
eg\varphi. A model with one stage is a row of a truth table. With one stage, the stages reachable from w are w alone, so (K5) says “\varphi is not forced, or \psi is”, and (K6) says “\varphi is not forced”: forcing becomes Chapter 4’s truth (@def-truth-value). Kripke models are rows that can grow. A stage that refutes \Gamma \vdash \psi forces every member of \Gamma and not \psi, which is weaker than forcing 
eg\psi. It is Section 1.1’s counterexample set, read at a stage: where truth tables make 
eg\psi true, a stage only fails to know \psi. In a one-stage model in which p is not known, does the stage force 
eg p? Does it force p \vee 
eg p? Yes to both. The only stage reachable is the stage itself, which does not force p, so (K6) gives 
eg p, and (K4) gives p \vee 
eg p. One stage is one row. A first countermodel [Two stages refute excluded middle] In M_1, decide whether w_0 forces p, 
eg p, p \vee 
eg p,

eg
eg p 	o p. - p is not known at w_0, so w_0 
Vdash p (K1). - w_1 is reachable from w_0 and forces p, so w_0 
Vdash 
eg p (K6). - Hence w_0 
Vdash p \vee 
eg p (K4): w_0 refutes \vdash p \vee 
eg p. - Next, 
eg
eg p. No stage reachable from w_0 forces 
eg p: not w_0, as just shown, and not w_1, which forces p. So w_0 \Vdash

Vdash

eg p 	o p. At w_0 the inquiry knows that p cannot be refuted, since p becomes known later on every way it can go, but it does not yet know p. Excluded middle asks it to know now which of p and 
eg p holds. Knowledge persists Letters stay known by the definition of a Kripke model. The same holds for every formula. [Heredity] In every Kripke model, if w \Vdash \varphi and w \le w', then w' \Vdash \varphi. In words: what a stage forces, every later stage forces. The proof is a structural induction on \varphi (@thm-structural-induction); it is in the fold. We prove, by @thm-structural-induction, that every formula \varphi has the property: for all stages w \le w' of every Kripke model, w \Vdash \varphi gives w' \Vdash \varphi. Letters. A letter forced at w is known at w (K1), hence known at w' by the condition on known letters in @def-kripke-model, hence forced at w'.  ot. No stage forces it (K2), so there is nothing to show. \wedge and \vee. If w \Vdash \varphi \wedge \psi, then w forces both parts (K3), so w' forces both by the induction hypothesis, and w' \Vdash \varphi \wedge \psi. For \vee, w forces one part (K4), and w' forces the same part by the induction hypothesis. 	o. Let w \Vdash \varphi 	o \psi, and let w'' be reachable from w' with w'' \Vdash \varphi. Since w \le w' and w' \le w'', transitivity gives w \le w'', so w'' \Vdash \psi by (K5) at w. Hence w' \Vdash \varphi 	o \psi by (K5). No induction hypothesis is used. 
eg. The same: every stage reachable from w' is reachable from w, and none of those forces \varphi (K6), so w' \Vdash 
eg\varphi. \leftrightarrow. By (K7), w forces the two implications, so w' forces both by the case 	o, and w' \Vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi. Every clause of @def-formula is covered, so every formula has the property. This proves the lemma. A stage w forces 
eg\varphi, and w' is reachable from w. Why does w' force 
eg\varphi, whatever \varphi is? w \Vdash 
eg\varphi says that no stage reachable from w forces \varphi. The stages reachable from w' are among those, by transitivity, so none of them forces \varphi either. Nothing is assumed about \varphi itself. The rules without RAA are sound for stages [Soundness without RAA] Let \Gamma be a list of formulas and \psi a formula. If \Gamma \vdash \psi by a derivation every line of which is a formula of @def-formula, in which no line uses ulename{RAA} or TAUT, nor a derived rule or cited result whose derivation uses one of them or a line outside @def-formula, then every stage of every Kripke model that forces every formula of \Gamma forces \psi. In words: a derivation without ulename{RAA} never leads from what a stage knows to what it does not know. title: Definition 1.1.3 (Counterexample Set)
page: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content: The counterexample set of an argument form is the list of its premises together with the negation of its conclusion. A counterexample to the form is an argument of that form whose premises are all true and whose conclusion is false, that is, a choice of statements for the letters that makes every member of the counterexample set true. A form is bad if it has a counterexample, and good if no choice of statements can break it.

title: Definition 1.1.2 (Main Connective)
page: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content: The main connective of a compound statement is the connective applied last when the statement is built up from its parts. An atomic statement has no main connective.

title: Definition 1.1.1 (Statement)
page: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content: A statement is a declarative sentence that is either true or false , and not both.

title: Example (Statements and nonstatements)
page: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content: Decide which of the following are statements. \(7\) is a prime number. \(0.999 > 1\) . There are infinitely many primes \(p\) for which \(p + 2\) is also prime. Is \(2^{11} - 1\) prime? \(x > 2\) . \(3 > 2\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content: State the definition of a statement. Is “ \(10^{100} + 1\) is prime” a statement? For a real number \(x\) , is “ \(x^2 - 1 = 0\) ” a statement? Is “ \(0^2 - 1 = 0\) ”? Let \(n\) be an integer, with \(P\) : “ \(n\) is even” and \(Q\) : “ \(n\) is prime”. Write “ \(n\) is prime but not even” in symbols. Find the main connective of \(P \wedge Q \to \neg R\) , and write the statement with all its parentheses. True or false, with a reason: if \(P\) and \(Q\) are both true, then \(P \vee Q\) is false. Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Write the form of “ \(x > 0\) and \(y > 0\) ; so \(y > 0\) and \(x > 0\) ” with premises above a line, saying what each letter stands for. Which of \(\wedge\) , \(\vee\) , \(\to\) is the main connective of \((P \vee Q) \wedge (Q \to R)\) ? Using the preview table of “Each connective, two rules”, say what a proof of this statement must do, and name the rule that Section 1.2 will state for it.

title: Exercise (B3: Necessary and sufficient, used later)
page: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content: Let \(x\) be a real number. Write “ \(x > 1\) is sufficient for \(x^2 > 1\) ” and “ \(x > 1\) is necessary for \(x^2 > 1\) ” as implications. Decide which of the two is true for every real \(x\) , and give a value of \(x\) that makes the other false. Find a condition on \(x\) , written with \(\vee\) , that is both necessary and sufficient for \(x^2 > 1\) . You may use that \(x^2 > 1\) exactly when \(\abs{x} > 1\) , where \(\abs{x}\) is \(x\) if \(x \ge 0\) and \(-x\) if \(x < 0\) .

title: Exercise (B4: Break it or explain why not)
page: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content: For each form, either find statements about a real number \(x\) that make every premise true and the conclusion false, or explain, by checking every case, why no choice of statements can (use the meaning of each connective; for \(\to\) , the table of “When is an implication broken?”). From \(P \to Q\) and \(\neg P\) , conclude \(\neg Q\) . From \(P \to Q\) and \(Q \to R\) , conclude \(P \to R\) . From \(P \vee Q\) , conclude \(P\) . From \(P \wedge Q\) , conclude \(P \vee Q\) .

title: Exercise (B5: One key, sixteen sentences, used later)
page: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content: Let \(n\) be an integer. Use only the letters \(E\) : “ \(n\) is even”, \(P\) : “ \(n\) is prime”, \(T\) : “ \(n\) is a multiple of \(3\) ” and \(G\) : “ \(n > 10\) ”. Translate sentences 1–14 into symbols. Then translate 15 and 16 into English, and find an \(n\) that makes 16 false. \(n\) is even and greater than \(10\) . \(n\) is odd. \(n\) is an even prime. If \(n\) is prime and greater than \(10\) , then \(n\) is odd. \(n\) is a multiple of \(3\) but not prime. \(n\) is neither even nor a multiple of \(3\) . \(n\) is not both even and a multiple of \(3\) . \(n\) is prime only if \(n\) is odd or at most \(10\) . \(n\) is even whenever it is a multiple of \(3\) greater than \(10\) . Provided \(n > 10\) , being even is sufficient for \(n\) not to be prime. \(n > 10\) is necessary for \(n\) to be an even multiple of \(3\) . Exactly one of “ \(n\) is even”, “ \(n\) is prime” holds. At least two of “ \(n\) is even”, “ \(n\) is prime”, “ \(n\) is a multiple of \(3\) ” hold. \(n\) is odd, but if it is greater than \(10\) , it is not a multiple of \(3\) . \(\neg G \to (E \vee T)\) . \((P \wedge \neg E) \to G\) .

title: Exercise (B6: Same form?)
page: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content: Here is an argument. If \(12\) is divisible by \(6\) , then \(12\) is even. If \(12\) is divisible by \(6\) , then \(12\) is divisible by \(3\) . So, if \(12\) is even, then \(12\) is divisible by \(3\) . Which of (a)–(d) have the same form as (T)? For one that does, break the form. Is the conclusion of (T) true, and does (T) prove it? Let \(x\) be a real number. If \(x > 2\) , then \(x^2 > 4\) . If \(x > 2\) , then \(x > 1\) . So, if \(x^2 > 4\) , then \(x > 1\) . Let \(\Delta\) be a triangle. If \(\Delta\) is equilateral, then \(\Delta\) is isosceles. If \(\Delta\) is equilateral, then each angle of \(\Delta\) is \(60^\circ\) . So, if \(\Delta\) is isosceles, then each angle of \(\Delta\) is \(60^\circ\) . Let \(n\) be an integer. If \(n\) is divisible by \(6\) , then \(n\) is even. If \(n\) is even, then \(n^2\) is even. So, if \(n\) is divisible by \(6\) , then \(n^2\) is even. Let \(x\) be a real number. If \(x > 3\) , then \(x > 2\) . If \(x > 3\) , then \(x > 1\) . So, if \(x > 3\) , then \(x > 2\) and \(x > 1\) .

title: Exercise (C1: “Only if” and “unless”, used later)
page: 1.1 Statements, Arguments and How to Break One
content: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be statements. Explain why “ \(P\) only if \(Q\) ” means \(P \to Q\) , and not \(Q \to P\) . (Ask: which situation would make “ \(P\) only if \(Q\) ” false?) Explain why “ \(P\) unless \(Q\) ” means \(\neg Q \to P\) . Let \(x\) be a real number. Decide whether each sentence is true for every real \(x\) . Justify your answer, giving a value of \(x\) that makes it false where there is one. “ \(x^2 = 4\) if \(x = 2\) .” “ \(x^2 = 4\) only if \(x = 2\) .” “ \(x^2 > 0\) unless \(x = 0\) .”

title: Definition 1.2.2 (Box-Free Derivation)
content: Fix a list of rules, each given by schemas. A box-free derivation is a finite list of numbered lines \(1, 2, \dots, n\) , where \(n \ge 1\) , each carrying one statement and a justification, such that: the first lines, possibly none and possibly all, are premises , justified by nothing; a short horizontal rule is drawn under the last premise; every later line is justified by one rule of the list, citing earlier lines, and it and the cited lines form an instance of a schema of that rule. The premises of the derivation are its premise lines, and its conclusion is its last line.

title: Definition 1.2.3 (Derivable)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of statements \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) , where \(n \ge 0\) , and let \(\psi\) be a statement. We say \(\psi\) is derivable from \(\Gamma\) , and write \[ \Gamma \vdash \psi , \] if there is a derivation, using the rules of logic, whose premises all belong to \(\Gamma\) and whose last line is \(\psi\) . We write \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \vdash \psi\) for \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) , and \(\vdash \psi\) when \(\Gamma\) is empty.

title: Definition 1.2.1 (Rule Schema)
content: A rule schema is a pattern of lines: given lines at the top, possibly none, and exactly one new line at the bottom, whose justification names the rule and cites the given lines. Line numbers in a schema are written \(i, j, k\) . The letters in the pattern stand for arbitrary expressions of the right kind, and a use of the rule replaces them consistently : the same letter by the same expression, symbol for symbol , everywhere it occurs. A line is justified by the rule when it and the lines it cites, with their numbers, are an instance of a schema of the rule: the pattern with every letter replaced in this way. The schema of \(\mathrm{Tr}\) is Here \(a\) , \(b\) , \(c\) stand for expressions for numbers.

title: Definition 1.2.5 (Rules for Conjunction)
content: The first schema is the rule \(\rulename{\wedge I}\) ( and-introduction ). Its two given lines may be cited in either order: the new line shows which statement is its left conjunct, so question 2 of “Reading a derivation” tries both orders. The second and third are the two forms of the rule \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) ( and-elimination ), one writing the left conjunct and one the right.

title: Definition 1.2.4 (Sequent)
content: Let \(P_1, \dots, P_n\) and \(Q\) be statements, where \(n \ge 0\) . The expression \(P_1, \dots, P_n \vdash Q\) , read “ \(P_1\) to \(P_n\) prove \(Q\) ”, is a sequent . It is the claim that \(Q\) is derivable from \(P_1, \dots, P_n\) in the sense of @def-derivable . The statements \(P_1, \dots, P_n\) are its premises and \(Q\) is its conclusion ; when \(n = 0\) we write \(\vdash Q\) .

title: Example (Chaining)
content: Let \(x\) , \(y\) , \(u\) , \(v\) , \(w\) , \(z\) be real numbers. Using the rule \(\mathrm{Tr}\) only, write a box-free derivation of each conclusion from the given premises. Premises \(0 < x\) , \(x < y\) , \(y < 1\) ; conclusion \(0 < 1\) . Premises \(u < v\) , \(w < z\) , \(v < w\) ; conclusion \(u < z\) .

title: Proposition 1.2.2 (Conjunction Is Associative)
content: \((P \wedge Q) \wedge R \vdash P \wedge (Q \wedge R)\) .

title: Proposition 1.2.1 (Conjunction Commutes)
content: \(P \wedge Q \vdash Q \wedge P\) .

title: Definition 1.3.1 (Implication Elimination)
content: This rule is called \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) ( implication-elimination , or modus ponens ).

title: Example (Two chains about numbers)
content: Let \(n\) be an integer. From the five premises \[ \begin{aligned} &6 \mid n, \qquad (6 \mid n) \to \bigl( (2 \mid n) \wedge (3 \mid n) \bigr), \qquad (2 \mid n) \to (4 \mid n^2), \\ &(3 \mid n) \to (9 \mid n^2), \qquad \bigl( (4 \mid n^2) \wedge (9 \mid n^2) \bigr) \to (36 \mid n^2), \end{aligned} \] derive \(36 \mid n^2\) . Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. From the six premises \[ \begin{aligned} &x > 1, \qquad y > 1, \qquad (x > 1) \to (x^2 > 1), \qquad (y > 1) \to (y^2 > 1), \\ &\bigl( (x^2 > 1) \wedge (y^2 > 1) \bigr) \to (x^2 + y^2 > 2), \qquad (x > 2) \to (x^2 + y^2 > 2), \end{aligned} \] derive \(x^2 + y^2 > 2\) .

title: Definition 1.4.2 (Derivation)
page: 1.4 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Fix a list of rules. A derivation is a finite list of numbered lines \(1, 2, \dots, n\) , each carrying one statement and a justification, together with a set of boxes . A box is a block of consecutive lines whose first line is an assumption. Any two boxes are either disjoint or one inside the other . A box ends at one of its lines and is closed after it. The last line of the derivation lies outside every box. The scope rule. Line \(i\) is available at line \(k\) if \(i < k\) and every box containing line \(i\) also contains line \(k\) . A box is available at line \(k\) if it ends before line \(k\) and the boxes other than itself that contain it are exactly the boxes containing line \(k\) . A line may cite only lines and boxes available at it. Every line is exactly one of the following: a premise ; the premises are the first lines, above every box, with a short rule under the last of them; an assumption , which may be any statement, and opens a new box; a repetition of the statement on a line available at this one, justified “R” and the line repeated; the conclusion of one rule of the list, applied to lines and boxes available at this one, such that this line and the cited lines and boxes form an instance of the rule’s schema. Clause (D3) is the rule \(\rulename{R}\) ( repetition ), whose schema is where line \(i\) must be available at line \(k\) .

title: Definition 1.4.1 (Rules for Implication)
page: 1.4 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: The left schema is the rule \(\rulename{{\to}I}\) ( implication-introduction ); the right one is \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) ( @def-rule-implication-elimination ). In \(\rulename{{\to}I}\) , the line \(\varphi\) is an assumption , which opens the box, and the assumption is discharged when the box closes. The line \(\psi\) is a line of that box itself , not of a box inside it.

content: State the rule \(\rulename{\vee E}\) as a schema, and name the three things its justification cites. For each sentence, taken from a proof, name the disjunction that supplies the cases and the statement both cases end in. “If \(n\) is even, then \(n^2 + n = n(n + 1)\) is even; if \(n\) is odd, then \(n + 1\) is even and so is \(n(n + 1)\) . Either way, \(n^2 + n\) is even.” “Both possibilities for the sign of \(t\) give \(t^2 \ge 0\) .” Let \(n\) be an integer. True or false, with a reason: “If \(n\) is even, then \(n^2\) is even. Since every integer is even or odd, \(n^2\) is even” is a correct proof by cases that \(n^2\) is even. The following is offered as a derivation of \(P \vee Q, \; P \to R \vdash R\) . Name the line that is not justified and the clause of @def-rules-disjunction it violates. In the first derivation of @prp-distributivity , which line is the disjunction that \(\rulename{\vee E}\) cites at line 10, and where did it come from? Why does each box end in \((P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R)\) rather than in \(P \wedge Q\) and \(P \wedge R\) ? In the same derivation, why does line 6 use \(\rulename{\vee I}\) to put \(P \wedge Q\) on the left ? Could line 6 have been \((P \wedge R) \vee (P \wedge Q)\) ?

title: Exercise (A2: Drill)
content: Each part takes a line or two. The parts run from reading a split, through a missing line and a justification column, to whole derivations. Let \(x\) be a real number and \(n\) an integer. “If \(x \ge 0\) , then \(\abs{x}^2 = x^2\) ; if \(x < 0\) , then \(\abs{x}^2 = (-x)^2 = x^2\) . So \(\abs{x}^2 = x^2\) .” Name the disjunction that supplies the cases, and the common last line. How many case boxes does the proof of @exm-abs-product-cases open? Inside a box whose current goal is \(S\) , the available line \(Q \vee R\) is split. What do the two case boxes end in? Line 1 is \((P \wedge Q) \vee R\) ; a box \(\lines{2}{4}\) runs from \(P \wedge Q\) to \(S \vee P\) , and a box \(\lines{5}{7}\) from \(R\) to \(S \vee P\) . What does “ \(\rulename{\vee E}\) 1, 2–4, 5–7” write? Line 9 is \(Q\) , justified “ \(\rulename{\vee E}\) 2, 3–5, 6–8”, with line 3 \(P \to Q\) and line 6 \(R\) . What are lines 2, 5 and 8? Justify each line: 1 \(P \vee (Q \wedge R)\) , 2 \(P \to S\) , 3 \(R \to S\) , premises; 4 \(P\) ; 5 \(S\) ; 6 \(Q \wedge R\) ; 7 \(R\) ; 8 \(S\) ; 9 \(S\) . The boxes are \(\lines{4}{5}\) and \(\lines{6}{8}\) . Two case boxes end in \(R \wedge S\) and \(S \wedge R\) . May \(\rulename{\vee E}\) close the split? Find the illegal line. Is the split “ \(n > 0\) or \(n < 0\) ” exhaustive for integers? “Case \(x \ge 1\) : \(x^2 \ge 1\) . Case \(x \le -1\) : \(x^2 \ge 1\) . So \(x^2 \ge 1\) for every real \(x\) .” What fails? Line 1 is \((P \vee Q) \to R\) . A student opens a box with \(P\) and a box with \(Q\) , each ending in \(R\) , and writes “ \(R\) — \(\rulename{\vee E}\) 1, 2–4, 5–7”. Correct? Derive \(P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee (P \vee R)\) . Derive \((P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) \vdash P\) . Derive \(P \vee Q, \ Q \to P \vdash P\) . Derive \((P \wedge Q) \vee (R \wedge S) \vdash Q \vee R\) .

title: Exercise (B1: The other distributive law)
content: Show that \((P \vee Q) \wedge (P \vee R) \vdash P \vee (Q \wedge R)\) . Hint: after taking the premise apart, you will need a case split inside a case.

title: Exercise (B2: The larger of two numbers)
content: For real numbers \(a\) and \(b\) , let \(\max(a, b) \coloneqq a\) if \(a \ge b\) , and \(\max(a, b) \coloneqq b\) if \(a < b\) . Prove that \(\max(a, b) \ge a\) and \(\max(a, b) \ge b\) . Hence deduce that \(\max(a, b) \ge \frac{1}{2}(a + b)\) : the larger of two numbers is at least their average.

title: Exercise (B3: Two cases, two conclusions)
content: A search for \(P \vee Q, \; P \to R, \; Q \to (S \wedge T) \vdash R \vee T\) has reached the stage below. Name the move, then complete it. Use (a) to prove: for every integer \(n\) , \(n^2\) is a multiple of \(4\) or one more than a multiple of \(8\) . You may use that every integer is even or odd, and that \(k(k + 1)\) is even for every integer \(k\) .

title: Exercise (B4: The smaller of two numbers)
content: For real numbers \(a\) and \(b\) , let \(\max(a, b)\) be as in @exr-disjunction-and-cases-b2 , and let \(\min(a, b) \coloneqq b\) if \(a \ge b\) , and \(\min(a, b) \coloneqq a\) if \(a < b\) . Prove by cases that \(\min(a, b) = -\max(-a, -b)\) .

title: Exercise (B5: Derive or break)
content: For each claim, derive it with the rules of this chapter, or break it by statements about a real number \(x\) that make its counterexample set true. \(P \vee Q, \ R \vdash (P \wedge R) \vee Q\) . \((P \vee Q) \wedge (P \vee R) \vdash P \wedge (Q \vee R)\) . \(P \vee (Q \vee R), \ Q \to P \vdash P \vee R\) . \((P \vee Q) \to R \vdash (P \to R) \vee (Q \to R)\) . \((P \to R) \vee (Q \to R) \vdash (P \vee Q) \to R\) . \(P \vee Q, \ P \to R \vdash R \vee Q\) . \(P \vee (Q \to R), \ Q \vdash P \vee R\) . \(P \vee (Q \to R) \vdash (P \vee Q) \to (P \vee R)\) . \((P \vee Q) \to (P \vee R) \vdash Q \to R\) .

title: Exercise (B6: Translate, then derive)
content: Translate each argument into a sequent with the letters given, then derive it or break its form. Let \(n\) be an integer. \(n\) is even or \(n\) is odd. If \(n\) is even, then \(n(n + 1)\) is even. If \(n\) is odd, then \(n + 1\) is even. If \(n + 1\) is even, then \(n(n + 1)\) is even. So \(n(n + 1)\) is even. Letters: \(E\) : “ \(n\) is even”, \(O\) : “ \(n\) is odd”, \(F\) : “ \(n + 1\) is even”, \(M\) : “ \(n(n + 1)\) is even”. Let \(x\) be a real number. If \(x > 1\) , then \(x^2 > 1\) . If \(x < -1\) , then \(x^2 > 1\) . And \(x^2 > 1\) . So \(x > 1\) or \(x < -1\) . Letters: \(P\) : “ \(x > 1\) ”, \(Q\) : “ \(x < -1\) ”, \(R\) : “ \(x^2 > 1\) ”. If the form breaks, say whether the conclusion is still true for every \(x\) with \(x^2 > 1\) , and which premise would repair the argument.

title: Exercise (B7: Fifteen standard sequents)
content: Derive each sequent. They are grouped by the move that does the main work. Read the skeleton off the goal. \(Q \vdash (P \to R) \to (P \to (Q \wedge R))\) . \(\vdash (P \wedge Q) \to ((Q \to R) \to (R \wedge P))\) . \((P \vee Q) \to R \vdash P \to (S \to (R \wedge P))\) . \(P \to (Q \to R) \vdash (S \wedge P) \to (Q \to (R \vee S))\) . \(Q \to R \vdash P \to ((P \to Q) \to (R \wedge P))\) . Use a premise by its main connective. \(P \to (Q \wedge R) \vdash (P \wedge S) \to (R \wedge S)\) . \(P \wedge (Q \to R), \ P \to Q \vdash R \wedge P\) . \((P \wedge Q) \to R, \ P \to Q \vdash P \to R\) . \(P \to (Q \to R), \ S \to Q \vdash (P \wedge S) \to R\) . \(((P \wedge Q) \to R) \to S, \ P \to T, \ (T \wedge Q) \to R \vdash S\) . Cases end in the current goal. \((P \to Q) \vee (Q \wedge R), \ P \vdash Q\) . \((P \to R) \vee (Q \to R) \vdash (P \wedge Q) \to R\) . \((P \to Q) \vee (P \to R) \vdash P \to (Q \vee R)\) . \(P \vee Q, \ S \to (Q \to R) \vdash (S \to (P \wedge S)) \vee (S \to R)\) . \(P \vee (Q \wedge R), \ P \to (R \wedge S) \vdash R \wedge (S \vee Q)\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Challenge: The reverse triangle inequality)
content: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Prove that \[ \bigl\lvert \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr\rvert \le \abs{x - y} \] by splitting into the two cases \(\abs{x} \ge \abs{y}\) and \(\abs{x} < \abs{y}\) , using in each case the triangle inequality of @exm-triangle-inequality-cases . Then explain why these two cases exhaust all possibilities, and why a split on the signs of \(x\) and \(y\) would need four cases.

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Here is a proof, by four cases, that \(\abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) for all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) . Case 1: \(x \ge 0\) . Then \(\abs{x} = x\) . Case 1a: \(y \ge 0\) . Then \(\abs{y} = y\) , and \(\abs{x - y}\) is \(x - y\) or \(y - x\) . Since \(x - y \le x \le x + y\) and \(y - x \le y \le x + y\) , we get \(\abs{x - y} \le x + y = \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) . Case 1b: \(y < 0\) . Then \(\abs{y} = -y\) , and \(x - y > 0\) , so \(\abs{x - y} = x - y = \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) . Case 2: \(x < 0\) . Then \(\abs{x} = -x\) . Case 2a: \(y \ge 0\) . Then \(\abs{y} = y\) , and \(x - y < 0\) , so \(\abs{x - y} = y - x = \abs{y} + \abs{x}\) . Case 2b: \(y < 0\) . Then \(\abs{y} = -y\) . Since \(x \ge 0\) and \(y < 0\) , we have \(x - y > 0\) , so \(\abs{x - y} = x - y \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) , because \(x \le \abs{x}\) and \(-y = \abs{y}\) . All four cases give \(\abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) . Is the statement true? Find the line that is not justified, and name the rule whose conditions it breaks. Show with specific numbers that the step fails. Repair Case 2b.

title: Exercise (C3: Exit check: a distributive law, rule by rule)

title: Exercise (R1)
content: Let \(f\) be a function and \([a, b]\) an interval. Take the atomic statements \(C\) : “ \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) ”, \(B\) : “ \(f\) is bounded on \([a, b]\) ” and \(I\) : “ \(f\) is integrable on \([a, b]\) ”; you need not know what the words mean. So \(f\) is integrable on \([a, b]\) and bounded there.” into a sequent, and derive it.

title: Definition 2.1.1 (Rules for Contradiction)
content: The left schema is \(\rulename{\neg E}\) ( not-elimination ): if \(\varphi\) and \(\neg\varphi\) stand on lines \(i\) and \(j\) available at line \(k\) , write \(\bot\) , citing both, the unnegated line first. The right schema is \(\rulename{\bot E}\) ( contradiction-elimination , or ex falso ): if \(\bot\) stands on a line \(i\) available at line \(k\) , write any statement \(\varphi\) , citing line \(i\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write the schema of \(\rulename{\neg I}\) from memory, and say which statement opens its box. Which rule does this sentence use, and which box does it close? “Suppose \(0\) had a reciprocal \(y\) . Then \(1 = 0 \cdot y = 0\) , which is absurd. title: Exercise (B3: The square root of three, used later)
content: You may use that every integer can be written as \(3k\) , \(3k + 1\) or \(3k + 2\) with \(k\) an integer, in one way only, and that every rational number can be written as \(p/q\) with integers \(p\) , \(q\) , \(q \ne 0\) , and \(p\) , \(q\) not both divisible by \(3\) . Prove that if \(n\) is an integer and \(n^2\) is divisible by \(3\) , then \(n\) is divisible by \(3\) . Hence prove that no rational number has square \(3\) .

title: Exercise (B5: From \sqrt 2 to \sqrt p)
content: Let \(p\) be a prime number. You may use two facts. ( \(\mathrm{L}_p\) ) Every rational number can be written as \(a/b\) with integers \(a\) , \(b\) , \(b \ne 0\) , and \(a\) , \(b\) not both divisible by \(p\) . ( \(\mathrm{E}_p\) ) For every integer \(n\) , if \(p\) divides \(n^2\) , then \(p\) divides \(n\) . Prove that no rational number has square \(p\) , naming the rule at each logical step. Where does your proof use ( \(\mathrm{E}_p\) ), and where ( \(\mathrm{L}_p\) )? Your proof never used that \(p\) is prime, only the two facts. Put \(6\) and \(9\) in place of \(p\) . ( \(\mathrm{E}_6\) ) is true (Exercise C1 of Section 2.4 proves it; take it as given here). Does ( \(\mathrm{L}_6\) ) follow from (L)? Is ( \(\mathrm{E}_9\) ) true? What does the argument then prove about \(\sqrt 6\) , and why does it prove nothing about \(\sqrt 9\) ?

title: Exercise (C1: The square root of six)
content: Prove that no rational number has square \(6\) . Use only the facts (E1)–(E3) of Section 2.1, (L), and @thm-square-even-implies-even , and name the rule at each logical step.

title: Exercise (C2: A proof that proves too much)
content: Here is a “proof” that \(\sqrt{4}\) is irrational, modeled on @thm-sqrt2-irrational . Suppose \(r\) is rational and \(r^2 = 4\) . Write \(r = p/q\) with \(p\) , \(q\) integers, \(q \ne 0\) , not both divisible by \(4\) . Then \(p^2 = 4q^2\) , so \(4\) divides \(p^2\) . Since \(n^2\) divisible by \(4\) implies \(n\) divisible by \(4\) , we get \(p = 4m\) . Then \(16m^2 = 4q^2\) , so \(q^2 = 4m^2\) , and as before \(4\) divides \(q\) . This contradicts the choice of \(p\) and \(q\) . Hence no rational number has square \(4\) . Explain why the conclusion must be false. Find the step that fails, and show that it fails with a specific integer. Every other step is a correct use of a rule. Which rule turns the “contradiction” into the conclusion, and why is the argument still wrong?

title: Theorem 2.2.1 (Irrationality of the Square Root of Two)
content: There is no rational number whose square is \(2\) . So if a real number \(\sqrt{2}\) with square \(2\) exists, it is irrational.

title: Definition 2.3.1 (Derived Rule)
page: 2.3 Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules
content: Let \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n \vdash \beta\) be a sequent, written with statement letters, that has already been derived earlier in the book. In a later derivation, replace each letter in \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n, \beta\) by a statement, the same statement for every occurrence of the same letter. If lines \(i_1, \dots, i_n\) , all available at line \(k\) , hold the resulting instances of \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n\) , we may write the resulting instance of \(\beta\) on line \(k\) . The justification names the result and cites \(i_1, \dots, i_n\) . A sequent used in this way is a derived rule . For example, @prp-modus-tollens becomes the rule \(\rulename{MT}\) :

title: Exercise (C3: Exit check: labeling a proof)
page: 2.3 Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules
content: Here is a proof that for an integer \(n\) , if \(n^2\) is odd, then \(n\) is odd. Suppose \(n^2\) is odd. If \(n\) were even, \(n = 2k\) , then \(n^2 = 2(2k^2)\) would be even; so, by contraposition, since \(n^2\) is not even (it is odd, and no integer is both), \(n\) is not even. As every integer is even or odd, \(n\) is odd. Label each sentence, or part of a sentence, with the rule or rules it uses, primitive or derived. Take as premises the facts (E1) and (E2) of Section 2.1 and the school computation “if \(n\) is even, then \(n^2\) is even”.

title: Lemma 2.3.3 (Weakening and Cut)
page: 2.3 Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules
content: Let \(\Gamma\) and \(\Delta\) be lists of statements, and let \(\varphi\) , \(\psi\) , \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m\) ( \(m \ge 1\) ), and \(\beta\) be statements. Weakening. If \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) and every member of \(\Gamma\) is a member of \(\Delta\) , then \(\Delta \vdash \psi\) . In particular, \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) implies \(\Gamma, \varphi \vdash \psi\) . Cut. If \(\Gamma \vdash \varphi\) and \(\Gamma, \varphi \vdash \psi\) , then \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) . Chaining. If \(\Gamma \vdash \alpha_i\) for every \(i = 1, \dots, m\) , and \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m \vdash \beta\) , then \(\Gamma \vdash \beta\) .

title: Definition 2.4.2 (Provable Equivalence)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: Statements \(P\) and \(Q\) are provably equivalent , written \(P \dashv\vdash Q\) , if \(P \vdash Q\) and \(Q \vdash P\) .
