title: Exercise (A1)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: State the rules \(\rulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}\) and \(\rulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}\) , and the definition of \(P \dashv\vdash Q\) . For a real number \(x \ge 0\) , consider “ \(x^2 = x\) if and only if \(x = 0\) or \(x = 1\) ”. Write the directions \((\Rightarrow)\) and \((\Leftarrow)\) as implications. Which one would a proof begin with “Suppose \(x^2 = x\) ”? True or false, with a reason: from the definition “an integer \(n\) is even if there is an integer \(k\) with \(n = 2k\) ” and the fact that \(10\) is even, we may conclude that \(10 = 2k\) for some integer \(k\) . True or false, with a reason: from the theorem “if \(x > 1\) , then \(x^2 > 1\) ” and the fact that \(x^2 > 1\) , we may conclude that \(x > 1\) .

title: Proposition 2.4.6 (Proving Equivalence by a Cycle)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: \(P \to Q, \; Q \to R, \; R \to P \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q\) . Likewise, from the same three premises, \(Q \leftrightarrow R\) and \(R \leftrightarrow P\) are derivable.

title: Proposition 2.4.1 (An Iff Is Two Implications)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: \(P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash (P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to P)\) , and \((P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to P) \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q\) .

title: Proposition 2.4.3 (Provable Equivalence and the Biconditional)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: For all statements \(P\) , \(Q\) , \(R\) : \(P \dashv\vdash Q\) if and only if \(\vdash P \leftrightarrow Q\) ; \(P \dashv\vdash P\) ; if \(P \dashv\vdash Q\) , then \(Q \dashv\vdash P\) ; and if \(P \dashv\vdash Q\) and \(Q \dashv\vdash R\) , then \(P \dashv\vdash R\) .

title: Theorem 2.4.4 (Odd Square, Odd Number)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: Let \(n\) be an integer. Then \(n\) is odd if and only if \(n^2\) is odd.

title: Theorem 2.4.5 (Squaring Preserves Order)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\) . Then \[ x \le y \iff x^2 \le y^2 . \]

title: Definition 2.5.1 (Reductio ad Absurdum)
page: 2.5 Proof by Contradiction and the Classical Rules
content: This is the rule \(\rulename{RAA}\) ( reductio ad absurdum , “reduction to the absurd”). The line \(\neg\varphi\) is an assumption, which opens the box and is discharged when the box closes. The line \(\bot\) is a line of that box itself , not of a box inside it.

title: Theorem 2.5.7 (The Classical Rules Are Interderivable)
page: 2.5 Proof by Contradiction and the Classical Rules
content: Over the primitive rules other than \(\rulename{RAA}\) , each of the three rules \(\rulename{RAA}\) , \(\rulename{\neg\neg E}\) , and \(\rulename{LEM}\) derives the other two. In particular, adding any one of the three to the other primitive rules gives the same derivable sequents.

title: Definition 3.1.1 (Partial Derivation)
content: A partial derivation is a list of lines laid out as a derivation ( @def-derivation ), except that some stretches of lines are still missing. Each missing stretch is a gap , drawn as a row \(\vdots\) . The line just below a gap is its current goal ; it is already written, but it has no justification yet, since the lines of the gap are to supply one. The lines available at the current goal, in the sense of @def-derivation , are the gap’s resources .

title: Definition 3.2.1 (Inconsistent and Consistent Lists)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of statements \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) , where \(n \ge 0\) . The list \(\Gamma\) is inconsistent if \(\Gamma \vdash \bot\) : some derivation whose premises all belong to \(\Gamma\) has \(\bot\) as its last line. It is consistent if it is not inconsistent, that is, if no derivation with premises in \(\Gamma\) ends with \(\bot\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Challenge: Splitting an inconsistency, used later)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list and \(\varphi\) a statement. Prove that if \(\Gamma, \varphi\) and \(\Gamma, \neg\varphi\) are both inconsistent, then so is \(\Gamma\) . Deduce: if \(\Gamma\) is consistent, then at least one of \(\Gamma, \varphi\) and \(\Gamma, \neg\varphi\) is consistent. Does (b) say which one?

title: Proposition 3.2.2 (Derivable Exactly When the Counterexample Set Is Inconsistent)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of statements and \(\varphi\) a statement. \(\Gamma \vdash \neg\varphi\) if and only if the list \(\Gamma, \varphi\) is inconsistent. \(\Gamma \vdash \varphi\) if and only if the list \(\Gamma, \neg\varphi\) is inconsistent.

title: Proposition 3.2.1 (An Inconsistent List Proves Everything)
content: For a list of statements \(\Gamma\) , the following are equivalent: \(\Gamma\) is inconsistent; \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) for every statement \(\psi\) ; \(\Gamma \vdash \chi\) and \(\Gamma \vdash \neg\chi\) for some statement \(\chi\) .

title: Example (An argument about a prime, extracted)
content: Extract the argument of this paragraph and derive it. Let \(n\) be an integer, and suppose that \(n\) is a prime greater than \(10\) . Then \(n\) is odd, since the only even prime is \(2\) . Nor is \(n\) a multiple of \(3\) , because the only prime that is a multiple of \(3\) is \(3\) itself. So \(n\) is neither even nor a multiple of \(3\) .

title: Example (A proof and its derivation, side by side)
content: Let \(n\) be an integer. Claim: if \(n\) is even and prime, then \(n\) is not a multiple of \(3\) . Proof. Suppose \(n\) is even and prime. If \(n\) were a multiple of \(3\) , it would be an even multiple of \(3\) , and no even multiple of \(3\) is prime; but \(n\) is prime. So \(n\) is not a multiple of \(3\) . Write the derivation the proof mirrors, in two columns.

title: Exercise (B1: Extract, then derive)
content: For each paragraph, find the conclusion, the stated premises and any unstated fact; choose letters; write the sequent; derive it. Let \(x\) be a real number with \(x^2 \le x\) . If \(x\) were greater than \(1\) , then \(x^2 = x \cdot x\) would be greater than \(x\) . If \(x\) were negative, \(x^2\) would be positive, hence greater than \(x\) . So \(x\) is at least \(0\) and at most \(1\) . Let \(n\) be an integer. Since \(n^2\) is odd, \(n\) is odd. Let \(a\) and \(b\) be real numbers with \(ab = 0\) . title: Exercise (B4: Put the proof in order)
content: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be real numbers. Claim: if \(a + b > 2\) , then \(a > 1\) or \(b > 1\) . This contradicts \(a + b > 2\) . Suppose \(a + b > 2\) . Then \(a > 1\) , since \(a + b > 2\) . Adding, \(a + b \le 2\) . Hence \(a > 1\) or \(b > 1\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that neither \(a > 1\) nor \(b > 1\) . Suppose \(a > 1\) or \(b > 1\) . Then \(a \le 1\) and \(b \le 1\) . Put six of these sentences in an order that proves the claim; two do not belong. Match each sentence of your order to a line of the derivation below, with \(A\) : “ \(a > 1\) ”, \(B\) : “ \(b > 1\) ”, \(S\) : “ \(a + b > 2\) ”.

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: from a paragraph to a derivation)
content: Let \(n\) be an integer greater than \(10\) , and suppose \(n\) is even or a multiple of \(3\) . Then \(n\) is not prime. Indeed, suppose \(n\) were prime. If \(n\) is even, \(n\) is an even prime, and every even prime is at most \(10\) . If \(n\) is a multiple of \(3\) , \(n\) is a prime multiple of \(3\) , and every such number is at most \(10\) . Either way \(n\) is at most \(10\) , which is false. So \(n\) is not prime. Name the conclusion, the stated premises, and the facts the paragraph gives as reasons, each on the key. Write the sequent. Derive it. Write the two-column table. Is the premise “ \(n > 10\) ” needed? Break the claim without it.

title: Exercise (C2: Challenge: A statement that promises anything)

title: Exercise (R4)
content: Ana and Ben talk about a real number. Ana. Let \(x\) be a real number with \(x^2 < x\) . Then \(x\) is positive. Ben. Why can’t it be negative? Ana. A negative number is less than its square. Ben. And zero? Ana. At zero, \(x^2\) equals \(x\) . And \(x\) is less than \(1\) , because for \(x \ge 1\) we would have \(x^2 \ge x\) . Ben. So \(0 < x < 1\) . But you never said why \(x^2 \ge x\) when \(x \ge 1\) . Ana. Multiply \(x \ge 1\) by \(x\) , which is positive. What is the conclusion, and who states it? Turn the dialogue into a derivation. Is Ana’s last answer enough?

title: Definition 4.1.1 (Formula)
content: The formulas are the strings given by the following clauses. Every atom is a formula, and \(\bot\) is a formula. If \(\varphi\) is a formula, then \(\neg\varphi\) is a formula. If \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are formulas, then \((\varphi \wedge \psi)\) , \((\varphi \vee \psi)\) , \((\varphi \to \psi)\) and \((\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi)\) are formulas. Nothing else is a formula: a string is a formula only if it is the last entry of a formation sequence . A formation sequence is a finite list of strings \(\chi_1, \dots, \chi_m\) , with \(m \ge 1\) , in which every entry \(\chi_i\) is an atom or \(\bot\) , or is \(\neg\chi_j\) for some earlier entry \(\chi_j\) (so \(j < i\) ), or is \((\chi_j \circ \chi_l)\) for some earlier entries \(\chi_j\) and \(\chi_l\) (so \(j, l < i\) ; \(j = l\) is allowed) and some binary connective \(\circ\) .

title: Definition 4.1.2 (Parse Tree)
content:
A parse tree for a formula is defined along the clauses of @def-formula . For an atom or \( ot\) : a single node, labeled by that atom or by \( ot\) . If \(T\) is a parse tree for \(\varphi\) , then the tree whose root is labeled \(
eg\) and has \(T\) hanging below it as its only subtree is a parse tree for \(
eg\varphi\) . If \(T\) and \(T'\) are parse trees for \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) , then the tree whose root is labeled \(\circ\) , with \(T\) hanging below it on the left and \(T'\) on the right , is a parse tree for \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) . Nothing else is a parse tree: a tree is a parse tree for a formula \(\varphi\) only if that follows from finitely many uses of (T1)–(T3). In particular, a parse tree for \(
eg\varphi\) is made by (T2), and a parse tree for \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) by (T3). The leaves are the nodes with nothing below them; a branch is a path from the root down to a leaf.

title: Definition 4.1.3 (Subformula)
content: The subformulas of a formula \(\varphi\) are the formulas whose parse trees hang from the nodes of a parse tree for \(\varphi\) : for each node, the formula of which the part of the tree from that node downwards is a parse tree. The formulas at the children of the root are the immediate subformulas of \(\varphi\) .

title: Axiom 4.2.1 (Principle of Induction)
content: Let \(P(n)\) be a property of natural numbers. Suppose that \(P(0)\) holds, and for every \(n \in \nN\) , if \(P(n)\) holds, then \(P(n + 1)\) holds. Then \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n \in \nN\) .

title: Example (An inequality by induction)
content: Prove that \(3^n \ge 2n + 1\) for every \(n \in \nN\) .

title: Example (Prove more to prove less)
content: For \(n \ge 1\) let \[ S_n = \frac{1}{1 \cdot 2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3} + \dots + \frac{1}{n(n + 1)} . \] Show that \(S_n < 1\) for every \(n \ge 1\) .

title: Example (A sum of products of neighbors)
content: Prove that for every natural number \(n \ge 1\) , \[ 1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 + \dots + n(n + 1) = \frac{n(n + 1)(n + 2)}{3} . \]

title: Example (Threes and fives)
content: Prove that every natural number \(n \ge 8\) is a sum of threes and fives: \(n = 3a + 5b\) for some integers \(a, b \ge 0\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: For each statement, say which kind of induction fits best (ordinary or strong), and write down its base case(s) and the statement of its inductive step, without proving them: (i) \(4^n - 1\) is divisible by \(3\) for every \(n \in \nN\) ; (ii) every natural number \(n \ge 12\) is \(4a + 5b\) for some integers \(a, b \ge 0\) . True or false, with a reason: to apply @thm-strong-induction , one must first check \(P(0)\) separately. A proof of “ \(P(n)\) for every \(n \ge 5\) ” checks \(P(5)\) and proves “if \(P(n)\) , then \(P(n + 1)\) ” for every \(n \ge 5\) . Which form of @ax-induction is this, and why is \(P(4)\) never needed? In @exm-strengthen-the-claim , why can “ \(S_n < 1\) ” not serve as the induction hypothesis?

title: Exercise (C1: Find the error)
content: Claim: for every \(n \ge 1\) , \[ 1 + 2 + \dots + n = \frac{n^2 + n + 2}{2} . \] “Proof”: suppose it holds for \(n\) . Then \[ 1 + \dots + n + (n + 1) = \frac{n^2 + n + 2}{2} + (n + 1) = \frac{n^2 + 3n + 4}{2} = \frac{(n+1)^2 + (n+1) + 2}{2} , \] so it holds for \(n + 1\) ; by induction it holds for every \(n \ge 1\) . Is the claim true for any \(n \ge 1\) ? Which item of the checklist fails, and which part of the “proof” is correct? Show that the same step “proves” \(1 + \dots + n = \frac{n^2 + n}{2} + c\) for every number \(c\) . What singles out \(c = 0\) ?

content: Prove that for every \(n \ge 2\) , \[ \Bigl(1 - \frac14\Bigr)\Bigl(1 - \frac19\Bigr) \cdots \Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{n^2}\Bigr) > \frac12 . \] Write \(R_n\) for this product. First show that the hypothesis \(R_n > \frac12\) alone, with \(R_{n+1} = R_n \bigl(1 - \frac{1}{(n+1)^2}\bigr)\) , does not give \(R_{n+1} > \frac12\) ; then prove more.

content:
Let \(P(n)\) be a property of natural numbers. Suppose that for every \(n \in 
N\) : if \(P(k)\) holds for every \(k \in 
N\) with \(k < n\) , then \(P(n)\) holds. Then \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n \in 
N\) .

title: Definition 4.3.1 (Height)
content: The height of a formula \(\varphi\) , written \(\hgt(\varphi)\) , is the number of nodes on a longest branch of its parse tree.

eg\varphi) = \atoms(\varphi)\) ; and \(\atoms((\varphi \circ \psi))\) consists of the members of \(\atoms(\varphi)\) together with those of \(\atoms(\psi)\) . Number of connectives: \(0\) for atoms and \( ot\) ; one more than for \(\varphi\) at \(
eg\varphi\) ; one more than the sum for \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) at \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) . Subformulas: the list of subformulas of \(p\) is \(p\) , and of \( ot\) is \( ot\) ; of \(
eg\varphi\) , the formula \(

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: The following argument claims to prove that every formula contains an even number of parentheses. We prove, by strong induction on \(n\) , that every formula with \(n\) symbols has an even number of parentheses. Let \(n \in \nN\) , let \(\chi\) be a formula with \(n\) symbols, and suppose that every formula with fewer than \(n\) symbols has an even number of parentheses. If \(\chi\) is an atom or \(\bot\) , it has no parentheses, and \(0\) is even. If \(\chi = \neg\varphi\) , then \(\varphi\) is a formula with \(n - 1\) symbols, so by hypothesis it has an even number of parentheses; and \(\chi\) has the same parentheses as \(\varphi\) . If \(\chi = (\varphi \circ \psi)\) , remove the outer pair of parentheses. The string \(\varphi \circ \psi\) has \(n - 2\) symbols, so by hypothesis it has an even number of parentheses. Putting the outer pair back adds \(2\) , so \(\chi\) has an even number of parentheses. By @thm-strong-induction , every formula has an even number of parentheses. Is the conclusion true? Which line fails, and why? Show that the move made in that line is illegal by applying the same move to a different property that every formula has, and reaching a false statement. Repair the argument.

title: Exercise (C5: Challenge: formulas without parentheses)
content: Write connectives in front of their parts and drop all parentheses. The Polish formulas are given by the clauses: every atom and \(\bot\) is a Polish formula; if \(\varphi\) is one, so is \(\mathsf{N}\varphi\) ; if \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are, so are \(\mathsf{K}\varphi\psi\) , \(\mathsf{A}\varphi\psi\) , \(\mathsf{C}\varphi\psi\) and \(\mathsf{E}\varphi\psi\) (for \(\wedge, \vee, \to, \leftrightarrow\) ); and nothing else is. Give each symbol a weight : \(+1\) for an atom or \(\bot\) , \(0\) for \(\mathsf{N}\) , \(-1\) for each of \(\mathsf{K}, \mathsf{A}, \mathsf{C}, \mathsf{E}\) . The weight \(w(u)\) of a string \(u\) is the sum of the weights of its symbols. Write \(((p \wedge \neg q) \to p)\) and \(\neg(p \vee (q \leftrightarrow r))\) as Polish formulas. Prove that every Polish formula has weight \(1\) , and that every proper initial segment of it (the empty one included) has weight at most \(0\) . Deduce that if \(\mathsf{K}\varphi\psi\) and \(\mathsf{K}\varphi'\psi'\) are the same string, for Polish formulas \(\varphi, \psi, \varphi', \psi'\) , then \(\varphi = \varphi'\) and \(\psi = \psi'\) . Read \(\mathsf{C}\mathsf{A}pq\mathsf{N}r\) by the count, and write it in ordinary notation.

title: Lemma 4.3.2 (Parenthesis Count)
content: Let \(\chi\) be a formula. \(\operatorname{ex}(\chi) = 0\) : \(\chi\) has as many left as right parentheses. Every initial segment \(u\) of \(\chi\) has \(\operatorname{ex}(u) \ge 0\) . If moreover \(\chi\) has the form \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) and \(u\) is proper and non-empty, then \(\operatorname{ex}(u) \ge 1\) . For every occurrence of a binary connective in \(\chi\) , the initial segment of \(\chi\) that ends just before that occurrence has excess at least \(1\) .

title: Theorem 4.3.1 (Structural Induction)
content: Let \(P(\varphi)\) be a property of formulas. Suppose that \(P(p)\) holds for every atom \(p\) , and \(P(\bot)\) holds; for every formula \(\varphi\) , if \(P(\varphi)\) holds, then \(P(\neg\varphi)\) holds; for all formulas \(\varphi, \psi\) and each binary connective \(\circ\) , if \(P(\varphi)\) and \(P(\psi)\) hold, then \(P((\varphi \circ \psi))\) holds. Then \(P(\varphi)\) holds for every formula \(\varphi\) .

Then there is exactly one function \(f\) on formulas such that, for every atom \(p\) , all formulas \(\varphi, \psi\) and every binary connective \(\circ\) , \[  egin{aligned} f(p) &= a_p, \qquad f( ot) = a_ ot, \ f(

title: Theorem 4.3.3 (Unique Readability)
content: Let \(\chi\) be a formula that is neither an atom nor \(\bot\) . Then exactly one of the following holds: \(\chi = \neg\varphi\) for a formula \(\varphi\) ; \(\chi = (\varphi \circ \psi)\) for formulas \(\varphi, \psi\) and a binary connective \(\circ\) . In case (i), \(\varphi\) is uniquely determined by \(\chi\) ; in case (ii), \(\circ\) , \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are uniquely determined by \(\chi\) .

title: Definition 4.4.4 (Truth Function)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) . A truth function \(f\) with \(n\) inputs assigns to each list \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) of truth values (each \(a_i\) is \(\mathrm{T}\) or \(\mathrm{F}\) ) a truth value \(f(a_1, \dots, a_n)\) . A formula \(\varphi\) expresses \(f\) if \[ v(\varphi) = f\bigl(v(p_1), \dots, v(p_n)\bigr) \quad \text{for every valuation } v . \]

title: Definition 4.4.3 (Truth Table)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula and let \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) be a list of distinct atoms that includes every atom of \(\varphi\) . A row is an assignment of a truth value to each of \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) . The truth table of \(\varphi\) (on \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) ) lists, for each of the \(2^n\) rows, the value \(v(\varphi)\) for a valuation \(v\) that agrees with the row on \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) . We say \(\varphi\) is true (or false) in the row.

title: Definition 4.4.2 (Truth Value of a Formula)
content: Let \(v\) be a valuation. The truth value \(v(\varphi)\) of a formula \(\varphi\) under \(v\) is defined by recursion on \(\varphi\) : for an atom \(p\) , \(v(p)\) is the value the valuation assigns to \(p\) ; and \(v(\bot) \coloneqq \mathrm{F}\) ; \(v(\neg\varphi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T}\) if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}\) , and \(v(\neg\varphi) \coloneqq \mathrm{F}\) if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) ; \(v(\varphi \wedge \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T}\) if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) ; otherwise \(\mathrm{F}\) ; \(v(\varphi \vee \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T}\) if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) or \(v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) (or both); otherwise \(\mathrm{F}\) ; \(v(\varphi \to \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{F}\) if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v(\psi) = \mathrm{F}\) ; otherwise \(\mathrm{T}\) ; \(v(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T}\) if \(v(\varphi) = v(\psi)\) ; otherwise \(\mathrm{F}\) . We say \(\varphi\) is true under \(v\) , or \(v\) makes \(\varphi\) true, if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) ; otherwise \(\varphi\) is false under \(v\) .

title: Definition 4.4.1 (Valuation)
content: A valuation \(v\) assigns to every atom \(p\) exactly one of the two truth values \(\mathrm{T}\) and \(\mathrm{F}\) . We write \(v(p)\) for the value it assigns to \(p\) , and say that \(p\) is true under \(v\) if \(v(p) = \mathrm{T}\) , false under \(v\) if \(v(p) = \mathrm{F}\) .

title: Example (Working backwards from F)
content: Find every row in which \[ \varphi = (p \to q) \to \bigl( p \to (q \wedge r) \bigr) \] is false: first with the full table on \(p, q, r\) , then without it.

title: Exercise (B4: Exactly one is true)

If \(n\) is even, then \(n\) is divisible by \(4\) . \(n\) is divisible by \(4\) , or \(n\) is odd. With the atom \(p\) for “ \(n\) is even” and the atom \(q\) for “ \(n\) is divisible by \(4\) ”, write (A), (B), (C) as formulas, find every row on \(p, q\) in which exactly one of them is true, and say what \(n\) can be.

title: Exercise (B5: Which primes divide n?)

If \(5\) divides \(n\) , then \(2\) does. \(2\) and \(5\) do not both divide \(n\) . With the atoms \(p\) , \(q\) , \(r\) for “ \(2 \mid n\) ”, “ \(3 \mid n\) ”, “ \(5 \mid n\) ”, find every row making all four claims true by working backwards, and give two such integers \(n\) . Why may the three atoms be treated as independent here?

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error, used later)
content: Here is a claim and a “proof”. Claim. Let \(v_{\mathrm{T}}\) be the all-T valuation. Every formula built from atoms by \(\wedge\) , \(\vee\) and \(\to\) only is true under \(v_{\mathrm{T}}\) . Proof. By @thm-structural-induction , with the property “if \(\varphi\) is built from atoms by \(\wedge\) , \(\vee\) , \(\to\) only, then \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) ”. The formulas \(\bot\) , \(\neg\varphi\) and \(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi\) are not built in this way, so the property holds for them. If a formula built in this way is \(\varphi \wedge \psi\) , \(\varphi \vee \psi\) or \(\varphi \to \psi\) , then \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are built in this way too, so the hypothesis applies to them. (1) For an atom \(p\) , \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(p) = \mathrm{T}\) by the definition of \(v_{\mathrm{T}}\) . (2) If \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) , then \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi \wedge \psi) = \mathrm{T}\) by (V3). (3) If \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) , then \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T}\) by (V4), since at least one part is true. (4) If \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) , then \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi \to \psi) = \mathrm{T}\) by (V5), because \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}\) and an implication with a false hypothesis is true. This covers every clause, and proves the claim. Is the claim true? Name the line that fails and say exactly what is wrong with it. Give a formula on which the reason given in that line is false. Repair the line.

title: Lemma 4.4.1 (Coincidence Lemma)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, and let \(v\) and \(w\) be valuations that agree on \(\atoms(\varphi)\) . Then \(v(\varphi) = w(\varphi)\) .

title: Definition 4.5.5 (Contradictory, Contrary and Subcontrary Formulas)
content: Formulas \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are contradictory if every row makes exactly one of them true; contrary if no row makes both true but some row makes both false; subcontrary if no row makes both false but some row makes both true.

title: Definition 4.5.2 (Satisfiable)
content: A formula \(\varphi\) is satisfiable if there is a valuation \(v\) with \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) . A list of formulas \(\Gamma = \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) , where \(n \ge 0\) , is satisfiable if there is a valuation that makes every \(\varphi_i\) true. A formula or list that is not satisfiable is unsatisfiable .

title: Definition 4.5.4 (Semantic Equivalence)
content: Formulas \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are semantically equivalent , written \(\varphi \equiv \psi\) , if \(\varphi \models \psi\) and \(\psi \models \varphi\) .

title: Definition 4.5.1 (Tautology and Contradiction)
content: A formula \(\varphi\) is a tautology if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) for every valuation \(v\) . It is a contradiction if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}\) for every valuation \(v\) .

title: Definition 4.5.3 (Semantic Entailment)
content: Let \(\Gamma = \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) be a list of formulas, where \(n \ge 0\) , and let \(\psi\) be a formula. We say \(\Gamma\) semantically entails \(\psi\) , and write \[ \Gamma \models \psi , \] if every valuation that makes all of \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) true also makes \(\psi\) true. We then also call the argument from \(\Gamma\) to \(\psi\) valid . We write \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \models \psi\) for \(\Gamma \models \psi\) , and \(\models \psi\) when \(\Gamma\) is empty. If \(\Gamma \models \psi\) fails, we write \(\Gamma \not\models \psi\) , and a valuation that makes every formula of \(\Gamma\) true and \(\psi\) false is a refuting valuation , or refuting row .

title: Example (Affirming the consequent is not valid)

title: Example (One grouping entails the other, not conversely)
content: Decide whether \((p \to q) \to r \models p \to (q \to r)\) , and whether \(p \to (q \to r) \models (p \to q) \to r\) .

title: Definition 4.6.1 (Search Tree)
content: Let \(\Delta\) be a finite list of formulas. A search tree for \(\Delta\) is built in stages. It begins as one node, the root , carrying the formulas of \(\Delta\) . At each stage, choose an open branch \(B\) and a formula \(\chi\) on \(B\) that is not an atom, a negated atom, \(\bot\) or \(\neg\bot\) , and that is not yet used on \(B\) ; then, below the last node of \(B\) , add \(\chi\) ’s rule: one new node with the formulas of its one way, or two new nodes side by side with the formulas of its two ways. On each new branch, \(\chi\) (and every formula equal to it) is now used: a formula is used on a branch exactly when the branch passes through a node added by its rule, so it stays used on every branch extending that one. Being used is a property of a formula on a branch : a formula at the root may be used on one branch and not on another. A branch is a path from the root down to a node with nothing below it, and its formulas are those on its nodes. A branch is closed if it holds some formula together with its negation, or holds \(\bot\) ; otherwise it is open . An open branch is finished if every formula on it, other than an atom, a negated atom or \(\neg\bot\) , is used on it. A search tree is finished if each of its branches is closed or finished.

title: Proposition 4.6.1 (The Search Decides)
content: Let \(\Delta\) be a finite list of formulas. Every search tree for \(\Delta\) can be continued until it is finished, and it has only finitely many stages. If every branch of a search tree for \(\Delta\) is closed, then \(\Delta\) is unsatisfiable. If a search tree for \(\Delta\) has an open finished branch \(B\) , then the valuation \(v_B\) that makes the atoms on \(B\) true and every other atom false makes every formula on \(B\) true, in particular every formula of \(\Delta\) . So, for a list \(\Gamma\) and a formula \(\psi\) : a search tree for \(\Gamma, \neg\psi\) , continued as in (a), either closes, and then \(\Gamma \models \psi\) , or has an open finished branch, whose row refutes \(\Gamma \models \psi\) .

title: Corollary 4.7.3 (Refuting Row)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\psi\) a formula. If some valuation makes every formula of \(\Gamma\) true and \(\psi\) false, then \(\Gamma \nvdash \psi\) .

content: Here are nine lines. Seven of them, in the right order, form the \(\rulename{\vee E}\) case of the proof of @thm-soundness . Line \(k\) is \(\chi\) , by \(\rulename{\vee E}\) citing line \(i\) (holding \(\varphi \vee \psi\) ), the box from line \(a\) to line \(b\) (opening with \(\varphi\) , ending with \(\chi\) ), and the box from line \(c\) to line \(d\) (opening with \(\psi\) , ending with \(\chi\) ). By the induction hypothesis for lines \(b\) and \(d\) , which come before line \(k\) , \(\Gamma_b \models \chi\) and \(\Gamma_d \models \chi\) . By @lem-context-inclusion (b), \(\Gamma_b\) is \(\Gamma_k\) with \(\varphi\) added, and \(\Gamma_d\) is \(\Gamma_k\) with \(\psi\) added. If \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) , then \(v\) makes every formula of \(\Gamma_b\) true, so \(v(\chi) = \mathrm{T}\) . title: Lemma 4.7.1 (Contexts in a Derivation)
content: Let lines \(i\) , \(k\) and \(a \le b\) belong to a derivation, and let \(\Gamma_j\) denote the context of line \(j\) . title: Definition 4.8.1 (The Step TAUT)

For \(m = 0\) , \(\psi\) must be a tautology.

title: Exercise (C4: Challenge: Strike out ∨I)
content: Strike \(\rulename{\vee I}\) from the primitive rules. Which sequents of @lem-connective-rows lose the derivations given in its proof (the table of the fold “The fifteen derivations”), and which step of the proof of @thm-completeness also uses \(\rulename{\vee I}\) , through a result of Chapter 2? Read \(\vee\) as \(\wedge\) : a valuation now makes \(\varphi \vee \psi\) true exactly when it makes both parts true; every other clause stays. Show that every remaining primitive rule is sound for this reading. Deduce that neither \(p \vdash p \vee q\) nor \(\vdash p \vee \neg p\) is derivable without \(\rulename{\vee I}\) (and without derived rules derived with it), although both are valid: the shorter list of rules is sound but not complete.

title: Lemma 4.8.2 (One Row of the Truth Table Is Derivable)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, let \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) ( \(n \ge 0\) ) be atoms among which are all the atoms of \(\varphi\) , and let \(v\) be a valuation. Then \[ p_1^{v}, \dots, p_n^{v} \vdash \varphi^{v} . \]

title: Theorem 4.8.4 (Completeness)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\psi\) a formula. If \(\Gamma \models \psi\) , then \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) .

title: Definition 4.9.5 (Adequate Set of Connectives)
content: A set \(S\) of connectives is adequate if every truth function, with any number \(n \ge 1\) of inputs, is expressed by some formula in \(S\) .

title: Definition 4.9.3 (Conjunctive Normal Form)
content: A formula has conjunctive normal form (CNF), or is in CNF , when it has the shape \(K_1 \wedge \dots \wedge K_k\) , with \(k \ge 1\) , where every \(K_i\) joins one or more literals by \(\vee\) .

title: Definition 4.9.2 (Disjunctive Normal Form)
content: A formula has disjunctive normal form (DNF), or is in DNF , when it has the shape \(C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k\) , with \(k \ge 1\) , where every \(C_i\) joins one or more literals by \(\wedge\) .

title: Definition 4.9.1 (Literal)
content: A literal is an atom or the negation of an atom.

title: Definition 4.9.4 (Positive and Negative Occurrences)
content: Each node of the parse tree of a formula \(\chi\) (an occurrence of a subformula, Section 4.5) is positive , negative , or unsigned , by the path from the root: the root is positive; the part of a node \(\neg\theta\) , and the left part of a node \(\theta_1 \to \theta_2\) , have the sign opposite to that node; the parts of a node \(\theta_1 \wedge \theta_2\) or \(\theta_1 \vee \theta_2\) , and the right part of \(\theta_1 \to \theta_2\) , have the same sign as that node; the parts of a node \(\theta_1 \leftrightarrow \theta_2\) , and every node below them, are unsigned.

title: Exercise (C1: One connective is enough)
content: Add to the language two binary connectives: \(\alpha \mathbin{|} \beta\) (“not both”, NAND), which is F exactly when \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are both T, and \(\alpha \downarrow \beta\) (“neither”, NOR), which is T exactly when \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are both F. title: Exercise (C4: From connectives to sets)
content: Let \(U\) be a collection, and \(A\) , \(B\) , \(E\) collections of members of \(U\) , in the everyday sense; \(U \setminus A\) is the collection of members of \(U\) not in \(A\) . For a member \(x\) of \(U\) , write \(a\) , \(b\) , \(e\) for the statements \(x \in A\) , \(x \in B\) , \(x \in E\) . Write “ \(x \in U \setminus (A \cap B)\) ” and “ \(x \in (U \setminus A) \cup (U \setminus B)\) ” as formulas in \(a\) , \(b\) , and deduce from a standard equivalence that the two collections have the same members. Show in the same way that \(A \cap (B \cup E)\) and \((A \cap B) \cup (A \cap E)\) have the same members. Show that \((a \to b) \to ((a \wedge e) \to (b \wedge e))\) is a tautology, and deduce: if every member of \(A\) is in \(B\) , then every member of \(A \cap E\) is in \(B \cap E\) .

title: Exercise (C5: Counting rows)
content: For a formula \(\varphi\) whose atoms are among \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) , let \(\#\varphi\) be the number of rows of the table on \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) in which \(\varphi\) is true. Show that \(\varphi \models \psi\) implies \(\#\varphi \le \#\psi\) , and that the converse fails. Show that \(\#(\varphi \vee \psi) = \#\varphi + \#\psi - \#(\varphi \wedge \psi)\) . Show that the minterms of two different rows are never true together, and that the disjunction of all \(2^n\) minterms is a tautology. Deduce that, for satisfiable \(\varphi\) , the full DNF of \(\varphi\) over \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) (one minterm on \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) for each row on them in which \(\varphi\) is true) has exactly \(\#\varphi\) minterms.

title: Exercise (C6: Challenge: Interpolation)
content: For \(\varphi = p \wedge q\) and \(\psi = q \vee r\) , find a formula \(\theta\) whose only atom is \(q\) , with \(\varphi \models \theta\) and \(\theta \models \psi\) . Prove: if \(\varphi \models \psi\) , \(\varphi\) is satisfiable and \(\psi\) is not a tautology, then there is a formula \(\theta\) , all of whose atoms occur both in \(\varphi\) and in \(\psi\) , with \(\varphi \models \theta\) and \(\theta \models \psi\) . Show that under the hypotheses of (b), \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) have at least one atom in common.

title: Proposition 4.9.3 (Validity of a CNF)
content: A formula in CNF is a tautology exactly when every clause contains some atom together with its negation. A formula in DNF is satisfiable exactly when some conjunctive clause contains no atom together with its negation.

title: Theorem 4.9.6 (Adequate Sets)
Theorem 4.9.2 (Conjunctive Normal Form)
content: Every formula \(\varphi\) is equivalent to a formula in CNF. If \(\varphi\) has at least one atom, the CNF can be chosen so that every atom in it is an atom of \(\varphi\) .

title: Theorem 4.9.1 (Disjunctive Normal Form)
content: Every formula \(\varphi\) is equivalent to a formula in DNF. If \(\varphi\) has at least one atom, the DNF can be chosen so that every atom in it is an atom of \(\varphi\) .

title: Theorem 4.9.5 (Monotonicity)
content: Let \(\alpha \models \beta\) , and let \(\chi'\) be obtained from \(\chi\) by replacing one occurrence of \(\alpha\) by \(\beta\) . If the occurrence is positive, then \(\chi \models \chi'\) ; if it is negative, then \(\chi' \models \chi\) .

title: Definition 4.10.1 (Derivability and Entailment from Infinitely Many Premises)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a collection of formulas, finite or infinite, and \(\psi\) a formula. \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) if \(\psi\) is derivable from some finite list of members of \(\Gamma\) ; \(\Gamma\) is consistent if \(\Gamma \nvdash \bot\) . \(\Gamma \models \psi\) if every valuation that makes every member of \(\Gamma\) true makes \(\psi\) true; \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable if some valuation makes every member of \(\Gamma\) true.

Show that a finite list of members of \(\Gamma\) that leaves out \(p_{50} \to p_{51}\) does not entail \(p_{100}\) .

title: Lemma 4.10.1 (The Formulas Can Be Listed)
content: There is a list \(\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \varphi_2, \dots\) of formulas in which every formula occurs.

title: Lemma 4.10.2 (Lindenbaum’s Lemma)
content: Every consistent collection of formulas is contained in a maximal consistent collection.

title: Lemma 4.10.3 (Maximal Consistent Collections)
content:
Let \(\Delta\) be maximal consistent, and let \(\varphi\) , \(\psi\) be formulas. If \(\Delta \vdash \varphi\) , then \(\varphi \in \Delta\) . Exactly one of \(\varphi\) , \(

otin \Delta\) or \(\psi \in \Delta\) ; \(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi \in \Delta\) iff \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are both in \(\Delta\) or both not in \(\Delta\) .

title: Lemma 4.10.4 (Truth Lemma)
content: Let \(\Delta\) be maximal consistent, and let \(v_\Delta\) be the valuation that makes an atom \(p\) true exactly when \(p \in \Delta\) . Then for every formula \(\varphi\) : \(v_\Delta(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) iff \(\varphi \in \Delta\) .

title: Theorem 4.10.6 (Compactness)
content: A collection \(\Gamma\) of formulas is satisfiable if and only if every finite list of members of \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable. Consequently, \(\Gamma \models \psi\) if and only if some finite list of members of \(\Gamma\) entails \(\psi\) .

title: Theorem 4.10.5 (Completeness for Infinitely Many Premises)
content: For every collection \(\Gamma\) of formulas, finite or infinite, and every formula \(\psi\) : if \(\Gamma \models \psi\) , then \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) . Equivalently, every consistent collection is satisfiable.

title: Definition 5.1.1 (Bounded Quantifier)
content: Let \(A\) be a set, \(x\) a variable, and \(\varphi\) an open sentence. The bounded quantifiers are the abbreviations \[ \begin{aligned} \forall x \in A \; \varphi \quad &\text{stands for} \quad \forall x\, (x \in A \to \varphi), \\ \exists x \in A \; \varphi \quad &\text{stands for} \quad \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge \varphi). \end{aligned} \] In the same way, for a term \(a\) in which \(x\) does not occur, \(\forall x > a \; \varphi\) stands for \(\forall x\, (x > a \to \varphi)\) and \(\exists x > a \; \varphi\) for \(\exists x\, (x > a \wedge \varphi)\) , and likewise with \(\ge\) , \(<\) , \(\le\) in place of \(>\) .

title: Definition 5.2.2 (First-Order Formula)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: The formulas (of predicate logic, or first-order formulas ) are the strings given by the following clauses. Atomic formulas. If \(R\) is a predicate symbol of arity \(n\) and \(t_1, \dots, t_n\) are terms, then \(R(t_1, \dots, t_n)\) is a formula. If \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) are terms, then \(t_1 = t_2\) is a formula. And \(\bot\) is a formula. If \(\varphi\) is a formula, then \(\neg\varphi\) is a formula. If \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are formulas, then \((\varphi \wedge \psi)\) , \((\varphi \vee \psi)\) , \((\varphi \to \psi)\) , and \((\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi)\) are formulas. If \(\varphi\) is a formula and \(x\) is a variable , then \(\forall x\, \varphi\) and \(\exists x\, \varphi\) are formulas. Nothing else is a formula: a string is a formula only if it is the last entry of a finite list in which every entry is an atomic formula, or is built by (Fm2), (Fm3) or (Fm4) from earlier entries.

title: Definition 5.2.6 (Free For)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: Let \(t\) be a term, \(x\) a variable, and \(\varphi\) a formula. The term \(t\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) if no free occurrence of \(x\) in \(\varphi\) lies in the scope of a quantifier \(\forall y\) or \(\exists y\) such that \(y\) is a variable of \(t\) .

title: Definition 5.2.3 (Free and Bound Variables)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula and \(x\) a variable. An occurrence of \(x\) in \(\varphi\) is an appearance of \(x\) inside one of the terms of an atomic formula of \(\varphi\) . (The \(x\) written just after a quantifier symbol, as in \(\forall x\) , is part of the quantifier node and is not an occurrence.) An occurrence of \(x\) is bound if the path from its leaf up to the root of the parse tree passes through a quantifier node \(\forall x\) or \(\exists x\) , with the same variable \(x\) . The lowest such node binds the occurrence. An occurrence that is not bound is free . The scope of a quantifier node is the part of the tree below it: the formula it governs. The variable \(x\) is a free variable of \(\varphi\) , or is free in \(\varphi\) , if at least one occurrence of \(x\) in \(\varphi\) is free.

title: Definition 5.2.4 (Sentence)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: A sentence is a formula with no free variables.

title: Definition 5.2.5 (Substitution of a Term for a Variable)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content:
Let \(t\) be a term and \(x\) a variable. For a term \(s\) , the term \(s[t/x]\) is \(s\) with every occurrence of \(x\) replaced by \(t\) ; by recursion on terms, \[  egin{aligned} x[t/x] &= t, \qquad y[t/x] = y \ 	ext{ for a variable } y 
e x, \qquad c[t/x] = c, \ f(s_1, \dots, s_n)[t/x] &= f igl( s_1[t/x], \dots, s_n[t/x]  igr). \end{aligned} \] For a formula \(\varphi\) , the formula \(\varphi[t/x]\) , read “ \(\varphi\) with \(t\) for \(x\) ”, is defined by recursion on \(\varphi\) : \[  egin{aligned} R(s_1, \dots, s_n)[t/x] &= R igl( s_1[t/x], \dots, s_n[t/x]  igr), \ (s_1 = s_2)[t/x] &=  igl( s_1[t/x] = s_2[t/x]  igr), \qquad  ot[t/x] =  ot, \ (

e x, \end{aligned} \] and the last two lines likewise with \(\exists\) in place of \( orall\) .

title: Definition 5.2.1 (Term)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: The terms are the strings given by the following clauses. Every variable is a term, and every constant symbol is a term. If \(f\) is a function symbol of arity \(n\) and \(t_1, \dots, t_n\) are terms, then \(f(t_1, \dots, t_n)\) is a term. Nothing else is a term: a string is a term only if it is the last entry of a finite list of strings in which every entry is a variable, a constant symbol, or \(f(s_1, \dots, s_n)\) for some function symbol \(f\) of arity \(n\) and earlier entries \(s_1, \dots, s_n\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: For each formula, mark each occurrence of each variable as free or bound, list the free variables, and say whether it is a sentence: (i) \(\forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(y))\) ; (ii) \(\exists x\, \forall y\, R(x, y)\) ; (iii) \(\forall x\, (x < y) \wedge \exists y\, (y < x)\) ; (iv) \(\forall \varepsilon\, \bigl( \varepsilon > 0 \to \exists \delta\, (\delta > 0 \wedge \delta < \varepsilon) \bigr)\) . Which of the following are terms, and which are formulas, for one-place \(f\) , two-place \(g\) and two-place predicate \(R\) ? title: Exercise (A2: Drill)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: Answer each part in a line or two. In \(\forall y\, (x < y) \wedge \exists x\, (x = y)\) , which occurrences are free, and what are the free variables? Is \(\forall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 0)\) a sentence? Someone writes \(\forall x\, P(x) \to Q(x)\) for “every \(P\) is a \(Q\) ”. Which occurrence of \(x\) is free, and what is the repair? Compute \(\bigl( x \le y \wedge \exists y\, (y < x) \bigr)[3/x]\) . Compute \(\bigl( \forall x\, (x \ge y) \bigr)[0/y]\) . Compute \(\bigl( \forall x\, P(x) \to P(x) \bigr)[c/x]\) . title: Exercise (B2: The set of free variables)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: For a term \(t\) , let \(\mathrm{Var}(t)\) be the set of variables of \(t\) , and for a formula \(\varphi\) , let \(\mathrm{FV}(\varphi)\) be the set of its free variables. (Here \(\cup\) is the union of two sets, \(\setminus\) removes elements, and \(\emptyset\) is the empty set, all in the everyday sense.) Write down clauses that define \(\mathrm{Var}(t)\) by recursion on terms and \(\mathrm{FV}(\varphi)\) by recursion on formulas, one clause for each case of @def-term and of @def-first-order-formula . Use your clauses to compute \(\mathrm{FV}\) of \(\forall x\, (x < y) \wedge \exists y\, (y < x)\) and of \(\forall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = z)\) , showing each step.

title: Exercise (B3: Swapping two letters)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution

Swap \(x\) and \(y\) in \(\varphi\) with three substitutions through a letter \(u\) that appears nowhere, checking at each step that the term is free for the variable. Why would \(z\) not do as the go-between?

title: Exercise (C1: Challenge: What substitution does to the free variables)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content:
Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, \(x\) a variable and \(t\) a term, with \(t\) free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) , and with \(x\) free in \(\varphi\) . Prove that the free variables of \(\varphi[t/x]\) are the free variables of \(\varphi\) other than \(x\) , together with the variables of \(t\) : \[ \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) =  igl( \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}  igr) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t), \] with the notation of B2. Prove it in the following form, by structural induction on \(\varphi\) : for every \(\varphi\) in which \(t\) is free for \(x\) , if \(x \in \mathrm{FV}(\varphi)\) , then \(\mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = (\mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t)\) ; if \(x 
otin \mathrm{FV}(\varphi)\) , then \(\varphi[t/x] = \varphi\) . The term version, the atomic case and the connective cases are done below; prove the case of \( orall y\, \varphi\) (the case of \(\exists y\, \varphi\) is the same). Show, with the capture example \(\exists y\, (y > x)\) , \(t = y + 1\) , that the conclusion can fail when \(t\) is not free for \(x\) . Show also, with an example of your own, that it can fail when \(x\) is not free in \(\varphi\) . Given for (a). Terms. Let \(s\) be a term in which \(x\) occurs. Then \(\mathrm{Var}(s[t/x]) = (\mathrm{Var}(s) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t)\) . By induction on \(s\) : if \(s\) is the variable \(x\) , then \(s[t/x] = t\) and both sides are \(\mathrm{Var}(t)\) . (A constant, or a variable other than \(x\) , does not contain \(x\) .) If \(s = f(s_1, \dots, s_n)\) , then \(s[t/x] = f(s_1[t/x], \dots, s_n[t/x])\) ; for each \(s_i\) containing \(x\) , the induction hypothesis gives \(\mathrm{Var}(s_i[t/x]) = (\mathrm{Var}(s_i) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t)\) , and for each \(s_i\) not containing \(x\) , \(s_i[t/x] = s_i\) (as in the proof of the claim in the text). At least one \(s_i\) contains \(x\) , so the union over \(i\) is \((\mathrm{Var}(s) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t)\) . Formulas. We prove, by structural induction on \(\varphi\) , the statement \(S(\varphi)\) : if \(t\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) , then \(\mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = (\mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t)\) when \(x \in \mathrm{FV}(\varphi)\) , and \(\varphi[t/x] = \varphi\) when \(x 
otin \mathrm{FV}(\varphi)\) . The second half is the claim proved in the text, for every \(\varphi\) ; so in each case below we assume \(x \in \mathrm{FV}(\varphi)\) and prove the equation. Write \(E(\chi)\) for the set \((\mathrm{FV}(\chi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t)\) . Atomic. Let \(\varphi = R(s_1, \dots, s_n)\) with \(x\) occurring in some \(s_i\) . By the clause for atomic formulas, \(\mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x])\) is the union over \(i\) of the sets \(\mathrm{Var}(s_i[t/x])\) . Exactly as in the term case for \(f(s_1, \dots, s_n)\) (the result for terms for each \(s_i\) containing \(x\) , \(s_i[t/x] = s_i\) for the others, and at least one \(s_i\) containing \(x\) ), this union is \(E(\varphi)\) . The same for \(s_1 = s_2\) . ( \( ot\) has no free variables.) Negation. \(\mathrm{FV}((
eg\varphi)[t/x]) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = E(\varphi) = E(
eg\varphi)\) , by the induction hypothesis ( \(t\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) , and \(x\) is free in \(\varphi\) ). Binary connective. Let \(x\) be free in \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) ; then \(t\) is free for \(x\) in both parts, and \(x\) is free in at least one. If it is free in both, the induction hypothesis gives \(E(\varphi) \cup E(\psi) = E((\varphi \circ \psi))\) . If it is free in \(\varphi\) only, then \(\psi[t/x] = \psi\) , and \(E(\varphi) \cup \mathrm{FV}(\psi) = E((\varphi \circ \psi))\) , because \(x 
otin \mathrm{FV}(\psi)\) . Symmetrically if it is free in \(\psi\) only.

title: Exercise (C2: Renaming is not swapping)
page: 5.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: Show that \(\forall x\, \exists y\, (x < y)\) and \(\forall y\, \exists x\, (y < x)\) are the same sentence up to renaming bound variables: give a sequence of renamings, each allowed by the condition of the text, leading from the first to the second. title: Definition 5.3.1 (Universal Elimination)
content: Here \(\varphi\) is a formula, \(x\) a variable, and \(t\) any term, subject to one side condition: \(t\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) ( @def-free-for ). Line \(i\) must be available at line \(k\) (the scope rule of @def-derivation ). This rule is called \(\rulename{\forall E}\) ( universal elimination , or instantiation ), and \(\varphi[t/x]\) is an instance of \(\forall x\, \varphi\) .

title: Example (Instantiation at work)
content: Give a derivation of each sequent. \(\forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(x)), \ P(c) \vdash Q(c)\) . \(\forall x\, \forall y\, R(x, y) \vdash R(c, c)\) . \(\forall x\, \forall y\, (R(x, y) \to R(y, x)), \ R(a, b) \vdash R(b, a)\) . \(\forall x\, (P(x) \to P(f(x))), \ P(c) \vdash P(f(f(c)))\) .

title: Example (Instances of \rulename{\forall E})
content: \(\varphi\) \(t\) the instance \(\varphi[t/x]\) \(P(x) \to Q(f(x))\) \(f(f(c))\) \(P(f(f(c))) \to Q(f(f(f(c))))\) \(\exists \delta\, \bigl( \delta > 0 \wedge \forall y\, (\abs{y - x} < \delta \to \abs{g(y) - g(x)} < 1) \bigr)\) \(a + 1\) \(\exists \delta\, \bigl( \delta > 0 \wedge \forall y\, (\abs{y - (a + 1)} < \delta \to \abs{g(y) - g(a + 1)} < 1) \bigr)\) \(x^2 \ge 0\) \(\varepsilon/2\) \((\varepsilon/2)^2 \ge 0\) In each row every free \(x\) gets the same term, and no letter of the term is caught (in the second row the quantifiers are on \(\delta\) and \(y\) , and \(a + 1\) contains neither). Not an instance. From \(\forall x\, \exists y\, (x < y)\) at the term \(y + 1\) , the line \(\exists y\, (y + 1 < y)\) is not written by \(\rulename{\forall E}\) : the \(y\) of \(y + 1\) is caught by \(\exists y\) (clause 4). Rename first; the instance is \(\exists z\, (y + 1 < z)\) , which says what was meant.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write the schema of \(\rulename{\forall E}\) and its side condition from memory. For each pair, decide whether line 2 follows from line 1 by one application of \(\rulename{\forall E}\) . If not, name the clause of @def-rule-universal-elimination that fails. Line 1: \(\forall x\, \exists y\, (y > x)\) ; line 2: \(\exists y\, (y > y)\) . Why does \(\rulename{\forall E}\) not need a line saying that the term \(t\) names an element of the domain?

content: Give a derivation of \[ \forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(x)), \ \forall x\, (Q(x) \to R(x)), \ P(a) \vdash R(a), \] and say, for each \(\rulename{\forall E}\) line, which line of the search asked for its term.

Give a derivation of \[ \forall x\, (x^2 \ge 0) \vdash (a + b)^2 \ge 0 \wedge (a - b)^2 \ge 0 . \] Then extend it by one line justified “arith” to a derivation of \(a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab\) from the same premise, and say which earlier line the arith line uses.

title: Exercise (B5: Derive or break)

title: Exercise (C1: A partner makes a loop)
content: A relation \(R\) is symmetric if \(R(x, y)\) gives \(R(y, x)\) , and transitive if \(R(x, y)\) and \(R(y, z)\) give \(R(x, z)\) . title: Definition 5.4.1 (Rules for the Universal Quantifier)
page: 5.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content: The rule on the left is \(\rulename{\forall I}\) ( universal introduction , or generalization ). It cites a flagged box, with flag \(x_0\) , from its first line \(i\) to its last line \(j\) , and writes \(\forall x\, \varphi\) on line \(k\) . The flag \(x_0\) is a variable . The box’s last line \(j\) is \(\varphi[x_0/x]\) , and it is a line of the flagged box itself , not of a box inside it. The side condition is on the name: at line \(k\) , \(x_0\) appears in no premise , \(x_0\) appears in no assumption of a box still open at line \(k\) , and \(x_0\) does not appear in \(\forall x\, \varphi\) . The rule on the right is \(\rulename{\forall E}\) , as in @def-rule-universal-elimination : \(t\) is any term free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) .

title: Example (A Proof to Check)
page: 5.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content: Here is a proof. Is its claim true? Which step fails? Claim. Some real number is at least as large as every real number. Proof. Let \(x\) be a real number, and put \(M = x + 1\) . Then \(x \le M\) . Since \(x\) was arbitrary, \(x \le M\) for every real \(x\) , so \(M\) is such a number.

content: A student offers this proof. Claim. For every real number \(x\) , \(x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0\) . Proof. (1) Let \(x\) be a real number. (2) At \(x = 0\) : \(0 - 0 + 1 = 1 \ge 0\) . title: Definition 5.5.1 (Existential Introduction)
content: The rule given by this schema is called \(\rulename{\exists I}\) ( existential introduction ). Here \(\varphi\) is any formula, \(x\) any variable, and \(t\) any term, subject to one side condition: \(t\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) ( @def-free-for ). Line \(i\) must be available at line \(k\) ( @def-derivation ).

Not an instance. From \(P(c) \wedge Q(d)\) , the line \(\exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x))\) is not written by \(\rulename{\exists I}\) : \(\varphi[t/x]\) puts one term in every marked place, and no single \(t\) turns \(P(x) \wedge Q(x)\) into \(P(c) \wedge Q(d)\) .

title: Proposition 5.5.1 (Every Implies Some)
content: \(\forall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x)\) .

title: Definition 5.6.1 (Rules for the Existential Quantifier)
content: The rule on the left is \(\rulename{\exists E}\) ( existential elimination ). It cites a line \(h\) holding \(\exists x\, \varphi\) and a flagged box with the name \(x_0\) , a variable, whose first line is the assumption \(\varphi[x_0/x]\) and whose last line \(j\) , a line of that box itself, is \(\chi\) ; line \(h\) and the box must be available at line \(k\) ( @def-derivation , with the flagged boxes of Section 5.4). The new line \(k\) repeats \(\chi\) . Side condition, at line \(k\) : the name \(x_0\) does not appear in \(\chi\) , in \(\exists x\, \varphi\) , in any premise, or in any assumption of a box still open at line \(k\) . The rule on the right is \(\rulename{\exists I}\) , recalled from @def-rule-existential-introduction : \(t\) is any term free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) .

title: Example (Derivations with existential elimination)
content: Show that: \(\exists x\, \bigl( P(x) \vee Q(x) \bigr) \dashv\vdash \exists x\, P(x) \vee \exists x\, Q(x)\) ; \(\exists x\, P(x), \ \forall x\, \bigl( P(x) \to \neg Q(x) \bigr) \vdash \neg \forall x\, Q(x)\) .

title: Example (Instances of \rulename{\exists E})
content: The existential The box’s assumption (name) The box’s last line The new line \(\exists k\, (m = 2 \cdot k + 1)\) \(m = 2 \cdot k_0 + 1\) ( \(k_0\) ) \(\exists j\, (m + 1 = 2 \cdot j)\) \(\exists j\, (m + 1 = 2 \cdot j)\) \(\exists y\, (R(f(c), y) \wedge \forall z\, R(y, z))\) \(R(f(c), u_0) \wedge \forall z\, R(u_0, z)\) ( \(u_0\) ) \(\exists y\, R(y, y)\) \(\exists y\, R(y, y)\) \(\exists \delta\, (\delta > 0 \wedge \delta < \varepsilon)\) \(\delta_0 > 0 \wedge \delta_0 < \varepsilon\) ( \(\delta_0\) ) \(\varepsilon > 0\) \(\varepsilon > 0\) Inside each box the last line is reached from the assumption (in the first by arith, \(m + 1 = 2 \cdot (k_0 + 1)\) , and \(\rulename{\exists I}\) ; in the second by \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) , \(\rulename{\forall E}\) at \(u_0\) and \(\rulename{\exists I}\) ; in the third by arith from \(0 < \delta_0 < \varepsilon\) ), and none mentions its name. Not an instance. From \(\exists x\, R(x, c)\) , a box that opens with \(R(c, x_0)\) : the assumption must be \(\varphi[x_0/x] = R(x_0, c)\) ; \(R(c, x_0)\) assumes the witness stands on the other side of \(c\) , which the existential never said.

title: Proposition 5.6.1 (Some Distributes Over And, One Way)

title: Theorem 5.6.3 (The Barber)
content: For every two-place predicate symbol \(R\) , \[ \vdash \neg\exists y\, \forall x\, \bigl( R(x, y) \leftrightarrow \neg R(x, x) \bigr). \]

title: Definition 5.7.1 (Rules for Equality)
content: The rule \(\rulename{{=}I}\) ( equality introduction , or reflexivity) writes \(t = t\) for any term \(t\) , at any line, citing nothing. The rule \(\rulename{{=}E}\) ( equality elimination , or substitution of equals) cites an equation \(t_1 = t_2\) on line \(i\) and a line \(j\) of the form \(\varphi[t_1/x]\) , both available at line \(k\) , and writes \(\varphi[t_2/x]\) on line \(k\) . Here \(\varphi\) is any formula and \(x\) any variable, subject to one side condition: both \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) are free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) ( @def-free-for ).

title: Example (Instances of \rulename{{=}E})
content: In each row the hole is \(z\) ; the cited line fills it with the left side of the equation, the new line with the right side. Equation \(t_1 = t_2\) \(\varphi\) Cited line \(\varphi[t_1/z]\) New line \(\varphi[t_2/z]\) \(f(c) = g(c) + 1\) \(P(z) \wedge R(f(c), c)\) \(P(f(c)) \wedge R(f(c), c)\) \(P(g(c) + 1) \wedge R(f(c), c)\) \(\varepsilon/2 = \delta\) \(\abs{x - a} < z \to \abs{h(x) - h(a)} < \varepsilon\) \(\abs{x - a} < \varepsilon/2 \to \abs{h(x) - h(a)} < \varepsilon\) \(\abs{x - a} < \delta \to \abs{h(x) - h(a)} < \varepsilon\) \(a + b = b + a\) \(\forall y\, (z \cdot y = y \cdot (a + b))\) \(\forall y\, ((a + b) \cdot y = y \cdot (a + b))\) \(\forall y\, ((b + a) \cdot y = y \cdot (a + b))\) In the first row the \(f(c)\) inside \(R(f(c), c)\) is written out in \(\varphi\) and stays; in the third the hole sits under \(\forall y\) , and both terms are free for \(z\) because neither contains \(y\) . Not an instance. From \(2 = 1 + 1\) and the line \(2^5 = 32\) , the line \((1 + 1)^5 = 3(1 + 1)\) , which treats the digit \(2\) of \(32\) as an occurrence of the term \(2\) , is not written by \(\rulename{{=}E}\) : the numeral \(32\) is one constant, with no occurrence of the term \(2\) inside it; \(\varphi = (z^5 = 32)\) gives only \((1 + 1)^5 = 32\) .

title: Proposition 5.7.1 (Equality Is Symmetric and Transitive)
content: For all terms \(s\) , \(t\) , \(u\) : \(s = t \vdash t = s\) ; \(s = t, \; t = u \vdash s = u\) .

title: Proposition 5.7.2 (Leibniz’s Law)
content: For every one-place predicate symbol \(P\) , \(\vdash \forall x\, \forall y\, \bigl( x = y \to (P(x) \to P(y)) \bigr)\) .

title: Definition 5.8.2 (Counting with Equality)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, \(x\) a variable, and \(y\) , \(z\) two different variables, other than \(x\) , that do not appear in \(\varphi\) . “ At least two \(x\) satisfy \(\varphi\) ” abbreviates \(\exists x\, \exists y\, (x \ne y \wedge \varphi \wedge \varphi[y/x])\) . “ At most one \(x\) satisfies \(\varphi\) ” abbreviates \(\forall x\, \forall y\, (\varphi \wedge \varphi[y/x] \to x = y)\) . “ At most two \(x\) satisfy \(\varphi\) ” abbreviates \(\forall x\, \forall y\, \forall z\, (\varphi \wedge \varphi[y/x] \wedge \varphi[z/x] \to x = y \vee x = z \vee y = z)\) . “ Exactly two \(x\) satisfy \(\varphi\) ” abbreviates the conjunction of “at least two” and “at most two”. For a number \(n \ge 2\) , “at least \(n\) ” uses \(n\) different variables \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) that do not appear in \(\varphi\) , and asks for all \(n(n - 1)/2\) inequalities \(x_i \ne x_j\) together with \(\varphi\) at each; “at most \(n\) ” says that among any \(n + 1\) objects satisfying \(\varphi\) , two are equal; “exactly \(n\) ” is both.

title: Definition 5.8.3 (Definite Description)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\varphi\) a formula whose only free variable is \(x\) , and suppose \(\Gamma \vdash \exists! x\, \varphi\) . Introducing a name for the \(x\) such that \(\varphi\) means taking a constant \(c\) that appears neither in \(\Gamma\) nor in \(\varphi\) , and letting derivations from \(\Gamma\) use the defining line \(\varphi[c/x]\) as one more premise. The phrase “the \(x\) such that \(\varphi\) ” names \(c\) .

title: Definition 5.8.1 (Unique Existence)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, \(x\) a variable, and \(y\) a variable other than \(x\) that does not appear in \(\varphi\) (Section 5.2). Then \[ \exists! x\, \varphi \quad \text{abbreviates} \quad \exists x\, \bigl( \varphi \wedge \forall y\, (\varphi[y/x] \to y = x) \bigr). \] We read \(\exists! x\, \varphi\) as “there is exactly one \(x\) such that \(\varphi\) ”, or “there is a unique \(x\) with \(\varphi\) ”.

title: Proposition 5.8.2 (Definitions Prove Nothing New)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\psi\) a formula. Let \(P\) be a one-place predicate symbol that appears neither in \(\Gamma\) nor in \(\psi\) , and \(\varphi\) a formula in which \(P\) does not appear and whose only free variable is \(x\) . If \(\Gamma, \forall x\, (P(x) \leftrightarrow \varphi) \vdash \psi\) , then \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) . Let \(\varphi\) be a formula whose only free variable is \(x\) , and \(c\) a constant that appears in none of \(\Gamma\) , \(\varphi\) , \(\psi\) . If \(\Gamma \vdash \exists x\, \varphi\) and \(\Gamma, \varphi[c/x] \vdash \psi\) , then \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) .

title: Proposition 5.8.1 (Two Halves of Unique Existence)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, \(x\) a variable, and \(y\) a variable other than \(x\) that does not appear in \(\varphi\) . Then \[ \exists! x\, \varphi \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists x\, \varphi \wedge \forall x\, \forall y\, \bigl( \varphi \wedge \varphi[y/x] \to x = y \bigr). \]

title: Exercise (A1)

title: Proposition 6.1.1 (Rules for Bounded Quantifiers)
page: 6.1 Translating Mathematics: Nested and Bounded Quantifiers
content: Let \(A\) be a fixed set, so that \(\in A\) is a one-place predicate symbol (Section 5.2), \(x\) a variable and \(\varphi\) a formula. The following four rules, the bounded rules , may be used in derivations, with the rule names of the unbounded rules and the same side conditions: in \(\forall x \in A \; \rulename{E}\) and \(\exists x \in A \; \rulename{I}\) , the term \(t\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) ; in \(\forall x \in A \; \rulename{I}\) , the name \(x_0\) appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at line \(k\) , and not in \(\forall x \in A\; \varphi\) ; in \(\exists x \in A \; \rulename{E}\) , it appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at line \(k\) , and not in \(\chi\) or in \(\exists x \in A\; \varphi\) . The last line of each box is a line of that box itself. Every use of a bounded rule can be replaced by a block of steps of the unbounded rules (Sections 5.3–5.6) and of Chapter 1, with the same premises, the same assumptions open, and the same last line. Hence any derivation that uses the bounded rules converts into one that does not. The same holds with \(x \in A\) and \(t \in A\) replaced by \(x > a\) and \(t > a\) , or by the bounds \(\ge a\) , \(< a\) , \(\le a\) , for a term \(a\) in which \(x\) does not occur.

title: Proposition 6.2.7 (Passage Laws)
content: Let \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) be formulas and \(x\) a variable that is not free in \(\psi\) . Then \(\forall x\, (\psi \to \varphi) \dashv\vdash \psi \to \forall x\, \varphi\) ; \(\forall x\, (\varphi \to \psi) \dashv\vdash \exists x\, \varphi \to \psi\) ; \(\exists x\, (\varphi \wedge \psi) \dashv\vdash \exists x\, \varphi \wedge \psi\) ; \(\exists x\, (\varphi \to \psi) \dashv\vdash \forall x\, \varphi \to \psi\) ; \(\exists x\, (\psi \to \varphi) \dashv\vdash \psi \to \exists x\, \varphi\) . title: Proposition 6.2.4 (Replacement of Provable Equivalents)
content: Let \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) be formulas, and let \(z_1, \dots, z_k\) be the variables free in \(\varphi\) or in \(\psi\) . Suppose that \(\vdash \forall z_1 \cdots \forall z_k\, (\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi)\) . If \(\chi'\) is obtained from a formula \(\chi\) by replacing one occurrence of \(\varphi\) in \(\chi\) by \(\psi\) , then \(\vdash \forall w_1 \cdots \forall w_m\, (\chi \leftrightarrow \chi')\) , where \(w_1, \dots, w_m\) are the variables free in \(\chi\) or in \(\chi'\) . In particular, \(\chi \dashv\vdash \chi'\) .

title: Definition 6.3.1 (Propositional Skeleton)
content: Call a first-order formula prime if it is atomic and not \(\bot\) , or begins with a quantifier, bounded or not. Assign to each prime formula a propositional atom, the same atom to two prime formulas exactly when one can be turned into the other by finitely many renamings of bound variables (Section 5.2), in either direction; this is an equivalence relation, so the assignment is well defined. The propositional skeleton \(\mathrm{sk}(\varphi)\) of a formula \(\varphi\) is defined by recursion: \(\mathrm{sk}(\bot) = \bot\) ; \(\mathrm{sk}(\pi)\) is the atom of \(\pi\) for a prime formula \(\pi\) ; \(\mathrm{sk}(\neg\varphi) = \neg\,\mathrm{sk}(\varphi)\) ; and \(\mathrm{sk}(\varphi \circ \psi) = \mathrm{sk}(\varphi) \circ \mathrm{sk}(\psi)\) for each of \(\wedge\) , \(\vee\) , \(\to\) , \(\leftrightarrow\) . The formulas of one list take their skeletons from one assignment.

title: Exercise (B1: Lipschitz implies uniformly continuous)
page: 6.4 Uniformly Continuous Implies Continuous, Rule by Rule

title: Exercise (B2: Put the proof in order)

content: Below are ten sentences. Eight of them, in a suitable order, form a proof that a function \(f\) uniformly continuous on \(A\) is continuous at every point of \(A\) ; two are distractors. Write down an order for the eight, and say why each distractor is wrong. Since \(x\) and \(y\) lie in \(A\) and \(\abs{x - y} < \delta\) , the choice of \(\delta\) , applied to \(u = x\) and \(v = y\) , gives \(\abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon\) . Let \(\delta > 0\) be arbitrary. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Since \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(x \in A\) were arbitrary, \(f\) is continuous at every point of \(A\) . Suppose \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(A\) . By uniform continuity, applied to \(\varepsilon\) , choose \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(u, v \in A\) , \(\abs{u - v} < \delta\) implies \(\abs{f(u) - f(v)} < \varepsilon\) . Choose \(\delta > 0\) for this \(x\) and this \(\varepsilon\) , and then let \(x \in A\) be arbitrary. Let \(x \in A\) . So for every \(y \in A\) , \(\abs{x - y} < \delta\) implies \(\abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon\) : this \(\delta\) works for \(x\) and \(\varepsilon\) . Let \(y \in A\) with \(\abs{x - y} < \delta\) .

title: Definition 7.1.2 (Assignment)
content: Let \(\fM\) be a structure with domain \(D\) . An assignment in \(\fM\) is a function \(\ell\) that gives every variable \(x\) a value \(\ell(x) \in D\) . For an assignment \(\ell\) , a variable \(x\) and an element \(d \in D\) , the assignment \(\ell[x \mapsto d]\) is the one that gives \(x\) the value \(d\) and every other variable the value \(\ell\) gives it: \[ \ell[x \mapsto d](y) \coloneqq \begin{cases} d & \text{if } y \text{ is the variable } x, \\ \ell(y) & \text{if } y \text{ is any other variable.} \end{cases} \]

title: Definition 7.1.4 (Semantic Entailment in Predicate Logic)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\varphi\) a formula. We say \(\Gamma\) semantically entails \(\varphi\) , and write \(\Gamma \models \varphi\) , if for every structure \(\fM\) for the symbols occurring in \(\Gamma\) and \(\varphi\) , and every assignment \(\ell\) in \(\fM\) , \[ \fM, \ell \models \Gamma \quad \Rightarrow \quad \fM, \ell \models \varphi . \] We write \(\models \varphi\) when \(\Gamma\) is empty. If \(\Gamma \models \varphi\) fails, we write \(\Gamma \not\models \varphi\) ; a structure \(\fM\) with an assignment \(\ell\) such that \(\fM, \ell \models \Gamma\) and \(\fM, \ell \not\models \varphi\) is a counter-model to \(\Gamma \models \varphi\) .

title: Definition 7.1.3 (Satisfaction)
content: Let \(\fM\) be a structure with domain \(D\) and \(\ell\) an assignment in \(\fM\) . The relation \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi\) , read “ \(\fM\) satisfies \(\varphi\) under \(\ell\) ”, is defined by recursion on the formula \(\varphi\) : \(\fM, \ell \models R(t_1, \dots, t_n)\) if \(\bigl( t_1^{\fM, \ell}, \dots, t_n^{\fM, \ell} \bigr) \in R^{\fM}\) ; \(\fM, \ell \models t_1 = t_2\) if \(t_1^{\fM, \ell}\) and \(t_2^{\fM, \ell}\) are the same element of \(D\) ; \(\fM, \ell \models \bot\) never holds; \(\fM, \ell \models \neg\varphi\) if \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi\) does not hold; \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi \wedge \psi\) if both \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi\) and \(\fM, \ell \models \psi\) ; \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi \vee \psi\) if at least one of them holds; \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi \to \psi\) unless \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi\) holds and \(\fM, \ell \models \psi\) does not; \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi\) if both hold or neither does; \(\fM, \ell \models \forall x\, \varphi\) if \(\fM, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi\) for every \(d \in D\) ; \(\fM, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi\) if \(\fM, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi\) for at least one \(d \in D\) . When \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi\) does not hold we write \(\fM, \ell \not\models \varphi\) . For a list \(\Gamma\) of formulas, \(\fM, \ell \models \Gamma\) means that \(\fM, \ell \models \gamma\) for every formula \(\gamma\) of \(\Gamma\) .

title: Definition 7.1.1 (Structure)
content: Fix a collection of constants, function symbols and predicate symbols, each function and predicate symbol with its arity \(n \ge 1\) . A structure \(\fM\) (also called a model ) for these symbols consists of a non-empty set \(D\) , the domain of \(\fM\) ; for each constant \(c\) , an element \(c^{\fM} \in D\) ; for each function symbol \(f\) of arity \(n\) , a function \(f^{\fM} \colon D^n \to D\) , defined at every \(n\) -tuple of elements of \(D\) ; for each predicate symbol \(R\) of arity \(n\) , a set \(R^{\fM}\) of \(n\) -tuples of elements of \(D\) . The symbol \(=\) is not interpreted by \(\fM\) : in every structure it means identity , “is the same element of \(D\) as”.

title: Corollary 7.3.4 (Counter-models)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\psi\) a formula. If some structure \(\fM\) and assignment \(\ell\) satisfy every formula of \(\Gamma\) and do not satisfy \(\psi\) , then \(\Gamma \nvdash \psi\) .

title: Corollary 7.3.2 (Renaming Keeps Meaning)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula and \(y, z\) variables, with \(z\) not appearing in \(\varphi\) (Section 5.2). Let \(\fM\) be a structure for the symbols of \(\varphi\) , with domain \(D\) . For every assignment \(\ell\) , \(\fM, \ell \models \forall y\, \varphi\) if and only if \(\fM, \ell \models \forall z\, \varphi[z/y]\) , and \(\fM, \ell \models \exists y\, \varphi\) if and only if \(\fM, \ell \models \exists z\, \varphi[z/y]\) . If \(\psi'\) arises from a formula \(\psi\) by such a renaming of one quantifier anywhere inside \(\psi\) (Section 5.2), then for every structure \(\fM\) for the symbols of \(\psi\) and every assignment \(\ell\) in it, \(\fM, \ell \models \psi\) if and only if \(\fM, \ell \models \psi'\) .

title: Lemma 7.3.1 (Substitution Lemma)
content: Let \(\fM\) be a structure, \(\ell\) an assignment in \(\fM\) , \(\varphi\) a formula, \(x\) a variable, and \(t\) a term that is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) ( @def-free-for ). Write \(a \coloneqq t^{\fM, \ell}\) . Then \[ \fM, \ell \models \varphi[t/x] \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \fM, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models \varphi . \]

title: Theorem 7.3.3 (Soundness for Predicate Logic)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\psi\) a formula. If \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) with the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 and the quantifier and equality rules of Sections 5.3 to 5.7, then \(\Gamma \models \psi\) ( @def-first-order-entailment ).

title: Definition 7.4.3 (Inconsistent Theory)
content: A theory \(T\) is inconsistent if \(T \vdash \bot\) , that is, if \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \vdash \bot\) for some finite list of axioms of \(T\) ; otherwise \(T\) is consistent .

title: Definition 7.4.2 (Model of a Theory)
content: A structure \(\fM\) for the symbols of \(T\) is a model of \(T\) , written \(\fM \models T\) , if every axiom of \(T\) is true in \(\fM\) . A sentence \(\sigma\) is a semantic consequence of \(T\) , written \(T \models \sigma\) , if \(\sigma\) is true in every model of \(T\) .

title: Definition 7.4.1 (Theory)
content: A theory \(T\) is a set of sentences in the chosen symbols, called its axioms ; the set may be finite or infinite. A sentence \(\sigma\) is derivable from \(T\) , written \(T \vdash \sigma\) , if \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \vdash \sigma\) for some finite list \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) of axioms of \(T\) ( \(n \ge 0\) ); such a \(\sigma\) is a theorem of \(T\) .

title: Example (Axioms, Models and Non-models)
content:
Equivalence relations. One two-place predicate symbol \(R\) , and three axioms: \[  egin{aligned} &	ext{(Refl)} &&  orall x\, R(x, x), \ &	ext{(Sym)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\, (R(x, y) 	o R(y, x)), \ &	ext{(Trans)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( (R(x, y) \wedge R(y, z)) 	o R(x, z)  igr). \end{aligned} \] A model: \(D = \{ a, b, c \}\) , with \(R^{ M}\) relating \(a\) and \(b\) both ways and every element to itself (Figure A, left). Each loop gives (Refl); the only pairs of different elements are \((a, b)\) and \((b, a)\) , which give (Sym); and every chain of two arrows ends where a loop or one of these pairs already is, which gives (Trans). In numbers: “ \(x\) and \(y\) have the same parity” on \(
Z\) . A non-model: on \(
Z\) , read \(R(x, y)\) as \(\abs{x - y} \le 1\) . It is reflexive and symmetric, and (Trans) fails at \(0, 1, 2\) : \(\abs{0 - 1} \le 1\) and \(\abs{1 - 2} \le 1\) , but \(\abs{0 - 2} = 2\) . Partial and linear orders. One two-place symbol \(\le\) . The axioms (Refl) and (Trans), written with \(\le\) , together with \[ 	ext{(Antisym)} \quad  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( (x \le y \wedge y \le x) 	o x = y  igr), \] make the theory of a partial order . Adding \[ 	ext{(Conn)} \quad  orall x\,  orall y\, (x \le y \vee y \le x) \] gives the theory of a linear order . A model of the first and not the second: divisibility on \(\{ 1, 2, 3, 6 \}\) (the right panel of Figure F in Section 7.1), where \(2\) and \(3\) are incomparable, so (Conn) fails at \((2, 3)\) . A model of both: \((
N, \le)\) . Smallest of all, the antichain \(D = \{ a, b \}\) with \(\le^{ M} = \{ (a, a), (b, b) \}\) (Figure A, right) is a partial order: the loops give (Refl), and (Antisym) and (Trans) only ever meet pairs \((d, d)\) . eg(x < x), \ &	ext{(Trans)} &&  orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( (x < y \wedge y < z) 	o x < z  igr) \end{aligned} \] make a strict order ; with \[ 	ext{(Tri)} \quad  orall x\,  orall y\, (x < y \vee x = y \vee y < x) \] a strict linear order ; and with \[ 	ext{(Dense)} \quad  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( x < y 	o \exists z\, (x < z \wedge z < y)  igr) \] a dense one. A model of all four: \((

title: Example (Reflexive, Symmetric, Transitive: Each Independent of the Other Two)
content: Three structures for one two-place symbol \(R\) (Figure I). The first two are the counter-readings (d) and (f) of @exr-universal-introduction-b5 , now as models, with \(a\) , \(b\) in place of \(0\) , \(1\) . Not reflexive : \(D = \{ a, b \}\) , \(R^{\fM} = \{ (a, a) \}\) . Symmetric and transitive, since the only pair is \((a, a)\) ; (Refl) fails at \(b\) . Not symmetric : \(D = \{ a, b \}\) , \(R^{\fM} = \{ (a, a), (b, b), (a, b) \}\) . Reflexive; transitive, since every chain of two arrows has a loop as one of them; (Sym) fails at \((a, b)\) , since \((b, a)\) is missing. Not transitive : \(D = \{ a, b, c \}\) , \(R^{\fM}\) the loops at \(a\) , \(b\) , \(c\) together with \((a, b)\) , \((b, a)\) , \((b, c)\) , \((c, b)\) . Reflexive; symmetric, since the arrows between different elements come in pairs; (Trans) fails at \(a, b, c\) , since \((a, b)\) and \((b, c)\) are in \(R^{\fM}\) and \((a, c)\) is not. By @prp-model-shows-independence (a), no one of the three axioms follows from the other two.

title: Example (The Six Symmetries of a Triangle)
content: Label the corners of an equilateral triangle \(1\) , \(2\) , \(3\) (Figure T). A symmetry is a motion that puts the triangle back on itself, recorded by where it sends each corner. There are six: \(e\) : nothing moves; \(r\) : a turn by a third, \(1 \mapsto 2\) , \(2 \mapsto 3\) , \(3 \mapsto 1\) ; \(q\) : a turn by two thirds, \(1 \mapsto 3\) , \(2 \mapsto 1\) , \(3 \mapsto 2\) ; the flips \(a\) (fixing \(1\) , swapping \(2\) and \(3\) ), \(b\) (fixing \(2\) ) and \(c\) (fixing \(3\) ). Read \(x \cdot y\) as “ first \(x\) , then \(y\) ”. For instance \(a \cdot r\) sends \(1\) to \(1\) and then to \(2\) ; \(2\) to \(3\) and then to \(1\) ; \(3\) to \(2\) and then to \(3\) . It fixes \(3\) and swaps \(1\) , \(2\) , so \(a \cdot r = c\) . Computed in the same way, the whole table, with row \(x\) , column \(y\) and entry \(x \cdot y\) , is \[ \begin{array}{c|cccccc} \cdot & e & r & q & a & b & c \\ \hline e & e & r & q & a & b & c \\ r & r & q & e & b & c & a \\ q & q & e & r & c & a & b \\ a & a & c & b & e & q & r \\ b & b & a & c & r & e & q \\ c & c & b & a & q & r & e \end{array} \] Take the domain \(\{ e, r, q, a, b, c \}\) , the table as the meaning of \(\cdot\) , and \(e\) as the meaning of the constant \(e\) . Check the group axioms. (Id): the \(e\) row and the \(e\) column repeat the column and row heads. (Inv): each row contains \(e\) , and in the same place as its column does. So \(r \cdot q = e = q \cdot r\) , and each flip undoes itself: \(a \cdot a = b \cdot b = c \cdot c = e\) . (Assoc): “first \(x\) , then \(y\) , then \(z\) ” is one sequence of motions, however it is bracketed. The fold below says this once more, carefully. Now \(a \cdot r = c\) and \(r \cdot a = b\) , so (Comm) fails at \((a, r)\) . So this is a model of the group axioms in which (Comm) is false. Two elements would not do: in a group \(\{ e, g \}\) , every product with \(e\) is fixed by (Id), and \(g \cdot g\) commutes with itself, so (Comm) holds.
