title: Exercise (C1: Describe every model)
content: Describe every model of each sentence, and prove your description. \(\forall x\, \forall y\, (x = y)\) . \(\exists x\, \exists y\, \neg(x = y) \wedge \forall x\, \forall y\, \forall z\, (x = y \vee x = z \vee y = z)\) . \(\forall x\, \forall y\, R(x, y)\) . \(\forall x\, \exists y\, \bigl( R(x, y) \wedge \forall z\, (R(x, z) \to z = y) \bigr)\) .

title: Exercise (C2: The partial order axioms are independent)
content: Show that each of (Refl), (Antisym) and (Trans), for \(\le\) , is independent of the other two.

title: Exercise (C3: Exit check: a theory checked three ways)
content: Let \(T\) be the theory of a strict linear order with a least element: (Irrefl), (Trans), (Tri), and \[ \text{(Least)} \quad \exists x\, \forall y\, (x = y \vee x < y). \] Show that \(T\) is consistent. Show that (Dense) is independent of \(T\) . Derive from \(T\) that the least element is unique: \(\forall x\, \forall y\, \bigl( (L(x) \wedge L(y)) \to x = y \bigr)\) , where \(L(x)\) abbreviates \(\forall z\, (x = z \vee x < z)\) . You may use \(\rulename{TAUT}\) on the propositional skeleton.

title: Proposition 7.4.1 (A Group Has Only One Identity)
content: From (Id), the sentence \[ \forall x\, \bigl( \forall y\, (y \cdot x = y \wedge x \cdot y = y) \to x = e \bigr) \] is derivable: an element that acts as an identity on every element is \(e\) .

title: Proposition 7.4.2 (A Theory with a Model Is Consistent)
content: If some structure is a model of \(T\) , then \(T\) is consistent.

title: Proposition 7.4.3 (Independence by Models)
content:
Let \(T\) be a theory and \(\sigma\) a sentence. If some model of \(T\) makes \(\sigma\) false, then \(T 
vdash \sigma\) . If, besides, some model of \(T\) makes \(\sigma\) true, then \(T 
vdash 
eg\sigma\) as well; \(\sigma\) is then independent of \(T\) : neither it nor its negation is a theorem.

title: Corollary 7.5.2 (Automorphisms Preserve Definable Sets)
content: If \(h\) is an automorphism of \(\fM\) and \(S \subseteq D\) is definable in \(\fM\) , then for every \(d \in D\) , \(d \in S\) if and only if \(h(d) \in S\) .

title: Definition 7.5.1 (Definable Set)
content: Let \(\fM\) be a structure with domain \(D\) , and \(\varphi\) a formula whose free variables are among \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) , all different. The set defined by \(\varphi\) in \(\fM\) is \[ \{ (d_1, \dots, d_n) \in D^n : \fM, \ell[x_1 \mapsto d_1] \cdots [x_n \mapsto d_n] \models \varphi \} , \] for any assignment \(\ell\) . A set \(S \subseteq D^n\) is definable in \(\fM\) if some formula defines it.

title: Definition 7.5.2 (Isomorphism of Structures)
content: Let \(\fM\) and \(\fN\) be structures for the same symbols, with domains \(D\) and \(E\) . An isomorphism \(h \colon \fM \to \fN\) is a bijection \(h \colon D \to E\) such that \(h(c^{\fM}) = c^{\fN}\) for each constant \(c\) ; \(h\bigl( f^{\fM}(d_1, \dots, d_n) \bigr) = f^{\fN}\bigl( h(d_1), \dots, h(d_n) \bigr)\) for each function symbol \(f\) of arity \(n\) and all \(d_1, \dots, d_n \in D\) ; \((d_1, \dots, d_n) \in R^{\fM}\) if and only if \(\bigl( h(d_1), \dots, h(d_n) \bigr) \in R^{\fN}\) , for each predicate symbol \(R\) of arity \(n\) and all \(d_1, \dots, d_n \in D\) . An isomorphism \(\fM \to \fM\) is an automorphism of \(\fM\) . \(\fM\) and \(\fN\) are isomorphic if an isomorphism \(\fM \to \fN\) exists.

title: Example (Sets Defined by Formulas)
content:
Each formula is read back in words. In \((
R; +, \cdot)\) , the formula \(\exists y\, (x = y \cdot y)\) , “ \(x\) is a square”, defines \([0, \infty)\) : a real number is the square of a real number exactly when it is non-negative. In \((
N; +)\) , the formula \(x + x = x\) , “ \(x\) added to itself gives itself”, defines \(\{ 0 \}\) , since \(d + d = d\) forces \(d = 0\) . The formula \(\exists z\, (
eg(z + z = z) \wedge x + z = y)\) , “ \(y\) is \(x\) plus something non-zero”, defines the set of pairs \((d, e)\) with \(d < e\) . In \((
N; \cdot)\) , write \(U(x)\) for the formula \( orall y\, (x \cdot y = y)\) , “multiplying by \(x\) changes nothing”. It defines \(\{ 1 \}\) : at \(x = 0\) the instance \(y = 1\) fails, since \(0 \cdot 1 = 0\) ; at \(x \ge 2\) the instance \(y = 1\) fails too, since \(x \cdot 1 = x 
e 1\) ; and at \(x = 1\) every instance holds. In \((
N; \cdot)\) , the formula \[ 
eg U(x) \wedge  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( y \cdot z = x 	o (U(y) \vee U(z))  igr) , \] “ \(x\) is not \(1\) , and whenever \(x\) is a product, one factor is \(1\) ”, defines the primes. At \(x = 0\) the instance \(y = z = 0\) fails ( \(0 \cdot 0 = 0\) , and neither factor is \(1\) ); at \(x = 1\) the first conjunct fails; at a composite \(x = yz\) with \(y, z \ge 2\) the instance at that \(y\) , \(z\) fails; at a prime, every factorization has a factor \(1\) .

title: Example (Maximum, Maximal, Supremum)
content: In a structure with one two-place symbol \(\le\) read as a partial order: “ \(x\) is a greatest element” is \(\forall y\, (y \le x)\) , “everything is below \(x\) ”. “ \(x\) is a maximal element” is \(\forall y\, (x \le y \to y = x)\) , “nothing is above \(x\) except \(x\) itself”. In the divisibility order on \(\{ 1, 2, 3 \}\) ( \(d \le e\) when \(d\) divides \(e\) ), \(2\) and \(3\) are maximal, and there is no greatest element, since \(2\) does not divide \(3\) nor \(3\) divide \(2\) . On \(\{ 1, 2, 3, 6 \}\) , \(6\) is both maximal and greatest. Add a one-place symbol \(A\) for a set of reals, and work in \((\nR; \le, A)\) . “ \(x\) is an upper bound of \(A\) ” is the formula \(B(x)\) : \(\forall y\, (A(y) \to y \le x)\) , “every element of \(A\) is at most \(x\) ”. “ \(x\) is the supremum of \(A\) ” is \(B(x) \wedge \forall z\, (B(z) \to x \le z)\) , “ \(x\) is an upper bound, and below every upper bound”. For \(A = [0, 1)\) , the supremum is \(1\) : it is an upper bound, and any \(z < 1\) is exceeded by an element of \([0, 1)\) , such as the larger of \(0\) and \((z + 1)/2\) , so \(z\) is not one. No element of \(A\) is greatest. “ \(A\) has a greatest element” is the sentence \(\exists x\, (A(x) \wedge B(x))\) , “some element of \(A\) is an upper bound of \(A\) ”. It is false for \(A = [0, 1)\) and true for \(A = [0, 1]\) .

title: Example (Zero Cannot Be Defined from the Order of the Integers)
content:
In \((
Z, <)\) , the shift \(h(d) = d + 1\) is an automorphism: it is a bijection, with inverse \(d \mapsto d - 1\) , and \(d < e\) if and only if \(d + 1 < e + 1\) . It sends \(0\) to \(1\) , and \(1 
otin \{ 0 \}\) . By @cor-automorphisms-fix-definable-sets , \(\{ 0 \}\) is not definable in \((
Z, <)\) : no formula in \(<\) alone singles out zero among the integers. Contrast \((
N, <)\) . There \(\{ 0 \}\) is definable, by \( orall y\, 
eg(y < x)\) , “nothing is below \(x\) ”. The corollary is not contradicted, since \(d \mapsto d + 1\) is not an automorphism of \((
N, <)\) : it is not onto. A finite picture: the four-cycle below, with \(D = \{ a, b, c, d \}\) and \(R\) the four arrows \(a 	o b 	o c 	o d 	o a\) . The rotation \(a \mapsto b\) , \(b \mapsto c\) , \(c \mapsto d\) , \(d \mapsto a\) is a bijection that sends each arrow to an arrow and each non-arrow to a non-arrow, so it is an automorphism. Applied once, twice or three times, it moves any element to any other, so no single element is definable. A minimal change makes one element definable again. Add the loop \((a, a)\) to \(R\) . Now \(R(x, x)\) defines \(\{ a \}\) , and the rotation is no longer an automorphism, since it sends the arrow \((a, a)\) to \((b, b)\) , which is not an arrow. The method can only use the automorphisms a structure has; each of the three non-trivial rotations sends the loop \((a, a)\) to a loop at \(b\) , \(c\) or \(d\) , so adding one arrow removed all three.

title: Exercise (R4)
content: Is the sentence \(\forall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) \to \exists y\, \forall x\, (x < y)\) true in \((\nN, <)\) ? Is it derivable?

title: Theorem 7.5.1 (Isomorphic Structures Satisfy the Same Sentences)
content: Let \(h \colon \fM \to \fN\) be an isomorphism. For every formula \(\varphi\) and every assignment \(\ell\) in \(\fM\) , \[ \fM, \ell \models \varphi \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \fN, h \circ \ell \models \varphi , \] where \(h \circ \ell\) gives each variable \(x\) the value \(h(\ell(x))\) . In particular, \(\fM \models \sigma\) if and only if \(\fN \models \sigma\) , for every sentence \(\sigma\) .

title: Example (A Model of Arithmetic with an Infinite Number)
page: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content:
Let \(T\) be the set of all sentences in \(0, S, +, \cdot, <\) that are true in \(
N\) . Add a new constant \(c\) , and to \(T\) add the axioms \[ \underline{0} < c, \quad \underline{1} < c, \quad \underline{2} < c, \quad \dots , \] one for each \(n \in 
N\) . Call the result \(T'\) . Every finite subset of \(T'\) has a model. A finite subset contains finitely many sentences of \(T\) and finitely many axioms \(\underline{n} < c\) ; let \(N\) be the largest \(n\) among them (or \(0\) if there is none). Read the symbols in \(
N\) as usual and \(c\) as \(N + 1\) . The sentences of \(T\) do not mention \(c\) , and they are true in \(
N\) ; each \(\underline{n} < c\) in the subset says \(n < N + 1\) , which is true. So \(T'\) has a model. By @thm-first-order-compactness there is a structure \( M\) in which every sentence of \(T'\) is true. In \( M\) every sentence true in \(
N\) is true, and \(c^{ M}\) is above the value in \( M\) of every numeral. It differs from each of them: if \(c^{ M}\) were the value of \(\underline{n}\) , the axiom \(\underline{n} < c\) would put an element below itself, while \( orall x\, 
eg(x < x)\) is true in \(
N\) , so in \(T\) , so in \( M\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content: State @thm-first-order-completeness in its two forms. State @thm-first-order-compactness , and give the short argument from completeness in three sentences. What is a non-standard element of a model of arithmetic? Why does the induction schema not rule non-standard elements out? Name one decidable and one undecidable question about sentences.

title: Exercise (A2: Drill)
page: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content:
Each part takes a line or two. The parts run from writing a counting sentence, through naming the theorem that answers a question, to judging what a theorem does and does not say. Write \(\sigma_2\) , “there are at least two elements”. Write “there are at most two elements”. Which theorem says “every consistent theory has a model”? Which says “if every finite part of \(T\) has a model, \(T\) has one”? True or false: completeness says that every sentence true in \((
N; 0, S, +, \cdot, <)\) is derivable with no premises. True or false: a theory with models of every finite size has an infinite model. Is “the domain is finite” expressible by one sentence? True or false: in a model of all sentences true in \(
N\) , every element is the value of a numeral. Over what does the second-order induction principle quantify that the schema does not? Is derivability of a propositional claim decidable? Of a monadic first-order sentence (one-place predicate symbols only; no constants, function symbols or \(=\) )? Of a first-order sentence in general? Does \((
R; 0, 1, +, \cdot, <)\) have a model of the same sentences whose domain can be listed? Why is a theory whose models are exactly the structures of size \(3\) possible, and one whose models are exactly the finite structures not?

title: Exercise (B1: Arbitrarily large finite models)
page: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content: Prove: if a theory \(T\) has, for every \(n\) , a finite model with at least \(n\) elements, then \(T\) has an infinite model. Apply it to the theory of an equivalence relation \(R\) in which every class has exactly two elements, with that last condition written as one sentence.

title: Exercise (B2: Which theorem settles it?)
page: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content: For each question, say which statement of this section or of Section 7.2 settles it (or that none does), and answer it. \(\models \sigma\) is known. Is \(\vdash \sigma\) ? \(T \nvdash \bot\) . Has \(T\) a model? \(\sigma\) is true in every finite structure. Is \(\sigma\) valid? Is there a structure satisfying every sentence true in \(\nN\) , with an element above the value of every numeral? Is there a procedure that decides validity for sentences built from one-place predicate symbols only (no constants, function symbols or \(=\) )?

title: Exercise (C1: “Finite” is not first-order)
page: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content: Prove that no sentence \(\varphi\) is true in exactly the finite structures for its symbols.

title: Exercise (C2: Challenge: least elements in a non-standard model)
page: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content: Let \(\fM\) be the model of @exm-non-standard-naturals . For a formula \(\psi\) with free variable \(x\) , write a sentence saying “if some element satisfies \(\psi\) , some least element satisfies \(\psi\) ”, and explain why it is true in \(\fM\) . Take \(\psi = \neg\varphi\) , where \(\varphi\) is a formula supposed to define the standard elements in \(\fM\) . The sentence of (a) then names a least non-standard element \(e\) . Choose an element below \(e\) that is also non-standard, and conclude, without using the induction argument of this section, that no such \(\varphi\) exists.

title: Theorem 7.6.2 (Compactness Theorem)
page: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content: If every finite subset of a theory \(T\) has a model, then \(T\) has a model.

title: Theorem 7.6.1 (Gödel’s Completeness Theorem)
page: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content: For every theory \(T\) and sentence \(\sigma\) : \(T \vdash \sigma\) if and only if \(T \models \sigma\) . Equivalently, a theory is consistent if and only if it has a model.

title: Theorem 7.6.3 (Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem)
page: 7.6 What First-Order Logic Can and Cannot Say
content: Let \(T\) be a theory in countably many symbols (the symbols can be listed \(s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots\) ). If \(T\) has an infinite model, then it has a model whose domain can be listed as \(d_0, d_1, d_2, \dots\) , and also a model whose domain cannot be so listed.

title: Example (A contrapositive in costume)
content: Here is a proof that, for an integer \(n\) , if \(n^2\) is even then \(n\) is even. Decide what it really uses, and rewrite it. Suppose \(n^2\) is even. Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(n\) is not even. Then \(n\) is odd, say \(n = 2k + 1\) with \(k\) an integer. Then \(n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1\) is odd, so \(n^2\) is not even. This contradicts the fact that \(n^2\) is even. Hence \(n\) is even.

title: Example (A direct proof in costume)
content: Here is a proof that \(x^2 - 2x > 3\) for every real \(x > 3\) . Decide what it really uses, and rewrite it. Let \(x > 3\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(x^2 - 2x \le 3\) . Since \(x > 3\) , both \(x - 3\) and \(x + 1\) are positive, so \((x - 3)(x + 1) > 0\) , that is, \(x^2 - 2x - 3 > 0\) . So \(x^2 - 2x > 3\) . This contradicts our assumption. Hence \(x^2 - 2x > 3\) .

title: Example (Both directions, the second by cases)
content: Let \(x\) be a real number with \(x \ge 0\) . Prove that \(x \le 1\) if and only if \(x^2 \le x\) . Tag each step with its rule.

title: Example (Two cases, a weakening, a refuted disjunct)
content: Let \(x\) be a real number. (a) Prove that \(\abs{x} + x \ge 0\) . (b) Prove that if \(x^2 = x\) and \(x \ne 0\) , then \(x = 1\) . Tag each step with its rule.

title: Example (Two parts, and one part)
content: Let \(x\) be a real number with \(0 < x < 1\) . Prove that \(x^2 < x\) and \(x^2 > 0\) . Tag the steps that carry the logic.

title: Example (One proof by contradiction, read two ways)
content: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be real numbers with \(a \le b + \varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Prove that \(a \le b\) , first by \(\rulename{RAA}\) ; then rewrite the proof as a case split.

title: Example (Three conditions, one cycle)
content: Let \(n\) be an integer. Prove that the following are equivalent: (i) \(n\) is odd; (ii) \(n^2\) is odd; (iii) \(n^2 + 2n\) is odd. Tag the steps that carry the logic.

title: Example (A hypothesis assumed, a lemma cited, a contrapositive announced)
content: Let \(x\) be a real number. (a) Prove that if \(\abs{x - 1} < 1\) , then \(x > 0\) . (b) Deduce that if \(x \le 0\) , then \(\abs{x - 1} \ge 1\) . Tag each step with its rule.

title: Example (A negative claim, its positive form, and an empty case)
content: Prove that no real number is an upper bound of \(\nR\) . (b) Prove the positive form: for every real \(s\) there is a real \(x\) with \(x > s\) . (c) Let \(A\) be an empty set of real numbers. Prove that every real number is an upper bound of \(A\) . Tag each step with its rule.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Name the rule that each phrase most often carries: (i) “in particular”; (ii) “conversely”; (iii) “in either case”; (iv) “this case cannot occur”; (v) “suppose, for contradiction, that \(x\) is not positive”; (vi) “we prove the contrapositive”; (vii) “that is”; (viii) “since \(x \ne 0\) , the first case is impossible”; (ix) “so \(x \ge 0\) ”, after “ \(x > 0\) ”; (x) “which contradicts \(x^2 \ge 0\) ”. Which of the phrases in (a) carry steps that may be silent in plain prose? A proof ends “Suppose \(7 = 2k\) for an integer \(k\) . Then \(k = 7/2\) , which is not an integer. Hence \(7\) is not even.” Which face of “by contradiction” is this? True or false, with a reason: a proof that begins “suppose, for contradiction” always uses \(\rulename{RAA}\) .

title: Exercise (A2: Drill)
content: Name the rule each phrase carries, and say whether plain prose may leave it out. Some parts ask a different question, and say so. “Suppose \(n\) is odd.”, at the start of a proof of “if \(n\) is odd, then \(n^2\) is odd”. “In either case, \(x^2 \ge 0\) .” “Since \(x \ne 0\) , the first case is impossible, so \(x = 3\) ”, after “ \(x = 0\) or \(x = 3\) ”. “ \(x > 2\) , so certainly \(x \ge 2\) .” “This contradicts \(n^2 \ge 0\) .” “Conversely, suppose \(x^2 = 4\) and \(x > 0\) .” “Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(n\) is not prime”, in a proof that ends “Hence \(n\) is prime.” A proof that \(\sqrt 5\) is irrational opens: “Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(\sqrt 5\) is rational.” Which annotation would its derivation print beside that assumption? “Suppose \(15\) is a perfect square. … a contradiction. Hence \(15\) is not a perfect square.” Which face of “by contradiction” is this? A proof of “if \(x^2 < 1\) , then \(x > -1\) ” begins “Suppose \(x \le -1\) . Then \(-x \ge 1\) , so \(x^2 = (-x)^2 \ge 1\) .” What should come before it? “Let \(n\) be even, say \(n = 2k\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(n^2\) is not even. Then \(n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2)\) is even, which contradicts \(n^2\) not being even. Hence \(n^2\) is even.” Is this proof in costume? Four conditions are to be shown equivalent. How many implications does a cycle need, and how many would proofs of every ordered pair need?

title: Exercise (B1: Take off the costume)
content: Here is a proof that \(\frac{a + b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}\) for all real \(a > 0\) and \(b > 0\) . Let \(a, b > 0\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(\frac{a+b}{2} < \sqrt{ab}\) . Since \((\sqrt a - \sqrt b)^2 \ge 0\) , expanding gives \(a - 2\sqrt{ab} + b \ge 0\) , so \(\frac{a+b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}\) . This contradicts our assumption. Hence \(\frac{a+b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}\) . Which costume is this? Justify your answer by saying where the assumption of the box is cited. Rewrite the proof without the contradiction.

title: Exercise (B3: Two clauses of a least upper bound)
content: Let \(A \coloneqq \{ x \in \nR : 0 < x < 2 \}\) . Prove that \(2\) is an upper bound of \(A\) , and that no real number \(t < 2\) is an upper bound of \(A\) . Tag each step with its rule. Hint: in the second part, take a number halfway between \(\max\{t, 0\}\) and \(2\) .

title: Exercise (B4: Two integers of the same parity)
content: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers. Prove that the following are equivalent, by a cycle: (i) \(a + b\) is even; (ii) \(a - b\) is even; (iii) \(a\) and \(b\) are both even or both odd. Say which arrow closes the cycle, and tag the logical steps of that arrow.

title: Exercise (C1: Euclid without the contradiction)
content: Here is a common proof that there are infinitely many primes. It uses two facts about integers that we take as known here: every integer \(m \ge 2\) has a prime divisor ( Sets and Functions , Chapter 3 proves it); and if an integer \(d\) divides two integers, it divides their difference (if \(u = dk\) and \(v = dl\) , then \(u - v = d(k - l)\) ). Suppose, for a contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, say \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) . Let \(N \coloneqq p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1\) . Then \(N \ge 2\) , so \(N\) has a prime divisor \(p\) . Since \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) are all the primes, \(p = p_i\) for some \(i\) . Then \(p_i\) divides both \(N\) and \(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k\) , so it divides their difference \(1\) , which is impossible for a prime. This is a contradiction. Hence there are infinitely many primes. “There are infinitely many primes” means “the set of primes is not finite”. Is the last step of the proof \(\rulename{RAA}\) or \(\rulename{\neg I}\) ? Where is the assumption “ \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) are all the primes” used? Which smell from this section does that suggest? Rewrite the argument as a direct proof of: for every finite list \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) of primes, with \(k \ge 1\) , there is a prime not in the list. Say what the rewrite gains over the original.

title: Exercise (C2: Which face, and the weakest form)
content: Here is a proof that if \(x\) is a real number with \(x^2 < \varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) , then \(x = 0\) . Suppose \(x^2 < \varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(x \ne 0\) . Then \(x^2 > 0\) , so we may take \(\varepsilon = x^2\) , and the hypothesis gives \(x^2 < x^2\) , which is impossible. Hence \(x = 0\) . Which face of “by contradiction” is this, as written? Rewrite the proof in the weakest form you can, and say which rules it uses at its logical steps, and which school fact.

title: Example (Two inclusions)
content: Let \(A \coloneqq \{ x \in \nR : x^2 \le 2x \}\) and \(B \coloneqq \{ x \in \nR : 0 \le x \le 2 \}\) . Prove that \(A = B\) , and tag the steps that carry the logic.

title: Example (A sequence has at most one limit)
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a sequence of real numbers with \(a_n \to L\) and \(a_n \to M\) . Prove that \(L = M\) , and annotate each phrase with its rule.

title: Example (The reciprocals tend to zero)
content: Prove that \(1/n \to 0\) , for the sequence \((1/n)_{n \ge 1}\) . Annotate each phrase with its rule, and state what the chosen constant depends on.

title: Example (An induction, and a legitimate symmetry)
content: Let \(a\) be a real number with \(0 < a \le 1\) . Prove that \(0 < a^n \le 1\) for every \(n \in \nN\) , and annotate each phrase with its rule. Let \(a\) and \(b\) be real numbers. Prove that \(\abs{a - b} = \max\{a, b\} - \min\{a, b\}\) , with a “without loss of generality”, and write out the case split it abbreviates.

title: Example (A constant sequence)
content: Let \(c\) be a real number and let \(a_n \coloneqq c\) for every \(n \in \nN\) . Prove that \(a_n \to c\) , and annotate each phrase with its rule.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a sequence of real numbers and \(L\) a real number. Here is a proof that if \(a_n \to L\) and \(L > 0\) , then \(a_n > 0\) for all large \(n\) . Its sentences are numbered. Suppose \(a_n \to L\) and \(L > 0\) . (2) Then \(L/2 > 0\) . (3) Choose \(N \in \nN\) such that \(\abs{a_n - L} < L/2\) for every \(n \ge N\) . (4) Let \(n \in \nN\) with \(n \ge N\) . (5) Then \(L - a_n \le \abs{a_n - L} < L/2\) , so \(a_n > L/2 > 0\) . (6) Hence \(a_n > 0\) for every \(n \ge N\) , that is, \(a_n > 0\) for all large \(n\) . Name the rule or rules carried by each sentence. Sentence (3) has no dependency parenthesis. What should it say, and why does \(N\) not depend on \(n\) ? Which instance of \(\rulename{\forall E}\) in the proof is not the obvious one? Which closing lines are silent?

title: Exercise (A2: Drill)
content: Each part takes a line or two. Most parts ask which rule a phrase carries, whether it may be silent, or for a judgment or a sentence. “Fix \(\varepsilon > 0\) .” Which rule, and may it be silent? “Applying the hypothesis with \(\varepsilon/3\) in place of \(\varepsilon\) .” Which rule, and may the term go unnamed? “Take \(\delta \coloneqq \varepsilon/5\) .” Which rule, may it be silent, and what does \(\delta\) depend on? “By hypothesis there is \(k\) with \(m = 2k + 1\) ; choose such a \(k\) .” Which rule, and what does it require of the name? In “Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Choose \(N\) such that … . Let \(n \ge N\) .”, may \(N\) depend on \(n\) ? In “Let \(x \in A\) . Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Choose \(\delta > 0\) such that …”, may \(\delta\) depend on \(x\) ? Write “ \(x^2 > 0\) for all \(x \ne 0\) ” with the quantifier in front. Negate “ \(a_n > 0\) for all large \(n\) ” with no \(\neg\) in front of a quantifier. A proof of “ \(\max\{a, b\} \ge a\) ” begins “Without loss of generality \(a \le b\) .” Is that legitimate? In an induction, which sentence opens the box of the induction hypothesis? To prove \(A = B\) , a proof shows \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq A\) . Which rules does that pattern use, and how does each inclusion open? A proof begins “Let \(m\) be the least element of \(A\) ”. What must already be on the page?

title: Exercise (B1: Ambiguous English)
content: Each sentence has a quantifier phrase at its end. Write both readings in symbols, with the quantifiers in front, and decide whether each reading is true for the function given. “ \(f(x) \le M\) for every real \(x\) , for some real \(M\) ”, for \(f(x) = x\) . “ \(x + y = 0\) for some real \(y\) , for every real \(x\) .” “ \(\abs{x - y} < \delta\) implies \(\abs{f(x) - f(y)} < 1\) for all real \(x, y\) , for some \(\delta > 0\) ”, for \(f(x) = x^2\) .

title: Exercise (B2: An induction, annotated)
content: Prove that \(5^n - 1\) is divisible by \(4\) for every \(n \in \nN\) . Annotate each phrase of your proof with its rule, and say which hypothesis of @ax-induction each part of the proof establishes.

title: Exercise (B3: Six, two and three, used later)
content: Let \(A \coloneqq \{ n \in \nZ : 6 \mid n \}\) and \(B \coloneqq \{ n \in \nZ : 2 \mid n \text{ and } 3 \mid n \}\) . Prove \(A = B\) by double inclusion. Name each “let”, each “choose” with its fresh name, and each witness.

title: Exercise (C1: When “similarly” is honest)
content: Prove that \(\max\{x, y\} + \min\{x, y\} = x + y\) for all real \(x\) and \(y\) , with a “without loss of generality”. Then write out the \(\rulename{\vee E}\) it abbreviates, and check that its second box is the first with the letters exchanged. Let \(x \ge 0\) and \(y\) be real numbers. A student proves \(x \max\{x, y\} \ge xy\) as follows: “Without loss of generality \(x \le y\) . Then \(\max\{x, y\} = y\) , and \(xy \ge xy\) .” Explain why “without loss of generality” is not legitimate here, prove the case the student skipped, and show by an example that the hypothesis \(x \ge 0\) cannot be dropped from the statement.

title: Exercise (C2: Moving a quantifier changes the meaning)
content: Give an example of a sentence of analysis, in English, that begins “for every \(x\) …”, whose meaning changes when the phrase “for every \(x\) ” is moved to the end of the sentence. Write both readings in symbols and show that one is true and the other false.

title: Definition 8.3.1 (Levels of Proof)
content: A proof can be written at four levels . Level 0, the full derivation. A derivation in the sense of @def-derivation , with the rules of Chapters 1, 2 and 5: every line is a premise, an assumption, or one rule applied to available lines. A derived rule used as one line ( @def-derived-rule ), such as the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules , counts as one rule. Facts about numbers enter as premises, or as lines justified “arith”, each of which records one such fact applied to the lines it cites. Level 1, the skeleton. The boxes and the logical lines only: every assumption, every flagged name, every line that opens or closes a box, with the rule that closes it, and every line that such a closing line cites. Each stretch of mathematics between them is compressed into one line, justified “arith”, “by def”, or by a cited result; a stretch of routine logical steps inside one box is compressed into one line justified by the names of its rules in order, such as “ \(\rulename{\forall E}\) , \(\rulename{\exists I}\) ”. Level 2, annotated prose. Sentences, each tagged in brackets with the rule or rules it carries, such as [ \(\rulename{\forall I}\) ] or [ \(\rulename{\exists E}\) ]. Level 3, plain prose. Sentences without tags, in which some steps are left unsaid. Which steps may be left unsaid is fixed by the convention that follows, not by the writer.

title: Definition 8.3.2 (Silent Steps)
Example (The irrationality of the square root of two at four levels)
content: Write the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational , that no rational number has square \(2\) , at levels 0, 1, 2 and 3 of @def-levels-of-proof , and match the levels line by line.

title: Example (Two columns)
content: Prove that \(x^2 - 6x + 10 > 0\) for every real \(x\) . (b) Let \(a_n \coloneqq (2n + 1)/(n + 1)\) for \(n \in \nN\) . Prove that \(a_n \to 2\) . Plan each proof as a column of reductions, then write it.

title: Example (Uniformly continuous implies continuous, at four levels)
content: Write the proof of @exm-uniform-implies-continuous , that a function uniformly continuous on \(A\) is continuous at every point of \(A\) , at levels 1 and 3, and say where each level records what \(\delta\) depends on.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Parts (a)–(c) are about @exm-uniform-four-levels , parts (d) and (e) about @exm-sqrt2-four-levels . Which lines of the level-1 skeleton does the level-3 sentence “Let \(x \in A\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\) ” stand for? Which open a box, which close one, and which are written at level 3? Where is the dependence of \(\delta\) recorded at levels 1 and 3? State the idea of the proof in two sentences. At which line of levels 1, 2 and 3 is the “not both even” clause of (L) used to reach the contradiction? True or false, with a reason: at level 3, the sentence “hence \(r^2 \ne 2\) ” may be left out of the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational , since the reader has just been told that a contradiction was reached.

title: Exercise (A2: Drill)
content: Each part takes a line or two. (a) names a level; (b)–(f) decide whether a step may be silent at level 3; (g) and (h) judge a text; (i) and (j) decide whether a line may be justified TAUT; (k) and (l) work with an “it suffices to show” column. “Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) [ \(\rulename{\forall I}\) ]. Take \(\delta \coloneqq \varepsilon/2\) [ \(\rulename{\exists I}\) ]. …” At which level is this text written? At level 3, may “since \(x\) was arbitrary” be left out? May “choose \(k\) with \(n = 2k\) ” be left out? May “by the triangle inequality” be left out? May “in particular \(x > 0\) ”, after “since \(0 < x < 1\) ”, be left out? May the split “ \(x \ge 0\) or \(x < 0\) , and every real \(x\) is one or the other” be left out? A skeleton has the line “ \(\abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon\) , arith”. Is the proof finished? A text says “Let \(r\) be rational. Then \(p\) is even.” Name two never-silent steps that are missing. From Section 6.3 on, may the level-1 line \(x_0 > 0\) , citing the line \(x_0 > 0 \wedge y_0 > 0\) , be justified TAUT? May the line \(\forall y\, \forall x\, R(x, y)\) , citing \(\forall x\, \forall y\, R(x, y)\) , be justified TAUT? A column for “ \(2^{n+1} > n + 1\) , given \(2^n > n\) and \(n \ge 1\) ” has the first row “it suffices to show \(2^n + 2^n > n + 1\) ”. What is that row’s reason, and what row could come next? In an “it suffices to show” column, which row is proved outright, with no further reduction?

title: Exercise (B1: Some-all gives all-some, on the natural numbers)
content: Read @prp-exists-forall-swap over the domain \(\nN\) , with \(R(x, y)\) as “ \(x \le y\) ”: from \(\exists x\, \forall y\, (x \le y)\) , conclude \(\forall y\, \exists x\, (x \le y)\) . The premise is true, with the witness \(x = 0\) . Write the proof at levels 1, 2 and 3. Your proof must use the premise, although this instance of the conclusion also has a one-line proof, with \(x = y\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Back from prose to a skeleton, with blanks)
content: Here is a level-3 proof. Claim. If \(n\) is an odd integer, then \(8 \mid n^2 - 1\) . Let \(n\) be odd, say \(n = 2k + 1\) with \(k\) an integer. Then \(n^2 - 1 = 4k(k + 1)\) , so it suffices to show that \(k(k + 1)\) is even. If \(k = 2j\) for an integer \(j\) , then \(k(k + 1) = 2 \cdot j(2j + 1)\) ; if \(k = 2j + 1\) , then \(k(k + 1) = 2 \cdot (2j + 1)(j + 1)\) . Either way \(k(k + 1) = 2i\) for an integer \(i\) , and then \(n^2 - 1 = 8i\) . Work over the domain \(\nZ\) , with “ \(n\) is odd” as \(\exists k\, (n = 2k + 1)\) and \(8 \mid m\) as \(\exists t\, (m = 8t)\) . Here is its level-1 skeleton with nine blanks, labeled (i)–(ix). Name the move, then complete it , and say where the proof uses the fact (E1) of Section 2.1, that every integer is even or odd.

title: Exercise (B3: A column of reductions)
content: Prove that \(\abs{x - 1} + \abs{x + 1} \ge 2\) for every real \(x\) by an “it suffices to show” column, each row with its reason. Turn the column into a level-3 proof. Which reasons in your column are \(\rulename{{=}E}\) steps that level 3 may leave silent? A student’s column has the row “it suffices to show \(\abs{x - 1} \ge 1\) and \(\abs{x + 1} \ge 1\) ”. Is that row’s reason correct? Can the student finish?

title: Exercise (C1: Arbitrarily close numbers, at two levels)
content: Consider @prp-arbitrarily-close-equal : for real numbers \(a\) and \(b\) , if \(\abs{a - b} < \varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) , then \(a = b\) . Write its proof at level 1, as a skeleton in which school facts about \(\abs{\cdot}\) and \(<\) are lines justified “arith”. Write it at level 3. Which lines of your skeleton are silent at level 3? Which instance of \(\rulename{\forall E}\) must the level-3 text name, and why?

title: Exercise (C2: Exit check: levels)
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a sequence of real numbers with \(a_n \to L\) , and let \(c \ne 0\) be a real number. Here is a level-0 derivation that \(c \, a_n \to cL\) , with the definition of a limit as in @exm-translate-limit (a), the hypothesis \(c \ne 0\) as premise 2, and two lines of school arithmetic justified “arith”. Write the proof at level 2 and at level 3. Then say in one sentence how the case \(c = 0\) goes.

title: Exercise (C3: Back from prose to a skeleton)
content: Here is a level-3 proof. Claim. For every integer \(n\) , \(4 \mid n^2\) or \(4 \mid n^2 - 1\) . Let \(n\) be an integer. If \(n\) is even, say \(n = 2k\) , then \(n^2 = 4k^2\) , so \(4 \mid n^2\) . If \(n\) is odd, say \(n = 2k + 1\) , then \(n^2 - 1 = 4k^2 + 4k = 4(k^2 + k)\) , so \(4 \mid n^2 - 1\) . Reconstruct its level-1 skeleton. Work over the domain \(\nZ\) , with “ \(n\) is even” as \(\exists k\, (n = 2k)\) , “ \(n\) is odd” as \(\exists k\, (n = 2k + 1)\) and \(4 \mid m\) as \(\exists t\, (m = 4t)\) . Name the rule that closes each box, and name every step of the skeleton that the prose leaves unsaid. Hint: The claim is a disjunction for every \(n\) . Which disjunct is reached in each case, and by which rule?

title: Example (Explaining a proof, well and badly)
content: Claim. For every real number \(x > 0\) , \(x + 1/x \ge 2\) . Proof. Let \(x > 0\) . \((x - 1)^2 \ge 0\) . So \(x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0\) . Dividing by \(x\) , \(x - 2 + 1/x \ge 0\) . Hence \(x + 1/x \ge 2\) . Self-explain each line of the proof.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Here is a proof that if \(a > 0\) , \(b > 0\) and \(a^2 = b^2\) , then \(a = b\) . \(a^2 - b^2 = 0\) . (2) \((a - b)(a + b) = 0\) . (3) \(a + b > 0\) . (4) Hence \(a - b = 0\) , that is, \(a = b\) . Classify each explanation as one that justifies its line or one that paraphrases it. “Line 1 follows from the hypothesis \(a^2 = b^2\) by subtracting \(b^2\) from both sides.” “Line 2: then the factored form is zero as well.” “Line 2 is line 1 rewritten with the identity \(u^2 - v^2 = (u - v)(u + v)\) , at \(u = a\) and \(v = b\) .” “Line 3: now we know that \(a + b\) is positive.” “Line 3 holds because \(a > 0\) and \(b > 0\) are hypotheses, and a sum of two positive numbers is positive.” “Line 4: so \(a - b\) is zero, which is what we wanted.”

title: Exercise (A2: Drill)
content: Answer each part in a phrase. (a) and (b) ask whether an explanation justifies or paraphrases; (c) and (d) which of the four questions is at work; (e) and (f) what kind of line it is; (g)–(i) name the unstated fact; (k) locates a hypothesis; (j) and (l) are about the habits of good readers. A line: “Since \(n\) is even, \(n^2\) is even.” An explanation: “With \(n = 2k\) , \(n^2 = 2(2k^2)\) , and \(2k^2\) is an integer.” Does it justify or paraphrase? A line: “ \(x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1)\) .” An explanation: “We factor it.” Justify or paraphrase? Which of the four questions asks “May we divide by \(x - 1\) here?” Which question does the answer “this line opens a box” answer? What kind of line is “Choose \(\delta > 0\) such that …”, and what does its derivation print beside it? What kind of line is “Since \(\varepsilon\) was arbitrary, …”? Name the unstated fact: “Since \(0 < a < b\) , \(a^2 < b^2\) .” Name the unstated fact: “ \(\abs{x - 2} < 1\) , so \(x > 1\) .” Name the unstated facts: “ \(x^2 = 9\) and \(x > 0\) , so \(x = 3\) .” After three readings, a proof feels clear. Has the reader self-explained it? “Let \(x < 0\) . Then \(1/x < 0\) .” Which hypothesis is used, and how? “Before reading the proof, I tried the claim myself by squaring both sides.” Which strategy is this?

title: Exercise (B1: Self-explain a counterexample)
content:
Here, with its lines numbered, is the half of @exm-square-not-uniform that shows \(f(x) = x^2\) is not uniformly continuous on \(
R\) . By the negation of uniform continuity, with the bounds \(x \in 
R\) and \(y \in 
R\) dropped because they always hold, we must show \[ \exists \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall \delta > 0 \; \exists x \; \exists y \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta \wedge \abs{x^2 - y^2} \ge \varepsilon  igr). \] Take \(\varepsilon = 1\) . (3) Let \(\delta > 0\) be arbitrary, and take \(x \coloneqq 1/\delta\) and \(y \coloneqq 1/\delta + \delta/2\) , which depend on \(\delta\) . (4) Then \(\abs{x - y} = \delta/2 < \delta\) , (5) and, since \(y > x > 0\) , \[ \abs{x^2 - y^2} = (y - x)(y + x) =  rac{\delta}{2} \Bigl(  rac{2}{\delta} +  rac{\delta}{2} \Bigr) = 1 +  rac{\delta^2}{4} \ge 1 . \] Since \(\delta\) was arbitrary, uniform continuity fails. Self-explain each line, citing labels where a line uses an earlier result. Say at which lines \(\delta > 0\) is used.

title: Exercise (B2: The unjustified line)
content: Here is a proof that for real numbers \(x < y\) , \(x^3 < y^3\) . Let \(x < y\) . (2) Then \(y^3 - x^3 = (y - x)(y^2 + xy + x^2)\) . (3) Since \(x < y\) , \(y - x > 0\) . (4) Also \(y^2 + xy + x^2 > 0\) . (5) So \(y^3 - x^3 > 0\) , as a product of two positive numbers. (6) Hence \(x^3 < y^3\) . Every line is true. Line 1 opens the box; of the rest, all but one are instances of a routine algebra or order fact, cited or not; one line is not an instance of any fact stated so far, and it needs an argument of its own. Self-explain the proof line by line to find it, and supply that argument as its warrant.

title: Exercise (B3: Name the unstated facts)
content: Here is a proof. Claim. For every real \(x \ge 0\) , \(x^3 + 2 \ge 3x\) . \(x^3 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)^2 (x + 2)\) . (2) \((x - 1)^2 \ge 0\) . (3) \(x + 2 > 0\) . (4) So \(x^3 - 3x + 2 \ge 0\) , (5) that is, \(x^3 + 2 \ge 3x\) . Name the unstated fact behind each line. Which line uses the hypothesis \(x \ge 0\) , and how? Find the least \(c\) such that the same proof, with at most two lines reworded, proves the claim for every \(x \ge c\) . Show that the claim fails at \(x = -3\) .

title: Exercise (C1: A longer proof)
content:
Here is a proof that a sequence has at most one limit, with its lines numbered. Claim. If \(a_n 	o L\) and \(a_n 	o M\) , then \(L = M\) . Suppose \(a_n 	o L\) and \(a_n 	o M\) , and suppose, for a contradiction, that \(L 
e M\) . (2) Let \(\varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{L - M}/2\) . Then \(\varepsilon > 0\) . (3) Choose \(N_1 \in 
N\) such that \(\abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \ge N_1\) , and \(N_2 \in 
N\) such that \(\abs{a_n - M} < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \ge N_2\) . (4) Let \(n \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}\) . (5) Then \(\abs{L - M} \le \abs{L - a_n} + \abs{a_n - M} < \varepsilon + \varepsilon = \abs{L - M}\) . (6) So \(\abs{L - M} < \abs{L - M}\) , which is impossible. (7) Hence \(L = M\) . Self-explain each line, citing labels where a line uses an earlier result. Say where the assumption \(L 
e M\) is used, and which rule closes the box it opens.

title: Exercise (C2: Challenge: A proof about derivations)
content: Self-explain the proof of @lem-atom-splitting in Section 4.8: for each of its five numbered steps, and for each claim in the paragraph that follows them, say what it uses and why that is legitimate. Then state the idea of the proof in two sentences.

title: Example (Label every sentence)
content: Here is a short proof. Label each sentence with the rule it uses. Claim. For a real number \(x\) , if \(\abs{x - 1} < 1\) , then \(x > 0\) . Proof. (1) Assume \(\abs{x - 1} < 1\) . (2) Every real number is at least \(1\) or below it, so either \(x \ge 1\) or \(x < 1\) . (3) Suppose first that \(x \ge 1\) . (4) Then \(x \ge 1 > 0\) . (5) Suppose instead that \(x < 1\) . (6) Then \(x - 1 < 0\) , so \(\abs{x - 1} = 1 - x\) . (7) Hence \(1 - x < 1\) , that is, \(x > 0\) . (8) In either case \(x > 0\) , which proves the claim.

title: Example (One of three, generalized)
content: Here are two proofs that one of \(17\) , \(18\) , \(19\) is a multiple of \(3\) . (P1) \(18 = 3 \cdot 6\) . (P2) \(17 = 3 \cdot 5 + 2\) , so \(17 + 1 = 3 \cdot 6\) . Which one generalizes to “for every integer \(n\) , one of \(n\) , \(n + 1\) , \(n + 2\) is a multiple of \(3\) ”? Write the general proof.

title: Example (A subset of a bounded set)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets of real numbers with \(A \subseteq B\) . Prove that if \(B\) is bounded above, then \(A\) is bounded above.

title: Example (From a derivation to a paragraph)
content: Let \(n\) be an integer. Write \(E\) for “ \(n\) is even”, \(O\) for “ \(n\) is odd”, \(F\) for “ \(n + 1\) is even”, and \(G\) for “ \(n(n + 1)\) is even”. The derivation below uses four facts about integers as premises. Write the paragraph a mathematician would write for it.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Here is a proof. Claim. For real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) , if \(x + y > 2\) , then \(x > 1\) or \(y > 1\) . Assume \(x + y > 2\) . (2) Suppose, for a contradiction, that it is not the case that \(x > 1\) or \(y > 1\) . (3) Then \(x > 1\) fails and \(y > 1\) fails. (4) So \(x \le 1\) and \(y \le 1\) . (5) Adding, \(x + y \le 2\) . (6) This contradicts \(x + y > 2\) . (7) Hence \(x > 1\) or \(y > 1\) , which proves the claim. Label each sentence with the rule it uses, as in @exm-annotate-abs . Which sentence closes an \(\rulename{RAA}\) box, and which uses one of De Morgan’s laws ( @prp-de-morgan )? Which law? Everything inside the box of (2) follows from (2) alone, until the clash in (6). Which face of “by contradiction” (Section 8.1) does the proof wear, and which face is it really? Write the first sentence of the rewritten proof. Sentence (7) closes two boxes. Which of the two closings may be silent at level 3, by @def-silent-steps ?

title: Exercise (A2: Drill)
content: Answer each part in a line. The parts follow the procedure: (a)–(b) symbols and unwinding, (c)–(d) the skeleton, (e) the order on the page, (f), (g), (i) the conventions, (h) the search and the page, (j)–(k) generalizing, (l) the Givens/Goal table. Write in symbols, with every quantifier and bound: “the square of every odd integer is odd” (domain \(\nZ\) ). Unwind “the sequence \((a_n)\) is bounded” (Section 5.6). The goal is \(\forall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \; \forall x \; (\abs{x - a} < \delta \to \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon)\) . What are the first and the last line of the outer box? A hypothesis says “some integer \(k\) has \(n = 2k + 1\) ”. When does its box open? On the page, which comes first: “let \(\delta \coloneqq \varepsilon/4\) ” or “let \(x\) be a real number with \(\abs{x - 1} < \delta\) ”? “ \(x\) is positive and \(y\) is negative, and so \(xy < 0\) and \(x - y > 0\) .” Which convention does this break? A proof uses \(c\) in its fourth sentence, and \(c\) appears nowhere before. Which convention, and which entry of Section 8.6? Is “this holds if \(x < 2\) ” a sentence of the page? Claim: \(x^2 - 4x + 3 < 0\) for \(1 < x < 3\) . A proof ends “… so \(x^2 - 4x + 3 = (x - 1)(x - 3)\) .” What is missing? A proof about the number \(12\) uses only “ \(12\) is a multiple of \(4\) ”. For which integers does the same proof prove the same claim? A proof about “an arbitrary odd \(n\) ” uses \(n > 0\) in one line. What does it prove? Givens \(\forall x \in A \; (x \in B)\) and \(\forall x \in B \; (x \in C)\) ; Goal \(\forall x \in A \; (x \in C)\) . Write the next row of the Givens/Goal table.

title: Exercise (B1: From skeleton to prose)
content: Each part gives a statement and a level-1 skeleton of its proof. Write the proof at level 3, keeping every step that @def-silent-steps says is never silent. For every integer \(n\) , if \(n\) is odd, then \(3n + 5\) is even. (Domain \(\nZ\) .) No real number \(x\) satisfies \(x^2 + 1 = 2x - 1\) . (Domain \(\nR\) .) For a real number \(x\) : \(x^3 = x\) if and only if \(x = -1\) , \(x = 0\) or \(x = 1\) . (Here \(x\) is fixed; “or” chains group to the right.) Hint: line 3 of (c) uses the school fact that a product of real numbers is zero only if one of its factors is zero.

title: Exercise (B2: Put the proof in order)
content:
Let \((a_n)\) and \((b_n)\) be sequences of real numbers with \(a_n 	o L\) and \(b_n 	o M\) , where “ \(a_n 	o L\) ” is the pattern of Section 6.1: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(N \in 
N\) such that \(\abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \ge N\) . Eight of the ten sentences below, in a suitable order, form a level-3 proof that \(a_n + b_n 	o L + M\) ; two are distractors. Write down an order for the eight, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each distractor is wrong. Let \(n \in 
N\) with \(n \ge N\) . Since \(b_n 	o M\) and \(\varepsilon/2 > 0\) , choose \(N_2 \in 
N\) (depending on \(\varepsilon\) ) such that \(\abs{b_n - M} < \varepsilon/2\) for every \(n \ge N_2\) . Let \(N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}\) , where \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) serve every \(\varepsilon\) at once. Then \(n \ge N_1\) and \(n \ge N_2\) . Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Since \(n \ge N\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\) were arbitrary, \(a_n + b_n 	o L + M\) . Choose \(N_1 \in 
N\) such that \(\abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \ge N_1\) . Let \(N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}\) . So \(\abs{(a_n + b_n) - (L + M)} \le \abs{a_n - L} + \abs{b_n - M} < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon\) . Since \(a_n 	o L\) and \(\varepsilon/2 > 0\) , choose \(N_1 \in 
N\) (depending on \(\varepsilon\) ) such that \(\abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon/2\) for every \(n \ge N_1\) .

title: Exercise (B3: The last step)
content: Here is a level-1 skeleton for the statement “for real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) , if \(x\) is rational and \(y\) is irrational, then \(x + y\) is irrational”, with \(x\) and \(y\) fixed: and its level-3 prose, with the closing sentence of the \(\rulename{\neg I}\) box left blank: Let \(x\) be rational and \(y\) irrational. Suppose \(x + y\) is rational. Then \(y = (x + y) - x\) is a difference of two rational numbers, so \(y\) is rational. This contradicts the irrationality of \(y\) . \(\underline{\qquad\qquad}\) Name the move, then complete it.

title: Exercise (B4: Which proof generalizes?)
content: Two proofs that \(6\) divides \(7^3 - 7 = 336\) : (P1) “ \(336 = 6 \cdot 56\) .” (P2) “ \(7^3 - 7 = 6 \cdot 7 \cdot 8\) , a product of three consecutive integers; one of them is even and one is a multiple of \(3\) , so \(6\) divides the product.” Which proof generalizes to “for every integer \(n\) , \(6 \mid n^3 - n\) ”, and why does the other not? Write the general proof at level 3, with its fresh name and every fact it uses. Which fact about \(6\) does (P2) leave unstated?

title: Exercise (C1: A constant found backwards)
content: Let \(f(x) = 2x + 3\) and let \(a\) be a fixed real number. Prove that for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(\abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon\) for every real \(x\) with \(\abs{x - a} < \delta\) . Write your answer as an Idea, which finds \(\delta\) backwards, followed by a Proof, which runs forwards. Say what \(\delta\) depends on.

title: Exercise (C2: Rewrite it properly)
content: A sequence \((a_n)\) is bounded if there is \(M \in \nR\) with \(\abs{a_n} \le M\) for every \(n \in \nN\) (Section 5.6). The following proof that a sequence \((a_n)\) with \(a_n \to L\) is bounded is correct in substance but badly written. We want some \(M\) with \(\abs{a_n} \le M\) . For big \(n\) , \(a_n\) is near \(L\) , so \(\abs{a_n}\) is less than \(\abs{L} + 1\) if we use \(1\) for \(\varepsilon\) . The small \(n\) are only finitely many, so take the biggest. So \(M\) is the max of all of them and it works. Name three faults of the text, each by the convention it breaks (this section) or the step that is not written. Rewrite the proof at level 3.

title: Exercise (C3: From \sqrt 2 to \sqrt 3, and not to \sqrt 4)
content: The level-3 proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational in @exm-sqrt2-four-levels uses (L) and @thm-square-even-implies-even . Rewrite it as a proof that no rational number has square \(3\) . You may use \((\mathrm{L}_3)\) : every rational number is \(p/q\) with integers \(p\) , \(q\) , \(q \ne 0\) , not both multiples of \(3\) . Prove the lemma your proof needs in place of @thm-square-even-implies-even . Rewrite it once more for \(4\) , with \((\mathrm{L}_4)\) : every rational number is \(p/q\) with integers \(p\) , \(q\) , \(q \ne 0\) , not both multiples of \(4\) , which is true. Which line fails? Why must some line fail? Say in one sentence what a generalization keeps and what it must prove again.

title: Example (What is not allowed)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content:
Each entry names the error, the rule it breaks and where that rule lives, and a failing instance whose conclusion is marked true or false : a wrong argument can reach either. Verifying instances and concluding “for all”. Breaks \(ulename{ orall I}\) , which needs one proof about a fresh name ( @def-rules-universal , Section 5.4). Instance: \(n^2 - n + 11\) is prime for \(n = 0, 1, \dots, 10\) (the values are \(11, 11, 13, 17, 23, 31, 41, 53, 67, 83, 101\) ), “so it is prime for every \(n \in 
N\) ”. False: at \(n = 11\) the value is \(121 = 11^2\) . A witness that depends on a variable introduced later, while uniformity is claimed. Breaks the side conditions of \(ulename{\exists E}\) and \(ulename{ orall I}\) : a witness \(\delta_0\) obtained inside the box of \(x_0\) may not leave it (Section 6.4, @exm-converse-fails ). Instance: “ \(x^2\) is continuous at every \(x\) , with \(\delta = \min\{1, \varepsilon/(2\abs{x} + 1)\}\) ; so one \(\delta\) for each \(\varepsilon\) serves every \(x\) , and \(x^2\) is uniformly continuous on \(
R\) ”. False ( @exm-square-not-uniform ). Treating the name from \(ulename{\exists E}\) as arbitrary. Breaks the side condition of \(ulename{ orall I}\) : the witness appears in the open assumption of its box ( @def-rules-existential , Section 5.6). Instance: “Some element of \(A\) is positive; let \(x\) be such an element. Since \(x\) was arbitrary, every element of \(A\) is positive.” False for \(A = \{-1, 1\}\) . Reusing one witness name for two \(ulename{\exists E}\) ’s. Breaks the fresh-name condition: the second name may not appear in an open assumption, and the first box’s assumption mentions it (Section 5.6, @exm-sum-of-evens ). Sibling boxes may share a name. Instance: “ \(m\) and \(n\) are even, so \(m = 2k\) and \(n = 2k\) for an integer \(k\) ; hence \(m = n\) ”. False: \(m = 2\) , \(n = 4\) . Proving the converse. Breaks \(ulename{{	o}I}\) , whose box opens with the hypothesis, not the conclusion ( @def-rules-implication , Section 1.4). Instance: “If \(x^2 > 1\) , then \(x > 1\) : suppose \(x > 1\) ; then \(x^2 > x > 1\) .” False: \(x = -2\) . Argument B of Section 1.1 makes the same move with a true conclusion. Affirming the consequent; denying the antecedent. Breaks @def-derivation (Section 1.4), being no rule: \(P 	o Q\) with \(Q\) gives no \(P\) , and with \(
eg P\) gives no \(
eg Q\) . Each pattern has a refuting row, so no derivation exists ( @cor-refuting-row , Section 4.7): @exm-affirming-the-consequent , and for denying the row \(P\) false, \(Q\) true. Instances: “a multiple of \(4\) is even and \(6\) is even, so \(6\) is a multiple of \(4\) ”; “… and \(6\) is not a multiple of \(4\) , so \(6\) is not even”. Both false . A missing case. Breaks \(ulename{\vee E}\) , which needs one box for each disjunct ( @def-rules-disjunction , Section 1.6). Instance: “ \(\abs{x} > 0\) for every real \(x\) : every real \(x\) has \(x > 0\) , \(x = 0\) or \(x < 0\) ; if \(x > 0\) , \(\abs{x} = x > 0\) ; if \(x < 0\) , \(\abs{x} = -x > 0\) ”. False: the case \(x = 0\) was dropped, and \(\abs{0} = 0\) . Cases that do not exhaust. Breaks \(ulename{\vee E}\) , whose first input must be a disjunction already derived (Section 1.6). Instance: “ \(x^2 \ge x\) for every real \(x\) : either \(x \ge 1\) or \(x \le 0\) ; in the first case \(x^2 = x \cdot x \ge x\) , in the second \(x^2 \ge 0 \ge x\) ”. False: \(x = 1/2\) satisfies neither case, and \(1/4 < 1/2\) . Citing a line that is not available: the goal itself (circular reasoning), a result proved later, or a general “fact” neither proved nor a true school fact (a false “fact” never qualifies). Breaks @def-derivation : every line is a premise, an assumption, or a rule applied to available lines (Section 1.4). Instances: “if \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) is even: suppose \(n^2\) is even; since \(n\) is even, …” ( true , and circular); “ \(x < 1\) , so \(x^2 < 1\) , since squaring preserves \(<\) ” ( false: \(x = -2\) ). Using an assumption after its box has closed. Breaks the scope rule of @def-derivation (Section 1.4). Instance: “Suppose \(n\) is even, say \(n = 2k\) ; then \(n^2 = 4k^2\) . Hence if \(n\) is even, \(4 \mid n^2\) . Now \(n^2 = 4k^2\) , so \(4 \mid n^2\) for every integer \(n\) .” False: \(n = 1\) . Proof D below makes the same move with a true conclusion. A wrong negation , in three forms. Each breaks \(ulename{RAA}\) , which closes only a box opened with \(
eg\varphi\) (Section 2.5), or the laws of Section 6.2. An \(ulename{RAA}\) box opened with a statement that is not the negation of the goal. Instance: “if \(x^2 > 9\) and \(x > 0\) , then \(x > 3\) : suppose, for a contradiction, that \(x < 3\) ; then \(0 < x < 3\) gives \(x^2 < 9\) , against \(x^2 > 9\) ; hence \(x > 3\) ” ( true : the box should open with \(x \le 3\) , and the case \(x = 3\) is never examined). A bound negated instead of a quantifier ( @prp-bounded-quantifier-negation ). Instance: “ \(a_n = 0\) does not converge to \(0\) , since some \(\varepsilon \le 0\) has \(\abs{a_n - 0} \ge \varepsilon\) for all \(n\) ” ( false ). The negation of \(\varphi 	o \psi\) written as an implication, \(
eg\varphi 	o 
eg\psi\) or \(\varphi 	o 
eg\psi\) , instead of \(\varphi \wedge 
eg\psi\) ( @prp-negated-implication ). Instance: “if \(x > 2\) , then \(x^2 > 4\) ” is “refuted” because “if \(x \le 2\) , then \(x^2 \le 4\) ” holds at \(x = 0\) ( false : both are true at \(x = 0\) , so one is not the negation of the other). Distinct letters taken for distinct objects. Two names introduced separately are treated as naming different objects, though no line says they differ. Breaks \(ulename{ orall I}\) : a box opened for two arbitrary names must cover every pair, including the pairs in which both name one object ( \(ulename{ orall E}\) may put the same term for both, @def-rule-universal-elimination ). Instance: “if \(a\) and \(b\) are roots of \(x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0\) , then \(a + b = 5\) : the two roots give \(x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - a)(x - b)\) , and comparing coefficients, \(a + b = 5\) ”. False: \(a = b = 2\) are roots, and \(2 + 2 = 4\) . An “and so on” with nothing behind it. A step is repeated “and so on”, and its outcome is used for every stage, but the passage from each stage to the next, or the reason the process ends, is never proved. Breaks @ax-induction (or @thm-strong-induction ): \(ulename{{	o}E}\) on the axiom needs its step as a line, and “and so on” is not that line. Instance: “a non-empty set \(A\) of positive rational numbers has a least element: take \(a_1 \in A\) ; if it is not least, take \(a_2 \in A\) with \(a_2 < a_1\) , and so on, until the least element is reached” ( false: \(\{ 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \}\) has no least element, and the process never ends). An object named before it is shown to exist. A step names an object, with “the …” or “let … be the …”, and so presupposes that such an object exists (for “the”, exactly one), though no line states or proves it. In (N9) the step asserts a fact that is not available; here the missing premise is never asserted at all, because it hides inside a name. Breaks \(ulename{\exists E}\) , which opens its box only by citing a line \(\exists x \, \varphi\) ( @def-rules-existential ), and the use of “the” (Section 5.8), which needs existence and uniqueness. Instance: “let \(N\) be the largest natural number; then \(N + 1 \le N\) , so \(1 \le 0\) ” ( false: the presupposed premise, that a largest natural number exists, is false).

title: Example (Proof A)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Claim. For a real number \(x\) , if \(x^2 - 3x + 2 < 0\) , then \(1 < x < 2\) . Assume \(x^2 - 3x + 2 < 0\) . (2) Then \((x - 1)(x - 2) < 0\) . (3) A product of two real numbers is negative only when one factor is positive and the other negative, so either \(x - 1 > 0\) and \(x - 2 < 0\) , or \(x - 1 < 0\) and \(x - 2 > 0\) . (4) In the first case, \(1 < x < 2\) . (5) In the second case, \(x < 1\) and \(x > 2\) , which is impossible. (6) Hence \(1 < x < 2\) .

title: Example (Proof B)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Claim. For an integer \(n\) , if \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) is even. Suppose \(n\) is even. (2) Then \(n = 2k\) for some integer \(k\) . (3) So \(n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2)\) . (4) Hence \(n^2\) is even. (5) Therefore, if \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) is even.

title: Example (Proof C)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Claim. For an integer \(n\) , the number \(n^2 - 2\) is not divisible by \(4\) . Suppose \(n^2 - 2\) is divisible by \(4\) , say \(n^2 - 2 = 4k\) with \(k\) an integer. (2) Then \(n^2 = 4k + 2 = 2(2k + 1)\) , so \(n^2\) is even. (3) By @thm-square-even-implies-even , \(n\) is even, say \(n = 2m\) with \(m\) an integer. (4) Then \(n^2 = 4m^2\) , so \(4m^2 = 4k + 2\) , and hence \(1 = 2(m^2 - k)\) . (5) So \(1\) is even. (6) But \(1\) is odd, and no integer is both even and odd; this is a contradiction. (7) Hence \(n^2 - 2\) is not divisible by \(4\) .

title: Example (Proof D)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Claim. For a real number \(x\) : if \(x > 1\) , then \(x^2 > x\) ; and \(x^2 + 1 > x\) . Suppose \(x > 1\) . (2) Multiplying both sides by \(x\) , which is positive, gives \(x^2 > x\) . (3) Hence if \(x > 1\) , then \(x^2 > x\) . (4) For the second part, \(x^2 + 1 > x^2\) , and \(x^2 > x\) by (2), so \(x^2 + 1 > x\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Each line below comes from a proof. Name the catalogue entry of @exm-not-allowed-catalogue that it commits, and the rule it breaks. “We checked \(3^n > n^2\) for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\) , so it holds for every \(n \in \nN\) .” “By hypothesis some \(x \in A\) has \(f(x) = 0\) ; fix such an \(x\) . Since \(x\) was arbitrary, \(f(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in A\) .” “To prove that \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) implies \(x_1 = x_2\) , suppose \(x_1 = x_2\) ; then \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) .” “To prove \(x > 0\) , suppose, for a contradiction, that \(x < 0\) .” “If \(n\) is divisible by \(6\) , then \(n\) is even. Since \(n\) is even, \(n\) is divisible by \(6\) .” “Every real \(x\) satisfies \(x > 0\) or \(x < 0\) ; we consider the two cases.”

title: Exercise (A2: Drill)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Name the entry of @exm-not-allowed-catalogue that each line commits, if any, and say whether its conclusion is true. “We checked that \(n^2 + n\) is even for \(n = 1, \dots, 6\) , so it is even for every \(n\) .” “Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and choose \(N\) with \(\abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon\) for \(n \ge N\) ; since \(\varepsilon\) was arbitrary, this one \(N\) works for every \(\varepsilon\) .” “ \(x\) and \(y\) are odd, so \(x = 2k + 1\) and \(y = 2k + 1\) .” “If \(n\) is divisible by \(4\) , then \(n\) is even; \(n\) is not divisible by \(4\) , so \(n\) is not even.” “ \(n^3 - n\) is even for every integer \(n\) : if \(n\) is even, say \(n = 2k\) , then \(n^3 - n = 2(4k^3 - k)\) ; so \(n^3 - n\) is even.” “Suppose \(x > 0\) ; then \(x^2 > 0\) . Hence if \(x > 0\) , then \(x^2 > 0\) . Since \(x^2 > 0\) , …” “The negation of ‘for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) , \(\abs{x} < \varepsilon\) ’ is ‘for some \(\varepsilon \le 0\) , \(\abs{x} \ge \varepsilon\) ’.” “To prove ‘if \(n^2\) is odd, then \(n\) is odd’: suppose \(n\) is odd; then \(n^2\) is odd.” “Let \(x\) and \(y\) be solutions of \(x^2 = 9\) . Then \(x^2 - y^2 = 0\) , so \((x - y)(x + y) = 0\) , and since \(x \ne y\) , \(x + y = 0\) .” “ \(a_1 = 2\) and \(a_{n+1} = a_n^2 - 2\) . Then \(a_2 = 2\) , \(a_3 = 2\) , and so on, so \(a_n = 2\) for every \(n \ge 1\) .” “Let \(n\) be the positive integer with \(n^2 = 2\) . Then \(1 < n^2 < 4\) , so \(1 < n < 2\) .” “From ‘ \(x > 0\) ’ and ‘( \(x > 0\) implies \(y > 0\) ) and ( \(y > 0\) implies \(z > 0\) )’, conclude ‘ \(z > 0\) ’ in one line.”

title: Exercise (B1: Two proofs in two columns)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Check each proof in two columns. For a wrong proof, name the first line that fails and its catalogue entry, and say whether the claim is true. Claim. For integers \(m\) and \(n\) , if \(m\) and \(n\) are odd, then \(m + n\) is even. (1) Assume \(m\) and \(n\) are odd. (2) Choose integers \(k\) and \(l\) with \(m = 2k + 1\) and \(n = 2l + 1\) . (3) Then \(m + n = 2k + 2l + 2 = 2(k + l + 1)\) . (4) Since \(k + l + 1\) is an integer, \(m + n\) is even. Claim. For a real number \(x\) , if \(x^2 < 1\) , then \(x < 1\) . (1) Assume \(x^2 < 1\) . (2) Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(x > 1\) . (3) Then \(x > 0\) , so \(x^2 = x \cdot x > x > 1\) . (4) This contradicts \(x^2 < 1\) . (5) Hence \(x < 1\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Find the error)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Find the error in the following proof, name its catalogue entry, and decide whether the claim is true. Claim. For all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) , \(\abs{x} + \abs{y} = \abs{x + y}\) . Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. (2) Either \(x\) and \(y\) are both \(\ge 0\) , or they are both \(< 0\) . (3) If both are \(\ge 0\) , then \(x + y \ge 0\) , so \(\abs{x} + \abs{y} = x + y = \abs{x + y}\) . (4) If both are \(< 0\) , then \(x + y < 0\) , so \(\abs{x} + \abs{y} = -x - y = -(x + y) = \abs{x + y}\) . (5) In either case \(\abs{x} + \abs{y} = \abs{x + y}\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Correct, or which entry?)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Each proof below is correct, or commits one of (N12), (N13), (N14); you are not told how many of each. For a correct proof, name its most delicate step. For a wrong one, name the entry, say whether the claim is true, and give a counterexample to the claim or a repair of the proof. Claim: for all integers \(m\) , \(n\) , if \(m\) and \(n\) are odd, then \(mn\) is odd. Proof: write \(m = 2k + 1\) and \(n = 2l + 1\) with integers \(k\) , \(l\) ; then \(mn = 4kl + 2k + 2l + 1 = 2(2kl + k + l) + 1\) . Claim: for all real \(a\) , \(b\) , if \(a^2 = b^2\) , then \(a = b\) or \(a = -b\) . Proof: \((a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2 = 0\) , and a product of real numbers is \(0\) only if a factor is. Claim: for all integers \(m\) , \(n\) , \(m^2 + n^2 \ge 1\) . Proof: two different integers are not both \(0\) , so one of \(m^2\) , \(n^2\) is at least \(1\) . Claim: every integer \(n \ge 2\) is a product of primes. Proof: if \(n\) is prime, it is a product of one prime. If not, \(n = ab\) with \(1 < a, b < n\) ; split \(a\) and \(b\) in the same way, and so on, until only primes remain. Claim: \(1\) is a solution of \(x^2 + x + 1 = 0\) . Proof: let \(x\) be the real solution. Then \(x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1) = 0\) , so \(x^3 = 1\) , and since \(x\) is real, \(x = 1\) .

title: Exercise (C1: The second half)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Let \(f \colon \nR \to \nR\) be continuous at \(a\) , as the quantifier pattern of Section 6.1: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(\abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon\) for every real \(x\) with \(\abs{x - a} < \delta\) . Suppose \(f(a) > 0\) . Here is a level-1 skeleton for the statement “there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(f(x) > 0\) for every \(x\) with \(\abs{x - a} < \delta\) ”: Its level-3 prose begins: Since \(f(a) > 0\) , the number \(f(a)/2\) is positive. By the continuity of \(f\) at \(a\) , applied with \(\varepsilon = f(a)/2\) , choose \(\delta > 0\) such that \(\abs{f(x) - f(a)} < f(a)/2\) for every real \(x\) with \(\abs{x - a} < \delta\) . The rest is blank. Name the move, then complete it. Say which skeleton lines your sentences carry, and what \(\delta\) depends on.

title: Exercise (C2: A true conclusion)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Here is a proof that \(\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3\) is irrational, a true conclusion. Find the line that fails and its catalogue entry, give a counterexample to the illegal step, and write a correct proof. Suppose \(\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 = r\) for some rational number \(r\) . (2) Squaring, \(r^2 = 2 + 2\sqrt 6 + 3 = 5 + 2\sqrt 6\) . (3) Hence \(\sqrt 6 = (r^2 - 5)/2\) , which is rational, since \(r\) is. (4) But \(\sqrt 6 = \sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 3\) is irrational, being a product of two irrational numbers. (5) This contradiction shows that \(\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3\) is irrational.

title: Exercise (C3: Exit check: four student proofs)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Judge each proof. If it is wrong, give the line that fails, its entry in @exm-not-allowed-catalogue , and a counterexample to the illegal step. If it is correct, name the rule of its most delicate step and check that step. Claim. For every integer \(n\) , if \(n\) is a multiple of \(4\) or a multiple of \(6\) , then \(n\) is even. (1) Let \(n\) be an integer that is a multiple of \(4\) or of \(6\) . (2) Case 1: \(n\) is a multiple of \(4\) . Choose an integer \(k\) with \(n = 4k\) ; then \(n = 2(2k)\) , so \(n\) is even. (3) Case 2: \(n\) is a multiple of \(6\) . Choose an integer \(k\) with \(n = 6k\) ; then \(n = 2(3k)\) , so \(n\) is even. (4) In either case, \(n\) is even. Claim. For integers \(m\) and \(n\) , if \(m\) and \(n\) are even, then \(mn\) is divisible by \(4\) . (1) Assume \(m\) and \(n\) are even. (2) Then \(m = 2k\) and \(n = 2k\) for an integer \(k\) . (3) So \(mn = 4k^2\) , which is divisible by \(4\) . Claim. For every real \(x\) , \(\abs{x - 1} \le \abs{x} + 1\) . (1) Either \(x \ge 1\) or \(x \le 0\) . (2) If \(x \ge 1\) , then \(\abs{x - 1} = x - 1 \le x + 1 = \abs{x} + 1\) . (3) If \(x \le 0\) , then \(\abs{x - 1} = 1 - x = 1 + \abs{x}\) . (4) In either case, \(\abs{x - 1} \le \abs{x} + 1\) . Claim. For every real \(x\) , if \(x^2 = 2x\) , then \(x = 2\) . (1) Assume \(x^2 = 2x\) . (2) Canceling \(x\) from both sides, \(x = 2\) . (3) Hence if \(x^2 = 2x\) , then \(x = 2\) .

title: Exercise (R1: A dialogue)
page: 8.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Two students discuss a claim. Ana: For every integer \(n\) , \(n^2 + n\) is even. Ben: Why? Ana: Take \(n = 3\) : \(9 + 3 = 12\) . Take \(n = 4\) : \(16 + 4 = 20\) . It always works. Ben: That is two numbers. Ana: All right. \(n^2 + n = n(n + 1)\) . If \(n\) is even, the product has an even factor. If \(n\) is odd, \(n + 1\) is even, so again it has an even factor. Either way \(n^2 + n\) is even. Ben: You only did positive numbers. Ana: I never used that \(n\) is positive. Which entry of @exm-not-allowed-catalogue does Ana’s first argument commit? Write her second argument as a level-3 proof, and name the rule each sentence carries. Is Ben’s last objection right? On which fact does the case split rest, and where was it stated?

title: Corollary 8.8.3 (Kripke Countermodel)
content: If some stage of some Kripke model refutes \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) , then \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) has no derivation without \(\rulename{RAA}\) in the propositional rules whose lines are all formulas of @def-formula .

title: Definition 8.8.2 (Forcing)
content: Let \(w\) be a stage of a Kripke model. \(w\) forces a formula \(\varphi\) , written \(w \Vdash \varphi\) , as follows; \(w \nVdash \varphi\) says that it does not. The definition is a recursion on \(\varphi\) ( @thm-structural-recursion ) that defines, for each formula, the set of stages that force it; clauses (K5) and (K6) need the sets of its parts, at other stages. \(w \Vdash p\) , for a letter \(p\) , if \(p\) is known at \(w\) ; \(w \Vdash \bot\) never; \(w \Vdash \varphi \wedge \psi\) if \(w \Vdash \varphi\) and \(w \Vdash \psi\) ; \(w \Vdash \varphi \vee \psi\) if \(w \Vdash \varphi\) or \(w \Vdash \psi\) ; \(w \Vdash \varphi \to \psi\) if every stage \(w'\) reachable from \(w\) with \(w' \Vdash \varphi\) has \(w' \Vdash \psi\) ; \(w \Vdash \neg\varphi\) if no stage reachable from \(w\) forces \(\varphi\) ; \(w \Vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi\) if \(w \Vdash \varphi \to \psi\) and \(w \Vdash \psi \to \varphi\) . A stage refutes a sequent \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) if it forces every formula of \(\Gamma\) and does not force \(\psi\) .

title: Definition 8.8.1 (Kripke Model)
content: A Kripke model consists of: a finite non-empty set of stages ; for each stage \(w\) , a set of stages reachable from \(w\) (written \(w \le w'\) ), such that \(w \le w\) for every stage, and \(w \le w'\) and \(w' \le w''\) give \(w \le w''\) ; for each stage \(w\) , a set of letters known at \(w\) , such that a letter known at \(w\) is known at every stage reachable from \(w\) .

title: Lemma 8.8.1 (Heredity)
content: In every Kripke model, if \(w \Vdash \varphi\) and \(w \le w'\) , then \(w' \Vdash \varphi\) .

title: Theorem 8.8.2 (Soundness without RAA)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\psi\) a formula. If \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) by a derivation every line of which is a formula of @def-formula , in which no line uses \(\rulename{RAA}\) or TAUT, nor a derived rule or cited result whose derivation uses one of them or a line outside @def-formula , then every stage of every Kripke model that forces every formula of \(\Gamma\) forces \(\psi\) .
